This is a game that's masterfully done. It hasn't been out for that long, but I have played it for about 30 hours.
First thing's first, yes, there's only one kind of puzzle. However, that puzzle evolves in such a way that the puzzle never becomes boring or repetitive. Now, there will be those who might disagree with this, but if you don't want to sit down and solve puzzles, puzzle games aren't for you anyway.
The graphics... Oh my God the graphics... So nice to look at. And they don't really need to be for a puzzle game. But this beautiful island they've created affects the gameplay and mood in such a fulfilling way. Really well designed.
The secret videos that you collect I absolutely loved, and the different sound bits here and there really makes you want to find more, listen to more, watch more.
Now, gameplay-wise I have a few problems which I will be listing down below:
1) The sound puzzle doesn't fit into the game. It really sticked out to me like it belonged somewhere else but not in this game.
2) The end game puzzles are a bit too complicated, and I think it damages the overall flow of the game in general.
3) I believe all your progress shouldn't be erased when you complete the game. I wanted to finish first and then go back for totems, but now that I have lost all my progress I really don't think I will go back to do all those puzzles I have already done, again.
Overall, a magnificent game. Easily worth the money.

As a side note:  If you suffer from colorblindness, or are hearing impared, you may not be able to finish the game, and will definitely be unable to 100% it.

This game is a turn-based strategy in the vein of Heroes of Might and Magic or Age of Wonder. You have a city and a hero, and need to expand and kill stuff, which lets you build a better city, hero, and army, and so on. Eventually you run into enemy AI opponents, and if you've done well enough in the first part of the game you will be able to beat them into submission. Good concept.
There are two problems that keep this game from being playable. First, it is a downgraded version of Eador: Broken Worlds. There's not much point in playing this since it became available after the superior polished sucessor.
Second, it is -incredibly- slow. The campaign features a tremendous number of individual maps, with no unique mission objectives. When you win one of these, you get a small bonus to resource production and, if you're lucky, one extra building available for contruction. You don't actually build anything on the campaign map, this just unlocks another small option on the main map. The real issue is that every single map takes hours, each map takes more and more time as you progress through the campaign, and there are a really limited number of strategies available to keep this interesting.

Ok, I read in a review that this game is a Heroes of... lookalike, and I have to say, someone just playing the game for 0.1 hours might not have seen the full depth of the game. The campaign might have it's lengths - but on the other hand, you won't be sitting idly around playing it.
The game (especially the campaing) tell a story, you have to conquer shards, to gain in power and influence. Each shard is divided into several provinces, which have inhabitants, quest and resources. There are common (Gold/Crystals) and uncommon resources (also called strategical resources - required for some units and buildings). You can unlock higher levels of buildings, units and equipment through developing your kingdom, your stronghold and of course by solving quest (sometimes there is stuff that "seems" to disappear, but in fact those nifty items are used for something else).
Every decission you make will have it's repercussions - for example: You have a thieves guild in your province that is causing trouble, you attack them and catch their leaders. Summary:
An expressive game that tells the story of a few survivors during a warring state. You build, scavenge and expand your shelter, while managing the needs of each survivor in it, until the war ends.
Every action is executed with a simple mouse click. Trading with passers-by, shooting at innocent survivors, eating, cooking, stealing, sparking conversations, all of these could simply play out with a mouse click, but be aware that each of them has consequences; killing innocent civilians will make someone depressed, helping a troubled neighbour may reap additional resources and make your survivors happy, etc.
Before the day ends, the interesting part comes in: scavenging. You will be allowed to assign 1 survivor to search for stuff around the neighbourhood. Some are dangerous which requires a little stealth play or firearm to breach, some posses no threat at all, whereby you are the only dangerous person in that setting. I would say this portion of the game is the best, as it makes you question your actions, i.e. stealing from helpless old folks, killing a mother of a few children just to squeeze more resources into your backpack?

Survivors might also die PERMANENTLY, due to sickness, unattended injuries, shootings, hunger, etc, which may cause things to spiral out of control. In the end, your decisions matter!
Pros:
- A simple gameplay that has a lot of depth
- Pacing is just nice for a RPG-ish strategy game
- Amazing aesthetic for a war setting
- A fitting sountrack that puts you in the mood during gameplay
Cons:
- Somewhat repetitive after a while
- Character inventory maybe too small xd
Score: 8.5/10

One of the greatest adventure games ever to be made. The visuals look very dated and the game only runs in 640x480. Even when it first came out this game wasn't anywhere near the prettiest around. Having said that the 2D backgrounds are stylish in their own way and do a good job of setting the mood for each particular scene.
If you can look past the graphical shortcomings and take it for what it is, the writing, the characters and the world will blow you away. All characters are fully voiced and the acting mostly lives up to a high standard. The semi-orchestral soundtrack is also amazing and boasts some very memorable themes.
The puzzles are mostly standard point-and-click-fare. There are a few particularly obnoxious spots where the solutions can only be found by randomly combining things without any clear logic behind it (yes, duck clamp rope, I'm referring to you). All in all, much like the graphics, the puzzles are something of a weak link but still solid enough to not detract from the overall experience.
The story is the main attraction here. Combining scifi and fantasy the plot reaches some epic heights. It might start a little slow, but in my opinion it only makes it feel even more grand when it eventually starts picking up momentum. The story goes into some pretty dark places, and you might be in for a more mature experience than you may first think. When it came out and I first played it, I'd never heard so much swearing in a video game. Of course the industry has changed a lot during the years, and that aspect will probably not be as much of a shocker as it was then.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story, especially if they're into scifi or fantasy. Those more gameplay oriented might just want to give this one a pass, since the puzzles really are just a vessel for delivering the main attraction.

I originally played this game on PS4, probably logging at least a couple hundred hours on the console. I was neither a fan of fighting games nor DC comics before I played Injustice 2. I casually enjoyed Batman, but that was about it. It changes not only the cosmetics of the characters, but also the game mechanics. One universe, for instance, may be 2x faster than the normal one, while another has bombs constantly falling out of the sky, while another has too much gravity and keeps characters from being able to jump. The Multiverse keeps the gameplay fresh and exciting, and since it's apparently endless, I doubt I'll be getting bored any time soon. I picked up the $80 full package because I'm excited for the TMNT and Hellboy releases. It came with a few really beautiful cosmetics for all of the characters, and even some alternate skins for characters like the Flash, whose alternate is Reverse Flash. The single player story is good, the mutliverse is great, the multiplayer is nice, and the game as a whole is very rich in content. Of course, Injustice 2 also has local co op, which I always appreciate. I think I will be having fun with this game for a long time. Highly recommend.

Excellent puzzles, great atmosphere, great game.
To elaborate a bit: I like puzzles, but too often puzzles aren't "fair".  You solve them by bashing them, by trying a bunch of stuff or you happen into an answer - but you groan because you didn't actually do any interesting thinking, or the correct "answer" isn't better than others you've tried.  Out of hundreds of puzzles in Witness, there was only 2 or 3 that I didn't like.  Almost all were fair and many were a real solid level of difficulty.
And a few were just amazing: difficult but fair, requiring a combination of lateral thinking, cleverness and deduction.  I really like puzzles where you can solve them through a series of small realizations, rather than just finding the "whole answer" all at once - and that was a core feature here.  There was some absolutely beautiful moments in this game.
Overall: a puzzle game that belongs in a very short list with classics like Braid or Portal.

This game is so much more than what it looks like on the surface, or what any review can describe.  Yes, it's puzzles. Yes, they're similar at the beginning when the game holds your hand with friendly tutorial screens.
I wouldn't describe the puzzles as mazes when it's more about drawing a path.  You learn how a path starts, and how a path ends, and the rest is up to you.
This game quickly breaks the rules it teaches you and adds new ones on the fly.  It's vaguely nonlinear, and there are tutorial puzzles, but you have to find them and figure out what they mean on your own.
You will be lost; you will be frustrated.
You will need to step back.
Very far back.
You will need to take screenshots and have graph paper handy.
You will come to hate basic colors and shapes and four-by-four grids in a way you never knew possible.
It is truly not for the impatient or feint of heart. (Or the colorblind, unfortunately.)
But this game will also surprise you and delight you and challenge your skills at perception in ways that flex the grey matter to its limits.  There are some truly mind-bending perspective shifts required here. And when you're ready to give up, there are still more hidden secrets to find and "when you see it" moments that keep the game exciting even after 20+ hours.

I was never really a big fan of MOBA games because I couldn't understand what was happening and they confuse me. So, I stuck to shooters and heavily story driven games however, it's similar to the time I transferred from console to my own custom built PC, which was both apprehensive to start with but very rewarding and satisfying in the end because of the whole new experience. MOBA isn't really getting anywhere now and we all know it because of the lack of MOBA games being made and the community of the big ones like League of Legends and Dota aren't the best anymore along with developers overusing the same tiresome strategy aspects but that can be said for most competitive games. Gigantic can revive the MOBA community and industry as a whole because it is so unique!
I knew about the game through watching sponsored YouTube videos but originally it didn't really tickle my fancy because of how I avoided the MOBA genre. It wasn't until I got my loot crate last month and discovered I had a code to use within the game for credits and that's what got me thinking; "You know what, I'll give it a go" and I played every day since and I am not disappointed. It is a really fun and exciting new experience!
Developed by independent game studio "Motiga inc" Gigantic is the new free fast-paced hero shooter MOBA that offers a unique experience through the use of a very colourful graphic style and mostly outstanding mechanics. This is done through the use of brilliant strategic aspects such as summoning creatures in order to aid your team along with your guardian and playing with your teammates in order to take down the enemies and crumble their defenses. So far the game is in it's early access stage where players are able to submit bugs, so you should expect some issues.
The game utilizes being able to buy founder packs in order to bring in funds which ARE NOT necessary to buy in order to win, this game is not pay to win in any way because it only unlocks all of the characters along with a founders title and 2 Limited edition skins. You can buy the characters by just playing the game and unlocking crowns, along with most of the in-game skins.
The developers are in fact working on this and they give weekly update videos on what has changed which keeps the community up to date and it just shows that they answer the communities questions and want you to be a part in the development of the game
The main objective is to defeat the enemy guardian through the use of getting kills, summoning your own and destroying the enemies creatures which makes the guardian vulnerable to your teams attacks. The game is very easy to pick and seems to have a pretty high skill cap however, there is no ranked game mode but there is a hidden MMR rating when you play but it isn't very polished yet because there are a few balance issues with the heroes so carrying a few games with a slightly overpowered hero can skyrocket you to high MMR. But don't let that get in the way because once again, it's in early stages so just enjoy the game and have fun to help the developers.
Most of the controls are clean and smooth like the movement and combat system however, I've heard that on console the auto aim needs to be toned down because it's almost like you have a free aimbot on hand with long range classes like Voden and with heroes like Lord Knossos where his charge attack seems to miss at close range and slide around the target instead of colliding with their hitbox and it seems pretty inconsistent in general, but it will be fixed soon by the developers I assume because it has been reported. There is nothing major and game breaking with the controls and the game responds very well to most inputs so there is nothing to worry about. One thing I would suggest is changing your roll/dodge ability to a easier key that you press once on PC because you have to double tap on default which isn't too consistent.
Each character has it's own set of unique abilities that can be upgraded using whichever path you like (from the levels you earn from summoning killing and damaging the enemy guardian), whether you want to be a team player or if you want to be an assassin to go in, get a kill and escape with quick movement or pick off a solo enemy.
When playing Gigantic, you will become immersed through the brilliantly made sound tracks and sound effects. The music never gets annoying and you barely notice it in the midst of battles and team fights. The sound effects within the game all make sense and fit with the actions for example the swinging of weapons has a very distinct sound along with spells being cast. The art style and audio alone is enough to make this game unique!
The game has a very unique and slick cel-shaded art style like the classics such as; The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker and that of the Borderlands series. This art style is one of my favorites because of its sheer simplicity and cartoon effects. This art style makes Gigantic pleasing to the eye and you don't have to worry about being distracted by flashy colours. The artists paid very good attention to detail such as cracks in the ground and hero skins looking extremely believable. Also, the character design is unique and really sets itself apart from current big titles like Smite, League of Legends and Dota which can help their smaller company to stand out and show!
So in the end this game is DEFINITELY worth the try because it is a free fairly small game and you can see what the game can become later on. There are a few kinks that need fixing such as collision with some attacks not registering/other minor control issues and server disconnects, but that is the early access experience because it isn't finely tuned and polished yet. What really sells it for me is the unique and clean cel-shaded art style combined with its unique take on the MOBA strategy genre. If you are a League of Legends or Dota fan, definitely pick this up!

Far Cry 4 is worth playing if you find it on sale.  It is very fun and gives you plenty of options for the way you play.  The only thing I don't like about the gameplay is the fact you have to climb towers to reveal areas of the map, like in most ubisoft open world games.  Tha gets old.
If you are wanting this game for co-op, I would have to tell you to save your money.  The gameplay is fun and you and a friend will enjoy it, but there are to many downfalls of the co-op.  First, you can't play campaign missions in co-op.  The person playing with you can not carry the progress you make together to his local game save.  The biggest fault, in my opinion, is the instability.  When I was playing co-op as the host, my friend would bash into cars parked in the middle of the road with people just standing next to them.  I asked him why he would do that and he said that he never saw anything there.  If I ever jumped into a vehicle he couldn't see, he said I would just float above the ground.  If I ever killed the people he couldn't see he said a gun would appear on the ground.  Another issue is the proximity area.  You have to stay pretty close to your friend.  The area is big enough you  could attack a compound from opposite angles, but if you are driving and get left behind the game will reset you.  This is very easy to do if you are following your partner and you have auto drive on and you are looking at the map.
In short, if you are looking for a fun single player game where you can carve your own path through a sandbox world and every now and then invite your buddy to create some mahem with you, I would highly recommend giving this a shot.  If you are just looking for something you play with your friends, pass it up.

"It’s not so much about taking cues from our culture but rather our lifestyle. This is a hard place to live, there’s always a roadblock to achieve your dreams and I think there’s this pattern in our characters and stories in which they’re always in trouble, but they try to keep a smile and go on."
—Christopher Ortiz, Artist & Designer of VA-11 Hall-A.
How much could a game about serving people drinks and chit-chatting with them possibly have to do with the philosophical question about the human condition? Except, you know, way less pretentious and more humane than how I am presenting it to you? Well, I dare say "VA-11 Hall-A" is a good answer. A weird one, but good.
I already explained the game to you in the first sentence, and there really isn't much more to the gameplay than mixing drinks and slightly steering the conversation on a "hit and miss" basis, managing your money to avoid being evicted from your apartment, trying to dodge the bad ending (yes, multiple endings, my friend), and delving into the world-building of this Cyberpunk playground, as the stories of your friends and clients unfold and tangle with yours, Jill Stingray, the bartender.
The world is not okay. At the end of 2069, living in Glitch City, a corrupt and decadent city-state, you find yourself living in a small appartment and working in a bar with the best boss ever and a co-worker who "looks like a John". Life could be worse, could be better. As you service the clients as they come in you start to realize the variety: detectives, robots, hackers... and you start to wonder what might be your own problems as you hear theirs.
And just as the quote in the beggining of this review, underneath all the jokes and smiles, the genuine feeling of belonging to the misfits that are trying to wash away time, memories and problems, or also celebrating them with alcohol, you can't help but feel the sadness that lies in each one of them, buried away in the moment, but always there, penetrating the present. Sometimes it'll take you some time to notice it. Other times, it will be more than obvious. All the times, the only choice these people have is to smile and keep going. You will laugh with them about the absurd troubles of the world, but also maybe shed a tear or two about how all-too-human living can be.
The "waifus" of the game are way more than just the eye-candy self-appointed names as
or
comically suggest. A lot of passion and care was taken in developing the characters. You will fall in love with their complexity, oozing with intriguing personality and how they paint Jill's everdyday life with their quirks, problems and aspirations. The world in itself is amazingly fleshed-out, too, and informing yourself deeper about it is entirely OPTIONAL, if you just want to get down to the bare bones through conversations.
The very heart and soul lies, undoubtedly, in the dialogue Jill has interacting with everybody, and what an entertainment that is. My personal suggestion is to grab yourself a drink as you play along and cheer her on as you do yourself the favor of getting her through her curious night shifts at VA-11 Hall-A.

This hit all the right buttons for me. The only VN-esque game that I've ever really played. And the gameplay component wasn't just thrown in. It was well thought out.
It's good. Real good. Good music, good writing, good story, there's a lot of good things. Not much to complain about. I mean, I wish it had a clear control list. (hint: ctrl skips dialogue at an alarming speed, and tab will display past dialogue) But that's it.
There are a lot of good laughs, and a fair amount of pretty heavy issues that are grappled with, too. The game does have a grander narrative, but it isn't told as a single story - it's a bunch of stories from different people woven together, which creates a bunch of interconnected stories flowing in a direction. Like how a rope is made up of smaller fibers. Among all those stories is probably something that the player can relate directly to. There's enough variation. I related to most of it.
Has some pretty solid iceberg storytelling. There's a lot going on that you can infer by reading between the lines and being a little genre savvy. It's good when people can create a world that encourages involvement. There's also a decent degree of tasteful mystery - leaving stuff up to the imagination. It doesn't hurt the story in the slightest.
I'm honestly torn whether I would like to see a sequel done from a different perspective, like Gil's. On one hand, that'd be neat, and I'd like to get immersed in the world again. On the other hand, it might spoil the charm of VA-11 Hall-A. Because part of the charm of this game is that you're *not* the traditional protagonist. It's not about action or fighting or any of that stuff. You're a bartender. You service traditional protagonists when they're thirsty.
I think a sequel like that could be pulled off, honestly, but it would be tricky to do. But that's not a discussion for this review.
Suffice it to say that this was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. I'm a bit of a snob when it comes to stories, so the fact that I'd like a sequel to a primarily story driven game really does mean something.

I first came across this game at PAX, and fell in love with it on concept and aesthetic alone. The early demo looked cool, though I couldn't quite figure out the bartending aspect. For a while after PAX I'd occasionally search Steam to see if it'd been released, every few weeks or so when I'd remember. I eventually stopped, life got busy, etc.
Flash forward to a few days after launch. I was talking about it to a friend of mine, and decided to google information on it, and noticed that it had been released. I bought it as fast as I possibly could, excited out of my mind that it was finally done.
Best decision ever.
I don't think I've played a visual novel in over a decade, and I didn't even realize this was going to be one until I started playing it. I honestly had no idea what I was in for - I tend to go into games I'm really interested in as blind as possible, to avoid spoilers. What I ended up getting was a fantastic story, great characters, a great setting and a soundtrack that fits the game perfectly, and is amazing on its own. The music is just downright infectious, I've had a few of the tracks stuck in my head since I first started.
I can't recommend this enough. As a cyberpunk/sci-fi junky, the world building and setting are great. It's a different experience, only getting exposed to the world via talking with the other characters and reading news on Jill's phone - but I still felt I had a good grasp of what was going on outside the bar, like as if I was playing a more "standard" game and running around out there myself.
The writing is great, and while the game features it's share of memes/pop culture references, I never thought they were excessive or that the game leaned too heavily on them instead of originality [and some of the references were really funny to me]. The cast is varied, not only in personalities, but in true cyberpunk fashion, they're rather biologically / physically / specially varied as well. The interactions Jill has with them are great, and it's interesting watching the various bar patrons' stories develop over the course of the game. Jill herself is a truly fleshed out character and not just an empty avatar of the player, which I enjoyed.
If I have one complaint, and it's a stretch, but it would've been nice to have a little... variance in the dialog, or more control over interaction. I get that this probably breaks the rules of the visual novel, but I would've loved a more Persona-style way to develop relationships with the customers, where the player would have more control over Jill's dialog, which could shape the relationship. This didn't hamper my enjoyment of the game at all, though.
Also, I wish it didn't end. I was sad to see the credits roll. I really really hope there'll be a sequel, or spinoff games, or something. It's a great environment with great characters, and I want more time with it all!
I never really thought I'd be this into a visual novel, but here we are.

Although I usually tend to stay away for things like war and such I found this game to be quite interesting. It brings a whole new take on war. Usually in games of war you play as the "hero" soldier or such on the battlefield taking on enemies. But this shows truely what it may be like for those who are not soldiers. With its stunning art and music it really captures the moments well and pulls you in to the lives of the civilians you play as.
Kill 3 people in one night raid, steal their food and medication, get depressed because of it, get drunk, forget about it, -  profit! 10/10 starving hobos.

The game's really good, like they say in the annotation -- you are a civilian during civil war and you have to survive somehow. I loved the idea of displaying "common people"-s point of view on a certain historical period (recall Valiant Hearts!). The setting resembles a horror zombie movie, yet it is inspired by real events. Like in Beholder, it is hard to stay a good person, and every mistake can cost you a life.
Overall I really really recommend it, but there are some bad sides: it is supposed to be replayable (as soon as you opening new characters after surviving for a certain number of days, just like in Don't Starve), but it is not, because it gets repetitive (well, survival games are supposed to be a bit repetitive, but I think there are ways to make it more interesting). The characters act the same (like, when I know that a certain {character} will leave us, I won't spend food and bandages on her\him -- and that's a bit like cheating!) and their dialogs are repeating. I would recommend the developers to put there more dialogs, especially when the characters are depressed. After I played for 4 teams I got bored, but there were still much more teams to play.
Maybe that's because the game is hard and my team didn't manage to live long. I wounder whether there is a good ending (like, evacuation or smth like that).
There are some other things that I liked about the game, but I won't tell you, find out for yourself!

I'm not talking about one or two jokes or references; the whole game seems to spin around feminism and women's strengths. Comment after comment, joke after joke. If it was about equality and social progress in general I may find it more to my liking but it only addresses women discrimination to a point where it stopped being funny to me by sheer repetition of the topic (it's a game called Reigns and I found not even one comment or joke against monarchy or against choosing an absolute ruler by heritage).

It is pretty enjoyable at first, but gradually the progression and quality just deteriorates.
The objectives become extremely difficult to fulfill in the mid to late game, over an hour of gameplay after recieving two; I never recieved a chance to fulfill either of them. The third just requires me to survive a long time, which is complete and utter chance. After sixty percent or so of the way through the game it just seems to drop all the flow it had and expect players to grind until they spontaneously complete objectives out of sheer unlikely chance. Which is completely what it turns into is just grinding, scrolling through the same cards thoughtlessly over and over again with absolutely no idea what you should or even can do. It just reached the point where I stopped playing because it did not feel like gameplay anymore, it felt like I reached the end of the game but the game was just lying and said I still had thirty percent left.
The process of activating the eclipse is bad. The room where it can be done is only accessible by taking a single specific path in the maze, and likely that path only even exists after you have acquired the item needed for the event. I went through that maze so many times searching for the centre as the game told me to, never found it a single time and that was just a dead end to that entire element of the game; until I looked the answer up online.
The poems for dueling are also overly cryptic. At first they are too obvious and then it just becomes utter guessing because the riddle being posed to the player just is not accessible, it is not the kind of thing you can think through and solve on your own you either have to look it up or brute force it by losing over and over across multiple time lines until you get the right answer.
Finally, the choices in the game itself are not very well thought out. Sometimes, the effects that your choices have on things is obvious. Othertimes, the choice makes no mention of a certain thing; yet that thing is effected by that choice. So players have no way of deducing how their choice will effect that thing, and so it is just chance whether it empowers or weakens said thing. So for example one choice is whether to abandon or fight against a crisis; in both circumstances wealth is effected, so the obvious logic is fighting the crisis will cost cash but you can save cash if you abandon it and do not use the resources. No apparently, abandoning the crisis costs cash for no reason. Which means fighting the crisis somehow makes you cash, or, you lose cash either way in which case if you get that choice while you have low wealth you are doomed. It is like this with all kinds of things, they just randomly effect things for no reason and the dialogue gives no hints to how it will be effected. This makes it even worse when you are trying to survive to get the survival objectives, then you lose because you made a choice that has effects the game did not allow you to predict. These choices which have effects that cannot be determined ruin the gameplay so much. One of the only major elements of the gameplay is the process of deducing how choices will effect things, yet there are some choices that players cannot deduce the outcome of. It just ruins the game because it does not feel like thoughtful gameplay anymore it is just swipe right or left and hope you do not get screwed.
Eventually playing at all becomes tedious, you have to pay attention to what each choice is since every choice you make will immediately effect your state; yet eventually you will have already read a lot of these choices but you have to keep reading many of them to be reminded of what the choice is. So it just turns into a grind, waiting for the new stuff to show up which at the point I reached virtually never happens even though the game says there is still new stuff.
The game also has this really strange feminism theme. The game flaunts female empowerment and whatever so much that it seems like the developers are taking the opportunity of having a game with a female protagonist to mock the concept of female equality by bringing it up constantly in the story. It does not come across like the developers are mocking equality extremists, in which case they should also be mocking people that preach inequality to keep it even; it just sounds like the developers are mocking the idea of gender equality period. At first the jokes are funny but they keep manifesting themselves constantly throughout the game with absolutely no restraint. So regardless of what the actual moral or statement the developers were trying to make, it is obsessive and pervasively splattered all over the game to a completely inappropriate degree.
It feels like one of the only reasons the developers made this game was to make whatever statement they are trying to make here, they spam jokes about equality and reference female empowerment that much it really is basically propaganda. Vague propaganda as it is again difficult to tell whether the jokes are aimed at feminists, equality in general, or extremists on both sides.
It does not even end there, the game also has a homosexuality theme and gives players multiple opportunities consistently to accept different partners. In the previous game, as far as I know, there was no homosexuality. So the developers can only tolerate homosexuality when it is two females, since for males that is exciting, but not when it is two males, since they usually find it gross. Male homosexuality is only referenced once in the whole game and it is brief and vague. In the previous game I am pretty sure it also did not give the player this many chances to start relationships especially not multiple ones at once; which suggests that the developers attribute having multiple sexual partners, having frivilous sexual relationships and being sexually active as a female thing. Or they only want to include these topics if they involve a female. The female relationships are also more vivid and have more elaborating choices associated with them, and outside of relationships female homosexuality is referenced more and so is the idea that the females in this game are feral and flirty in general.
So the developers only decided to start including sexuality, polygamy, and sexual behaviour all in the game that specifically involves a female protagonist and a higher amount of female characters in general. They even give you an achievement for having four relationships at once. And, they are only inclusive of homosexuality when it is attractive; making many references to female homosexuality which males find exciting, but only one to male homosexuality because what hetrosexual male wants to think about that.
No improvements were made to the blatantly flawed system of the original game. They learned nothing, they did nothing new, just made more of the same extremely basic content then sold it again as another game. Copying even the exact same mechanics and themes the previous game had as well.
Zero creativity, zero advancement, zero growth as developers, bad enough to not even improve any of the flaws at all but to also straight up reskin all the main aspects of the previous game.
But if that is not enough, include the addition of hatred, bigotry and sexism into the mix. So not only is it bad as a game, but it is also bad as a creation; period. This should not be on retail.

Reigns: Her Majesty is the sequel to Reigns. If you ever wanted to rule a place with the swipe of a left or a right? Ever wanted to find your true love with the swipe of a left or a right? Well there's Tinder for that and Reigns: Her Majesty is the Tinder counterpart but this time instead of finding a girl/guy you fancy (which when you swipe right because you think he/she is so cute, they never bother swiping right also!), you have to rule a kingdom... this time as Queen!
Whilst ruling the kingdom, you have to take care of four important subsidaries. The church, the people (citizens of your kingdom), the army and your treasury (we've got to have... money). Maintaining a good steady relationship (no pun intended) between these four subsidaries is what you are meant to do. Failing one of them could result in you being dismebered, exiled, assasinated, and so on and so fourth
As you die, another queen will take your place and the game doesn't really stop there. You will be able to continue playing the game only this time with a different queen, only trying to avoid doing the same mistakes you did in the first place. Whilst ruling, there may be other offers that might come your way, such as starting a crusade, having an affair with another important figure or even meet the queen of the forest...
The game is weird and sometimes creepy. The game does go through some weird moments. The game can also get creepy especially in the moments with what seems like another version of Satan from the first game when you die. The game is a mixture of weirdness and creepiness
The game also offers 'combat', basically trying to time your attacks whilst also blocking and... praying. The combat is sluggish and isn't really explained that well. Thankfully it isn't that hard to master but it's a pain to start
Reings: Her Majesty has a lot to offer with almost 300+ cards to discover (I have found almost all of them) and many different branching paths. Reigns: Her Majesty is a fun, addicting little game which can be played in short bursts and although it's mostly the same user interface, that like it looks like the Tinder app, it keeps on dragging you to play more

If you enjoyed Reigns and the premier Tinder x Roylaty Simulator you're going to find more of that action here.
TLDR; Video first impressions.

This game is so much more than what it looks like on the surface, or what any review can describe.  Yes, it's puzzles. Yes, they're similar at the beginning when the game holds your hand with friendly tutorial screens.
I wouldn't describe the puzzles as mazes when it's more about drawing a path.  You learn how a path starts, and how a path ends, and the rest is up to you.
This game quickly breaks the rules it teaches you and adds new ones on the fly.  It's vaguely nonlinear, and there are tutorial puzzles, but you have to find them and figure out what they mean on your own.
You will be lost; you will be frustrated.
You will need to step back.
Very far back.
You will need to take screenshots and have graph paper handy.
You will come to hate basic colors and shapes and four-by-four grids in a way you never knew possible.
It is truly not for the impatient or feint of heart. (Or the colorblind, unfortunately.)
But this game will also surprise you and delight you and challenge your skills at perception in ways that flex the grey matter to its limits.  There are some truly mind-bending perspective shifts required here. And when you're ready to give up, there are still more hidden secrets to find and "when you see it" moments that keep the game exciting even after 20+ hours.

It's a pity that it comes to this, but I DO NOT RECOMMEND Injustice 2 in its current state. It is true that the port is in better shape than the disastrous Arkham Knight or MKX during its troubled start but it should not be enough. Especially not from WB Games, not after a 6 month delay and not with the current pricing.
The Steam version was launched on 14/11, the same day the latest patch and Hellboy came out on the consoles. After a 6 month delay people would expect the PC version will be up to date. Guess what, it's not. To make matters worse, there was not a single word about it on the store page that it is not the latest version. You could find articles about Hellboy being available later, but it wasn't loud and clear.
2 weeks later we still don't have any updates or news about what to expect, but we have random crashes with no error messages, random slow-downs with Benchmark predicting constant 60 fps and various minor to major annoyances that hinder our experience. Losing progress has more consequence in Injustice 2 than any other previous NRS games because of the gear system. QLOC did an amazing job with MKXL and I'm confident they can and will fix the lingering issues but the lack of communication is still unacceptable. The december update is out for consoles while we do not even have the previous one and have no idea what to expect and when.
I'll change my review if the issues are fixed but as of right now I do not recommend Injustice 2, especially if you own it on console.

Within it all, a bewildered April is forced to grow as her understanding of the world is routinely shattered by the things she sees and the actions she has to take. Where her quest was once fuelled by crushing fear and unwanted obligation, she’s forced to accept her role in things, personally investing in the worlds and the people she aids along the way. The twenty or so hours from the start of The Longest Journey until the end exhibits two very different April Ryans. Not necessarily better, but certainly different. It’s a story before it’s anything else; a tale of change and acceptance and hardships and how a simple rubber ducky could easily have led to the death of two worlds. It’s hard not to fall to that particular obstacle, but an unforgivable wrong not to find a way through. There’s too much at stake.
Full Review //

I realize this game is 15 years old, but I'm surprised by what passed as "entertaining" back then. I have trouble staying awake while playing this game. It is sooo slooow. For example, if you want to make the protagonist, April, walk from one end of an area to the other, you simply click where you want her to walk and then... WAIT. And wait. While she walks. Make that stroll. Saunter? She's obviously in no hurry. Okay, looks like she's finally there now. Now? No, now. There. Several minutes later you can start her walking to her next destination. (Update: Apparently she'll jog if you double click.) Let's see, what else bothered me? Shortly into the game we get to interrogate her landlady in detail about her lesbian lover. That, I'm sure, is pivotal to the plot somehow. When I tried to save the game I would lose my mouse pointer, but luckily I found the enter key worked. I can only exit the game via Task Manager/End Task and when I do, all the font on my desktop reverts to the crappy font from the game.
Rhetorical question: Regarding the abysmally low helpful review rating by the community... Is this because the cons I've listed weren't beneficial in helping you decide on a purchase or just because you love this game and can't stand anyone having a differing opinion on it's worth. Perhaps I should go downgrade all of the thumbs-up reviews... Nah, I'm bigger than that.

The characters are excellent, April Ryan is an absolute bad♥♥♥♥♥ how is it there was a game made with a witty strong female lead 15 years ago but they can't manage it now?! I loved her, you will love her.
The puzzles are challenging at times, but that only makes the experience more immersive.
If you're wondering whether to buy this before playing dreamfall, 100% yes. I was going to skip this one, thinking the graphics and age would make it a chore - I was wrong. This is way better than its successor.

I Must Kill...: Fresh Meat is a point and click horror adventure game based around a main character known only as Butcher. The title offers a solid background story available under the "bonus" option of the main menu, which lets us know that at Butcher experienced trauma at an early age which caused him to have to undergo an operation for his mental instability. We also learn that his Grandfather, who is now dead, was his sole caregiver as his parents died when he was a child.
The game hit Steam in Early Access at the end of November, 2015. According to the questionaire regarding its Early Access status on the store page, the developers claim that I Must Kill would last for approximately three months. It's now nearly a year later, and they've barely made any headway whatsoever on making this title an actual game. Many people have brought up that there is literally nothing to do in the game except for explore three levels of a house, and I have compared videos from ten months ago to my experience playing this title on October 4, 2016.
Before I jump in to the large amount of bad things that I have to say about this game, let me start with the good. The art direction and sound is amazing. It reminds me a bit of Neverending Nightmares, which was a huge hit on Steam when it launched. However, that game did not come in as an Early Access title, but it was offered as a free download outside of Steam as it was being worked on. As well, the concept of the game is wonderfully dark and captivating. All of the base elements to make a good game are here, and I Must Kill could be one of the greatest indie horror games since Neverending Nightmares if it ever gets finished.
Now I've played a lot of games, and I understand Early Access, but it seems as though Gaming Cats Studio have only done a few things with this title in the last ten months. They've updated some of the graphics, added a new mouse cursor, and added somewhat of an introduction; instead of starting at Butcher's house, you now begin at the Butchery. With that being said, there's still nothing to actually do in the game. The new intro is somewhat confusing, as you go into the Butchery, there's no cursor telling you where to go (you click until you find it), and then you leave again to get in your car. Obviously there's supposed to be more to this section, but it has yet to be added.
The new cursor is a hand, which covers up the text of any items that are labeled; such as the bucket, steel table, Butchery, and old desk. You can still tell that there are things that are meant to be clicked on and interacted with, because the finger on the hand starts moving, but they still can't be left or right clicked on. During the intro there are several things that you can click on to examine outside, such as a car and a hotel, and the view/take/talk wheel is unique and it looks cool. However, there are no actual items to take.
I also want to bring up a few things about the developer. The main thing is that they do not give any updates regarding their game. There hasn't been a news update since June 22, 2016. They stated that they didn't want to keep putting update notes in the community hub for "every little thing" that they add, but that's why you save it all up in to a rather significant update and then post it. If you do not let people know that you're working on the game, they have no idea what's going on. There have even been unanswered threads in the discussion form asking if the game is still being worked on. For a while, Gaming Cats Studio even abandoned the game because of a temper tantrum they threw about negative reviews, aka "hateful community", and Jim Sterling who apparently "ruin their dreams". It's extremely childish, and if you're reading this developers, you need to get a thicker skin if you plan to work with a massive public community like Steam.
With all of that being said, I'm very doubtful that we will ever see I Must Kill...: Fresh Meat become a complete game, or even one with anything to do in it for that matter. With an estimated completion time of 3 months, the fact that very negligible things have even been added in the last 10 months, and no news updates in the last 4 months, I'm not sure if anyone holds hope for this title any more. It's really a shame, since the premise is promising and the graphics and audio are excellent. I hope to be able to update this review some day, and if that day comes I do whole heartedly look forward to it. Until then...

10 hours in review: I hate this game.
I am a completionist. I mostly play RPGs and strategy games. I like to win, so my gaming style primarily involves achieving goals, expanding my powerbase, meeting my targets, improving my strength, all of which to end in a smashing victory.
This War of Mine offers very little and frequently none of these things. The gameplay is inherently simple. You have a few survivors in a badly damaged house. During the day they can do simple tasks, like building furniture, patching a hole in the wall or something else to help you survive, cooking meals, distilling hooch, or resting from nightly activities. During the night one person can go out to scavenge for badly needed supplies, while the rest sleeps (hopefully in a bed) or stands guard, hoping you won't get raided during the night.
Rather than adding and expanding, the game constantly offers straightforward but difficult choices. Does the scavenger bring home raw materials today so somebody can patch a hole in the wall, or does he bring medication in case somebody gets sick or wounded? Do I risk life and limb to steal from armed bandits or inflict myself with moral guilt stealing from the defenseless elderly? Do I give my last piece of food to the wounded guy who has to stand guard tonight or to the sick man on the bed? Do I trade away my last bandages while nobody's wounded so we can all eat tomorrow? There's no do-overs either so I am stuck with my choices. Beyond just restarting the entire story of course.
This is what makes This War of Mine so damn good.
Every day in the game, it's one bad choice or another, all for the sake of staving off immediate disaster. For one more day. For the sake of survival. For the hope that things will be a little bit better tomorrow, if only you can get through the problems right now. Can you survive without resorting to theft? If you can't, who do you steal from, how much do you risk in the process? What about murder, when does that get justified by survival?
If as a player you do not get upset by stealing or murdering for the sake of your group of survivors, then your survivors will. They get sad and depressed, even suicidal, from committing atrocities. Morale is an important part of the game, and the horrorific actions you commit to in the name of surviving are as relevant as the ones that are inflicted upon you. Maybe even moreso.
Because war is horrible and this glimpse of what living in a warzone is like, just so. It is atrocious. It is insecure. It comes with the realization that while this game has plenty abstractions, these stories are real. There are people who have lived through this. Who are trying to live through it in the world today. Who probably will be trying to live through it in the future.
Who only want to survive. Just one more day. Maybe tomorrow will be better.
I have to stop writing now. Marko is sick, but he's the only one who is uninjured after last night when bandits tried to raid our shelter again. We have some rat meat left over so I'd best cook him a meal. Maybe he'll finally find some medicine tonight. Hopefully the trader will come by today, we have a few bottles of moonshine ready. If not, I might drink it. All of it. Who am I kidding. Tomorrow won't be better. Things will only get worse.

There are plenty of reviews explaining positive points about this game, so I'd like to address two specific criticisms having sunk a fair amount of time into it and continually being surprised at how well put together the world is and how satisfying the puzzle solving is:
1) 'The Talos Principle did it better, and there was a real story.' I love The Talos Principle, but the games aren't really comparable in design - The Talos Principle, with few exceptions (some of the harder stars) confines its puzzles to very clear boundaries and the levels don't interact with each other. The Witness throws that out the window, with puzzles building together and the player's perspective of the level changing what puzzles are available and solvable. The two games play by different sets of rules.
As far as a story goes, I don't really feel like it's lacking in this game. That's not to say that there is a complex or compelling narrative presented, but it doesn't need more than it has. The real narrative is how you the player interact with your environment, and that's sufficient (and certainly better than a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥story shoehorned into the environment would have been)
2) 'It's just a bunch of mobile game puzzles in a pretty island.' Anyone who says this didn't get very far in the game. It has a pretty gentle difficulty curve at first, so I can see how you would get that impression. The way the player interacts with the world is via panels with little maze puzzles on them. If you play the first 45 minutes to an hour of the game, it teaches you the first few maze mechanics in quick succession, so that's the main focus. Once you start exploring, it becomes apparent that the mazes aren't really the majority of the puzzles. They're merely how you communicate your understanding of the puzzles' solutions to the game.

I'm enjoying this game a lot. It's definitely not for everyone, but if you like being presented with interesting problems, banging your head against a problem only to realize the solution was right in front of you 20 minutes later, and then being satisfied that you figured it out, this game is really fun. It does a great job of teaching the mechanics to the player, and then pushing your thinking.

There are better, more detailed and more extensive reviews for this game, so I'm just writting why I wouldn't recommend it.
The main reason I bought Eador: Genesis was for the Hero and the combat system. You're the Hero, the commander of your army, you go explore the land and you actually fight.
You improve your Hero and buy armor and weapons, and customize it to some sub-classes.
With all that said, all that fails: The customization is completely random; at every level-up you are given 3 RANDOM "masteries" and choose to boost one. They're not useless but you can't choose what you want to become.
If none of the masteries is what you want, then you HAVE TO choose the "passive" or "main" (say Magic Dmg for Wizard, Attack for Warrior, Range plus Attack for Scout).
Sorry, but for a RPG feature this is a SHAME. You don't actually know how many masteries are or when are you getting the one you'll like. You don't even know which are the sub-classes or what skills will you need. You can't customize your Hero the way you want knowing NOTHING.
Then again, the army recruitment and management system is terrible: You pay many kinds of soldiers to help you in battle. They level up and get some stats, skills and stuff... then in some random not-favorable battle they die and... your time spent in that unit, developement and EVERYTHING is just destroyed and you have to hire a lvl 0 unit again.
There's only one "save slot" for Campaign Mode, so if you want to try a class, you have to erase your previous game data.
If you played lets say... 30 hours the Warrior and you need a rest or you want to try a new Hero, you're gonna LOSE 30 hours of your life just to find you hate the Scout and want your Warrior back.
The autosave is also annoying because every time you exit the Campaign, it autosaves. This means you learn the game from your mistakes, but the hardest way possible, and nothing can be undone.
Well, if you don't mind some of these features and just like the strategy and empire building... this game is maybe for you.
Definetly not for me.

Must say I've become a bit addicted to this simple turn based strategy game. The references to the HoMM series are certainly apt, as even on the easiest difficulties Eador can be somewhat unforgiving at times with its checkmate AI making a nuisance in every uncovered corner. The amount of content is basically unlimited, which would be normally be a frustration for a completist such as myself, but oddly it's become instead one of the game's attractions and now I look at Eador as an excellent drop in/drop out strategy game, one I could actually beat were I to 'drop in' for about 300 hours or so.
In addition to the skirmish style single player, Eador also offers a campaign mode consisting of 80 randomly generated 'scenarios', which apparently allows you to say you've 'beaten' the game should you be perserverent enough to successfully conquer 80 maps, any of which could take the better part of a day to complete. The gameplay and controls are solid, and although Eador can feel repetitive at times, it's no fault of the game's design but rather the frequent battles that often play out in familiar fashion. It's like a casual drop in strategy game that's been given a surprising sense of depth, and that in turn gives a satisfying weight to your daily bouts. Thumbs up.

The game's really good, like they say in the annotation -- you are a civilian during civil war and you have to survive somehow. I loved the idea of displaying "common people"-s point of view on a certain historical period (recall Valiant Hearts!). The setting resembles a horror zombie movie, yet it is inspired by real events. Like in Beholder, it is hard to stay a good person, and every mistake can cost you a life.
Overall I really really recommend it, but there are some bad sides: it is supposed to be replayable (as soon as you opening new characters after surviving for a certain number of days, just like in Don't Starve), but it is not, because it gets repetitive (well, survival games are supposed to be a bit repetitive, but I think there are ways to make it more interesting). The characters act the same (like, when I know that a certain {character} will leave us, I won't spend food and bandages on her\him -- and that's a bit like cheating!) and their dialogs are repeating. I would recommend the developers to put there more dialogs, especially when the characters are depressed. After I played for 4 teams I got bored, but there were still much more teams to play.
Maybe that's because the game is hard and my team didn't manage to live long. I wounder whether there is a good ending (like, evacuation or smth like that).
There are some other things that I liked about the game, but I won't tell you, find out for yourself!

A powerful experience in a short game.

Ive been playing this game not on steam so my time wont show it but after 42 levels I can say that this game is good and worth a try. There is no reason (besides the 6gb limit) to not try out this game. The F2P model has had some questionable and bare bone games on its list but this one is very worth it. The game is on the boarder of moba and third person action game with maps having non traditional lanes unlike league and a stronger focus on aiming even for the melee characters. The game has a card system that, after every level up, a card is aquired and requires you to complete challenges with either basic all around challenges like summoning x number of creatures or get character specific ones that give more xp and coins. This system is what makes not buying the game not so much of a boundary because you can get all the stuff for free if you just play long enough and you don't even have to play that long since the game gives you cards to gain even more gold from the matches. The characters are varied and no two are the same giving everyone a chance to find a character they like in the training mode so you know what character you would like to purchase next instead of just throwing coins at them. Although there is no ranked, when you get to the upper levels people naturally are better than lower ones because to get the most xp and gold you have to be good and the better players summon and maintain creatures better thus granting more xp so I don't think that there will be any lower skilled players in a high rank, yet. On top of all that the games art style is stunning, sporting a very chalky and powdery style for their 2d character portraits and 3d in game models, it all looks very clean and visually beautiful. Some may get turned off by the huge branch off it took from mobas format but I strongly feel that it was for the better and Gigantic as a game and concept stands out from the crowd and hopefully won't be thought of as another overwatch clone. Get this game download it and try it out for no charge, I did and have not regretted it so far. Other people may give this game bad scores for the 6gb limit to play but I feel that if you don't have 6 gigs then delete some game and reinstall it after you try this game, you, hopefully, won't be let down.

Gigantic is an incredible blend of the TPS and MOBA genres, and will feel both comfortably familiar and intriguingly fresh for fans of either.
Pros:
- Beautiful, polished artstyle reminiscent of Zelda: Wind Waker or Okami, with memorable characters and environments.
- Fantastic roster of varied and fun heroes.
- Engaging, competitive gameplay that is well balanced and rewards player skill and team coordination.
- Mostly well-behaved community, free of toxicity.
- Characters and skins are easy to get for free.
- Frequent updates bringing new skins & characters.
Cons:
- Slightly demanding system requirements (6 GB usable RAM) for what it is.
- Creature and Power mechanics might overwhelm new players at first.
- Game may become somewhat repetitive due to lack of map, creature and guardian variety.
- Poor Steam integration because of the ARC launcher.
- Mediocre matchmaking.
Overall, an absolutely fantastic game for people coming from SMITE, Overwatch, TF2, Awesomenauts, etc. and are looking for a breath of fresh air that doesn't feel very foreign.

Alright, what's the deal with this game? It's got crappy graphics and looks like it's from 1998!
Let's ignore those facts for a moment. Suspend your disbelief, if you will. What's going on beneath the surface with the game mechanics?
As of this review writing, I've got 305 hours spent on this game (I'm a bit ashamed of that). So, there's something being done right here. It certainly scratches a lot of my itches and gives me what I'm looking for.
In terms of strategy, there are multiple layers of complexity. You're first introduced to the game in a small starting scenario which introduces the game mechanics to you. Most of the time, you are moving your hero armies around on the campaign map. On occassion, your hero will get into a tactical battle against monsters or other heros. This takes place on a hexagonal grid system and each side takes turns moving all of their creatures.
The battles are quite tactical. Your creatures come in 4 different tiers of strength. Each unit comes with certain strengths and weaknesses, and abilities. For example, the thief has a dagger strike which poisons his foes and doesn't let them counter attack. However, the thief doesn't have a lot of HP or armor, so they can easily be killed. Archers can't shoot at adjacent enemies, so they have to move away. Sometimes, your archers can only move away and can't act, so adjacent units can keep following them and killing the archers. So, you certainly want to protect the archers with blocking melee units. The game also has a pretty interesting list of battle spells. If you can't get behind a melee wall to the squishy archers, you could always resurrect one of the dead corpses as a zombie which can do the job. Just as well, the enemy could do that to you! So, to prevent that, you want to move your creatures on top of corpses to prevent their reanimation. That could also cause you to move onto a strategically disadvantageous position. Every army has a hero leading it, so the heros also directly participate in the battles. Heros can become very, very powerful as they level up. I find that an appropriately maxed warrior can pretty much solo every fight, but that strategy won't work forever.
Your kingdom consists of your capitol and any conquered provinces. Each province yields a little bit of mana and/or gold per turn. This mana and gold is used for spells and recruiting units or constructing buildings. Some provinces will have strategic resources (such as logs) which will reduce the building costs of a building within your capitol. Each province can be improved to provide more resources. It seems that every turn, there are also a bunch of random events which happen within your kingdom. You have to read each event story and navigate a dialogue tree to respond to the event in some way. Each dialogue choice has a variable chance that it creates a favorable result or a negative result. The game events work on a sort of "karma" system, where choosing the "evil" choices results in negative karma but a short term gain, and choosing the "good" choice results in positive karma but generally incurs a cost. Over time, if your karma becomes really good, your kingdom will be flooded with positive events. If your karma becomes bad, you get flooded with bad events which get progressively more expensive.
Meanwhile, you also also contending against one or more AI players who usually play with a slight advantage (cheaters!). You have to play particularly well in order to beat the AI.
The game is also a bit unforgiving. You can't really just start a level, save at turn 15, play to turn 25, and then reload turn 15 if things go bad. The save game system only allows you to go back one turn, and if you reload, it also penalizes you by subtracting from your final score. You can restart an entire scenario from the beginning, but that too has a campaign cost (in terms of astral energy). So, you don't want to screw around and experiment. In some scenarios, an enemy wizard will directly attack your home world and you have to fend them off. If you lose, that's it. Game over. You lose. Roll credits. No reloading and trying again.
In the campaign mode, you select which "shards" you want to conquer. Each shard unlocks two or more buildings for your capitol for each subsequent scenario. Some shards are extremely difficult to conquer if you don't have sufficient tech. So, you have to pick carefully which shards you want to conquer and in which order you want to conquer them based on the buildings they unlock.
This game is very fun, very interesting, and very complex. If you can look past the graphics, I highly recommend it for any strategy minded players. There is a newer version of this game out which pretty much is this exact game (in terms of mechanics) but overhauls the graphics and UI (ooh, pretty sparkles!).
There is only one significant downside to the game, and that is the drawback of its unforgiving save game system. I encountered a problem midway into one of my campaigns where my save game file got corrupted somehow. Since there wasn't any previous saved games, I lost hours of progress. I almost lost my entire campaign! I had to restart my shard scenario from the beginning.

After Portal, the second (commercial) great first person puzzler. Visit ancient ruins and discover the mystery of one fallen culture.

The Ball may seem like a silly little mod gone standalone, but it's far more then just a simple mod now. An entire experience centered around a simple to use ball leads you through a series of huge ancient ruins in an experience that can only be described as 'one hell of a ride.' The story is purposefully trimmed down, leaving you to peform as a true archeologist and piece together the events that occured so deep inside the mountain through the discovery of artifacts which unfold pieces of the story as they are discovered. The ball itself is a simple artifact with only two controls, hammer, and recall, allowing you to bowl the ball down hallways, or draw it back to you as needed. These two simple options turn into a menagerie of puzzles, combat, and various other uses you never imagined. Don't let the price fool you, It's amazingly entertaining, and worthwhile.

There are games that make me sad, games that make me cringe, games I regret buying.
The Longest Journey is
of the above. Quite the contrary: It may very well be one of my favorite story-driven adventure games.
Don't let the dated (okay, very dated) graphics fool you. It looks old and it
old but unlike many newer titles, it has an original story, an interesting and compelling world and a good sense of humor. It doesn't quite manage to make dramatic scenes actually feel dramatic but the cast of characters is solid and the voice actors' talents more than make up for the lack of graphical fidelity.
Now to my gripes with the game: The advertised "40+ hours of gameplay" seem widely exaggerated. This is not my first time playing the game, so some of the puzzles didn't take me as long as they might have a newer player, but I still think that the game should only take about 20 hours to complete the story (and thus experience all the content) - compared to other games and "experiences", a pretty damn decent number.
Another slight annoyance is that backtracking is a necessity and some of the areas are quite expansive, particularly those you need to traverse a couple of times. It does give some areas a sense of scale but it also somewhat inflates the playtime without adding anything to the game. Furthermore, the game is from a time when showing off your "cool animations" was not unheard off and so you get to watch the some annoying, unskippable animation more than once (can you say "library"?).
However, that is by and large the only thing that even remotely bothered me.
My verdict: It's a must-have if you like interesting, slightly wacky worlds and stories. It's a steal, even when it's not on sale.

Despite the outdated 2-D environment/3-D characters, The Longest Journey is timeless. The storytelling is extremely compelling and got me hooked all the way, never a moment of dullness (maybe except when I was struggling through some bizarre puzzles. I'm looking at you Mr Rubber Ducky).
Each character is memorable in its own way, from April, and Cortez to Brian Westhouse and even Constable Guybrush! And of course, Crow, who brings such joy and laughter to any tense moment April might have. I really enjoyed April's comments on almost everything she sees (this is lacking in Dreamfall, sadly). It gave her great depth of character and her insights to the world around her. Her sense of sarcasm will be remembered!
The voice acting is top notch as well, combined with atmospheric, haunting, yet beautiful soundtracks, I was easily pulled into the world of Stark and Arcadia (completely forgotten of the low-res 2-D background environment). The extensive dialogue at some parts can be a bit long, but it gave the much needed background story to set up the rest of the events that are yet to be unfold.
The puzzles can be a bit on the unconventional side but they were not unsolvable. The game isn't hand-holding whatsoever, you just have to think a bit harder to get there!
Overall, I am extremely impressed with this game. Despite a linear story, I would still replay this just to catch more details of this game and just to enjoy a good storytelling in a game for once.

I have more or less "finished" this game after 38 hours of playtime. I have some non-puzzle content to wrap up (e.g. hunting down audio logs), but am mostly done with the meat of the game at 515 (out of an alleged 523) puzzles solved. I have achieved both of the games only achievements and experienced what some would call the "secret ending".
What an excellent game this is.
The basic mechanic - the line puzzle - is utilized very well. Maybe half of the puzzles involve symbols on the puzzle panel that you must divine the meaning of in order to proceed. The other half present you with effectively blank slate of a panel and expect you to figure out the pattern it wants you to trace. The line drawing is therefore an input mechanic for puzzles solved "externally" from the panel itself just as much as it is a way to solve puzzles that present themselves to you with no frills.
The world is split into several puzzle "hubs", and from about 5 minutes into the game you are set free on the island to pursue them in any order. Most of them are independent of each other, but a few leverage knowledge learned from other areas. Eventually you will be expected to combine techniques and puzzle language from each hub area in the games most challenging and rewarding puzzles.
The island itself is gorgeous and beautifully realized. It is one of the single most meticulously designed video sets I have ever had the pleasure of exploring. Nearly everything on the island is placed with purpose.
If I had to complain, it's that the plot is mostly insubstantial; wispy and tenuous. Given some of the messaging within the game itself and the philosophies it describe, this isn't a true negative but I imagine some people will be disappointed. The puzzles and exploring the island are truly their own reward and the very loose narrative provide just a small bit of flavor.
If you remotely enjoy puzzles then do yourself the favor of buying this game.

The Witness is a puzzle game like no other I have played.  It bucks the trend not only by having no narrative, but also by having no direct explanation of any of the game mechanics.  Rather than painstakingly explaining everything as most games do, The Witness simply provides the information you need and lets you figure it out.  It's quite refreshing in an era of constant hint popups, control prompts, and hour-long tutorials.
Now how does this work?  The Witness provides all the information you need, and even provides a set of tutorial puzzles for each main mechanic but it does not tell you how any of it works.  Half the challenge is figuring out how the mechanics work.  The game provides a near-constant feeling of satisfaction from figuring the puzzles out, barring a very small minority of puzzles.  I found many of the puzzles rather clever in their design, and I find it quite telling how superb the design is that I only ever felt frustrated in two spots in the entire game when I am normally frustrated very easily by difficult puzzles.
Another large difference I see between The Witness and other puzzle games is in the design of the puzzles themselves.  Most games use very simple mechanics and combine them in increasingly complex and lengthy ways to increase difficulty.  I find that results in the major difficulty of the puzzles being simply thinking through all the steps, rather than any mechanical complexity.  The Witness, however, uses more and more complex mechanics, constantly modifying or introducing new ones, without unnecessarily increasing the size or complexity of the puzzles themselves.  The difficulty feels more natural and logical this way, rather than just trying to overload the player's brain with too many steps.
The part that makes this all work and ties it all together is the puzzle interface itself.  Puzzles are presented on panels throughout the game world with an exceedingly simple goal: Draw a line from the starting point to the ending point through a grid.  Every puzzle has the same basic goal, and this simplicity tying every puzzle together gives the player a feeling of familiarity, even when confronted by completely new mechanics.
Graphically the game is very impressive, especially considering how low detail the models and textures are.  It runs quite smoothly as well, barring a particular bug with my GPU that I've been working around and will hopefully be solved in the near future.  The island is beautiful and very colorful, with each zone having a distinctive style.  Sound effects are minimal, but fit their purpose well.  There is no music, which I was confused about at first but completely understand after playing the game.  I wasn't even tempted to play my own music while playing the game.  Any music would drastically alter the mood, and the game is so tightly designed, it felt like that would lessen the experience.
There are two things about the game I dislike:
- The first being a small number of puzzles that felt like they could not be solved with perception and logic alone, but required the use of external software to decipher.
- The second being the story, or lack thereof.  While nearly everything in the game is very tightly thematically linked around the idea of opening your mind and learning new things, I thought that there should be some sort of explanation for the island itself, why you're there, and certain things non-puzzle-related that you find.  It's possible there's a well-hidden secret that has not yet been discovered that contains this, but nothing has been located to my knowledge.  I know that some people complain about the lack of narrative, but while I don't think it would fit the game to have an Elohim or GlaDOS watching over you the whole time, I would have liked a little bit of something to explain the world.  There does seem to be an attempt by the game but I found it very lacking and it raised even more questions.
I'm not sure I've ever played such a well-designed game.  Everything fits, everything supports the rest of the design.  The amount of content is certainly worth the price, containing more than either The Talos Principle or Portal 2.  It's certainly an experience unlike any I've had before in a game and I hope that other developers, not just of puzzle games, can learn from this example.  I realize this game isn't for everybody, but I hope that most will enjoy it as much as I did.

If you like your puzzles difficult, densely packed, and well designed, the Witness is a wonderful game. Be warned though that if you need story, context, or variety in your puzzle format, the Witness can be to some a tiresome slog. The game has beautiful clarity of purpose across every connected component of the location, puzzles, and mechanics, but that purpose is beautiful delivery of puzzles. There's not much in the game but walking around in silence, and dragging lines across your screen.
Its best feature is the difficulty ramp, one of the best I've seen in a long time. It's engagingly difficult, but with variety as well - you at times go from working through a difficult puzzle for 30 minutes to burning through an easy sequence of 5 in under a minute.
Throughout the content I've seen (more than 20 hours worth, about a main-story-and-a-half worth of puzzles), the design in the Witness has so far never felt unfair. While I very much liked both the Talos Principle and Fez, they both felt to me like their difficulty spiked somewhat in the later, optional puzzle content. The Witness never has for a moment to me (though admittedly, I'm not done). In addition, the brilliance of the many independent puzzle sequences is that being temporarily stumped is just an opportunity to go explore and solve puzzles elsewhere.
Again though, if you need a story, context, or a fundamental variety in mechanics to get you through the 20+ hours of difficult puzzles - and I really wouldn't blame you - best hold off.
