The game looks fantastic - characters look true to the source material, and the backgrounds look neat. The lighting is great, and anything metal pops, looking cool. Shout-out to the team responsible for facial animations during character interactions - they are lifelike, and almost L.A. Noire quality. The UI, and the HUD look pleasing.
Voice acting is AAA, and most VAs are from the DC animated series. (The Batman's voice is rightly Mr. Conroy's.) Music is so-so, and nothing stands out for me, except the title theme.
Solid character roster. Almost all are unique, and mostly feel balanced. With MK's style of kombat, numerous combos are simple enough to pull off for beginners. It also feels satisfying for those skilled in fighting games, to chain long combos and get 600+ damage. Vets may find that the combat system is not much complex to master. Supermoves are easy to pull off, but very few look powerful, especially for the heroes. While some are at least amusing, like The Flash's, just watch Batman's or Grodd's, they look like just another special move/throw. Super meter management has been improved, and you can now do various escapes.
The level-ups and the new gear system are sweet ways to add RPG-like gameplay to a fighting game, adding several hours of gameplay. All the characters in the game can be customized with the gear dropped by simply playing the game. Your character starts at level 1, and goes up to level 20. (Took me almost 6 hours per character to get to level 20.) Getting your character to level 20 mainly allows you to equip the best gear in the game, gives you 2 extra abilities (additional special moves to assign), and adds more inventory slots to store gear. Interestingly, the rare/epic gear you obtain from the gear drops are almost always dropped for characters that you don't play with, even with "Character bias" option set to on. So, there is a huge element of grinding, notably to get epic gear drops for the characters you play with.
From the multiplayer standpoint, the netcode is pretty good from my experience.
Classic NRS game: has hours of content. The game is not incomplete like Capcom's SFV. Listing my favorite modes below. Note, completion of any mode results in loot box drops. (Or mother box, as appropriate for a game set in the DC universe.)

- Has a competent story mode with alternate endings, and levels up characters you get to play in there plus provides you some epic gear. I think Injustice 1's story flowed better, and made you try out more characters.
- Multiverse, a nice way to do quests/challenges that predominantly provides gear and credits. It has a battle simulator for the classic arcade mode. Love the multiverse battles with special conditions and powerups, like your fists on fire: they are so much fun! There is also the legendary multiverse that requires a lot of conditions to be completed. It gives you a piece of legendary gear for a character (huge stat buff) if you are up for the grind. e.g. Play as a set character, and win 1000 matches, is one of the conditions!
- Tutorial
There is a decent tutorial going over all the game's mechanics.

- Guild multiverse: Now you can join guilds and complete quests as a guild for special guild bonuses. The bosses in this multiverse are super tough that may require the entire guild to beat.
- AI battle simulator: You choose a team of AI characters, and find other players to battle. You can learn how the AI plays here to get better.
- King of the hill matches, ranked matches, PvP, and many more.
After releasing this really late for us PC gamers, WB takes the liberty of charging almost full price at release. Opposed to Injustice 1 on PC, which was the ultimate edition released at $50 (sans microtransactions) after a similar delay. Well, and the ultimate edition here is anything but good value, as it does not get you everything like Injustice 1. Darkseid is not a part of the ultimate edition, and he is to be purchased separately. That is, if you missed out on Steam's pre-order bonus/timed special offer. Missing on the ultimate edition out-of-the-box are also some premier skins like Jay Garrick's, which either needs the game's rarest currency: source crystals to unlock, or real world money to get those crystals in large quantities...which brings us to the next list item.
Alas, there are microtransactions, in the form of source crystals. They take a ton of grinding to get to the high 1000s, unless you pay real money. You get it in the low 1000s after you complete the story mode, and a decent amount, based on your luck, on completing some daily challenges. Typically, you get 100/200 source crystals for your in-game profile level ups. (I hear there is a profile level cap, haven't hit it yet which could stop accrual.) Another thing to get them is again based on your luck: complete secret actions, like equip 5 epic/rare gear on a character for the first time.
Thankfully, the microtransactions do not provide you competitive advantage, like land you better gear. They are used to get skins, shaders to color your gear, transform your gear's looks, and level up your character to level 20 in an instant. The amount of source crystals required to get these skins/level ups are almost always in the high 1000s. That makes it easy to spend real money on top of the game's current asking price. Particularly likely if you are tired of grinding, and want to get to level 20 in order to equip the level 20 gear, and assign extra abilities.
The best WB has done in a while, a good effort by QLOC. The game however appears to render the story cutscenes locked at 30 FPS, and the transition to the game that can do way more than 30 FPS appears a bit choppy and weird. There used to be several random crashes to desktop. The patch that came with Hellboy seems to have fixed the crashes, but introduced slowdowns on some gear loadouts.
Recommend it as a game, but I am not a fan of the questionable business practices taking shape here. Still not Capcom level questionable, but a few steps in the wrong direction.
If you don't mind the grind, and/or the existence of microtransactions, this is what I can suggest:
> Enjoy fighting games, and/or a fan of DC or guest characters like TMNT? You would've gotten this already!
> Like fighting games, and are on the fence? For the sheer amount of single player and multiplayer content, I recommend the standard edition, even at the current price.
> Single player, and just here for the story? With multiple playthroughs, you may be getting 6-8 hours of content. (Depending on how well you play.) But the game is more than that with its RPG-like mechanics, and various single player game modes. Could recommend the standard edition at the current price, but a price drop (>=10%) may be better value.
> Absolutely want everything that the game would offer, and do not want to spend more than what the ultimate edition costs now? I can't recommend it at the moment. Wait for a price drop. (>=25%) If the game looks super enticing, and money is no object, then get it by all means. We need more players on the PC.
Lastly, I advise against buying Brainiac although the game allows you to purchase him...he is available after you beat the single player story mode.

Nostalgia glasses or not, this is a good game.
I played Injustice: Gods Among Us the day the game came out. My fangirling over having Batman beat the crap out of Superman (or vice-versa) easily made that game my personal Game of the Year. And that's the year that The Last of Us came out. So when I heard that the sequel to one of my favourite games was coming out, I was stoked. Then I found out it wasn't coming to PC, at least not yet. Time tempered my anticipation into skepticism, and by the time the game was officially announced, I was almost ready to not buy the game.
Then the game surpassed almost all my expectations.
Pros:
- Microtransactions are in there, but just playing the game gets you everything, and I mean EVERYTHING.
- Less DLC than the original, more content overall.
- Graphics are 10/10.
- Controls are tight, the hits are satisfying, and the super moves are really cool.
- Arcade mode never felt so big and meaningful before the Multiverse.
- There's an offline Single Fight mode.
- Online is great, as long as you have a solid internet connection.
- The best PC port WB has made in a long time.
Cons:
- Microtransactions are in there.
- Sometimes the really good graphics hit the uncanny valley. Swamp Thing gives me the heebie-jeebies.
- Story isn't as good as the original, and the fact that
is almost completely swept under the rug.
- There's a daily rewards system where you pit your character's against other people's characters, all controlled by AI.
- Game can get really laggy if you don't tone down the default settings on a lower end computer.
tl;dr, I love this game. Great followup to the first Injustice game, and a great port to PC.

The steam page says, "Far Cry 4 allows for a second player to drop in and drop out at any point" this is an absolute lie.
First off, you have to finish the Prologue and Act 1 to unlock co-op, second YOU CANNOT PLAY ANY OF THE CAMPAIGN MISSIONS IN CO-OP. Even though the game literally says, "co-op campaign" you can't join a friend's game while they're doing a campaign mission or start a campaign mission while in a friend's game.
So what can you do in co-op? You can go around in the open world and help your friend find collectibles, unlock radio towers, capture outposts, and do side-quests but if you're the second player NONE OF THOSE THINGS WILL CARRY OVER TO YOUR SAVE FILE. The things that do carry over are skills, money, weapons, perks, exp...anything that has to do with your character. Anything having to do with unlocking stuff on the map doesn't carry over.

Oh boy do I reccommend TOXIKK,
First point, If the lack of players is putting you off I have a few things to reasure you,
1. The devs are launching an advertising campaign once it reaches release
2. The game is just as fun solo against bots, no joke.
TOXIKK is a game made of pure fun, unlike games like Bioshock and Spec Ops: The line, TOXIKK is made for pure enjoyment, with no complications like a deep story or cover systems; a true descendant of games like Unreal and Quake from the early 2000s, the only feature that could be seen as unnessecary is the somewhat realism like graphics, so it could be slightly hard to know if you hit your enemies or not, but I think of that as a plus (I'll explain later)
The devs for TOXIKK are amazing, they truely listen to the community, I would say head over to
for any important things you need to say, as it is hit and miss on the steam forums, but on the actual website every post gets a response fairly quickly
The style of early access Reakktor is going for is *gasp* similar to Killing Floor 2, but this is a good thing, it means they update occasionally but when they do it is perfect and completed, unlike many survival games out there that update a half-arsed buggy patch every week
True arena combat, and its own unique gamemode.
The arena combat I personally prefer to Unreal, as in unreal you can pick up one of many gimmiky weapons that aren't particullaly reliable in combat, TOXIKK is the oppisite, nearly every gun fills a solid `primary` weapon kind of role, and you can use them all pretty easily. The classic modes feel... I don't know... so... solid? I have played Payday 2 and Counter Strike but the combat in here feels so... pure. There is no sprinting limitation, no recoil to control, no tactics or reload to always keep in the back of your mind.
The unique gamemode is a team based capture the flag with vehicles and arena combat, I haven't seen anything like it in any other game, it is like Tribes meets Unreal, it is extremely well done and reccommend it to everyone.
Easy to learn hard to master is what they said and I can't agree more, there is dodge-jumping, wall jumping, double jumping, basically all the jumping you can imagine.
The maps are perfectly made, jump right in and have fun, or do your research and learn all the 3 ways to get to the secret mega armour hidden in the vents, learn shortcuts and know how to avoid enemies everywhere. The attention to detail in TOXIKK is insane, on Twin Peaks (big snowy map) there is two cliffs, perfectly placed far enough away from each other that a well timed jump with a Banshee (hovercraft) lands you smoothly on the other side. Knowing these will give you a tiny advantage, but won't hinder casual players.
This is where TOXIKK shines.
You can customize every crosshair in every imaginable way possible for each individual gun, add hitmarkers (even the sound is customizable) or change your sensitivity to as precise as you want it, there is also the standard graphical changes. You can also customize your character if you so wish
There are currently a selection of interesting modifiers in the game, including everyones favorite, instagib.
There are currently 3 gamemodes in TOXIKK, but don't let that put you off, many are planned for the next update
TOXIKK may not be complete yet, and needs some content patches, but it is the most polished early access game I have ever played, definitely worth picking up

The two biggest complaints that this game seems to have are these:
1. no one on the public servers.
2. minimal amount of content.
Both of these are accurate assessments at this juncture (release 0.89, 22 Sep 2015). However, this game has two very poignant counterarguments:
1. It's *stable*, and the content is *polished*. The game has never crashed on me, and even with the settings basically-maxxed out, it runs butter smooth on my laptop (core i7, 16GB RAM, SSD, GeForce 965M). There are only a handful of maps, but they load nicely, look great, make sense, and I've never run into a geometry issue or other annoyance.
2. LAN. This game actually works over a LAN. This is something that so few games have these days, which annoys me, because I love getting together with my friends and having a frag fest in the same room.
I'll also add a few other minor nitpicks:
1. Weapon balance could stand a bit of tweaking. The default gun is about as effective as a marshmallow launcher, while the rocket launcher will kill basically anyone in one shot, even with a whole-lot-of-health. Similarly, health power-ups are very sparsely littered around most of the maps, so death is near-constant.
2. The AI could use a bit of improvement. Playing against bots seems to go from "they'll run in highly predictable patterns, never capture the flag, and ignore your existence when you're shooting them" to "you'll never make it five steps out of the base before you get killed with a headshot from halfway across the map".
3. Vehicle maps aren't yet optimized. Most of them are extremely large, taking a long time to traverse. The land vehicles have some handling issues, and getting from one side of the map to the other takes a while on foot, due to the lack of a translocator or hoverboard kind of mechanic to help speed things along.
None of my nitpicks are actual show stoppers, if you're an Unreal Tournament fan (especially the underrated UT3, which is unsurprising given Toxikk's use of the engine), you'll feel right at home in this game that seems to take the tenets of the UT series (clearly its inspiration) and give it an overhaul in all the right places. I look forward to the forthcoming content and system optimizations, but even with its handful of maps and modifiers, it's worth the asking price - especially if you're looking for a game that supports LAN play.

I had no idea what to expect from this game - I had heard that this series by Funcom/Red Thread was quite good, but I wasn't prepared for the
that lay in store. (har har)
To be completely fair, the graphics are, as expected, very dated. But as an avid fan of the old point 'n' clicks, that came as no surprise to me. That being said, the static backgrounds were often very good and at times even striking. Gave me that warm nostalgic feeling without ever causing any real troubles with seeing items or what is going on.
Probably the highest compliment I can give to such a game is to say that I almost never came out of a puzzle still feeling frustrated. For illustration, let me compare this title to some of the old Sierra games (which I adore): frequently in Sierra games, you would either spend hours banging your head against the wall or break down and look up a hint to get you through some tough puzzles only to find that you needed to:
Yes, this kind of makes sense. But no level of thought would have ever led you to that conclusion on your own. So usually, you are left to wander around trying every verb on every noun in the blasted game until the solution just falls into your lap. Not a very rewarding feeling.
On the other hand, TLJ only incited that feeling once or twice. True, some of the puzzles were especially easy -- perhaps
easy -- but I went through the story feeling smart and engaged.
The last compliment I can give this game applies to the series (and studio) in general, but also applies here. Funcom/Red Thread are great at making their games inclusive (e.g. female protagonist, racial diversity, different sexualities) which really adds to the immersion for me. Being in a world that more accurately reflects the real world creates depth and allows me to get swept up on a journey of my own.
This is now one of my all-time favorite point-and-clicks and games and series. 5/5

Do you like maze puzzles? Do you like hundreds of maze puzzles in a row? If yes, then you might enjoy The Witness.
If, like me, you aren't completely enthused with doing puzzle after puzzle after puzzle with nothing to break up the puzzle-puzzle-puzzle stream, then this game probably isn't for you. I've been told that there's a subtle "plotmosphere" somewhere in the game, but to be honest -- no matter how great that subtle plot might be, I'm not willing to sit through a million of the same types of puzzles. (Yes, I know they end up slightly different. But in the end, they're all still maze puzzles.)
I got pretty sick of the Talos Principle too, but that one had more variety in the puzzles and an actual story that was driving me forward. The only thing The Witness really has going for it is beautiful graphics. (And, if you like maze puzzles, it has a lot of them.)

The Witness is a puzzle/exploration game with a special focus on perception and perspective. It starts out simple, easing you into the mechanics of the game, but before long you'll be juggling multiple puzzle mechanics that you've learned hours or days ago to try to unlock new areas or "complete" already discovered areas.
During the process of playing the game, you're basically being taught a puzzle language and the game constantly tests you to see whether you've understood the rules correctly. With the exception of one specific challenge, there's always at least one logical solution, so if you feel like something's impossible to do, it's usually best to look elsewhere or revisit the area that teaches you the skills and mechanics involved in whatever you're having trouble with.
Except for one challenge, which could be considered the final boss of the game (and is an absolute blast to complete), The Witness features no music, allowing you to concentrate on understanding the game world and learning the puzzle language, or just take in the breathtaking sights of the island.
If you've enjoyed games like Myst or Fez, you'll be happy to hear that The Witness is their lovechild, only prettier, smarter and even more full of surprises. And if you get a kick out of moments of epiphany where you go "A-ha! That must be how this works!", you'll not be able to put this one down for quite a while.

as reply to TigusVidikis's comment:
>Pay to Win??? why?
Because you can speed up your progress significantly with real money. Faster progress means faster success and an advantage over players who don't do it.
> Premium ships are just different ships. Better in some stats, worse in others.
But they start fully leveled. Non-premium ships are therefore worse from their stats until they are leveled up also. but there is little point in flying a leveled ship any more since you mostly want to level up the next one. so for most of the time the premium ship IS better.
>The only real thing to give you an edge is and indirect bonus, if you go premium you get more XP and more loot.
more xp and more loot (items, upgrades) means better stats than one who doesn't pay. better stats means better chances. better chances means winning more often. winning more often means even faster progress. so from my conclusion this IS pay to win.
from what i have seen you can achieve most things by stupid grind. but it will take you a long while and will certainly not be fun for the most time. the game is purely balanced to annoy you so much until you pay. and the developers are greedy.
for 1 € (euro) i get 300 galactic standards (gs).
one month of premium licence (+50% xp, extra loot) cost you 3000 gs = 10 €
a second set of implants cost you 2000 gs = 6,7 €
a rank 11 ship costs you 6.2 million ingame credits this are around 12000 gs and thus 40 €.
to change ONE visual aspect of ONE ship costs you 150 gs = 0,5 €.
even beeing the mentor of a new character afaik costs you 200 gs = 0,7 €.
so if you want to play it seriously and have fun doing it you have little chance without paying. thats what everyone starting this game must be aware of. if you have plenty of real money to spend play it. but don't let you fool by the "free to play" tag because this is a lie.
I see that the developers must eat and want to be payed for their work. but the payment scheme applied in this game is obviously greedy and reminds me of extortion. and this is not only my opinion i have heard several other people mentioning this as the most annoying aspect of the game.

is a Cyberpunk visual novel in which you take the role of Jill Stingray, a bartender at a small bar in a dystopian city known as GLITCH CITY. (Or waifu bartending, that's what others call it)
Anyway, during Jill's Bizarre Adventure, you get visitors who well...sit down and just want a drink or two. So you give them a few drinks and depending on how well you serve them, they can either entertain you with some of their interesting stories, or just straight-up try to make you feel uncomfortable while casually spouting sexual jokes at you. This game also reqiures a bit of thinking as the game has multiple endings depending on how you serve certain characters, so you're doing more than just reading.
I recommend this game to people who are a fan of the anime universe, but want something different other than tons of fanservice and "kawaii" girls. Even if you aren't a fan of anime, the game can still be great because the atmosphere feels so different compared to what you'd expect out of general anime-style games/visual novels. The game is in a very mature environment also (I mean it's in a bar, what else would you expect?) so you won't expect any cheesy aspects to come out compared to what you'd stereotype seeing MOST anime for the first time (again, fanservice and kawaii girls).
Overall, this VN (visual novel) is a must. The characters are very likable, and the game delivers a calm, interesting experience that you can just lay back and enjoy (best to play during the night). Anytime there's a sale, take advantage and get this game. You might have different opinions on the game, but it's not something you'd regret buying (Judging by the game's content, not my personal preferences).
So yea,

I normally don't review games when I have so few hours playing, but I have put up to 100 hours in on Xbox before the PC release and I have some thoughts I'd like to share.
First, this is in my opinion the best fighting game ever made, as a DC fan and a Mortal Kombat fan it is a match made in heaven and a big improvement from Injustice Gods Among us on everything but the story which isn't quite on par.
The story mode and online features do have their moments, but my favourite thing to do in Injustice 2 is the Multiverse. This is perhaps one of the only games I have ever experienced where the Loot Box system is pretty much one of the most awesome parts of the game and why? The gear! The gear RPG's this game up quite a bit, with similar gear drops as in a dungeon in an MMORPG. It's a blast fighting through ladders of multiverses which are usually different every day. The PC port too is pretty solid with only one crash and it was on a loading screen. Not to mention Injustice 2 looks stunning, the assets and character designs are gorgeous in 4K and 1080p and the super moves do not disappoint. I'm quite new to fighting games, I played some of the first video games but never really enjoyed fighting games until Mortal Kombat 9. I found fighting games inaccessable, but the new MK series and Injustice games have allowed me to enjoy what is an amazing genre. Injustice 2 is no exception, the special moves are usually easy or a little challenging to pull off especially against a Hard AI or Online opponent, but it is satisfying when you  start to truly get a grasp on a character and begin to level them up. Top 3 characters:
1) Harley Quinn
2) Batman
3) Starfire
Whilst I'm on the topic of Starfire I will have to say I'm not too fond of the DLC practice. The content is great with more characters coming even now, but the season pass is expensive (I should know having bought it twice now) and to have paid £32 and have Darkseid still locked behind a paywall? Get that fixed WB.
Overall however 9.5/10

A blast from the past, this point and click adventure game is a joy to play.  You play April Ryan, an 18 year old girl who is chosen to save two parallel worlds from chaos and destruction.
While the 3d character models are little more than jagged pixelated blobs resembling human -or magical- beings, the background images you enteract with are lovely and still hold up rather well.
The story is imaginative and engaging, there's a lot of humor to be found here, and the characters you meet are memorable.
Keep in mind, this game has little to no direction on what your next step should be - so there's a lot of trail and error invovled.  It can be a tad frustrating, but there are several walkthroughs to be found if you find yourself stuck.  Also, if you find an object, pick it up, it'll come in handy sooner or later :)
All in all if you love a good story, pick this game up!  :)

Classic click and point with a novel like storyline that kept me very interested. The constant twists and turns in storyline are very unique and entertaining while the realistically diverse characters and their multidimensional personalities and background stories were very well designed. Graphics aren't the best because this is an older game and because the modern standard for graphics is so contrasting, but they still clearly illustrate the settings and characters. Only sour note for me personally was the sexual harassment main character April experiences (sexually themed comments, male characters suggesting she barter sex in exchange for their help/services). In reality sexual harrassment happens every day (unfortunately) so I am on the fence not sure if I should shake my finger at the creators for reinforcing this sexism and sexual harassment or acknowledge them for creating a realistic world full of realistic societal problems including settings with background characters depicting gangs, prostitues, and my favorite half unconscious junkies all while April completes her long journey.

Personal Rating: 3.5 of 10
On the front, this game seems like a solid Hack & Slash RPG game with a rather unique and rare background story. I only clocked a couple of minutes into the game and unfortunatly it is enough for one to discover what is lacking.
There are five characters, each with distinguish items and skills. You may only control 1 at a time while the remaining follows you closely and automatically engage in combat. This is a great idea because playing as a weak bowman character will have other melee character tanks for you.
Voice acting is sub-par. It tries to hard to be dramatic. If you are familiar Diablo and Torchlight series, the controls mapping are similar. UI is good as you don't need to ponder which short-cut key maps to what. All the accessible features are displayed with huge clear buttons. However, controls are clunky and sometimes irresponsive. Clicking to attack or move does not work sometimes. Path finding is non-existance and your character may get stuck easily.
Animations is one of the issue as striking a moving enemy halts the animation but they are still gliding towards you. A.I. is nothing to shout about. Would appreciate if other characters are livelier. They don't engage in combat enemies gets close within a certain range to them. Safe to say, many elements are pre-programmed with static outcome. Another example is enemy spawns and how other non-engaging enemies will aim for you always.
Sound settings does not work in the main menu. Shutting down all volume will still play the menu repetitive music.
This game can really be something if a little more resource is spent to refine and polish it. Overall, the graphics, soundtrack, character design, combat, gameplay; well basically the core components are there and it isn't a bad game, just plagued by these menial problems.

This is the game I have always wanted to play. Every time I read through Samuel and Kings I think how awesome an rpg of the life of David would be. In fact, I got into game design myself in order to learn the skills necessary to perhaps one day make such a game. It would seem kingdom games got there first though, and it's everything I hoped it would be.
The action rpg gameplay is for the most part smooth and enjoyable, the various character skills and ability to switch between them on the fly is great, the combat feels great and smashing through hordes of enemies is incredibly satisfying. I love the amount of loot you get, and the various buffs certain equipment gives makes equiping the five feels like I'm making meaningful choices.
The voice acting is excellent, as is the music, and the environments look beautiful and are fun to explore. However I do find myself getting stuck on the terrain on occassion, and this can be a little frustrating when I'm trying to explore every corner of the map to find the caches containing interesting background info on the events taking place.
One rather cool and unique part of this game is the comic style cutscenes, complete with voice acting and sound effects. It's a great way to cover the story of David, and brings a lot of characterisation to each of the guardians.
My only real complaint would be that the game feels a little too easy most of the time, with only a couple of instances so far where I've felt challenged in combat. A harder difficulty mode where you take more damage or enemies feel stronger would probably be something this game could benefit from. Also there is no co-op/multiplayer which is a little disappointing, but as I bought this as a singleplayer game I'm not going to complain about it, it would just be cool to have a friend take the place of the ai.
All in all, a fantastic experience so far that I'm certainly going to enjoy continuing, from a company that seemingly knows how to make quality games. I hope to see more games from them in future as there are not enough designers willing to take the risk of using Biblical settings and stories in their games.

Oh... here we go. I wanted to talk in a calculated and measured way but I don't think that's really the way you're going to figure if you'll enjoy the game. Either this will resonate with you or it won't and you'll think I'm full of abject puffery or that I'm deluded in some manner.
I have to say, it's weird seeing the utter contrast between people who enjoy the game and people who don't. Either the motif of enlightenment and zen strikes you or it doesn't. Either you enjoy the myriad ways that the game makes path-puzzle solving difficult by using the environment and adding more rules or you find it stupid. Either you love the way the game tries to make you feel connected to something, some secret just beyond your grasp (there goes the motif again)... or you find the whole experience unbearably pretentious.
I can't promise you'll like the game (if a deeply puristic exploration 'game' can even be called such). And as a personal plea from an absolute nobody, maybe I can't convince you of it but there IS something here: a surprisingly strongly structured attempt to invoke a longing for a connection to something (knowledge or spirituality or whatever metaphysical concept you hold closest to you). Either you'll find the call to this 'something' deeply self-resonant or you won't and if it's the latter I can see easily how you might not enjoy the game. The whole experience is built around trying to invoke your feeling that 'something' and if it fails then your mileage will vary.
For the sake of trying to give SOME sort of guidance, it's close to the Myst series and The Talos Principle thematically (and graphically it's downright GORGEOUS). And like those games either you are good at puzzle solving or you'll need to look up the solutions. Try not to spoil it for yourself though since some of the seemingly toughest puzzles sometimes just require knowledge acquired at a vastly different area of the island. None of the problems are unfair really though pounding away at a puzzle like its a veil you're desperate to see behind is discouraging at times. As an important aside though, sadly, the game WILL give you issues at points if you are colorblind to certain colors or are deaf.
Thanks, Thekla in general and Jonathan Blow. I lack the words to properly express. This wasn't a game I was looking forward to heavily and it's completely consuming me. (Hell, Braid only resonated with me minimally.) I'm really going to miss this feeling when the experience is over.
In the end, whether something resonated with you in this review or it didn't. And either way I can't promise any correlation with how you'll feel about the game. So what was the point of this? I suppose I just needed to express how this experience has made me feel was all.

Not everyone's cup of tea, yet it is in my opinion greater than the sum of its parts.
Getting the "Endgame" achievement is half the experience and should be a significant milestone for many. You can comfortably put this game and its myriad secrets to rest at that point. I reached this in ~20 hours with half a stack of post-it notes and my favourite image editor to draw over screenshots.
Casual to moderate puzzle solvers should enjoy this first half of the game, the remainder of which is balls-to-the-wall insane.
The $40 price tag will not be justifiable to many. Personally, however, it more than earned its keep.
I would recommend giving this a shot anyway, and take advantage of the Steam Refunds feature if you're not getting any satisfaction after the 1 hour mark. In order to maximise the likelihood of enjoying this game, please relax. Know that if you are ever stuck, you can always set the game down and have a break, and have the solution spring to your mind the next time you sit down to tackle it, or journey to an unexplored part of the map and find another puzzle to crack.
I really love this game.
CONS:
- Sometimes in a sequences of puzzles, when you make a mistake you are forced to solve the previous puzzle again.
- Rarely, you are only given half a solution forcing you to brute force the remainder of the puzzle.

The dev sent me a steam key for this game last week after I made a big list of local multiplayer games on reddit and mentioned that I have LMP gaming parties every weekend.  He asked if my friends and I would try it out before release and give him some criticism. I had no idea it would be out so soon and we didn't get a chance to play it till the weekend, and even then I'm such a do-nothing stoner that I put it off till just now.
Luckily for him I don't have too many comments or criticisms to lob at the game. It's pretty much the Rolls Royce of Asteroids style, single screen, 4-player arena games. You get dumped into a ship builder screen at the start, most of us just started designing a cool looking abstract spaceship avatar (pick a nose, a midsection, and a tail), not understanding that each design carried different weapons. Once we saw the hint in the top corner saying to hold L2 to show the descriptions of the weapons the real game was on. Matches can be over really quickly once everyone gets a handle on the controls and starts focusing more on attacking instead of learning the mechanics of the really weird weaponry. Thankfully it's a single button press to immediately begin another round. It turned into a bit of a chess match with guys counter-picking against the top dog who usually discovered some new "OP" weapon and abused it until evolution forced somebody to discover it's counter.
I'm not saying it's The Witcher 4, but what it claims to do, it does as well as any of it's vast list of competitors. We also played Stardust Vanguards which certainly has more depth to it than something like Astral Gun, with a cool pixel-art mech art style and multiple gamemodes, but it's also 5x the cost. My only real advice to the dev was going to be that he needed to price it very competitively because the steam market is so flooded with clones of these type that I'm choosing to not even buy some that are very highly regarded. I see they went for around the $2 price, which is right where I think it should be. Some kid can sell a few steam cards, make a couple bucks, and get a quality game out of the deal. The rest of us won't even notice 2 bucks missing from our wallet, so why not.
One definitive thing I will declare about Astral Gun though, is that this game has terrific music. We love blasting music ridiculously loud while playing if it's good, and if a game has an awesome soundtrack like Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime or Pivvot it always gets booted up for at least 10 minutes just to listen to it, if nothing else. If you didn't compose the music yourself, Mr Developer, please give the buddy of yours who did a bigger cut of the pie. We were all in agreement that it was the high water mark of the game; but like I said, we're all a bunch of dirty know-nothing stoners who probably overvalue an awesome soundtrack compared to the layperson.

I have to begin by saying that I find the internet speak in the title, 'FootLOL: Epic Fail League', rather irritating. Now that I got that out of my system, let's talk a bit about sport games, specifically those relating to soccer (or football if you're of the more European persuasion and such). FIFA and Pro Evolution Soccer never really interested me. Soccer is something that I preferred to play in real life, with one exception. A number of years ago, I came across Level 5's Inazuma Eleven series on the Nintendo DS. To keep things short and simple, I was (and probably still am) a sucker for games with RPG elements. Soccer matches in Inazuma Eleven were more akin to battles with over-the-top special moves and abilities and that was how my attention was held in a game involving sport. It also had something of a story to it, which I found to be simple, yet engaging. That's good enough for me.
FootLOL: Epic Fail League is nothing like Inazuma Eleven, but that's okay. It doesn't play like a Japanese RPG, but I suppose I wasn't expecting it to. After playing around with it for quite some time, I think it resembles a puzzle game more than anything else. You see, the odd (but interesting) thing about FootLOL is that it requires you to fulfil certain conditions in order for you to win and attain that I-am-a-Completionist-With-OCD three star ranking after each match. For example, one match may have two 'bonus objectives’, with the first involving the creation of a situation where your team scores zero goals and the opposing teams scores 3. It's only after completing this objective that you can work on the second, which could be you having to bump up your score from zero to 3 and ensuring that other team jumps up from 3 to 6. Finally, the actual main objective would call for your team to finish up by scoring five more goals than the other. If all of this went over your head, just know that FootLOL puts you in situations where you have to manipulate matches by sabotaging the efforts of both teams.
You may be wondering about how one goes about undermining the players of both teams. Well, by placing landmines on the soccer field of course! It gets a little bit more madcap than that as you progress through the game. FootLOL will also provide access to tools such as force fields, portals, walls of fire, bombing runs, rampaging soccer fans and cows (some inspiration from Worms perhaps?), UFOs and a little something that transforms players into Spartan warriors. As you may have figured out, matches can become quite chaotic and that's how things move away from the sport genre, and more towards that of the puzzle game.
These tools have the potential to result in goals being scored in such a way that they ruin your chances of fulfilling those conditions I mentioned earlier. However, the right combination of tools can bring some semblance of order to the chaos. Usually, this translates to using the ability that gives a red card to every player that you can click on, having cannons fire balls into the opposing goal or your own, or 'cloning' balls right in front of the posts and having stampeding cows do the scoring for you. So, as you can see, FootLOL will eventually reach a point where you hardly want any players on the field at all.
Personally, I can stomach all of this craziness, which is why I'm going to say that despite the title putting me off, FootLOL: Epic Fail League turned out to be slightly better than I expected. Having said that, it is not aesthetically pleasing, the multiplayer is quite dead and the music is annoying and repetitive. Speaking of which, you would think that having an assortment of zany tools at your disposal would somehow stem the tide of boredom, but it didn't. It held my attention for a while, but I'm done with FootLOL and I'm not coming back.
What tends to keep me interested in a game (and I'm guessing this is the same for many of you) is some depth. That can be either in the story and themes presented, or in the way that you play the game. I have no interest in 'fun little time wasters'. Although, I mentioned that it seems to lean more towards the puzzle side of things, FootLOL is still too simple for me. There isn't really much in the way of tactics, strategy or skill involved. There are many matches to win, but it doesn't matter if you win them all in about the same way. Something tells me that the developers didn't put much time into observing the interplay between all of the tools they implemented.
And that's probably the best way that I can describe 'FootLOL: Epic Fail League'. Lion's Shade didn't put much thought into it, so how can we give it much thought? Lion's Shade didn't put enough time into it, so it doesn't deserve our time.

It's a good game, but it can sometimes feel unfair.
This is because no matter how hard you plan, how efficient you are with your supplies, and how well equipped your characters are, there is always an unkown element. Something can always go wrong, and sometimes you can do nothing to avoid it.
If you've ever played Oregon Trail, it's slightly similar. The game shifts between actual gameplay, which consists of exploring randomly generated "towns" with randomly generated "buildings" you can enter, explore, and loot, and driving in a car (no gameplay) on your road to Canada and this is where the unknown element comes in.
Your characters can argue amongst each other, or you can run into a group of bandits who'll demand all your supplies, or you get jumped by a horde of zombies, etc. These random encounters will debilitate your squad. Thus, as I mentioned earlier, there is a large element of luck involved in actually completing a successful playthrough as even the most well prepared can still die from one random encounter. Many if not most or even all of these random encounters can be "dealt with" if you have the required skill check (for example, if your car breaks down, but you have a high level mechanic, then you can fix the car) but chances are you won't, as each character is able to specialize in maybe one or two skills and there are countless random encounters the game has to choose from. This unexpectedness and dynamic story-telling is good (towns and buildings and runs are always different and new) in some ways, but it's TOO uncontrollable. It can really make you feel powerless at times and, again, unfair. In my opinion, much of the gameplay is too reliant on RNG and not actual skill and knowledge of the game.
All in all it's a solid game with good features. You can make your own survivor, complete with cute aesthetics and a special set of positive and negative traits to choose from to really give your character some personality. Gameplay is also well-balanced and flows well. Perfect balance between quick, casual, jump in jump out play sessions, and also long, intense, gaming marathons. At the beginning, when you're first getting used to the mechanics, you will get party-wiped pretty often, so you don't have to invest too much time as you'll be restarting every few minutes however once you're comfortable and surviving longer, single runs can last up to 90, 120, even 180 minutes. Sound short? Well like I said you'll die a lot, so getting that far is an achievement in itself, and plus it's designed to have maximum replayability so you'll surely sink many hours into this title.

Death Road To Canada is a fantastic Roguelike with an odd yet funny sense of humor and fast-paced and insanely fun combat.
The game focuses on 1 to 4 people (or some animals) trying to get to Canada to escape from the zombies. You start with 1 or 2 people, but gain more people on your way.
The main focus of the game is the Oregon Trail-like events and mission-like action scenes.
The Oregon Trail-like events focus on a certain thing happening, from funny, sad, painful or just plain.. ..weird.
These events often result in one of your stats (Loyalty, Morale, Medical, Mechanical, Strength, Wits, Fitness, Attitude, Medical, Composure, Shooting) either being revealed, decreasing or increasing.
The other focus, the mission-like action scenes feature you picking a mission and apptempting to find supplies, weapons and NPCs. These are the main bulk of the game.
Overall, the game is fantastic with the ability to make custom characters (go to Canada with your friends, idols or memes), multiple modes that change a bit, but enough, and tons of refrences.
Oh yeah the soundtrack is great too.

It's a story unlike any other. The protagonist, April, is an unconventional hero; everyday girl but still not exactly what we, or she, expect her to be, to grow into. As her adventures went on, the story took such unexpected turns sometimes that I just had to put my laptop to the side and scream out loud! It's one of those point-and-click adventure games where I just want to explore every little detail, examine the smallest object to get some more funny and/or insightful little tidbit from the heroine's mind.
Yes, the graphics are rather old, and sometimes running around between scenes gets a bit tedious. But it's all so very worth it for the story, for the overall experience.
I think the TLJ series will forever be my favourite, hands down. <3

6 months since it's original release for the consoles, Injustice 2 finally made its way onto PC. Having played and enjoyed the first Injustice game, the announcement of a sequel got me excited. Needless to say, this game is superior from its predecessor. (As sequels are supposed to be)
Pros:
- Great graphics and excellent facial animations.
- A bigger character roster with some B and C-list characters, introducing players to some less popular DC characters.
- The story is also a high point of the game, with amazing cutscenes and voice acting. Dialogue can be pretty dumb at times but overall, it's still above average. All in all, pretty solid. Quick note to everyone who wants Braniac, complete the story, you'll get Braniac for free. Don't buy Braniac.
- Gameplay mechanics is friendly to new players and responsive.
- Customization, not just gear, but abilities and shaders. Your character would then be unique and special to you only (unless if someone else has the exact same loadout, which is possible but unlikely). This can change the way you play and provides variety, thankfully, for ranked matches, the gears are just cosmetics.
- Multiverse, essentially the ladders of Mortal Kombat, this mode rewards players for completing them. But that's not what makes it good, the battles and opponents are. Modifiers are present, opponents have different loadouts, the boss battles are tough.
- Multiplayer, the netcode is well done. There's single fights, king of the hill, and ranked versions for both. I think that's all because I don't remember everything.
- Motherboxes, or loot boxes. As I've mentioned in my Shadow of War review, I think loot boxes are fine, as long as they're not hiding content away. In this game, you get the customization items through the loot boxes, best thing about it is you do not have to pay any real money for it.
- Ever want to get loot while you go out or do something else? Introducing the AI Battle Simulator, select your fighters and let them fight for you.
Cons:
- The pricing for characters, 6 dollars for one character? Jesus, that's too much, maybe lower it down to 2 dollars or maybe even 1.
- Soundtrack, the only soundtrack I remember from the game is the "main theme" and that music that plays after completing a battle. Its just not memorable, just like the Justice League movie soundtrack.
The PC community in Injustice 2 is admittedly lower than the consoles and that makes sense. I hope that this game will gain more traction in the upcoming months. That being said, I really like this game, even if I suck at it.

I haven't played a legit fighting game in a long time. In fact I remeber the last one I played was Mortal Kombat Deception, which in my opinion was an awesome game. So I won't lie to you, I may be slightly biased with this review. I've known John a long time, he's made quite a lot of games, and I'm still undecided if this is my favorite game that he's made. That's not to be taken the wrong way though, as I certainly enjoy this game. It has a lot of charm, a lot of details, and everything works really well. Having said that, I will still try to give a fair and honest review.
This is a very basic platformer, and absolutely nothing about the platforming is in anyway difficult. The controls are really tight, meaning that there isn't really any float to them. Normally I tend to like a little bit of float, like in Super Meat Boy for example, but with this game the controls fit perfectly.
The art is very simple and clean. I like the look, and in particular, all the little movement that happens within the game. I would have liked a little deeper color for some areas as it looks kinda of washed out at times, but that is just a subjective opinion. My monitor could be the culprit, I don't know.
The characters are great. It's amazing what can be done with some pixels and some proper animations. The squid, the squirrel in the nut, the big fat lazy fish, and even the bird in the castle all had charm. My favorite though are the little bugs roasting marshmallows. I laughed when one of the marshmallows burst into flames. This is something I love to see, and you can tell that although simple, there was care put into the characters that make up this world.
The puzzles are very typical of John's style. Appeasing a creature with some sort of item, which in turn allows for progression is a simple premise that I myself have done as well, and that's because it works. None of the puzzles are extremely difficult, but exploration is key to completing the majority of them. This is mainly because, when you get an item, you have no idea what it's for. There is no dialog, no pointers, just an inventory. So it's best to collect all you can, and interact with all the creatures until you figure out what goes where.
The music is well made and really works within the game, Marius did a fine job composing this. Surprisingly there are a lot of tracks for such a small game. I had backed this game on Kickstarter, so I actually received the soundtrack a few weeks ago. I haven't heard all of them within the game yet as I haven't completely finished it, but so far, I do enjoy the music very much.
Overall Gebub's Adventure is a really good game, worthy of it's price. If you want to chill out, solve some puzzles, and explore a pretty neat little world, then this is it! I hope you enjoy the game as much as I have, and I look forward to future titles from John most definitely! As I had mentioned before, John's made a lot of games, and they are worth checking out. In particular Maximus Cerebrum! Below is a link to his GameJolt page, enjoy!

I finished Gebub’s Adventure mere minutes ago, and my emotions are so mixed. On one hand, I loved the game, and wish it could have gone on far longer. On the other hand, the challenges were real, and I take satisfaction in resolving them….well, I resolved most of them.
Gebub’s Adventure has a lot to love. It’s a wonderfully fun game, with just enough tension to keep things really interesting, and made me return more than once after almost giving up. It has just enough frustration built into it to keep things from seeming too simple. And in a universe of gaming where the word “permadeath” is no longer redundant (or a joke), GA gives us “permaLIFE”. There is no death, no matter how far the little guy(?) falls, or how long he(?) remains underwater, how much acid he swims through, or how far he’s flung through the air or how many blocks crush him. Even being swallowed, and finding his way through the digestive tract of some big…thing only slows him slightly. But all these journeys are essential to solving all the puzzles necessary for completion of the adventure, and finding all the objects and all the colored balls, no matter how well hidden (but always with a subtle hint.)
The controls of Gebub’s Adventure couldn’t be much more simple. Arrow keys for movement and jumps (or WASD), “M” for map and inventory, and “X” to exit. There ya go! GA apparently can be completed in an hour, but I spent five (so far. But I did manage to find EVERY colored ball, and some were quite well hidden in a wide (.i.e.–wonderful!) variety of puzzle environments.) Admittedly, I have some physical difficulties that made some of the jumping challenges a bit more challenging that the average player might find them, but not overwhelmingly so.
Every time it seemed Gebub’s world had surely reached its limit, suddenly there was an icy mountaintop, or an incredibly beautiful moonlight sailboat ride. And a huge part of the game is spent underground, to appeal to the most jaded dungeon dwellers. (And I’ll always wonder about the lava fisherman….) The music was truly a wonder all by itself. I can’t imagine how it could have been any more special, yet with enough variety to never begin to be tedious.
If I had to identify a flaw in Gebub's Adventure, it would be the lack of a simple method of recording screenshots to share the beauty of this special game.
If asked, I can’t imagine a game that would have appealed to the widest possible range of gamers as well as GA does, from (possibly) pre-teens to this 58-year old geezer who has been gaming over thirty years. This would be a great game to play with children (or parents), or alone. All in all, a very high recommendation if you need a break from a “forever” game, or today's dose of zombies, and at a reasonable price.
Thank you (players, for reading. DEVS, for your wonderful creation.)

I came away impressed with this indie action RPG.
It's a very easy game--you won't find much of a challenge here--but the different characters and their skills are fun to play, and I do like how the story forces you to play as other people at times. I also appreciate the levels when they aren't generic valleys or hills; some of the town/city environments at night look quite nice with their campfire and brazier flame effects.
The occasional stealth/assassinate segments are a nice change of pace and don't overstay their welcome, though it is amusing to toss a knife into a guy's back and not get any reaction at all from the other fellow standing right next to him at the campfire.
Gameplay-wise, the biggest problem is the characters' pathfinding issues and their tendency to get hung up on the scenery. They don't get permanently stuck, usually, but they do get delayed often, and sometimes they get delayed at the worst time, such as in a boss fight or during a stealth segment. I also encountered a couple of buggy moments that required reloading a save, but they weren't serious.
As for the story, aside from the muddled beginning narration, it's pretty well told via comic-book scenes and dialogue, with only occasional typos or other minor editing problems, though I wish the ending was not quite so abrupt.
I also have to address the character of Ariella, a fictional addition to the tale. In general, I dislike such additions to historical/period works, especially in this case, where she seems to serve mostly as a female player character who contributes to the action. I didn't mind playing as her, though, and she is worked into the story fairly believably for the most part; I just disliked the couple of moments in the comic-book story where she's suddenly a backflipping, stabbing ninja who saves the day.
Overall, I am glad I played Five: Guardians of David. So few games are set in Biblical times, and this one handles the subject matter very well. Players can enjoy it without even being particularly interested in the background, let alone being of the faith.

Take away the Biblical backstory and you have a solid, isometric ARPG from first-time developer,
, that is both engaging and provides innovative mechanics to a familiar genre. Then put the Biblical stuff back in and you’re given something else, something more—historicity and a brave exploration in meshing religion with gaming.
It’s not that story-driven video games lack religion, just not real-world ones. Taking an existing religion and making a game based on one of its more iconic heroes (in this case David, of “David & Goliath” fame), is begging the overly-critical gaming community to rip your game apart.
However, the game is solid. The level design and backgrounds are lush and gorgeous. The pacing is consistent. The loot and risk-reward system are passable. The music is excellent. If a gamer, unfamiliar with any modern religion, was handed a copy of
and
, she would be hard-pressed to select the better game since both have excellent features and limited flaws.
Beyond the objective view, the game should be praised for the way it
handle religion, not in spite of it. There’s never a moment where it feels preachy. It’s educational. The outfits, weapons, and landscapes are historical. Where magic is used in fantasy games,
uses miracles. Heroism is portrayed by selfless sacrifice rather than a common rags-to-riches motif. All actual Bible verses are confined to caches, like developer’s notes, scattered throughout the game, but remain separate from the story and gameplay. In other words, the game lets the player choose how much religion they’re exposed to.
The bottom line is, the game is fun. It’s well worth the price point and no one is trying to convert you. Except me…because I think you should play it.

Movie adaptations of books have been around for nearly as long as cinema itself.
Forrest Gump, Casino Royale and Harry Potter are a few recent (ok, maybe no so recent) movies that I enjoyed despite having never read the books which gave them life.
The more popular a book is, the more likely you'll end up with a movie adaption (and sometimes a game adaption too) so it's no surprise that we've ended up with movie versions of The Da Vinci Code and 50 Shades of Gray, but there's a much more popular book which has spawned plenty of movies over the years (but not that many games) and that book is The Bible.
There was a famous movie director, Cecil B. Demille, who back in the early days of Hollywood built a name for himself producing biblical themed movie adaptations.
He's even quoted as saying "Give me a couple of pages of the bible and I'll give you a picture."
So why do we get biblical blockbusters but not godly games?
Well, gaming is a more immersive and personal experience than cinema and religion can be a divisive thing, there are so many different flavours to choose from, hell, people have even fought wars over it!
Which is ironic when as far as I'm aware (and I haven't read any of the religious books either) that  all faiths, no matter which brand you buy into, preach a message of peace.
It's all love thy Gamer, thou shalt not covert your friends Steam collection, that sort of thing, right?
Yet despite all that peaceful preachery, people have still died over an argument about who's imaginary friend is best.
An irony that isn't lost on Five: Guardians of David, an action RPG title which doesn't shy away from its religious roots but has all the hackery slashery of a Diablo title.
So, in this increasingly splintered, ideologically fractured world, is this godly game a good idea that'll sell gazillions  or a biblical blunder that's bound to bomb?
I'm sure God knows but he's not telling so maybe we'll come to our own decision by the time we get to the end of this review.
When you fire up Five: Guardians of David you'll experience a very verbal (and to a heathen type like myself largely irrelevant) intro movie which reels off a list of old testament names and vague timescales, a summary of this opening narrative (without the names because frankly I can't remember them) would go something like this:
God told A to move to B who had a son called C that became known as D, years later D's decedents moved to E, 430 years after that F led D's descendants from E back to A and then divided A up into bits.
Now it's 400 years later and blah, blah, blah...
If you where familiar with the names and events been recounted I'm sure this would be engrossing stuff, but I'm not, so it for me, it wasn't.
Any way the jist of all this "second son of a of a brother of a man..." palaver essentially serves to tell you that there's a king whom God isn't too keen on but it's ok because there's a boy, the titular David, who should be king instead, oh and King number one (The one God doesn't love) is at war and readying his army for a battle.
 As all this is going on, two shepherd boys who'd been napping on a hill top, awake to the horror of death, but this tragedy isn't a result of the two opposing armies in the valley below.
They open their eyes to the shocking sight of a dead bloody sheep.
Puts all the war and Godly favor stuff into perspective doesn't it?
Anyway, this is where you come in, the first two of the five characters you'll eventually control happen to be our ineffective shepherds whose sleepy neglect has led this poor lamb to meet its woolly maker.
This mindless mutton murder serves as your first task as you seek out the old shepherd to tell him of this sheeply slaughter.
Marching off down the hill side will quickly bring you into contact with a pack of wolves, the murderous mongrels which munched on the mutilated mutton perhaps?
In true Diablo style, you set about clicking on the wolves to smite them for their crimes. 
This encounter will be repeated several times as you journey down the slope.
Take a few steps, whack a wolf with a hammer, rinse and repeat, over and over and over, you can't go five steps without another pack of wolves wondering onto the screen and into your righteous hammer.
At least when they die loot in the form of gold (sorry, I mean shekels) will shower out of their still warm corpses, so that's nice.
When you've finished saving lost sheep from the wolves, (not the subtlest of religious metaphors) you'll come across the old sheep keeper and tell him all about the tragedy.
Overwhelmed with gratitude the old man tells you to bugger off and find your mother, she's got chores for you.
A little walk and a lot of clicking on baddies (mostly wolves) later and you'll discover that one of these chores is to go and find your sister.
Then you follow the path some more, kill some more "bad things" (mostly wolves) and carry on with the drawn out "tutorial" missions as the game winds its way from clicking on wolves and philistine soldiers through to a lion and eventually doing the whole David v Goliath thing, which I enjoyed (even I've heard that little parable! and it was nice to reach a narrative point which felt familiar.
So we know it's a slow burner but how does the game actually play?
Well, you view the action from a zoomable isometric vantage, click to move, click on baddy  to attack etc. It's an ARPG, you know the drill.
You can switch between the five party members to control any one directly, each comes with their own abilities and special actions, all of which you upgrade as you level up throughout the course of the game.
This is a tried and tested game mechanic and is initially quite enjoyable, the problem is that it doesn't take long before things begin to feel a little repetitive, the enemy types aren't varied enough and the spawn points are too frequent which can sometime make the clicky, choppy fun feel more like a chore.
There are plenty of loot drops to fill up your groups inventory, armour, swords, spears, etc. if loot is your thing then this game has you covered.
There's also an auto-equip feature which is a nice touch and saves a lot of time sorting through the inevitable junk pile which you always accumulate in games like this and leaves you fairly confident that when you sell of your unwanted baggage you won't be throwing the baby out with the bath water.
The missions themselves, being tied to the old testament, follow a linier path.
This isn't necessarily a bad thing, sometimes I like a single path to follow, it ensures narrative coherence and a tighter plot, the problem here (and it's a personal issue, you're mileage will vary) is that I just wasn't hooked by the story (it almost felt like it was written millennia ago).
As you follow the path through each level you'll come across caches which give you little♥♥♥♥♥bits of info regarding the game and how its unfolding events relate to the bible. It's a nice touch which lets you know which story elements were made up specifically for the game (as opposed to the elements which were dreamt up for the original work the game is based on).
You can even load up biblical references from these caches if you feel the need to dig a little deeper into the inspiration for this tale.
Technically the game is fairly solid, you'll likely encounter an occasional glitch, but nothing game breaking.

Yay. Awesome. Minimalistic puzzles at their best!
I'm a gamer who has tried hundreds of puzzles and logic games, both on Flash websites and on consoles or such, and of course there aren't infinite kinds of games.
Anyways, Circularity manages to introduce to me a new twist - with its smooth and minimalistic graphics and controls (you need only the left mouse button), you're provided of lots of puzzles in which you have to shoot a ball from a clockwise or counterclockwise-turning big circle to another one; there's just a little bit of misinformation in the achievements 'cos they unlock if you complete a level with 3 stars (while they only say "complete level a" etc.).
Anyways, in every level you'll find three green dots and you will have to jump from a circle to another one by clicking with the left mouse button and collecting (going through) them, and landing on another circle or on the purple small circle, which isn't rotating and marks the end of every level.
Of course, by progressing in the game you'll face obstacles like red static lines, portals, blue "bouncing-able" (they say ricochet xD) walls and so on - it's really not that easy! Oh, and there's also a nice little feature: your last path/trajectory remains "saved" as a trail so that you can adjust the next strike :)
I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzles of any kind, it's refreshing and really gives us a somehow new approach to gameplay.
Graphics of course are extremely minimalistic, but it's not the point of the game! Sounds too aren't even noticeable.
I'd just suggest to adjust the achievement names, since as I said you'll get them NOT by completing the levels but by completing them with 3 stars!!
Anyways, being an indie Unity game developed by a guy with a Georgian surname (good job mate whoever you are!) I think that this deserves a good rating :) Of course replayability isn't that great, it's just a pastime (of 80 levels, anyways xD) but it comes at a very low price, so, no problems at all, happy to contribute!

You didn't heed the signs on the walls as you mounted a dusty end table to reach the building's next level. Zlata is terminally sick and you heard there were meds in this old town ruin. After checking the first floor, this was the only way to reach the second level where you saw the infirmary arrow lead. Every other way was caved in and you didn't bring a shovel.
For a moment, you thought of her smile and ability to lift everyone's mood with a guitar, that warmth you felt drinking your morning coffee. God, you missed your coffee. The shelter's supply ran out last week and the scarcity has made the good's price skyrocket. You can barely get a cup's worth for a bundle of firewood anymore.
Scuffing up the rubble to your feet, you saw the door's lettering on the other side of the room read. Half the infirmary was blown away by the military's shelling. You weren't religious, but you prayed there was some pills left. Zlata wouldn't make it the next couple days without them.
You jog over to the shelves next to a maimed patient bed. Sliding the cover open, dust flew out, but then it cleared. There were two bottles left. You took one in your hand and shook it. The sound of pills rattling inside brought a broud smile to your face.
That smile, like every smile you've felt since the war started, was short lived.
All of a sudden, the shelf cover exploded in front of you, a loud crack tearing through your ears. Was it a rifle or the plastic cover? You've never heard gunfire so close, but that thought didn't occur to you. Suddenly, your chest pounded, heart ablaze with fear. You turned on your heel and lept for the door. It was a reckless gamble. The chances of it being locked were high. Your shoulder crashed against the wood and the door gave. The frame chinked and a bullet ricocheted passed your head. It was so close you felt the air bending to the projectile's force. You scrambled on your knees over the debris and slammed the door behind you, clawing away from it.
At last, you noticed how loud and heavy your breathing was in the empy space, almost as loud as your heart thumping in your chest. Your eyes darted over the darkened room, then back to the infirmary door. When you saw it, you laughed a little. Beside the door, written boldly with white chalk on the wall read, 'SNIPER.'

This is a very pretty space shooter in the vain of World of Tanks... but in space... and with shooting... and less tanks.
I think that's a pretty good summary over-all, however there is a bit more to it than that.
First, unlike WoT, which I also liked quite a bit and played for a few years, this game has a bit more depth in your ship customization, minus the very detailed damage models of your actual ships like you do with the tanks (did you think space ships would be ricocheting lasers off each other?! >:O)... no, I don't mean the stickers or camos you can put on your ships/tanks, even though you have those too, but the fact that every class of ship has it's own group of weapons they can use (not many, but enough imho), which are also mated with more specific class modules. For example, while all Frigates can use Heavy Blasters, only an Engineering Frigate has access to a certain type of drone and "aura"-based healing modules (both for shields and hull) that offer support to all of those around it. Similarly, a Guard Frigate, while also having access to the same Heavy Blasters (can you tell I like Heavy Blasters? lol) will have access to anti-missile defensive modules along with resistance-improving modules that will keep them alive longer. The way you mix and match your Implants (think of these as passive "skills" that improve certain stats or give you some minor abilities) along with your class-specific modules and weapons can have very interesting results. Some people say that only one small group of combinations will produce effective ship builds, however from what I have seen that you can really spec-out a number of ships very differently that will make them absolutely shine under certain circumstance or make them worse in the long-run. The key is to spend a little time to read what all of the different modules do and maybe check the forums for some other player's successful builds for certain classes... then you can tweak anything you want to fit your play style.
In addition to a fairly limited but also strangely satisfying customization of your ships, you have your PvP, PvE, and Sector Conquest (Corp PvP) battles all of which feel very different from one another. PvP lets you hone your skills against other better players (even lets you check some of the gearing options of people on your team when you die or simply looking at the stats screen and mousing-over their ships to give you an idea of what works for them). PvE lets you try some new tactics and mow-down waves of bots. Sector Conquest (mostly for higher-Tier players) lets you bring a limited number of ships without respawns that make your choices all the more important, and truly feels different from the other PvP modes... not to mention gives you nice rewards for holding territories.
The largest complaints I've seen are 1.) "OMG, I just started playing and this game has horrible balance and I can't even change most of my modules!", and 2.) "OMG, I was banned by ABUSIVE Admins!!" Please let me now address both of these concerns:
1.) when you first start-off, you have Tier 1 ships (Rank 1-3). These are your starter ships, and you also get your first chance to fly one of each new class of ships other than your base Fighter. Each of these ships has only 1 type of weapon they can select/use and less than a handful of specialized modules, which means that you will spend most of your time just shooting and occasionally pressing the #1 and #2 keys, and maybe even figure-out you have a special module you can activate by pressing "F." That in itself is the point - to introduce you to the core gameplay before drowning you with choices. As soon as your are done with Tier 1 (which is too fast imho), you are in Tier 2 and have access to more modules and slots for new passive modules... you will probably start meeting more and more players with T4 upgraded weapons and modules and think they are "P2Winners" who are abusing new players... they are not either... all upgrades can be attained with some time and patience, and it will not take long before you figure-out upgrading gears and how easy for you to also have T4 gears. Then before you know it, you are in Tier 3 matches on shiny new ships with even more options/modules/weapons available and here is where it starts getting 'tough' if you did not take the time to learn the basics of the game yet, but it will also teach you how to play better if you give it the time and admit to yourself that you CAN improve and that with a little effort your gears can also be all fancy and upgraded. The only time the balance truly seems off is when you reach Tier 4 battles (Rank 10-12 ships), because due to the current match maker, you are stuck with battles against plenty of Tier 5 ships (Rank 13-15), but even then, the ships have similar enough stats that with the right gears and tactics you too can be competitive.
2.) Well, maybe you should be insulting people less? I ONCE got banned in general chat because I responded to some idiot on a political subject which I found insulting and completely incorrect in-general. I was banned for all of 1 hour from public chat (did not stop me from chatting in Corp or Group chat)... big deal. If you constantly get banned, odds are that you have an abrasively toxic self-entitled and opinionated personality... maybe try not typing as much and playing more. I have yet to get banned for saying anything in battles, then again I also spend quite a bit of time reporting jerks who won't shut the **** up about how horrible everybody else other than they are during the entire match (= killing the morale of the entire team and guaranteeing a loss... if you do that, then STOP IT... that's what the ban is there to help you with).
My Advice to new players since I had to learn this the hard way:
1.) Grind every ship to max level (your ships gain individual levels that make them more powerful), don't just abandon them as soon as the next ship is unlocked.
2.) KEEP all of the ships you are done grinding to max level, as that will give you +1% to experience (synergy) gains... this will make a huge difference for how fast you unlock future ships. If you sell them, you DON'T get the bonus.
3.) Spend as much time on and max EVERY ship on Tier 1 and 2 for ALL 3 factions, both to learn which ship classes are available, to learn the game before starting naked and scared on Tier 3 ships, and also to help lessen your grind at higher tiers... it's really not that bad if follow this rule of thumb, and you will uncover which classes of ship fit your play style the best.
4.) READ module descriptions and don't be afraid to spam your modules in combat... they are not to be saved for later, but to help you destroy your opponents or save your own team... sometimes just firing your guns is not enough... why cripple yourself? If you don't use your modules, or use them incorrectly, "you will not have a good time."
5.) Do NOT just go down one line of ships, such as Frigates. Why? Because Frigates are not useful for every mission/game, such as for capturing Beacons any more than Interceptors can tank with their faces against hordes of AI bots... yes, you can learn the game and figure-out on which maps certain counter-intuitive ships MAY work, however don't just force yourself to lose every match because you have 2 or 3 of the same type of Frigate which can't even get to the battle on time and STILL die because you don't have the right builds or high enough level of upgrades on them.
Over-all, this is a game I enjoy quite a bit, and I even got my wife to start playing it with me. Graphics look absolutely gorgeous with CrossfireX at a 2560x1440p resolution with everything maxed, granted you don't need as much juice to have the game look good at lower settings... very well optimized.
