FootLOL: Epic Fail League developed by Lion's Shade & released on 17 Sep 2013 on the PC platform. On Metacritic
, it has:

What would you expect from a game that combines soccer with cows, mines, spartans, cannons, UFOS and air plane bombers & other unspeakable objects of destruction(s)? If you answered a logical, reasonable, responsible gaming experience – Shows you the red card out *blows whistle* You are dismissed from the field!
But on a serious note, is this title really worth the money/time for all the utter insane chaos? It's really hard to say depending on how you view it.
FootLoL is not your normal standard soccer game. It's not about winning but rather making the other team fail. Wait, isn't that the same? No. And sometimes, you make your own team fail. Wait, what? Yes, you heard me right. If it doesn't make sense, not everything has to make sense and sometimes you have to defy logic for a gaming experience out of this world. That's partically what FootLOL tries to deliver. An Utter Out of this world holy cow chaos beyond oblivion pancakes with 'WTF” stamped on it.
FootLoL offers 3 game mode:

Controls & Visuals:
FootLol controls is very simple. As for the visuals, for me it's okay. It's not pixelated, everything looks simple & clean. I have no complains on this 2 department. Controls, mechanics is working as intended, nothing is broken and no bugs encountered.
FootLOL even allows you to customize how your players look. Although limited but it's something cool to run around with a cowboy hat and all your players looking -_- like this. Weeee!
Animation is fluid, no choppy performance issue but the music after XX hours I couldn't take it anymore. I switched it off and played my own mp3 list. It was a much more rewarding experience when you are listening to “ice ice baby” while leading 50-3. you know?
My Personal Thoughts
Last steam sale, I wanted to purchase a similar product within this context of genre@gameplay. Something just for the fun & casual however I skip it. This time around, I went for it. Looking at the blue mini characters that goes “Weeee” when you blow them up to the sky...I dont know. Satisfying in some sense? Sending hordes of cows onto the pitch, deploying cannons that scores goals for you, sending off the entire team or converting your players into Spartan warriors. Epic. Tons of laughter & fun.
There's 2 issue arising from the game by the time you completed your second planet.

My Summary
FootLoL is certainly fun and refreshing to play with friends/with others but I doubt it can keep it's player base in the long run. I just wished there was a little more to do/or to see as I traveled to other planets. But everywhere I go, I lay waste. Lol.
I am not sure if the opponent strategy was well thought off or just randomly assigned. Some of them are in a mess. You can't counter mess with more mess. You can only delay or hinder the mess from becoming a bigger mess for your team. Did my sentence make any sense to you? No? I can assure you that I am still sane at this point of writing.
Due to that, if you are playing this product just for the fun and don't focus on the objectives at all. You'll be riding cows on UFOS. If your emphasis is on objectives, the cows will be riding you on UFO's instead. Without further delay, before I start to sound like an insane person, on the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for FootLOL: Epic Fail League is an EPIC 5/10.

For the first 1/3 of this game, I would have given it a "no." Then up until an hour or so before the end, I felt pretty neutral about the whole thing. By the end of the game, for whatever reason, I had fallen a little bit in love with the world(s) this adventure spans. So it's a yes, but with some warnings.
This game was created at a time when 3D graphics technology, even pre-rendered, was quite limited. It shows, big time. The characters are chunks of polygons and the animations in particular are quite absurd. Like, unintentional humor absurd. Nonetheless, I could see how this could be visually captivating for people-- 14 years ago. I didn't come into this game expecting anything other than dated graphics but it is not a game that has aged well in that respect.
In terms of "gameplay," there isn't a whole lot of it. It's an adventure game, so it comes with the territory that a lot of your time will be spent walking about and taking in the storytelling. This game felt like 80% of it was just spent listening to people talk. There's just a lot to listen to. At times, especially towards the first half, it can seem very slow just listening to all the talking. But there are eventually puzzles to solve. Unfortunately they're not good puzzles. If you're familiar with adventure games, you'll know there are right ways to do puzzles and wrong ways to do them. TLJ does them the wrong way. I was forced to consult a walkthrough
times in order to progress, and the things I was "missing" were always ridiculous.
The defining (if not redeeming) aspect of any adventure game of course is the storyline. Despite a funky opening, The Longest Journey doesn't exactly dash out of the gate. The aforementioned long-winded dialogues quickly reveal a diverse cast, but they're not all what I would necessarily consider "fascinating." Unfortunately the voice acting is extremely uneven. Rarely, it's quite good, but occasionally it's plain terrible, and often it's just "off" enough to keep it from being believable. The game is ambitious; it really tries for a lot of drama with developed characters and action and humor, and the acting really doesn't sell it. Admittedly, 14 years ago, it was probably pretty impressive. So the game throws you into the "Journey" with really little reason to be interested in it, largely because you're not sure what's supposed to be going on. Then soon enough things get weird, and you start getting a sense of the scope of all this weirdness, but it honestly feels pretty cheesy. For some reason it was enough to keep me coming back to playing TLJ again and again (it IS a long journey), and eventually the game lulled me into appreciating the depth of its story. I became numb to the games flaws and was left to contemplate how thorough a world was created here, particularly the many characters and their stories, and how they all together belong to something bigger. Still, it isn't fantastic, but it is something rather special. By the end, I was glad to have met them, awkward as some of them may have come across at first.
The Longest Journey was clearly a very ambitious adventure, and while it may not have aged so well, you can still sense the vision of the creators as something that is quite remarkable. The game's ending can be described as unsatisfying, but moreso than leaving a bad taste in my mouth it just left me wanting more. And, as it turns out, there is more. So that's where I'm headed next.

The execution....not so much.
As a game, it's a failure on most every level. The gameplay is straight out of Diablo/Titan Quest/Grim Dawn with the one exception being that you can control multiple party members. As a game, Five has to be measured against that strong competition and it really fails to measure up. I've played it for an hour and have no desire to return to it (more on that in a moment).
The graphics/animations aren't good. Titan Quest is a decade old and looks better. The color pallet is muted and it's often tough to distinguish details on the screen. The animations are stiff and stilted. Enemies look just like your guys and it can be tough to figure out who is friend from foe unless you concentrate on the health bars above people's heads. The music/sound is ok though the voice acting is quite poor. Frankly, I wish they hadn't voice acted the game as just text would have been an improvement.
The cartoon interludes telling the story are pretty cool, if a little heavy-handed on the whole "ordained by God" thing and actually not accurate, That's actually pretty insulting. An example of this is when they're telling the story of David v. Goliath. In thie game David claims that he didn't need armor because he was protected by God. Nice try, but no. That's not how the story goes. He declined armor because he was not accustomed to wearing it! That's fairly unforgivable given how sacred some faiths hold the source material.
Back to the game, your characters level but you have no influence over their leveling - you don't get to raise their stats or pick any new skills. You get what you get and that makes character advancement a dull affair.
The one gimmick in the gameplay  is that you can control multiple party members. However, it's more limited in reality since you can control only one at a time (and the others are woefully ineffective when you're not controlling them) this novelty quickly wears off. Other than that the gameplay is straight out of any Diablo-style game. Each one of the 5 characters you can control have different abilities but you're better off using the one guy who can stun everyone (I forget who that is). You'll find other characters not as useful. The abilites aren't anything to write home about and there's nothing that makes you go "wow". Kicking an opponent or lighting an arrow on fire isn't anything new in the genre.
Itemization isn't anything to write home about either. I know I was only an hour into the game but of the 5 characters, only one had any kind of decent weapon upgrade. Without being able to control your character advancement, itemization becomes far more important. I didn't see any real great shakes here and thus this is another missed opportunity. It did not feel rewarding to play through the game and not get any real upgrades to your characters. Now maybe later on new cool weapons fall like Frankincense and Myrrh from the sky but it didn't happen early enough in the game to compel me to keep playing.
As mentioned, the enemies are based on the Torah and therefore are pretty run of the mill. Just like the abilities, there's nothing here to make you go WOW! There are some wild variations on difficulty though and while you'll chew through most enemies easily some seem abnormally difficult even though they're still white (fodder) enemies.They're basically enemy soldiers.
So far what I've described is a fairly dull Diablo clone. Unfortunately, FIVE gets worse,
Ok, then finally we get to the bugs and the reason I'm no longer playing the game. I've hit four in the first hour.
1. Gold from a chest dropped into an area of the screen my character couldn't access. Very minor.
2. An enemy was shooting at me from an area on the map that I couldn't get to. That's pretty annoying.
3. I managed to roll myself into the crowd and couldn't move in the boss battle against Goliath. He couldn't get to me and I couldn't get back out. So the only option was to restart the entire battle which required me to play through the ENITRE map again. Exceptionally annoying.
4. The last was the boss battle at Shebitku. There's a spike trap that comes up to prevent your other characters from coming into a one-on-one fight. Except when I died (because the difficulty on this battle is so absurd that I died in two hits) the spikes didn't come back down. Thus I could not re-engage the boss. So I saved. And reloaded the save....and was again placed all the way back at the start of the level. That's enough. Done. Not coming back.
So as a game what you have is a poor Titan Quest clone with bad animations, no character development, poor itemization, boring enemies, muddled textures and that's VERY buggy. Beyond the novel concept and the nice developers there's nothing redeeming here. That's unfortunate because I'd love to see more historical games made outside the wargame genre. But I can't when the execution of the game is this poor. Thumbs down.

I put a "yes" on the "Do you recommend this game?" box, but it should come with a disclaimer. This game is not for everyone. It's not like Braid; you can't just jump into it and go. The Witness is a lot more like MYST or other older puzzle games, where it's entirely puzzle and no action. All of the puzzles are done on grids and they involve creating lines on these grids. There are rules however, and sometimes you have to get very, very creative. The environment interacts with the puzzles and you have to put the two together in a way that will not always make sense at first. A lot of people are saying that the puzzles are not rewarding due to no big "ah ha!" moments, but I find that this isn't entirely true. There aren't any 'big' moments where everything falls into place, but the game does provide an enjoyable slow burn that is fun to just spend an afternoon digging into. It's not a short game, by any means (I've played about 10 hours and only activated three out of seven lasers). The high price tag reflects the amount of time you will spend in The Witness.
My only complaint is that, so far, the plot/narrative elements are vague, far apart, and unrewarding. There's clearly a lot going on on the island and I don't think I've missed much, but I get the feeling that lots of people will never even come across a single story element. Good thing that the puzzles themselves are plenty fun on their own.

Before writing this review I was asking myself "If I would clone a good game on the same engine, then remove most of the content and add a bit of my own similar content, would it still be a good game?" - Heall yeah it would be. But I still wouldn't recommend it, because there is the original out there with way more content.
In that regard I feel this review might be a little unfair, because objectivly TOXIKK is not a bad game and is targeted on fans of classic arena shooters, which don't need much innovation in the first place. But since here we have basically none, I don't really see the point of investing into this game.
Being based on the Unreal Engine, this game looks really great. It surpasses modern standards and runs fluently on halfway decent PCs. I would definetely call this game the best looking arena shooter at this point.
Another thing this game makes good use of from the Unreal Engine is the great AI, which results in very smart behavior of the bots. Even though currently there are barely any multiplayer games going on, as this game is not really popular, it is not a big deal because you can practice just fine with bots and have fun with them.
At this point there are only a couple of maps with just 3 modes: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch and some sort of Capture the "Flag" on bigger maps with vehicles. And apart from that there is really nothing you can do. That is rather poor.
While the description of the game claims "fresh ideas", I haven't really found anything that makes this game unique compared to other arena shooters. This is the game's biggest problem. A simple arena shooter is nice, but without something that makes it stand out from the crowd, this game won't get far.
I don't recommend this game to anybody who is not into arena shooters, since there is nothing special to see here. Arena-FPS fans might consider it, but should wait for more content first.

You can call this game a “cyberpunk bartender action” (just like in the title): it’s all about being a bartender in a cyberpunk world, mixing drinks and changing lives. Patrons come to the bar and place their orders, you mix them their cocktails and listen to their stories. To receive character-specific endings, you must learn what your regulars like to drink in a specific mood or figure out some riddle-like order of theirs.
Gameplay: it’s a visual novel with some gameplay elements: you read stories and mix drinks from basic ingredients to earn money. Money is important, because Jill (the protagonist) must pay her bills and buy nice things, so that her life wouldn't be miserable and she wouldn't be distracted from work. So you need to provide better service to get more money so you can spend it to provide better service. Gameplay-wise it simple, but the stories and setting are engaging.

Stories: every customer (and the bartender too) has something to tell, discuss or complain about. Their stories are different, some are funny, some are heavy, and some are disturbing.

Characters: elegant cat-woman… sex-worker android… corgi with an eyepatch… and everyone is lovely. Which is lovely.

TL;DR: Well written character interactions and clever choice mechanic make for a mature/silly/deep experience. 9/10 for a visual novel-type game.
edit: The price is definately worth it. No regrets here.
The game plays very much like a visual novel as you spend most of your time clicking through conversational text but it's broken up by mixing drinks. You chose, most often, what drink, the amount of alcohol, or what size is best for the customer. Your goal is customer satisfaction but also trying to avoid making a bad situation worse (enabling an alcoholic vs refusing to make their prefered drinks). Of course you can always play the devil's advocate and get an idol trashed before her big concert.
The characters are very deep and genuine while still being a little outlandish ala post-dystopian future styling. Android sex robots will depend on you for companionship and half-man-machine killers will seek you out for a wind-down beverage after work. Most of the topics covered are serious and relatable to people of drinking age and you'll find bits of your own personality and experience in many of the clients you serve. Even the non-humans are very much human on the inside.
Lastly, the protagonist, Jill, is very relatable (at least in my opinion) in that she is an observer that doesn't hide away her own personality. Conversations aren't one-sided (except for a few loud, energetic characters) and she carries a lot of respect for her clients as well as herself. She might not always say what she's thinking but she has an opinion on everything. Many players will see her as her own character rather than a proxy for the player themselves.

BlackEye looks fantastic, loads nice and snappy, it's chepa, and offers a challenge.  Those are the good things.
As for the bad - the game is entirely too chaotic.  You essentially fall down each level avoiding various enemies, traps, and other environmental hazards.  The controls (I used an Xbox One controller) didn't feel terribly responsive or at least not to a point I'd prefer.  My biggest gripe is I simply have no idea what's going on.  I don't mean story-wise either, though that's lacking in-game too.  Instead I'm talking about the various icons or artifacts you can pick up.  I had no clue what the vast majority of it did or how to use them correctly.  Instead I found myself just bumbling to the bottom of each level, occasionally shooting something out of my rear, going through some random portals and hoping I make it to the end.
I realize this is a pretty negative review of this game and I can't really recommend it right now.  However, it does seem as if the developer is working hard on it and adding not only new content but trying to fix existing issues.  I'd gladly come back and try this title out again and see if it's been improved.  So there's definitely potential - just right now it's not fully reached.
Me bumbling around:

The concept is nice, but at the current state (14.06.2017), I can not recommend it.
In Black Eye your character tries to reach the lower world by jumping down. As you can see from the screenshots or videos, the game has a well-defined style and the whole concept seems intriguing. But at the current point, the game is far from done.
Right now, if you look at it, the most lacking part is UI, and, because of that, User Experience. The control tips in the beginning seems to be too small and the icons don’t help much. Then you just start falling down, encounter lots of different stuff (icons) which are not really self-explanatory and try to make sense from all of it. And if you don’t want to place the text in the game – that’s totally fine and it can be a part of your style, but then try gradually introducing the elements, instead of throwing the gamepad picture at the start of the game and then just making players encounter everything at a too fast pace. At this point, the weakest point is introduction.
A minor thing, but make sure that players can navigate the menu with their gamepad. Just catch the stick movements and move the mouse cursor accordingly.
Gameplay-wise, I would move the camera down a bit more when player is jumping down, just so that he can see what’s going down where he’s falling. Also consider giving him short invulnerability on damage, because right now the death can happen a bit too fast.
Speaking of death, check out the youtube video “why your death animations sucks” (linked below); I think the death animations can be adjusted. I.e. splashing the black blood or shaking the screen or playing more sounds. Otherwise the death just does not feel serious.
If you work on it – I’m sure it will turn out great. At the current state, the game has a nice concept, defined style and graphics, but that’s about it. The gameplay / user feedback needs more work and improvement. So I suggest waiting until early access ends and I’ll probably revisit the review.

Injustice 2 is a really good game with a couple downsides but overall depending on where you're coming from a must buy:
Let's say you never played fighting games, don't know what superarmor, frame advantages and the difference between strings and combos are but would like to play a fighting game for a change, should you get Injustice 2 ?
I think if you should get any of them then injustice, compared to most other popular fighting games Injustice is not about complex input and buttontimings to fire off your strongest attack called a super move for instance. You press RT and LT on your controller when your meters are full - on all characters. While every character has a different moveset and differ from how they are played (at range, close up, setting up traps etc.) all characters have the most important moves unified. Want to punch someone through a wall into the next area ? Press <-- A regardless of who you play. Want to roll forward past any projectiles ? --> --> RT, etc. etc.
The game is flashy, loud, violent and bombastic from Supermove to Area Transitions and extremely responsive to controls (I have not played on the keyboard but i suggest using a controller at least)
This makes for a much easier way to learn the game when you are relatively new to fighting games. Even though I2 is easier in some of these aspects than other fighting games button mashing is not rewarded and you will always loose against a higher skilled opponent. If you see yourself being that higher skilled opponent the game gives you all the tools to do just that, versus other players or in singleplayer. I personally enjoy fighting against the AI in Multiverses (sort of daily challenges that you can complete in varying difficulty that reward you with gear / cosmetics) but lets say that's not your thing and you only want to fight online against other players: you can disable gear for both players in games aside from the cosmetics, and in ranked it's disabled anyways.
Don't like PvP at all ? There's a storymode with a good story (i'd rate it 7.5/10) where you get to play alot of different characters, and while the writing is mediocre at times it's alot of fun to play through it. Not even to mentioned the TON of customization you can do visually and statswise through the ton of gear that gets thrown at you.
The problem here is to be quite frank the pricepoint, if you JUST want to play the story and never interact with other players then i'd say it's probably to expensive. If you however add all the multiverse content to it you might even get a good deal out of it. If you go for PvP anything on top is just a cherry and added benefit, it IS definitely worth it.
If you ever wanted to get an entry into fighting games and really start to understand them, I2 is perfect, there's a ton of good tutorial videos out from consoleplayers (they apply exactly the same) and the game gives you ALL data you ever would want if you feel like it.
It really feels great the first time you hit a longer combo with one of your characters after figuring out how you can connect the moves of all these different characters.
Personally if you're unsure wether you will like the game but want i'd say get the normal version, ultimate you can still upgrade later on (at a loss though) if you really love the game.
It's no surprise, netherrealms keeps their games transparent. You get all data you ever would want for all the moves, the Netcode is absolutely superior (for some reason flawless even around 250ms) and the AI in practice mode is all you would expect: On screen tagged moves that you can favourite, recordmode for AI, numerous settings down to delayed wakeups etc. make learning new combos a breeze.
I would say though for better or worse there is more zoning in this than in MK or similar games but also much more arenainteraction than similar games. (Area Transitions, Interactables, jump off points etc.)
Another big advantage is that alot of other people have already laid the groundwork with most characters, you're coming into a game that already had it's major balance patches and you can check out endless videos from the competitive scene or just combo guides for almost all characters.
My only criticism at the moment would be there's no ELO Ranking just a ranked set mode where you fight against random people, so if you like to show off badges that you're number 1 in europe you won't get that here. (yet ?)
Other than that, inputs have been very responsive, combos are easily to put together and online play against others is just a blast.
I love the game, as soon as it offers a proper ranking system it will be even better however you have to be aware that you are buying a niche game that has a hefty pricepoint. I personally think it's absolutely worth it, i do think though it's priced to high when it comes to convincing others to get the game. The value is there, but for most people this is still just "a fighting game", if you love competitive games and want to beat others through skill and not just gear, get it, no question.

If you don't mind a game that's rough around the edges and you're looking for a little challenge, you may like this game (especially if you can get it for $1).  The presentation is passable namely because of the excessive bloodshed.  The graphics themselves and enemy design are middling at best, but differing enemy capabilities and increases in their difficulty as you progress make up for it.  The game itself doesn't actually feel that hard, but over time it wears you down, either you feel overconfident and spend too much time going for all of the collectibles in a level, or you take on enemies head-on without figuring out if it's the best method of attack, in either case, you end up taking damage that isn't always easy to replenish.  If I could give this game any comparison, it would be Binding of Isaac Lite (with Lite being the key word) - It's nowhere near as creative, difficult, visually compelling or always differing, nor does it have the same tight controls, but I'd be lying if I didn't say that this game brought me back to it a few times to give it another go.

TLDR: DO NOT GET THIS GAME ON PC. GET IT ON THE Xbox360 INSTEAD BECAUSE THE PC PORT ISN'T POSSIBLE TO FINISH BECAUSE OF THE BOSS FIGHTS THAT DON'T WORK.
This was the first game I'd ever bought on XBLA as a kid, and it's still one of my all-time favs. As soon as I saw it on Steam I knew I had to get it, and I was VERY dissapointed with the PC port.
Here's the good things about the PC port.
-Make your own levels
-Play the game with headphones (And be amazed by the fantastic soundtrack)
-Turn up the graphics to the max which makes the game look better than on the Xbox360
-Play the game with a MUCH higher framerate so the controls feel much tighter and more responsive
But, then there's all the problems with the PC port. (These problems are not on the XBLA edition which I recommend you get instead)
-Dashing doesn't work quite right.
-Buggy boss fights. Here's some examples of them:
One boss got stuck and I had to nudge him out in order for him to get to where he needed to go in order for the final stage of the fight to start.
Another boss isn't even possible to finish (And therefor making the game impossible to finish) You're supposed to get it to charge at you and smash into the gears you're standing above, but it doesn't charge, it just slowly hovers towards you instead, meaning that it doesn't get the impact on the gears needed to finish that stage of the boss fight.
The rest of the bosses are just as frustratingly buggy making the boss fights completely unplayable.
0/5 - Impossible to finish. Get it on XBLA for the Xbox360 instead

While this is a negative review, I want to stress that I don't think this is strictly speaking a game that doesn't try to earnestly be good. That is, this isn't one of those games that are remarkably bad that you see on Steam so often. I played the Xbox 360 Demo back in very early Xbox 360 Arcade days and thought it was fun. And for the most part? Its actually not really straight up bad, its just below par and it has a number of issues that make it impossible to reccomend.
Pros:
-The game itself might not be amazing, but when it was made on the 360 it was only 50mb in size. The PC port obviously doesn't have the same strict size limitations that early Xbox Arcade titles had of course (and they seem to have increased the game's overall size to over 300mb, probably higher quality sound and textures were the result). But still, considering that it originally was very small and yet still a fairly pretty game for its time is an engineering feat one can at least apreciate.
-Has good music.
-Very pretty art design.

Was going to wait longer to do this, but I've played enough to know. And, I dont write many reviews..
- Skills: No need to waste time with items. Each hero has a different set of skillful abilities that are fun and dynamic and upgraded by performance. There are various ways to upgrade your abilities and build your hero. Which gives the game more depth and replay value. Especially if you play with friends and build around each other. only complaint is there seems to be a slight delay while trying to activate abilities. sometimes i gotta smash a key to make sure it fires off quickly enough.
- Aesthetics: It has a, "cartoony"  look, but, with its own style. From the character design to the animations, particle effects and maps. It is visually pleasing. Especially moving around and with the Guardians, it creates a very immersive effect. It runs very smooth as well. I've enjoyed many cel shaded titles over the years, and Gigantic does it well.
- Mode: an amalgam of other classic modes but with its own twist. various points to attack or defend which effect the main objective, the Guardian. It's simple yet allows for various outcomes because there are different creatures that can be summoned on a control point. which are effectively towers in other MOBAs. I like how there are no, "creeps" or "minions". or, waves of units going down lanes. all of the action comes from the users and the few creatures they summon and play around. so in that sense its a skill based game where everyone is focusing almost entirely on the enemy users. skill involving both quick and precise use of abilities but with platformer type mobility. and it also reminds me of a fighting game, but team based. each guardian has a health bar which is worn down throughout the match.
matches can be fast or they can be drawn out. unfortunately it may be drawn out from one team not working together well enough concerning the objective, and they do not attack the Guardian when its vulnerable, instead they stand on a point seemingly AFK defending a creature that no one is attacking.. probably thinking to themselves that the other people on their team don't know how to play. Other times a match is dragged out because both teams know what they're doing and are working together very well in a mutual stalemate. and once the match is forced into a sort of sudden death mode, it gets really fun. because by then everyone is typically max level so they are fighting with everything they've got.
All of this sounded better in my head. I can tell you all the other MOBAs I've played over the years, but i wanted to break it down and keep it simple.  It is a great free to play game, but certain things may turn off some people, but.. not everyone. There is some level of grind involved, but for some people they enjoy earning and collecting. It is not pay to win however, so no need to worry about that. There is an interesting sort of quest system in place to help you save up the two kinds of currency that unlocks everything. They are like tarot cards, so you get a daily draw and you can hold up to 7 in your hand. it can be hard to start out if all of your quests are for Heroes you don't have access to. although there is a healthy character rotation, which gives you time to familiarize yourself and progress with each Hero, while also finish quests. but, if you start with quests for heros you cant play they are essentially, "dead in hand".. but that makes another sort of mini game as far as what cards you pick and what you decide to unlock first. So far i am at around 10 hours and I'm about to unlock my second Hero if i pick one on sale or lower priced. But, i'd probably need to save for several more hours in order to get some of the other Heroes or creatures. I will say that the various free to play MOBAs i've played over the years, I don't do it with money but by simply playing the game. And this game is enjoyable enough to do that, however if you do put money in I can say that this company deserves it. Some may complain about originality but all in all it is a fun, quality game. Casual yet competitive. Great, skill based action that gives you that sense of reward for doing what you needed to in a fight. So give it a try. Especially if you've enjoyed any other MOBAs.

This is a very well crafted, down-to-earth gaming experience with great atmosphere and exciting (and sometimes depressing) highs and lows. Your experience here will be finite, but it's still certainly worth a buy.
If you've ever played Don't Starve (or other survival games) before, some of the mechanics of this game will be familiar to you. You can create a lot of different things, however your supplies are limited, so you'll have to guess at which things might be the most important and learn from experience. This really works well for the game in your first or second playthrough because it forces you to make tough decisions... Your food supply is low. Your survivors are starving. You ask yourself if you have anything to trade for food... Would you trade away your store of life-saving medicine to buy a tin or two of meat? How about the firearms you've crafted to protect yourself? Would you kill an innocent person just to survive for a precious few more days? These are some of the questions you will have to ask yourself, and it is this part of the game that is probably the most memorable and unique for me.
This is the kind of game that is quite easy to become immersed in, especially in your first couple of playthroughs.  The music, the drab, monotone color palette, the sound effects - everything is just done and presented very well.
To me - and this feels like the really important bit - it doesn't feel like the game is just telling you a story - like so many other games would do - but rather like you are writing your own. It's the story of your survivors, and it's completely up to you as to what kind of story that will be. As the days went on in my game, I found myself getting attached to Marko, Bruno, and Pavle. I felt guilt on the days I couldn't feed them all, and uplifted on those precious occasions when I found a can or two of meat to share amongst them whilst scavenging. Then Marko was shot and killed - and it felt genuinely horrible and I wanted revenge. So I had revenge! Pavle gunned down the murderer and his parents too, and took their supplies - a lot of wood, scrap, food, and other necessities - home. But it was small comfort for Pavle and Bruno; they had lost their friend, and Pavle's hands would be forever stained with blood. Perhaps he would be next to die in the neverending search for supplies just to go on living. In that run, being quite new to the game, scavenging became a bloodsport and killing a necessity for life. It was honestly unreal. I found myself justifying murder! Soon, I was no better than the other bandits and criminals that were raiding my shelter for supplies. No game has ever made me feel like that - about making hard decisions to get from one day to the next. I was so happy in a later run when I could just feed everyone enough to keep them going, and when I had the spare resources to make a guitar and an armchair to bring my survivors some small comforts.
However, it should be stated that the experience is most certainly finite. Once you figure out the optimal way to do things, you will find that the game falls flat. When everything is in abundance, there are no difficult decisions to make and that core element of the game that makes it so appealing is suddenly gone. It is not an 'if' but a 'when'. It's a bit of a shame too because at this point, the game has gotten so easy that I don't even want to see it through to the ending. It would have been nice if the gameplay went beyond 'figure out the correct build path through trial and error and then you will pretty much never lose'. My playtime says ~50 hours, but I left it open, paused, and in the background over a few nights so 20 hours is more accurate.
That said, This War of Mine certainly delivers - and it delivers something truly unique and fascinating over a good 15-20 hours of gameplay. For these reasons, it is definitely worth a buy in this humble reviewer's opinion.

I put a "yes" on the "Do you recommend this game?" box, but it should come with a disclaimer. This game is not for everyone. It's not like Braid; you can't just jump into it and go. The Witness is a lot more like MYST or other older puzzle games, where it's entirely puzzle and no action. All of the puzzles are done on grids and they involve creating lines on these grids. There are rules however, and sometimes you have to get very, very creative. The environment interacts with the puzzles and you have to put the two together in a way that will not always make sense at first. A lot of people are saying that the puzzles are not rewarding due to no big "ah ha!" moments, but I find that this isn't entirely true. There aren't any 'big' moments where everything falls into place, but the game does provide an enjoyable slow burn that is fun to just spend an afternoon digging into. It's not a short game, by any means (I've played about 10 hours and only activated three out of seven lasers). The high price tag reflects the amount of time you will spend in The Witness.
My only complaint is that, so far, the plot/narrative elements are vague, far apart, and unrewarding. There's clearly a lot going on on the island and I don't think I've missed much, but I get the feeling that lots of people will never even come across a single story element. Good thing that the puzzles themselves are plenty fun on their own.

Not just a snake-puzzle simulator. Seems like it for the first hour, but then a larger meta appears. Definitely worth a play. Especially like the lack of tutorials, all the methods of solving puzzles are eased into and hinted at, with you discovering the rules of the game world. The game world isn't just "there" to solve puzzles in, it's incredibly relevant.

If you enjoy maze logic puzzles (or Sudoku, Sokoban, etc) you'll love this game. The Witness is broader and deeper and more subtle and surprising and wonderful and beautiful and epiphanic than just a series of maze puzzles, but I really appreciated how well crafted those maze puzzles are, how they teach without words and bring you to unexpected solutions with such elegance. The world has a peaceful, meditative quality that needs to be embraced - these puzzles aren't work, they're like steps on the road to enlightenment.
The Witness is a magnificent game.

There is no false advertising here - this game is long and it's one heck of a journey. The story bridges two worlds - a sci-fi dystopia and a fantasy world full of strange magical creatures. It's rare to find a story that manages to incorporate dragons and hovercraft, castles and spacestations and the game manages to do it almost seamlessly. The characters are believable with realistic motivations for the most part, and the voice acting (and almost everything is voiced - which is a rare treat for such an old game) is very good quality. It is easy to get frustrated with the pace of the game, however. Several people I know gave up after the first few chapters, and I almost fell into that trap, but it's well worth persevering through the endless *walking* (even with double-click or Escape to make her run, the protagonist seems agonisingly slow sometimes) and the extremely linear puzzles which sometimes have the oddest and most unlikely solutions. If you get too frustrated, as I did at some points, don't feel too guilty about doing a little cheating. It's worth a little shameless googling sometimes to get on with the story. The ending is a little abrupt, and I felt that I was wishing for something more, but maybe it's just because I missed talking to Charlie one last time! (Charlieeeee!)

is a strategy defense combined with a neat and challenging card game combat hailing from Nival Interactive, a small Russian development team that will take on the formidable feat of developing
, eventually later on. As a side note, alongside its quite improved sequel
, the game holds a special place for me; meaning many frustrating hours of deck building and combat practice during 2001-2004. I was about to shed tears of joy when I first managed to beat this one!
In the world of Ether, there comes a time when the way to the Temple of Time is finally open. The old legend states that whoever holds dominion over the Temple shall rule the power of Ether, the substance of all magic and creation. Four distinct nations of the realm: druidic Vitals, aloof Kinets, fierce Chaots and decaying Synthets all begin a race towards the Temple to challenge the master of the world: the White Lord. Only one shall succeed and overcome the challenges of becoming the next White Lord. As the saying goes: "The Ether enslaves the ones who obey it, and destroys the ones who do not".
I suspect that neither European nor American market are familiar with this challenging and enjoyable series, so I'll try to make a resume for the game dynamics. In its essence,
is a strategy game which presents the player an isometric map with a capital city, resources to gather and monsters to challenge. With each combat your hero overcomes, he/she levels up to unlock a selection of abilities. You have to make sure that you protect your base and gather needed resources to wage war at the same time. Here, we basically have a
alternative.
The combat itself on the other hand, is a variation of
card game where your hero and the enemy faces each other, with monsters to summon and spells to alter the battlefield. Here is where things get complicated: you will be collecting the spells throughout the strategy map and you will have a limited number of spells that your deck may hold any given time. For each spell acquired, you will also need the appropriate resources which determines how many times that spell can be cast. Thus, you have to establish a careful balance between the game's strategy and card game elements. Easier said than done, this restriction quickly becomes tricky to handle. When you decide to change one card, you can easily find yourself travelling to the other side of the map, while an enemy hero silently marches towards your capital.
Graphics are fairly outdated, but still charming enough in my opinion. The environment and character animations are colorful exaggerations that we are already familiar from
or
series. Camera settings are usually a bit distasteful, inconveniently choosing to focus on random figures, but hey! No one promised an A+ game. What we have here is an old, challenging strategy and card game that certainly doesn't hold hands with the player.
There is a truckload of negative reviews about the game out there, complaining about constant crashes or not being able to run the game at all on modern systems. These issues are long gone. The worst that you should be expecting is that you may have to run the game from the directory rather than the Steam shortcut which doesn't record playtime. Otherwise, it works fine. The campaign is fairly long - with two concurrently occurring separate scenarios. You can always run an independent strategy or dueling session too.
I strongly suggest giving
a chance if you either enjoy strategy or card games, or that you'd be curious about a successful combination of the two. Take it when you're feeling up for a challenge.

This is the only visual novel-esque I will ever recommend. The character and world building are beautiful, and after time you will start to care about the characters. I really don't want to give anything away but let me tell you one thing: the prologue is working at a bar where the only customers are corgis.

VA-11 Hall-A resembles a 80s cyberpunk anime like Dominion Tank Police: it has cute characters who have hilarious conversations on screen, but the bleakness of the world they live in is always looming, and the story itself is ultimately tragic. Today you trade jokes with a sweet big-eyed girl, tomorrow you go to sleep in the bar, afraid to go outside, listening to the shooting on the streets, where a civil riot rages, wondering if she's even still alive.
The story takes place in a hellhole of a city, populated with all kinds of weird people: cyborgs, hackers, journalists, sentient dogs, assassins, private cops, sex workers, bloggers, mutants... Each one has their own personal story, their own perspective on the ongoing events. Each one needs someone to listen while pouring them synthetic drinks. That's where your character comes in: a nerdy bisexual bartender with her own issues that she's not eager to share -- even with the player.
This is a cyberpunk story that features all hallmarks of the genre -- some shooting, some hacking, some sex -- but you won't see any of it on screen. Instead you will talk with all kinds of people, learning about the ongoing events from various perspectives and affecting them ever so slightly, one drink at a time. This is your only way to affect the story: while it has several ending, you never get to choose what to say -- only what to mix.
Brilliantly written, funny and tragic, childish and mature at the same time, this is one of the best visual novels I've ever read.

FIVE: Guardians of David is an isometric action RPG based on the Biblical stories of David’s life starting from a young giant killer’s perspective to an influential leader. The story of David is at the center of attention right from the start, most of it depicted through comic-book style cut-scenes between the missions and the rest through scarce dialogue encounters in the game.
Most of the time when you actually bother to pay attention to what the game has to say you get the impression that you are listening to some kind of a weird Biblical teaching device. Characters are paradoxically soulless, and despite being some of the most important Biblical figures, they have no personality whatsoever. Representation of that storyline onto the battlefield is even worse. Missions you venture through will give you absolutely no sense of accomplishment as you literary won’t die. Even if you do, you will simply take control of some other character from your party of five. Atop of that almost every single mission objective in the game is a boring fetch quest where you must either destroy, collect, grab or pull something, killing hundreds along the way.
The player controls a party up to a 5 class-based characters: ranged weapon users, spear wielders, sword and shield fighters. There is plenty of space for quite a number of collectible gear and weapons on the shoulders of five men you control, which unfortunately makes no difference due to the fact that such a casual combat doesn’t require you to even bother with comparing or even collecting new gear. You slice through hordes of enemies like knife through butter any give weapon.
There is no deapth or high quality here, not by any means a Diablo–style action RPG clone. FIVE: Guardians of David is simply a below average game for a below average player. On the other side FIVE being a “Bible Game,” doesn’t bring much of anything to the table other than slaying people by thousands, while promoting some kind of twisted morality through the comic-book cutscenes. Levels are entirely linear and narrow corridors, with some kind of and open space usually associated to a boss battle (which you can’t lose, as you respawn over and over again). Leveling-up is done collectively by group and new abilities are auto-assigned by the game, though these can be modified.
I really cannot reccommend FIVE to anyone. Fans of action RPGs have literally dozens of better games to choose from. Price of 22,99$ is ridiculous for the content you get. Aside from the novelty of the Biblical theme and story, FIVE‘s gameplay ignores a lot of what has been a standard in the genre for quite some time. Such important gameplay aspects as strategic groups, tactics and propper character development are nowhere to be found here. With its bleek heroes and dumb enemies FIVE: Guardians of David is something not worth your time or money.

Thank you Kingdom Games for sending us this game to review!
King David was described in the Bible numerous times (1 Sam 13:14, Acts 13:22) as a man after God’s own heart.  He was also a warrior and shed a lot of blood (1 Chronicles 28:3) and because of that, the job of building a temple for God was passed onto his son, Solomon.  David wasn’t the only one on the battlefield though - he had many mighty warriors and they are all described in 2 Samuel 23:8-39. FIVE: Guardians of David focuses on Jashobeam, Eleazar, Shammah, Abishai, and Benaiah.
Each of these warriors has a specialized weapon and together they were an unstoppable force that have wiped out many of Israel’s enemies including the Amalekites, Arameans, Edomites, Jebusites, Moabites, and the Philistines.    In the beginning of the game, these mighty men were mere shepherd boys fighting off wolves along with the occasional lion.
FIVE: Guardians of David is an action RPG very similar to the play style of Diablo.  The swarms of enemy soldiers can be attacked by clicking on them repeatedly or by holding down the mouse pointer on them until their hit points are depleted.  As long as another mighty warrior is still standing, you can take control of them at any time.  If one of the warriors falls in battle, the others can pick up their slack if needed.  If all of the warriors fall, the game will resume at the nearest check point and the enemy’s health points will be where you left them.  Some gamers may find that too easy for their tastes, especially during boss battles. There are many boss battles and of course, the epic battle between David and Goliath takes place early on in the game.
A majority of the game takes place as David is fleeing from Saul and beginning to establish his kingdom.  Besides dealing with outside opposition, the people of Jerusalem did not want him to establish his kingdom there.   Their king had to take it by force, and he did.
While most of the game is based on and sources its Biblical references, there are some added characters and story elements to keep things interesting.     In total there are eleven acts and forty-two levels in the single-player campaign.  After completing each act and their boss, a Steam achievement is earned.  I’m not sure why, but there is no achievement or mention of Act 3.  Does that mean there are only ten acts?  In either case, this is one of three Steam games I have gotten a 100% completion on.
There’s a decent amount of variety in the game’s missions.  Besides beating the snot out of people, you will also have many opportunities to set fires to their camps or scout them out stealth style while not being detected.  Animal lovers may take offense to the mission objectives that require hobbling messenger horses (binding their legs with rope) or setting loose pigs with ignited jars of oil on them to set enemy tents ablaze in the chaos.  Each mission has several objectives that need to be completed and optional caches that can be found to relay some story background and accompanying Biblical verses.  Finding all of the caches is great for OCD gamers and their knowledge will prove to be useful when it comes to taking quizzes in exchange for some good loot.  I like the way that this game offers but doesn’t force Biblical references on the gamers and they can to choose to read it if they want to.
In all honesty, FIVE: Guardians of David is one of the better Bible themed games I have played in a long time.  The gameplay is fun and just when it starts to get a little bit dull, something new is thrown into the mix like stealth missions or enemies with new abilities.  The alchemists were very annoying with their fire attacks and explosions upon their death.
There’s a fair amount of humor as well with the conversations amongst the five mighty warriors turning into bickering and they pick on and prank each other a bit throughout the game.  The voice acting is well done and the background music is a good fit, though it could use a little more variety in my opinion.
Graphically, FIVE: Guardians of David is pretty good and there’s a decent amount of variety in the maps.  Some of the missions take place in towns while others are in the desert or inside of caves.  The enemy animations are nicely done as well though I did run into a funny glitch.  During a battle instead of the enemies attacking me, they were clapping instead.  It was both hilarious and taunting as if to say the attacks weren’t powerful enough.  Once that swarm of enemies was defeated, the normal attack animations resumed.
Sadly, I wish that was the only glitch I had to report.  The check points in this game is arguably useful.  While they do record your inventory and number of caches discovered, if you have to leave your game mid-level for any reason, upon re-launching it you’ll have to start at the beginning of the level again.  The only time the check points work properly is if you get defeated by a boss, and sadly even then they don’t trigger properly.  I got my butt kicked in two different boss fights and my party was not registering in the game as dead and when I had to reload the autosave, I had to start the level from the beginning and re-do all of the objectives before I could fight the boss again.
Despite having to redo my progress a couple of times, my experience playing FIVE: Guardians of David has been mostly positive.  The single-player campaign took me roughly seventeen hours to complete.  There is some re-playability if anyone missed locating all of the caches during their first play-through.  This game lends itself well to multiplayer-coop but it’s not available at this time.  The developers haven’t excluded the possibility.  While the normal price is $24.99, I have seen it for less than $10 on sale and it’s worth picking up if you’re looking for a good Bible themed game.  I look forward to future releases from Kingdom Games.

There is no music, just beautiful ambient sounds, which I think is a good choice. While the music in Talos Principle is great, eventually I got tired of it. Graphics are similarly sparse, going for bright, pastel colors and smooth plain surfaces instead of high resolution textures. Think functional archtecture or zen gardens.

Gigantic! The 3rd person, action, strategy, team-based MOBA, tower defense shooter! Isn't that a little excessive when you say it out loud? Well, that's because it is. Despite it being a very nice looking game, taking inspiaration from countless other games of these genres, most obvious being Smite and Paladins, with a cartoonish style that is always welcomed to me because we are finally passed the age where games had to look desaturate and depressing, Gigantic gives us too much for its own good and still manages to feel lacking in content. There is such an underwhelming amount of stuff crammed in here that even after the tutorial you are left scratching your head, which should not be the case since, again, it's just another team-based game and if you played any MOBA before, you know what to expect, right? Wrong.
At first glance, this is actually a really cool concept. Each team of 5 players has one giant boss. The two creatures duke it out and it is your responsibility to defend your own giant from the enemy attacks, all while attacking their giant in return. You are able to attack the enemy boss when your giant pins it down and you must hit the weak spot. This can happen by gathering enough power during the battle. If only they drew the line on that premise, but they wanted more and this is where Gigantic loses me. It also has a semi tower defense system implemented, where each team has to summon a creature on specific control points to, of course, gather power orbs so you can feed your giant. Creatures are an integral part of Gigantic. They automatically collect power orbs once they appear and protect a control point to provide you and your team additional bonuses that aid you. They will attack enemies if they get near and they can also be destroyed. Which means you have to protect these creatures at all cost. Making the gameplay into a hassel and it quickly stops being fun.
The champions are decent, each with their own set of abilities that you can upgrade, each with a different perk depending on your style. However, they made the awkward choice of allowing you to upgrade outside your base, and so you have team players pausing for 4-6 seconds to choose their perks leaving them open to attack or just ignoring the objective. Speaking of team players. There is such little coordination here. Most just flat-out ignore their role and try to go for kills. I would excuse this if it wasn't a team-based game! Also, you better get used to the default champions because you seriously have to grind your heart out to get a new one.
Grinding in this game is unacceptable! The devs are purposely trying to make you buy the ultimate pack and to me it seems like a such a scummy strategy. Compared to other, more intelligent, F2P games where you are actually engaged in the objective and the combat presented, where you can actually progress on a good pace, this is shameful. My apologies, I forgot to mention the boring combat Gigantic has to offer. None of your attacks feel satisfying. There is no punch to anything you do. To make matters worse, the movement feels disjointed, making you miss the most basic attack.
Above all I mentioned, one of the worst aspects of Gigantic is the matchmaking. You are constantly waiting to enter a lobby only to be kicked out because of a bad connection from another player. When you finally do enter you are pinned against higher ranking players. Delightful. But don't worry because those same players will be in your next match. As if they were the only ones playing. They seriously need to fix the matchmaking if anything else.
Overall, Gigantic is a pretty disappointing game that left me confused and unfulfilled. I can only recommend it to hardcore fans of MOBA games since it does have a unique spin to it and it is also free to download and play.

I hadn't played The Longest Journey until now. I had read about it from the PC magazines in 1999/2000 when it came out and I've always found it quite interesting. Why it took so long for me to finally play the game? I don't know. But I'm really really glad I finally did play it!
The Longest Journey is a point-and-click adventure game in which the player takes control of an 18-year-old fine arts student April Ryan. The events of the game take place in the year 2209 and the futuristic city of Newport is quite believable. April suffers from strange nightmares and is stressed out to finish her artwork for an upcoming exhibition. Soon she is pulled into a dangerous adventure of fantasy and magic, and all her former petty teenager problems turn pretty meaningless, as a far larger destiny is waiting for her to be fulfilled.  I don't want to give away too much the story — less you know, more enjoyable it is.
April's is a likeable character. Luckily she's quite a mature gal for a 18-year-old! She can be a bit whiny and sarcastic sometimes, but mostly she's great and well-written. The pre-millenial 3D graphics don't add much for the character, but the voice-acting is superb. Sarah Hamilton does an outstanding performance as April. There are also many other memorable characters.
As mentioned, the 3D graphics haven't aged that well. Don't get me wrong, the game's still charming looking and all, but especially the 3D character models and some of the cutscenes are quite cringeworthy. They have the "late nineties awkward 3D graphics look". The voice-acting and overall sound are great.
Controls are basic point-and-click stuff and you cannot die or screw up — just the way I like my point-and-click adventure games. Some of the puzzles are kinda strange and ”out there”. I had to check out a walkthrough a few times. It took me about 13 hours to beat the game.
The detail of the story and all the small things are quite baffling. April keeps a journal throughout the game's story and it really feels like it's written by a young girl. The journal is not necessary at all, but adds detail to this masterpiece and a lost player can find some clues while reading it.
Tl;dr: A fine quality point-and-click classic with a compelling story, a highly detailed world and great characters. The graphics are a bit dated. Some of the puzzles are♥♥♥♥♥ Highly recommended!

Point and click adventure games are usually synonymous with LucasArts in most people's minds.  However, although LucasArts certainly perfected the genre, and gave the world the SCUMM system, they by no means make the only good games.
All the way back to the Atari ST with games like Erebus, or Obitus, there have been some intriguing and wonderful games.  Even "Scoop" back on the Archimedes was fascinating in its own way.  But technology has moved on.  Branching story lines, throwaway disk space, FMV, voiceovers, you name it.       The main thing which more modern computers allows is for a variety of backgrounds, sounds and models.     This allows the game creators to generate a less homogenous world, giving you more of a sense of adventure.   How many old PaC games have spent their entire time wandering around the same desert island, or the same metallic city?
The Longest Journey isn't made by a mainstream distributor, like EA or LucasArts.  It snuck under the radar, and has sat on shelves in stores, or on Steam for a long time, with an unattractive, amateurish-looking advert.  the postive reviews, however, show that underneath a game that outwardly looks decidedly second or third-tier (like some of the "hidden object" games, is a compelling, almost-first-tier game.
The game starts off strange, and remains delightfully off-kilter all the way through.    It really leverages the universe that it's set in, to allow fast, interesting scene changes.   The artwork is luscious, and the voice acting is both hilarious, and excellent.  The music's pretty good too.  It's very satisfying to solve puzzles, and you get a genuine flow of story.  Solving a puzzle doesn't leave you thinking "now what?".  The in-game journal provides an amazing amount of back-story and hints.
So, why do I say it's only "almost" a first-tier game? Well, it has a few kinks.  Although it plays perfectly well on a Windows-7 PC, it is ageing.  The FMV is older-style "3DSMax" rendering, with high compression (Think Tomb Raider 2 FMV).    Also, it's short.  Don't let my playtime fool you, I had the game minimized for a lot of the time.  I actually finished it in about 6 or 7 hours.      But the length, and the slightly "B-grade" FMV isn't what knocks it off the top spot, it's the habit that the game has, of breaking its own rules.  I'll explain:-
The game is a series of "compartments", You finish everything that's within one compartment, using everything that's in that area, and then you move through to the next one.   This is pretty standard PaC fare, actually.  Early in the game, you get access to the "Metro", which allows simultaneous access to the the next compartment, while allowing access to previous ones.   9/10 times, re-visiting those older areas does you no good at all, you just go to the next 'opened up area'.
However, there are a few times in the game where you hit a brick wall.  You're trying to "use everything-on-everything" (uEoE)  in the usual PaC way, but nothing's helping.  The only thing to do it backtrack to an earlier area, and do the uEoE approach again, in the hope that you get a different outcome.    Sometimes it makes a kind of sense... often you scratch your head and think "uhh.. that makes NO sense, I could have easily done that THIS way, if the game had let me".
To attempt to reduce the futility, the game flashes objects when you hover them over each other, to show that it's a valid response to uEoE, but you're still dragging, clicking and right-clicking for literally HOURS until you find that (for example- changing the objects, but not the logic), using the "PEPPER SPRAY"  (obtained in area 5) on the "DUCK" (in area 3), will cause a door to open in Area 7. Why? Because eventually, after going through the door, you need to go back to where the duck was sitting to get the next piece of dialog, which is dependent on going through the door in area 5.  This is just after you have used the "BREAD" on the "DUCK", and have had a piece of dialog that says "Ok, I better leave him alone then".     Hmmm.  Why go back and bother the duck, when the game just told me not to.
So, I had to resort to the walkthrough a few times because i'd spent too long uEoE and the combinatorial complexity was teeing me off.   There is another puzzle where the hint just isn't good enough to let you know how to solve it, and the combinatorial complexity is something like  4x6x6x6x6  to just get it "randomly" right..  A futher hint which doesn't ruin the puzzle completely reduces this to just 2x2x2 (telephone puzzle).
Despite this, I had a wonderful time exploring the interesting world.   For a "indie", this is amazingly well made.  The outtakes at the end are great too.
I totally recommend playing it if you like PaC games which focus a little more on the cyberpunk / fantasy / sci-fi realm.   It's not "Blade Runner" or "The Dig", but you'll really enjoy its humour and setting.    Very well recommended, but keep one tab open on a walkthrough page! ;)

I'm very much a fan of "modern", more narrative-focused adventure games (The Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, Kentucky Route Zero, etc). I saw the trailers for Dreamfall Chapters and wanted to play the first games to get caught up on the story.
The Longest Journey is definitely a "classic" adventure game. It has all the pixel hunting, item combining, and obscure puzzles that are the hallmark of the genre. I admit I don't particularly enjoy this aspect of adventure games, and am glad to see it mostly absent from more modern adventures. GameFAQs was my constant companion while playing this game, and thankfully kept it from becoming frustrating. The graphics are very... 640x480, and while I can usually look past dated graphics in older games, there were points where it was difficult to tell what an object was, or what was going on in a scene, simply from lack of resolution/polygons.
I don't want to sound too hard on the game, because I actually loved it. Definitely the strongest point of the game (and why I think it's remembered so fondly) is the fantastic writing and memorable characters. April Ryan feels like a *real* person, and talks like a real person would. I loved talking to Burns Flipper or Captain Nebevay or Crow just to hear what they had to say. Admittedly sometimes people can be long-winded or launch into overlong explanations, but it never really detracted from the game. The story too, while at times dropping into fantasy cliches and being the Chosen One (TM) who can save the world, was still really interesting and mostly unique.
The Longest Journey is still a great game despite its technical/gameplay flaws, and if you're looking to get into the Longest Journey/Dreamfall series like I was, it's definitely worth playing.

My roommates told me I was making a mistake when I saw this at PAX and proclaimed "Imma buy this" without much more htought. Yet it didn't take an hour before Valhalla captured their attention and had them in my room watching over my shoulder.
A surprise to the many friends I've told, Valhalla IS a good game, maybe even great; It's topical, but futuristic; Forced, but appropriate; cliche, but novel. Valhalla is balanced, not going to far off in one direction to make your average internet denizen uncomfortable. Backed by great visuals and a superb original soundtrack, Valhalla is heavily driven by its narrative elements, told through bar patrons at the 'hell hole' establishment our protagonist Jill works at. It's up to the player to piece together a story, and serve up drinks to keep patrons talking. There's very little actual 'game' elements to the game, scoring even lower in actions-a-player-will-make than TellTale stories. All discussions are scripted, and mixing drinks is trivial at worst; This is Jill's story, not yours, so why should you get to make any choices on what she's going to say? None of this ultimately detracts from the experience, however: Contrary to what it may seem, a heavily scripted on-rails story game is a surprising breath of fresh air in a Steam market dominated by randomly-generated open-world survival games.
Valhalla is a perfect game to grab your favorite drink, sit down, and casually play. It's not perfect, but I've solidly enjoyed my time with it, and it's well worth the price. Valhalla is difficult to put down, and I can't wait to keep playing. Recommended to most gamers.

TL;DR Full Review way down below:
If you like VN's, this one will likely be enjoyable for you. With a charming aesthetic and colorful cast, Va-11 Hall-A had me from the start to finish, which was about 10 hours for one playthrough. The writing is great for the most part, with some weird sexual focuses, but most of it plays off for jokes effectively enough to be pleasant. Plus the music is amazing if electronic is your thing. I didn't regret buying this at full price, and I don't believe you will either.
If you don't like VN's, this likely won't change your mind at all, especially since it lacks the standard dialogue choices, and has no voice acting.
If you haven't tried a VN before, and the aesthetic seems appealing to you, I advise trying it out sometime. Find out if the genre appeals to you at all. If you're lookin for more VN's after this, I'd recommend Daganronpa, shown below. It's more active, has some voice acting, and has a more intense overarching story. Plus, you get to see all of your favorite characters die horribly and then get all nostalgic for when George R. R. Martin was actually releasing books.

Soundtrack(s):
Link to Purchase:
Filled with all different types of synth, the soundtrack manages to punctuate many different points of the game amazingly, and on it's own it stands up incredibly well. Plus, $7 for 40ish songs is a great deal, so I beyond recommend this soundtrack to pretty much anyone, regardless of if they liked the game or not.
Note: Two different versions of the soundtrack are available. The Prologue soundtrack has 18 songs on it, and is filled with both relaxed, bar like music, and a share of heavy electronic music, that was slightly reminiscent of Perturbator's music from the Hotline Miami soundtrack. I initially didn't like this one that much, but it really grew on me as time went by, and I realized that there was supposed to be that tonal difference. Thematically, the heavier songs don't really fit as the game always had this relaxed atmosphere to it, but on their own the music on this album really shines.
The second version is dubbed Second Round, and has 44 songs, containing the majority of music from the game, and most of the songs you'll recognize. No real tonal problems, and I loved a lot of the stuff off this one right off the bat.
Buying both will run you $12, but I wholeheartedly recommend doing just that.
Long Winded Tirade:
Va-11 Hall-A is an odd duck, if I've ever seen one. A Visual Novel with Japanese inspirations from a dev team whose company name literally translates to "Boss Girl", Va-11 Hall-A never strays away from the stranger side of things. To set the stage, Va-11 Hall-A takes place within Glitch City, a stand-in for any given sci-fi city, filled with corrupt institutions and organizations that attempt to control and oppress the population. The next natural step is a main protagonist whom wishes to liberate the people, or fight the Illuminati, but that's not the case here. Our main character is a normal 27-year-old Bartender named Jill, who instantly becomes more relatable than most souped up augmented because she’s insecure, living in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ apartment, and hates mornings. Plus she has bills to pay. So as far as filling in the role of every man/woman, Jill does a pretty good job. Still, Sukeban took great care in making Jill her own woman and managed to give her real character, which a lot of first person VN's often fail to do, and usually fail rather spectacularly by just giving them amnesia as an excuse for having no personality. That alone sets the game apart from its competitors, but they do other unique things as well.
One of the ways that Va-11 Hall-A attempts to separate itself from the normal VN is by forgoing the standard novelty of choices. Rather than just give binary options every once in a while, to dictate endings, they instead adjust the ending based upon how good a bartender you are. These junctures are a little obvious, as Jill will remark, “Should I really serve him/her ______ drink?” While they may be a bit obvious, the attempt was appreciated and well done enough to serve the games theme.
This isn’t a game that strives to drag you in through intense gameplay by any means. If you want to invest yourself in the game, you’re doing it for the characters. Every person that walks through the door has a pretty unique personality, and sometimes you’ll dread having an annoying customer show up almost as much as Jill does. What really impresses me about the writing is how consistent each character manages to be. Every patron feels like a fully fleshed out person, whether they’re human or not. From a rather charming sex robot named Dorothy to a Shiba Inu that can talk, every cast member has something more going on than their appearances let on, just like every person you’ll ever meet. The friendly neighborhood hacker has a family from Hell, and the seemingly aloof medic is probably more insecure about herself than she shows off. It’s nice to see media that takes the next step with character development like these guys have.
I guess I should wrap up the rambling somehow. Va-11 Hall-A is a strange little slice of life, giving us a glimpse into a future that might be, and showing us what it would be like for the average citizen. In doing that, it helps to show that even if life may end up seeming so vastly different in the future, in many ways it stays the same even more than it changes. People will always be struggling with things as mundane as bill payments and working at dive bars. They’ll experience the same struggles of finding their places in the world, and both finding, and losing, love. Va-11 Hall-A takes the time that you give it to show you a mirror, and even though it may be a bit unfocused, I can almost guarantee you’ll find something of yourself in it.
Plus the Boss is just great. Who doesn’t want to work for an ex-pro-wrestler with a cybernetic arm? Cause I wanna work for that person.
Also the number of subtle, and not so subtle, Metal Gear references always managed to rip a grin out of me. It's pretty good.
