The game shares more familiarities with a novel, having an extraordinary amount of dialogue to go through and numerous objects to click on and explore. Story felt refreshingly unique and flows well. It is split into thirteen Chapters of varying length and themes. The voice acting is brilliant – characters feel natural, not samey and often time’s humorous (mature content).
Puzzles on reflection were mostly straight forward, logical and challenging – and only had to use a guide for small sections of the game that didn’t make sense or where I forgot one piece of dialogue (you need to complete certain things in order to continue with the plot). Graphics and cut scenes look dated at first impression but soon becomes part of the games charm. Musical soundtrack does a fantastic job at conveying the different moods throughout the journey.
Chapter Three is the funniest, and cements the fact that this is now one of my favourite point and click games. Definitely a masterpiece.

Seven and a half years after the release of indie darling Braid, Jonathon Blow is back for revenge with another puzzler: The Witness! This newest game is in many ways quite similar to Braid: the puzzles themselves are (for the most part) very well thought-out, the visuals are interesting, and the rest of the game is a complete mess. Braid was a much shorter experience, though, and a lot of the really stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥didn't show up until after you beat the game and received access to Blow's attempt at a plot (really just an infodump). The Witness, being much much longer, gives the player plenty of time to think about what went wrong during the making of this game.
The majority of the game's puzzles revolve around the use of various symbols that each denote specific rules that must be kept in mind when solving the puzzle in question. Black and white dots must be separated, tetris blocks must be drawn into the grid, and colored balls must be grouped into pairs. I wouldn't really call any of these spoilers, as the way the game introduces these symbols makes it fairly obvious what their specific rules are. As the game progresses, these symbols are combined and used in increasingly more complex ways, and I would say that this is the one part where The Witness isn't a complete failure. The way that the difficulty progresses feels very natural, and I never found myself stuck on any one puzzle for a very long time. It is when the game deviates from these mechanics that things go downhill.
Several areas of the game choose to completely forgo these symbol-based puzzles, with often tedious results. The environment-based puzzles are never difficult: Blow obviously realized that during the development of the game, so the way that these puzzle mechanics evolve just makes them more annoying to solve. For example, one area's gimmick is that you have to listen to bird calls and map out puzzle solutions based on high, medium, and low notes. As you progress through the area, the bird calls begin to get interrupted by other noises, such as wolf howls and jackhammers. Instead of making the puzzles more difficult to solve by increasing their complexity, The Witness chooses in these cases to just make it take longer for the player to get the information they need. Again, these environmental puzzles become extremely tedious: you already know what you have to do, but some silly gimmick has been added that means the puzzle takes five times as long to solve as it should.
The game's final area has its own share of problems, which I'll put in spoiler tags.
Another problem lies with the way that the puzzles are integrated into the game's world. Most of the game involves solving a series of puzzles, each on its own separate panel, which then unlocks a door to the next series of puzzles. Granted, these are very good puzzles, but it rarely feels like I even need to be on an island at all. In only a few instances do these puzzles have any impact on the world other than activating machinery: in the treetops area, for example, the puzzle panels that you solve slowly form bridges that you use to cross from tree to tree. A few puzzles can be solved in more than one way, and depending on how you solve them, the direction of the bridge changes. As it stands, though, there exists very little relation between the game's puzzles and the game's world.
The final major problem, I would say, is the issue of player motivation. The only draw here is the puzzles; if you do not love solving puzzles (in fact, a specific type of puzzle), there is zero reason to buy this game. There is no plot, no lore, nothing exists to motivate those who maybe aren't so keen on the puzzles but want to learn more about this strange island that they're on. In fact, Blow decides to further exacerbate things by dropping audio logs all over the place. No, these aren't recordings made by the people on the island who all apparently turned into statues: they're quotes from famous scientists, artists, and thinkers of the world, telling you about how amazing the world is and how powerful we all are! What's worse, there exists a hidden theater where, by inputting the correct puzzle solution, you can watch unrelated video clips that I guess were meant to "blow your mind". Of the three that I found, there's a clip of James Burke talking about how science is the greatest thing ever, one of Richard Feynman talking about the hierarchy of the universe and why he studied physics, and the ending of Tarkovsky's Nostalghia taken out of context. Really, all of these clips and quotes and whatever other♥♥♥♥♥♥was thrown into the game seem to have no purpose for being there. Blow just wanted to sound smart by having a clip in his game where an astronaut talks about how cool space is.
I went into this game deliberately avoiding any information I might find (hopefully I don't ruin the magic for anyone reading this♥♥♥♥♥♥. I knew that there were two possibilities: either there was a really interesting backstory, or there wasn't. Not knowing which of these was true meant that, at least for most of the game, there still existed within me a small glimmer of hope that The Witness would end up as something more than a collection of interesting puzzles (not counting the environmental puzzles, ♥♥♥♥ that). It was only during the game's ending, when
that I realized that I had been duped. Since I enjoyed the puzzle aspect of the game, it didn't hit me as hard as I would assume that it would hit someone expecting more, but it was still a pretty big disappointment. The Witness just doesn't seem to understand what it wants to be. If you took away the entire island setting and turned The Witness into a traditional puzzle game with a level select system (a la SpaceChem, Mario's Picross, World of Goo, etc), you would certainly lose very little. Sure, I enjoyed exploring the island, but it never felt like a necessary part of the game to me.
So, while The Witness is interesting purely as a collection of puzzles, it makes very little effort to justify the existence of its island setting. Outdated concepts such as "plot" and "lore" are superseded by audio logs talking about how cool our planet is. While 50-60% of the puzzles are very well-designed, the rest involve gimmicks that only serve to bore any competent player. Despite the game's flaws, I did enjoy it. However, I would only recommend it to those interested in solving a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of puzzles.

The witness is a masterclass in how to implement, teach, and experiment with mechanics and any puzzly game should really study it and figure out how to take its lessons and put it into their games. There's an incredible amount of depth in a very simple way of interacting with the world + just about everything ties together. Every single puzzle is taught, every single puzzle has a mechanical language easing you into exactly how to solve it- and there's just a ridiculous amount of them all to work through.
i've yearned for a really good elaboration on what the myst series did to videogames for ages and this is just the sort of thing i've been waiting for, really. Games that do what the Myst series tried to do so few and far between, despite that series being so groundbreaking. Puzzle games centering around world- and exploration-based puzzles are basically nonexistent - there's barely even games that try and fail at it, let alone games like this that succeed so hard. Mini Metro is more of a shape connector than a train simulator. The objective of Mini Metro is to connect different shaped stations and move different shaped passengers to their desired shape. E.g. A square wants to move to the nearest square-shaped station and a triangle wants to move to a triangle-shaped station. You lose if any one station gets overcrowded for too long. As the game progresses, more different shapes will appear and it will get harder and longer to get a shape to a specific station. You will be limited by the number of trains, lines and bridge connections. Basically, you are playing the crayon coloured train map that you see at train stations. However, you are playing it without any real consideration to physics.
Gameplay-wise, you click and drag the lines between any stations on the map and they get connected. You do not have to worry about terrain conditions blocking you as the lines magically join to one another. You can even break the lines to rejoin in any spaghetti shape you can think of. Every week, you will be given some reward, like an extra train, interchange, bridge or extra line.
Conclusion, this isn't a train simulator. It's a line-shape connector masquerading as a train simulator.
Note : The developers are Dinosaur Polo Club. A four man gig.
1. It Sounds Like a Train Simulator
The name, Mini Metro, is very catchy.
1. It is Not a Train Simulator
I really don't see what you are trying to simulate.

It really removes the player from the immersion. This is like playing any game with just hitboxes.
3. Random Spawning of Shapes
Why they spawn is totally beyond me. Are they going to a retail shop? Are they trying to reach another station? Why do they go to any shape, not a specific location? A real passenger would actually try to reach somewhere specific, not just any random station that fits a profile.
4. Loss Condition
Overcrowding causes your station to close. What kind of loss condition is this? Train stations get overcrowded all the time. People get frustrated. However, they don't close down.

My nominee for "Best Game Within a Game" award 2016.
A pleasant and short narrative in a cyberpunk setting light on interactivity, but well written and interesting enough to keep someone entertained through a play through.
As a storytelling piece, the game is light on plot and has little plot development other than the larger events in the city you hear people talk about and read in the news between days.  There is a conflict the protagonist is involved in, but it is tiny and insignificant compared to the events she hears about and what some of the bar patrons are involved in.  Instead, there is an emphasis on character development and interaction and that is where the game shines.
The only other game I've heard this compared to would be to Papers Please, a comparison I agree with.  Most of your interaction with the game is spent listening to the clients, mixing drinks, reading blogs, and buying random junk to fill up your apartment.  The game is extremely linear with no dialogue choices or major decisions.  Any branching choices are made in how you fill a drink orders or what you buy at the shop to fill your apartment.
The people who stumble into the bar are varied and include everything from a Hatsune Miku proxy, a talking dog, a JC Denton approximation, an Underage Sex-Bot, George Konstanza, a police woman, among several others.  Chatting with the characters at work tells you more about the world and the protagonist's life.
In all the game is a calm, relaxing, and entertaining experience worth trying.

The Guest is a fairly well-done first-person adventure that is best described as a sequence of interconnected "Escape the Room" situations. Gameplay takes place in quite small areas, but each area has many items to discover - some of which are needed for the puzzles, some provide background information and tell a mysterious story about a missing person.
The puzzle design is varied and engaging. Often you have to first find several missing objects, then add them to the puzzle, and then solve a minigame. Other puzzles require combining the correct items in your inventory. The game provides many clues, and the difficulty was (at least for me) right at the sweet spot where you really have to think, and feel a sense of accomplishment when you find the solution, but never totally get stuck. (One puzzle got me stumped because a ring had to be positioned correctly, and looked correct even when it was rotated 180° away from its target position, but I eventually got past that.)
The interface highlights objects that you can interact with, which gets rid of the annoying "click everything in case it's usable" gameplay. You can turn that feature off if you find the experience more immersive without it. The rest of the interface isn't stellar, but gets the job done. It could be more obvious that there is a second inventory page if you picked up many items.
I found the story engaging, interesting, and well-paced. You keep finding more information, and the game invites you to build your own theories, which I enjoyed a lot. Unfortunately though, it all completely breaks down when the game ends. Instead of actually solving the detailed mystery that they built up, the devs basically show their players the middle finger and impose a "wtf"-type ending on their game that renders 90% of the previous information completely irrelevant. One can't help but wonder why that detailed mystery is even there. It does not get solved or elaborated on - the ending simply
most of the game. On top of that, it puts the main character in a rather undesirable situation, so it does not even feel satisfying.
Graphically the game seems solid for in indie adventure game. There is some good use of lighting. Textures look a bit washed out, and some of the models are a bit crude, but hey - for an indie adventure game that has a focus on good puzzles, this is all completely adequate. Voice acting was on the same level - not great, but not really bad either, so it didn't detract from the game. Some of the writing showed that the devs aren't native English speakers, but I've seen way worse.
.
Side notes:
1. There is a music puzzle that will cause problems for deaf people - you may have to ask someone else for help with that one. It is randomized, and you only have three attempts to solve it before it randomizes again, so you cannot just look the correct sequence up in a guide. If you're just tone-deaf, then you
be able to solve it, since the interface allows infinite experimentation and checks before you commit your solution. I often struggle with music puzzles myself, but had no problems with this one.
2. Achievement hunters should brace themselves for a potentially frustrating experience. One achievement requires you to solve a maze puzzle (with lots of walking) on the first try, but it is randomized and apparently has no clues. You'll have to reload and replay it until you happen to get lucky and guess all choices correctly, the chance for which is 1/16. Another achievement requires you to restart the game if you've taken too many turns in a certain puzzle, reloading does not help. And there's also an achievement for finding all objects, but its counter does not update correctly, so it's hard to check whether you missed something.
3. As usual, don't draw conclusions from my displayed playing time. I often let games idle while I do other stuff or sleep. I also played through the game several times to get the achievements.

'The Guest' is a first person adventure puzzle game. You wake up in a hotel room that's locked. You don't remember how you got there. You find some puzzles to solve, most of which require you to use items you find across the room to solve them. Solving a puzzle leads to other puzzles to solve etc.  'The Guest' an ok game, worth playing if you don't expect too much, but not at full price. If you're into the genre, I recommend picking it up when it's discounted by 50% or more.
Most of the puzzles are pretty clever and well-executed. Sometimes they vaguely reminded me of the quality of the puzzles of the game The Room, which is a huge compliment. The Guest clearly aspires to be as good as The Room and other games that set the bar. It does not succeed but it doesn't fall flat on its face either. The puzzles are challenging, visually attractive, non-repetitive and they reflect the atmosphere of the adventuring aspect of this game i.e. the mystery of what's going on.
The Guest is a puzzle game first and foremost. But it has some adventuring elements, too. This means you'll be exploring the hotel room you're in and be picking up items to use either on things in the room or on each other in the inventory, to create new items that can be used on things in the room. There is also a story being told while you explore and solve puzzles, but don't expect too much story, it's certainly not a narrative driven adventure game. I appreciated the story, however basic and surreal, for what it was.
Some of the achievements are pretty challenging, which always adds an extra layer to games and especially to puzzle games. One of the achievements seems bugged for me (Houdini) but 4.2% of the users have it, which is more than the usual percentage of achievement cheaters, so I'm not sure why it won't trigger for me.
A warning to conclude: the achievement for the labyrinth (you need to complete it without failing) is completed by pure luck. So save before using the telephone and reload to do the labyrinth again and again if you want the achievement. Do not trust the so-called guide you'll find here on Steam, it's a (bad) joke. If you look at the final part of the 'guide', you'll see the author put some letters in the middle of seemingly random words in capitals. These spell out 'troll'.

I'm fully aware that this game is incredibly dated by this point and stuff like graphics and animation I won't factor into this, not that I really tend to care about them anyways.
It's hard to really find how I feel about this though. On one hand, it's got pacing problems all over the place. The game's divided into 13 chapters, but not really, since some of the chapters are four times as long as others. And the game spends too much time worldbuilding; I can understand a certain extent of it but characters go too far in-depth about tiny things that won't ever be mentioned again. There's a lot of talking, also. A lot of talking. And plenty of instances where it will take you 15-20 seconds to run across a screen; and there's the option of walking it, too...
Plus, the game is admittedly kind of hard to take seriously due to its datedness. The CGI cutscenes where you get close-ups on the characters' faces... the stiff animations... I found myself laughing at some of the most tense scenes in the game because of that.
The story itself is also kind of cliched, but that's kind of the point. The main character, April, is in fact entirely aware of how cliche it gets, which kind of makes it permissable and enjoyable. The gameplay is standard point-and-click stuff. The puzzles aren't the most obscure but they can be tricky and the slooow pacing can make them more annoying than necessary.
Really though the major issue I do have with this game is its pacing, I still enjoyed it but if it had better pacing I'm sure I'd have enjoyed it even more.

I have somewhat mixed feelings about this game.  It was perhaps the most epic, involved, creative, and intelligent story I've come across in a game.  At the same time the writing and voice-acting are uneven across the entirety of the game.  Some clever humor is appreciated, but it too often strayed into just plain corny and bad.  The voice-acting was not very convincing on the whole, kept afloat only by the smart dialogue.  The puzzles were good overall, but at times quite inane and illogical.  Some of the solutions just weren't logical and I don't know how anybody would have figured them out on their own.  Also keep in mind that this game is nearly 15 years old.  The graphics may have been good when the game was originally released and some of the environments are nice, but by today's standards, the graphics are extremely poor.  The characters are at times gruesome looking regardless of how long ago they were produced.  Overall though, it's a classic point-and-click adventure that is worth your time if only for one of the most epic stories ever told in videogaming.

I bought this when I got sick, had FOUR DAYS to play it pretty much non stop, and still have yet to get to Canada. No matter how seriously OP I twink my characters, no matter what strategy I take, this entire game can beat you on a bad coin flip. Even if you manage to RNG your way to the final stretch, the game will almost always end with two consecutive Sieges, the first typically in somewhere claustrophobic and the actual final wave I've only ever gotten to ONE TIME, (throughout about 20 playthroughs) so I couldn't tell you one way or the other.

I've read a few threads and basically everyone I see is under the consensus that this game is unfairly hard and genuinely not fun after the first several playthroughs. The only reason I'm not going to get a steam refund is because I've seen a few news feeds hinting at a better build of the game and several Dev posts saying that they're tweaking/introducing a legacy system where your death doesn't mean you've totally lost everything.
This game just really makes me mad, it's a very fun and always an entertaining co-op experience, but when you want to just chill and have an easy run, there's really nothing you can do. This is on-par with Don't Starve in that death is a serious thing, but at least Don't Starve had some ways of giving you a cushion to land on when you inevitably did die, and made you give more of a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your character. I spent most of my games distributing stat bonuses/level ups/etc amongst my whole crew but then ALL OF THEM DIED ON THE FINAL WAVE and made me feel like it sincerely did not matter what I did during the entire game leading up to that point. I just needed a lucky dice roll or something completely arbitrary and out of my control.
Don't get me wrong, it's a wonderful game and taken at what it was marketed as, it's extremely true-to-form. There were plenty of times when I died in Oregon Trail from bad RNG or some dumbass mistake, plenty of times I died in Don't Starve thanks to my poor reaction time or underestimating an enemy, and I really don't think I'm a bad gamer or have a weak disposition for real-time combat, I just can't take that helpless feeling I get when my crew gets shredded by ONE SINGLE SIEGE after literally hours of beating zombie♥♥♥♥♥like a rented mule.
If you plan on getting this game, buy it during Halloween when it's on sale, I paid around $10 for it and I feel like that may have been a LITTLE too much, but for the content, I thought it was fair. It's retail price is absurd for what basically ammounts to a novelty game that you'll never get to play casually.
TL:DR - Don't expect to beat it, but it's a great arcade game.

"The Witness" is a visually astonishing game, not a single fault found with the graphics but as many people know its not just the graphics makes a good game right? As for the Audio, well, there really isn't much to talk about here as there isn't much to listen to in the game as far as I know, there are Audio Logs that can be found scattered around the land but even then they don't tell you much if anything about the backstory of this game. The one positive about the Audio is Very Meaty footsteps that are needed to solve some puzzles.
Now for the Puzzles, The puzzles are original and can get very complex very fast with new mechanics around every corner and very little to no help solving them, however they are possible after a few failed attempts. What this game does with perspective is extremely clever and it can really make you think outside the box, yet, that said some of the "Forced Perspective" puzzles can be quite tricky getting into the right place to solve but not impossible.
As for the mood of the game it is calming and stress free mostly however, it can make you feel like a complete idiot by not seeing the larger picture but then again it does feel very satifying once you have cracked a puzzle that has been fustrating you for quite a while.
Now for what some people look for in these types of games, The Story. I can't comment on the story just yet as im only 5 hours in but from that 5 hours of solving puzzles and wandering the land I can say that there isn't much of a story, You wake up in a tunnel and thats pretty much all your told, The audio logs are just Quotes from famous people and tell very little of the story and I haven't found anything that tells me what happened to the "Others" or what will happen once I solve the "Final" puzzle.
TL:DR  Amazing Graphics, Very fun and original puzles, Not much of a story, Not much audio but still pretty good. I recommend this game to anybody that wants a good puzzle to solve.
The Witness really is the Dark Souls of puzzle games. However, if one dedicates themselves to it and jumps from puzzle to puzzle to avoid frustration, the game is very satisfying.

With a story that seems a bit anemic, yet still interesting to some extent, the true focus of this game is on its gameplay. It's very addicting and fun (and extraordinarily, exponentially difficult throughout). Also, with no cheap tricks or annoying malfunctions that impede you, it's really up to the player to progress in any way. There's no way to unattentively rush through these stages, so you'll really need to expend some level of repetitious effort and interest to appreciate this game.
At times, it does seem to get too pixel-perfect for comfort but, again, it's really up to you. With a lot of practice, attention to contextual patterns, and a bunch of free time, even the most difficult levels can be surpassed somewhat easily. Once you do get through a distinctly trying stage, it can be exhiliratingly satisfying.
There are very few distinguishable enemies (specifically, only five) and never a large spectra of harmful objects, but this fact isn't all that noticeable, and doesn't seem to impact enjoyablility. Nearly each level is packed with a healthy, respectable amount of obstacles, with differences being in the form of level design and enemy placement. This makes each chapter fresh enough for what the game sets out to do.
All-in-all, it's a pretty difficult, fun little platformer that doesn't especially break the mold or have much of a story to tell, but if you want an addicting trial-by-fire, "gauntlet of enemies" type game to play in your free time, I'd reccommend this game over and over again.

This game will be something you will pick up and probably drop very rapidly. It has enemies and obstacles which tend to juggle you to your death, it has very finnicky platforming later on and some cruel boobytraps laying in wait in segments.
However it is a game which has a certain beauty seeing it played well.
The game in essence is a hard platformer with enemies. It very much banks on how you flow through the level and enemies how well you do. The punishing part is the ENDLESS supply of spikes and sawblades waiting to murder you, aside from the mobs that is. The levels are tight and finnicky to navigate at times, sometimes downright cruel.
Learning to flow through the level and the enemies is something you pick up over playing. Since there is method to the madness.
The control scheme is very basic. you have an attack button, a jump button and the movement controls. Depending on your inputs the attack can be dash, a normal stab, a kick and an uppercut kick. It can be finnicky to have the right attack trigger when you want, and I can recommend a controller for this, as keyboard lacks the thumbstick to make movement in narrow scenarios difficult. Besides the various attacks you also have a jump which allows for a double jump (except when you fell of a surface/wall then you only get one).
The enemies are basic but I want to give special mention to the squiddy things, or as I prefer calling them. ♥♥♥♥ing annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. They line up with you and charge you, however they also hamper your movement in the air, which is awful when the level has SPIKES AND MORE SPIKES waiting to hug you. The other are wraiths following the boo school of attacking and zombie like blobs hell bent on pushing you into SPIKES.
The game has various goals, besides completing the levels, you can achieve. Score tiers and time challenges are the simplest ones. Some of these can be very manageable, others will end up in destroyed hardware considering how narrow the conditions are (one death can cost you the speedrun time) to complete these. There are others such as no death, no save sigils.
My concerns are that at times the controls feel like they refuse to operate (because of the narrow trigger conditions for specific attacks, such as a dash REQUIRES you to be on the ground, so a pixel above will just make you aimlessly poke the air).
Also the enemies sometimes have attack behaviour which breaks their patterns, screwing with your flow and ruining your combo or your life.
Lastly how narrow some of requirements are, and having little leeway for some badge scores and times is incredibly frustrating spending multiple hours to get repeatedly screwed by some annoying hitbox or slight deviation can screw you (YOUR FOOT WHEN SLIDING A BIT WHEN ENDING A RUN COUNTS, CAUSING THE DAMN SAW TO BOUNCE YOU INTO OBLIVION).
To end this with my attempt to complete the game fully, some of the frequently uttered sentences were "I am so sick of getting juggled all over the place by those ♥♥♥♥ing sawblades".

What this game is about?
It's about using powerups to manipulate playing field in order to score goals or fulfill some aims of the stage like for example winning in a set score 3:2.
This game is a little indie game, where you go through more or less chaotic stages where you and your opponent use different power ups in order to achieve victory by any means. Player with most goals win the match.
Some exapmles of basic power ups:
- haste to one footballer for about 10 seconds
- stop time for about 5 seconds
- create some shield that blocks the ball
- meteor that can knock players down for a moment and destroy shields
- mine than knocks down players for about three seconds and can push the ball in a direction opposite to the side of explosion (physics, you know?)
The player also have possibility to buy some advancements like more income or slight advance in speed of footballers (that look like 2d cartoony like characters, funny enough).
There is one basic exploit. About an hour into the game and I have found one stage that you can reload to have goals like win with goal pattern 1:0, 3:0 and so on. Such a game takes about 10-30 seconds to win and gives 750$. Upgrading income by 4% costs 500%. Please do the math yourself and calculate how much time would it take to upgrade your income to a maximum level (25 times 4%) thus giving you a permanent upgrade of 100% more income.
Rince and repeat such a stage that you can complete under 10 seconds and earn so much money in about 2 hours of gameplay that you will (yes, will) win the game without any difficulty at all.
Thus such an exploit is quite a fun killer to me. The game is still nice to play and use really wacky powerups (cow stampede, meteors, bombarding, spawning additional balls so you can have scores like 38:19, so on and so forth) but why shouldn't a player not use such an exploit to win the game easily? There is no motivation to play more levels, and some of them can drag itself for about 2 minutes. This can be long, believe me.

Best PC port in a long timem still some inconsistencies and little bugs, but nothing major.
The game itself is incredible, awesome and fun gameplay, immense replay factor (both in single and multiplayer), the graphics and sound are amazing, the history is very good (requires prior comics or first game knowledge to fully understand it), the characters versions are very respectfull and truthfull to their lore, also best guest-characters ever.
With all that said, Injustice 2 is a game with a "closed combo structure", so you must memorize which combinations work for each character, also applies to special moves, there is way less room for improvisation than Guilty Gear Xrd for example, so keep that in mind.
Also the gear system (while it's disabled on ranked) is fun (collecting pieces and customizing your character) and gives a "roleplay progression" like feel to the single player experience, however goes against onde of the main pillars of fighting games, that only skill matters, since gear can give small to huge advantages to one side, because both gear and character do level up.
TL;DR: very good game, very enjoyable. Good port, but not perfect. Lots of content, more comming (at least for now). Combo structure requires a lot of memorization, but pays off.

Snail Bob 2: Tiny troubles
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Well, I have met a number of snails in my life. Plenty of Jean, Julien, Andre and Paolo (yes, Paolo is a well-known name in the snail community) - but Bob. . .  that is surely the first one I have ever met!
Snail Bob 2 is a casual puzzle game for parents to play with their kids, but also enjoyable for all ages. At first, you will meet Bob and go through a small tutorial which will show you how make Bob turn around, move and stop, as well as what you will have to look for within the level, such as buttons to press, levers to activate and other things to look for in the level.
Bob will have 3 stories to play in this game and each of them has 30 levels to complete. Basically, you will have to get Pao.., sorry Bob to the door with the exist sign in one piece. In each level, you will have to collect three Stars which are very well hidden or blend in within the artwork. Some levels will have a puzzle piece to collect; in total you will have to gather twelves pieces to achieve the entire puzzle. Each time you collect a certain number of stars, you will be given a new outfit in your wardrobe. Bob could become a pirate, a plumber, a Viking snail and much more!
The path to the exit door is not difficult but you will have several obstacles to navigate in each level. Time of play is approximately thirty-five minutes per story.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Cute artwork
-	90 levels to complete
-	Great to play with kids
-	Trading Cards & Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Short game
-	Repetitive
Snail Bob 2 is a casual game for parents and kids to play together.
6.5/10

99 Levels To Hell is a platform shooter with, "tons of guns, upgrades, magic, traps, and monsters to kill," but that is very misleading from what the game actually offers. 99 Levels to Hell also prides itself on being a rogue-like, but you'll find that it's not so much hard as it is unpredictable, dull, and effortless.
- Relatively cheap, if you have five dollars to spare.
- Is a game.
- Poor level design.
- Endlessly annoying soundtrack.
- Buggy hitboxes.
- Combat is dull, same with bosses.
- Repetitive gameplay (and not the good kind).
- Massively time-consuming achievements.
99 Levels To Hell has poor level design, which you'll find whenever you play through for your first time. Since there are one-hundred levels, you'll find yourself asking, "Isn't this the same level from before?" whenever you get far enough into the game. You'll notice a pattern of the same maps, with different textures, and that makes the game very boring. Along with that, the soundtrack is the same ambient dungeon music over, and over, and over. Which would be fine, but I'm positive the actual song is about a minute long - and repeats.
The hitboxes were another thing that really turned me off about this game. Sometimes your bullets are very unpredictable and you'll find yourself not killing an enemy that was right in front of you, which can really cost you in this game since the hearts are somewhat scarce. Another thing (and this is more of a tip), if there is an enemy on top of a shootable item like a box, your bullets will hit the box first and the enemy will remain unharmed. I've died my fair share shooting once, thinking I shot the monster, but instead died because it shot the box first.
Speaking of shooting, the combat is woefully boring. There are a handful of guns in the game, but some of them are absolutely awful, which means you'll probably use the start weapons by default. That also means that, if you unlock a character with a crappy gun, you won't ever use that character because you'll be disadvantaged. Even if you did play with that character, getting another gun from a golden chest is very difficult because golden chests are seemingly ultra rare.
The combat also sucks with the bosses, which you think would be very awesome! Yeah, they're not. They sit there and (maybe) fire a couple things at you, but usually you'll be able to beat them fairly easy. In fact, if you get enough range upgrades on your gun, you can sit on the other side of the map and shoot the boss without it being on screen - it won't move, attack, or spawn enemies. It's basically a free boss battle nearly every time, if you have the right equipment.
Lastly, the achievements. I know not many people put the achievements down in their reviews, but for the achievement hunter that's thinking of buying this game: don't. There are a couple of achievements that will physically pain you trying to do. One is to collect ten-thousand gold nuggets, which can take awhile since you don't actually get that much through all of your playthroughs. You also very rarely get the gold nugget piles, which means you'll be individually collecting gold that already have terrible drop rates.
The other achievements are just time-consuming: play the game for ten and one-hundred hours. A game that requires nothing more than three hours of your time to complete is giving you an earnable achievement to play the game for one hundred hours. No, you can't just idle at the menu or alt-tab, you actually have to play within the dungeons. Sure, you can idle it in the tutorial dungeon for one hundred hours, but the achievement has been known to bug, so it's practically a hit-or-miss if you'll get it or not.
All-in-all, do not buy this game, unless you're seriously desperate and have a spare five dollars you don't care about. If you really want a good rogue-like, spend some money on Tales of Maj'Eyal or another game that its developers actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about. You'll be pulling your hair out with 99 Levels To Hell and I would never recommend this game, not even to my worst enemy.

The Longest Journey does its name justice. It is an epic adventure from beginning to end and it never gets tedious or boring like a lot of adventure games tend to do when they try to forcefully increase the playtime. The setting is unique, intriguing and creates a great atmosphere. The plot is original and inspiring and shows what adventure games can do when they're done right. The brightest aspect of the game, however are the characters. From the heroine to the minor characters, they are all wonderfully designed with a certain integrity that makes them incredibly powerful. They bring the story to life and make for a truly memorable game. This could not have been done without the excellent writing and voice acting. The only argument I have against the game's excellence is the pacing and execution of the lest stretch before the finale, which compared to the rest of the game seemed rushed. It seems as if the development team was not able to give this segment the attention and devotion that it deserved. It is a small issue barely worth mentioning however, since the rest of the game shines brightly.
If adventure games are your thing, this is a must-play.

"They Bleed Pixels" is a game with a lot of good ideas but in general, mixed execution. Part of it is that TBP seems to have something of an identity crisis, is it a fast-paced 100-deaths-per-minute speedrunner-friendly platformer like say, Super Meatboy? Or is it something slower and more methodical? Or maybe it's a beat-em-up? Perhaps a collectathon? None of these things are inherently mutually incompatible but TBP's first issue is that it can't really seem to figure out how to reconcile them, and this bleeds (pardon the pun) through almost every aspect of its game design.
Let's start with the controls. In addition to the usual running and jumping, our protagonist The Clawed Girl has not one but three basic moves, a slash with her claws (effectively: a punch), a small kick that intends to send enemies flying a short distance horizontally, and a longer kick that angles to launch them upward, either into level obstacles or to juggle them, fighting game style, and execute some combos. On top of this, you have a dash that allows you to charge toward an enemy in the blink of an eye to quickly close distance. All of this
perfectly nice, but the problem is that every single action aforementioned is bound to the same button, and while you can change what that single button is, you cannot disassociate the actions to other buttons, a slash is executed by tapping your attack button, the short kick by holding it for slightly longer, and the long kick by holding it longer still. The game will effectively guess as to when you want to do a dash, if you tap the attack button while a distance away from an enemy that it judges appropriate, you will dash instead. It is hard to overstate how frustrating all this is, as it makes you feel like you have precious little control over your character. It is possible (and I've mused aloud about the idea) that you get more abilities later on that necessitate binding all of these actions to a single button, but at that point I think it is perhaps time to reconsider your entire control scheme.
The frustration does not stop there. TBP has "physics" of a sort, in that when you kick an enemy they will knock about and the game will try to determine logically where they should go. Again, this is something that sounds great, but for the most part characters (both The Clawed Girl and various enemies) knock about with all the grace of a Superball, even
would not be so bad if it were at least consistent, but hitting the same enemy with the same attack can cause very different results, and while I'm sure there is *some* method to this madness, it is obscure to this particular player at least.
Finally there is the level design. It should probably not surprise that TBP's levels fall into the "lethal to a comical degree" school of thought, and they do. The levels are riddled with spikes, buzzsaws,
spikes, and friction-free ice patches (more on those in a moment), once again, none of this is bad inherently and to be as far to TBP itself as possible, the level design is where the game has the *least* amount of problems. Still, it does sometimes feel as though the obstacles' hitboxes are a bit outsized and even if they're not the wonky knockaround physics mean that getting hit by any particular thing quite often means you'll be flung into a second and third, or in the case of certain patches of ceiling spikes, you'll simply stick to them like glue until you die.
On a more positive note on an audiovisual level the game is great. The pixelly style reminds me of the golden age of browser games, but notched up a few degrees for a genuine commercial platform. But while the game looks and sounds great, it simply doesn't play well. This may have been more acceptable when the game was new back in 2012, but looking back from 2017, it simply doesn't cut it.
I have to admit that I feel sort of bad going this hard on the game because it's not
by any means, it simply doesn't do what it sets out to do or at least doesn't to my standards, but posed the question "would I recommend this game" I'd have to give it a pretty sound "No". I in fact bought this game on sale for just $2 and I'm reluctant to recommend it even at
price. I think difficulty hounds will find something to like here, but if you're even mildly put off by the sheer frustration that They Bleed Pixels will throw at you I'd advise you to look elsewhere.

[TL;DR below, spoiler-free review]
reality is more of a philosophical VN than sci-fi, where the main driving question throughout the VN is: "What is reality to you?"

Notice I added "to you" at the end, because this VN doesn't actually answer the question for you, it's something the VN wants you to decide for yourself. While reality is not the first to have asked this question, it does an interesting take--it plays it realistically at first and then does a twist.
Choices are pretty varied here. You get to make impactful decisions regarding the main characters(such as deciding their idea of reality and their goals) how the main characters interact with others and each other at certain points(which influences how well the main characters get along in the end), and the fate of Vitalia.
The story paces well, although some parts feel like they were tacked in out of the blue, but the reason behind those becomes clearer as the story goes on.(For e.g the twist felt like drinking kool aid at first but I realised it was a hypothetical question.) The current version of the VN is complete, inclusive of all 3 books. There's also stats at the end of each book where you find out the percentage of people who made the same choice as you, which is neat.
For the time taken for this VN I estimate the average player would be finished playing(all choices explored) within the range of 6-9 hours. This seems really short on paper, but after reading I'm not too sure how it can be expanded without compromising or losing the essense of the driving question. Sure, we could go explore more on growing InterMense but that would make Jacob OOC(you'll find out the reason why Jacob founded InterMense in the VN), and going deeper into Vitalia lore would simply be filler.(although it might make for a nice DLC or spin-off perhaps?)
Still after considering the content, the price for this VN is however, a little steep even on sale. This alone is a major drawback. There are however steam trading cards for this game which is sellable on the steam market.
All things considered, reality is a VN that makes you think, and it's rare to find such VNs that priortise or make that one of its primary goals. If that and the plot summary interests you, it's worth a shot.
TL;DR fairly unique VN, good plot & pacing however price is somewhat steep; get on sale.
Reccommended for:
-people who like rpg/exploration games
-VR enthusiasts
-people looking for VNs that make them think rather than for the feels
Not reccommended for:
-people looking for a full sci-fi VN
-people looking for romance as a major theme(romance exists, but it's hard to get one. I'd go so far as to say it's the endgame lol)
-people who dislike existential questions

DISCLAIMER: As of right now I haven't seen all possible epilogues, but this could still be kinda spoilery. Also I kinda know the devs so yay for bias.
---
If there's one thing </reality> is good at, it's making us question things. Is life actually real? Just what are we? Do I want a Penta for myself?
I don't know about the first two questions, but the third's answer is a big yes.
The art is very beautiful. With varied characters and breathtaking backgrounds, it makes me wish real life was as beautiful. The way each protag is depicted next to the text box is a feature I wish more VNs had, since it lets us actually see the protag's emotions in his expressions, instead of inferring from the dialogue.
The story is really good, even if it's a bit on the short side. Both protagonists help bring different perspectives into view, while still leaving space for character development between both protags and other characters.
My only problem with it, to be honest, is that it was unvoiced. Although I understand it, my first experience was during a Let's Read with other people, and so their voices got stuck with me for each character. But the lack of voice acting didn't affect at all how much I enjoyed the parts we hadn't read before.
After one run through it, I have it at 7.5, and I have high hopes that as I unlock more endings, it'll only go higher.

First of all, the game is shorter than I had expected. My 7.7 hours includes finishing the game + all achievements but must games be 50+ hours in order to be positively recognised? No!
I really enjoyed it and here's why:

* Amusing (in my opinion!) references to MMORPGs.
* A decent amount of choices to be made, some choices building upon others or unlocking other choices later on.
* Genuinely sweet moments when characters bonded and guilt-factor moments when making enemies.
* Beautiful art - I could only ask for even MORE shown of Vitalia. There is a character who experiences a lot that is described in text and left to the imagination rather than shown.
Any issues?
Not exactly. I did notice "information" spelled incorrectly one time, but didn't notice any other typos and certainly no bugs.
Unlike other VNs I'm used to playing, the user interface was quite streamlined, e.g. there was no obvious "skip" button (useful during replays) << not really a complaint either, it just took me a moment to work out Ctrl was the button I needed :)
Recommended to both seasoned players of VNs and newbies.

First of all, I just wanted to say that the title is so amazing and unique and I spent a lot of time just admiring how clever it is.
To be honest, I never really finished the demo. Even though I found the premise interesting, everything just seemed to be advancing so slowly. I thought Book 1 did a good job of picking up the pace though and introducing the characters, though I have to admit that I spent the majority of time getting frusterated at Ben for his actions, probably because I ended up developing a huge bias for Jacob.
Speaking of the characters, I really enjoyed how Lilya grew over time and thought that her dynamic with Ben and Jacob was really interesting. How they all liked Vitalia, but due to their different backgrounds and the varying amount of human support they each had, they acted in different ways. I thought that was very well written. I ended up liking all three of the main characters (to varying degrees) and want them to be friends, though sadly I keep trying and failing to get those achievements.
Books 2 and 3 were mainly about the plot and I thought that the plot twists were written and paced well. It kept you engaged and wasn't very repetitive either. I really liked the choice mechanic system of the game where sometimes just one choice could completely change the ending. I also really appreciated seeing how many people chose the same choices as I did and thought that that was a really cool thing to include.
I ended up enjoying the game more than I thought I would. There are still a couple of loose ends that I'm not sure if they're answered in other endings, so maybe I'll go back and try to get everything. But overall, it was great writing and a cool story and I'd recommend it. Keep up the good work! :)
(Also Lilya's family is the real MVP)

The story kept me interested throughout and the characters were refreshingly varied with differing views (weither or not they placed actual emphasis on this in story) and I feel though it was short, I personally was satisfied with the ending. Also the fact that I feel like the branching storylines and replaying quality were more important than the actual length itself and gave the story more depth, though for my playthrough personally I have yet to see them all.
Overall I feel it was worth the 10 euro I spent to purchase, the art was gorgeous, the GUI well polished, the characters were well done with their own problems and how it impacts the way they interact with others in small ways. And I liked seeing the choices other players made at the end of each book as well. :)

Disclaimer: I've only finished book one of three so far.
So this is a cool visual novel, unsurprisingly about VR and the nature of reality. It definitely has strong .hack vibes, but it has its own spin on the VR angle and explores some interesting themes, like the allure of escapism for people whose lives might not be all that great. The plot is a little slow to start off with, but once it builds steam, it's good at maintaining a sense of tension and intrigue. The characters are also interesting, especially the protagonist, who struggles with social anxiety that's written in a believable and relatable way.
As for presentation, I'm impressed by the attention to detail. It seems like there's no narration of actions, but the graphics and sound effects do such a good job of conveying what's going on that it took me a while to notice. There are tons of CGs and little animations that add a lot of polish. There are also a ton of character sprites that are very expressive, and the environments are colorful and imaginative. I also think the electronic soundtrack does a good job of setting a sci-fi mood.
The game works well and seems bug-free. There are a few features I liked, like seeing the protagonist's thoughts when you hover over choices and seeing how common your choices were and what the impact of them is at the end of a chapter.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who's interested in character-driven fiction and virtual reality.

It's a personal rule of mine to play at least 2 hours of a game before clocking up a review. after playing Death Road to Canada, I realize that regulation must be changed. I need so much more time to take it all in.
Death Road to Canada is a fantastic take on the Oregon Trail that blends humor, survival, character customization, RPG elemnets, beat-em-up combat, and parodies of pop culture that make you crack a grin.
The soundtrack isn't that diverse, but it's enough to keep you bopping your head to the beat and humming along as you (attempt to) rip your way through hordes of zombies. The sound effects really match the feeling of whats happening. I really love the use of sound in this game. It's satisfying.
The gameplay is simple yet complex. Managing supplies, your vehicle, your party of friends, weapons, and descisions that really do take efect. It successfully blends in these RPG elements that makes the game flow smoothly.
Combat is simple. Hit zombies with your weapons. Thats it. Smack them till' they dead. Mm-mm. Delicious.
The best part of the game, without a doubt, is the Familiar Characters Mode. You can create your friends, family, celebrities, Youtubers, et cetera. The possibilities are endless. you can give them perks to help your party on your journey, and personality traits that can boost those perks. This really makes the game feel like your own, and you really do feel terrible when they get killed in the field.
The graphics are pixelated, and thats fine with me. It gives the game potential to age well and stretch out to a more appealing audience. This game is only pretty mild, being a zombie game. They drop a few guts and...black stuff, but it's never that bad. No blood, just...oil, I guess.
The game is local co-op compatible, but sadly has no online co-op support by the time this review is released. It's a bit of a bummer, but it's pretty enjoyable with friends, and great to play by yourself.
Death Road to Canada successfully blends survival, humor, RPG elements, beat-em-up combat, and charming pixel graphics that appeal very well. The game is priced extremely well at 15 bucks, but I bought it on sale at 10 bucks. Not that... thats important or, whatever.
Also its uh... kinda glithcy. Like, the game will stop or glitch like, once every six to twelve playthroughs.
Also its uh... kinda glitchy. Like, the game will crash or freeze or glitch at least once every ten to twelve playthroughs. And playthroughs dont last that long. I mean, The game deleted all my save data, like custom characters. it took me a long time to make my friends! And it did it again the day after. WHAT.
8-Great
+Charming Graphics
+Well executed RPG elements
+Successful Survival gameplay
+Smooth Beat-Em-Up Combat
+Funny
+Brilliant Character Customization
+Interesting Mechanics
+Choices, Choices, CHOICES!!!!
+Entertaining Soundtrack
+Lots of Game Modes
+Pop Culture References
-Extremely Glitchy

Far Cry 4 is so great! How do I know? The game can affect you more than teenage hormones in puberty! You may also feel more impulsive and more inclined to take risks.. Like experimenting with drugs, driving without a licence like a crazy maniac or riding elephants! You forget to eat, forget to sleep, forget to play other games!
In the past 4 months I've played all Far Cry games except Far Cry Primal and I must admit I love Far Cry 4 the most. Far Cry 4 made me want to abandon all my other games. All I wanted was to enter this amazing world in Himalayas and start roaming again!
It isn't really the main story what makes me think it's all so realistic. It is the way how the world there reacts to my presence. Open world events, wild life can attack you when you are trying to do stealth missions, many possibilities how to travel - Tuk Tuk, Gyrocopter, Wingsuit, Paraglider, Cargo Truck, Snow Mobile and much more. You can also fast travel to outposts once you liberate them. Climbing mountains with a grappling hook can be exciting, especially when you are like me and kill yourself while swinging from one edge to another ;)
--->
I enjoy liberating outposts without being detected the most. Believe me it makes it so much easier for you if they don't call for reinforcements, especially later in game and on hard difficulty.. Hard difficulty is much harder than in Far Cry 3, but I would still recommend it if you like a bit more challenge and adrenaline! I also tried liberating fortresses in coop gameplay and it was so much fun! I wished there were more of them!
The main story is ok, weaker than in Far Cry 3, but still fun! What makes Far Cry 4 special for me are the special missions which allow you to travel to new locations like the mythological Shangri-La or the snowy parts of Himalayas full of danger, predators and soldiers, where you have to be aware of your oxygen levels.
In my opinion they fixed all the things which were bothering me a bit in Far Cry 3. They should have brought Vaas, though ;) I miss him! The only thing I really dislike in Far Cry 4 is how the main missions are marked on the map by first letter of a name of the person you should be talking to. Everytime I opened my map it took me ages to find those letters! Especially at the beginning when I was a newbie and didn't know how to even get a story mission..
Overall I expected disappointment at the beginning of Far Cry 4 because of all the feedback I got.. And no, I don't think it's like Far Cry 3 with improved graphics and weaker story. It's much more than that! I will definitely play this game again!

VA-11 Hall-A is a cyberpunk/dystopian visual novel developed by Sukeban Games. In VA-11 Hall-A you play as Jill, a bartender at the VA-11 Hall-A bar, known by its regulars as Valhalla. Valhalla is located in Glitch City, a city controlled by corrupt corporations and an even more corrupt police force. Through the eyes of Jill you'll come to know what life is like for those who live in the city and you'll hear countless stories, some of which will make you laugh, others that'll make you think.



VA-11 Hall-A is, at its core, a linear visual novel with a couple of different paths you can go down (affecting little more than the story). Jill's conversations with her patrons will have slight differences if you serve the wrong drink to someone (or in some cases if you serve them the right drink instead of what they ask for). The game has several different endings, two main endings and then several different endings which are dependent upon interactions with certain characters. Generally I'm not a fan of story-driven games where your actions have no consequences but VA-11 Hall-A tells such an excellent story, and is so well-written that I didn't mind at all that it was linear. The only issue that crops up with its linearity is that subsequent playthroughs (if you're looking to get all the achievements) may not be as enjoyable as your first run.

Despite being a visual novel, VA-11 Hall-A does have some gameplay. When a patron at the bar orders a drink, a screen comes up with the mixing recipes for all the drinks (well maybe not quite all of them) on the left hand side of the screen and the right hand side is occupied by the actual drink mixer. This part of the game is surprisingly enjoyable, though it can get a tad repetitive later on. Whenever a customer orders a drink (providing Jill isn't distracted) Jill will have a line which either tells you exactly what the customer wants or it'll tell you what they've order and hint at what drink they may actually be after. I found the most enjoyable orders to be the ones where the customer asks for something along the lines of "the usual". Orders like these challenge what you know about a character and whether or not you've been paying attention, though you could just look up the answer in the forum if you're stumped. The characters who appear often enough to have a usual drink are generally the characters who appear most often and are therefore the most fleshed out, they're the characters who really paint a picture of Glitch City.

The greatest thing about Glitch City and its inhabitants is that they feel real. Even VA-11 Hall-A's most ridiculous character feels real because he fits within Glitch City which, through the complaints and comments made by other characters, feels real. Glitch City, and many of the characters, start out as mysteries that you as a player will unravel as you progress through the game. It helps make the game even more compelling for its more curious players. By the time I finished my first playthrough of the game I felt like I really knew Glitch City and those who lived there.

Speaking of finishing playthroughs, once you've finished your first run you can start a New Game+ mode which is designed for players who want to get all the achievements/see the endings they haven't yet seen. With NG+ you start from the beginning of the game with your leftover money as well as any items you bought. This makes chasing down the other endings easier, especially if you got the Bad Ending for your first run like I did. NG+ also allows you to purchase the remaining songs from the in-game shop with the money you earn as Jill, you'll need all of the music for one of the achievements.

Even if you aren't chasing achievements, you'll want to buy all of the music in VA-11 Hall-A because let me tell you, it's an absolutely fantastic soundtrack. I've never been a huge fan of synth music but not only does VA-11 Hall-A have a great soundtrack, it also has a soundtrack that fits in perfectly with the game world. At the start of each day and after each break you choose twelve songs to play on the jukebox and you can then shuffle, skip etc whenever you want to while you're talking to customers. From the tracks I've heard so far none of them have lyrics which means they work perfectly for ambient music but they're also enjoyable to listen to by themselves if you're a fan of synth or just a fan of game soundtracks in general.

The game's visuals are also excellent. The art style fits in well and the bar is very well designed, it really makes you feel like you're in this cyberpunk world. All of the character images are well designed, there were a couple I didn't really like but that just comes down to personal preference rather than it being a case of poorly designed characters. VA-11 Hall-A has scan lines, I think they make the game look even better but they can be turned off if you're that way inclined. The UI is also well designed, it's nice having the mixer station always visible and it leaves plenty of room for the on-screen characters and dialogue box.


VA-11 Hall-A is an absolutely fantastic visual novel set in a well thought out cyberpunk dystopia and it may just be one of the best story-driven games I've played. Even the light gameplay elements in VA-11 Hall-A are enjoyable. If you're a fan of story-driven games then this is an absolute must have even at full-price.

If you ever played Super Meat Boy game and you are looking for similar, but not exactly the same, experience - get They Bleed Pixels ASAP.
This game looks bloody cute on the screenshots. I love the visuals, the music and our heroine. It's fun to kill enemies! Looking for each of the hidden pages is also enjoyable but... yeah, that's for like the first few levels. After this the difficulty level jumps up like crazy and you no longer care about killing everything that moves, collecting everything that's collectable, finding some secret stuff. You just try, and try, and try, and try, and try to finish level. For the first time, I picked up the Standard difficulty level because I wanted to reach the ending level, but maybe the Novice would be a better choice for starters. Anyway somehow, after 6 hours, I reached the end. It's short, you say? Not really. There are lots of things to do: arts to unlock, get a better grade on each of levels, complete bonus levels. Also, the achievements. That's where you will find a hell similar to the one in Super Meat Boy - speedrunning? Complete a level without any deaths? Good luck! I'm not sure if I will ever want to spend XX hours trying to master one piece of level. Maybe some day, but not now. Oh, by the way, there is nothing wrong with controlls - I feel like it's almost perfect and you don't need a gamepad to play or beat it (I was using a keyboard).
They Bleed Pixels is truly fun game, and if you like challenges, you will have even more fun. It also gets cheap as sales - up to 80% off! I kinda wish that Spooky Squid Games will ever make a similar, or even harder, platformer, because they did a great job on this game :)

If you are looking for a game ...
... which challenges you instead of rewards you.
... which isn't bugged to hell or released in alpha as most 'full releases' are these days.
... in which thoughtfulness is encouraged, instead of time-destroying grinding or farming for e-stats.
... where you walk away from it feeling happier than when you sat down.
... which doesn't conspire to get you addicted like many modern games.
... which feels like walking into an art gallery, where ones shoes should be removed upon entering.
... with actual depth. Not the fake depth of grinding to level whatever, but the depth of discovering and understanding complex practical and philosophic puzzles Witness presents you with.
... in which 'sleeping on it' is actually a legitimate method of solving the puzzles.
... where you will walk over a piece of ground a hundred times, not realizing it is the missing piece of the puzzle.
... which you can show your family and friends.
... which doesn't feel like watching a Michael Bay film.
... which is bad by 2016 standards (no perks, leveling treadmills, no addictive hooks, no farming, no worrying about it while you're at work, no peer pressure, no achievements, unlockables, no pay to win, no DLC).
Then you have found a game worth playing.
I won't tell you to like Witness. It is not for everyone. The price feels steep at $39.99. I do believe Witness is worthy enough for you to take a chance with it, and after 10-20 hours of play, deciding then whether you like it, or not.
Just as a wine collection needs a few fine bottles, your Steam Library needs The Witness.

Gigantic is another 3rd person MOBA similar to SMITE and Paladin. The game is simple enough to understand. You control a single hero in a team of 5. Your team's objective is to take down the enemy's Guardian. To do so, you try to gain 100 power before the other team. The first team to hit 100 power gains RAMPAGE and is allowed a chance to pin down the enemy team's guardian to damage it. The first team to damage the enemy team's 3 times wins. If the game drags out for too long, there will be a final clash between the Guardians. You can think of it as Super Creep mode in old Dota.
Gameplay-wise, your hero uses the LMB and RMB to fight, WASD for movement and Spacebar for jumping. LMB is a bread and butter skill while RMB is usually a power move. The more you attack, the more Focus you will gain. Once you have enough Focus, you can perform a complex ultimate where you press F and LMB. In my opinion, the movement is slightly more interesting than SMITE simply due to the ability to jump. You will run around the map trying to kill heroes, collecting power, attacking the enemy Guardian and summoning creatures.
There is a whole roster of interesting characters to play with. However, you will notice immense similarities to the roster of Dota. Sadly, all heroes need to be bought with gold or rubies. Rubies being the cash currency. 12,000 rubies for $59.99. Certain creatures cannot be summoned unless you buy them. The paid creatures even have additional abilities compared to the default creatures.
Conclusion, this game is P2W. Despite the interesting roster, I am turned off by the locking of core gameplay mechanics behind a paywall. The 3D gameplay is not as interesting compared to the top down view of traditional MOBAs. Gigantic is no different from PvP battles from old MMORPGs like World of Warcraft.
Note : Publisher is Perfect World Entertainment.

TLJ is an asthonishing blend of sci-fi and fantasy that flows on a linear progression, sans most point and click adventure games, but the pacing is smooth and you'll never be stuck in a single area for long periods of time. The story itself can be really intense at times and for the most part doesn't give in to jarring plot conveniences. The writing, brainchild of Ragnar Tornquist, is great as well. Usually protagonists, or characters in general, can be two extremes: really swell, or really annoying. If they fall inbetween they are bland. Tornquist's writing makes protagonist April Ryan annoyingly believable. Her mannerisms will constantly remind you that she's just a college student and not someone fit to save two worlds.
Spec-wise, the game came out in '99, and to my knowledge there are no HD mods or anything, and if this bothers you, start to notice the scenery more. The backgrounds in this game are gorgeous and they really amplify the atmosphere.
The gameplay has some good puzzles. They aren't very hard, but they do the job. Also you can't die. To me this is a safer approach than other pointnclicks like Sierra games where you are punished for not knowing what was ahead of you ahead of time and it doesn't create anxiety for the sake of defibrilatting action into otherwise bland gameplay like The Walking Dead. If you like sci-fi or fantasy this is a game to check out, if you find it on sale that is. I really enjoyed it.

One of the best fighting games out there.
Alright, I'll be honest, I'm not on the competitive scene, so maybe I'm not one to talk, since fighting games have raised to popularity precisely as multiplayer games.  So, if you're looking for info on the online portion, I can't help you much.
That being said, fighting games still had their fans in the single-player community.  This was only exacerbated by Netherrealm's games starting to include story modes ever since Mortal Kombat vs DC Universe.  After that, fighting games NOT including a story mode started to look half-made.  Naturally, this being the latest Netherrealm game, it has a story mode, and it's fantastic.
STORY MODE
The story continues some time after the events of the first game, being set in the same universe of the "Regime", this time without any other parallel universe intervening.  The world-consuming alien Brainiac approaches Earth with the intention of, well, consuming it.  Finding himself short on help, Batman realizes he has to release Superman from prison in order to fight the alien threat.  Meanwhile, Kara Zor-El aka Supergirl has recently showed up on Earth and has to make a choice where her loyalties rest.
As stories go, it's not particularly deep, but it's fun, interesting and full of colorful and likable (for the most part) characters.  Just like in previous games, you follow a list of characters (from the DC universe in this case), each one for a few battles as the story develops.  Unlike the previous game, there aren't any QTE minigames mixed in the middle of the story, but things are spiced up by being able to choose between a couple of characters on certain ocassions.
OTHER MODES
Besides the story mode, there are a couple of other options for solo play.  There are classic single fights and tower battles (in which you fight a list of increasingly difficult AI opponents until you reach the boss and get your character's ending), but the biggest addition is the Multiverse.  Replacing the S.T.A.R. Labs mission from the previous game, the Multiverse is an ever-changing list of missions with different requirements, difficulty, objectives and rewards.  These are being changed on a daily basis, so you'll always have something different to try.  There are even multiplayer-focused Multiverse missions, but as I already mentioned, online play is not my thing.  Fighting in most of these modes (except, apparently, in single fights) nets you experience and rewards.
ONLINE MODES
I already said is not my thing, darn it!  Why are you even looking here?
GAMEPLAY
Here's where things get interesting.  The gameplay options are quite varied.  In fact, there are so many options it can be overwhelming.  Besides the classic attack / combo system, and special and super moves there are bunch of options for blocking, canceling, dodging and overall turning the tides of the battle.  A new player can rely on a few combos and abilities, but as the difficulty rises (particularly in other game modes), you'll need to start mastering all these other moves (such as the Clash system and proper use of the environmental interactions, both of which return from the previous game) if you want to keep up.
CUSTOMIZATION
The shiniest part of the game is the customization.  While fighting games have traditionally included alternate costumes for the characters for a while, this game takes it several steps forward.  Rather than just including classic costumes, playing the game nets you rewards in the form of gear pieces, exclusive to each character, which you can combine to form a costume however you want it.  You can also unlock shaders to give your character different colors.
Most importantly, all these gear pieces have stats, allowing you to improve your attack, defense, abilities, health and many other extra features.  And if you like the stats of a piece of gear but the looks of another, you can simply make the former look like the latter (though this consumes in-game currency).  Your characters can be leveled up, and their stats grow as well.  You can then swap your gear pieces for some of your current level or try to regenerate lower-level pieces into higher-level ones with new stats (which also consumes currency).
Gear comes in several different flavors of rarity, and you can obtain it directly in missions or from loot boxes.  The options are nearly endless.
And yes, before you ask, the game has microtransactions.  But they are completely unintrusive.  There's nothing you can buy that you can't unlock by playing and considering the extreme amount of content and the ridiculously large roster you'll never find yourself in a position in which you need to pay real money.  Also, since the use of gear can be turned off in online play even someone with lots of money to spend won't have the advantage unless you let them.
PC OPTIONS
The game works extremely well on my PC at very high settings, with its several-years-old i3 CPU and 6GB of RAM.  My card is a GeForce GTX 960, which is mid-end, and I run Windows 7 64 bit.  Never crashed or bugged out.  The game has a lot of options for PC customization.  As an aside, I noticed that you can configure the language in-game to pick the same language your Steam client has, which shows they've actually given care to the PC version.
All in all, this is my favorite fighting game and one I'll be playing for a long time.  I recommend it without any shadow of a doubt.

It's a great casual game to play with children. I was playing the whole game with 3yo daughter. Finding stars and puzzle pieces is her favorite part of gameplay. Huge thanks to developers. :)

The game contains various stories which don't have much plot: they just have an introduction to present you the new area, and an ending in which Bob leaves it.
Every area consists of 25 levels, and each one has 3 stars to collect, while some of them have "puzzle pieces" to collect aswell. Getting a specific number of stars unlocks new costumes, and when you get enough pieces to complete the puzzle, you unlock 5 extra levels related to the area you're playing at.
The game has some cool mechanics (which I didn't expect) and even 2 boss battles.
The game is focused to be played by kids so it's not difficult at all. You may fail some times because of stupid actions but you don't really have to think much to complete the game. Boss battles are easy, too.
The only thing that resulted me a bit harder to do was to find every star. I'm not sure if it's because colors distract me more than they do to other people, but there are hidden stars in the background and I couldn't find them easily because of their color. The same happened with some puzzle pieces.
There is a specific tune for each area. Although they're looped, they aren't annoying due to their "softness" and "harmony" (I don't know how to explain it).
The music is as simple as the game so it fits great.
It's the aspect I liked the most of the game. There are backgrounds, clickable items, themes, costumes... which refer to shows and movies (LOST, Star Wars, Spongebob...), videogames (Half Life, Fallout, Metal Gear Solid, Super Mario, Mortal Kombat...) and books (Robin Hood?).
I think that the game is a 7'5/10 even being focused to children, 'cause it can result fun and entertaining for everyone, and these cultural references improve the game even more. I just dislike that some mechanics become a bit repetitive, and the game's length being too short: I completed (100%'d) the game in just 2 hours. I would love to play more levels!
