A surprisingly charming game.  The comparisons to Lemmings are fairly spot on, though you simply have more direct control over a single 'lemming', aka the titular Snail Bob.
Each level tasks you with guiding Bob to the goal with numerous types of mini-puzzle objectives along the way to create a safe path.  All levels are single-screen, but can become fairly complex as you progress through the game.  I haven't found the game to become particularly difficult, but some stages require extra thought.  It fits in a niche of being engaging enough for adults but accessible enough for younger children.
In addition to the goal of guiding Bob, each level has 3 hidden stars as well as occasional puzzle pieces.  Collecting enough of these unlocks costumes for Bob or additional levels (in the case of the puzzle pieces).  Progress is never gated by them however, so there's no pressure to fully scour every level if you don't want to.  Since you can tell Bob to stop at any time, you can easily 'pause' him in a safe place while you hunt for hidden objects, giving a more relaxing feel to the searching.
The game currently consists of 90 levels with more slated to be added at a later date.  There's certainly a 'mobile game' feel to the structure and aesthetic, but the game plays perfectly well on PC.  It won't win any awards for technical achievement, but it succeeds in the goal of being a family friendly puzzle game for all ages.

Cute little Lemmings-like game. The art/music/sound were very well done, and there was a lot of humor in some of the levels/situations that was amusing.

The one thing I did not like about the game was the star/puzzle piece mechanic. On each level are 3 stars and occasionally a puzzle piece hidden somewhere that the player has to find (technically, you could ignore this, but you need the stars to unlock outfits and the puzzle pieces to, well, solve the puzzle).
The problem is that for almost all of the levels, the stars/puzzle pieces are designed so that they blend into the background so this part of the game becomes "methodically search in a vertical pattern for anomalous objects."
On a few of the levels, the puzzle pieces/stars are hidden behind objects that you have to activate, which made a lot more sense and felt like it was actually part of the game. The "find the hidden object" portion felt divorced from the rest of the gameplay.
All-in-all, though, totally worth it for $5 if you like these kind of games and don't mind the low difficulty level.

Once upon a time I'd happily recommend this. But last I checked the grind had almost doubled. Ignoring that, originally you only fought against ships of your own tier. Which was fine, the queues were only a minute long. Then suddenly they made it akin to WoT, where you can be paired up against ships of a higher tier.
in WoT, irritating as it is as a lower tier tank you're still -somewhat- useful. Star Conflict? There's no real scouting mechanic. You are slower, weaker and significantly less durable than any ship a single tier higher than you. I distinctly recall firing everything I had at such an opponent, but his shields were able to regenerate faster than I could deal damage, even if he sat still.
This is the equivalent of a tier 1 WoT tank going against a tier 5 (If it were a tier 1 and 2 ship in SC). As you might guess, this is horribly misbalanced and the T1 has no hope in hell of doing a dang thing.
Again, it really pains me. The game itself was -good-, I enjoyed it. The grind increase was iffy but I could deal with it, but the botched tier matchmaking (Which evidently was an attempt to imitate other, similar, games, such as their own War Thunder, but without considering the fact that a T1 ship is utterly useless against a T2. Whereas in War Thunder a T1 plane is still capable against a T2) was what really killed Star Conflict for me.
Mind you, this was ages ago, so they might have changed it back, or re-balanced each tier. In which case feel free to correct me.

(Spoiler-Free Review)  To be honest, I'm a little disappointed.
The game was a lot shorter than I thought it would be, and leaves a lot of questions unanswered.  The conclusion feels pretty rushed - I was shocked when I had already stumbled upon the epilogue.  Not only that, but there were a lot less real choices than I believed there would be.  The most impactful decisions come at the end, but even then, it doesn't change the narrative so much as it does the short and (in my opinion) lackluster epilogue.  It's a shame because the story is well-written, it's just so short and rushed that it doesn't give enough time to be really invested in Vitalia's plight and the characters, or resolve anything in a satisfactory manner.  Most of the development happens in the last 5 to 10 minutes of the game and that's unforunate considering that I found the lore interesting and was looking forward to what extent the creators endeavored to explore it.  Many of the imaginative concepts introduced are not adequately explored (especially when some of them are made to seem important) or are simply just mentioned again in the epilogue.  In addition, when it comes down to it, the main character doesn't get to do much of anything.  There's a lot of contemplating of choices but not a lot of actually...making them, much less acting upon them since the game doesn't even give that many opportunities for climactic decisions.

Visual novel with more interactivity than most games of it's genre. You play as bartender, mixing drinks is the "gameplay", so to speak. Interactions with people (/robots/dogs/...) are scripted but vary depending on choices, with an astonishing amount of optional content, dialogue and lore. While it's not perfectly written, every single character is interesting (that takes effort!) and the lore of the world is fleshed out immensely. Multiple story arcs, multiple endings and multiple dialogue branches make for great replay value. Nice artstyle and some great tracks on the Soundtrack.
Recommended if you like: Narrative, story-rich games, Visual Novels
Not recommended if you don't like: Gameplay-poor games, Anime artstyle
Playtime: ~13h, great replay value.
Amazing visuals and sountrack, very relaxing gameplay, compelling story, characters and writing. Great game! If, like me, the theme, style and mood strikes your fancy, do yourself a favor and buy it!

Should you play this game?
Yes, please. I played this game as a person who hadn't touched anything in the Visual Novel genre. This game is short enough for beginners but contains enough depth for a serious gamer. (Around 8 to 10 hours of story with medium reading speed.)
What reason(s) can you give me to play this game?
That's not a question that'll give you a succinct answer.
0) Disclaimer required: The flavor of this Visual Novel is mature. There's a lot of crude language, adult sex topics, a lot of small talk which leads to opinions about political issues or tough personal issues.
1) The characters are fantastic, each with their quirks, personalities, and backstories. You really feel that they are the main characters of their life. This leads to great dialogue.
Smack in the beginning, you are introduced to 2 characters for great shock value. One is Donovan D. Dawson, who is unabshedly rude(he insults the bar the moment he enters), shamelessly arrogant, yet somehow charismatic. Another is Ingram McDougal, who speaks openly about his sex life. There's yet another character that you'll meet, Dorothy, who is a cheerful 10 to 13 year old lilim(cyborg), who sells her body for a living and is proud of it. She openly admits to using her looks to have an advantage over other competitors.
One interesting aspect of the characters is that a lot of them are people of the LGBT community. And the story treats this aspect correctly. That you are bisexual or gay or whatever is simply melded into the culture. In the small talk during the story, you'd have a casual "How do you like males? Hmm, then what about females?" vibe going on.  It's treated as such an ubiquitous aspect of the story, that you get a glimpse of a society where gender discrimination simply doesn't occur.
And that really adds to both the characters and the world.
2) The world setting is deep yet also never fully explored, which gives the story a unique feel. You play as a bartender and all you experience is the daily ongoings of bartending life to different customers. Major events in the city will occur, but you'll only ever hear of them from a 3rd person point of view. You'll see it reported on the TV, on the news app, or a message board(similar to that of '♥♥♥♥♥♥').
To some, this removed approach might feel like you're left out, but there are a lot of hidden clues surrounding the backstory of those events. If you simply took your customers at face value, then they seem like people with a job. But if you were more persistent and observant, you'll find that your characters are indeed connected to the major events in the city. You know this from the bits of knowledge they reveal as they speak and the bits of knowledge you gained from 3rd person sources. Yet, these speculations are never mentioned in the story. Instead, our main character Jill, chooses to accept the customers and friends at face value, because in the end, they are both her customer and her friends.
This may be a story filled with implications, but more importantly, it's a story about the people of a dystopian cyberpunk future.
3)The world setting also introduces an assortment of races, like cat boomers, lilims, humans with cyborg implants and etc. All these assortments of races and their origins are actually explained, which really gives one the feel of looking through a small hole into a full and complex world.
4) It's worth buying the game for the OST alone. At the start of each day in the story, you get to choose 12 songs, that'll play as you go through the daily bartender motions. You can change these each day, once at the beginning of workshift and another time after break. And there's a HUGE selection for you to choose from, each soundtrack sounding like a professional arrangement of synth, techno, and electronic liquid gold. Now, there's bound to be stuff you dislike but there's also bound to be stuff you LOVE. It's great to be able to play this playlist at anytime during the story.
*Note: Gaming Knowledge Worth Spoiling*
5) The pixel art is gorgeous. The pictures will speak for themselves.
6) The gameplay of mixing drinks is simple enough to pick up as the story goes. A gaming mechanic that you would eventually discover is
Although the gameplay is simple, sometimes, characters will give you a vague description of what they want. "Give me something sweet." Don't worry, you'll have a recipe terminal on hand to look up on how to make the drinks. As you attempt to give these characters what they want or what they should drink, the task of figuring out the drink and getting it right rewards you with more connection to the characters. Some characters will have a favourite drink or a go-to drink for certain occasions.
This builds a familiarity and empathy towards them. You personally feel responsible for their mood. You don't really get punished for messing up. But when you do mess up, you see it in their microexpressions and language. You see the slight disappointment in their language and the sad curves of their eyebrows or the frown on their mouths. These are things you may glance over, but going through the daily bartender motions long enough make you realize that your actions, however small, do affect your customers. And that, is good gameplay design and writing.
7) There are lots and lots of humor and quotable lines. The writing is all round top-notch.
CONCLUSION:
The sum of all these reasons truly made me feel that my money was spent right. I bought this at the price of $15. I can tell you, it is every cent well spent. More so than steam games i bought during cheap seasonal sales, more so than games I'd bought because they were popular.
I initially bought this game, thinking my money would be 'some exchange of money' for a casual timekiller. After playing this game, I realized instead, my $15 was solely spent to, support Sukeban Games for their effort in creating this game, and invest in any possibility of their future endeavors.
What reason(s) can you give me to play this game? That's not a question that'll give you a succinct answer. A better question with a succinct answer would be:
Why shouldn't I play this game?
-You shouldn't play it if you don't have the time(10 hours) or money($15) to open your mind and explore new worlds.

If you are looking for a game ...
... which challenges you instead of rewards you.
... which isn't bugged to hell or released in alpha as most 'full releases' are these days.
... in which thoughtfulness is encouraged, instead of time-destroying grinding or farming for e-stats.
... where you walk away from it feeling happier than when you sat down.
... which doesn't conspire to get you addicted like many modern games.
... which feels like walking into an art gallery, where ones shoes should be removed upon entering.
... with actual depth. Not the fake depth of grinding to level whatever, but the depth of discovering and understanding complex practical and philosophic puzzles Witness presents you with.
... in which 'sleeping on it' is actually a legitimate method of solving the puzzles.
... where you will walk over a piece of ground a hundred times, not realizing it is the missing piece of the puzzle.
... which you can show your family and friends.
... which doesn't feel like watching a Michael Bay film.
... which is bad by 2016 standards (no perks, leveling treadmills, no addictive hooks, no farming, no worrying about it while you're at work, no peer pressure, no achievements, unlockables, no pay to win, no DLC).
Then you have found a game worth playing.
I won't tell you to like Witness. It is not for everyone. The price feels steep at $39.99. I do believe Witness is worthy enough for you to take a chance with it, and after 10-20 hours of play, deciding then whether you like it, or not.
Just as a wine collection needs a few fine bottles, your Steam Library needs The Witness.

I was not excited to play as the Imperial Guard because after completing Dawn of War (vanilla), they seemed like total wusses. However, Winter Assault's gameplay is pretty awesome! I loved the gameplay as the Imperial Guard. You can send your guys into bunkers and then pop them out across the map at listening posts or other bunkers within seconds, which saves a lot of time and can help with defending. I liked the look and sound of their builder units better, their builders built much faster than Space Marine Servitors did, and the turrets they built seemed a lot more useful as well, though I believe they do take up more room.
One of my only personal qualms with Dawn of War (vanilla) was that I didn't really have fun with the story, as everyone simply wants to kill everyone of other factions on sight, and that never changes, with the exception of a painfully obvious turncoat. With Winter Assault, however, there is stealthy assisting of another faction, allying factions with mistrust/shaky alliances, and some intrigue, even if it is still pretty simple. It's more interesting, in my opinion. They don't need to be BFFs or even honor their agreements, but aside from the villains in Dawn of War (vanilla), there weren't alliances. This game also allows for you to play as the Eldar at points in the missions, and you can even play a "disorder" campaign on the opposing side, which has its own set of missions as Orks and Chaos Marines! Basically anything I wanted in the vanilla game was added with this expansion, and I liked the Imperial Guard more than the Space Marines. Fantastic!
However, the single player missions themselves, though starting out pretty good, began to take a dive in quality starting with the third, requiring that you play the mission in pretty specific ways, or be utterly destroyed. I undestand the same tactics shouldn't need to work on every map, and that gimmick differences on maps are to be expected - that's part of what I loved about Starcraft II. That said, in the fourth mission, the game sends horde after horde at you, letting you capture small bases, but will not allow you to build new bases or non-listening post turrets and building add-ons for improved troops.
There was no declared plot reason for this, I had builders, their building trees were gutted for the mission, and my troops dwindled and dwindled, even when I restarted the mission a few times, trying to be more careful and build quicker. Hell, little chaos critters even get teleported into the base you capture, so you can't press forward without risking loss of the base, and resources are crazy tight as it is, so I can't afford to leave anyone to guard it. Of course it's doable, and I'm sure it's even easy for some, but I was not having fun, and with the severe, stubborn restrictions to what I could build (almost nothing) gave me less options and control.
I love the improvements to this expansion, and feel it has a superior story, basic gameplay, and faction variety than the vanilla version of Dawn of War, and I respect it greatly for that, but the actual missions (I played almost exclusively on the "order" campaign) discourage the base-building and open strategy that the vanilla Dawn of War encouraged. If the missions had been more like those in the vanilla Dawn of War, I feel that this game would have been superior for me in every way, but the missions became so dissatisfying and restrictive in what I could build that I could not enjoy playing the campaign any further.

Snail Bob 2 is a fun, casual puzzle game with a few chuckles thrown in.
The game tasks you with a very simple objective. Get Snail Bob to the exit, safely.
He will constantly move through the level, so you need to interact with the environment by shifting platform positions, scaring enemies away, etc. You can also click on him to make him stay in one spot, which is useful if you need time to set up something, or keep him on a moving platform. Your second ability is to turn him around.
With those simple mechanics, you're ready to play the entire game. Although it's very simple, the game can still make for some decently challenging and fun puzzles. It never gets insanely difficult, as it's meant to stay a decently casual and relaxing experience. You can collect hidden stars throughout the game, and use them to unlock costumes for Bob. Some levels also have a hidden puzzle piece, that once all have been collected in a chapter, will unlock a few bonus levels.
The game is very simple, yet entertaining. It's got a few pop culture references and jokes every now and again, and the cutscenes are cute, and will make you laugh.
Overall, a charming and fun game!

Bob 2 takes much inspiration from the lemmings series. Simple objective, direct him toward to exit while collecting hidden coins and puzzle pieces.
Controls are all mouse driven, click on platforms to move them, buttons to use them while directing Bob backward and forward dodging hazards. Screen resolutions of 4k were supported, toggles not sliders for sound. Three worlds were available with a fourth coming in December. Each contained 25 levels and collecting all puzzle pieces rewards an extra 5. Coins collected could be spent on a range of costumes, most drawing reference to gaming and pop culture (Half Life 3!). Collectables were often quite well hidden, which plays like a HoG side-quest.
More aimed at the younger generation it's still enjoyable for older gamers, just quite short lived for the price. If in column B perhaps wait out a sale or coupon and you shouldn't leave disappointed. Cheers.

are completely different, for

First thing is first.  The Witness is easily worth $40, even $60.  People who dismiss this game after just the first 30 minutes are missing out on what I think is one of the best games of all time.  The game is a slow burn.  It will take some time to really fall in love with it.
The Witness is a game from Mr. Blow, the genius behind Braid.  He spent around 7 years working on this game and it clearly shows.  The game is incredibly polished, with beautiful watercolor graphics and literally no glitches.  The sound design is eerie and very minimalist but contains very immersive sound effects, like water and walking through different terrains.  Overall, it's really, really well made.
The gameplay consists of solving line puzzles on a grid.  The game starts easy and gets more and more complicated.  The design is absolutely brilliant.  Basically, this game does NOT hold your hand AT ALL.  You are forced to figure everything out on your own.  This makes it very challenging, but also extremely rewarding and satisfying.  I want to again stress that this game does not ever...ever help you or hold your hand.  You must observe and think critically to understand the puzzles.  This is a breath of fresh air in the current gaming market.  To put it bluntly, The Witness respects your intelligence as a gamer, unlike so many games.
The "story" is not really a story, but rather a reflection of human endeavor.  The puzzles in The Witness are analogous to human progress and discovery.  Humans have come a long way since cave man days.  Slowly, through observation and patience, we came to better understand our environment and eventually understand the physical laws of nature that govern everything around us.  There are many highly interesting scientific/artistic audio logs and even a surprising video I found from James Burke in the game.  Each audiolog, when pieced together, tells a subtle, but brilliant "story."
In conclusion, I love this game.  I honestly can't think of any flaws.  10/10

Let me start by saying THIS IS NOT A GAME FOR EVERYONE. This puzzle game is quite different from the likes of Braid, FEZ, Portal or anything else you may have played. That said, it's still an amazing experience.
While it *does* get very complicated late-game, The Witness takes a very simple concept (labyrinths that you normally must find your way through) and throws a bunch of different rulesets about them at you. They do this with a variety of symbols that at first, you won't know what at all they mean. That's where this game kinda becomes FEZ in a sense. In FEZ, you didn't know how to translate any of the cube text or the tetronimo lines until you found a specific room in the game that told you what you do translates to what the tetronimo lines say. The same goes for The Witness. You encounter symbols within these puzzle panels, only for them to be revealed what they mean to you by a row of puzzle panels that teach you how to use the symbol, and how involved each symbol can potentially get.
The reasopn why this game is so different from other puzzle games that you may have played is because of a few factors. For one thing, the control scheme consists of 5 buttons. W, A, S, D, and Mouse 1. You don't get any physical power-ups like a double jump (not to mention, you can't jump in general). The only power up you get in this game is knowledge on how to solve another puzzle. This game will seem unrewarding if you're expecting to collect a certain amount of something every time you finish a puzzle. Instead what unlocks is more puzzles in place of whatever you think you might collect. This game is one giant puzzle and doesn't reward you until you complete it. If you go into this game knowing that, you will enjoy it as I have so far. Knowledge truly is power in this game.
Another thing that's different is that this game isn't linear whatsoever. Once you complete the "tutorial area" right out of the start point, you're free to take on *any* puzzle you'd like. Of course, you won't know how to solve most of them until you find the "tutorial panels" introducing diffierent symbols, but that freedom is there. It's something I haven't really experienced in any other puzzle game I've played so far.
If you're on the fence about this game, here are some questions that might help you:
Do you like discovering puzzle mechanics on your own, with no hand-holding? (Similar to FEZ, but if you didn't play FEZ, then you should know that game doesn't explain anything *at all* to you, just like how The Witness doesn't either.)
Do you enjoy that sense of "aha!!" moments when you've been studying a puzzle you've been struggling with for a while?
Do you not mind getting stuck on a puzzle, and decide to leave to come back to it later?
Do you like/not mind a lack of narrative in a puzzle game, and instead be somewhere shrouded in mystery that's (most likely) not explained? (I'm still working on completing this game, so I'm not sure if the island you're on ever gets explained in the end.)
Do you not mind exploring in search of anything that could help your puzzle-solving abilities?
Do you like to be surrounded by really ♥♥♥♥ing pretty visuals? (who doesn't??)
If the answer to all of these questions is 'yes', definitely give this game a shot!
P.S. DO NOT look up any puzzles. You only experience this game once, and it's definitely something wonderful to experience!!

I rarely buy games at launch, but since I loved Braid I had to buy this one. The puzzles are challenging but, when everything finally clicks, so satisfying. I love that the game doesn't have any tutorials or direction, but is made in a way that you never feel like you're lost.
Even though the game is open world, it's organized much like how Braid was. Each "area" of the world has a puzzle theme that gets more and more complex as you progress through that area. The difference here is you don't really have to do the areas in a specific order.
I hear a lot of people saying there's impossible puzzles, or it's impossibly difficult. I'd say they're probably playing "wrong." If you can't figure something out, don't be afraid to leave the puzzle and come back to it later.
Interestingly, this makes for a great group game I've found. Even though it's technically singleplayer, my friends have had a blast adventuring and working out the puzzles together. It's a lot more fun thinking everything through as a team I'd say!
If you liked Braid, you'll love this game. If you aren't a fan of solving puzzles, hated Braid, or get frustrated easily, then you'll probably hate The Witness. This is easily one of my favorite recent games!

What is FootLOL: Epic Fail League?
Genre: strategic football/soccer game with RPG elements
Setting: funny stickman characters (=the players) battling for victory in football/soccer matches
Difficulty: 3/10 --> basically easy
Length: 5 hours for a single playthrough, up to 10 for getting all rewards
Mode: singleplayer campaign, multiplayer (abandoned)
The positive aspects:
- fresh and funny gameplay. You do not control the players themselves, but have to guide them to scoring goals by using power-ups in the right way
- lots of power-ups with different characteristics: meteors, cows, flak cannons, air strikes, shields, teleporters, ball clones, crazy fans and a lot more
- RPG-ish upgrades to improve your team and cosmetics (new flags, eyes, hats etc.)
- Pretty nice sound effects, especially when you spam the pitch with different power-ups simultaneously
The negative aspects:
- strange goals. Sometimes it happens that you put the ball wide, but then it drops into the net, counting as a goal.
- gameplay gets repititive after a short time
- 2D/3D graphics mashup. You're getting used to that, but putting the 2D players into 3D would have been nice
- The biggest counterpoint surely is the strange tasks you have to complete. In most of the games you have to complete three tasks, which are always special scores. For example, for the first task the game wants you to lead by 3-0, for the second task to be down by 3-7, and for the third/final task to win by a 5-goal margin.
On the one hand, this gameplay element adds some tactical depth into the game as you sometimes have to support the opponent's team and sabotage your own squad. Otherwise - pardon me - strange thing to support somebody you have to beat, isn't it? Like corrupting the game. And I don't think that FIFA developed this game
- multiplayer is as good as dead, unfortunately
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
Ok, basically FootLOL is a fun football game with entertaining gameplay and a huge variety of power-ups to reach your goals. Though there are some counterpoints, like strange goals and tasks to complete, you can have a nice time spamming the field with cows and meteors. I recommend you to try it out (at sales time)!

An old classic, this game is one of the best experiences for quest-lovers.
the game is rather solid, length-wise, i clocked at 30 hours of gameplay, which is impressive, we are talking about "the longest" journey after all.
The dialogue in this game is really powerful and it helps you to connect with different characters, and some of them are really cool and interesting.
This game requires the player to think, like any good Click and Point Adventure should, but by no means is it a quick pased game, it's rather slow pased but really rewarding, like an interactive book of some sort.
The puzzles are challenging and quite cryptic, i was sitting on some of them for more than 25 minutes, and when i was able to solve such a puzzle i was extremely pleased.
the Graphics, however, did not age well. You are forced to play this game at 640x480 resolution, which really is an eyesore.
All in all, if you are looking for a game with great plot and dialogue and can overlook the distasteful graphics, this game is a must.

This game really is among the very finest "point-and-click" adventure game that has ever been made.  The controls aren't particulary complex.  Left-click, right-click, Esc for the save menu, click to skip through dialogue.  Pretty standard.  The graphics looked dated when the game was new, and by today's standard they're antique.  Puzzles are pretty logical, and not very difficult.  Death is impossible.  But none of that is the reason you want to play this game.
TLJ has one of the most incredible stories ever told in interactive format.  It's like playing through an epic-length novel in 15 or 20 hours of gameplay.  The voice cast is outstanding from front to back.  The lead character, April Ryan, is likable and intelligent, and by the end of the game, you'll feel like you know her, and you'll be sorry to see her go at the end of the game.  Despite being dialogue-heavy, this game is never boring.  The plot advances with every puzzle solved, every character spoken to.  The cultures of two entire worlds are brought into conflict through April Ryan.
April is an art student in a slightly-dystopian, near future version of our world, a high-technology two-class society.  Magic doesn't exist there any more than it does in real life.  But April gets involved in a complicated plot that finds her being trapped in a parallel universe on a world called "Arcadia," where magic is real, and technology is sparse.  April occasionally goes back and forth between worlds, and even into space, in order to save Arcadia and her own world, and in the process learns a lot about herself.
Best $10 you could spend on Steam.

My Short Review of "The Witness"
What makes The Witness a sublime game is that the mechanics continue to build upon themselves in profound ways. However, going into more detail about the WAYS in which these continue to expand and evolve really would spoil the experience.
I am willing to say is the following:
1) Despite how it may first appear, it isn't all just simple line puzzles on series of monitors about "connecting the dots." This mechanic forms the heart of the game, but it develops beyond that in really cool ways.  These include expanding out into the world surrounding the puzzles so that the game and the world work in symbiosis.
2) It's going to push you to constantly re-examine the assumptions you've made about how the game plays and maybe even larger assumptions about the way you think in general, about the limitations of human perception and the way we make meaning.  I can say that of very few games.
Very few puzzle games are of the caliber of the Witness. I've put about 20 hours into it thus far and I would rank it with the likes of Portal. It's going for something very different tonally (The Witness is austere where Portal is satirical), but it is that caliber of puzzle game and similarly highly unique.
And that's not to mention the aesthetics of the world it establishes. It's a beautiful world with shades of Myst. Imagine the ambling about the lost city of Pompey with a proliferation of pastel coloring at every angle.  And it has a polish goes goes all the way down to the satisfying "thump" when you lock a puzzle in place or the ping when you query the cursor. This isn't a cheaply made thing. It is a thing made with the type of loving care to detail that is very rare. There's no jankiness or weird graphical glitches or animation hitches we've come to expect with modern game design's growing pains anywhere to be seen. Nothing but a high caliber sheen.
I would just like to end by discussing the supposedly controversial price point of the "The Witness." If you are someone who plays games but doesn't think this game is worth $40 then there are really only two possible explanations:
1) You have not played it yet and don't realize you are profoundly wrong. Profoundly.
2) You are a very stupid person.
In the first case, allow this review to inspire you to give it a shot. In the second case, you are likely too dumb to appreciate this game anyway and someone should probably come and take that $40 away from you before you accidentally shove it up your nostrils and suffocate in your idiot confusion over trying to use your mouth as a breathing apparatus.
This game is more than meets the eye; it's a work of art. 'Nuf said.
It was very pretty. But if you're looking for something like Myst this isn't it. Personally I found the puzzles more frustrating than interesting.

Remember how you feel that an Arkham game got way too many Riddler trophies? Well, the Witness is that times about 5. Sure, it is indeed much more brillantly designed than most of things Rocksteady ever did. But by the day of the end, it's just way too demanding to be enjoyable.

Does this game deserves a 10? Hell yes!
Is this game for everyone? It should be! It's a game for people who love to play and test and observe and try...
This game got two things against it the developer didn't knew would exist when he created this game: Twitch and Steam refund.
A lot of people use Twitch to form their opinion on a game now... And this game is not meant to be watch. You are missing "the game", it is not meant to be seen but to be played. Even more so than a lot of games.
And steam refund prevents that also... You don't play this kind of game for 1 hour 1/2 and "get it". At best, you've found some tutorials and puzzles you could not understand, and you can't understand the world neither...
Braid comparaison:
Watching 2 hours of this game is like watching the first chapter of Braid... You would think it is a platformer!
Yet, what is important in a Platformer : timing. Then Blow made a game ABOUT time, how our understanding of it changed through history (up to the atomic bomb) or how it changes depending of the status of your relationship (up to the break up) and implemented all those idea through gameplay mechanisms.
What is important in a Puzzle : discoveries. Then Blow made a game ABOUT discoveries, and again, through the gameplay.
If you consider Talos puzzles as "room" where you move lasers, block distrubtions, rewind time and Portal as Puzzles where you change speed, jump or teleport to go to places.
And if you consider The Witness puzzles as "lines" you can draw.

This game is brutally difficult, but complete fair. You have to really master its mechanics in order to advance. The music is great and the pixel art backgrounds are beautiful. Some of the platforming reminds me of Super Meat Boy, but with fun combat system.

Stylized art, use of combos, over-the-top platforming tactics, cool particle system (GORE), sound FX, and music.
And while all of that is cool, the premise of the game revolves around one elements and like with most games that are centered around one element that sole element is going not to keep gamers coming back for very long.
As you might have guessed I am referring to the over-use of carnage.
Once the novelty of the carnage wares off, the overwhelming difficulty sets in and the player becomes brutality aware of the frustration and punishing platforming difficulity.
The other three elements I refer to are the riducliously difficult platforming, the Lovecraftin themes and story, and the use of pickups to deterrmine the placement of save-spots
Now you might argue that there is more than one element to this game, and I would agree.
but the fact is the game revoles only one of thos elements. Carnage. Everything you do results in the over-use of blood shaed and flaying body parts. There is next to zero story so any change of an RPG is out the window.
Allow me to break each of these elements down you.
1. Lovecraftin themes and cut-scenes. Yay.. nothing new there.
2. Heart-based HP meter. An all-together bad idea.
First , it is so uniginal that the use of them is becoming cliche and speaks of an amatuer dev who copies what other people did.
Second, just because three points of life was enough to start with Zelda, does not mean that 3 hearts is enough for They Bleed Pixels or whatever game you can dream up.
The boys who made this game might as well have given the player only one heart, because three isn't enough to get anywhere with. I constantly found myself giving up everytme I got injuried from the ice and spiked walls, because I knew that once I got passed them, I would not last long.
3. The use of pickups to deterrmine the placement of save-spots.
Whether this is a new idea or or so rare that I have never seen it before, the point is that a new idea doesn't not mean a good idea.
While it is unique the problem lies in...
A) if the player does lot do combos the player's save points become to close together to realy make any difference.
B) If the save point is created right before an extremely hard area that doesn't have enough blood around to ensure a save point after that area the player is forced to redo those extremely hard areas again and again and again and again.
Thus the player could easily spend 30 minutes on just one section of one level,
4. Like a lot of developers (both indie and professional) they lack the awareness of the difference between challenging/difficult and punishing/frustrating.
What many developers miss is that once a game become so difficult that it is frustrating the average playter will sto playing it and seek a refund.
An element that devs often miss when making a game stand out or unique is that their platform design or their enemies are positioned in such a way that the design iteself becomes punishing to the player.
The overall goal of any game (unless it is an expriemental game) is that the game should be beatable by the average gamer within a reasonable amount of time given the amount and length of the levels.
No average gamer should have to spend 40 minutes on the first level (or any single level for that matter) when playing a platform / sidescroller.
Having said that I have beaten severall of the hardest NES titels ever made and they were easier than this. Castlevania 3, Meganman 1 - 4, Ninja Gaiden 1 - 2, Castlevania 4 (SNES), and Super Mario World (SNES and all of its secrets ) and so on....
5. NEVER center your game around only one concept.
An example of this would to use Link 's hookshot and base a game on it.
Another examle would be to use the gravity flipping of Gravity duck and base a game on it.
Another is too center your game around carnage, espicially in this case given that once the novelty wares of so does the time spent playing it.
Games should be multi-faceted.
This is a classic example of 'how not to make a game'.

There's a big problem with They Bleed Pixels, that I don't really find in any other games. I love how it looks, the music is great, and the controls are really good as well, but those aren't the big problem for me.
I'm all for difficulty in games, and I have fully completed multiple considered insanely hard platformer games. They Bleed Pixels, however, goes too far with it. Even the first levels are very hard and will take experienced people a big amount of time. By the time I got to the fourth level, the platforming was already so unforgiving I got really frustrated. This isn't just the game being hard, but I felt like the level design was so particularly made to be unforgiving and unfair that it completely killed the game.
The rate this game introduces new unforgiving mechanics and expects you to get used to them is unreasonable as well, and doesn't help the whole case.
If you think that you can look past flatout unfair difficulty such as this, feel free to get this. It isn't for me, though.

They Bleed Pixels is a difficult platformer inspired by classic horror books such as Call of Cthulhu. Keep in mind, this game is not for everyone. The difficulty can be a real turn off, but if you enjoy that challenge, this game will be a delight to play. Skip to the end for the summary.
The pixel art here is very well made. Everything from the character to the platforms have an unnerving aesthetic, with black being the main color in almost all the objects. All the levels have a big difference in the way they look, ranging from a factory to an ocean. Most of the levels looks good, except for 1 or 2 where the backgrounds are just bland. One of the best parts of the pixel art is without a doubt the blood. Kicking enemies into saw blades turns them into an explosion of gore, getting on the floor and walls and changing the way the level looks. There's not much else to say about the graphics other than that they look good.
SCORE 8/10
The game mostly revolves around platforming and combat. Neither of these tasks are too easy, and become even more difficult when you have to do both at the same time. Platforming feels tight and the amount of mobility moves you have at your disposal are great. However, the controls will sometimes feel unresponsive, especially trying to jump while sliding on a wall. There are a few enemy types, but only two out of the four feel unique. Combat is fun, but you use one button for every attack, which can sometimes lead to you doing the wrong attack and dying. Speaking of dying, you will be doing that
. The game is certainly not easy. Most jumps require frame perfect manuevers, and those get complicated when there are enemies flying around you looking to ruin your day. One of the very fair things about the difficulty is the checkpoint system. Depending on how you kill the enemies and how many pickups you find, you will unlock a checkpoint, which you can place anywhere that isn't around enemies or objects like saws. This is way better than a regular checkpoint system because you can try to get past an obstacle to place your checkpoint, or play it safe and place it before going in. The combat alone isn't too difficult unless you're fighting on ice, which is probably my least favorite obstacle in the game, for every move you make will send you flying across the map. But if you ever find the game too hard on the regular difficulty, you can always switch to the easier difficulty. Now don't think this is an "easy" difficult, it's simply easier than the regular game, you will still die plenty of times. I had to switch to this difficulty about 3/4ths of the way in because the last levels are truly pure hell (do them if you want a real challenge).  The only downside of using the easier difficulty is you don't get to play the final level. The biggest flaw of this game is just how short it is. The game is about 4-6 hours long for a normal playthrough, obviously much longer if you're looking to get the achievements.
SCORE 8/10
While there is a story, it is told through short cutscenes without much explanation. The cutscenes show a girl arriving at a "School for Troubled Young Ladies" and then proceeds to get her dreams haunted by a cursed book. All the levels are her dreams and trying to escape from them. I really think there could've been potential with the story, too bad no-one followed up on it. I will not set a score for this.
There is a lot of replay value for people looking to get all the achievements, a total of 150 achievements to be found. Most of these require you to go back and play the levels and do things like not die, kill all the enemies, or finish the level under a certain time. Other than that, there a few bonus levels that the devs added in. These levels are pretty good and way different than the original game. One has you collecting ponies with everything trying to be as "kid-friendly" as possible. It would be nice if there was a workshop feature where people could make their own levels, but whatever. Other than that though, there really isn't a reason to replay this game.
SCORE 7/10
The sound effects in this game are mediocre, and there aren't that many. Attacking sounds kind of bland, as all of the other sound effects. The soundtrack is good, but the songs sound too similar. When I was playing this game, I genuinely thought that the game was just using the same song over and over again. Audio isn't the strongest part of this game that's for sure.
SCORE 6/10

I'm torn on this one.
I love the game, and I love the original. This is a great continuation of the series, it has huge high points, but its flaws are much, much worse.
So I enjoy the fighting. Many of the characters seem to be directly ported from the original, with one or two moves added/removed/changed a little, and most have new unique character powers that work much better in fights than the originals. The new characters fit in well, and have unique playstyles and powers from the first (with just a little recycling like Poison Ivy having one of Killer Frost's old moves.)
The graphics are beautiful, it's a stunning game visually and it really brings the characters to life. So many of the characters look way more distinct, unlike the first where most female characters looked like they had their faces copy pasted, and Wonder Woman looked like a dude.
A big personal issue for me is players. This is a PC fighter game. I am in Australia. The game has a gear system that changes your stats and can even add or change special moves, and naturally you have the option to queue without gear affecting gameplay against other players. But for me it's less of a matter of "Do I feel like playing competitive mode, or king of the hill, or ranked sets?" and more of an issue of "Is anyone queueing for any game mode? At all? Anywhere?" and then when I find a match it's usually a stomp cos there's just one guy queueing with gear on. I swear I've never seen a game of King of the Hill.
A major issue for me is the AI opponents. The standard "arcade mode" boss is dumb. Don't get me wrong, I like a strong/difficult boss. Superman from the first game was always an intense fight, but this one is just bad. Rather than make the AI smart or make his moves hit a little harder, he instead has moves that the regular character doesn't have, summoning fullscreen unblockable attacks that hit for 25% of your health, have a second attack taking that up to 50% max HP, and have no cooldown, so he can just do that again and kill you outright. He isn't difficult to fight, he is just cheap. That's the start of the issues. The "high level" AI blatantly cheats. This isn't "whaa I got outplayed," it's well documented online with anti air attacks being started before your hero even leaves the ground when you hit jump, perfectly juggling you with moves that a human couldn't possibly input in time and sitting at range spamming the same attack over and over again. Try to hit them with a ranged attack? Nope, they'll swap to a fullscreen ranged attack just at the right time to cancel yours. Try to close the gap a little? Nope, Wonder Woman throws her massive range whip that hits you if you're doing anything except crounching in the furthest corner, pulling you in then throwing you back to the same spot for the spam to start again. Seriously, whoever tested this AI and went "yep, that's what I wanted" was either braindamaged or a sadistic monster. This game adds an AI option for the player; gear up your character and send them to fight for you, and many people recommend this against more difficult bosses. That's nice and all, but I want to PLAY my game, not watch it play itself.
The gear system is bit of a mixed bag. In terms of gameplay it's fun. Taking too much damage? Increase your character's defense and health. Hitting like a wet rag? Go for more strength and ability points. There's the option to disable/balance levels and gear when playing against other players so there's no issue there. (For those who can actually find a match.) The main issue I have is aesthetics. Injustice 1 only had skins; classic looks for the characters from throughout the ages. Iconic comic looks, movie skins, alternate game skins. It'd be great if they'd learnt from this. Nobody was ever going "Yay I unlocked Harley's costume from the story mode, it's so cool," they were excited for Arkham skins, her classic jester outfit, etc. Injustice 2 has 9 "premier skins" which replace the character altogether with an alternate character who suits the same moveset, like Mr. Freeze replacing Captain Cold, Vixen replacing Cheetah, Black Lightning replacing Raiden. These are great because they're only cosmetic but add another set of characters to the game that would otherwise be impossible to add while remaining distinct from their counterparts. Unfortunately those skins can't use the cosmetic side of gear, and the system is wasted on them, and one isn't even possible to unlock on PC right now as you can't connect to the mobile game yet. The gear system divides each character into 5 slots, and almost all different customisations are unique designs made for this game. Unfortunately, the devs have clearly put way more effort into some characters over the rest of the cast. Batman has a tonne of batsuits, all of which look completely distinct from each other, but Poison Ivy can only slightly change the types of leaves dotted in her unchangeable hairstyle. Supergirl doesn't even have a classic longer hair cosmetic and has to use the weird bob they've given her. Other characters are in a midpoint, like Harley. She has lots of customisation, but they're ugly as all hell. Her hair is almost always died black and red, which would be alright, except all characters come with different colour schemes to put on gear, but they don't affect hair which makes her clash with herself, and so many of the unique designs are really atrocious jester hats that look legitimately awful. On top of these issues, some colour schemes, as well as the premier skins, are locked behind "source crystals," the ingame currency earnt for increasing your profile level. However the amount you get is so low you will almost certainly never unlock all the colour schemes without dumping a tonne of real money on the game (you know, after you've already spent $80 to have the game + DLC.) Yes, these are only cosmetic changes, but a game that costs this much money demanding even more just to have the cosmetics unlocked is ridiculously greedy. It's basically a free-to-play game's model of money making in a game that's already made more money than it should have.
So some bigger positives; guilds exist. Teaming up with players around the world, working together to take on challenges and earn shared rewards. There's really no downside (as long as the guild leader removes people who are just there to leech the rewards.) I was lucky enough to play day 1 and make a guild, having it take off very successfully.
The story is pretty great, a natural continuation of the original, and while the ending is fairly obvious for any player, it's still a great journey to get there.
So honestly I really have to put this one in the "only buy it on sale" category. I love it, but it costs a lot of money, expects you to spend more on top of that to have the full roster, expects you to spend more than that on hats, and then the single player side will almost certainly have you raging at the broken AI at some point.

Upon completing the Longest Journey, I wasn't surprised it constantly gets ranked in top PC game lists.
Clocking in at a solid 25 hours, it will keep you entertained for quite a while. You do have to put yourself into the Click and Point Adventure mindset however, as it is by no means, a fast paced game. It's more like an interactive book.
The game for me shined the most in its dialogue. Nearly every character has an incredibly natural enunciation rarely found in games. It gives you a stronger connection with them, and helps you believe every word.
The next best parts of the Longest Journey was its story and variety of characters. It takes place in the 23rd century Venice, and gives a fascinating perspective of the past, present, and future. With a story as interesting as this, that's all I can really say without spoiling anything.
The characters feature a wide range of tallent and personallity, which makes them so interesting to talk to. By the first sentence someone utters, you already know what kind of person he/she is, and how he/she is going to treat you, it really is that detailed.
For a game stuck in 640x480 resolution, it is full of very detailed and beautiful scenery. 3D objects are pretty pixelated and jaggy, and are probably the thing that aged the worst. Some up-resing would benefit The Longest Journey pretty well, but I quickly became lost in everything else it had to offer, that the quality rarely bothered me.
The puzzles as well can be pretty cryptic. I had to look up a guild many times to figure out what to do next. That didn't bother me too much either, but it would have been nice if the main character gave hits on what to do.
I am currently working through the sequel, Dreamfall, which early on already has reoccuring characters and locations, and because it came out 6 years after the first, it's nice to see things in better detail.
If you want a less action oriented experience that feels like a mix of an interactive painting and a best selling novel, I highly recommend picking up the double pack. With a promising 3rd installment in the works, how can you go wrong?

-The world presented in the longest journey is extremly detailed and interesting, tons of depth.  If you like to take your time an experience the world of your games, then this one won't let you down
- The story is exciting and engrossing, lots of twists and turns.
- The game has a great sense of humor, but it doesn't take away from the serious aspects of the game at all
-A game that is actually well written, what a surprise.
I don't really want to spoil any plot elements, I sugest you just jump right in and don't look back.
But of course the game isn't perfect, it falls into some of the same problems a lot of older adventure games faced.
cons:
-Solutions to some puzzles and just absurd or nonsense.
-lots of running back and forth especially early in the game, especially if you happened to miss an item you were meant to pick up along the way (trust me you will)
-Graphics, the game is old you can't fault it that much.
- Movement feels kind of clunky, it's not that big of a deal, but might as well mention it.
Overall I think the pros outweigh the cons greatly in this game, and it is worth looking into for anyone that appreciates good stories in games.

This is the first expansion to Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War. It was very interesting moving on to this one after spending many many hours playing the original bare-bones game.
Many changes, including an improved building location system, reworking the Chaos, and new units and unit changes.
The changes are good for the most part, but some of the changes are really bizarre, like most of what has happened to the Chaos. Chaos Predators now cannot be upgraded with anti-vehicle normally anymore, Chaos Space Marines can now only have heavy bolter weapon upgrades, and the most strange is that the Horror Squad is now primarily effective against vehicles instead of heavy infantry.
The A.I. also see an improvement in this game compared to the original. Much smarter, and much more difficult and fast.
And, of course, we see a brand new race to choose from in this expansion: the Imperial Guard. They appear much like Orks in the sense that they rely on numbers and buildings, but are weaker in terms of health like the Eldar. However, something that makes the Imperial Guard very strong, is their vehicles. Many to chose from, and very powerful. Vehicle lovers will greatly enjoy this race to play as.
Overall, fantastic expansion. New campaign, new maps, new units, and a new race to play as. Lovers of the original game will love this one just as well, if not more.

A simple review:  For a more oldschool gamer such as myself, Star Conflict brings to mind such classic space sims as X-wing series, Starlancer, and Freelancer - games I still enjoy to this day.
The atmosphere is impressive, both on the scale of the playing areas, and the soundtrack.  however, some of the sound effects have more business being in games that invovle an actual atmostphere and not the vacuum of space. Even one of my projectile weapons (one designed to be something like a shotgun for starfighters) sounds like an old shotgun sound effect.
Graphically speaking, the game is simply beautiful, although the scenery outside the actual playing fields don't change much - you only notice this when flying in the new open space "invasion" mode.  In the PvE and PvP modes, which are much more faster paced and hectic, it won't be an issue.
Game play is relatively balanced, and constantly being tweaked, controls are fine tuned and adjustable, and the game can be effectively played with keyboard and mouse, gamepad, or joystick.
If your pace is more MMO style, you can explore the relatively vast reaches of invasion space - the open world portion of the game.  For me, a guy who's perfectly content to explore this space in search of loot and crafting material, it stops just a little short of being fullfilling.  The mining opportunities are small, and the risks far outweigh the rewards, though considering the company seems to be pushing for more players to join the Invasion part of the game, as well as the crafting set up, this may change in the future.
For clans, or "corporations" there is the conflict area of the game, where you and your corp fight for territory between the three main factions.  Can't say I've played this one yet, because a certain rank of ship is required, which is a shame...because it's the part of the game I was most excited for.
overall, the game is much more than satisfying and enjoyable, constantly evolving - for better or worse, with an active support team involved in the game community, can't ask for much more than that.

This game is pleasant and addictive but it's beyond infuriating.
That being said, I would still reccommend it.
Note: I'm writing this, but I'm done with the game at all. Because it's hard.
Story: Not much to be honest, not that I was expecting much. Still, they took the time to add something rather than just slap levels in it. The segments also have well-done art.
Gameplay: Infuriating, addicting, soooo difficult. I'm not a hardcore gamer and I don't exclusively play platformers so I found this frustrating. Despite all that, I found myself coming back for more toture multiple times. This game makes you into a masochist.
There are always new mechanics being thrown in too and they get more difficult as you go. Levels tend to have re-peating mechanics & characters so that you get used to it in one level, then they murder your soul with whatever they bring out next while simoultaneously sending you into a relapse of horror from the earlier levels. I do enjoy how the levels aren't really repetive. As least that way if I'm struggling with something, I won't run into the exact same problem after completing a stretch of something like those damn ice platforms.
Also, there is a collection system if you need an extra challenge (HA....hahah...*cries*). The perfectionist in my cries at the pages as I realize that I missed one, but also just completed a segment for the first time in about 15 deaths and only need one more kill for a checkpoint.
The save points are a great idea. You can place them anywhere if you get enough blood, some from the environment and some from enemies. I think this really helps because you can be good either at getting to and killing lots of enemies or travelling the environment well and can still get a save point on the map. There is almost always a good space to place them too. There seem to be good spots spaced out in the areas that are about the time that an average player *cough* me *cough* would have enough blood to save.
Controls: I loved the controls. I think they are considered what most people would call 'elegant'. They say it's better with a controller, but I still wholeheartedly enjoyed it and could play fine on a keyboard. I just love how they used the controls, though I'm sure some people might find the controls 'icky' as they use the z,x, and arrow keys. I just love how they do so much with so few keys.
Art: I like it. It's cute and pixely and full of blood (and two of those things reflect the titlel). I really enjoy the animations and the backgrounds. The enemies aren't all super fancy or anything, but they reflect the kind of enemy they are and easily recognized. Also, the backgrounds will change per level. And there is a different background every level.
Music: So catchy. Yet another thing to love. Depends on the player's taste, but I wholeheartedly enjoy it.
Pros:
+Fun
+Addicting
+Great music
+Great controls (probably hit or miss for this one though)
+Pleasant art
+Different environments
+Variations in challenges
+Levels aren't repetetive (unless you count when dying a lot that is)
+Lots of blood
+Have a novice mode.
+Usually suuuper cheap during summer/winter sales
+Mother♥♥♥♥ing written in C
Cons:
-For some, the difficulty. I'm having problems finishing the game. But then again, that's probably because I subbornly refuse to play on novice mode.
-For some, the controls
Score 8/10

In many ways I don't feel qualified to write about this game. First of all I cheated. Out of the 300 puzzles I cleared to finish this game (out of about 700, I believe) I had to look up solutions for maybe 5-10% of that. Therein lies the shame, and the act of playing into the developer's hand of being an illogical being, driven by comfort rather than intellectual curiosity. Games have long conditioned us to look for help if we are stuck and to fully resort to the helping hand in such a predicament; this instead of our own ability or logic. Realizing this you are swiftly thrown into discomfort, playing The Witness. Because the game has a logic to it, but you can only rely on yourself to figure out the system in play. The mechanics are obscured by non-knowledge, but that's what makes this game so unique, and what constitutes its elegance and beauty as a game.
I can't say that I have played a game that has required as much of me as The Witness. It requires trust and dedication, trusting that the game is working properly, that when you do not know something, that is what the game intends. And the only way a game can pull something like that off is with having absolutely impeccable game-design. There can't be any tricking of the player, in any sense. Blow mentions in an interview that he does not want to trick the player into feeling smart, which he never does with this game, but more so I think it's important to not trick the player into feeling dumb. Once a player start to doubt his or her own ability to solve something due to a lack of information, it's over. But even in this regard I think that The Witness succeeds in making the player feel like the answer of any puzzle lies within the game itself. My problems mainly arose when I knew that I didn't know, because I knew I disregarded certain places of the game where I felt like I couldn't grasp the logical rule-sets, or where I couldn't get over the leaps of logic even after I looked up solutions for certain puzzles. I conceded, there was no real trust in my own ability. That and my impatience lead to a certain mistrust of the game. But with this view back on myself, I see that the problem is not with the game-design, it is with me.
Because I can't stress this enough, this game is elegant in a way I have never seen before. It is a self-sufficient game. It's cyclical, it is an exercise in the Nietzschean return. Repetition of fleeting activities, grasping at shadows of pleasure, the attempt to make something out of nothing, personal progression, are all parts of this game. Narratively, visually and according to the mechanics we are witnessing the eternal return of our activities as human beings, our purpose as lifeforms. The Witness adumbrates a great deal of humanity, an intimacy that becomes so much closer despite the distance required when viewing ourselves existentially. The Witness is this incredible holistic experience that encapsulates the art of game-design without profusion. It is clinical, precise and executed perfectly, which you will notice with enough trust in the game-design and with enough appreciation for game-creation.
At the heart of this game – what is really the core of this experience, to me – is what goes on in your head, and what this game requires of you as a person; as a mind among minds, as a human being with intelligence. What I noticed fairly early on was my desperate need to vocalize the principles that each puzzle was run by. I had to vocalize this intuitively logical puzzle, just to wrap my head around what was required. This is not something I've ever really experienced before in games, and I was surprised to see it come out in a medium that is not often lauded for its intellectuality. Because this process of vocalizing or making conscious and intuitive form of intelligence puts it in the view of self-conscious scrutiny. This is a quality that can be very valuable for people in general, and in its own way The Witness has the possibility of teaching it.
What I referred to earlier in terms of elegance, was in regards to the game-design, puzzle-design and the comportment of this game. This elegant restraint and non-compromise with the idiocy of the gamer's conditioned need for help, bleeds into its over all presentation. There is almost no music or extravagant sound-design, but runs the gamut of beautifully suiting each situation with an aural atmosphere that never feels empty nor mawkishly musical. It's this portrayal of life as “doing”, as functionality and concreteness. Every sound has its place, it springs out of the movement of the player and has a natural flow to it that in accordance with the visuals manage to structure a believable holistic world. Every facet goes with the theme of an encapsulation of being within something very fleeting, finding familiarity in a world that you're thrown into and out of, at least for the moment being. While this is the attempt, at least seemingly, it is hindered by self-hatred spawned out of inability. That is, however, limited to the dynamics of the individual, to what is deemed subjective.
The Witness succeeds in creating a stimulating world in all senses of that word, to all senses. In terms of visuals, I struggle to think of a game I think is more beautiful than this. In terms of composition, level design, environment, colors and lighting, it's out of this world, but more worldly than most games. There is this marriage between naturalism and human influence, between nature and machine, between natural colors and vibrant neon, between vocalized LOGIC AND VISUAL CUES.
When I get some time I am going to revisit this game with a fresh mind. I am not going to look up solutions and I am going to wholly dedicate myself to this experience. The Witness is incredible, and unless this game spawns a trend of games following in its footsteps, we will most likely not see anything quite like this in a very long time. I'm the type of person to be subjugated under things I consider to be more intelligent than me, and this game falls under that category. That means I am naturally inclined to praise it, solely due to the fact of it being “above me”. I have yet to master this game, even though I have beaten it, I don't feel like I have beaten it, and I that alone makes me impressed. I do not feel finished with the game, I couldn't happily move on from this game. Because I know there is more to it. I know there is more to learn and that curiosity will drive me back to this experience. And I think that is special. Especially special enough to warrant a recommendation.
I believe this is a game where the more time you dedicate to it the better it gets and the more fulfilling it becomes. It simulates and portrays the essence of human – even personal – progression in so many ways and so perfectly, and it has so many moments of beauty and immense respect before the creator. If If I were to inhabit this world as my only existence I'd bow down in eternal love for its creator. I respect this creation and most of all I appreciated the experience. It was okay.

Initial Thoughts on The Witness:
This game is amazing. I've only played for 6 hours so far and it has, quite literally, surpassed every expectation I had going in and, interestingly enough, scratched an itch for immersive puzzles that I didn't know I had. The game is beautiful, one of the most beautiful games I've played, but not in the sense of graphical prowsess but in the sense that it really feels as though someone laboured both time and love into sculpting this island (though, in having said that, graphically this game runs like a dream and looks the part (for specs and FPS, check bottom of preliminary review).
This is one of those games where I, in good concious, can't spoil or talk about any of the puzzles or what occurs in the game for that would do a great disservice to the experience. All I can say is that if you like puzzles (and, yes, they are varried -- even if they all essentially are the same breed) and if you like immersive experiences, please play this game and please do not spoil it for yourself. This is an experience that needs to be your own. I can't wait to jump back in and see what else I learn.
Thoughts on Performance:
The game consistently runs well at 60fps (on the high setting) with a GTX970m, i7-4720HQ (2.6ghz) with 8gb RAM loaded from SSD at 1920x1080. Runs fluidly and smoothly and beautifully. A great PC game.
Recommended for:
Anyone who likes puzzlers. This is, at the very core, and exploratory puzzle game. I'm not sure if there is a legitimate narrative but that isn't what is gripping about this game. You create the narrative with your exploration and puzzle-solving. Do not buy this game if you wanted a game like MYST or a game that isn't fundamentally a puzzle game. The price tag is a bit steep for a puzzle game, yes, but it has been worth it for me so far. Wait for a sale if you are on the fence about the title but this has been one of my personal favourites for the past year.
If you like puzzle games, you must play this game.

I was worried following the development of this as to how a full game was going to be genuinely enjoyable whilst consisting of solely line drawing puzzles. I was even more concerned how it was going stack up against the brilliant Braid.
I shouldn't have doubted Mr Blow for a second who has once again proven himself incredibly capable both of creating fiendishly difficult puzzles but also of excellent game design by having really well crafted "tutorial" sections that ease you in with the fundamentals without ever having to outright tell you anything but also by having an open-world approach so that should you find yourself completely stuck you can wander off to another puzzle and try again later. The ways the same basic puzzle has been expanded upon and altered for different sections are so imaginative and really rewarding to crack. Also, the whole thing is absolutely gorgeous and the sound design is also excellent.
You absolutely need to be prepared to use your brain (and quite possibly a pen and paper to help in some cases) but if you do enjoy a mental challenge then this is an excellent game to pick up.

With more than 25+ hours of adventure, The Longest Journey certainly lives up to its title--man this game is long winded. Overall, this is a fantastic fantasy point-and-click adventure, although the beginning doesn't really do a good job at being captivating so I'm sure a lot of players quit prematurely never actually giving it a chance. I also got a little fatigued near the end as well, but by that time there was no way I was bailing out. Now I'm actually getting excited to play the sequel and also to learn about the upcoming 3rd episode due in 2014.
The one sad part is the game can only be played at 640x480 resolution and the graphics and animations did not age well making for some serious sore eyes. Thankfully, the story more than made up for it--absolutely classic.

There are a lot of stale fantasy games out there. Games about men with swords and false British accents fighting monsters and animals alongside Dwarves and Elves. Few are the games which can truly create a unique world full of unique creatures and characters, and a unique story to go along with it. The Longest Journey is proof that, if nothing else, those sword & Elf games are just being lazy.
The Longest Journey is a good title, I feel. There's plenty lot of plot, and it's pretty important. Seeing the plot through to its conclusion is also important. But in this game, I wouldn't hesistate for a moment to say that the journey is far more important than the destination. For all the characters, I can't think of one that I didn't like - hero, villain, or neutral. From an egotistical wizard, to a short-tempered and superstitious captain, to the duly unloved police force, to your ladies' bird sidekick, to Burns Flipper, they're all memorable in their own way. And all of the races you'll meet along the way - the complexly-named ones who sing to the soil, the tense-confused ones who experience their entire lives simultaneously and the flying ones who hold storytelling in one's own words to be integral to their culture, to name only a few - are so fascinating that for all the time spent learning about each of them, I'm a little bummed out that I couldn't learn more.
The places you go are as wonderful as they are mysterious, and are only made moreso by the clash between the two worlds - the technological world of Stark, and the magical world of Arcadia. When I first visited the Haven Age of Myst IV: Revelation, I was greeted with stormy skies, a rough ocean, and an upturned shipwreck, all looming ahead. Once I climbed the nearby rock and peered over the other side, I saw bright skies, and a colorful, inviting jungle. The sheer wonder of this clash stopped me solid in my tracks, leaving me to admire the sharply contrasting views for some time before finally moving on.
This is what The Longest Journey is like *all the time*. Just on a much larger scale.
The journey is indeed long, for an adventure game. It's not always entirely forgiving; there are one or two infamous moon logic-y puzzles that are sure to frustrate, but please don't let them dissuade you. Barring those moments, The Longest Journey is such a lovingly crafted adventure, full of twists and turns, technology and magic, characters and exploration, and Burns Flipper, and it's all held together by April Ryan, our caring but sarcastic protagonist. April Ryan is, in my own opinion, the best-written female character of any video game I've ever played. And it's a good thing too, given the sheer amount of dialogue she has, all vocalized perfectly by Sarah Hamilton.
I play a lot of adventure games. The Longest Journey is without a doubt one of the best I have ever played, and I cannot recommend it enough. It's creative, it's well-written, it's mostly well-voiced, the majority of the puzzles make sense, and April only looks terrifying in the FMVs. Don't be on the fence about this one. Get it.

Winter Assault often feels like the Cataclysm to Dawn of War's Homeworld; it did something different, focussed on a different faction, and aside from a few characteristics, has been ignored by the rest of the franchise.
I still didn't know much about the Warhammer 40,000 universe around when Winter Assault came out. I wasn't familiar with the lore (was I even aware that there was a lore?), and I was only just starting to appreciate the different factions. It was Winter Assault, however, that cemented how much I hated the Eldar, not just because of their over-complicated gameplay, but also their arrogance and condescension. Kudos to Games Workshop for giving me another reason for hating Elf-type races, aside from their general drippiness and flouncy-flouncy ways.
So, Winter Assault is an expansion to the original Dawn of War game, requiring the original to be installed at the same time. It adds a new playable faction, the Imperial Guard (in addition to the original Space Marine, Chaos Space Marine, Eldar and Ork factions), and adds a new unit to each faction.
Unlike every other game in Dawn of War, there are no Blood Ravens here, not even as a cameo. There are two (distinct) campaigns, one from the side of "Order" (Imperial Guard and Eldar), and "Chaos" (Chaos Space Marines and Orks), with endings for each of the four factions, depending on whom you focus on in the final mission. There's a cameo by the Ultramarines, and there's also a sneak peek at one of the factions that they added in one of the subsequent games.
Winter Assault added two characters who would return to the series, Farseer Taldeer (who'd show up in Dark Crusade, and then would get a mention in Dawn of War 2 Retribution), and Gorgutz (who'd show up in the rest of the Dawn of War games, and is due to rejoin the cast along with Taldeer in Dawn of War 3). Sadly, General Sturnn never returns to the series, even though I felt that he was the best character out of everyone. His Chaos Space Marine counterpart, Crull, however not only gets a mention in the next game, he also gets to tour the galaxy atop Gorgutz's pointy stick.
Crull, by the way, is probably amongst the worst Chaos Lords in the series, and undoubtedly leads the worst band of World Eaters in the galaxy. I'll bet they only made him a World Eater so that they would have an excuse to show off the new Khorne Beserkers, but really, they could have added any band of Chaos Undivided.
Lore nitpicking aside, Winter Assault is a lot lighter and fluffier than the original's campaign. There are a lot more set-pieces in the missions to showcase the various abilities of the units (especially for the Imperial Guard). I think Relic wanted a Starcraft beating tournament-style RTS, shame they couldn't get the game balance quite right.
Overall, if you're going to play the original game (and why wouldn't you), I'd add Winter Assault to the mix. It's a good campaign that's overshadowed by the first and third games, and wasn't horrible enough to get Soulstorm's (bad) publicity.
