This War of Mine is an enjoyable game. I wouldn't call it "fun" because of the serious subject matter. If you are highly empathetic, you might find it difficult to play. I guess I am not that empathetic because I don't really feel emotional pain from the game at all. I have about 100 hours of gameplay right now, so I think I have definitely gotten my money's worth.
--------- Main Reasons why I enjoy this game ---------
1. The scavenging runs at night can be exhilarating. Heart-pounding exhilarating. There is a timer counting down until dawn. There are serious dangers that can kill you. You are trying to balance the risks against your life with your need for resources to survive once you get back. Maybe if you don't get some food tonight, someone could die tomorrow. There is real risk for real reward. This is an important thing in a game.
2. If things go well, you slowly go from near zero resources to a well-stocked larder. There is satisfaction in that. There is a sense of accomplishment. Because the game is HARD and when you succeed it is rewarding.
--------- Things I don't enjoy as much ---------
1. The game is very slow paced during the daytime. I wish there was a way to fast-foward time without skipping all the way to end of day, but this can mean you miss things sometimes.
2. If combat goes south, it can sometimes render the game very frustrating. I think you should be able to quick-save in some way. If your scavenging character dies, the game instantly saves and goes to the next day. While I get the reasons for doing this (emotional loss of death is real), it can also be very frustrating. I have abandoned a few games after day 20 because my good scavenger(s) died and left me with only near-useless characters like Cveta or Anton. That was not fun.
--------- Description of Gameplay ---------
The game consists of a two-phase cycle of play: Home and Scavenge.
The home phase is during the daytime when you build and manage your household. There are only two maps for homes, but different starting characters will have different starting supplies and wounds/sickness to either handicap or help the player. You use four basic supplies to build different things in the home (wood, components, parts, and electronics) and then a combination of many supplies to create secondary goods. For example, weapon parts and components might be combined to create a saw blade (utility item).
The second phase is during the night when you scavenge from various locations in the city. This is the most important phase by far, since what you bring back from these adventurers will determine if your characters live or die. There are some locations in the city where you do not need utility items (saw blades, lockpicks, hatchets, shovels, etc) or weapons, but they are few and far between. The most valuable resources in the game are behind locked doors, grates, and things that require tools to get to AND/OR you must kill people defending those resources. When you get back from scavenging, there is a chance your home might have been attacked while you were away, resulting in possible wounds to the defenders and theft of some of your supplies.
This creates a cycle of interaction between the two phases. You bring home resources from the scavenging phase to use during the home phase to make tools for the scavenging phase. So there is a lot of complex interaction going on between these two phases.
The objective of the game is to survive until the end of the war (about 35-45 days of this cycle). Your characters need sleep every day, food about every two days, medicine to cure sicknesses that develop randomly, bandages to heal wounds, and warmth from a heater on cold days (requiring fuel). So these items become the core measure of success in the game; food, medicine, bandages, and firewood. If you have healthy stocks of these materials in your home, you have security. When you have minimal amounts of these supplies, you need to work hard to fix that. Otherwise, you will lose.
So there is a chain relationship between these resources. You can use a little bit of wood and some weapon parts to create a hatchet, which can be used to chop up furniture to get a LOT of lumber and firewood bits. But you have to balance that need for wood with the ability to use those weapon parts to repair a gun that might better defend your home during the scavenge phase (and thus reduce chance of wounds) or take with you on a scavenging run to kill enemies that are defending valuable goods. So you have a lot of choices about how you manage your resources towards the goal of surviving the war.
--------- Replayability ---------
As I have gotten closer to 100 hours of gameplay, things have become more routine and less enjoyable. I am losing focus and attention. I would really like more options that just the Little Ones DLC. But I don't know that the base game (as it stands right now) has a lot of replayability once you really memorize all the locations. Exploring the scavenging locations is the most fun part of the game in my opinion and once that is done, it fades a lot. This happens to most games (unless they have procedurally generated areas, which this one doesn't). So I feel this does limit replayability.
But 100 hours is a lot. The game costs as much as a movie ticket when on sale. It is worth the price for sure.
--------- Improvements ---------
Things that I would like to see implemented in a 2nd edition or a DLC (I would pay for these things).
1. New home environments (currently only 2)
2. New locations to explore during the scavenging phase (increases replayability).
3. More characters. You could do this without creating too many new character models by re-using some of the NPC models. I don't think people would even notice it.
4. More flexibility in creating custom characters (already pretty good but more options would be nice).
5. Quick save option
6. Ability to increase the speed of time passing or jump forward one hour at a time, something like that
7. Some kind of screen showing all the different options that you can use a particular resource for (ex. here is everything you can use wood for). This would help people make decisions about how to use limited resources.
8. Some kind of in-game encyclopedia function. Like the Civopedia from Civilization.

Short and Unsatisfying. The puzzles are fairly easy, or can be brute forced without much difficulty, and there are lot of loose ends with no real lead up or resolution, and the twist is unexpected but akin to finding out at the end of Myst that the main character was a Lizardman, out of nowhere and lacking any real connection to any of the previous elements.
I never actually knew or cared about why I was Leonard, why a game set in 1986, of all times, has some futuristic trappings, and while you get to see a glimpse behind the curtain of the room trap, it goes no further than that and you're railroaded all the way, barring some obscure hidden puzzle.
Puzzle solving at it's core is hunting for random stuff in the dark, and most of them are red herrings, so much so there's a cheevo for grabbing all the crap, which makes inventory management a little hard. I wish I wasn't being so dead honest about the nature of this game, it is nothing but finding junk in the dark, and finding ways to turn on the light so you can find said junk, and then using it to solve a puzzle.
I guess a good way to put how the ending makes me feel, is that I didn't really feel indoctrinated- Bioshock and White Night made you realize that you'd been playing to someone else's rules all along and hadn't noticed it, whereas this game's antagonists have a very low bar for conversion. I guess if you can solve random puzzles that have no interconnection or deeper meaning, you're okay enough for them, I guess?
Worst part is that if there's room for multiple endings, and I just got a bad one, two puzzles are so full of tedium, the lazy maze I could have coded in my sleep, and the one involving rotating 3D objects to form a 2D puzzle, which are slow, and imprecise, I'm not even interested in going back to the beginning to try something new, which I doubt exists, as the game is very linear. Even found a bug when I hit "continue" after beating the game that had me back in the locked room, with buggy access to my inventory, and forced to sit through the unskippable credits again.
Save up your money and maybe try something a bit more groundbreaking, like Layers of Fear or something.

Like the eponymous bar the game takes place in, this is a game that's flying under most people's radars, but is highly deserving of a look, if you're a certain kind of person.
Make no mistake, by and large, this game resembles a visual novel; it emphasizes writing and aesthetics, and goes so far as to do away with dialogue choices, long seen as a staple of interactivity in an otherwise linear genre. But don't take that to mean that this game has no element of non-linearity or choice - merely that it resides in mechanics which aren't usually seen that way. The gameplay is not meant to be challenging, but the writing is stimulating and compelling in ways rarely seen in this medium. Anime fans will savor the references, which can get mind numbingly obscure and are often gut-bustingly funny. Fans of story will find characters with an uncanny balance of quirks, flaws, hopes and stand-out moments that stick with you. An incredible amount of care was put into the environments and people that you meet here.
There are people who won't enjoy this game - anyone who's turned off my the anime aesthetic, or anyone looking for more cyberpunk action than cyberpunk bartending. But for those looking for a story they hadn't heard before, this is a diamond in the rough. It's about 10 hours, it has replay value and a good amount of secrets, and most importantly, it's got a personality all its own. Recommend.

If you finish the storyline, you can start a New Game + and you even get tips on how to get different endings.
As far as gameplay mechanics go, they're pretty good. It involves remembering certain characters' favourite drink and conserving cash for your upcoming bills. There is another interesting feature; at the start of most days, you will have an option to buy an item so Jill, the main protagonist, does not lose focus. This basically means that when somebody asks for a drink and the navigation menu shows itself, the text box on the bottom tells you what drink they want and perhaps any recommendations for the drinks. If you lose focus, you don't get that and are greeted with distracted thoughts, giving you no help or recommendations whatsoever. It's good if you have a good memory or know what the characters like, but if you can not remember what the person wanted, you will either have to reload the save, get the drink wrong (thus voiding your flawless service bonus) or miraculously guess the drink correctly. It's an interesting mechanic.
Graphics are great, especially for the theme of the game. Going back to PC98 surely feels good. There's also an option to activate screen lines, which is nice. Character design is well executed, too. The game sticks to its theme throughout, so no sudden HD images, they will all have a pixelated theme. I'm happy about that.
Theres nothing bad about this game if you asked me. I binge played this game until I completed the story, and I plan on starting a New Game + to get all the endings. If you like a good visual novel as well as gameplay mechanics, this is the game for you.

The game just /feels/ bad. Your inputs feel very sluggish, and this could be the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor animations and it could be the input lag for the port. The moves look, feel and sound weak for the most part.
I love the fireball game in traditional 2D fighters, but "zoning" in this game is different and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for multiple reasons:
In Street Fighter, if you read a correct fireball, you jump in, and then you're in. Often the threat of the jump is enough to think twice about throwing a fireball. In Injustice, because the screen size is so large, you often have to jump or duck over 3-4 instances of "projectiles" in order to get close enough to make the projectile a risky option for the "zoner". Also, if you fail to duck or jump one projectile, you're hit with a large amount of pushback. Projectiles also don't interact with each other or cancel each other out, meaning matches with two zoners often end up with them hitting each other full screen.
The combination of a huge screen size, knockback on projectiles, strong backdashes and no projectile clashing means that fullscreen projectile "spam" is a winning strategy. It's a shame, because once you finally fight your way into a closer range, the footsies and spacing elements are actually quite fun if you ignore the crappy animations. It's just that getting hit once and then the zoner backdashing away to expand the screen means you have to fight to get to the point where the zoner has to actually commit to an option or make a read (as opposed to just doing what's optimal).
I recommend Guilty Gear, but I understand a lot of people have reservations towards anime games (Under Night or UNIEL for short is a good gateway to anime games if you're wanting a bridge between traditional fighters and anime). Maybe just hold out for DBFZ or SFV:AE?

In many ways I don't feel qualified to write about this game. First of all I cheated. Out of the 300 puzzles I cleared to finish this game (out of about 700, I believe) I had to look up solutions for maybe 5-10% of that. Therein lies the shame, and the act of playing into the developer's hand of being an illogical being, driven by comfort rather than intellectual curiosity. Games have long conditioned us to look for help if we are stuck and to fully resort to the helping hand in such a predicament; this instead of our own ability or logic. Realizing this you are swiftly thrown into discomfort, playing The Witness. Because the game has a logic to it, but you can only rely on yourself to figure out the system in play. The mechanics are obscured by non-knowledge, but that's what makes this game so unique, and what constitutes its elegance and beauty as a game.
I can't say that I have played a game that has required as much of me as The Witness. It requires trust and dedication, trusting that the game is working properly, that when you do not know something, that is what the game intends. And the only way a game can pull something like that off is with having absolutely impeccable game-design. There can't be any tricking of the player, in any sense. Blow mentions in an interview that he does not want to trick the player into feeling smart, which he never does with this game, but more so I think it's important to not trick the player into feeling dumb. Once a player start to doubt his or her own ability to solve something due to a lack of information, it's over. But even in this regard I think that The Witness succeeds in making the player feel like the answer of any puzzle lies within the game itself. My problems mainly arose when I knew that I didn't know, because I knew I disregarded certain places of the game where I felt like I couldn't grasp the logical rule-sets, or where I couldn't get over the leaps of logic even after I looked up solutions for certain puzzles. I conceded, there was no real trust in my own ability. That and my impatience lead to a certain mistrust of the game. But with this view back on myself, I see that the problem is not with the game-design, it is with me.
Because I can't stress this enough, this game is elegant in a way I have never seen before. It is a self-sufficient game. It's cyclical, it is an exercise in the Nietzschean return. Repetition of fleeting activities, grasping at shadows of pleasure, the attempt to make something out of nothing, personal progression, are all parts of this game. Narratively, visually and according to the mechanics we are witnessing the eternal return of our activities as human beings, our purpose as lifeforms. The Witness adumbrates a great deal of humanity, an intimacy that becomes so much closer despite the distance required when viewing ourselves existentially. The Witness is this incredible holistic experience that encapsulates the art of game-design without profusion. It is clinical, precise and executed perfectly, which you will notice with enough trust in the game-design and with enough appreciation for game-creation.
At the heart of this game – what is really the core of this experience, to me – is what goes on in your head, and what this game requires of you as a person; as a mind among minds, as a human being with intelligence. What I noticed fairly early on was my desperate need to vocalize the principles that each puzzle was run by. I had to vocalize this intuitively logical puzzle, just to wrap my head around what was required. This is not something I've ever really experienced before in games, and I was surprised to see it come out in a medium that is not often lauded for its intellectuality. Because this process of vocalizing or making conscious and intuitive form of intelligence puts it in the view of self-conscious scrutiny. This is a quality that can be very valuable for people in general, and in its own way The Witness has the possibility of teaching it.
What I referred to earlier in terms of elegance, was in regards to the game-design, puzzle-design and the comportment of this game. This elegant restraint and non-compromise with the idiocy of the gamer's conditioned need for help, bleeds into its over all presentation. There is almost no music or extravagant sound-design, but runs the gamut of beautifully suiting each situation with an aural atmosphere that never feels empty nor mawkishly musical. It's this portrayal of life as “doing”, as functionality and concreteness. Every sound has its place, it springs out of the movement of the player and has a natural flow to it that in accordance with the visuals manage to structure a believable holistic world. Every facet goes with the theme of an encapsulation of being within something very fleeting, finding familiarity in a world that you're thrown into and out of, at least for the moment being. While this is the attempt, at least seemingly, it is hindered by self-hatred spawned out of inability. That is, however, limited to the dynamics of the individual, to what is deemed subjective.
The Witness succeeds in creating a stimulating world in all senses of that word, to all senses. In terms of visuals, I struggle to think of a game I think is more beautiful than this. In terms of composition, level design, environment, colors and lighting, it's out of this world, but more worldly than most games. There is this marriage between naturalism and human influence, between nature and machine, between natural colors and vibrant neon, between vocalized LOGIC AND VISUAL CUES.
When I get some time I am going to revisit this game with a fresh mind. I am not going to look up solutions and I am going to wholly dedicate myself to this experience. The Witness is incredible, and unless this game spawns a trend of games following in its footsteps, we will most likely not see anything quite like this in a very long time. I'm the type of person to be subjugated under things I consider to be more intelligent than me, and this game falls under that category. That means I am naturally inclined to praise it, solely due to the fact of it being “above me”. I have yet to master this game, even though I have beaten it, I don't feel like I have beaten it, and I that alone makes me impressed. I do not feel finished with the game, I couldn't happily move on from this game. Because I know there is more to it. I know there is more to learn and that curiosity will drive me back to this experience. And I think that is special. Especially special enough to warrant a recommendation.
I believe this is a game where the more time you dedicate to it the better it gets and the more fulfilling it becomes. It simulates and portrays the essence of human – even personal – progression in so many ways and so perfectly, and it has so many moments of beauty and immense respect before the creator. If If I were to inhabit this world as my only existence I'd bow down in eternal love for its creator. I respect this creation and most of all I appreciated the experience. It was okay.

Initial Thoughts on The Witness:
This game is amazing. I've only played for 6 hours so far and it has, quite literally, surpassed every expectation I had going in and, interestingly enough, scratched an itch for immersive puzzles that I didn't know I had. The game is beautiful, one of the most beautiful games I've played, but not in the sense of graphical prowsess but in the sense that it really feels as though someone laboured both time and love into sculpting this island (though, in having said that, graphically this game runs like a dream and looks the part (for specs and FPS, check bottom of preliminary review).
This is one of those games where I, in good concious, can't spoil or talk about any of the puzzles or what occurs in the game for that would do a great disservice to the experience. All I can say is that if you like puzzles (and, yes, they are varried -- even if they all essentially are the same breed) and if you like immersive experiences, please play this game and please do not spoil it for yourself. This is an experience that needs to be your own. I can't wait to jump back in and see what else I learn.
Thoughts on Performance:
The game consistently runs well at 60fps (on the high setting) with a GTX970m, i7-4720HQ (2.6ghz) with 8gb RAM loaded from SSD at 1920x1080. Runs fluidly and smoothly and beautifully. A great PC game.
Recommended for:

You create the narrative with your exploration and puzzle-solving. Do not buy this game if you wanted a game like MYST or a game that isn't fundamentally a puzzle game. The price tag is a bit steep for a puzzle game, yes, but it has been worth it for me so far. I shouldn't have doubted Mr Blow for a second who has once again proven himself incredibly capable both of creating fiendishly difficult puzzles but also of excellent game design by having really well crafted "tutorial" sections that ease you in with the fundamentals without ever having to outright tell you anything but also by having an open-world approach so that should you find yourself completely stuck you can wander off to another puzzle and try again later. Greetings Everyone!
Continuing along my path of reviewing every steam game I own I came to my much beloved Dawn of War Series…Okay, I cheated a bit as I was going alphabetical but with DOW3 coming out soon I decided to skip the queue and play through this again one more time in preparation.  I am a huge fan of the DOW series but I have to admit, Winter Assault is my least favorite of the bunch.
How do we get there:  It probably isn’t but pathing feels much worse, probably has to do with the design of the levels; many being smaller corridors with less room to maneuver.  Regardless, I feel that this is one of the defining issues with the series and this one felt very bad.  I’m not one to shun away from the bad simply because I like a game.
The Hammer:  The big deal of this game was the addition of the Imperial Guard, which was heavily criticized as being over powered in release.  I didn’t really care then but now I do see the importance of this, however, the next two expansions provided more (in my opinion) and I felt much of the assets were already included in the previous game.  If this was a new release I’d probably not recommend it unless you were a diehard fan simply on ‘bang for your buck.’
Something about Necrons:  I only really liked the story as it included Necrons, but ended up being annoyed by the lack of the Blood Ravens.  Yes, you will see I am heavily biased as they are my favorite chapter and feel they should always be front and center.  The missions were touted by the community as being some of the most difficult of any DOW but in my opinion this had more to do with poor implementation and not true difficulty.  With that I’d still recommend getting it if you plan to play the series in its entirety.
Overall, this game can be skipped if you are only playing for a strong RTS feel, but I feel that everyone should have this game if they enjoy the series as it may be the weakest but it is still a part of the series.  You will likely end up getting it as a bundle regardless.  Objectively it is a weak game by comparison to the others in the series however.

If I had to sum up Miko Mole in one word, it'd have to be masterpiece. This is one of the only games I can confidently say appeals to everyone. Whether it's the beautiful soundtrack, or the speechless, realistic graphics, I have to say this game will not be topped for years to come; at a price of just £3.99 I don't think the developers could be more generous.
Miko Mole focuses on a mole adamently named Miko. Miko's life has been boring and mundane, he's trying to make a living in a world dominated by a single corperation named evil corp. The most precious resource in their underground world is diamonds, most of the diamond mining is done by evil corp, anyone trespassing on their mines will be killed, that's the harsh reality of Miko's world; Miko's a brave mole who wants excitement in his life, and to live a comfortable life style. To achive his ambitions he has to infiltrate evil corps mines and snatch as many diamonds he can, along the way dealing with various unnamed threats.
Firstly, I have to pay compliments to the games soundtrack, it's enough to make you shed a tear in the most emotional moments this game will have you put through. There's been no game to this date with a soundtrack that will have you fully immersed to the point that you're unable to pay attention to the world around you.
Next, the graphics couldn't be described as anything but jaw dropping. When I first looked at the games trailer, I thought it was live action, but it was in game footage. This is a game that needs VR support; if it has it I think I'd never be able to return to this world again.
The level variation is something that has never been done before, each time you enter a new level, you're entering a new way of thinking, a new threat to face, a fresh design. You'll need to change your strategy, and utilise your tools in ways you would think you could before. Every foot you tread gives a new set of hardships to overcome and emotional moments that will leave you unable control yourself. Also every area has a new set of voices and character models that will leave you asking 'how did they do it?'
The gameplay leaves you immersed for every second, unable to look away or you'll miss something that you'll have to go back and find later, though tedious at times it's refreshing, as I've never kicked myself harder wondering 'how did I miss that?' More than I ever have playing this game.
In conclusion, Miko Mole has set the bar high for a new era of gaming, with speechless quality that will leave your jaw dropped and fully immersed in the game. This game has made history and in my opinion will never be forgotton; it will forever be recognised as the game that pushed players out of their comfort zone, our of their closed mindedness, and into a new way of thinking that will change the players mind for the rest of their lives.

Miko Mole:
~~~~~~~~
Ok, where is my orange helmet? Here it is! My backpack, my ingenious flying equipment, my cool dance moves. . .  I am pretty much set to go! Here I come, my little diamonds, my names is Miko. . . Miko the Mole, and I am on my way to become a master thief!
Miko Mole is an arcade puzzle game where you take control of a cute Mole with a tendency to like shiny rocks. The only small predicament Miko finds is that the diamonds are owned by Evil Corp and they will make it difficult for Miko to steal them.
The aim of the game is to collect a specific number of diamonds within a time limit to open the exit grid and progress to the next level. If you do that well, you will be rewarded with three golden stars and points at the end of the level. You will have plenty of obstacles to avoid, and you will also have to avoid being caught by the likes of bats and rats.

Miko Mole has six challenging worlds in which to play, consisting of 40 levels per world. A whopping 240 levels in total. I find the first world quite easy to achieve the 3 golden stars but when you move to another world, you will find it quite challenging. In some worlds, you will not only have to deal with rats, bats and other animals but you will have to be careful not be seen by cameras, and avoid lasers, sonars, machine guns, boulders and more. However, you can use the boulders to your advantage by dropping them on your enemies’ heads. Some of the worlds will have switches which trigger doors to open. Usually these switches are in the middle of four colourful lights, and next to the light you will also see levers. Activating the switch initiate a light sequence. You will need to reproduce the exact sequence by pulling the levers next to the lights.  It can become very tricky when you have flying bats all around you or machine guns shooting at you! Poor Miko . . .

In some levels, you will need to use dynamite to open a path, picking up crates or boulders that obstruct your way.
This game has cute graphics and an enjoyable soundtrack. In terms of the controls, you can use the keyboard, but I would strongly recommend using a gamepad. In my opinion the controls could have been smoother.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Cute graphics
-	240 levels and 6 worlds to beat
-	The ability to move to another world as you wish
-	Good price point
-	 Fun to play for all ages
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls could have been smoother
Miko Mole is a fun arcade puzzle game for all ages - everyone needs a cute mole in their game library!
7/10

This game captured my attention because my toddler daughter is so infatuated with the game.
Miko Mole is a clever blend of the puzzle, strategy, adventure, and platformer genre. Throughout the gargantuan amount of levels, players will face a myriad variety of challenges some of which are more difficult than others. Some levels are straightforward while others are more intricate and the difficulty does not necessarily progress in that order. Some people are complaining about the graphics, but I argue that they are adequate if not appropriate for the game. Miko and his co-stars are adorable. Additional elements are added as the game progresses which keeps the game refreshing, but they don't appear until later in the game.

Miko Mole is a casual arcade puzzler. As Miko, you strive to "steal" diamonds from an evil mega-corp (of course), becuase you can, and female moles are renowned for their love of shiny stones. Probably.
Despite not having any real USP, what Miko does, it does very well. Equipped with a rotor a lá Inspector Gadget, you can fly, dig and walk through each level, accumulating the required amount of diamonds to proceed to the next. Miko has 6 worlds, and each world has 40 levels. (That's 240 by the way. It's a lot). As each level goes by, the difficulty increases, and with each new world comes new enemies, puzzle mechanisms and abilities to ensure a continued challenge and freshness.
In terms of Steamworks, Miko offers trading cards, and a clever achievment collection that challenges users to achieve a specific target on specific levels, as well as the usual achievement for completing each level with 3/3 stars. Miko also offers full controller support.
At €4.99, Miko represents very good value, with a lot of content and replayability. It's easy to pick up, and will be popular with all ages.
Miko Mole is another Steam release from Ensenasoft, a Mexican studio with a strong catalogue of mobile titles. Miko Mole is also available on PS4.

A gripping tale of a group of strangers trying to survive in a bombed out country suffering from a seemingly ceaseless civil war. The events that occur in this game are happening to tens of thousands of people all over the world, and it's a harrowing look into what some of them have to deal with on a day to day basis.
Each decision you make can have a lasting impact on both your physical survival, and the mental health of the group as a whole, and if you invest yourself in the story, there can be some truly memorable moral choices that need to be made. Do you steal from the elderly couple, who have never done you any wrong, and threaten them at knife point to get food and medicine or go hungry for a day? Can you even wait a day? What if one of your group members is dying? There are a lot of choices that you have to rationalize with yourself after making them, and the game really makes you think about the consequences of your actions.
It's flawed certainly, and I found it a little too easy to become completely self sufficient, but otherwise the game is a fantastic look at day to day survival and morality.

I wish that I could give The Guest a horizontal thumb; an in-between recommendation. A thumbs-up feels too enthusiastic, and a thumbs-down feels a bit unfair.
The Guest is a mixture of escape-the-room, point-and-click, walking simulator, puzzle, and mystery. There are also elements of suspense and sci-fi, and the combination of all these works pretty well overall. The controls weren’t
clunky, but they could stand some refining. I will note that I experienced two technical problems, one of which could have been game-breaking. Also worth noting is that I was unable to save the game once I reached the latter half. Since I finished it that evening, it didn’t really matter to me. But if you plan on spreading this game out, beware. The Guest only takes about 3-4 hours to complete, though, so finishing it in a sitting is feasible.
I absolutely love when games are atmospheric, and The Guest is just that. From the sound effects to the lighting to the graphics, The Guest captures a certain atmosphere and doesn’t let go of it. Having said that, atmosphere is this game’s strongest point; on other fronts, it felt a bit lackluster. I enjoy a good puzzler, but I felt that these puzzles were at once too difficult and too mindless. I solved a couple of puzzles by more or less clicking randomly, and that’s just not satisfying. There’s one puzzle in particular (under the bathroom sink) that just did not make sense to me, even with the in-game “guide” to it. Maybe that’s just me being a dummy, but I would have never solved it without checking a walkthrough. The puzzles worked pretty well mechanically, but from a player’s viewpoint they were not very intuitive. They were mostly tedious, and I had a few moments of: "Am I supposed to know what to do here?". I find it hard to say that a puzzle game is objectively good when the puzzles just aren’t what they should be. With a little work, though, Team Gotham could make some really lovely puzzles.
Story-wise, I felt a bit cheated. There's a fine line between mysteriousness and vagueness, and The Guest unfortunately crosses over to the wrong side of that line. There are questions about the world and characters and plot that we just don’t get answers to. The material is undoubtedly
, it just isn't brought to its full potential. The premise is gripping, but it's not fleshed out as much as it should be, leaving players with more of a skeleton than a meaty game. Truth be told, I really do want to see a sequel to this game, where the puzzles and controls are more refined and the story is more prevalent and better developed. If Team Gotham makes a sequel, I’ll be playing it. And if I’m not mistaken, The Guest is their first project; for a first project, this is a solid and respectable effort. (And if you’re into achievements, there are some easy ones and some hard ones. I enjoyed the achievements a lot, even though I couldn’t get some of them.)
In the end, The Guest left me wanting more. Sometimes for the wrong reasons, sometimes (maybe mostly?) for the right ones. I’ve chosen to give this game a thumbs-up because I did overall enjoy my experience, and I appreciate this game for what it is. I feel a bit disappointed in it, and I can absolutely see its fault, but it’s not bad. If you’re willing to take a $10 risk, buy The Guest. You might be disappointed, but you’ll probably be appreciative. It’s worth it for the beautifully crafted atmosphere if nothing else.

It pains me to give this a negative review, but I was left feeling so underwhelmed.
I LOVE Room Escape games. From The Room to Submachine and every free Flash game in between - if it has intriguing, logical puzzles then I'll be glad to play. A room escape with an intriguing story line and detailed graphics? Hell yes, I'm sold.
The puzzles were... fine. None of them really challenging for a seasoned puzzle addict, more a case of hunting around for the bits you need and putting two & two together. Solid, but not spectacular. Mechanically, they were extremely well implemented, and integrated into the world, and for that I do congratulate the developers - the influence of The Room is clear. One in particular - involving aligning markings to form a pattern - was elegant and truly innovative.
But the game falls down hard in the extras that it promises. Without wishing to spoil anything, I found the writing to be clumsy, tired and directionless. It starts as a mystery and smudges seamlessly into the worst of tired tropes, without really making any sense in between. The puzzles and the story don't mesh together in any way - you're told what the arbitrary challenges were for, in-world, but at the same time they're presented as far deeper and more insidious than they are. (Using blunt sinister thematic keywords as passwords is sitll arbitrary - change the theme to Lovecraftian horror and replace the puzzle answers with "DAGON" and "RLYEH" and nothing is lost, see?)
The writing, in short, was a thin thematic skin and nothing more. Which would've been easy to brush off if it hadn't been such a clumsy cultural throwback too. It was like a Mcarthyite fever dream. 1984 for kids. Given the rich detail of the assets and lighting, the theming was all the more jarring.
The other big problem was the mechanical immersion. Having the game be first-person is such an interesting and unusual tool for puzzle makers (cf The Witness, Portal, Perspective, FRACT) that, sadly, only ever served to get in the way of this game. Stumbling around furniture in the dark isn't tense or fun, it's just annoying. Not being able to see properly into drawers & cupboards makes the object hunting a chore. Both these problems are nonexistent in room-escape Flash games, but are introduced by using first person perspective. It was a bold move that didn't pay off.
And the labyrinth, my god, the labyrinth.
The labyrinth really exemplified the problem I had with this game. It wasn't fun. It wasn't challenging. It wasn't tense. It didn't communicate anything about the character, the world, the game mechanics, it wasn't a puzzle or a significant storytelling device, it was nothing. Nothing but a tedious 5m+ trial-and-error walk through a blocky corridor, rendered in quite pretty atmospheric lighting. I just don't see what the developers were trying to achieve or communicate through that device. I don't see why they thought it was a good idea. It was an incongruous, boring intermission.
It was a gimmick, not a new or clever one, and it made no sense, didn't tie in thematically or mechanically to anything else, did nothing but frustrate and distract. What was the point?
I played the game through in a couple of hours, and enjoyed the puzzles well enough in spite of the problems I've stated. But while I could've played the puzzles quite happily for another two hours, the theme, the 1st-person mechanics, the writing, all would've annoyed me more and more. It ended when it had to, and left no impact in the process.
The developers clearly have real talent with regards to building a solid, pretty, functional game, and I hate to imagine that this review might discourage them from pursuing that. They have good ideas, solid mechanical competence, and I want to see more. I just feel like they never had anyone sit down with a critical eye and ask them, "What is this bit for? What are you trying to accomplish there? What are you hoping to make the player think or feel? Do any of these elements support each other, or are they just thrown in to fill the gaps?" Some good writing and creative direction could've turned this game into a little gem, but it's not a gem. It's coal. Solid, functional, unexciting - burn it up and it's gone, leaving nothing behind.
I'm not angry, just disappointed.

This is the first game I have felt compelled to write a review for.  I purchased it as part of the Elegent Engineering bundle a short while back.  Quite addcitive, it's like the Swiss-watch of puzzlers.  On the face of it beautifully simple, yet you know the inner workings are intricate and complex.  Each time you play you glimpse at your previous best score comprising of how many days in operation and the amount of passenger journeys completed for that particular map.  Daring you to do better!
Also, no two games are ever the same and different aspects can catch you out if you’re not on the ball.  Be it station overcrowding from a new special stop appearing on the map, stretching a rail line a stop too far or running out of Locos, bridges or tunnels.  It forces you to think and look at how to optimise your railways.  You can set the direction of travel or your Locos, how they intersect, increase carriages and later on introduce newer high-speed Locos.
As your rail network grows you notice every tiny impact that affects your passengers journey, you find yourself trying to cover all bases while engineering in a little wiggle room for expansion.  Too many stops will slow a Locos journey if it’s heading towards a busy Interchange or bottle neck.  Not enough carriage space and they will simply speed by stations not picking anyone up, leaving passengers hopping mad.
But don’t worry, even if you fail, you can still rail!  When a game ends in normal mode you have the option to play on in some kind of Zen state of endless network rail management.  I've since purchased this game for mobile, it's a great game to lose a few minutes or a few hours to and quite therapeutic.
I’ve not yet found a map maker or any such option or tool, which would be nice for the community to also make maps, I’m not concerned about this yet myself as I’m a long way from completion.  Also worth a mention is the night mode, which is an absolute god send for those with sensitive eyes and will darken the screen nicely.
Overall a lovely, well-crafted enjoyable game.
Highly recommended!

Wow... What can be said about this game? It is perhaps not a masterpiece, but it is definitely something I cannot call a large majority of other games. It is simply a treat. Despite the lack of refined technology at the time it was released, never have I experienced a story so engaging or characters so vibrant, varied, and alive. If you are looking to be challenged, the puzzles you come across aren't terribly difficult or anything, but they are well-thought out and are very appropriate to the numerous settings you encounter them in. In addition to the amazing concept art and backgrounds, the voice acting is also surprisingly good.
This game really set the standard for click-and-point adventure games -- a genre that is often getting overshadowed by fast-paced shooters and high-action hack-and-slashers these days. There is indeed a reason its Metacritic score is so high. This is a beautiful game that was lovingly crafted. I would go so far as to say that it's nearly more than a game. It's an experience... and one that needs to be had. It does many things that present-day games too often lack, and it does them well.

This War of Mine realistically depicts what civilians have to go through just to survive. Shying away from the typical perspective for war games which is usually that of a soldier's, it tests players in ways that will leave them shocked or depressed (as was the case for me).
- Morale
Perhaps one of the main mechanics that further adds realism to the game, every action that you make will affect the morale of your characters. From killing bandits to stealing valuable items, they will either be contented or fall into a state of sadness or worse, depression. What makes this game mechanic better is that not all characters will suffer the same reward or penalty to their morale. There are some that are more practical and will just be like "We did what we had to do to survive" whenever one of the group steals from neutral or civilian characters. Of course there are others that will immediately be demoralized and will need to be consoled by others.
- Trading
As is the case for most,if not all wars, money has no value. As such, players will have to rely on looting or crafting items valuable enough to be traded for items that they need, which is great because this gives them a lot of ways to get items that they are unsure how to acquire. Rather than farming for materials to craft a certain item, they can instead trade for it. There is a trader that regularly comes to the player's house approximately every 3 days, so you won't have to scour the entire map just to find one. In addition, there are certain places that have available traders. TAKE NOTE that some of them have really bad rates, so if you think that you are not getting much for what you are giving up, don't hesitate to reject it.
- Others:
As players progress through the game and get more materials, more items will be available for crafting. Most of them are very important and will play a part in the survival of the characters. Also, there will be times during the game that their house will be attacked by robbers nearly every day. Hence, it is a must for players to fortify it as soon as they can, as even if only one guard is on watch, a fully fortified house will almost always be able to repel any bandit attack without any wounds or losses. I believe there are even more mechanics for this game but I'll leave that for you guys to explore :D
While one of the more subtle elements of the game, the ending of the characters that players control can change depending on their actions throughout the war. For instance, if one of them kept stealing or even killed civilians, this can lead to a bad ending for them should they survive the war. While I do not consider it that realistic, it may have been introduced by the game's developers as an evaluation: You survived the war, but at what cost?
Overall thoughts:
This War of Mine's introduction of the civilian perspective when it comes to wars is definitely what got me hooked into it. You will find that there is more to this game than just surviving. While it's quite difficult, and would sometimes leave you shocked, it will challenge you to be crafty and patient. Furthermore, it's not that expensive given the amount of content and the high value of replayability that it has.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED, regardless of whether it is on sale or not.

I recommend The Witness if you like strictly puzzle games.
So a lot of reviews compare this to Myst: it's not. There's an island, and that's where the similarities end. That's fine, because if I wanted to play Myst I would play Myst. Unfortunately those reviews set me up with the impression that I would be playing a puzzle-driven narrative -like- Myst; again, it's not.
The narrative in The Witness is extremely vague, if there even is any. I'm several hours in and I can say with confidence the story isn't why I'm continuing to play. The puzzles are. There are a lot of puzzles; hundreds, maybe thousands? The premise of these puzzles are interactive maze-displays that grow progressively harder as you adventure through a visually compelling island. Sometimes you'll "get" the maze solution in a couple of moments, but more often than not you'll walk around, think, walk around some more, and wonder aloud before you have your "eureka!" moment.
If you want to spend ~$40 USD on an adventure game then don't buy this. This isn't an adventure game, although I will admit it -might- turn into a more solid adventure after one progresses far enough; however, that point comes well beyond the first few hours. If you want to spend ~$40 USD on a puzzle game then this is going to be worth your money because there's a lot here  - a lot of puzzles. If you buy The Witness I promise you will have myriad hours of puzzles in your future.
Closing thoughts: I wish this game had a soundtrack. I like the clever environmental cues for some puzzle segments. I like the overly-saturated world. I wish the collectable, uh, tape recordings were more common.

There are tape and video recordings hidden around the island for you to find if you keep an eye open for them. They are filled with quotes about the ways in which different thought processes colour our view of the world, such as thoughts on Religion, the Scientific Method, Human Morality and
I have now 'finished' the game, although there are still quite some puzzles out there I think I might have missed or have remained unsolved as you do not have to solve every puzzle to 'complete' the game.
However, when starting out I cannot stress enough that you have to explore the
to be able to solve the mazes. In the first hours you are playing you might think that the puzzles you are encountering are truly impossible. At the end I was gleefully solving puzzles while backtracking to places I thought were impossible the first time around.

Allow me to preface my review with a commentary directed at many of the highly rated negative reviews currently on the store page. It worries me greatly that so many people put so much stock in reviews that very obviously let their expectations drive the review. I hope that potential buyers read a generous number of reviews (both negative and positive) and gauge the contents. If your tastes match those of the reviewer, a subjective review will probably resonate with you. If not, try and view it from an objective standpoint. That being said...
Let me put something bluntly, and in brief.
If you are not the type who could lean back and listen to instrumental music and dream up worlds of your own, this game might not be for you.
If you like clear stories being told for you and to your face, this game might not be for you.
If you believe that a good game has explosive action, this game might not be for you.
If you dislike sitting in silence and letting your thoughts flow free, this game might not be for you.
The Witness is a cerebral game, as much about curiosity and self-reflection as it is about exploration and seeking clarity. It is not a successor to Myst. It is not trying to compete with The Talos Principle. I'd even go so far as to say that, despite some very obvious similarities, it tries to break free of Blow's previous work, Braid, and does not try to emulate the cryptic secrets of Fez.
The game (I'm tempted to call it interactive art) deserves to be considered on its own merits before being compared to experiences that may seem similar to it. As does any other game. Indeed, the exploration of the game and the thick atmosphere of the world evokes thoughts of the desolate and empty worlds of Myst. Its single mechanic echoes the central element of time manipulation in Braid. The "first person puzzle solver" moniker can also be applied to The Talos Principle. But The Witness is different. Its core mechanic, the sliding puzzles shown many times over in the gameplay trailer, is not the game's primary draw. It is only the first of many layers, a conduit through which you engage in a dialogue with the world you explore, a sun-bathed island seemingly abandoned ages ago.
As you take your first steps from an ominous dark room into the glaring sunlight of a quiet garden of strong colours, you are left naked with nothing but the wind in your trees as your companion. Even before passing the first gated puzzles into the open world ahead, you a greeted by choice. While one has an obvious immediate impliciation, the other does not. What is its repercussion? You don't know. The thought lingers, and the moment you are released onto the island you are made free to follow the trail to its conclusion. Or perhaps the harbour town you see in the distance as you find an overview. Or the doorway, tucked neatly behind a few bushes, unseen as you pass by the first time. This urge to explore and see every part of the island, the effects of choices made and the many vistas and vignettes, all come together to form yet another layer of the game.
Before long, you will encounter tape recorders scattered about the island, containing quotes from notable figures of our own past. This is not some pretentious attempt at being philosophical or artificially raise the class of the game. The clips, as with every feature of the island, have been particularly chosen to make you think. About the puzzles. About the island. About how you, as the player, perceive what may have transpired and how you view the world and its mysteries - yet another layer of The Witness. This is when something becomes clear. Every rock, every tree, the dancing shadows, and running streams have all been placed with meticulous, deliberate precision. You will return to previous scenery, time and time again, and notice something new. Lessons learned in your travels will open your mind to impressions that may have never occurred to you otherwise.
This exploration and cycle of increasing depth is an important part of The Witness' narrative. This game is not about the puzzles, however obvious they may seem. The puzzles are a means to an end. The puzzles, and the always cryptic revelations they lead to, allow you to draw your own conclusions. This is the beauty of the game, and why it stands out in comparisons.
Players who delve single-mindedly into the puzzles, enforcing their own Metroidvania view into the many and complex puzzle rules, are likely to overlook the shifting perspectives and obviously deliberate constellations in play.
Players expecting a Myst-style relevation from the precious but fragmented voice and video clips will leave wanting.
Players expecting the frivolities of dialogue or humour to break the tedium of puzzles have entirely missed the point.
This game is for the patient. The meticulous. The explorers. The ponderers. The listeners. The dreamers.
In many ways, this game defies categorisation while integrating elements of many well-known games. Above all, however, it is most definitely a Jonathan Blow creation. If nothing else, this tells you three things: everything is deliberate, you are only limited by your own mind, and the story is yours - through and through.

gigantic is a game with a very gentle learning curve, with a pleasing art style and a very generous currency rate. The charactrers are a little derivative, but the gameplay is unique enough to smooth out any accusations of concept theft.
however, the characters are one of my only dissapointments in the game. Many of the tank/bruisers play exactly the same, down to having all but one ability being the same basic design. knossos and margrave are both melee characters with a short and powerful cc ability, a long charging ability, and a self-centered aoe disable focus. While the technicalities of their abilities make their strengths vastly different, they are played exactly the same. run into the battle, soak up damage, protect weak teammates. Their only functional differences seem to be their level of tank vs damage potential. This issue repeats itself with the mages, the utilities, the melee assassins and the fighters. the gameplay of these characters feels very similar with small differences between them. Regardless, this is my only main negative concern and in no way diminishes the fun i am having in this game. I would still recommend getting this game simply for the art style and forgiving learning curve alone.

overall, this gameplay feels like a blend of beat-em-up style combat with the strategy of a simple MOBA. The simple beauty of the art style creates an easily accessible game with a high skill cap that with the right marketing will attract casual and competetive players alike.

PROS:
- Its only 5 dollars.

CONS:

My feelings about this were pretty mixed.
The most satisfying thing about the game was the viseral rip-and-tear combat, but the focus of the game is solidly on precision platforming. The large variety of movement options available made getting around pretty satisfying and the level design is all right, but ultimately I found the game more frustrating than challenging.
The aesthetic also felt really weak. The music was barely a presence (weird for a game that gives its composer top billing on the start-up screen), every level is aesthetically almost identical, and there's only a handful of uninspired enemies you keep encountering over and over. Given that I thought the feel of movement and combat was the most entertaining thing about the game, a lineup of dull foes was a real buzzkill, especially in a game ostensibly about eldritch monsters that had some cool cut scenes to start off with. The minimal black and white art does make the levels extremely easy to read visually, but I really wanted something more interesting to look at after a while.
I also thought the "place your own checkpoint" mechanic was a bad decision and added pretty much nothing to the game besides additional frustration when you clear a tricky section without quite enough blood to make a checkpoint, or when you accidentally set up a checkpoint in a really bad place (I locked myself out of backtracking to get special items a couple of times like this).
Ultimately this game is probably worth messing around with a bit if you're a huge fan of extremely punishing platformers, but doesn't offer much else.

Today this game caught me by surprise, I typically look up the upcoming games and I put on my wishlist any interesting looking games including RPGs, and today I saw this pop in my Queue and somehow I had completely miss this... I assume somehow it didn't show in the 'upcoming' list of games for some reason because otherwise it would have gotten my attention ahead of time. So here we have Faria: Starfall a 16-Bit like JRPG, while it is a RPG Maker title, it is a beautifully made one with custom made graphics I believe, it start on a premise similar to what Lufia II did way back in time, I have yet to see how the story will evolve beyond this early dynamic, I assume the story development here is a bit slower than it was in Lufia.
Now where Faria: Starfall differs from the typical JRPG game is in the gameplay, their is no leveling, hardly seemingly any skills, the game instead seem to be based heavily on crafting, a bit like a Survival game, its all about gathering raw resources to turn into various items to employ in battle and for crafting Relics, its hard to know the exact length of what might be available, their are no Status page to see your character's stats. Anyhow this reminds me a bit of some of some Alchemist games I played years ago, which also relied on gathering items to make stuff, its a fairly unique approach still to a JRPG, one that could be deemed more realistic than normal JRPG with their seemingly normal characters level grinding into minor deities by the end of some games. I'll admit however that at the start the combat is a bit on the basic and difficult side of things, and you'll need to unlock some of the craftables to start having an easier time at fighting and start to delve in a more complex form of combat. Also this game doesn't have random encounters, instead it has the less used but still common system of having the monsters visible on the map, but in this game they seemingly only roam around, they don't go after you, so you can choose if you want to fight or not.
Actually the beginning is not all that is like Lufia II... its a JRPG game with puzzles in dungeons required to be accomplished to progress... just like Lufia II, I have to say on a very personal note that is the one aspect of Lufia II I could have done without, but that is more a question of personal taste than a flaw of the game. Further in my game, I can again say this... puzzles... are a hard thing... you don't need to fear game over, but puzzles you'll fear for sure, they are multiple and some are pretty difficult, from intelligence based puzzles like in Lufia II to a far more difficult type of speed and reflex based puzzles, its a challenging game for sure. Seem however some of those puzzles got a 'easy bypass' that allow to skip them, but its not universal, I'll say if you use mouse and keyboard to play the game, the mouse might be the key to deal with some of those speed & reflex ones in a manner that won't drive you insane.
Now while employing 16-Bit like graphics I have to see the game is fairly pretty and colorful, it seem like much of the stuff is custom made, albeit many monsters are based on common tropes from RPG and JRPG games. The music is also fairly good, most of what I have been exposed to tend to be more cheery happy music, in the town, field and beach, in battle you've got a cheery action with maybe a carnivalous tone music, I got some more mysterious type of music with a slight dramatic tone in a cave, so overall its very appropriate music too, also the music hasn't been a problem to listen to unlike some games where you rush to shut it off, this one is pretty nice to let run. The writing is also fairly nice, it has a very quality literature look to it, it has, I'll admit, a few cliché stuff and a couple of typos, but still its nice to look at, largely still fairly easy to follow, and is quite well made overall still.
Anyhow its not to say the game is perfect, like I said its confusing due to the lack of Status Page, it also has at the point I have a lack of Map, which make it difficult to figure my characters up and finding my way around, but those don't rate that much compared to all the positive.
So in the end I do recommend the game to people that want a good JRPG, that are willing to embrace a fairly novel gameplay compared to normal JRPG, a JRPG with a fairly in-depth background setting, where you can gather up items and make Relics that will reveal small glimpses in the lore of the game, the Developer of this game obviously love the game and is very passionate about it, its a beautiful work of love for sure. I'd give the game the tentative note of 7.5/10 for this game, I'll need to get far more advanced in the game to be able to get a proper grasp at the storyline, the characters and the gameplay to be able to decide if the grade I gave it is right, the faults I noted are not the end of the world, I'll need to see more to see if it get better or worse. So yea, at this price, with an expected 20 hours on a first run at least, if you don't go after every single relics, its a solid price for a good game.

Welcome to my review of
.  And I know what you're thinking..."How can you possibly write a negative review about a game that is well-liked?"  To that, I'll get to the details, but from the get-go, this isn't exactly a game...it's more like a demo (it's even said in the title.)
is basically a demo version of an upcoming game called
, which was supposed to have come out in the first quarter of 2017.  However, given that it's currently mid-August, it's become evident that the developer has just given up on this project as he still logs in, but refuses to acknowledge feedback and bug reports.
As you play
, you'll basically take control of a snarky little square and guide him to portals in hopes of...well...escaping the game.  I loved the controls and the humor involved with Kevin the Square. Everything feels good right down to the musical choices...but the one unforgivable aspect I found repeatedly in this game is that it crashes often and that there is no save point (meaning you'll have to start from the very beginning if the game crashes).
At first, I thought (during level 2) that Kevin was joking about crashing the game during his lines of dialogue, where his attempt seemingly fails.  Upon entering the portal, I found a very thin blue line....the next level's visual refused to load, but I could still hear the dialogue boxes, jumping, and death sounds.  I Alt-Tabbed out and found out that it's a video issue with the game.  Several boots and crashes, same result (for different levels).  One one case, I died and the game crashed right there and then.  The farthest I got was the "super jump" involving a charge shot.  Shortly after, the game crashed (once more) upon entering a portal.
Until the crashing is fixed, I'm afraid that I'm unable to finish this game.  I like the concept and many other aspects about the game, but when it becomes impossible to proceed, then I simply cannot enjoy this title as I should.  If the constant crashing was fixed, I would be happy to re-analyze this review, but until then, this game is a miss for me.

The Witness is a PURE puzzle game. It has no story, and it has no puzzles that don't involve drawing a contiguous line from the start to the end of a grid in order to divide the space according to logical rules.  Those puzzles are deliciously challenging, and the lack of distraction from them forces you to start to see everything in lines. This is important as you progress, as you are constantly asked to apply the visual language you have been learning in new ways and in new contexts. In the same way that people used to play Tetris for hours and then dream of pieces falling, spending some time getting familiar with the Island and learning the aesthetics, you will be dreaming in connected lines.
It's a 9/10 for me.
If you like puzzling, and you go in expecting a collection of puzzles that fit within a larger context that is also a puzzle, and don't expect a story, you will find one of the best designed and put together challenge to come along in a long time.
The downsides for me are mostly technical:
* I have the audio crackling problem, which hurts the already somewhat sparse ambient sound experience
* There is some z-fighting on some of the grass, flowers etc that detracts from the beautiful island design
* My method for note taking is to use the steam screenshot feature. While this works OK, an in-game note system would have been really helpful. No, I'm not going to use my phone or write notes in a notebook
* A few of the puzzles are bad for colorblind or deaf. It doesn't affect me personally, but I think more care should have been done to either mark those puzzles optional or work around people's limitations.

This is pure genius!
I did have utmost respect for Jonathan Blow before. Now that has grown to the level of hero worship, and I do not use the word lightly. What goes on throughout is a testament to both his brilliance and his ability to communicate, even through the most limited of channels.
It does take intelligence to admire the game, admittedly. You only get to appreciate the layers of puzzles unraveling if you are able to unravel them. As you progress deeper into the game, you glimpse part of that genius, and in time begin to think alike. You grow and get to expect what comes next, and then you get amazed that the designer did foresee your growth, what path it would take and did prepare for that. You bubble with joy when you see the next surprise, that you deep inside knew was coming, but only realized it after the fact.
You get to see the simplest of puzzle ideas, an application of graph theory, grow into an infinite playground in a fractal pattern, always promising to be more in the next step.
It is amazing that this level of intricacy can be achieved, in any stretch of time. The development time, long as it may be considering 'industry norms', is nothing, considering this was the end result. It is exciting that yet more artifacts like this may come from Johnathan blow.
There are all these complaints, from people who are offended when their intelligence is challenged. People don't play games to feel inadequate, many do when playing this. And many people tend to lash out so as to convince (primarily) themselves that the inadequecy isn't intrinsic. Those who can introspect, can grow, and that denomination is the target audience for this work.
I have seen comparisons with Portal and Talos Principle. Games that fall far behind their promise (especially in the case of Portal). The puzzles were kept simple, as a design decision -to appeal to a wider audience, when they could be so much more. No punches are pulled here. The premise is extended far, far beyond what could initially be imagined.
There are complaints that you have to use pen and paper. False: You also need a pencil and an eraser. The puzzles are so intricate that some of them would give you a headache if you tried to keep all aspects of it in your head, even if you were named von Neumann, and that is by design. If you think that is bad, this game is definitely not for you.
I have seen comments that this is a disappointment after Braid. Ridiculous, I think: This game contains the seed that made Braid great: the ever-evolving puzzles, the extension of a simple mechanic to both technical and symbolic extremes, and the philosophical sense of wonder behind. Likewise it contains what made Myst great: The sense of exporation and loneliness in an alien environment, and the devious, ingenious, and original puzzles. Myst was never about the patchwork mythology pasted on it afterwards. This work captures the 'abstract' in them both, where most people merely grasp and look for the veneer, the packaging. I tried to avoid and spoilers throughout, but here I will give the whiff of one: The game _explicitly tells_ this fact within, showing that 'the dev team thinks of everything', even what most people will fail to grasp, and the few will.
I have seen someone complaining when they learned to do something, and looked forward to 'apply elbow grease' to solve others like it was frustrated when 'the rules arbitrarily changed' in the next step. That is the point here, really. That was Blow's promise all along: There won't be any repetition, any 'application of elbow grease'. You won't ever get to turn off your brain and proceed through muscle memory -or its cognitive equivalent. Aside from some tutorial bits (where the whiners haven't even got past) the game always keeps you on your toes, always offers something fresh. This gripe, of course, contradicts with another that has been raised: That the game is repetitive. Well, only if you cannot see the puzzles for what they are and all you can comprehend is lines and boxes.
There are those who whine about not getting rewarded. That's pitiful, for it shows that the people have become so dependent on the Skinner boxes that dominate the industry, not only need but also explicitly want the base gratification offered by them, for accomplishing trivial tasks. Here the gratification is in the puzzle itself: Admiring the beauty of one's own work in the solution, getting a nontrivial thing done, and getting to see the next puzzle. That is not to say there are no climaxes and revelations, they are just scarce enough to be really significant and deeply satisfying. And supposed dead ends are, more likely than not, part of some greater puzzle that you might get to see hours later.
And in all that freshness, there is an amazing amount of content. It was immensely satisfying to get the endgame after 13 hours of play, and I believe I did very good time there. There wasn't the disappointment of it being over either: There is so much more to explore yet. And the game did make the promise with puzzles that -at the time- I could not fathom, teasing to come back after I did grow.
Now all I hope for is for Blow to begin working on his next project immediately, and with utmost pace. I do believe he is a font that contains more to give than a lifetime of giving would suffice.

Some look at this game and see a collection of nearly identical puzzles.  I won't lie to you, you interact with puzzles in mainly one way in this game.  But the logic of the puzzles is so varied and challenging, and the environmental impact on the puzzles is very distinct and keeps a somewhat simple idea really fresh for hours on end.   Most games have a primary way of interacting with the game (in shooters, you shoot, etc.), and The Witness is no different.  But the way in which the game distorts these puzzles, uses them to challenge what you already understand, and incorporates a beautiful environment makes The Witness a memorable and very enjoyable experience.  The world is vast, with lots of places to explore and secrets/easter eggs to find when you want to take a break from the basic puzzle.  The Witness does follow the recent trend of not giving the player much (if any) story directly, instead relying upon the environment and some hidden pieces to build the story of the world.  This approach may not resonate with everyone, but I feel that it fits the story being told.  I'd highly reccomend this game to anyone who like puzzles or wants to think a bit when playing their next video game.  9.5/10

Welcome to Valhalla.
VA-11 Hall-A (henceforth referred to as "Valhalla") is, when you get down to it, a visual novel. There are no platforms to jump, no bad guys to shoot, no bosses to fight. You're just a girl with a rather simple drink-mixing interface. Let's get this out of the way first: while this game is light on reading compared to most other visual novels, it's still a visual NOVEL. The drink-mixing minigame does a good job of breaking up the reading, but while it's an interesting concept, it's not all that exciting from a gameplay perspective. The emphasis here is on the top-notch story and character exploration, along with fantastic character art and atmospheric music.
You play as Jill (not Julianne, by any means), who tends bar at a small-time establishment located in the seedy, cyberpunky Glitch City. From behind Valhalla's counter you'll meet strange, mysterious, and often silly clients looking for someone to confide in or complain to as they go about their daily lives.
A good chunk of these stories serves as world-building. As you speak with your clients--who come from different and disparate walks of life--the history, politics, and culture of Glitch City is brought into increasingly sharper focus. It's a world full of corruption and oppression, but one that everyone navigates as best they can. The clients themselves all have unique and interesting personalities, histories, and opinions on the current events of the city, which they unfold to you as you mix up and serve them their drinks of choice.
Underneath the big picture of Glitch City and the snapshots you get of the lives of Jill's clients, however, is a heartachingly personal story of love and regret. And despite the dark undertones of the world and the violence that has become commonplace in Glitch City, Valhalla is a game full of hope and humor. It's a laid-back, relaxing, beautiful game where anime jokes and discussions on solipsism coexist in a way that somehow makes sense. Whether you're a fan of visual novels, or a newcomer to the genre looking for an entrypoint, this is a title you don't want to miss.

I feel very cheated by this game. I was promised an experience, not any experience, but the ability to experience what is known as "The Longest Journey".
I go back to their proficiency (or lack thereof!) in the name, because it's key to what makes this so special-- if not successful. What is shown by the game is far less engrossing than how they amplify that, sometimes excruciatingly, until the pointing, clicking, and adventuring is raised to a gale force bellow. You're pulled so close to the guts of the mouse that by the end you'll think you could build one yourself.
The first half of "The Longest Journey" simulates how it must feel to be eaten alive-- at least until the second half, when player one attempts to eschew the paradigm, drowning in it. But in the back half of the game, the storm ends and it = switches to a hush. "The Longest Journey" is ambient and gentle, almost absent-mindedly turning upbeat at the end, and "The Longest Journey" grows so static that it's not even a dirge: It's lovely to play but bereft of tension.
Which is why I'm so curious about whether it's actually "good", if "good" even has a meaning at all (it doesn't).  Like early Pink Floyd, it, (both player and game as a one-self 'playergame'^[1]^[2]) engaged in an exploration that was unrehearsed and maybe even naïve. The game tried to become something other than the sum of its parts-- and by emerging from free and unrehearsed improvisation, the game resisted containers; the wails and ballads emerged organically, and their apparent goal-- of creating spontaneous, non-idiomatic, and exhilarating adventure-- was reached again and again, if only by proxy through existence.
It feels like the game wings itself in front of us-- thrilling us with new discoveries one minute, and the next, batting around ideas that go nowhere. Is the organ lineup here to stay? (Probably not) Is the pervasive melancholy a stylistic choice, a side effect of playing without truth, or an emotional reaction? Does "The Longest Journey" survive, evolve, or die?^[3] Whatever the future holds, this is some of the riskiest improv ever recorded: In every moment of the game, you just wish you actually went on the journey which was in fact, in the longest, but you just ♥♥♥♥ing don't.
