Be Forewarned: This is a pretty old game and you may have trouble running it on modern machines. I personally encountered the "No FMV/Cutscenes playing" problem until i had to set my Power Options to "High Performance" which solved the issue. This solution may, or may not work for you.
This review may also contain minor puzzle spoilers.
==================================================
The Longest Journey is a graphic adventure game that was released back in 1999 by Funcom. During its time, it was hailed as one of the best graphic adventure games ever made (which i never played. I was more interested in Lucasarts and Sierra games in those days).
The most important element for any good adventure game is a good story, and this game most certainly delivers, although sometimes abit too much. It starts off simple enough, about an 18-year old art student April Ryan, her daily frustrations about school and boys until she starts having strange dreams and visions. What follows next is a mind bending over-the-top story plot spanning 12 chapters that will involve parallel universes and saving the very essence of reality. This is a very complex story indeed but can sometimes be too complex due to the many story jargons it throws at you and may be kindda hard to follow at times.
The art style have not aged very well. While the background art still does somewhat holds up well enough although barely, the 3D character art looks extremely dated. The look is reminiscent of early 90s 1st generation attempts at 3D characters in a video game. While this may be passable in 1999, it definitely looks ancient now in 2013, though I certainly cannot fault it for that. The game also runs at at maximum of 640 x 480 resolution, so it will look extremely pixellated running at full screen on modern widescreens. Sadly, there was never any "HD" patch ever made.
Gameplay wise, it adheres to the "Lucasarts" gaming philosophy where you will never ever come to a premature Game Over screen just because you forgot to pick up a tiny crucial object 30 screens before. Thankfully it also does not have any timed action sequence QTEs, although there is a very insignificant one at one of the later chapters, which can be easily done. The player need only focus on the story and puzzle solving.
As with any adventure games, puzzles are always the meat of the game, and unfortunately some of the puzzles in this game can have very obscure solutions. (I'm looking at you "Telephone Statue" puzzle). More then once, i had to consult a walkthrough because some of the solutions are too cryptic. Alot of times, i also had to resort to the "Use everything in my inventory until something works" tactic.
The puzzles are also definitely anything but subtle so to speak, and are put there for no apparent reason other then to present a challenge for the player to solve instead of it having a functional and logical use in the world. Alot of puzzles don't make alot of sense in their solutions. (Eg: Minor Spoilers: Who in their right mind would go touch a digusting green gloop on the ground that probably looks radioactive? Or dance around like a mad loon just because they see a shadow telling them to dance?" Basically don't use logic when you try to solve the puzzles, think "out of the box" instead.
Before wrapping up this review, theres something else that i'd like to add in that once you finished the game, you will unlock an extra option called "Book of Secrets" which is a collection of voice acting outtakes and unused/concept art that were used in the development of the game. This is considered to be quite a rare addition especially for a game released in 1999 where such bonus additions were rarely seen.
Overall Rating: 7.0 / 10
For old-school hardcore adventure gamers who appreciate a very complex story and don't mind tackling very obscure puzzles, this is definitely a game you should pick up. For younger gamers however, i'd recommend if you can watch a video preview before committing to it, as this game definitely shows its age now.

Well this game kept me up far far too late for three in a row as my pre bed reading that did nothing at all to help me get ready for sleep. I haven't gotten through 100% completion yet, but I intend to go back through soon to pick up what I've missed, and I can honestly say I look forward to revisiting a lot of scenes... Or rather, I don't remember disliking any of the scenes so I'll probably end up skipping nothing.
The gameplay mechanic is similar to Papers Please in that how well you do your job affects how your game goes, and how well different characters like you. The mechanic is nothing outstanding or particularly interesting, but the sequences of mixing drinks tend to be short enough in comparison to the dialogue that it never felt too tedious. I would definitely say the actual drink mixing is the weakest part of the game, though.
Let's just give a quick score list
Gameplay: 4/10 : Serves purpose, nothing much positive or negative about it.
Story: 5/10 : There isn't much of one, but I don't feel like there needs to be either in this case.
Characters: 9/10 : Where the game really shines and what makes it enjoyable
Dialogue writing: 8/10 : The writer(s?) went a little heavy on references to how animes tend to be subtitled at times. Pretty much the only flaw.
Music: 10/10 : Love the soundtrack. Objectively perfection is impossible, but because I can find no faults I have to give it a ten.
World: 10/10 : This is what I love the most about this game, all told. This format of dropping you into the world, doing a mundane job, and interacting with people, is incredible for world building. It cuts out all narration requirements, all setup requirements, all everything that storytelling traditionally requires and is often put on too thickly in games, VN or otherwise. It only presents to you information known by the characters in their everyday lives, and in their everyday conversations. This creates an iron strong sense of "rightness," wherein suspension of disbelief is ultimately mostly avoided. If all of your characters are so utterly casual and accepting of something in their world, it's natural feeling for you to think of it in the same way.
Anyways. I would strongly and thoroughly recommend this to anyone who likes cyberpunk, reading, or even just good character focused stories.

Nicer than Paladins. Gigantic's kind of cel-shaded.
Only 1 game mode so far. 2 teams, each with their own boss guardian, take turns to attack and defend, based on actions completed in the game.
There are many objectives in the game beyond whacking the boss guardian. Firstly, you can only attack the guardians during their vulnerability phase. Secondly, you have to spawn and protect your stationary summons. Summons grant benefits, but when killed they grant the enemy team points towards the guardian vulnerability phase. Thirdly of course, you kill the enemy heroes running around.
Heroes are unlocked using free credits. They can be boosted with cards. Levelling up your heroes' mastery rank (by playing more) gives you more points. Fulfilling objectives (stipulated by your objective cards) gives you more points.
This is also a team-based game, so picking the right mix of heroes and coordinating callouts is the best way to play.
There are melee, sniper, sentry, flanker, crowd control, etc heroes. There's some variety involved, but I think from my 2 hours so far I would not call it a shooter.
While it may not be a shooter, but its game mechanics can be quite confusing. Its abilities are MOBA like. Its in-game action phases (aka the boss guardian phases) can be very confusing for your first half dozen games. It gets better but yea, a lot of things you need time to get used to.

Rating 7/10
Overview:
2d Sidescroller Action Rogue
The Good:
+ 2d sidescrolling action through 99 levels and 10 bosses. Levels have a time limit, spend too long in the level and multiple ghosts start to come into the level.  Levels can have shops, elevators that can either send you further down or back up, slots for gambling gold you find, and portals.
+ Multiple characters that start out with their own weapons, however you can always switch weapons later on. You can only carry one weapon at a time so choose carefully.
+Different items and upgrade for weapons that can either be found or bought in shops.
+Cool Boss battles
+items are randomized in each level
+Easy achievements except for 1 (100 hours in dungeon)
The Bad:
- Their are a handful of levels that get re-used over and over again. After playing the game for a few hours you generally get a good sense of each level. Item randomization in the levels help to a degree but not by much
-Every 10 levels the game switches up the environment, this is good except its just a reskin of the textures, it adds some variety however the novelty wears off pretty quickly when you realize you are playing the same level that you played 6 floors up.
-Enemies change every 10 levels as well and most of them act exactly the same as the previous levels removing some of the challenge from the game. Essentially enemies are just reskined from previously levels.
-Some enemies are hard to see and blend too well in the background. I'm not sure if this was by design or by accident but it gets very frustrating when you loose health and you have no idea what hit you. Even worse, sometimes you will loose health exiting shops or other areas instantly because an enemy was right there and their is little you could do about it.
Conclusion
Despite its many faults I still had fun playing the game. The game has all the core elements of a good rogue like game albeit a bit on the easy side. Their is no denying that this feels like a poor mans spelunky but if you like rogue games then this is a good game to waste a few hours on.
While it might be an interesting concept, the execution leaves something to be desired. Saves and checkpoints are kind of implemented weirdly, and goals are poorly defined.

Real money helps you skip the grind, but the premium ships you can buy aren't better than the normal ones. Buying a premium ship means:
1. You don't need to level it
2. You don't pay for repairs
3. You can buy a premium ship at any tier
Nothing you buy with real money hands you items with better statistics.
Customisation could be a little more varied, but I find the ship models generally look good and the graphics in general are nice.

The game has real potential but quickly loses its shine when you realize you have to spend real money to get coins to upgrade your ship. You cant PVE unless you have 3 other players, but if you PVP you can play with bots. Not sure why i cant PVE with bots. Over the game is lacking some serious polish.

This War of Mine is a marvelous game.
It's a game where it's atmosphere completely overshadows its relatively simplistic gameplay. In this game you're essentially trying to lead a small group of people to survival in an incredibly oppressive and overwhelming environment. Food and supplies are scarce, your party will become depressed or ill (many times both). If this is not addressed it can have permanent consequences that can potentially lead to your party unravelling and being the end of themselves.
The game also presents its characters in a complex manner as anybody who you may otherwise call an antagonist is placed in a scenario where you'd be acting similarly if you were in their shoes.
Overall I think This War Of Mine is a wonderful example of art in video games. I think this is a game that should be played and appreciated as it is rare to find a game that excels in meeting its intentions to the level that this one does.

After playing through most of the game, I have to say that this is one of the better story based games released in the last couple of years. The game touches on a multitude of topics from lying to dealing with the realization of mortality. It introduces these topics in such a way that most of them feel organic. Every character was writen with so well that you don't feel like any characters feel the same. Though some characters share similar traits and characteristcs, they all have actual personalities. They Display this perfectly using the drinks. Using Alma as an example, she orders the same drinks nearly every time, but the distict characteristics of the drinks gives a little insight to her character. Her favorite drink is a brandtini, the drink is decribed as sweet, classy, and happy. This nearly summarizes how her character is. I give the game credit for making every drink that a customer orders feel like an extention of their character, I might just be looking too deep into it, but I still give it credit for doing that.
I also have to comend the world that the writers created. Without seeing anything outside of your apartment and the bar itself, you get this vivid image of what this futuristic world is like. The detail that they put into it is amazing, they create these characters that show exactly what this future is like. From Anamatronic Sex Workers, a hitman that has a striking resemblance to Adam Jensen, to ♥♥♥♥♥ing corgi and shiba inue buisnessmen. The world is so crazy and just out of this world that it draws in your attention, but realistic enough to be enaging. The characters tell you about this world with just enogh detail for you to understand it, but leaving out just enough to make you wonder.
The one thing i love most about this game so far is how they show what our would could come to. The Begining of the game is set near what is called "Super Chistmas". This is a "better version" of chirstmas so to speak. It was made by big buisnesses to get more money out of the holiday season. Its a smart commentary on the current economic status of the United States. They tackle this kind of commentary in a very smart and interesting way.
As a minor note, the soundtrack is beautiful. They did a perfect job creating it.
So far, I have no complaints to this game. I have experienced no bugs so far in my play through. The characters are all memorable, even some throw away charcters are memorable. There is no dull moment in the story in this game. The game has done a perfect job keeping me engaged throughout the story. They have set up a perfect world that i would love to see expanded upon.
I give this a 10/10. In my personal opinion, this game deserves a lot of recognition and praise. This was a passion project and it shows. The devs put so much time and effort into make this world that i hope that they recieve continue doing this,
*Edit*- Finally 100% this game, No Regrets. Heads up, In the name of beauty is hell to get. Look up a walkthrough, will save you hours of frustration.

While this game may seem like "Anime Bull sh!t" as some would describe it from a glance, the story and character depth is amazingly impressive. For a game where the extent of gameplay can be peformed by clicking and dragging ingredients, its got one of the more fleshed-out settings when compared to a surprising amount of "Big" games that are out there...and only a tiny amount is really directly shown to the player. Each character helps bring a new perspective into the player's view of the world, discussing and informing them about yet another aspect of "Glitch City" and its people. Also there are inside jokes, fun pokes at real things such as reddit, news rags, and online streamers, and well-thought out intertwining of characters with the plot.
If you don't like dialouge then I'd warn you not to get this game, its almost all dialouge. However, if you do like game dialouge (and Sci-fi aesthetic) I can't recommend it enough.

Frustrating yet satisfying puzzle game.   I usually write lengthy reviews but I think a shorter one will suffice.
The Guest is a puzzle game in which you are stuck in this room and in escence have to find a way out.   Along the way, there are plenty of puzzles that will require you to either use outside items or use logical thinking.   The range of difficulty is from fairly easy, to fairly difficult.  Nothing is impossible, and there are plenty of red herrings, but as long as you remember the very basic clues that are given, then you should do well.  There are plenty of things to grab that you will NOT use, so that can be tricky, and some of the challenges in the later part of the game, can take quite a bit of thinking.
Another thing that I should bring up, is whether this is a horror game or walking simulator.   In short, it is neither.   It is not a horror game becauase outside of the early on 'bathroom scene', there are no scary parts to it.  Creepy?  yes very much, but once you restore power to the room and turn on the lights, then things seem less scary.   As for walking simulator, there is not that much walking outisde of one section in which you might find yourself walking a LOT more than you would like. Outside of that, there just isn't much walking needed.
Visually the game is a stanard Unity type of game so its nice pretty 3d visuals that run very smoothly.   Voice acting is minimal and even then its not that bad I suppose.   Music is minimal.   There are a few odd bugs though.  I got trapped on one puzzle and couldn't exit out of the puzzle, and another time, I had the control key display, stick to my screen and would not remove itself until I reloaded the game.
Overall, this game is a good 3 hour or so puzzle game that is well worth it IF you do NOT cheat or use outside sources.  As it stands, there is only one person I think who has finished it but he takes quite a while to do.  Everything in the game, is possible to do if you read the clues, use simple logic, and semi-complex logic.    My only gripe aside from the few bugs, is that the ending is, nice but cliche although maybe it could lead into a sequel (although doubtful).   Still, its a good game for a good price and there should be more games like this.

I'll admit that I'm not done with this game, as I'm sure many aren't either. At about 25 hours in, this is a game about trying to do puzzles, finding out why your answer is wrong, and learning all of the rules of the puzzles. I've never gotten to a puzzle that I couldn't finish because of this. Sometimes it takes pulling out a whiteboard and drawing potential paths, but this game never breaks its own rules and that's paramount in puzzle games.
This is a game that rewards  you, not only for concentration, but a serendipitious curiosity that is rare in new games. This game asks you to, above all else, exist on this island.

It's by far one of the most clever puzzle games I've ever played. The puzzles start out fairly simple, and you're left to your own devices to figure out each new rule and concept introduced with new puzzles. At times you'll need to pull out a pen and paper to solve your way through a particularly difficult set, but when you solve each series of problems with increasing difficulty, it only makes it more rewarding.
The story is largely symbolic, and most of it is only hinted at through environmental cues, audio clips, and intentional placement of objects. The best way I can describe it without spoiling anything at all, is that the story is about an abstract concept. Since abstract concepts are hard to describe directly, the best way to describe them to someone is through bits and pieces of information that at first seem irrelevent. These small pieces of information may seem abstract in and of themselves, but they slowly come together, leading you closer and closer to an epiphony that was (hopefully) intended.
At it's core, it's a puzzle game. Exploring the world reveals nothing more than clues into the story. The world is so detailed that every item feels deliberately placed, but sadly very little interaction with the world actually takes place.
With some discount, base game worth even just for single, long as many SP games.

The minimalist artstyle fits this game like a glove, not only does it make sense thematically (looking like a subway map), but also suits its simple gameplay.
And simplicity really is the name of the game, everything is simple, from the gameplay, to the menus and the graphics, but that's not a bad thing, because everything works great! One of the best examples of this is how the passagers are just smaller, filled out, versions of the shapes of the stations they want to go to. It's a simple and elegant way to make the game art explain its gameplay purpose by itself.
Don't be fooled by the simplicity of the gameplay though, because the game can get really hard really fast! Has more and more special stations show up and people start to pile up waiting for their trains, the levels quickly become chaotic. You need to be really good at reading the map and make wise choices every game week (when you pick between more carriage, tracks, tunels, etc.) to prevent that.
Once you let one station get overcrowded for too long, you lose that level. Fortunately you can continue playing that level on a zen-like Endless mode, where you won't have any concerns with stations overcrowding. You won't be getting any score for doing so, but you don't feel like your time was wasted since you can continue building your routes.
Alternatively you can start a map right away in this mode, which is a good way to just relax or experiment route strategies.
There's also an Extreme mode, where you can't rebuild tracks, for players that want a higher degree of challenge.
Some levels add new mechanics, like the Osaka level which introduces the Shinkansen, which adds some variation to the gameplay, and allows you to try different strategies.
One thing I would like to see added, would be some kind of statists you could check out mid game, to make it easier to learn and improve your route strategy. Although that would probably go against Mini Metro's minimalist style.
Mini Metro is an elegant, minimalistic, wonderful managing game, which can be as relaxing as it can be stressful!

This is the one where they got all the pieces to fit together in a package that is both intriguing and engaging narratively the first time but also highly repeatable to become a decent “podcast” game.
The very tired climb a thing to reveal map and remove miscreants from their outposts is what this game is; in fact it can get down right tedious especially if you play a lot of open wold games. However, this one feels really good. The shooting feels responsive and rewarding. Hunting animals to craft ammo belts or weapons holsters also makes hunting the animals actually worth while albeit from an animal activists perspective it probably seems a bit egregious if not superfluous. But you are just pushing buttons. Get over it.
There are side missions everywhere. There are outposts everywhere -- Fortresses even; An increased difficulty version of the traditional outpost. There are random karma events that can lend to your reputation and make things cheaper in shops. Aside from karma there is an over laying morality system that certainly is not what I'd called specifically nuanced but it's there. It basically revolves around choosing between two methods of going about the main campaign missions. Listen to what Amita and Sabal have to say, make your choice. The ending is very unexpectedly satisfying and perhaps it feels a bit topical which makes it feel much more pertinent especially when I felt no real connection to any specific characters. Even on low settings the game is very pretty. Normally that kind of thing isn't really my jam; I care much more about performance. But there is something to be said about the world feeling a bit more real and not as cartoonish that grounds the narrative and tells a bit more cohesively just how – unreasonable  – Pagan Min can be.

I'm going to preface this by saying I hate Mobas. League of Legends, DOTA 2, Paragon, I've tried 'em and I hate 'em. On the other hand, I love hero shooters. I've played Rainbow Six: Siege, Overwatch, Paladins, Dirty Bomb, and I've had a blast. What I'm trying to say is that I am no stranger to either genre that this game classifies itself as. This is also my first review on Steam, because generally speaking, it's not worth it to me. This time it is.
When I first tried Gigantic, I didn't know what to expect. I loosely followed it prior to release, but didn't even try it during the open beta. I decided to give it a go, and I'm so glad I did. I find Gigantic overall to be a huge breath of fresh air for both the hero shooter and Moba genres, and I feel that they balanced the traits of the two genres exceptionally well.
Unlike your standard Moba, there are no lanes. Not in the standard sense anyways. There are different checkpoints around the map that hold summoned creatures, but oftentimes it's best for your team to stick together rather than hang out separately across different areas of the map. The tower system is nice as well. You can summon creatures that give a localized advantage for your team, but if it's destroyed, you can always summon a new creature. Instead of attacking the enemy's core only after you've fought your way through the hordes of creatures in a lane and destroyed your opponent's towers, you have to build enough energy in order to attack your enemy's guardian, which you have to successfully do several times in order to squeeze out a win for your team.
Unlike most hero shooters, Gigantic is third-person, which I was pretty hesitant about. As someone who has poured hundreds of hours into Overwatch, I'm used to the first-person aspect. One of the best things about Gigantic is what it pulls from hero shooters. Team fights are sometimes several minutes long moving to different parts of the map as one team tries to pull out the advantage. You don't get that in a Moba, but you do find them in hero shooters such as Overwatch or Paladins.
All in all, Gigantic has its charm, but it has things they need to work on as well. There are bugs and balance issues. There are features that would have been nice to have at launch (push to talk wasn't released until last week, in addition to the custom games browser). While ranked mode is being worked on, there have been few details released in regards to when this is expected, and matchmaking can seem inconsistent at times (partially due to the player-base not necessarily having a huge amount of players online at a time). But the crew at Motiga is actively involved with their community, as you'll see if you look at their Reddit. They are pushing out a hero a month and have teased new maps to come as well. There is a beautiful foundation for a phenomenal game here, and a glowing possibility of an esports following, and I'm happy to be along for the ride.
P.S. This is the one Free to Play game that I dropped 30 bucks on after only about 10 hours of playtime. And once again, the one game that I have left a review on. I gotta either really love it or really hate it for that. I'm guessing you can figure out which.

This War of Mine is a marvelous game.
It's a game where it's atmosphere completely overshadows its relatively simplistic gameplay. In this game you're essentially trying to lead a small group of people to survival in an incredibly oppressive and overwhelming environment. Food and supplies are scarce, your party will become depressed or ill (many times both). If this is not addressed it can have permanent consequences that can potentially lead to your party unravelling and being the end of themselves.
The game also presents its characters in a complex manner as anybody who you may otherwise call an antagonist is placed in a scenario where you'd be acting similarly if you were in their shoes.
Overall I think This War Of Mine is a wonderful example of art in video games. I think this is a game that should be played and appreciated as it is rare to find a game that excels in meeting its intentions to the level that this one does.

The whole premise revolves around cheating so that a balanced game, between mediocre AIs, tips in the favor of your team. You can speed boost your defender by the ball, the player he passes to and then explode the goalie, or you can accidentaly speed boost the opponents offense and blow up your defender.  Everything happens super fast, which gives it a really zany vibe.
The game offers incentives to play in favor of the opponents early in the match, which is a fresh approach to the issue of difficulty.  Sure you can win with a little skill, but setting yourself up for a big comeback and then pulling it off takes finese.  It really says something when a game encourages you to antagonize yourself in a positive way.

Overall rating is 6/10.
This is a somewhat fun, addictive and non-traditional soccer (or football, if you will) game. Instead of controlling any of the characters themselves, you instead get access to a wide range of powerups that you can use to influence the outcome of the game. Initially, you begin with just mines that you can place to blow up the enemy players (or even your own, if you're so inclined) but as you progress in the game, you get access to other powerups (some of which include cows that run people over, rockets, UFOs that pick players up, rabid fans that help your team kick the ball, etc).
Each match in the single player mode has an objective, which may range from "win the match within the time limit" to "get the score to exactly 5:4". Therefore, there are times where you'll have to use your weapons on your own team mates to manipulate the score.
The gameplay is relatively fun, whacky, hilarious and addictive, although the game suffers immensely from imbalance. Some items, such as the Red card (that sends a player off the field) are incredibly overpowered and ruin all the challenge in the game. I would actually recommend trying to avoid some overpowered items if possible, as they completely eliminate any difficulty in the game, which further removes any real incentive to use different tactics to complete the objectives.
The graphics and sound are pretty mediocre, although none of this is particularly bothersome for a game of this nature.
Apparently this game has multiplayer too, although I haven't tried it out yet. I imagine it'd be relatively fun, particularly if you were able to restrict the use of some items (i.e. the aforementioned red card).
Overall, I would recommend you try out the game, as it did hold my attention enough to actually beat it.

A lobby based space shooter.
What's good.
1) Great space fighter with much more customization options than the rivals, through diverse module slot distribution and multiple types of weapons with interesting mechanics.
2) Almost perfect free to play model. The grind is not too much (though it's certainly there), and the ships you can buy with money are not strictly superior (though they are better in some ways, just like every ship has their own quirks).
3) Very nice gradual learning, you start with very few options, slower ships, only one game mode, and you ramp up the number of modules and modes you can use gradually through the tiers.
4) Developing competitive side. Observer system already in place, tournaments are held, teams are preparing well ahead.
5) Multiple game modes with their own interesting mechanics and multiple maps, some very imaginative.
What's bad
1) Low population, and all that comes with this. Sometimes long Q times for some modes.
2) No skill based matchmaking, so everyone is thrown into the game as equals (except squads who have to be matched by an enemy squad), which sometimes lead to very unbalanced matches.
3) The game is not really dynamic compared to shooters like Freelancer or even Moon Breakers, if you fly anything other than an interceptor than you usually strafe behind cover more than you dogfight, which is fine for frigates but a bit weird for a fighter.
4) Somewhat lacking balance, one shiptree (graph) (Jericho) is considered strictly inferior in most areas to the others. Hopefully will be patched, and anyone can play anything anyways, it's not restricted, players don't belong to a side.
All in all, a very enjoyable space shooter, even if somewhat grindy, but if you enjoy your game, you won't notice it at all.

The Longest Journey by Funcom takes us on April Ryan's adventure to save the world(s)! I didn't know what to expect from this game, especially since I'm not a huge fan of point-and-click adventure games, but The Longest Journey is easily the best p-a-c game I've ever played, and is a highly worthwhile title for its story alone. The backgrounds are beautifully done, but the character models are quite dated; that said, that doesn't really matter, because the writing, world-building, and characterization are incredibly manufactured and suck you so deeply into this adventure you soon don't care about looking at a blocky April texture. Seriously, there are more memorable characters in this game than the last several games I've played *combined*. Crow, The Wheel Man, The Flipster, and especially April - she's an incredibly *real* character. I'm just flabbergasted how well Funcom has pulled her off. She seems just like an 18 year old girl would, and the rest (or most important) of the characters are equally deep and interesting. To add to this characterization, the voice acting is also outstanding (mostly, there were a few poor ones) and...I just really can't get over how real April was, I honestly feel like I know her, and the rest of the characters too - they're very dynamic and just so well done. There are also lots of dialogue choices to pick through that don't pertain to *immediate* story progression used to flesh out the worlds and the characters - this was much appreciated, and made the created universe feel large and dynamic. There were other nice features as well: the setting was very unique, there was a video replay option to view the FMVs, nicely done music...However, the downfall of any point and click adventure game are the puzzles. Some are very convoluted. I remember one where you had to make a fishing pole out of some kind of string, an inflateable duck, and a bandaide. It was just too much for me, I admit, I used a walkthrough. That said, I would recommend using a walkthrough if you get stuck in this game - it's definitely worth playing, even for a p-a-c adventure game.
Pros:
Excellent (like really) characterization and world building
Music
Backgrounds
Storyline
Cons:
Convoluted puzzles
A little too much backtracking at times
This was a great adventure, after playing it I'm really excited to move on to Dreamfall and I've also kept my eye on the kickstarter for the new Chapters that's coming out. A-
Note: Initially I didn't like the movement speed of the character - then I figured out you could double-click to run around. I also thought it was difficult to find where exits to different areas were on-screen - then I figured out if you press "X" it will show you. Keep that in mind while playing if you have the same difficulties I did. Also, as mentioned, the puzzles can be tough and not so obvious. The story, characterization, and world building are what makes this game great - don't let aggravating gameplay choices stop you from enjoying April's adventure, use a walkthrough.

The Longest Journey does not possess the best graphics ( it was produced in 1999) but I hope you can look past that because The Longest Journey is the real deal. Story telling... fantastic voice acting... that is what The Longest Journey is about. Without a doubt, this is the best storyline I have ever seen in a game. The characters are all fully developed and unforgetable. It has mature themes which games rarely explore. I have played a lot of adventure games and I am confident in saying The Longest Journey is possibly the best adventure game of its time and is undoubtedly a pinnacle achievment of its genre.

is the best Far Cry.
This is the one where they got all the pieces to fit together in a package that is both intriguing and engaging narratively the first time but also highly repeatable to become a decent “podcast” game.
The very tired climb a thing to reveal map and remove miscreants from their outposts is what this game is; in fact it can get down right tedious especially if you play a lot of open wold games. However, this one feels really good. The shooting feels responsive and rewarding. Hunting animals to craft ammo belts or weapons holsters also makes hunting the animals actually worth while albeit from an animal activists perspective it probably seems a bit egregious if not superfluous. But you are just pushing buttons. Get over it.
There are side missions everywhere. There are outposts everywhere -- Fortresses even; An increased difficulty version of the traditional outpost. There are random karma events that can lend to your reputation and make things cheaper in shops. Aside from karma there is an over laying morality system that certainly is not what I'd called specifically nuanced but it's there. It basically revolves around choosing between two methods of going about the main campaign missions. Listen to what Amita and Sabal have to say, make your choice. The ending is very unexpectedly satisfying and perhaps it feels a bit topical which makes it feel much more pertinent especially when I felt no real connection to any specific characters. I mean, other than recognizing them as the people that give me missions.
Even on low settings the game is very pretty. Normally that kind of thing isn't really my jam; I care much more about performance. But there is something to be said about the world feeling a bit more real and not as cartoonish that grounds the narrative and tells a bit more cohesively just how – unreasonable  – Pagan Min can be.
There is co-op available for the main campaign. I didn't try it. It's not my thing.

Similar to other modern platformers of the genre like Super Meat Boy, They Bleed Pixels is a hard game. That being said, overall the game is decent. While the game hits the mark with aspects such as story and art, the controls is where it goes downhill.
The graphics, although pixel art, are great and the effects that occur when kicking enemies into saw blades are very satisfying. From the backgrounds, to the enemies, to the death animations are all beautiful.
The story didn't interest me from the start but from what I picked up it seems to be pretty original and enjoyable if you put in the time to watch the cutscenes.
Now onto the gameplay. The game has a checkpoint system that is based on both collectibles and combat. There is a fair balance of when you recieve checkpoints and I never got to a point where I felt there was too long of a gap. Something that sets this game apart from games like Super Meat Boy is the combat element. While doging obsticles and manuevering through the levels you must fight a variety of enemies, earning combos off of them and filling your checkpoint bar as a result. Theres a decent variety of moves that when used correctly can be very satisfying. The different enemy types are not. While the first enemies you run into are relatively easy, the later ones become annoying and tedious. Each enemy has a weakness/strategy to defeating them but when combined with the level layouts it can be overwhelming and tough to the point of annoyance. Part of this comes from the enemies themselves and part of this is from the poor controls.
The controls are where the game really could use some polish. Keep in mind that I played with a controller. (Which is recommended during the games loading screen). Movement is fine, jumping can be tough, and combat is just awful. When it comes to jumping most of my issues came from wall jumping and multiple jumps. At first I was convinced after jumping off a wall you only recieved one jump instead of two but later on found out you could jump a second time and that the controls were unreliable. The same goes for sliding off of walls into a jump. The combat is controlled with a single button which is where most of the frustrations come from. Things like dash attacks, kicks, and normal slashes all being bound to a single button ends up making combat a mess. This is my biggest complaint overall.
That being said I think that the game is a net positive and for 10$ isn't overselling itself. If you enjoy platformers and the trial and error gameplay then I would recommend picking it up. Although the controls and combat can be rough, if you're willing to look past them then you'll find a gem of a game.

Ok...I really wanted to like this game.  I like roguelikes, have beaten hell in Spelunky, run through Binding of Isaac now and again, and all that.  The core concept of the game is solid, but plays like a cut-rate Mexican version of Spelunky.  The first hour or two are interesting and challenging, but once you get the goofy mechanics of controling your character, and upgrade your weapon a little it becomes really really grindy.  What at first seems like a decent spread of items, and modifications, pretty quickly gets kind of boring.  Get to shop, buy any weapon upgrades you can, get the heart sign to regenerate hearts, rinse, wash, and repeat.
The enemies suffer from the same lack of originality, and you start to see repeats of limited behaviors with variation in sprites.  Same thing with the levels.  I realize the developer had to come up with some way to have 99 levels, but an extra couple of room layouts would have broken up the monotony.
So...the upside is potential, right?  If another five or ten weapons could be come up with that would keep things fresh.  Same with the other items...and enemies...and rooms.
Catch it on sale for a buck or so if you want, but honestly, just go buy Spelunky for a much more polished and fun game (or wait for the new Binding of Isaac).  I'll keep an eye on the developer, and see what he comes up with next, but for now I'm on level 51 and just kind of losing interest.

This is a perfect little hot chocolate mug of a game. It's a sweet, short, comforting set of love stories that now lives permanently on my hard drive to replay whenever I need a pick me up.
Rosemary is a goshdarn delight, good at her job but frequently awkward and always adorable.
The boys are fun and varied, and the road to romancing each of them is VERY well written and designed. In most other otome games, the choices tend to be either obvious or frustratingly arbitrary. In Rose of Winter, the choices hit that sweet spot in between: logical but not blatant. I got it wrong sometimes, but when trying again and really thinking over the guy's values and worldview, in hindsight it would make perfect sense.
Something that was surprising but REALLY welcome was the total frankness with which this game treated sexuality. Now, this is NOT an adult game, nothing shows up on screen past PG. But I've gotten depressingly used to otome heroines never being allowed to WANT sex or think about sex or have sex be anything other than something that happens TO them. Rosemary, bless her FACE, Rosemary has a LIBIDO! She thinks about things! She asks for things! She RECEIVES THINGS THAT SHE ASKS FOR! Get it, girl!
This is a bite sized game, but given how MUCH I enjoyed it and the number of times I've replayed favourite scenes from my favourite route (BEAST PRINCE IS BEST PRINCE), I consider it well worth the money.

I'm writing this having just succeeded on completing all the Achievements. I'm quite sure you could do it faster than that, but even with a Guide I had a very difficult time getting Kuya's Sad ending, of all things! Boy will just not let go of me ...
Anyways, if you enjoy visual novels/otome games, then I give this one my highest recommendation. The heroine is smart, resourceful, and holds her own in a fight, which is a nice change. Written and helmed by Magnolia Porter (whose work I was introduced to through her webcomic Monster Pulse), it has a nice pacing, interesting scenarios, and unique heroes. Whole dev team does a fantastic job of taking these male characters, who you wouldn't necessarily imagine as being romantic interests, and sells you on them in a way that feels genuine and earned instead of pushy.
But instead of rambling on, let me break it down for you:
PROS
- Fantastic use of setting (you never see Mount Needle the same way twice)
- Unique heroine and heroes, all with distinct personalities (all-around excellent writing)
- Nice use of music; although there are recurring themes, they aren't overused to the point of grating on the ear
- High quality of illustrations (characters are all very emotive, CGs are beautiful)
CONS
- I understand WHY they made Rosemary an innocent, it makes sense within the narrative, but I agree with the others who have said that the whole "never been kissed" thing has been done before. And it makes the other, er, 'intimate developments' feel surprisingly rushed.
- Watch out for that fast-forward button! You can turn it on, but unless you've set it to stop when you reach unread dialogue, it won't stop on its own.
- No 'Back' button, though a judicious use of the Save feature somewhat made up for it. Sometimes the dialogue choices are too similar or too vague, and you don't realize you've selected the opposite of what you meant to until Rosemary blurts out something bizarre.
- No CG gallery. It's not the end of the world, but the illustrations are so lovingly rendered that it seems a pity.
- Nothing in-game keeps track of which endings you've completed. Again, not the end of the world, and you'll only care if you're trying to save yourself some time while collecting all the Achievements.
IN SUM: If you've wished there were more romantic VNs/otomes on the market, consider this a temporary answer to your prayers. I really hope that Rose of Winter is successful enough that we see more like it, both by this developer and by others.

Rose of Winter stands out among visual novels I've played because I particularly enjoyed the protagonist. She wasn't a damsel in distress, she wasn't overly apologetic or shy, she had aspirations beyond just finding a guy to get married to, and she definitely had faults.
I also found all of the romance options fun to read about because they were so unique, and in some cases even surprising. I would say Kuya was actually the most "normal" so that should tell you something about the rest! :) In some paths there's even questions about "well, how is that going to work... physically?" that adds some spice and humor to the romance.
Unfortunately each path is rather short, but at the same time, each is also a separate story. I wish there were more CGs because I adore the art style! But these are small gripes for me. If short play time bothers you, then wait until Rose of Winter is on discount (I bought it, rather fittingly, during the winter sale!)

I thought this was going to be a generic Papers Please rip off but serving drinks instead. Oh how wrong I was. I'm first introduced with a small expostion about the world I'm about to read in, in a dystopia called Glitch City.
Althrough the first hours of the game will probably be a lighthearted tone, there are events that I won't spoil that will remind you that the world isn't a great place to live in. In fact due to the way the world works and its rich world building, it serves as a connection to the characters and their reactions to the world around them.
You play as Jill, a bartender who mixes drinks and changes lives, in a way. At first, I was a bit weary on the characters considering some of them are based on other characters, Jamie looking like Adam Jensen from Deus Ex is a bit odd, but fortunately their personalities gave me a postive outlook, not to mention their backstories.
The protagonist is likeable, relatable, and also flawed. Her relationships with her customers and friends are very in depth and give her support at her worst moments. In a well written world like Glitch City I'm surprised there wasn't a complicated plot scheme going around in the main story, but you know what? It doesn't need that. This story focuses on the characters and their lives, particularly Jill. And it does these characters arcs so well.
Gameplay is actually simple, but sometimes requires you to pay attention. Then again you're meant to get comfy. With that said, I felt later on mixing drinks as a game is a pretty neat thing, but as you continue it starts getting boring and repetitive. I'm ultimately glad the game ends on a pretty not too short but not too long note. Otherwise it would get pretty tedious.
Overall, I'm satisfed with this game, great world, good characters, and not to mention the great soundtrack. If you're interested then buy this game and support these devs, considering they're from Venezuela.

Thoughts on the story: The "Epic Story" of Injustice 2 is lackluster, boring and predictable,Superman is once again mistreated in the worse possible way byNetherRealm's incompetent writers to be dumbfoundedly evil, and none of the characters in the roster get any form of satisfying character arc.
The roster: Some of the characters either have no purpose whatsoever in the game's main storyline, or have shockingly weak motivations like being under Brainiac's mind control. Other characters' motivation are just straight-up missing.
I'm fairly liking the game's roster so far, having Supergirl make her game debut AND being portrayed well in an Injustice game, always good to have a symbol of Hope in the DC Universe. Still waiting for them to fix Superman. Some characters however, such as Gorilla Grodd, Cheetah, Black Adam, Daiman's Robin, and the Joker are downright boring to me and I personally, would've wanted to see more interesting characters make their debut in Injustice, such as John Constantine (The Hellblazer), Metallo, Booster Gold, and Mera, as well as other characters I wished returned from Injustice 1, (Zatanna, Raven, Lex Luthor).
Graphics: These are good, Wonder Woman looks like a woman this time, not like a male cosplayer with a wig. Other characters in the roster look amazing too, maybe a few gripes about their design but that's down to opinions.
Gameplay: I like the gameplay in Injustice 2, though I don't know if there is a dispute going on with fans, as I found each character's combos and special moves simplified and sometimes limited. Black Canary for example, has only 8 complete combos, and 7 special moves, not counting Canary Drop's upclose and air variations.
I also despise the game's random gear drop system, and I dislike the stats bonuses, it can make for unfair matchups in online fights, just because it's not ranked doesn't mean higher level fighters should have an advantage over lower ones beside each players' level of skill.
Issues: Long load times, characters not loading in 'customize characters' menu, overly long menu animations.

The Longest Journey is a very epic game, you could even say it was one of the longest journeys I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. Hahaha. No. Okay, enough of that.
The best way to classify this game would probably have to be something like fantasy science fiction. A sort of Lord of the Rings meets Blade Runner. Lord of the Blade Runners. Yeah, sure.
The main protagonist, April Ryan, is caught between two worlds; a world of logic and science (Stark, Earth), and a world of magic (Arcadia). There is also another dimension containing all that is in between. It's an interesting premise but an all too familiar one, yet The Longest Journey executes it fairly well.
The introduction and conclusion to the story are very satisfying, but the main journey is quite empty and void of any depth. The characters are very one-dimensional and are lacking in personality and do not elicit any significant emotional connection. It's basically "travel from point A to point B whilst saving an entire race of people. Now travel from point B to point C and do the same, over and over again."
There are very few strong supporting characters who you will meet along the way, the rest are very forgettable and are bid farewell as soon as they are met. There are some interesting characters, especially one in particular who seems to hold the power of omniscience, but their back story is not explored as much as I would have liked.
April Ryan's attitude, her denial of everything that is happening, is very grating. She comes off as a pretentious teeny bopper but I'm not exactly sure of her age. She has to be in her mid-20s at the very least, yet she acts like such an unenthusiastic, apathetic, ungrateful little♥♥♥♥♥♥ If I had the power to travel between dimensions my mind would be ♥♥♥♥ing blown and I would absolutely love it, but with April it's as if it is a burden. I can understand it from her point of view, but she never reconsiders just how important her task is, but rather complains about it right to the very end.
Honestly, it's a long game. I actually had to force myself to finish because of how bored I was becoming near the end. It's a very slow and sluggish game. Everything, from character animations to voice acting, seems to purposefully artificially extend the game's length just by dragging them out as much as any single person can tolerate. Many, many, many voices are spoken at such a slow pace that it's far easier to rely on subtitles and read through the text, skipping their dialogue completely.
The pre-rendered backdrops are very beautiful and there is some fancy cinematography going on in a few areas, but the character models are ugly and honestly aren't much of a step up from Final Fantasy VII's blocky models. I preferred the sci-fi setting to the fantasy world, it just seemed so much more welcoming and familiar. Although the fantasy setting was sprawling with life, it became a pain to make friends and explain your predicament to every single person you came across. I kinda preferred exploring April's home town and speaking with her friends.
The Longest Journey could have been so much more brilliant had 3D point-and-clicks not taken over from their superior 2D counterparts. It's a shame it became such a huge fad in the late '90s and early '00s, point-and-clicks just don't work in a 3D environment as well as their 2D brethren.

Huge fan of Braid and been following this game for a long time. Can't recommend:
-Draw a line through your numpad (start at bottom left of one and end at top right of 9) where multiples of 4 are grouped together, 2 multiples of 2 are grouped, the number of turns you make must equal at least two other numbers in a section added together, and all the numbers in a particular section must be a prime number when added up. Sound fun? Not for me, and that's what some of the puzzles in The Witness are like. To be fair, some puzzles are really interesting and utilize the environment in cool ways. No problem with these. Others are like that example, just too logical for my tastes. I found myself knowing what the rules to a particular puzzle was, but having trouble figuring out the exact pattern it wants me to have. It's a bunch of trial and error until you get a line that works with the conditions you already know about. Like an overly complicated Sudoku. It might be hard and challenging, but not interesting to me at all.
-The design goal was to capture the "ah ha!" moment, but the annoying part is that it forces you to have these. Meaning, there's no grey area. You either know it or you don't. In a game like Portal, you can clearly see if your idea will work or not, just by looking at it. You can get halfway through an idea, see it wont work, and go from there. There's a system in place that you slowly begin to understand. In The Witness, there is no system in place, you will either know exactly what to do or are completely lost.
-Returning to the game (or a puzzle) later will completely suck because you'll forget the specific rules to certain puzzles. Later puzzles require you to know the rules to previous puzzles, so your only option (if you happen to forget) would be to resolve the earlier puzzles. I'm not interested in backtracking through puzzle ideas.
-There's no way to tell if you don't know what to do. You might just not have all the info you need. There might be a puzzle on the ohter side of the map that tells you how to solve this one. There might not. No way to differentiate the two.
-Traversing the overworld is a pain. There's no reason to have a run button, why not just always be running? You can't fall off of heights and everything is on predetermined pathways. Meaning you have to zigzag through a pattern of rocks on a hill instead of simply going up/down hill. There's no accessible minimap, so if you want to go back to a puzzle, you need to remember where it was or just run around until you find it.
-You pretty need a pen/paper or some type of image program. There are puzzles that require you to flip images, rotate them, and so on, which can get kind of tedious (but is sometimes a little cool).
-There is a ton of puzzle saturation. A lot of the ideas repeat themselves with minor variation, and in a game like this, it's more interesting to know what else is out there, not what's already been done.

This is not a careful review so much as a quick retort to those who are complaining about the controls.  I play platformers pretty fervently.  This one is fantastic.  Yes, it is difficult.  Yes, there are some aspects of the control that take getting used to; in particular, the combat/beat-em-up elements are a little unaccustomed for a game that has this degree of intense run/slide/jump platforming challenge (harder than Super Meat Boy, for example).
Suck it up, learn the mechanics, learn to love them.  Win.  Don't complain about slippery surfaces and momentum, those are fully intentional parts of the game and increase and immersive physicality while providing fair challenge.  The controls are not imprecise---you are.
I don't see any complainers who perservered to win.  I did, so take it from me---a rewarding game that will grow hair on your chest, and required playing for devotees of the hardcore-platformer genre.

The story mode is quite enjoyable pitting the Imperial Guard, Space Marines (just a little bit) and Eldar against the Orks and and the forces of Chaos. The story mode is split into 2 main segments, one focusing on the Imperial Guard and Eldar, the other being focused on the Orks and Chaos. The second to last missions have two endings each. Depending on what faction is used to win the second to last mission sets who is going to be used for the last mission (This can be altered by loading up the second to last missions and using the other factions. The missions are quite long and sometimes require the use of many different tactics to complete. The last mission itself is enjoyable for another reason that I will not spoil.
This expansion added a few new units to the game outside of the Imperial guard e.g. Chaplains for the Space Marines.
And of course there is the new faction, the Imperial Guard. The IG are weak as infantry, requiring large amounts to be effective, but do have the balancing of their forces by having a very strong set of vehicles. They utilise the Basilisk (the only real long range unit in the game), The Leman Russ (A fairly strong main battle tank) and a few others. All of the units in the Imperial Guard are completely overshadowed by its magnum opus, the Baneblade. The Baneblade is the most powerful unit in the entire game with its ridiculously high health and major firepower. The Baneblade is the only unit that can easily go toe-to-toe with an entire army, take out there base and then return home without taking too much damage.
Although all the units are available in the later expansion (that do not require the original game or any other expansions, I would recommend buying this expansion aswell, even if it is just for the story mode.

-Winter Assault is set on Lorn V, where the forces of Order and Disorder fight amongst themselves over the power of an ancient Imperial weapon. It's the first expansion to the original Dawn of War, adding the Imperial Guard as a playable faction. The campaign, as well, offers far more options.
-Two seperate campaigns this time, both with two endings. It allows you, in the end, to pick the faction of your choice. It gives more incentive for you to go back and play through it again to see what would happen if you chose a different side.
-There are a few missions, however, that make me never want to play it again. There is a good amount of fair challenge in the game, but (particularly in the Chaos campaign) you are sometimes forced to go through very repititive tasks to finish a mission. That, and some missions are actually timed, making balancing base building and combat a nuisance. More than once I failed a mission without even realizing what had happened. In the final mission of the Chaos campaign, just as I was delivering the final blow, the mission failed. I never found out why, but I do know that I had the upper hand in the battle.
-Situations like this happened far too often.
-That said, there is fun to be had with this. The story is intriguing, as each faction seems to be using each other, and the Disorder campaign has some enjoyable dialogue between the Orks and Chaos. It's not a groundbreaking story, of course, but the conflict itself well thought out. If anything, it sets up the events for the next game.
-If you really enjoy Dawn of War, you'll probably be interested in this. Chances are, you already received this in a bundle. Is it worth trying out? Sure. Is it a game I would recommend? No.
-It's far from perfect and requires a lot of patience, but it's not a bad game. However, I would say that I only enjoyed specific parts of it. While the branching paths are a nice addition, I don't have the energy to go back and witness the other endings.
-I enjoy Dawn of War, but the tedious activities in this campaign were more frustrating than fun. I'd give it a pass and just move onto Dark Crusade.

This is my preliminary report. I'll update after the big update on the 8th.
This game features excellent space combat, decent ship customization, and is overall rather fun to play.
Personally, I would prefer if the ships had a little more inertia (so I could cut engines and strafe). It has that a little bit, but as soon as you turn, your ship slows the heck down, making strafing rather difficuly, and limiting combat to what's right in front of you. (freelancer is an example of a game that got this right).
The biggest thing that ruins this game is that it's pay-to-win in the truest sense of the phrase. If you join, your first few games will go pretty well, but then as soon as you start to run into players that have put money into the game, you're doomed. This is also evidenced by the $300(?) of DLC. That's ridiculous. The in-game "for-real-money" currency is called "standards". At the beginning you have enough standards to get something nice for yourself, but the first 5 or so "optional training missions" ask you to spend all your standards before you know that you won't be getting any more.
I understand that they have to make money, but I think they could do it better. For example, if they made the "for money" weapons "unique" instead of "better", so that they can give you an advantage only if you use them carefully, and so nothing inaccessible to the free-player is overpowered. That would require a lot of imagination, which is another thing this game somewhat lacks. Anyone can imagine a cylinder with guns all over it flying through space. Sure, the graphic designers did a good job, but really this game adds nothing to the space-shooting genre.
TLDR: this game would be great if the devs weren't greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

This is a tough one to review because... well, it's hard to talk about a game with an enigmatic story and puzzles without inevitably♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in someone's bowl of cornflakes. Suffice it to say you are a heavily medicated doctor trapped in his hotel room in Boston.
And it's a pretty darn nice room if I do say so myself. Spacious, plenty of chairs and couches for guests, a record player and television set... the bathroom has a nasty leak but otherwise if this were a hotel review, I'd give it a 4/5 - just short of perfect since I'm being held there against my will. I have to dock points for that.
It's your standard point n' click adventure game: pick up random things, combine them, smash them together, etc. What's cool about it is you can walk around all first person-like, and that freedom of movement, coupled with the creepy atmosphere, definitely kept me on my toes. There's nothing outright frightening so far... just the overwhelming sensation that I'm being watched, judged.
Analyzed.
Puzzles are good and varied, and the game provides clever hints assuming you're paying attention. And the graphics are nice. Not great, not dated, just nice... there's no physics to speak of, or other characters that I've encountered - just the hotel room, so it's hard to screw that kind of thing up. The sound design is great though, definitely worth mentioning! Heavy footsteps, rainfall, creaks and leaks, all adds to the sense of dread and loneliness. Finally the story... hasn't really captured me just yet. Yes it's mysterious, but it's too mysterious and, thus far, entirely reliant on note fragments and newspaper articles.
But I have to finish it! I'm currently stuck on this particularly perplexing puzzle. Think I'm about done though, and short of the ending coming out of left field (Zionist dinosaurs have conspired to lock me away in a hotel room to keep me from completing Chicken Soup for the Soul), I think this is a worthwhile purchase for puzzle/tense, atmospheric adventure game fans.

Simple in its premise, yet very difficult to get the hang of, Mini Metro is an addicting simulation game that starts off relaxing and gets more stressful and challenging as time goes on.
You must design metro lines in between stations, stations have a shape and passengers will be shaped as the stations they want to get to. New stations pop up at random around the map every now and then. You connect stations with lines, making sure they successfully transport passengers to their destination, otherwise the metro becomes overcrowded and you lose. To accommodate for the passengers, you can increase the number of locomotives, increase a locomotive's capacity and use tunnels to go under rivers, which are awarded to you every in-game week.
There's different maps which present different obstacles when designing your metro.
In normal mode, you may redraw the lines as you see fit.
In endless mode, the metro doesn't overcrowd.
In extreme mode, you cannot redraw the lines once they're drawn.
It is relaxing for the first few minutes (the music and presentation contribute a lot to this), but if you don't plan well enough, it's easy to saturate your metro and lose.
Do you draw one big line or many small ones, an extension or a connection? It's up to you.
Very recommended.

If you're looking for a high-precision platformer, this is not it. There are these "slippery" platforms common throughout the game that act sort of like icy platforms in other games which is fine, but with a key difference in the way velocity is handled: You are always sliding even if you land straight downward on one with no horizontal velocity, in which case horizontal velocity in the direction you're facing is instantly added. There are varying sliding speeds based on your movement down to this strange minimum velocity that makes jumping onto these a nightmare. They are used extensively throughout and only add challenge through artificially removing precision from the controls.
Attacks are unintuitive at first, in that the direction to kick an enemy is not based on direction of the control stick but rather how long you hold the attack button, which is frustrating but perhaps you'd get used to it after a while.

I really want to like this game. The music is nice, the graphical style is great, and the sound design is solid and satisfying. The non-verbal story is also pretty damn good, told by brief animations and combined with the background design of the levels themselves. But a game is only as good as their controls, and the controls are TERRIBLE. Loose, flowy, inconsistent, difficult to learn and nigh-impossible to master, it made playing much of the game a chore. I couldn't bear to finish it, because after I began the fourth level and found beginning it required a dash move that only executed half the time (thanks to all your attacks being bound to a single button), I gave up. I want to love this game, but as it stands, I just can't bear to keep playing it. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play. Which is a shame, because it has a lot of potential.

"WELCOME TO THE 99 LEVELS TO HELL",ok got that out of my system and now on with the review.This is one game i was looking forward to when it was first announced and i must say that having play'd the final version i am not one bit dissapointed with the end product.
Ok graphics wise this game is really competent at what it set's out to do and the graphics style really does suit the game,the music is both dark and at times (especially when the ghosts appear) has a sudden urgency to it,the dialouge in game is also really good (what there is of it) and helps to give you some clue as to what is going on and the game play mechanics in game all really work well and if you die it wont be due to the game but your lack of either time playing the game (learning attack patterns and how the different weapons and power ups work) or concentration whilst playing (i know happened to me on one of the boss levels,my wife shouted "your foods ready" i looked away and said "Ok i'm coming in a moment" then i died ARRRRGGGHHHHH).
As you progress through the game you will learn what the various enemies do and how they attack (some on sight will hunt you down and others will float about whilst firing at you and yet others will get near you and then "BOOM" explode ECT) and as you watch and learn so you will get better at the game and not die so often,this is never more the case than when fighting against a level boss.
Some are rather easy and predictable and others are rather devious and not so predictable and yet when fighting against others the sheer number of on screen allies the boss has and can summon can be nothing short of an annoyance (trust me in a good "I HAVE TO BEAT THIS DAMN BOSS" sort of way) and also prove to (in some cases) be to much to deal with at times unless your tooled up.
Now this brings me to POWER UPS and the different character classes,there is 4 character classes to choose from which range from the "MAJOR" to the "DRAGON" with all the characters offering different weapons and therefore a choice of which to take into the game when you play (some are better suited to certain levels as the sniper gun fires one bullet at a time and the machine gun fires multiple times but seems to lack as much of a kick),all the characters bar the first one have to be found and set free from the cages they are in (with a bomb if you have one-if not find one as the more characters you have the easier the game will be).
Now on to power ups,they range from the usefull to the down right bizarre,my favorite power up is the (what i call) "DEMON UMBRELLA" this little demonic umbrella takes you from where you are right to the end of level boss and this is ok if your tooled up but not if your "NOT",having said that it gives you ample oppurtunity to test out the boss and learn a little of their attack patterns and how to deal with them (helped me on one occasion with an ♥♥♥ of a boss "DAMN YOU,YOU FLOATING EYE THINGY"),but by jumping like this you do stand a chance of missing out on leveling up your character and also not finding the elusive other characters.
The other power ups range from a torch (which helps in the dark-pretty useless really on most levels),fireball that floats around your character and fires out a fire ball every time you shoot your gun,ice ball which preety much does the same as the fire ball except its ice instead,the bubble gun which surrounds the enemy in a bubble and sends them skyward,the poisen arrow gun (which does exactally what it says on the tin),weapon strength power ups which power up the strength of your weapon (OMG I WOULD HAVE THOUGHT THAT WAS OBVIOUS DUH) to other usefull and often weird and strange power ups.
When you do beat an end of level boss (comes around the 9th level mark of each seperate level) you will not have to start the game right from the begining like you do if you die before reaching and defeating said boss,thats why when you fight a boss your praying that you beat them so you dont have to start that level to get right back up to the boss again (thats where the "DEMON UMBRELLA" comes in handy),but defeating a boss feels just how it should ("HA HA HA HA HA i beat you,you mother...................." less of that language kids may be present) and gives you a sense of acheivement and the knowledge that your getting just that little bit better at the game.
So in closing i reccomend this game to anyone out for a good,challenging game that will test both your skills as a gamer and your patience as a gamer also ("AAAARRRRRGGGHHHH you bloody game,your cheating me i beat that boss WWWAAAHHH wheres my dummy") and at the price its at why are you waiting and if you do buy the game "WELCOME TO HELL BBUUWWWHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA"

I'm not going to be too hard on this game. It's not too bad - it's essentially the developers showing off their weird experimentation with the formula that Spelunky was based on. Unfortunately, there's issues with tone, because it sounds like a weird mashup of 'knockout power chord' sounding metal, Haunted House Halloween Noises Volume 17, and Super Mario Bros. It forgets that the game is about descending to Hell and does the thing where it sometimes places the exit door in a hard to reach place, unlike Spelunky which puts the exit door at the bottom to give it a sense of continuity. The casino rooms are built by people that don't know what the appeal of gambling is. A lot of this game feels unrefined and like it is in need of tightening up and revision. Unfortunately, since I've been playing the recently revised 2.0 version, I'm not sure the developers are on the right track with this game. It's all right, but there's a lot of little flaws that make it a chore to play.

The first expansion pack released for WH40K Dawn of War 1 that was developed by Relic Entertainment in 2005, Winter Assault adds on to what made the core game successful to start with with two new campaigns and a new faction from the Imperium of Man:  The mass infantry-throwing, artillery-heavy Imperial Guard.
-Story:  Taking place during/after the last game on the iceball of a planet called Lorne V, the player is tasked with aiding General Sturn and his regiment of Imperial Guardsman reclaim a Warlord Titan:  A giant mecha spawned of forgotten technology that the Imperium hopes to recover and mass produce in their war against their enemies (read:  Everyone not Imperium).  The task proves much more difficult than it sounds, as war-loving orks and blood-thirsty forces of chaos stand in the way.  For the first time in its day, Winter Assault allows the player to choose between two separate campaigns, where they choose to play as the forces of order (Imperial Guard and Eldar) or the forces of disorder (Chaos and Orks).  Unlike most games where alliances remain permanent however, players can (or should I say, are forced to) determine which of these sides ultimately win because in Warhammer 40K there is no peace, there is only war.  Unlike the first game in Dawn of War I, there are multiple endings (4 actually) that depend on the player's choices.  Great for adding a bit of replay value, and while the story isn't spectacular, it's not bad by any means.  Score: 4/5
-Gameplay:  Nothing much has changed between Dawn of War and Winter Assault, save for the addition of new maps and a new faction in its entirety:  The Imperial Guard.  While the Imperial Guard had some units featured in the first game's campaign, Winter Assault focuses greatly adds upon them by granting the Imperial Guard faction a vast increase in infantry units and artillery, with the most noteable addition being the powerful, bullet-soaking brick of a tank called the Baneblade.  The fact that the Imperial Guard infantry can travel between their buildings adds for some new tactics, combined with their additional units all help flesh out the faction.  Despite its focus on the IG, none of the other factions are completely left out, as they each gain additional units, some with new abilities to mix things up a bit.  It might not seem like a lot of additions, but for the casual and dedicated WH40K fan it's enough to keep things interesting.  Score: 4/5
-Graphics:  Because Winter Assault and Dawn of War were built from the same engine, not much has been done with graphical improvements.  This isn't a bad thing however, as consistency is something to expect in any expansion pack or DLC.  The frigid atmosphere of Lorne V further adds to the sense of bleakness that the grimdark universe of Warhammer 40K is known for, as it creates the impression that even the weather is out to kill you.  The ice and snow also creates an interesting contrast to draw more attention to the scorch marks, blood stains, and general scenes of death and destruction that make WH40K what it is.  So while there might nto be anything new, the old adage "If it isn't broken, don't fix it" works in this case.  Score:  4.25/5
-Sound:  While Winter Assault recycles many of the same tracks and sound effects from Dawn of War, it does add new music and lines.  The masculine choir added to the orchestral soundtrack fits both the mood of the Imperial Guard and the frozen environment they're in, and some of the lines delivered by the commanders of each faction are pretty memorable.   Much like the situation with the graphics, there wasn't a lot added to the sound aspect of the game, but what was added works very well.  Score:  4.25/5
-Replayability:  As said earlier, the fact that Winter Assault features two campaigns with a total of four different possible endings adds to the replay value of this game.  The maps from the original Dawn of War are also included in the multiplayer aspect of the game, and the Imperial Guard faction offers a new challenge for those looking to try a different faction in multiplayer.  While Winter Assault's multiplayer might have seen some form of population back in its heyday, online matches are practically unheard of save for games between friends.  Still, the amount of replayability for this game in comparison to is predecessor is an improvement, albeit a marginal one.  Score:  3.75/5
-Overall:  Winter Assault is a worthy continuation of the Dawn of War games with some worthwhile new content.  With subtle changes to the game's mechanics and more than one campaign, Relic Entertainment adds enough to satisfy most fans while avoiding any major changes.  Those expecting a massive amount of additions will be somewhat underwhelmed, but not disappointed.  Overall, I'd recommend getting this game during a sale if you need something to pass the time, it's worth it.  Overall Score: 20.25/25 or  81%
