"A Dark Souls of puzzle games"
--------------------------------
* Is this game similar to Myst?
--------------------------------
If you like Myst, or Myst-like games with emphasis on exploration, you should stop right now and buy it immediately.
This is distilled spiritual successor of Myst and I waited for a game like this for years.
--------------------------------
* Would I like it if i like Talos Principle (Portal, etc)?
--------------------------------
I found people who like Talos giving a lot of negative reviews for reasons not completely clear to me. Those games are on the same level in terms of difficulty and complexity, but the core philosophy behind the games is completely different.
Talos is more of a Portal-like puzzle game where the mechanic of the puzzle is simple, but the solution can be incredibly complex.
Witness has more of the Myst like approach. The puzzle machanic is usually hidden and your goal is to discover it. Essentially it depends on if you like this kind of games.
--------------------------------
* I am afraid this is another indie crap with bad puzzles
--------------------------------
* This is easily an AAA tile.
This is not an indie game, well, not your regular indie game. It was not made by a single person, and even if it was, this is not what automatically should make it a low budget indie.
The production quality of this game is insane. Speaking in a Myst terms, I would say I found it easily on a pair with Raven or Exile.
* This is not an 'only maze puzzles' game.
There is a lot of misunderstanding about this part and trailer not really explainging it well.
What I was expected initially from the Witness is a collection of small mini-games where you just need to go through the maze. This did not sound really exciting to be honest.
Every time dev is asked "are there only maze puzzles" the answer is always "yes, there are only maze puzzles" and I wonder why did he not take time to explain this, because this statement is incorrect.
* Panels are not puzzles.
Panels are not puzzles, but rather interactive interfaces in the game. They work on the similar principle, but do a lot of different stuff.
They activate and deactivate different machinery, open doors and move elevators, they modify game environment, etc.
Think of them as unorthodox touchscreens or gearboxes.
* Puzzles are not mazes.
Let's be honest: the variety of the puzzles in the game is insane. There are logic puzzles, but there are also optical puzzles based on the effects light and shadow or color mixture, there are sound puzzles, mechanical and kinetic puzzles, puzzles based on the environment and so on.
There are typically three group of puzzles:
* One is some sort of tutorial, where you learn the rules of the game in a seris of progressively more complex tasks.
* Then there are puzzles that combine several rules at the same time.
(They may be really confusign at fist, but it usually means that you don't have enough information or understanding of the game at this moment).
* And finally there is a metagame level where you suddenly discover that established rules may work outside of their usual context if you start to think outside the box.
Almost all of the game elements are interconnected in some way, and the main goal of the game is to find those connections.
(Which is, needless to say, insanely addictive and fun)
----------------
TL;DR:
---------------
Definitely not a game for everyone, but great nevertheless.

The Witness purely a puzzle game, and I've never been fan of purely puzzle games. I don't mean I never should have bought this, I mean I like when games have purpose and puzzles, and The Witness only has one of those things.
Some puzzles are tricky, yes, and the trickiest require you to finish a puzzle elsewhere on the map for the solution to a previous one, but most of the puzzles are solved by you staring at them for an extended period of time before the solution clicks. It's also extremely annoying when a puzzle could very very easily be solved by trial and error, but the game makes you return to the previous puzzle if you get it wrong. This seems like a cheap way of forcing you to solve it correctly especially when my favorite puzzles have so many combinations that it's more worth your time to figure out the answer the way the game intends rather than through trial and error.
As expected from his previous game, the Braid developer has shown a complete incapability of adding any meaningful story. I don't know why I expected a better for this game, maybe it was because of Portal and to a much much much lesser extent The Talos Principle (which I believe is filled with too much philosophical mumbo jumbo) but I would have liked some form of purpose to this game, any reason to exist whatsoever, besides only solving puzzles, but there's none. There's voice tapes scattered throughout and some extremely out of place videos but these almost always ramble on for minutes at a time and have you screaming "stop stop stop I don't care" until you avoid the voice tapes entirely.
If none of that bothers you, then The Witness is a good puzzle game. It seems all negative reviews can at least agree a little bit on that, so if you want something to try to chip away at every night then this is pretty good filler.
final edit, for something that I forgot to add apparently: What is with the lack of colorblind options? There's puzzles in a greenhouse I am physically incapable of finishing because I am colorblind. I had to get my brother to do them for me, and that's not any fun. Not only that, there's puzzles that require hearing, and my first thought was "RIP deaf people." Almost every knowledgeable developer adds ways of getting around these disabilities given to us lowly people by a warping of the universe at birth, but I guess The Witness is above such catering. I don't belive I'm entitled to specific or better treatment, and I hate to be a special snowflake, but come on, even Battlefield, a game that arguably doesn't need it, has colorblind options. It involves something as basic as switching color based puzzles to symbols - that's all that needs to be done!

Gigantic is a third-person hero arena shooter (or MOBA if you want to) in the vain of such games like Overwatch, Smite, Paladins, etc.  Now, just that sentence may have you saying to yourself ,"Hey, it already sounds like it's going to be a ripoff of the big boy games!  I'm out!", but I implore you to give this one a shot.
Gigantic sets itself apart from others of its type with its vastly energetic and free-flowing gameplay.  Every movement, every  attack, every ability feels impactful and satisfying to use, and the gameplay complements this.
Gameplay, itself, is the general "5 vs 5 hero brawler", but incorporates a unique mix between the traditional MOBA (Dota 2, LoL, etc) and the more modern hero brawlers (Overwatch, Battleborn, etc), utilizing dynamic tower-based objectives while also allowing the game to act more like a "Team Deathmatch" of sorts, where kills matter more than just for your kill ratio (more on that in a bit).
The objective of the game is to gain "energy" for your guardian, which you can earn through two ways: one is through kills (10 energy for each kill) and using "summons", this game's "towers" or "turrets" so to speak, to harvest energy; there's specific areas on the floor marked on your map where you can summon one creature.  They're little animal helpers whose abilities differ from one to the next (i.e. one can wall off chokepoints near its area, one allows for health regen and one allows vision over any target, stealthed or not, etc).
Once you have 100 energy, then your guardian goes into action, flying above the arena towards the enemy's guardian, inflicting damage and leaving them open for even more damage.  Damage them enough, and they get "wounded", taking away one health point from them out of a maximum of 3.  Obviously, if you inflict enough damage, you win the game.
From there, it's the general hero brawler schlock; there's different heroes with different abilities who fit in different niches blahblah, you've probably heard that one a dozen times. "Why would I try this game out if it sounds too familiar?" you say to yourself.  Personally, I feel like this game distances itself from others of its kind enough to make it familiar only if you pay attention.
Everything about this game screams out "personality".  The graphics are colorful and vibrant, with the maps having that "Dark Souls" feel where they feel natural while also being traversable while also making for some good eye candy, which you might not have enough time to appreciate when you're in a match.  The gameplay itself is very fast-paced, with a huge emphasis on mobility.  Aside from the usual mobility abilities, every hero also has a sprint and dodge function (which you should practice using, by the way!).  The maps' large scale emphasizes high mobility, which means there's hardly a break in between skirmishes.
Another unique aspect of Gigantic is how it handles levelling up.  It settles on a compromise, once again, between the traditional MOBA and modern hero brawler; you start with all your abilities, and instead of levelling it up and just bumping  up a few numbers, you have a choice between two modifiers to your abilities, which branch out into more specializes modifiers up to two modifiers per ability.  This means that you can modify yourself to fit any situation.  Need armor after using an ability to tank the hits?  Go for it!  Want to lower the cooldown on the ability by a few seconds instead?  All yours.
All this blends in beautifully to make a game with personality and zest, making it stand up tall over others of its kind.

Visual novels are a, pardon the phrase, novel idea. They tend to trend towards tatty smut. Which is fine if that's what you're into, but the story telling elements in most leave something top be desired. On top of that, the payoff tends to take a little too long to get to the climax.
"Rose of Winter," however, is more like a little short story collection than an actual novel, which is refreshing. Instead of playing different love interests against each other, or trying to balance them, each presents a different version of the same premise: escort a hot dignitary over a treacherous mountain pass. And the fantasy setting allows for unique characters.
Also, Rose is just adorable, and the art is impeccable. How this game hasn't found its way to cult status yet is beyond me.

Rose of Winter is a short (a single playthrough of one storyline lasts about an hour), earnest visual novel about a romantically inexperienced, though not naive, young knight, escorting one of four attractive young princes across a treacherous, snowy mountain. The writing is good, the experience is touching, and the art and music are just right for the experience. Some people will never enjoy a story about a sweet young woman falling in love for the first time with hot mystical men. For everyone else, please buy this game.
Magnolia Porter (the writer) and Aatmaja Pandya (the character designer) have created compelling characters, thanks in no small part to their nuanced treatment of femininity. The main character, Rosemary, is a large woman, who is aware of her size and how it is perceived, but the writing never dwells on that. She occupies a masculised social role (that of the physically competent chivalrous knight), but is not ashamed of her femininity. In fact, she keeps her hair fluffy, her armour has pink highlights, and she is very naturally a sweet and nurturing person. She is hired to protect men, and sometimes they take issue with her role, but never because she is a woman. Though I have my favourites, the four princes are all interesting people, and none of the four main plot arcs are predictable.
Mechanically, this is a standard small-scope visual novel. There is a lot of text, with the occasional dialogue choice. Most of the time, you're watching Pandya's full-body character illustrations emote over beautiful backgrounds by Victoria Grace Elliott, but for tense or intimate scenes, the scene cuts away to a full illustration. There are something like six music tracks, and I think the stirring ones move me more than the tender ones do, but they're all lovely. The animation involves simple digital manipulation of the assets. A couple of scenes involve characters navigating across a river, carrying each other, or fighting. It is possible to do this very poorly in visual novels, but the movements here are very smooth.
This game will make you feel cute. You can romance a very pretty dragon boy and the colour palette kind of reminds me of fondant. Please take a few hours out of your life to play a little game made by a small team of artists who really care about their craft, and want you to share a story of burgeoning love between mutually respectful individuals whose fantasy lives subtly reflect the complications, little injustices, and real feelings of the real world.

The Longest Journey follows April Ryan, an art student from the future, as she learns of The Balance between two worlds, which is crumbling... and guess who has to save it?  Mature content, profanity... a very involved story.  A few ridiculous or tedious puzzles, but most aren't TOO bad, amazing characters, and yes, the graphics aren't "modern" but I actually think they did OK, especially in the cutscenes.  And of course, plenty of humor, as many characters are sarcastic and there's a few pop culture references as well as inaccurate references to the past (aka modern day for us) that made me smile.

The Longest Journey is indeed a long journey. It may take you about 15-20 hours to finish, maybe even more. It's a traditional point-and-click adventure game and it is said that it may very well be one of the best ever made. The story is great and the voice acting is actually surprisingly good. If you don't mind the outdated graphics and that the game still runs with a very low resolution (extremely low) it's worth playing through. There are a few tweaks you can do to make the game more compelling for the eye, for example running it windowed. I recommend this one to anyone who is a fan of point-and-click adventures.

I was a little wary going into this game to begin with. The idea of a cyberpunk bartending game was novel, but just how far could they take that concept without the proverbial well running dry? That being said, after I started to really sink my teeth into this game I started to realise that the strengths of this game are not in its action or gameplay, but moreso its storytelling, its OST, its art style, and its characterisation.
Every character you meet will have their own believable personality, needs, dreams, fears and so on... Even the quietest, grumpiest people to visit the bar will have their backstories if you just look close enough and listen to what others say about them. Every encounter with every patron is as unique and memorable as the last, with moments that will make you laugh, weep, and cheer along with them as they go about their daily lives, stopping in for some brief respite and bitter booze as they tell you their daily tales.
With the ability to customise your bar's jukebox soundtrack, you can give your bar the atmosphere you desire. Want to put on 12 copies of the in-game equivalent of the Nyan Cat song? That's something you can certainly do. I personally chose to pick 12 songs I liked and just stuck with them the whole game, but you can change the playlist literally every in-game break / twice a day if you so desired.
The game definitely does have its weaknesses though - the gameplay DOES get stale after a while, and you're moreso going through the motions than anything else really, though perhaps that's intentional. I still think some mixing (heh) on mechanics could have gone along nicely, but that's just me.
I've played through three times and got every achievement, though, so the lack of extensive gameplay doesn't detract too much from just how enjoyable this game's atmosphere can be! ;)

They Bleed Pixels is a marvelous take on the precision-platformer genre, combining tough jumping challenges together with an intuitive combat system and a unique checkpoint/respawn mechanic. The game controls well, is smartly designed, and has polish and care put into every part of its being.
The story portion of the game is broken up into 11 long linear stages, with a handful of unrelated bonus stages on the side.  These stages throw every type of platforming challenge imaginable at the player, and are often as vertical as they are horizontal (thanks to the double-jump and wall jump in the game).  The difficulty is harsh and death is common, but it’s nowhere near the realm of the infamous “platformer hell” games.  Instead the real difficulty of the game is self-imposed, should the player choose to attempt 100%, time attack, score attack, and no-death runs of the levels.  Going for a high score is a separate game unto itself, as it brings into play the combo-centric combat system, where every move can be simply executed with one button and a direction.  This keeps battle smooth and to the point, allowing it to be integrated INTO the platforming, rather that being distinct from it.
The checkpoint system is a brilliant revelation:  In TBP, the player makes their OWN checkpoints.  Collecting items and killing enemies quickly fills a checkpoint meter; once full, the player can empty it to create a checkpoint in any safe location they choose.  This allows the player to feel out which sections give them personally the most trouble and then hold their checkpoints for those locations, saving a lot of tedious trial-and-error time.  The restriction of only being able to create checkpoints in "safe" locations prevents any possible exploitation of breaking up timing-critical action segments, and creates a very fair mechanic that's so intuitive and convenient it's a wonder more games don't try to emulate it.
The graphics of the game put function over fashion; a necessity for those familiar to the genre.  Sprites and platforms are simply designed and dark with a white outline, while the backgrounds are brightly colored and always pull from a similar palette.  This contrast and minimalism makes it easy for the player to understand their surroundings at a glance and focus on the precision of the game, while still presenting a unique and appealing visual style.  All sprite animations are very smooth with plenty of frames, giving a comfortable polish to the minimalism.  The name of the game should not be forgotten, however: when they bleed pixels, they bleed a LOT of pixels, and what well-animated pixels they are.
In a world where brutal precision-platformers have become more commonplace, They Bleed Pixels distinguishes itself in the genre in many ways without sacrificing anything in the process.  Except for a young virgin girl or two, but how else are you going to awaken the Old Lord from his slumber and bring about the new age?

99 Levels to Hell is a 2D randomly generated dual stick platformer. Left stick moves you, right stick is aim. You can of course mouse aim and use the keyboards. There is a jump button, a bomb button, a shoot button and an item use button. Everything is mapped to the shoulder buttons. Even with a controller, you still need to use a mouse for the menu.
You go through randomly generated levels killing monsters, collecting gold and find a key that will unlock a door to the next level. It is a good fun little game that I feel like I've played before. The game has charm and a sense of humor, coupled with enough red blood to literally paint every surface in the game. You'll find shop keepers along the way... some that weren't even supposed to be here today, that you can buy stuff from.
Ever play Spelunky? This is a Spelunky clone right down to the tutorial level with ghosts that will chase you if you take too long to complete each level. There are games that feel like other games. This is a clone if not stolen code. Is that a bad thing? No. Is this better than Spelunky? Eh yes at no. Sadly a game trying to be too much like Spelunky will never have a crown as grand as Spelunky, but this is still a fun little game. 99 Levels feels less deadly. There is no fall damage, there are no random spike traps on the floor or any enemies that pop out of objects when you open them with your gun.
99 Levels has casinos, and a wider color pallet with dark tones and well bright red blood. It is a good diversity here. It has treasure levels too. I think these are all steps in the right direction. Just not far enough. There is a chance here to expand upon things.
There is no carry function to pick things up and throw them such as princesses, rocks and keys. When you get a key, you just get it, you don't carry it and throw it. There seems to be no rope climb feature to throw grappling hooks and climb up. There are ladders though, and you don't climb ladders so much as float up them freely. While there are bomb walls, and shootable dirt walls, there are no webs, water or anything interesting like that. It just seems less than Spelunky. Less features, less controls, less price.
This game is a good start for any developer, but if you already have Spelunky, you probably don't need 99 Levels to Hell.

99 Levels to Hell is a mix of Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, combined with some new gameplay ideas (though not many). The game could be a lot of fun, but unfortunately it falls short in some areas.
The levels are too dark, almost as if you'd play Spelunky with dark levels all the time - and that without the torch, as only a tiny area around your character is well lit. It's a very annoying kind of darkness as it's neither too dark to see anything at all, nor bright enough to clearly see everything. It hurts the eyes.
On top of that enemies are hard to see because they are small and their color often matches the color of the background.
Due to these two flaws you often get damaged by enemies only because you couldn't see them properly. Trying to spot enemies and traps in the darkness around you becomes the main challenge of the game, which is simply no fun.
This is a shame as the game itself is quite entertaining and it would be easy to fix these flaws by increasing the brightness of the levels and maybe adding some kind of outline to enemies to make them stand out more from the background.
Anyway, the game is still decent and worth its low price, just don't expect a game as good as Spelunky. If you like Spelunky and finally got bored with it you may want to give this a try as it's a slightly different experience and fun for at least a few hours.

"A Dark Souls of puzzle games"
--------------------------------
* Is this game similar to Myst?
--------------------------------
If you like Myst, or Myst-like games with emphasis on exploration, you should stop right now and buy it immediately.
This is distilled spiritual successor of Myst and I waited for a game like this for years.
--------------------------------
* Would I like it if i like Talos Principle (Portal, etc)?
--------------------------------
I found people who like Talos giving a lot of negative reviews for reasons not completely clear to me. Those games are on the same level in terms of difficulty and complexity, but the core philosophy behind the games is completely different.
Talos is more of a Portal-like puzzle game where the mechanic of the puzzle is simple, but the solution can be incredibly complex.
Witness has more of the Myst like approach. The puzzle machanic is usually hidden and your goal is to discover it. Essentially it depends on if you like this kind of games.
--------------------------------
* I am afraid this is another indie crap with bad puzzles
--------------------------------
* This is easily an AAA tile.
This is not an indie game, well, not your regular indie game. It was not made by a single person, and even if it was, this is not what automatically should make it a low budget indie.
The production quality of this game is insane. Speaking in a Myst terms, I would say I found it easily on a pair with Raven or Exile.
* This is not an 'only maze puzzles' game.
There is a lot of misunderstanding about this part and trailer not really explainging it well.
What I was expected initially from the Witness is a collection of small mini-games where you just need to go through the maze. This did not sound really exciting to be honest.
Every time dev is asked "are there only maze puzzles" the answer is always "yes, there are only maze puzzles" and I wonder why did he not take time to explain this, because this statement is incorrect.
* Panels are not puzzles.
Panels are not puzzles, but rather interactive interfaces in the game. They work on the similar principle, but do a lot of different stuff.
They activate and deactivate different machinery, open doors and move elevators, they modify game environment, etc.
Think of them as unorthodox touchscreens or gearboxes.
* Puzzles are not mazes.
Let's be honest: the variety of the puzzles in the game is insane. There are logic puzzles, but there are also optical puzzles based on the effects light and shadow or color mixture, there are sound puzzles, mechanical and kinetic puzzles, puzzles based on the environment and so on.
There are typically three group of puzzles:
* One is some sort of tutorial, where you learn the rules of the game in a seris of progressively more complex tasks.
* Then there are puzzles that combine several rules at the same time.
(They may be really confusign at fist, but it usually means that you don't have enough information or understanding of the game at this moment).
* And finally there is a metagame level where you suddenly discover that established rules may work outside of their usual context if you start to think outside the box.
Almost all of the game elements are interconnected in some way, and the main goal of the game is to find those connections.
(Which is, needless to say, insanely addictive and fun)
----------------
TL;DR:
---------------
Definitely not a game for everyone, but great nevertheless.

The Witness purely a puzzle game, and I've never been fan of purely puzzle games. I don't mean I never should have bought this, I mean I like when games have purpose and puzzles, and The Witness only has one of those things.
Some puzzles are tricky, yes, and the trickiest require you to finish a puzzle elsewhere on the map for the solution to a previous one, but most of the puzzles are solved by you staring at them for an extended period of time before the solution clicks. It's also extremely annoying when a puzzle could very very easily be solved by trial and error, but the game makes you return to the previous puzzle if you get it wrong. This seems like a cheap way of forcing you to solve it correctly especially when my favorite puzzles have so many combinations that it's more worth your time to figure out the answer the way the game intends rather than through trial and error.
As expected from his previous game, the Braid developer has shown a complete incapability of adding any meaningful story. I don't know why I expected a better for this game, maybe it was because of Portal and to a much much much lesser extent The Talos Principle (which I believe is filled with too much philosophical mumbo jumbo) but I would have liked some form of purpose to this game, any reason to exist whatsoever, besides only solving puzzles, but there's none. There's voice tapes scattered throughout and some extremely out of place videos but these almost always ramble on for minutes at a time and have you screaming "stop stop stop I don't care" until you avoid the voice tapes entirely.
If none of that bothers you, then The Witness is a good puzzle game. It seems all negative reviews can at least agree a little bit on that, so if you want something to try to chip away at every night then this is pretty good filler.
final edit, for something that I forgot to add apparently: What is with the lack of colorblind options? There's puzzles in a greenhouse I am physically incapable of finishing because I am colorblind. I had to get my brother to do them for me, and that's not any fun. Not only that, there's puzzles that require hearing, and my first thought was "RIP deaf people." Almost every knowledgeable developer adds ways of getting around these disabilities given to us lowly people by a warping of the universe at birth, but I guess The Witness is above such catering. I don't belive I'm entitled to specific or better treatment, and I hate to be a special snowflake, but come on, even Battlefield, a game that arguably doesn't need it, has colorblind options. It involves something as basic as switching color based puzzles to symbols - that's all that needs to be done!
If you like challenging puzzle games like Talos Principle - buy this game. You won't regret it. Totaly worth every penny!

In short, it's not great, a 5/10 at best, for a little more detail look below.
I've knocked up a quick three minute review, check it out here:

HOUR ONE:
I must admit the negative reviews on Steam are almost overwhelming. I was really looking forward to this, mostly based on the fact that Jonathan Blow was the mastermind of the project, and it looked really pretty. I'm not really the biggest fan of puzzle games. Portal 1 and 2 are wonderful, I think they're great. Talos Principle? I liked some aspects of it (the atmosphere and the lore) but the gameplay didn't really do it for me. I got some amount of enjoyment from it, but had little motivation to go deep into it. To hear from many that Talos is a better game quickly grew my skepticism of The Witness. Is it really worth $40? Kind of a risky investment considering I put exactly 2 hours into Talos... and I don't really intend to go back.
While the similarities to Talos are definitely there, this game also hearkens to what is one of my favorite games of the last few years, Proteus. The lack of music brings my full attention to the environment -- no dramatic emotional cues are provoked, and I like that. I'm kind of left to my own exploratory devices, at my own pace. And what a place to explore. This game is VISUALLY ARRESTING. I don't know how they made colors behave the way they have here. Everything I look at is a dopamine rush. It's just the definition of aesthetically pleasing. I can't quite put my finger on it. It's painterly, and layered: yes, your character is confined to sometimes-limited paths (unlike most FPS situations, if it looks like it would break your ankle, you can't drop down, etc) but the trade-off is gorgeous views, interesting visual terminals, and controlled color palletes. I wish parks were designed this nicely. I wish landscapes for designed so elegantly. It really feels like someone has considered how the game looks from every possible angle. The whole thing is super screenshottable; picturesque. And it is a dream to explore.
So then, about those puzzles. They are more "two dimensional" and "contained" than I expected, I guess, but I think that's okay. Instead of making yourself and your movement an element of the puzzle, like in Talos principle, you literally use a cursor to guide lines through a 2D "maze." It's, at first, exactly like the pen and paper maze puzzles that lined children's magazines. And that is actually kind of refreshing to me, to have each puzzle be a clear, self-contained unit. Because it's easy to walk away from them. It's easy because there is so much worth exploring. Since I haven't allowed myself to get to the brink of frustration yet, in the first hour, I've been pleasantly surprised and happy with them. I'd say there's probably much, much building on the basic formula to be had, and I don't doubt I WILL be frustrated.
At the end of hour 1, I am pretty easily expecting to blow past hour 2. I can't wait to hop back in. But how long will it hold me? We shall see...
DAY TWO:
Well... as much as I love the world of this game, I'm not really sure I'm made of the kind of stuff that can make much progress with these puzzles. The exploration is great. The puzzles feel like a lot of trial-and-error to my math-strained brain. Unfortunately, I think I'm going to test out Steam's refund system, because I'm just not sure if it's worth $40 for me right now. I expect to go back in the future, but... not right now.

Okay, after playing it for a while i think i can make an unbiased review on this game because the methaphorical pink glasses are off now. The fact that the game is this visually pleasing made me take a while before gaining the ability to be unbiased.
Pros:
-Design, right off the bat this game has the most beautifull graphics i have ever seen. It's extremely colorfull, pleasing and straight up artistic. And in my opinion, it beats any other game in terms of style and colors. In addition, in terms of design (not playstyle) the heroes of Gigantic are unique, and that is an understatement and heroes like Voden, Tyto and Vadasi capture a certain elegance and beauty that neither overwatch, battleborn nor paladins were capable of capturing. That may be an opinion of mine but i am truly in love with the animations and designs of some of these heroes.
-Leveling system. For some reason i really like a leveling system in online games, it gives a good sense of progression and decently rewards the player with an upgrade of their tools of destruction (or healing in my case). The drawback to this is that it takes a little while to read what exactly an upgrade does. Fortunatly Gigantic reccomends certain upgrades wich completely cancels out the drawback of leveling.
-Hero versatility. While heroes are typically ment for a single purpose (the margrave is a defender whereas beckett is preferably an attacker) The game has managed to keep their heroes fairly versatile wich means that it never feels like you're stuck with a hero adn the weapons they wield because they typically handle well in any situation.
-Controls. The controls are tight and responsive, but that is probaply a given nowadays. But kudos to gigantic for keeping the controls easy to understand. In some of these other hero shooters you can get lost in the controls and activate the wrong ability. Also, something i find fun about some classes is that you can play like a complete idiot and it can still look like you know what you're doing.
-Third person. While some people may not like it (typically including me) they executed it fairly well in gigantic. The heroes respond quickly to where you want to go and the over the shoulder aiming never gets confusing, nor does it get more difficult to hit your enemy at point bank, even if the hero that is attacking you is much smaller than the one the player is controlling. The enemy cant really hide behind larger player models wich is a problem i personally had with third person shooters.
-Game modes. Now i havent played alot of mobas and mmo's so keep that in mind when i say this, but the gamemodes are very unique if a bit confusing at times. I personally enjoy it alot.
Now for everything that this game does well, it has alot of gaps that i assume will be fixed in the future because it feels like this game is not done yet. It's amazing right now but there has to be more down the line in the future because as awesome as it is it feels very bare bones.
Cons:
-Locked, expensive heroes: Locked heroes is a thing that really busts my balls, especially when the character that is plastered all over the advertising (tyto) is locked as well. Now it's not as bad as other games where you need to unlock them before you can even try them, you can play as locked heroes in the training mode. But i stil feel that certain hero types shouldnt be locked. In my honest opinion (dont lynch me if you disagree) a healer, a sniper, an assaulter and a defender have to be part of the starter pack. Now Uncle sven, Beckett and Lord Knossos were free for me. Regardless, the grinding is insane in this game. In the end though it makes playing as the hero you grinded so hard for feel more rewarding. This is fairly opinionated but i had to put it here, i believe that people should only put out the full game and not just half of it and make people pay for it extra.
-Stamina. Now this is for balancing, but i have to say that it is extremely annoying. There had to be a way to limit the dodging though so i understand it's for balancing. But it is an annoying learning curve for each class (especially assassins) to learn to preserve sprinting, especially when jumping uses stamina as well.
-Lack of heroes. Now this is something that i feel will be fixed in the future but there are only a few heroes to play with and it feels very barebones, moreover the game itself feels fairly empty. But this is a point of wich i assume that will be fixed in the future, heroes will probaply be added in later updates.
In general i just cant not reccomend this game, even if there are things wrong with it because it's too much fun. In conclusion i would give this game a 7/10 and i cant stress enough that people should try it.

Though there is some negatives, firstly which bugged me a lot, is that the game is spilt into two modes, daytime which is management mode, where you build up your settle and look after your characters and the night mode, where you go out to look for supplies, as this is supposedly the safe test time.
During this time, you can also trade but during the day time, a trader visits at regular intervals so I find going out to trade as a waste of scavenging time, and if the trader, as well as other visitors can move around in daylight, why can’t we?
I would of like it more if these two modes where blended into one, so you can decide, as personally I would of prefer to have gone on trading missions during the day or would have been nice if you can visit your neighbours yourself, offer to help or to trade with them, rather than you waiting for them to come to you.
A grip with this management mode, is you can craft stuff and create more workstations to craft even more, some to improve the moral of your characters and the rest to trade, however I find, that there isn’t enough loot in the game to make this work, as at the start I’m selling the craft materials to buy more food, and building materials and then by the end, I’m no longer finding enough of this crafting materials to make much use of the workbenches that I have built, without going out to trade for them back again, which seems pointless, in the game where the idea is to survive, why would I be trading food, medicine or weapons for some ingredients to make alcohol, to then supposedly to trade back to get the food and medicine again? And the building the materials are used in pretty much all craft stations, so you rarely have them to spare either.
Potential spoiler strategy either, apart from crafting places to get more food and water to survive, I found it was for the best just to ignore these other workbenches, aleast that’s how I eventually starting surviving after quite a few fail attempts at first.
Another gripe is when your on these scavenging missions, you have time limit to get back before dawn, (before the management mode starts), however especially when visiting a new location, I quickly max out my carry limit and have to send home well in advance of the time limit, I would like it if the game was then to give you an option in these cases to risk another trip.
So with that suggestion if mind, it would be nice if the distance of these locations where factor in, as no matter where you go on the map, it always takes 2hours, as day mode ends at 7pm and night mode starts at 9pm. As well as the option to send more than one scavenger, fair enough, risking one person on a new location but I’m sure, if you’ve been there and found it safe (I know in real-life that could change the following night but in this game apart from a couple of script events, if an area is safe, its always going to be safe), but full of potential resources you would send out a group to grab as much stuff as you can before somebody else finds.
There are mods, that increase your carry limit, which I did start using as a way to fake simulator taking extra bodies to carry stuff but really that carry limit is then increased always and not just certain times where I might of consider risking more lives for more loot.
But otherwise apart from these gripes, it was an really enjoyable game definitely worth playing, aleast through once.

I rate Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War: Winter Assualt 2/5. Bad.
While the multiplayer aspect of this game is pretty much the same as in any other Dawn of War game (except this add-on appears to be the first to have allowed you to play as the Imperial Guard, which is a nice, though not entirely well done addition) the single player campaigns (there are 2, each of which have 2 different endings depending on which individual faction you decide you support the most) are not well done at all. The single player campaigns do not play much like normal skirmish matches but instead require you to complete very specific objectives. This would be all well and good were it not for the fact that, (at least in the good-guy's "Order" campaign I tried to play) the campaign (and your units) are hampered by bugs and design mistakes which make the whole experience enormously frustrating. Too frustrating for me to want to complete anyhow, not when there are so many other, clearly better games out there.
Good things:
+There are 2 single player campaigns, each of which feature 2 factions resulting in a grand total of 4 possible endings.
Middling things:
+/-You can play as the Imperial Guard (but you can also do that more effectively in the Dark Crusade add-on). The numbers of imperial guard units which you control is still not numerous enough to be canonical. The battles still don't feel extremely epic (despite the nice ambient battle sounds in some missions). In the overarching context of Warhammer 40k seems very, very strange to be able to simply teleport in replacement imperial guardsmen as squads become depleted (and this also feels strange for most other factions as well). Why not just teleport everyone who's available all at once and flood the battlefield with soldiers like the Imperial Guard would actually want to do?
+/- Which ending you get apparently depends on a particular choice you make toward the end of teach campaign and which campaign you chose from the outset.
+/- The graphics, sound and music quality are, for the most part, the same quality as in the original Dawn of War Game.
Bad Things:
-You usually have to build up the numbers of your force during the course of each battle. This is yet another game which resorts to the tired and true (and completely unrealistic) Command and Conquer styled game mechanic of getting buildings, building the force and attacking with what you've built. I'm honestly getting truly sick of seeing this completely unrealistic game mechanic. All RTS games do not need to be this way but most of them are exactly this way and usually implement it in a manner which makes little sense (as we see here in Winter Assault). If the imperial Guard is really so massive they should be able to bring their own pre-built tanks and such along with them (etc.) and they should have already landed a whole bunch of them during the initial planetary invasion (and the same is true for most other factions) Only the Eldar and the Necrons, perhaps, should be using the "build-your-army" mechanic that all factions must use in these games, and even then that side of things should be handled automatically for the most part.
-Units will automatically engage enemy units whenever they are in range. Once engaged units will absolutely refuse to retreat or tactically withdraw even if they are engaged against a clearly stronger force. Given the manner in which the main campaign missions of winter Assault are setup, where you continually have fewer forces than your enemies, this (bug? oversight? design error?) problem causes the game to become severely (and needlessly) frustrating. The elite units of the Eldar should be disciplined enough to withdraw when ordered. The non-elite Imperial Guard units should actively run away from such confrontations (unless a commissar is present) but your imperial Guard (being the elite Cadians I guess) will never, ever run away even when they clearly should do so and (unlike the cadians) will ignore any orders to do so. This frustrating problem effectively breaks the game for me, particularly when there are so many other, better games out there to play.
-The space marines still look cute and cuddly.

Full disclosure beforehand, I did receive this game for free from the company representative Cassandra Khaw, for streaming on my Twitch channel. I've since completed my on-broadcast playthrough, and am writing this review of my own volition.
--
I was a little wary going into this game to begin with. The idea of a cyberpunk bartending game was novel, but just how far could they take that concept without the proverbial well running dry? That being said, after I started to really sink my teeth into this game I started to realise that the strengths of this game are not in its action or gameplay, but moreso its storytelling, its OST, its art style, and its characterisation.
Every character you meet will have their own believable personality, needs, dreams, fears and so on... Even the quietest, grumpiest people to visit the bar will have their backstories if you just look close enough and listen to what others say about them. Every encounter with every patron is as unique and memorable as the last, with moments that will make you laugh, weep, and cheer along with them as they go about their daily lives, stopping in for some brief respite and bitter booze as they tell you their daily tales.
With the ability to customise your bar's jukebox soundtrack, you can give your bar the atmosphere you desire. Want to put on 12 copies of the in-game equivalent of the Nyan Cat song? That's something you can certainly do. I personally chose to pick 12 songs I liked and just stuck with them the whole game, but you can change the playlist literally every in-game break / twice a day if you so desired.
The game definitely does have its weaknesses though - the gameplay DOES get stale after a while, and you're moreso going through the motions than anything else really, though perhaps that's intentional. I still think some mixing (heh) on mechanics could have gone along nicely, but that's just me.
I've played through three times and got every achievement, though, so the lack of extensive gameplay doesn't detract too much from just how enjoyable this game's atmosphere can be! ;)

First impressions:
A pretty generic rogue-like platformer, didn’t really have a good time playing it. The game just got boring rather quickly, much to my surprise, as I love games like Rogue Legacy and Risk of Rain, so I had expected myself to have a great time with 99 Levels to Hell.
Even with this, the game still has its pros, like the music and graphics, which are pretty top-notch for a title of the genre. The setting is a bit unique as well for the genre, with multiple levels of hell to be traversed. It is, however, quite difficult to progress, and the progression itself is rather slow, but still possible.
It took less than thirty minutes for the game to lose its appeal. The floors kept repeating the same patterns and I felt like I was just grinding my way through the various floors and enemies, just to reach a boss. I can’t say the game is really bad, it does have some good aspects to it, but I just can’t bring myself to keep playing a game that feels like it was made in Flash.
There are far better games to choose from out there. Take Rogue Legacy, for example. If you’re really in the mood for a change of setting (and pace, mind you), then give 99 Levels to Hell a try.

Fun game with pretty basic objectives, win the soccer game. Players automatically control themselves to get the ball. Your main objective is to use props like weapons, mines, missiles, shields, portals, power-ups, etc to out play the other player and win the game. It’s basically Worms style but age friendly. Also, you only receive the achievements your unlocked once you close out the game.

FootLOL is a fun take on football, but unfortunately manages to stay fresh for only a few hours or so. It's best played in short sessions of about 30 minutes. You don't actually control any of the players but you can help them out by keeping them safe, or by hurting your enemies. You do this by using power-ups.
Your team will shoot when they're near the goal and they'll do the best they to keep the enemy from scoring. Finishing ('winning' is the better word here) matches will earn you money and completing objectives will earn you even more money. This money is used to use more power-ups, or to let you choose more of them, or to improve the AI of your team, for example.
The graphics are simple and the sound effects are very basic but it has a certain charm, I guess.
There are several worlds to complete so it will take at least a couple of hours to complete it. I grew tired of it before that, but it was a fun, unusual game anyway.
If you like casual games about football/soccer FootLOL is the game you're looking for.

Who remembers "Super Meat Boy"? This is that but slower, with combat, and a different paint job. This is a game for people who love H.P. HOUR ONE:
I must admit the negative reviews on Steam are almost overwhelming. I was really looking forward to this, mostly based on the fact that Jonathan Blow was the mastermind of the project, and it looked really pretty. I'm not really the biggest fan of puzzle games. Portal 1 and 2 are wonderful, I think they're great. Talos Principle? I liked some aspects of it (the atmosphere and the lore) but the gameplay didn't really do it for me. I got some amount of enjoyment from it, but had little motivation to go deep into it. To hear from many that Talos is a better game quickly grew my skepticism of The Witness. Is it really worth $40? Kind of a risky investment considering I put exactly 2 hours into Talos... and I don't really intend to go back.
While the similarities to Talos are definitely there, this game also hearkens to what is one of my favorite games of the last few years, Proteus. The lack of music brings my full attention to the environment -- no dramatic emotional cues are provoked, and I like that. I'm kind of left to my own exploratory devices, at my own pace. And what a place to explore. This game is VISUALLY ARRESTING. I don't know how they made colors behave the way they have here. Everything I look at is a dopamine rush. It's just the definition of aesthetically pleasing. I can't quite put my finger on it. It's painterly, and layered: yes, your character is confined to sometimes-limited paths (unlike most FPS situations, if it looks like it would break your ankle, you can't drop down, etc) but the trade-off is gorgeous views, interesting visual terminals, and controlled color palletes. I wish parks were designed this nicely. I wish landscapes for designed so elegantly. It really feels like someone has considered how the game looks from every possible angle. The whole thing is super screenshottable; picturesque. And it is a dream to explore.
So then, about those puzzles. They are more "two dimensional" and "contained" than I expected, I guess, but I think that's okay. Instead of making yourself and your movement an element of the puzzle, like in Talos principle, you literally use a cursor to guide lines through a 2D "maze." It's, at first, exactly like the pen and paper maze puzzles that lined children's magazines. And that is actually kind of refreshing to me, to have each puzzle be a clear, self-contained unit. Because it's easy to walk away from them. It's easy because there is so much worth exploring. Since I haven't allowed myself to get to the brink of frustration yet, in the first hour, I've been pleasantly surprised and happy with them. I'd say there's probably much, much building on the basic formula to be had, and I don't doubt I WILL be frustrated.
At the end of hour 1, I am pretty easily expecting to blow past hour 2. I can't wait to hop back in. But how long will it hold me? We shall see...
DAY TWO:
Well... as much as I love the world of this game, I'm not really sure I'm made of the kind of stuff that can make much progress with these puzzles. The exploration is great. The puzzles feel like a lot of trial-and-error to my math-strained brain. Unfortunately, I think I'm going to test out Steam's refund system, because I'm just not sure if it's worth $40 for me right now. I expect to go back in the future, but... not right now.

The Witness is a great puzzle game. It's the first game in a long time that I've actually wanted to take notes for while I play (screenshots + annotations maybe?). Overall, I'd highly recommend this game if you enjoy puzzle games!

This game is hard, but it's very relaxing. The general ambiance is very peaceful, and I find that complimenting the game with some light orchestral music makes for the perfect experience. The key to enjoying this game is to view the panels not as a challenge, but as a lesson. They're not something to be conquered, they're something to be approached on their own terms and handled as one becomes ready.
I don’t think that the development team is trying to show off how smart they all are, and how dumb everyone else is. The puzzles aren’t trying to beat you back and dissuade you, they’re enticing you with the opportunity to learn and to understand and to explore. Sometimes, they fail. Most of the time, they succeed.
I think the decision to build the game without an engaging narrative is a bit of a double edged sword. On the one hand, I don't feel frustration from not being able to complete the puzzles fast enough to satisfy my narrative curiosity, which was a problem I sometimes had in Portal. I always wanted to hear what Glados had to say next, even more than I really cared about solving the puzzles, a conflict which often led to significant frustration. In The Witness, I don't have to worry about missing out on a captivating narrative, because as far as I can tell, there isn’t one.
But, on the other hand, not having an engaging narrative means that this isn’t a game that I can sit and play for long periods of time, especially now that I’ve gotten far enough in that puzzles are taking more than 10 minutes to solve. Even with the music, I find my mind wandering and thinking of other things to do. I just try to take it one panel at a time and when I start getting bored I do something else. When I come back later, I’ve regained some energy and my curiosity and I can enjoy playing once more.
Ultimately, I offer my cautious recommendation of this game. If you find that you don’t like it before your refund period expires, just go and get a refund. It won’t get any easier or significantly more engaging any time soon, and you’re better off finding something else that can hold your attention.

This game is a challenge, and it is a good challenge.  You need to explore, and be patient.  You need to think hard, and remember what you've learned in detail.
The Witness doesn't explain anything, so you have to figure out everything on your own.  The Witness is filled with tutorials which explain game mechanics, but you have to discover them.  They don't look any different than any other puzzle.
Between the 30 minute and the 2 hour mark, The Witness can be confusing and overwhelming, but it is supposed to be this way.  If you push on, and figure out what you can about the way the world works, you are in for a great time.
The Witness has a beautiful 'brush stroke' art style.  The textures are simplistic, but The Witness compensates with overwhelming color, beautiful environments, and detailed props.  The foliage on plants is some of the prettiest I've ever seen.
There is no music, which at first was alarming.  However, the lack of music actually highlights the incredible sound this game delivers.  The sound design is striking, and powerful.  Doors make deep, resonant clanging noises as they open.  Machines whine and groan as they operate.  There is no shortage of footstep sounds, and each surface you walk on feels unique, and immersive.
When it comes to writing, and voice acting, The Witness is somewhat similar to The Talos Principle.  It is somewhat abstract and metaphorical.  It 'speaks at a distance'.

Do you enjoy puzzles?
Logic, mazes, even sudoku?
Have you ever played/enjoyed Myst?
If so, you'll probably love The Witness.
The game is amazing.
There are countless puzzles, and it's up to you to find them on the huge island, and to solve them.
You will get stuck. You will stumble. You may need to get a pen and paper to write notes, and to try to work out puzzles.
You may get to a point where you want to slam your head against the wall because you found a puzzle that is too hard for you to understand.
That's ok. That's part of the game. You aren't expected to have all the answers right away.
Go to a different part of the island, solve some other puzzles, and eventually you will be able to come back to the puzzle with a fresh perspective and understanding, and wonder "Why was that so difficult before?"
This is a game for puzzle lovers. That frustration is part of the enjoyment. Because the "Aha!!" moment is the ultimate reward.
This game is full of those aha moments. The Island itself is fascinating, and wondrous to explore, discovering new bits of knowledge to add to the puzzle language.
If you are impatient, easily angered, hate puzzles, or just can't stand being stuck.. Then this game isn't for you.
The Witness is a puzzle journey. It's about solving puzzles, but it feels so much more than that. It's an experience.
Gorgeous world, sophisicated puzzles, and a world begging for questions to be answered. Amazing game so far. Can't wait to explore more and uncover secrets.

Dear Jon,
I am writing to you about your magnum opus, The Witness, not out of love, but as an expression of my boredom with completing what may be the critical apex of your brain's functionality.  I understand that engineering a puzzle takes a great mind, but I feel as though you're efforts are simply too mundane.  Every day, the New York Times challenges me with a crossword puzzle that draws on my education and life experiences to craft a truly memorable and endearing experience.  The Witness reminded me of a stained glass paint kit I received as a Christmas gift.  It's an imitation of true, masterful art and only enables lesser minds to experience the physical climb towards impacting the world we share.  I can say, with no doubt in my mind, you are a smart man.  However, I beat all 700 puzzles in 10 hours and have an incredibly high IQ.  I implore you, with respect, to refund me the $40 I spent on your product as I do not make much in the world of academia.
Sincerely yours,
Hitler

Highly addictive game, its one of those, just one more turn sort of games so I would highly recommend giving this one a go, for some you might end up sinking hours and hours into it, playing through it repeatedly with each available character as well as making your own, for others you’ll might just play through it few times until you finally survive and call it a day.
Though there is some negatives, firstly which bugged me a lot, is that the game is spilt into two modes, daytime which is management mode, where you build up your settle and look after your characters and the night mode, where you go out to look for supplies, as this is supposedly the safe test time.
During this time, you can also trade but during the day time, a trader visits at regular intervals so I find going out to trade as a waste of scavenging time, and if the trader, as well as other visitors can move around in daylight, why can’t we?
I would of like it more if these two modes where blended into one, so you can decide, as personally I would of prefer to have gone on trading missions during the day or would have been nice if you can visit your neighbours yourself, offer to help or to trade with them, rather than you waiting for them to come to you.
A grip with this management mode, is you can craft stuff and create more workstations to craft even more, some to improve the moral of your characters and the rest to trade, however I find, that there isn’t enough loot in the game to make this work, as at the start I’m selling the craft materials to buy more food, and building materials and then by the end, I’m no longer finding enough of this crafting materials to make much use of the workbenches that I have built, without going out to trade for them back again, which seems pointless, in the game where the idea is to survive, why would I be trading food, medicine or weapons for some ingredients to make alcohol, to then supposedly to trade back to get the food and medicine again? And the building the materials are used in pretty much all craft stations, so you rarely have them to spare either.
Potential spoiler strategy either, apart from crafting places to get more food and water to survive, I found it was for the best just to ignore these other workbenches, aleast that’s how I eventually starting surviving after quite a few fail attempts at first.
Another gripe is when your on these scavenging missions, you have time limit to get back before dawn, (before the management mode starts), however especially when visiting a new location, I quickly max out my carry limit and have to send home well in advance of the time limit, I would like it if the game was then to give you an option in these cases to risk another trip.
So with that suggestion if mind, it would be nice if the distance of these locations where factor in, as no matter where you go on the map, it always takes 2hours, as day mode ends at 7pm and night mode starts at 9pm. As well as the option to send more than one scavenger, fair enough, risking one person on a new location but I’m sure, if you’ve been there and found it safe (I know in real-life that could change the following night but in this game apart from a couple of script events, if an area is safe, its always going to be safe), but full of potential resources you would send out a group to grab as much stuff as you can before somebody else finds.
There are mods, that increase your carry limit, which I did start using as a way to fake simulator taking extra bodies to carry stuff but really that carry limit is then increased always and not just certain times where I might of consider risking more lives for more loot.
But otherwise apart from these gripes, it was an really enjoyable game definitely worth playing, aleast through once.

Great little time-waster where the simplicity belies the complexity of the game. Lovely minimalist design and a treat for everyone that's looked at a metro map and thought "I could do better than that!"

A wonderfully sleek and stylish problem-solving game that you can enjoy even if you know next-to-nothing about the logistics of designing a train network.
The list of core gameplay mechanics is pleasingly short - but by no means does Mini Metro lack depth. As the screenshots attest, the seemingly simple act of connecting stations eventually leads to a hectic and definitely unprofessional jumble of lines that you know your polygonal citizens despise with every side of their being.
It's then probably fair to say that the art of this game is building a seamless train network, replicating real-life transit principles a la Cities in Transit or Cities: Skylines... but you can still have an incredibly relaxing time without that stuff. I think this speaks to the approachability of Mini Metro - it's one of the few games in my library that I'd say is equally as fun no matter if your committment to it is 10 minutes on the bus (also on iOS and Android!) or an hour on a rainy evening.
If you're thinking of buying the game, the base price is extremely reasonable, and on sale it's an absolute bargain. If the concept of the game appeals to you, I think you'll be satisfied with your purchase - even if you're only coming back to it every so often for a couple of games at a time.

99 levels to hell feels more like a journey through hell, as per it's insane difficulty. Each level is randomly generated, as per the usual dungeon crawler, with plenty of items and creatures to find. If you've played spelunky you should have a good idea of what you're getting yourself into.
The premise of 99 levels to hell is that you are a dark wizard, whose light brother and mother have both been killed, and you are journeying into hell to kill Satan and get your revenge, or at least I'm guessing. The plot of 99 levels to hell is slowly unraveled as you play via hidden rooms that occasionally show up.
The gameplay of 99 levels to hell is fairly standard, a platformer where you have to find the exit to progress to the next level, however 99 levels to hell mixes things up, as you must find a key in order to unlock the exit, making each level a bit longer, as the area of the level itself is not as big as Spelunky. Like Spelunky, this game features permadeath, however here you can save and quit at anytime, though it costs 1 heart. The game is seperated into 10 dungeons, each with a unique feel and theme to fit with a boss fight at the end. Not to mention some unique traps and enemies. However most enemies are re-skins of ones seen previously with higher stats, which is unfortunate. The dungeons are listed below from first to last.
1: The Castle
2: The Green Underground
3: The Dungeon
4: The Machine
5: The Wet Caves
6: The Beast
7: The Next Dimension
8: The Unknown
9: The Necropolis
10: Hell
The games most notable feature is its soundtrack, which is incredibly good for an indie game. Each area has an eerie and unique theme, with some very heavy metal to pump you up during the boss fight. However it isn't as scary as it could be due to good lighting and poorly made cartoon enemies and bosses, which use stock death sounds that are far too silly considering what they are. While this does add some charm, I feel that if a sequel was made it could use better enemy design and quality to increase the scare factor.
Like spelunky, you can grab treasure (gold nuggets) to buy items in shops, and bombs to blast stone blocks, and find items in crates and chests. however the dirt blocks can be destroyed by any weapon, including enemy shots. This reduces the exploration factor by a large amount, but 99 levels to hell seems more orientated torwards combat.
The worst part by far, however about 99 levels to hell is its art style, it isn't necessarily bad for the most part, but inconsitent and poorly animated. The backrounds clearly are done in great detail, but most enemies are done very badly, and have little animation. Many of the objects in the game also are done differently, and it looks as if different images were taken and pasted into the game. A prime example of the poor animation is your ladder climbing animation, which is 2 sprites with one foot raised above the other. This is very lazy, and can greatly reduce the immersion this game can provide.
All in all, 99 levels to hell is a fun experience, with interesting story and fun gameplay, it is well worth the $5. However the game is not perfect, as it has multiple flaws which just look like laziness, but it is still fun. All the comments below are from people who played for 5 minutes and were not instantly entertained. If you are a fan of platformers, side-scrolling shooters, roguelikes or all of the above, I would reccomend this game, just give it a bit of time, as the first 2 dungeons are not too difficult, but the game will get harder, that is a gaurantee.
Final score: 7/10

The game looks amazing and is one of the hardest puzzle games I think I'll ever live to see.  It may not be a game for everyone, as it certainly gets tedious and frustrating on multiple occasions.  When I get stuck, I have the most success when I take a ten minute break and look at the puzzle again with fresh eyes.  This so happened to be the game I've been craving; a game that has tangible solutions that require a variety of thinking strategies to solve.  If you want this difficult yet rewarding experience, DO NOT look at gameplay or spoilers.  Every step gradually prepares you mentally for the next task, and by utilizing previously "viewed" knowledge, you're only cheating yourself.
Likes:
Visual Quality:  Like I said, the game looks amazing.  Saturated colors galore. The power of the colors makes every section of the island feel vastly different, even when they're two steps from each other.  The small trinkets and the "evidence of human activity" scattered around tell small stories themselves.
Gameplay:  Traveling is a bit slow, but the island is the right size for your movement speed.  The core of the game, AKA the puzzles, have a good learning curve that steepens in the later portion.  You may get overwhelmed when you first see a puzzle you haven't come across before.  There's no time limit, so do not feel the need to solve everything right away.  I guarantee you will not be successful if that is the mindset you hold.  This is a game where your success depends on your own willpower and thinking strategies.
Dislikes:
-Overwhelming color: Certain areas in the game have puzzles specifically using the area's color scheme.  Be weary when playing with screen brightness at maximum, you're eyes are not prepared for that intensity and brightness of color.  It only occurs in two or three areas, but I had to leave after about 30 minutes because I was having trouble seeing the puzzles.
-Not an Adventure Game: I have this under dislike even though I like the concept of the game temendously.  This is more of a warning or FYI.  If you're hoping for a plot and character development and purpose, good luck.  This is a solitary game.  You make discoveries yourself, but it's all for your own pride.
-Replayability:  Unless a patch or something is released for another island or whatnot, I doubt many people will play this twice for pleasure.  I would totally let my friends play this so I can feel superior to them while they struggle, but that's about it.

Brain usage is go! If you like exploration and maze puzzles, get this now. I haven't had this much fun with a puzzle game since MYST.

Then they repeat the cycle. The trouble is, you need them to do their jobs to obtain things to help make/collect other things, that allow you to complete the campaign levels. Sleeping and exercising don't help! Initially I found this funny, then realised that was all they were doing.
I un-installed and re-installed this game four times (the first time I did, it worked and I managed to get to level 3 of the main campaign, which allowed for another few hours of game play), and followed the advice on forums to try to amend it. Sadly, nothing worked this time round and I've now requested a refund. But for the glitch free time I did have, I enjoyed it. But the glitch made it unplayable for me, I can't play a game I can't progress through! Disappointed as the majority of reviews for this game were postive, so it must just be bad luck.
** Update 06/8/17: Steam haven't provided a refund, which makes sense - I went and bought a hard copy of the game and started having the same issues after several hours of game play :( gutted. Such a good game when it works. If you buy this, I really hope it works consistently for you!**

Bad points:

This game (or should I call it a depression simulator?) is a little dark. You spend your time floating between starving, freezing and being wounded, sick or depressed, or a delightful combination of all of the above. The only joy remaining in this game is that it's pretty satisfying if you're a compulsive looter. Although I dearly wish you could expand your backpack slots!
The game throws you in the deep end with pretty much no guidance, leading to a lot of trial and error in trying to survive. This is probably intentional - after all, the characters don't get any help, why should you? However, I must admit that after I'd read a guide online, I got a LOT more into it, and replayed it several times.
The game mechanics were a little frustrating in that sometimes instead of attacking I would just be ducking in and out of cover repeatedly, and then die. Or when the graphics don't make it clear that there is a gap in the ceiling right above me that I could easily pass through, and I end up trying to go a more dangerous route, and dying. Or it not being clear how to use cover when a sniper is shooting at me, and dying. This is extra frustrating when you're hours into the game and death is permanent. Don't get me wrong, I definitely think permadeath is the right choice for a game like this, but death should be because you make a mistake, not because the mechanics haven't been properly explained or displayed to the player.
Despite these niggles, this is a great game which can easily devour hours of your life, leaving you lost in a deep melancholy. Everything about its design contributes to communicating the misery of war.

Death Road to Canada is an amazing game where you attempt to take a car full of jerks to the Canadian border so they can live out their blissful existence free from the American zombies. Along the way, you'll find talking dogs, kawaii Anime girls, and a buttload of other crazy characters that make the game ridiculously entertaining. There is a lot of replay value and though I haven't tried co-op yet, that seems quite entertaining as well. I'd like to include an anecdote, but instead I'll just list a few things that have happened to me in this game in the few hours I've played it:
[SOME SPOILERS]
-Had a character possesed by a Demon
-Met an Alien who helped us blast through undead
-Had a character die because they attempted to pull out a loose tooth
-Had a moose chuckle at my characters, then kill them
-Told too many people to "cool it"
-Opened way too many toilets, expecting too much each time
-Had my dreams of reaching Canada destroyed before my eyes
I've yet to reach Canada (my most recent playthrough was my closest, with my Demon-Possesed Debutante reaching the final mission before becoming zombie chow) so it is challenging but after a brief break, I always return to the game, telling myself that I will make it "this time."
EDIT: After 14 hours, I finally made it to Canada with my custom character (Hank) and a whole lotta luck.
8/10 Recommended.

After working at it for a few days, I was finally able to get Injustice 2 to launch, so here we go.
GAMEPLAY
It's really fun, seems better balanced than it's predecessor, and is just a blast to play. If you enjoyed the first Injustice or MKX, you'll probably enjoy this one too.
STORY
Again, the story here is really strong. I was pleasantly surprised with the campaign from the first Injustice, since fighting games are notorious for bland stories at best. Fortunately, Injustice 2 breaks from this trend, and the cutscenes are so well acted.
OPTIMISATION
For the most part this seems pretty good, control-wise anyway. I personally feel it shouldn't be noteworthy when a game controls well on PC, but oh well. Definitely play with a controller though if you can.
BUGS
Sadly there are many, I'll list all of the ones that I've encountered:
-Game wouldn't launch until I fiddled with the config.ini a few dozen times
-Game doesn't run terribly well on my system (i5-6500, GTX 970, 24GB Ram DDR4), by this I mean that frame drops consistently occur no matter what settings are chosen
-DO NOT LEAVE FRAME-SKIPPING ON, seriously don't. It locks the game (for me anyway) at 30fps no matter the settings, makes everything blurry, and the animations very abrupt. The trade off is that sometimes fighting slows down, but I'd rather that than constantly hyperactive glitch-machines jumping around my screen
-After playing for over 20 minutes, my game starts to slow down: fps drops, animations slow down, menus take longer to load. It's quite strange, and doesn't occur in any other game I own. Closing the game and restarting it remediates this, but it's a pain
-In the Story mode, occasionally the audio will desync from the visuals for the duration of a cutscene, which is a real shame since the story is so engaging, and the motion capture is so well done. If you're telling yourself it won't bother you, oh it will. At it's worst, the audio was ahead by about ten seconds, so I ended up watching the end of a scene in silence, since the audio had already finished
VERDICT
This is such a good game, but at the moment it is buried under layers of bugs so thick, thousands of people can't play at all, and that isn't including those who suffer through subpar performance. My list isn't even comprehensive, as there are so many other issues being suffered by other people that I haven't experienced. It is a real shame, so I can't in good conscience recommend this game until there are patches fixing this stuff. You'd be playing a game of Russian Roulette if you bought this game right now, except the only two eventualities is a game that either works, or doesn't. If things change, I'll update my review

A not so bad port. There are some issues with this game but they don't affect the core combat, thank god. I have the game set to high for most settings and it seems to stick to 60fps during gameplay, but will drop to 30fps and below during the super moves. Also some cutscenes will cap at 30fps while some will stick to 60fps. While playing you will notice that the frame rate will bounce between 30 and 60 alot, its really inconsistent, but as I said before does not happen duing the actual fighting, only during cinematic spots I think. I have also noticed that transitions from cinematic to gameplay are not as smooth as they were on consoles. This is probably tied to the FPS issues. While the fps may be weird, the ingame graphics menu is impressive, with lots of options and easy to understand explanations. It also has a benchmarking tool so you can test it all out, though it only accounts for the fps of core combat and not cinematics like super moves. Sound is also kinda weirdly soft when not using headphones or I guess a sound system (don't have a sound system so I'm stuck using my headphones or my computer speakers.) All this taken into account, its still a fun fighting game and a serviceable port. I'll give this a pass for now and hopefully WB/NRS will listen to the pc community and fix these issues soon.
