I've been intrigued by VA-11 Hall-A since I first saw an article published by Siliconera and it got me curious. I was surprised to see this title just magically popped up on Steam and I got excited. The hype was immediately quenched by a simplistic, though fun mixing interface, combined with the challenge of not only making the drink correctly but also the challenge of remembering key details regarding regulars' "the usual" and the like.
The characters, dialogue, tone, and general atmosphere shine like the developers not only truly grasped what makes the cyberpunk genre so enjoyable, but also with such a fine understanding of great dialogue and chemistry. Each character has their own wonderful backstory and personality that strikes a sense of curiosity in me. I want to know more about these characters, their lives, their history, and I love to be around them. Even the main character begins to flesh herself out which is remarkable.
I was also ecstatic at every sly reference to other cyberpunk/sci-fi wonders like Armitage and Bubblegum Crisis. It's nice to see other people taking such an interest in a genre that sadly goes rather underappreciated. VA-11 Hall-A does not refrain from addressing not only key social problems that exist within our own timeline, but addresses themes like self-pity, self-discovery, bonding, and even sexuality with some character's preferences being left ambiguous or hinted at. It's never thrown out at you or explained to it, it's part of a conversation and truly feels like a genuine one, at that.
Combine all of this with VA-11 Hall-A's incredibly detailed art that truly allows each character to not only be differentiated, but stand on their own in a unique way. You immediately recognize every character, remembering what you talked about last, and the game even encourages you to keep a keen eye on past conversations. Stella definitely stands out as one of my favorite characters in terms of design.
Major kudos out to the folks at Sukeban Games and thanks also to Ysbyrd for publishing this masterpiece. 10/10.

Firstly, I think describing this as anything 'waifu' related is selling it short.
It's a cyberpunk visual novel with a simple bartending mini-game attached.
You have very little influence over the story - you can serve the characters the drinks they want, the drinks they REALLY want or the drinks they definitely don't want with some dialogue variation. No relationship nonsense.
The bartending is not difficult and could become boring - I'd recommend trying to spice this up yourself by memorising recipes etc.
The story itself is great but not everything is spelled out - things are left unsaid, certain parts are only alluded to and some things come out of the blue and are never mentioned again. This actually works in the game's favour as long as you don't expect everything to be handed to you in a full, discrete package. Remember that the story started before you arrived and will go on after you leave.
All in all, it's a relaxed, simple game that I would very much recommend.

Just like the first part, the second is a good Beat 'Em Up with solid mechanics. If you liked the first one, this one will be for you.
Well, what do I like about this game?
The most obvious thing first: The graphics. The game looks really great, especially for being an Unreal Engine 3 game (I wondered why they didn't make this in UE4. Probably too much for the consoles).
The combat itself is really smooth and with a little practice you can quickly string together your first combos. Just pick a character and go for it.
The gear system is also a nice addictive factor, so far I do enjoy getting new loot - I hope the visuals get more interesting though, so far it's mostly variations on the same theme for each character (with Superman being a small exception). What I'd like to see would be items that combined to a set maybe give you Michael Keaton's Batman or Heath Ledger's Joker. So far I've only seen a few total conversion skins, like Flash/Reverse Flash, changing his voice lines and so on.
The story is motivating, I finished it in two long sessions with all different paths completed. It does lack a little wow factor, but more on that in the con section.
The new Multiverse portal mode is also an interesting addition to farm equipment, with several fights being tied together and a little specialty in some of these fights, like the Joker being your sidekick (you can summon him to hit the enemy), and from time to time a challenge to gain an additional loot box.
Which brings me to the Loot Box system. Also a nice addition, and very 2017. Plus I like that the loading screen hints tell you that leaving your loot unopened doesn't help because it's content is determined the moment you collect one.
I have a couple of complaints though, but really minor stuff:
First, the story's not as good as the first one, but honestly, it's a Beat 'Em Up, so I wasn't expecting that much.
Second, when comparing the story mode with part one's story mode, I miss the tiny little minigames/quick time events that were only there to propel the story, but they did provide a nice change of pace.
Third, the Star Labs Missions are now replaced with the Multiverse portals. While being a good way of earning XP and gear for the characters, the Star Labs Missions had the advantage of being designed more interestingly. When I think back about the mission where you fly as Lobo through space, shooting stuff... ah, memories.
Fourth, the Online Matchmaking. Almost as interesting as Overwatch, when you're getting matched with people
much better than you. I myself am happy about stringing together a couple of attacks, but my opponents tend to pull off combos which don't ever let you up until you die. Which is okay, I have no trouble with people playing better than me, just the system behind that is baffling me. Also, I do experience timeouts while playing online, but I'm not sure if it is the game's or my connection's fault (given that I have these timeouts in other games too, it's probably my own problem though).
And fifth, the stages. They are all well-designed, look great and give a nice backdrop for the matches. But they lack in terms of stage transitions. Not all the stages even have them, which is sad.
So all in all, if you liked Injustice 1, you're going to like this one. I will update this once I had the pleasure of trying it out the classic way: With a friend sitting next to me and us beating the cr*p out of each other on my TV :D

I know for one nobody likes long reviews that you only read for end results or the bulletin points, so here it is simply.
Gigantic is a 3rd person "MOBA", but MOBA is too broad a term to catagorize this into. Gigantic is a game I've felt some real heart and soul poured into, and this genuinely feels like a nice game. 8/10

Really fun game.
It's like SMITE in the sense that it's a 3rd person MOBA. But this game has more in common with games like Overwatch and Team Fortress.
It's a team based action/shooter with an emphasis on the characters rather than the classes.
For example if you play as Tyto the Swift, your going to find that you are ALOT faster (hence the swift in the name I guess) than most every other characters, but you also have an extreme amount of mobility that allows you to chase down pretty much anyone, or escape from nearly any situation. Think Genji from Overwatch, but a whole lot more focus on melee, rather than throwing shuriken.
Each character can be built in several different ways, but seeing as how each ability only has two upgrade paths your going to find which path suits you best fairly early.
Some upgrades are just plain amazing, while some others seem almost worthless by comparison. So the balance definitely needs some work when it comes to the perk, or upgrade system for abilities.
Thankfully the game itself is very balanced when it comes to characters, right now the only characters I'd say are a little *too* good are Tripp and Pokko. Everyone else is on a almost completely level playing field.
The graphics aren't the best, but they remind me of Zelda: Windwaker, with the cartoony cellshaded look and all. Couple this with *amazing* animations for all the movement and effects and you have a lovely, charming and exciting game.
You can also unlock skins with EARNED In-game cash if your broke as hell irl like myself.
Bonus.
TL;DR Fun and interesting combat with colorful and unique characters, some minor balance issues and a pretty solid buisness scheme.

Overall the game is a refreshing spin on the genre and feels well done.... at first.  Even the heroes feel balanced, with the exception of Tripp.  Lots of children in every one of these games defending the OP character and there is no difference here.
The more you play you start to feel the glaring issues however, matchmaking does not exist (record who you play with and keep track, it will become very apparent), invisible parts on every map where you see no terrain.  Worst part for me however is the efficiency or mmr system, it forces you to play specific heroes that can maintain high efficiency even when the game matches you with a bunch of glue sniffing geniuses.
Considering this genre is very competative I can't reccomend this game with issues such as bad balance and horrid matchmaking.  Those type of issues belong in alpha and beta, which this game feels like more and more.

As of v0.75:
TOXIKK wants to be new Unreal Tournament.
And while it's still quite rough around the edges, it is definitely getting there.
The combat is quick, fun and all about learning maps, honing your reflexes and learning how to use dodge jumps.
No progression means everyone's equal at any time. And for me personally that's a very cool thing (at least I can't make an excuse that someone has higher level than me and that why I suck xD).
There are only two maps in the game, but they do show that devs know what they are doing - maps are very well designed, nicely balanced for all the game modes you can run them on, have enough space for close combat as well as for long range encounter, and of course look pretty cool.
The game code seems to be quite solid - I rarely had dips below 60 fps. And the ones that happened seemed to be related to particle emitters.
Cell capture mode (that is essentially CTF) is pretty awesome too. Mostly because of the huge map with vehicular combat and all the crazy stunts you can pull off.
So, if you like old-school arena FPS games - I'd definitely recommend TOXIKK.
And if you think that 3 game modes and two maps are not enough, then just add it to your wishlist and keep an eye on it. It is pretty damn enjoyable.
On the downsides:
- Game features only three modes and two maps at the moment
- Vehicles are behaving a bit whacky from time to time
- Looks like weapons that emit a lot of particles (mainly flamethrower) currently crash the game
- For some reason game has mouse smoothing on by default (although it's barely noticeable)

I can't stop playing this game. It's great for quick breaks between other games, it's great for dedicated game sessions, it's just great. Combat is simple but satisfying - push button to swing weapon, push button to swap weapons, use arrow keys to move - and the way zombies work in this game mean you can easily beat a couple of them, but a hoard is terrifying - as it should be!
The game is about taking a team of losers to Canada while driving up the East Coast of the US - unlike reality, it's easy to cross the border - the main trouble is getting there, as America's filled with vile zombies. You have to scavenge food and supplies and keep your car loaded while keeping your team alive, and it's not an easy task.
The primary obstacle for you will be your team: they're very good at being idiots. A simple fart in the car will drive them apart until someone breaks down and leaves, they can get into deadly pose-offs with muscular men, they can for some reason pick up the worst hitchhikers you've ever met. They also eat too much food!
...But they're your losers. Literally! You can make custom characters, so if you want to bring Megatron and Starscream on a roadtrip to Canada together, my god you can do it. No, they won't be robots, but Megatron can flip out in righteous fury and punch your friends, so it's as accurate as you're gonna get.
So, let's see: graphics, check. They're clear and easy to read, and gorgeous to boot. Music? Addicting with enough variety that I'm happy to keep listening to it. Controls? Very tidy, and you can remap them! Gameplay? Excellent.
So how about that Early Access status? The game as-is is complete: you can play a game on normal mode and run into plenty of variety, enemies, characters, etc - without feeling like it's incomplete. There's no glaringly missing features, and I've only encountered one or two mild bugs in my playtime (while playing in the Beta branch, so those are being worked on). The EA status means they're adding even more stuff and tweaking the game (LET THE AI USE AIRHORNS PLEASE IT'S HILARIOUS) and making it even more better! :D
In short: game is good. I've wasted at least 27 hours on it, beat several of the game modes, and splatted my team against more zombies than I care to count. Please treat yourself to it!

If you're a normal person who plays during the day and can stop and check in often, definitly buy this. If you're like me and can only play at night, or can only spend an hour or two on it, you're going to get frustrated real quick.
I knew it was real time, but I assumed that meant waiting X amount of minutes before X task was up. I didn't realize that meant it would be dark in game from my reallife 5 PM to 4 AM. Since I work until 5 every day, that means I essentially can't play this game at all. To be able to advance at all you need to do things that you can only do during the day.
I've been drooling over this game for quite some time. I only played a short amount of time so far, since I could do very little in game (it was too dark), but it seems well put together, and it does make you anxious about planning what to do next (Hurry! I want to do X next! or :O A wolf!!? That's just what I need while I'm starving and searching for berries!) I wanted a survival game that puts you in realistic shoes and forces you to go farther than just surface worries and a point and click. I wanted something that would be educational and mentally stimulating. It is.
I *don't* like the real time aspect of it. Chances are I won't be able to play this at ALL with my schedule. And a minor annoyance is that when you're 'writing' in the journal, you can't speed up the typing by clicking. I read really fast and it's kindof annoying that it goes so slow. But so far, these are my only complaints.

I really would have liked to give this game/survival sim thumbs up; however, after trying to chop a tree 6 times, and every time being attacked by a bear, whose meat - after I killed it - I mysteriously couldn't take with me, and oh yeah, the wood I'd chopped for a bloody half hour had also mysteriously gone, I called it quits. That's 5 days real time wasted. Also, I have issues with having to choose between a pack wiht a warm coat (I started playing in September - so I start out in September in the game - that means it's cold) or a pack with food.  The one leads to starvation, the other to hypothermia, meaning you're too cold to do anything at all anymore. Finding food you can't - you have no skills! Fishing? forget it. It's just real time wasted and another bout of hypothermia.
II love the concept; I just got totally frustrated with the unrealistic happenings and the odds so totally stacked against me.

I love the idea behind this game. Homesteading in Alaska in real time. If you require instant gratification from your games, this probably isn't for you. Though there is a mode that allows you to fast forward through 12 tasks each day. But that takes away from the tension that builds as you wait to see the results of your tasks. This is a challenging game that can take a lot of attempts to figure out. You need to consider and plan well to succeed. Take the time to develop your skills before rushing out to take on the Alaskan wilderness. Great game at a great price.

Once upon a time, I got fed up with city life and decided to move to Alaska, live in the middle of no where and get away from it all.
I didn't know jack and froze to death the first night.
Twice upon a time, I got fed up with the city and left for a cabin in the middle of Alaska.
I still didn't know jack, (and didn't really know that I didn't know jack) and died two days later.
Thrice upon a time, ... yeah I got fed up with the city and bought a cabin in the middle of Denali National Park in Alaska.
This time I knew that I didn't know jack and made sure that I was covering the basics every day.  218 days later, I'm still alive and life is pretty nice.
e-River Cabin Journal is not a game as much as a puzzle.  A puzzle that requires patience, planning, observation and thinking things through.  Decisions have consequences.  This games is all about decisions.  And a little bit of luck.
Playing in real time means that you have to fit logging in around your real life, sort of like a hobby.
If you are not into solving complex strategy puzzles, this is not for you.
If you want to virtually go through something like actually bugging out for Alaksa (but essentially being a clueless bunny on arrival) and seeing if you can survive, this is your cup of tea.
As a plus, the discussion board can be pretty lively at times and most of the other players are very helpful and fun.
As for me, I'm usually out looking for my dog.  Again. And again.  And again.
Maybe the devs should give me a cat.

There is something about this visual novel that just wins me over immediately. You're a bartender. That's it. You don't get involved in a heavy plot, you don't get heavily involved in other people's lives, you just go to work day after day and talk to your clients for about five minutes at a time. Sure if they go missing for a while or are sad you wish you could help, but all you can do is serve drinks. And there is something about a game that's so simple and yet the world is so fleshed out that you need to piece together through snippets you get from news articles and conversations you have that is so goddamn clever. The writing and art are excellent and the personalities and characters you meet are varied and always interesting. I honestly love it and it's one of my all-time favourite games. Highly, highly recommended.

Well it only took them half a year, but Injustice 2's PC port is finally here. NRS and WB haven't had the best track record for PC ports (see Arkham Knight and MKX's launch) but I'm happy to report this thankfully ended up being worth the wait. There's a lot to cover here so I'll divide my thoughts into sections.
Story: While story mode is hardly the most important aspect of a fighter (or even second most important) the Injustice series certainly has some of the better ones. Like previous NRS stories it's basically like watching a movie but whenever the characters fight you take control and play out the battle. Not spectacular gameplay wise, but the story itself is compelling enough to make you forget. In all honesty I'd say that the Injustice storyline is better written than most of the superhero films that have come out recently. It feels appropriately comic booky and has lots of fun character moments and twists on the DC universe. It's fun seeing the uneasy alliance Batman and fascist Superman have while fighting the greater threat of Brainiac. Plus there's an army of Gorillas who want to take over the world.
Gameplay: I imagine I don't really need to describe what the gameplay is like. If you've played any fighter you'll instantly feel comfortable playing this. It's basically a more refined version of the first, combos feel more intuitive (at least to a scrub like me) and in general it just feels tighter and more fun. The main difference I can think of is that characters now have level progression (1-20). The more you play them, the more you level up, giving them more bonus stats. Of course it's disabled in cometitive modes so it mostly gets its use in sp and casual online modes. Speaking of which...
Loot/Gear: Not gonna lie, I wasn't exactly excited when I heard this had a loot box system, and do I like it now? Meh. It's okay. You mostly just get cosmetics and some stat boosts from items (also disabled in competitive mode, so no real pay to win) and unlike Overwatch they hand these things out like candy. I've gotten like a 100 just in my first 10 hours of playing. Now that's mostly from finishing the story mode but you also get them from multiverse events and of course leveling up. This is probably the least offensive use of them in a game, as they are pretty easy to ignore, and I can't imagine anyone actually needing to buy more of these. Unlike some OTHER games you don't have to grind for 40 hours to unlock one character.
Roster: It's too early for me to comment on any balance, so I'll just be talking about the choice of characters. Personally I'm quite happy with the roster. They dropped about half the roster of the first and added mostly new characters. Which I'm honestly fine with. I do kind of miss Raven and Deathstroke but I'm glad they went with more obscure characters with more interesting personalities and powers. Atrocitus has a kitty that can shoot fireballs and attack on command, Black Canary screams at people, there's a talking Gorilla with Mind Control, and there's also everyone's favorite mustard loving Tamaranian princess Starfire and Edgelord supreme Red Hood. And in case you've been living under a rock the mother♥♥♥♥ing Ninja Turtles are going to be in this game, much to the chagrin of Spawn fans. Joker is still trash though (this interpretation anyway), and Damian Wayne is still the worst.
Graphics: I had to turn down the graphics quality to be able to run smoothly on my computer, but even at medium quality it still looks pretty good. The character models are the most noteworthy, it feels like there should be an uncanny valley effect with them but somehow they just found the right balance and there's a crazy amount of detail. There are some very attractive character designs here (wink wink). Some of the gear pieces are just downright ugly though. No amount of stats is gonna make me want to have that ugly helmet thing on Superman.
Sound: The music is... alright. The main theme sounds good, and the orchestral score works well in the cutscenes but none of the stage bgm stands out. They're alright, but I prefer something faster, like electronic or metal with fighters, something to get you pumped up and ready to fight, like the soundtracks of Marvel vs Capcom, Street Fighter, Tekken etc. Sound design is good. Punches and lasers all sound satisfying. And the voice acting is good. Though some of the voice actors are a bit to distractingly recognizable (at least if you've heard their voices before). Laura Bailey is pretty easily recognized and I can't listen to Blue Beetle or Brainiac without thinking of Pit  from Kid Icarus or Shran from Star Trek respectively. That's just nitpicking though.
Port: There's no glaring issues that I've noticed. Since I optimized the graphical settings it's flawlessly other than one odd CTD when I was in the Wonder Woman chapter of the story. I haven't played as much of the mp since the beta but it ran very well there and other reviews seem to concur here.
Price: For full disclosure I bought the UE on Green Man Games for 60$. Many have complained about the price and I cannot disagree. The only real defense is that it is lower than when it launched (though of course the UE then was a hundred goddamn dollars). It really depends on you if you think the price is worth it, if you loved the first and know you'll enjoy this then definitely go for it. If you're on the fence it's probably best to just wait.
Overall: Whew, that was more long-winded than I thought it would be. Anyway it's pretty obvious that I quite like this game and would recommend it to anyone who loves fighters and/or DC. I give Injustice 2 420 arbitrary numbers out of a possible 666 arbitrary numbers

Injustice 2 returns with a well done fighting game experience, including a whole new roster(and some returning favorites) with fighters, zoners, and all arounders, as well as new improvements from the old game. For instance, clashes are much faster and less flashy along with the two characters colliding having 4 or 5 different voice lines, a notable improvement over the one repetitive voice line from each character and huge blinding explosion every clash. Secondly, interactables, specifically throwable items, deal much less damage and are a bit more scarce around maps. Now while Injustice 2 may have a lower skill floor than other fighting games, an example would be all you have to do to block is move the joystick backwards, it doesn’t make it any less rewarding to more hardcore players as there is a lot of ridiculous high damage combos that can be mastered by putting in a lot of hours (believe me i’ve felt it after getting my♥♥♥♥♥pounded by guys that really know how to play Flash). In conclusion, an easy to pickup and worthwhile to master fighting game that improves upon the original formula of the first game.
The game takes place after the fallout from the first game, in the cool universe where Superman isn’t a golden boy and actually does cool♥♥♥♥♥♥, where our heroes are still recovering after the fall of Superman’s regime and trying to change their ways. However, things get a lot more complicated as Brainiac shows up and decides to throw a wrench into their plans and take over the alternate Earth to grow his intelligence and it’s up to ,once again, Batman and pals to figure out how to stop him from destroying the planet. To begin with the obvious, the facial animations are phenomenal, makes the dev team of Andromeda look like they had their monitors off during development. Now more importantly, Injustice 2 includes branching storylines that let you choose between 2 fighters during encounters giving some variety and letting players find characters they really like playing. They've also removed those interactable mini games, like shooting arrows at Solomon Grundy, and while that may dissapoint a few i'm actually pretty glad it was removed so I can just focus on fighting. For the most part, Brainiac and his story shouldn’t be anything too new and exciting, if you're familiar with DC animated movies, but the best part of the story is at the end where MAJOR SPOILERS
Overall, a solid story that makes me feel excited for the Injustice 3 storyline.
All of the characters are really well done and have some minor improvements while the stages are a lot better and usually have a lot of cool events happening in the background making every fight feel that much better. Clarity wise, I can very easily tell where projectiles are coming from and how they travel as well as what the interactables are, so for gameplay purposes once you get familiar with all the characters and stages you’ll know how to react. As for graphics the game runs quite smoothly on my older video card so i’d imagine people with top of the line PCs shouldn’t have much of an issue running the game on max settings.
A new addition to the game, the AI battle simulator lets you pick three of your favorite characters and pit them against other players defending teams letting you see who would win in a fight between Batman and Superman as well as netting small amounts of experience and rewards while you’re not playing so highly recommended you set up a team Asap (who knows maybe you’ll learn a combo).
Although we did learn about alternate Earths in the story of the first game, Injustice never really went anywhere with the concept, but now the multiverse is hugely present as it'll replace the Star Labs missions, and you’ll be able to access alternate Earths through Brother Eye and play a variety of different challenges to earn rewards. Now these challenges vary in difficulty and after getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by a lvl 20 Robin who took out my whole health bar in one combo and barely scratching him I recommend you get more familiar with the game and grind equipment before you take on tougher challenges. Although it isn't as creative as the Star Labs missions as it's largely just beat your opponent with certain multipliers and debuffs it's still very well done. Nevertheless, still a fun way to play different characters and challenges and earn rewards along the way.
Nothing too impressive, a largely generic action score but still passable and gives the stages a mild flair to set them apart from one another.
Yes, a fighting game has lootboxes, and yes they do actually have an impact on gameplay besides being cosmetic. Injustice 2 has “Mother Boxes” a.k.a unholy lootboxes that let you unlock equippable gear for characters ranging from various rarities that change the stats,abilities, and look of the equipped character, for example, if you want your character to hit harder equip them with strength gear. Thankfully any stat changes are disabled in ranked and competitive game modes so it’ll be all up to skill to decide the victor and while it is cool to unlock gear for your favorite fighters it can be a bit of a pain to new players who get smacked down even faster to a more experienced player who has top tier gear for their main. So all in all, play comp if you want a slightly more fair gameplay experience.
A very worthy sequel to Injustice that has an easy to grasp hard to master gameplay style and improves upon everything in the first game.
. If you ever wanted to fight with your favorite DC heros and settle who would win in a fight between Batman and Superman once and for all this game is for you.

I'm roughly 5 hours in and I can't get enough. I'll fully flesh out this review at some point, but I thought it important to put my initial impressions up as soon as possible. Without meaning to offend, it seems clear that most of the negative reviews I've skimmed through, simply don't get it.
The Witness is not about being told a 'story', at least not in a traditional sense. It is a contemplative, meandering conversation between designer and player. It's about uncovering a story yourself, through hours of patience and curiosity. There are so many mysteries to uncover: what is this island, who were its inhabitants, what the heck is with all of these puzzles? I've only barely scratched the surface, and I am more than intrigued. I'm excited for more, and without being spoon fed the answers.
Saying that the maze puzzle mechanics are repetitive is like complaining that an FPS is repetitive because it makes you fire guns, or driving games are repetitive because you drive cars. The maze puzzles work BECAUSE they are the backbone of all of the puzzle solving. They give your brain a filter through which to receive all of the information that you collect by completing other puzzles or simply exploring the environment. It would be impossible for the puzzles to have the depth that they do if it weren't for the maze structure.
The puzzles are beyond fantastic, a masterclass in puzzle design. They are always varied, always making you question assumptions, and always building upon the accumulated lessons that you've acquired. It's your brain that levels up, not your character. Truly brilliant stuff! Yes, they are crazy fun; yes, at times they are pretty frustrating; and yes, you probably should get out the old pen and paper once in awhile. They are more than worth it.

So far this game seem really interesting. The puzzles are starting to get complicated after an hour of gameplay but as the devs an player states, move away from the puzzle if you don't get it. There will be other puzzles to do which might aid you in other puzzles you previosly couldn't solve. Other than that, the game looks beautiful but the lack of graphical settings is anoying. And so far into the game there is no music att all which makes the game a bit too quiet.

A great puzzle game.
Like other great puzzle games, the basic mechanic (the 2d puzzle mazes) is consistent and at the same time completely reinvented with interesting new ideas throughout the game. In the same way that Portal "only" lets you shoot portals throughout the game, The Witness "only" lets you draw line puzzles. It keeps the game elegant and primarily a puzzle game, not an "is this interactible or is this important?" game.
The beautiful 3d environment is not wasted. It's important for both solving the puzzles and for providing the freedom to explore puzzles in any order you prefer. You will need to pay close attention to the environment and certain 3d objects for puzzles and secrets. I find this more rewarding than filling the island with interactible "story" objects that you can pick up and examine. The environment does not hide useless items. It hides information.
Like Antichamber, there's no typical story in The Witness, but there are mysteries. You should play this game if you consider yourself an explorer and enjoy uncovering mysteries.

I highly reccomend this game so far, but it's not for everyone. This is a game about discovering how things work by paying attention to detail and forcing yourself to let go of preconceptions.

Up to the point I am at, there's no "story" to the game that I know of, but the game does have a message. Which you can guess from several audio logs you can find around the island and also there's a "hidden" room in the island that adds to the message.
There's little to no reward other than having the satisfaction of solving a problem each time you solve a puzzle. If you're the kind of person who needs a story to feel personally invested in a game, or need eye candy to keep the interest this game probably is not for you. This, I think, helps construct the message I think the game is trying to convey.

I didn't really think much of this game when I first saw it pop-up on Steam. I've got hundreds of hours in Overwatch, thousands in Dota 2, and hundreds in SMITE. This looked like some kind of mash-up and it didn't really make sense to me what it was trying to do. That was my own fault. It definitely can be argued that it draws from all three of those games but it really is its own beast.
It's fast-paced, strategic, and filled with unique heroes. The fight for control of capture points by summoning different creatues that provide buffs, defense, and healing gives the game this constant back and forth tug-of-war that means you are constantly making decisions and fighting for the upper-hand.
Lots of fighting wouldn't be fun without great hero kits. You see some of the familiar names; Bruiser, Tank, Support, Assassin, but the more open, 3rd-person movement of the game means these are similar names with brand new ways of playing. You'll launch yourself across the map to slam down on opponents or vault over walls to escape, you'll hover in the air to blast opponents from above. The freedom of movement and all skill shot abilties is a very welcome addition. You level up as you play allowing you to unlock different augments to your four abilties and ultimate. This provides new combos that are exciting to pull off instead of just spamming abilities. Also all the animations are incredibly slick. Movement looks great, attacks are distinct, and killing off an enemy has a satisfying punch to it.
As far as I can see the developers have a real passion for this game and intend to regularly add new heroes to add to the diversity, so it doesnt matter if you like or dont like shooters and MOBAs, this game is unique to itself and if you enjoy fast paced competitive games then you should at the very least give it a go. It may surprise you like it did me.

Survival point & click adventure with some potential but wrong execution.
This game is recommended only for those who want to play a game in "real time" mode meaning one gaming day = one real day. Some tasks requires really 30 minutes, some even more. Devs stated this game has a year of play time and is meant to be played a little bit each day.
And here comes the main reason this game cannot be generally recommended for survival games lovers. The casual mode included makes those 30 min tasks instant, anyway, you cannot proceed to another day in game until a new day in real life begin. If the casual mode could be played separately of the real days, the game would be highly recommended even containing some bugs and some weird control elements.
Pos:
- there is a lot of things to do - drinking, cooking, cutting tree into firewood and kindles, loading your guns manually, reading books etc.
- it is kind of sophisticated. For example using a radio drains battery, you may charge the battery a little bit by hand charger, building wind turbine, solar panel or simply buy a new battery.
- from content point of view it is kind of nicely made game, not sloppy.
Neg:
- casual mode is not a casual mode even though it penalizes you for being casual :/
- some control mechanics are awful, for example during reloading, after inserting each single projectile into magazine the window "reloads" - hides and shows again.
- from coding point of view the game feels kind of sloppy.

I think this game is great. It is very different than most games. You have to know what you're getting into. Understand that there is no live action fighting in this game. You move around a character icon and click on all the different tools and options. You have many choices for things to do and ways to survive.
This game requires a lot of patience. Every time you make a choice to do something, say maybe clean one of your guns for example, it sets a timer that references your computer clock and applies an appropriate wait time until the task is complete. During that time, you must wait for the task to be completed before you can do anything else in the game other than wait or log out and come back later.
What I really like about this game is that it is a challeng, but it doesnt require my full attention. I can play while I cook or fold laundry or watch t.v. and the game will always wait for me (except at midnight, when all of your current condition stats will apply to your health - this is the only time you can die!) I usually log into this game two or three times per day for a few minutes to make choices. Then, I get to return later in the day and find out the results of my choice, whether or not I'm likely to survive until tomorrow. Good times.

First of all, there are a lot of Space games that are coming to us all soon and I'll think many of them will be great...
But so far Star Conflict is, for now (and for me), the only game that is fully released and Free to play! Free to play is really free to play. I know - cause I started to play that way!
You can however choose to pay more or less real money to get more from the game - but it's up to you! For me, the most important argument to pay - is to support the developers!
I think they have made a perfect score in this:
1. Play the game for free
2. Don't like it? Erase it and you haven't spend your money!
Compare that to buying a game, play it for an hour and realize that the game is not for you. Your money is gone...
3. Like it? Continue play for free if you want. Yes, you can play this game forever without spending any money!
I'll have seen many pilots in this game who have played for long without spending any money. If I meet them in a fight it's the skill, ships level and how many we are against each other who wins! 2 against 1 is always a better start...
So why should you pay? First of all (I say it again) - to support the developers! Again - instead of beeing forced to pay $X to get a game or pay $X every month to play a game you have now the chance to pay what you think the game is worth or what you can afford!
So what do you get in the game if you pay? (I'll skip the details)
- Faster ship-leveling = ships get stronger and faster (you can still level up a ship but it takes more time)
(Faster ship-leveling also means that you can access newer ships faster and access more parts of the game faster)
- More loot (you can still loot a lot if you win a PvP game)
So the only positive effect is that, instead of playing for hours, you can direct get what you want.
Buying a DLC ship:
The other way to spend money in  this game is buy a DLC ship. This is the only way to get those ship. There are 50 of them but there are also 135(!) ships you can work your way to get (without spending any money).
Are those DLC ships better than the normal ships? Yes and no... If you level up a normal ship to maximum that ship is balanced to be equal to the DLC ship beacuse the DLC ship is maxed leveled from start. That is also a week point for the DLC ships. One of the most fun things in the game is to level up a ship.
So, for me I only use DLC ships in the Invasion mode (MMO part of the game). They are great cause they don't have to be rapaired and the have more slots for things you find.
The review then? Here it is...
I love playing Battlefield 4 with keyboard+mouse. It's easy to understand, kill all enemies and capture the flag, and the matches are short. In Star Conflict you have the same game type - but in space and it is working great! But here you also have the Invasion mode MMO. Fly to sectors just to explore it, shoot some bad guys or find some valuable stuff - if you have more time over.
The controls works perfect (I use keyboard and mouse), the graphics are truly awesome, the balance is not 100% but the developers is trying hard with it and are releasing updates often.
The only really bad thing about this game is when starting a PvP game. Often it takes around a minute to get started but sometimes it can take several minutes. A tip here is to select "Any region" instead of your region.
The game needs this time to find other gamers with your (ship)rank so the match will be fair.
And because there is not so many players this takes time...
I'll do hope that more space-liking-gamers finds this game!
Oculus Rift
I play this game using a Oculus Rift.
I can't in words explain how incredible fantastic the game is when using Oculus Rift.

When you are in a dogfight and the enemy fly by you, I'll guess you have some problem to follow him when using a monitor. In Oculus Rift you just turn your head and follow him and then turn your ship after him without loosing him from sight!
That's really neat...

And the world in Star Conflict is great and made in "3D"... It looks fantastic when you look at it on your monitor... Yes? ...but when you use the Oculus Rift... fantastic goes to fantastic X 10! It's hard to explain but you are truly in that world!
You know when you play you see the world from behind your ship. In Oculus Rift you "hang" just above your ship. You can look up, to the sides and when you look down you see the ship and the 3D-deep is awesome. Your ship is so close and far away you see the asteroids and even farther away you see a planet. Words can never explain that feeling - you have to try it to understand it!
So, if I rate Star Conflict a 5 of 5 when playing it with a normal monitor I need to raise that to a 10 of 5 if I play with Oculus Rift. It's still the same game - but with Oculus Rift you ARE IN THE GAME!

Unlike most story and character driven games Valhalla doesn't give you 2-4 black and white options with clear and telegraphed consequences. The story flows fluidly and is based around which drinks you choose to prepare, rather than what you choose to say (you do not control the main character, Jill's, dialogue). The characters are diverse in both personality and design and the game strikes a fantastic balance between humor and serious drama. And the new mechanics of managing Jill's personal finances and happiness are engaging and bring another level of immersion. (Also the lock screen on Jill's phone may be the cutest thing to ever grace my computer screen). Overall this is a true indie gem and I'm delighted to see the positive response it's getting on Steam.

Well it only took them half a year, but Injustice 2's PC port is finally here. NRS and WB haven't had the best track record for PC ports (see Arkham Knight and MKX's launch) but I'm happy to report this thankfully ended up being worth the wait. There's a lot to cover here so I'll divide my thoughts into sections.
Story: While story mode is hardly the most important aspect of a fighter (or even second most important) the Injustice series certainly has some of the better ones. Like previous NRS stories it's basically like watching a movie but whenever the characters fight you take control and play out the battle. Not spectacular gameplay wise, but the story itself is compelling enough to make you forget. In all honesty I'd say that the Injustice storyline is better written than most of the superhero films that have come out recently. It feels appropriately comic booky and has lots of fun character moments and twists on the DC universe. It's fun seeing the uneasy alliance Batman and fascist Superman have while fighting the greater threat of Brainiac. Plus there's an army of Gorillas who want to take over the world.
Gameplay: I imagine I don't really need to describe what the gameplay is like. If you've played any fighter you'll instantly feel comfortable playing this. It's basically a more refined version of the first, combos feel more intuitive (at least to a scrub like me) and in general it just feels tighter and more fun. The main difference I can think of is that characters now have level progression (1-20). The more you play them, the more you level up, giving them more bonus stats. Of course it's disabled in cometitive modes so it mostly gets its use in sp and casual online modes. Speaking of which...
Loot/Gear: Not gonna lie, I wasn't exactly excited when I heard this had a loot box system, and do I like it now? Meh. It's okay. You mostly just get cosmetics and some stat boosts from items (also disabled in competitive mode, so no real pay to win) and unlike Overwatch they hand these things out like candy. I've gotten like a 100 just in my first 10 hours of playing. Now that's mostly from finishing the story mode but you also get them from multiverse events and of course leveling up. This is probably the least offensive use of them in a game, as they are pretty easy to ignore, and I can't imagine anyone actually needing to buy more of these. Unlike some OTHER games you don't have to grind for 40 hours to unlock one character.
Roster: It's too early for me to comment on any balance, so I'll just be talking about the choice of characters. Personally I'm quite happy with the roster. They dropped about half the roster of the first and added mostly new characters. Which I'm honestly fine with. I do kind of miss Raven and Deathstroke but I'm glad they went with more obscure characters with more interesting personalities and powers. Atrocitus has a kitty that can shoot fireballs and attack on command, Black Canary screams at people, there's a talking Gorilla with Mind Control, and there's also everyone's favorite mustard loving Tamaranian princess Starfire and Edgelord supreme Red Hood. And in case you've been living under a rock the mother♥♥♥♥ing Ninja Turtles are going to be in this game, much to the chagrin of Spawn fans. Joker is still trash though (this interpretation anyway), and Damian Wayne is still the worst.
Graphics: I had to turn down the graphics quality to be able to run smoothly on my computer, but even at medium quality it still looks pretty good. The character models are the most noteworthy, it feels like there should be an uncanny valley effect with them but somehow they just found the right balance and there's a crazy amount of detail. There are some very attractive character designs here (wink wink). Some of the gear pieces are just downright ugly though. No amount of stats is gonna make me want to have that ugly helmet thing on Superman.
Sound: The music is... alright. The main theme sounds good, and the orchestral score works well in the cutscenes but none of the stage bgm stands out. They're alright, but I prefer something faster, like electronic or metal with fighters, something to get you pumped up and ready to fight, like the soundtracks of Marvel vs Capcom, Street Fighter, Tekken etc. Sound design is good. Punches and lasers all sound satisfying. And the voice acting is good. Though some of the voice actors are a bit to distractingly recognizable (at least if you've heard their voices before). Laura Bailey is pretty easily recognized and I can't listen to Blue Beetle or Brainiac without thinking of Pit  from Kid Icarus or Shran from Star Trek respectively. That's just nitpicking though.

A few Hours in and I tell you that for fans of Caesar IV, Pharaoh, or Emperor Rise of the Middle Kingdom, this game is right up your alley.  You play the clever city builder in the employ of the Roman goverment to seek out new areas and found new cities from the ground up.  Each scenario becomes increasingly difficult, but not to the point that it becomes overly taxing to build and maintain your city.  There are fewer overlays in this game, making it slightly harder to micro manage your city as perfectly as you might have in previous city builders of the same genre.  Still, you command all the power on your map, and if a Roman's house has to go for the city bath, you just say the word.  There are also economic and military scenarios available as you progress into the game, as you might have assumed.
There are only a few negative aspects of the game that might make the avid city builder a little frustrated.  In CivCity: Rome, you find yourself balancing happiness constantly.  The scale goes from +100 to -100 and it affects your population directly.  If you leave your happiness at +100 (which is relatively easy to do in most scenarios) your population will explode leading to "vagrants" that sit outside your town center, create housing shortages, and generate... unhappiness.  On its own, you can counter this effect, but you'll eventually find yourself trying to balance your population by keeping your happiness in the -10 to +10 range, which equals 0 growth and 0 loss.  If you then want to create a new industry, you'll need to bump your happiness to get more people, then bring it back down again.  Occassionally you'll receive empire bonuses or, negatively, barbarian threats that will mess with your happiness for a short time.  I found this yo-yo effect to be a little annoying at times.
Postively, Sid has added some researchable technologies that you can use to customize your city to the style you want for the particular map your on, which is really refreshing.  This game is really a solid add to your collection if you like these types of city builders.

Injustice 2 returns with a well done fighting game experience, including a whole new roster(and some returning favorites) with fighters, zoners, and all arounders, as well as new improvements from the old game. For instance, clashes are much faster and less flashy along with the two characters colliding having 4 or 5 different voice lines, a notable improvement over the one repetitive voice line from each character and huge blinding explosion every clash. Secondly, interactables, specifically throwable items, deal much less damage and are a bit more scarce around maps. Now while Injustice 2 may have a lower skill floor than other fighting games, an example would be all you have to do to block is move the joystick backwards, it doesn’t make it any less rewarding to more hardcore players as there is a lot of ridiculous high damage combos that can be mastered by putting in a lot of hours (believe me i’ve felt it after getting my♥♥♥♥♥pounded by guys that really know how to play Flash). In conclusion, an easy to pickup and worthwhile to master fighting game that improves upon the original formula of the first game.
The game takes place after the fallout from the first game, in the cool universe where Superman isn’t a golden boy and actually does cool♥♥♥♥♥♥, where our heroes are still recovering after the fall of Superman’s regime and trying to change their ways. However, things get a lot more complicated as Brainiac shows up and decides to throw a wrench into their plans and take over the alternate Earth to grow his intelligence and it’s up to ,once again, Batman and pals to figure out how to stop him from destroying the planet. To begin with the obvious, the facial animations are phenomenal, makes the dev team of Andromeda look like they had their monitors off during development. Now more importantly, Injustice 2 includes branching storylines that let you choose between 2 fighters during encounters giving some variety and letting players find characters they really like playing. They've also removed those interactable mini games, like shooting arrows at Solomon Grundy, and while that may dissapoint a few i'm actually pretty glad it was removed so I can just focus on fighting. For the most part, Brainiac and his story shouldn’t be anything too new and exciting, if you're familiar with DC animated movies, but the best part of the story is at the end where MAJOR SPOILERS
Overall, a solid story that makes me feel excited for the Injustice 3 storyline.
All of the characters are really well done and have some minor improvements while the stages are a lot better and usually have a lot of cool events happening in the background making every fight feel that much better. Clarity wise, I can very easily tell where projectiles are coming from and how they travel as well as what the interactables are, so for gameplay purposes once you get familiar with all the characters and stages you’ll know how to react. As for graphics the game runs quite smoothly on my older video card so i’d imagine people with top of the line PCs shouldn’t have much of an issue running the game on max settings.
A new addition to the game, the AI battle simulator lets you pick three of your favorite characters and pit them against other players defending teams letting you see who would win in a fight between Batman and Superman as well as netting small amounts of experience and rewards while you’re not playing so highly recommended you set up a team Asap (who knows maybe you’ll learn a combo).
Although we did learn about alternate Earths in the story of the first game, Injustice never really went anywhere with the concept, but now the multiverse is hugely present as it'll replace the Star Labs missions, and you’ll be able to access alternate Earths through Brother Eye and play a variety of different challenges to earn rewards. Now these challenges vary in difficulty and after getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by a lvl 20 Robin who took out my whole health bar in one combo and barely scratching him I recommend you get more familiar with the game and grind equipment before you take on tougher challenges. Although it isn't as creative as the Star Labs missions as it's largely just beat your opponent with certain multipliers and debuffs it's still very well done. Nevertheless, still a fun way to play different characters and challenges and earn rewards along the way.
Nothing too impressive, a largely generic action score but still passable and gives the stages a mild flair to set them apart from one another.
Yes, a fighting game has lootboxes, and yes they do actually have an impact on gameplay besides being cosmetic. Injustice 2 has “Mother Boxes” a.k.a unholy lootboxes that let you unlock equippable gear for characters ranging from various rarities that change the stats,abilities, and look of the equipped character, for example, if you want your character to hit harder equip them with strength gear. Thankfully any stat changes are disabled in ranked and competitive game modes so it’ll be all up to skill to decide the victor and while it is cool to unlock gear for your favorite fighters it can be a bit of a pain to new players who get smacked down even faster to a more experienced player who has top tier gear for their main. So all in all, play comp if you want a slightly more fair gameplay experience.
A very worthy sequel to Injustice that has an easy to grasp hard to master gameplay style and improves upon everything in the first game.
. If you ever wanted to fight with your favorite DC heros and settle who would win in a fight between Batman and Superman once and for all this game is for you.

I don't write many reviews, but this game is worth it. The Witness has been one of the best gaming experiences I have had in a while. It has a Myst like quality with the island being a giant puzzle and there being a point to it all that is masked behind an abundance of small, tablet like puzzles.
A lot of the hate I've read on here praises the game for its beauty and bashes it for the puzzles that are simplistic in nature originally, but progress in unique and clever ways throughout. Boiling this game down to "Snake puzzles on a boring island" is reductionist in the worst way because what this game does best is keep the mind swirling with where to go and what to do next while teaching you along the way.
The way that teaching occurs in this game is so organic that at times it is hard to realize that you've added a new piece of the puzzle solving to your mind. This cleverness and subtelty combined with the beauty and mystery of the game make this puzzle game worth checking out.
The price tag is a bit steep if these aren't your types of games so wait for a sale and pick it up as soon as you can.

Some negative reviews mention that they do not like the game because ultimately, it's a challenging and repetitive puzzle game about a line on a grid.
However for me that would be forgetting the thing that makes the
difference: it is making you travel and wander in a beautiful, extremely dense and detailed universe, full of questions and history.
It does something very few  games do right, that is capturing an ambient, pushing you in a universe that's here not only as a filler, but also something that questions you in a very subtle and progressive way.
Not many games make me think about their universe after I'm done playing them, and The Witness definitely does that about its puzzle and environment.
It also makes you feel like you are travelling and exploring something alive, which is too rare in games for me.
I got back the sensation I had when playing games like The Wind Waker, Journey or the Metroid series, this sensation of exploring something natural and alive, coherent. And that's worth way more than 40 bucks.
AND it makes something that no puzzle game do, that is managing to teach you very complex rules little by little, without using
text. When you get to realize you just learnt something all by yourself, that's the greatest reward you can get and yes, it's more than enough for me to keep on going.
If you want to get some fireworks, explosions and pumped up music everytime you do something great, then sure you won't like the game. But honestly, is it really what matters?
The Witness tells you to enjoy the trip not the destination, and it does it in a remarkable way.

I bought The Witness yesterday, and I've completed 249 of the game's puzzles in approximately 7.5 hours. There are still quite a few areas I haven't unlocked, and a few puzzles that I'm completely baffled by, but generally speaking, the game gives you enough freedom to keep discovering new areas and learning about different game mechanics in a way that allows you to progress continuously. There are several areas which I've finished completely, which taught some of the simpler mechanics that are built on in later puzzles.
I want to give a little context on the way you learn about puzzle elements in this game, because I've seen some misconceptions in other reviews. The simplest puzzles are just moving a dot to connect a line from A to B, but quickly the game will start to introduce different symbols into the puzzles, each of which has a function and dictates something about the way you need to solve the puzzle.
This is the important part:
If you come across a puzzle that seems way too hard for you, then it probably is. The game is not encouraging you to try to guess the answer and get really frustrated. It's giving you a sign that you haven't learned the right tools to solve it yet, and you should be looking somewhere else. Every puzzle element, from black and white squares, to spiky dots, to a little tri-force looking thing that changes how different puzzle regions act, to things that look like Tetris blocks, every one of these elements is explained in a series of very basic puzzles (starting with just one or two squares as opposed to the usual 5x5 grid) that explains the mechanic. The rules, once you learn them, do not change. They are not arbitrary. They work the same way every time. There is a lot of challenge in finding a solution that fits all the conditions imposed by the different puzzle elements, but there is no guesswork.
It's unfortunate to see a lot of reviewers quitting after an hour and a half of playtime because they got really frustrated with something they didn't understand and want a refund for the game. My own feeling is that the game does a really good job of slowly introducing you to new elements, as long as you just walk around and look for simpler puzzles before going straight to trying the most complicated-looking thing you can find. The game even turns off the puzzle panels if you try to brute-force an answer to a puzzle you can't solve yet--- take the hint.
A few other things. The graphics are beautiful, with a very colorful, almost cel-shaded style. The different biomes of the island are each distinct and offer an impressive diversity of scenery, with each location having a different mood, and often with puzzle mechanics that relate loosely to the area (one region, overlooking a wide bay of calm water, teaches puzzles about reflection). The sound is minimal but effective; there are a few puzzles that actually require sound to complete, and because the rest of the soundtrack is relatively sparse, the auditory clues jumped out at me quickly. The one place where I think the game falters is in story, in that there really isn't one, even (at least as far as I've gotten) to be pieced together from the audio recordings and videos that can be found around the island. Myst or Riven this is not--- the game has a lot of atmosphere, but it doesn't have a narrative. As a fan of games with strong stories and generally of fiction with detailed world-building, it does seem like a little bit of a missed opportunity. But overall, I've really enjoyed my time with the game so far, and I'm looking forward to playing more.

I purchased this game from
before it was released on Steam. So, I have many more hours into this game than my account shows.
I have to say that they have done an amazing job on a very gutsy project. The music and visual designs are wonderful. The concept and immersion are well thought out. The concept is one that will turn some away, but I think that it a very nice change of pace. The interface has some issues, but the Devs are working on them after receiving feedback.
It took me a few days to figure out some of the basics. Boy howdy! It got very frustrating during those first few days days. But, once I had the basics down, the game changed for me entirely. I think the game was designed to make the player feel some something to the effect of what it would be like to be alone in the Alaskan wilderness with no developed skills. A relatvely simple task of gathering firewood risks slipping with the axe and hurting yourself or having a wolf come through camp and attack you. The suspense of potential success or failure because it takes 40 minutes in real time to know how you did. Watching your supplies slowly get consumed as you use all your energy to go hunting, only to return to the cabin empty handed. Developing your skills requires real time. They make it easier than real life, you can just read a book. Although, most take more than six hours to complete as you read them in one to three hour chunks. Even when you get all your skills to 100, you still have to prepare yourself and your cabin to make it through winter. The days get shorter or longer depending on when you play it, because it uses your real date/time to determine what the day will be like, as if you we in Alaska.
Everything you do takes a certain amount of real time. LIght a fire, two minutes. Gather some kindling, 30 minutes. But, you don't sit there watching it for that time. Well, you can if you want. You can either put it in the background and a timer goes off when the task is done or close the game and come back in however long it will be. It saves the game and when you launch it again, it checks your local time and tells you how much time is left or shows you the results of your efforts. If you have a plan for what you want to do for the day, it will probably take you less than half an hour to play it each day, five minutes at a time. You can use the "Fast Forward" feature to skip the realtime and knock out all your tasks (up to 12) quickly in one sitting.
Things to do before going outside on the first day:
1) Spend some time reading (defense against animal attacks, the pistol manual and the lumberjack book help most at the beginning
2) Load your pistol
3) Fill your belt pouch
If you like survival games and like to challenge yourself, give it a shot. If you have to have instant gratification and think games should be made to your limited expectations, give it a shot anyway. You may find that it is OK to take your time.

Grab your backpack as you head out the door to start your life in Alaska!  To be honest I truely love this game!  The only thing some people may not like it would be due to it is "Real Time", but you can get some "Fast Forward" which allow you to jump ahead in time a few times a day.  Something you have to remember is the fact a "Game Day" is the same as in RL.  At Midnight the game processes the day and you start the next day.  I find myself doing chores and hate waiting till I can finish and start another one.  Now this game has a lot of "Luck" needed to stay a live.  But would I recommend this game?  Well if you like games that you have to really take time to play then this may fit your bill.  Great way to pass time each day as you go from one chore to another.  This is now my "Go To" game and I really like that the Dev of the game is very active on the discussion forums and will look at all suggestions we give.  Just remember this is a VERY SLOW paced game, and if you aren't careful you may just be attacked by a bear so be sure to keep your pistol loaded..  (Took me a few games to figure this one out!)  Be sure to read any books on the bookcase to give you a heads start!  9/10
Edit:  If you are a fan of true simulations, and randomness in a game, then you must give this a go.  This game, although slow paced really makes you feel for your charater, you care they get an infection, or if animals are stealing your food.   You really look forward to each day in RL, when you can start the game, and see what has happened in game over the night.  Basically you live 2 lives, One in the Real World, and one in Alaska Wilderness.  I have been gaming for many, many, many years and this is on my top 5 greatest games of all time.  It is so well done, and the patches which add content are unique in adding things to make the game world even larger.  If they ever code in a semi multiplayer play style this would add another layer on top of the rather large world. (They have a very basic version where you can send some items through like the postal system, but you can't visit them).  Hardest part is trying to fit everything you need to do to survive in one day, so time management is a MUST.
Just do yourself a favor and stop debating and just buy this gem!

I like the idea of e-River Cabin Journal.  The concept is sound.  On paper, this game should work.  Unfortunately there are far too many annoying issues that have been left within the game to recommend it.  The idea of a "real-world" survival game is appealing, and I was open minded when approaching the game and its "real-time gameplay" features.  This title however, needs much more work, and probably shouldn't have been released onto Steam just yet.  It's hard to say whether or not e-River Cabin Journal would have benefited from starting off in Early Access, but as it stands, it really does feel like it's lacking quite a few basic features and is still far too buggy for a recommendation from any informed gamer.  The gameplay is
reminiscent of classic text adventure games mixed with classic point and click adventure games,
but not quite.  Instead, it feels more like a turn-based RPG, with each turn taking one whole "real-life" day to complete.  If it sounds confusing, well it is, and the way the game was designed doesn't help much in enlightening gamers to the finer points of the gameplay or its mechanics.
I've spent between 4 - 6 hours with the game so far, over the course of a couple of weeks after purchasing the game when it was first released about a month or so ago, and while I initially enjoyed the idea of the game, I've found it very taxing to actually continue playing it and have had to force myself to try and get back into it, which hasn't been easy.  I'd say that I enjoyed the first hour, but slowly became more and more frustrated as I tried to push myself to continue playing.  Since the game was first released, there were many issues that I thought would have been tweaked or fixed by now, but those issues are still plaguing the game and are affecting my enjoyment and the overall experience.
Simply put, the game feels unfinished.  Due to it's pacing and the sheer amount of slogging and clicking through unintuitive menu's, it feels more like a Spreadsheet and Menu simulator right now rather than an actual survival game, and I would say that as a game it even feels like a less than stellar work of interactive fiction.  There are no options or settings menus.  You can't adjust the screen size, the speed of the game, or any other basic features, and while I do appreciate the simplicity of it's design and the attempted atmosphere within the game, I find interacting with its "gameplay" to be slow, frustrating, and a bit of a chore.
To be perfectly honest, there are freeware games and even classic ascii and text adventure games out there with more intuitive menus, controls, and systems put in place that help the player without actually tarnishing the experience or making the game any less challenging or interesting.
Things that negatively affect the experience for me:
- Running the game and having multiple windows open at the same time - all the time
- No fullscreen option
- Very slow load times
- Low resolution graphics
(the game is filled with low-res static images - making the chances of a fullscreen mode unlikely in a future update)
- Defunct tutorial
- Untintuitive tool-tips (this game really does need active tool-tips)
- A messy and confusing series of menu layouts
It's a shame that the game is such a mess in its current state.  The developer clearly loves "The Great Outdoors" and there is a realistic sense of survival that almost shines to the surface of the game, even through the chaotic gameplay mechanics and overall design choices.  However, everything good within this game is overshadowed by far more glaring issues and a sense of tedium due to the lack of settings, options, and the unfinished manner in which the game is currently presented.  This would have been a very interesting game had it been released during the early 1990's, but I find it hard to swallow that the game is selling for around $10 dollars on Steam.
To be fair, the developer has an older freeware prototype version of the game on their old website that feels like it was made for Windows 95 and is simply called
It works with WinXP, Win7,8, and I believe 10.  If you're at all interested, or want to see exactly how this game plays then head over to the original site and try out the free version which you'll find located at this address:
Be sure to download and try that freeware version first, because aside from some slightly better graphics and sound, the user interface and gameplay are almost identical.  Then you can determine whether or not you want to drop your hard earned moolah on the commercial release.

Platform Hell games are an incredibly popular genre. Super Meat Boy set a very high standard back when it released, and people have been trying to emulate its success for quite a while.
Improving on the formula is harder than copying it, though. What could be better than running really fast and dying all the time?
Well, have I got news for you. The formula has been changed.
Running, jumping, and dying? Make room... For punching.
That's right. An entire new dimension has opened up. This is like discovering a new color that's the opposite of a mix of a slightly pinkish green and a deep purplish orange. Or maybe whatever the ♥♥♥♥ razzmatazz is, that's a crayon too. The game has changed, people.
They Bleed Pixels, an indie platformer available on Steam, combines the platformer hell action of games like Super Meat Boy with an entire Tumblr worth of A E S T H E T I C. And punching.
As a young girl named Strong Female Protagonist, you're thrust into a world of Lovecraftian horror and sharp minimalist pixel art to fend for your life against tentacles and very pointy things that are everywhere.
Graphically, They Bleed Pixels is stylish and sleek. A monotone black and white with accents of red form the foreground, contrasting sharply with the vibrant backgrounds. With PARALLAX SCROLLING.
That's a mark of the finest quality.
While the whole retro platformer pixel art thing has been done a million times, the style is executed tastefully and with enough of a unique spin to differentiate it from literally every other platforming game on Steam.
But the game's most defining feature is its snappy fighting system. They Bleed Pixels' combat is very space-oriented. You're capable of launching enemies horizontally or vertically with kicks, chaining combos with your punches and by use of the environment itself. The same spikes, saw-blades, and pikes that'll be maiming you can be used to kill your enemies.
Controlling space becomes essential in later levels, where enemies will start to condense into smaller areas with more obstacles in your way. Being able to effectively kick them around while dispatching them with speed and style is critical, as it will also determine how many times you have to die in the same spot over and over.
The checkpoint system is a little unique. A meter will build up as you combo and kill, and once it's full your character can cast a checkpoint by standing still. Which at first struck me as a weird mechanic, because I was concerned I'd cast it accidentally without meaning to. But the fast pace of the game actually lead me to forget about the checkpoints completely at times. Your score doubles as long as you keep your checkpoint meter full, so there's a strong risk-reward element to it, but I honestly just kept forgetting it was there and getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when I had to jump through razor-blade ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for the umpteenth time.
They Bleed Pixels' brutal nature is great and all, but it's also just full of♥♥♥♥♥♥at times.
