I feel like I've written this before, but..."I wish I liked this more than I do".
Gigantic is a 5v5 hero shooter/brawler game with multiple contested points on the map. The contested points can be inhabited by creatures that the players can spawn, if they have enough points. In between contesting these points, the players spend time wildly running around a medium-sized arena, murdering one another.
Gigantic is a f2p game, which means that most of the experience is set behind a paywall. In reality, the free version acts as a demo, since you can purchase an "ultimate pack" for 30€ that has everything the game will ever offer in it, current and future content included. It's probably the best paymodel a game like this could have.
Paymodels aside, what is there to this game? Having played the free version on the Arc launcher and now on Steam, I gotta say, not a lot. The game needs to mature to reach it's full potential. Since there's no hero stacking, you can't be certain that you will get to play who you want. The balance seems a little wonky at times and a few members of the cast are just plain boring. No hits carry ANY weight whatsoever and the effects are Battleborn-level bad, which means you will have some trouble understanding who is punching who. The UI is pretty nifty, so at least it's not actively hindering you.
The biggest question I gotta ask myself is: why should I play this game? It's pretty, has an absolultely charming art style and it's fast. Is that enough for me to actually keep playing this, even when it's free? No, hell no.
I'll keep looking at the game, checking if it will get updates in the future. As it stands, it sorta feels like Paragon, except Paragon feels better and runs better than this. There just isn't anything here that I haven't seen before, or that hasn't been done better in other games.
Oh, and the wait times can be OBNOXIOUS. 20 minutes on Arc to get into a single match? No thanks.

I picked this game up despite it not having any reviews or ratings whatsoever. Since it's only 5 bucks, the screenshots look cool, I had some money to spare, and I happen to be a zombie fan, I couldn't resist. All I can say is, don't waste your money. Don't be fooled by the screenshots. This is one of those games that exists solely to prove that appearances can be deceiving.
First off, the optimization is atrocious. I have a decent, mid-range pc that can run games like crysis and far cry 3 at a nice framerate at high-very high settings. With this game, I cranked up all the settings and was unpleasantly surprised to be met by a choppy, unstable, and nausia-inducing framerate that never manages to go past 35 frames per second. The game isn't exactly a looker either (despite what the screenshots may suggest) so performance this terrible is simply inexcusable. Flat textures everywhere, horrifically stiff animations, a terrible draw distance, you get the idea.The only thing that looks mildly good is the guns. Now, I understand this is just a small indie game, but that doesn't excuse quality this poor. The graphics don't bother me as much as the horrendous performance (even on low settings).
But as bad as the performance and graphics are, the gameplay could be solid enough to save the game right? Wrong! Combat is split up in melee and gunplay. You start off with a melee weapon and must kill zombies to get money and find spots where you can buy guns. The problem here is that the combat (both melee and guns) is flatter than a pancake. There is no sense of impact to the melee combat and the enemy ai is easily exploited. You can just run backwards and swat mindlessly at the zombies (one by one) to kill them with one blow to the head. Even the Walking Dead Survival Instinct had better melee combat and ai. The gunplay is arguably better, but that doesn't make it good. That's like saying a gunshot wound to the stomach hurts less than a gunshot wound to the crotch. To make matters worse, every single time you fire the gun, the framerate goes to the single digits. This means that if you have a small group of zombies attacking and you're just wildly firing an assault rifle, the framerate might just force you into a vomit fit.
Sound wise, it's... average. The zombie sounds are all right, but the melee and gunfire sounds are unsatisying.
Pros:
A few decent sound effects.
Guns have a nice look to them due to shading.
Cons:
Terrible combat
No tension
Tedious weapon system
Insanely bad optimization
Poor visuals
Costs money
Terrible combat
It'll waste a few of your hard-earned dollars
You'll hate yourself after playing it.
Terrible combat
Sound design is mostly lacking
Did I mention the terrible combat?
Bottom line: STAY AWAY. If you want good zombie survival games check out left 4 dead 2, dead island, and dying light. Don't waste money on this game until the dev gives it a major overhaul (if that day ever comes).

I don't understand why this game exists, and I don't even mean for that to sound harsh. I got this in a bundle and read reviews, and it sounded so awful that I wanted to be apart of it, knowing full well why I shouldn't. But it was a zombie wave game, there's not much originality left in it, but I suppose someone could come along and change the game. It's been done before, and it sure as hell can be done again.

So, right away, I have to make an account. Wait wait wait, pump the brakes. For what? The multiplayer is broken right now, what in the world do I need an account for? Well, leap of faith. Account made. Let's just configure this thing and... the dropdown box for "effects" has no values in it. That's... concerning. But, giving it a benefit of a doubt, right? Let's play a game then, 2 maps to choose from. Okay, maybe replayability makes it fun? Maybe it's randomized, that would be cool. I learned later that, no, it really wouldn't. Within the first seconds of  the game, I realized what I had gotten myself into. The graphics, while very bad, could have been worse. After all, I'm usually not one to judge by looks alone, so I decided to try and make a good run.

Crowbar in hand, I use the old training method where you run in a line and small circles to gather up the zombies. Great, it works, so at least the AI is decent? Wrong. Turns out, you can just walk in a straight line, look back and m1 all of the zombies to death. Okay, but there's a lot of them, surely this method wouldn't last forever? Again, wrong. The only reason why I didn't put an engagement ring on that method is purely because it takes forever, seeing as though they add more zombies as you progress through the rounds. As I was trying to find a place to stay still, I realized I never tried jumping on an object, like a car. So I did. And I stayed there the entire game.

The reason why I chose this foolproof situation is because the AI is so bad, they'll clump up together in an effort to grab you even though they can't, and you can just crouch and whack them with whatever tool they started you out with. My actual gamewinning strategy was to run to the gunstore, buy a rocketlauncher, jump on the barricades via other platforms, and began the simple process of gather, shoot, collect, repeat. Every other item was rendered useless with this method. Flashlight or nightvision? Why, when you can just turn the gamma up. Health? You're not even being hit, why waste your time? ATV or other vehicle? That perch is now your life, no vehicle can change that.

I could have gone an infinite amount of rounds that way, but the glitches got the best of me. T-posing zombie models floating around, zombies getting caught on objects and moonwalking in random locations, only moving when I shot at them, and the gamebreaking spiders. There are big old hairy spiders in this game, and they're the most useless wastes of polygons. At one point, a spider froze in a parking lot and I had to kill it to advance to the next round. I apparently didn't get that it was an omen, so I thought nothing of it and resumed, only for a spider (I assume) later to freeze somewhere hidden that I was unable to find, making it impossible to progress anymore through the game.

Would I have kept on playing hadn't the big♥♥♥♥♥spider bugged (huehue) out? Maybe, but only because the (broken) leaderboard of the (broken) multiplayer aspect said that the highscore was 19, and I was already on 12 with 100% health. I wanted to like this game, mostly because I paid for it, and it just didn't happen. If you're actually reading this and on the fence about buying it, please don't. And if you're the developer of this game, why did you do this. You have plenty of time to fix this, I assume. I understand if you're not the best at making games, and this was just a fling, but this is kind of insulting. People spent money on this, and I feel like you don't care about that at all. If you did, you would make a patch trying to fix everything wrong with this game, but deep down we all know you're not gonna do that.

While The Witness is beautiful game, it boils down to solving a series of mazes presented to the player on digital panels. If you strip away this games production values, it's nothing more than a very well executed puzzle game that you might find on a mobile device for around $5. I simply can not recommend this game at it's current price, not to mention that many will give up in frustration due to the games opaque design and difficulty.

When I had my first oh my god moment after exploring enough, it actually startled me.
This review may be premature, but it's definitely worth recommending if you enjoy exploratory puzzle games the likes of MOTAS (the Mystery of Time and Space), but *moreso* if you enjoyed Antichamber.
There are a number of other indie puzzle games I'm dying to mention, but I hope you'll remember some of them when you stumble on what prompted me to write this immediately.
Beautiful art style and importantly: ART DIRECTION. I can already see why this game took so much time to make.

The game absolutely does have tutorials, but allows you to find them and revisit old puzzles in a natural flow that kept me from being stumped so far.
Supplemental Post-Game
Still enjoyed the game overall, but there were some puzzles whose design were straight up frustrating and was glad to avoid having to solve. Aids such as photoshop were a massive help with some of those, but I don't know if that was intended as a solution, given the game was designed around the PS4 first (as far as I can tell)...
In any case, I still highly recommend this game.
It is still narratively thin, but I believe that its thematic strength and how it's married to the gameplay more than makes up for what a lot of people believe is plot vagueness.

The Witness is an incredible puzzle game.  each puzzle is fair - it's not like myst or monkey island, where you might have to do something unorthodox, like combine a monkey and a wrench to get a "monkey wrench".  this game eshews the concept of an inventory in favour of having each puzzle represented as a glowing maze panel.  in doing so, The Witness removes all ambiguity between what *is* and what *isn't* a puzzle, which was a really smart design choice.
this game was designed and iterated upon for nearly 10 years after the release of Braid, the developer's previous game, and the amount of polish and attention to detail in the island is, quite frankly, astonishing.  the island is dense, packed with puzzles, shortcuts between areas, and gorgeous views; it's one of the most engaging worlds i've explored in a game, right up there with Dark Souls.  one aspect of the world design that i was not fond of, however, were the audio logs scattered throughout the island.  they don't explain the plot of the game, but are rather a collection of miscellaneous, thematic quotes from famous philosophers and mathematicians.  these audio logs feel a little pretentious, and very superfluous (it's a tight, polished puzzle game, but it has audio logs arbitrarily tacked on).
i have a few other minor gripes about the game, including the lack of a conclusive ending, but this isn't a game i played for its plot.  over the course of my first playthrough, i had countless "a-ha!" moments, which is a benchmark for any puzzle game.  The Witness is so rewarding and well-designed that the game's few flaws can be easily overlooked.

The perfect successor to Myst!
If you love solving puzzles and are looking for a game that will challenge your mind and your sanity, this is definitely worth your time.
The Witness takes a simple concept, that being mazes, and gradually introduces more and more depths, twists and mechanics along the way. There are over 600 different puzzles to be solved here and trust me, later on in the game they'll take you a while to figure out.
This game will make you feel like an utter genius one minute, and a complete idiot the next. 9/10

One important thing first: You don't need to like trains to like Mini Metro, but if you enjoy, say, Transport Tycoon, that might be an indicator MM is a game for you. Nonetheless it is NOT a game seriously simulating the building of a transport network, there's just too many things random to consider it that. Money won't help you overcoming the challenges it presents you. In fact, there isn't even money. It's more like a subway-themed puzzle game. Solving problems with the resources you have and use them most efficiently, that's what Mini Metro is about. Not gaining as many as possible.
You pick your map from a slowly, but steadily growing list of cities around the world - literally around the world. From the US to Brazil to Germany to Egypt to India to Japan to Australia and many more. The most recent addition was Stockholm, Sweden. Your job then is to connect each stop to the subway system (or tram in some cases) of the city, wherever said stop decides to appear on the map. Sounds simple and it is, but that doesn't necessarily mean it is easy. You only have so many subway lines available, and only so many trains to run on them, and only so many tunnels or bridges, which you will need to cross bodies of water. The maps develop in a random way in each time you play, and so do the extensions you are presented to choose from each in-game week. The replayability of Mini Metro therefore is secured for a very long time.
Further, each of the cities comes with not only with its own map, but also, more subtily, with its own set of rules, which are slightly different in different places. One will bombard you with passengers once your network is past a certain size, some will allow you to run only so many lines at maximum, others will keep you critically short on tunnels or carriages or whatever it is you are in desperate need for all the time, on some the trains have less-than-standard capacity, in yet another, the stations do.
What I imagine is a big part to the success of Mini Metro, is that it is great for multi-hour play sessions - it's in fact heavily addictive at first. While that wore out after a while for me, the nature of its gameplay also makes it great to come back to if you have a few minutes you need to fill. Cooking and cleaning is done... "C'mon, let me draw some subway lines until the visitors arrive."
With gameplay being covered, let's move on to graphics. There's not much of graphics really, a whole lot of well done aesthetics nonetheless. The network you build as time goes by is displayed in the form of a map as they are commonly put up at real-world train stations. Some of these become really nice to watch, and the replay function after the game has ended (which it will, you can't beat Mini Metro) can be interesting as well.
So, you probably guessed already I'm very pleased by the game, but are there things that should be changed? Well, not many. Sometimes trains refuse to depart from a stop for some time for unknown reasons. There's two solutions to this coming to my mind: Either fix the bug or declare it a feature, call it a technical malfunction on the train.
The secon thing that can be annoying is if you want to draw a line from one stop to the next parallel to a river that makes a tiny little swerve toward the side there, so the direct way leads under a bit of water you could easily lay your tracks around in reality. A fix to this could be waypoints that the player could place on the map freely, where your lines will go by without stopping.
Those are really the only nitpicks coming to my mind, after way over 100 hours (PC and tablet combined).

VA-11 Hall-A, is a game with relaxing atmosphere, a great soundtrack, and appealing visuals.
The only form of time limit you'll really face is the need to pay rent, your electricity bill, and your phone bill as well...other than that though it's just serving drinks to weird people, and cute anime girls.  A majority of the game is spent reading conversations, the main way you interact with those conversations is by serving the drinks, you can listen to the customers requests, or you can just ♥♥♥♥ up their orders.  The drinks you serve them change the way the story plays out.
The jokes are pretty top notch most relate to internet culture, and I really did enjoy reading through the conversations, and I always made sure to read the news articles, and danger/u/ posts before the start of a new day just because I knew they'd have something to make me chuckle.
The Characters are great as well I really did enjoy the way they interacted with each-other and I legitimately felt happy when I saw some of them come back to the bar,  it is really interesting to hear how they're lives are playing out, but never seeing any of it for yourself.  You hear all of their stories, and even some of their insecurities, you'll sometimes read news stories about them, and you'll only ever see them in the bar.  They open up to you because they know you're just the person who serves them drinks, and they don't expect judgement.  Hell sometimes you even play the role of the "Wise Bartender", and you manage to change their lives for the better all because they decided to take a chance in some shady looking back-alley bar.
The game starts off with a (generally) postitive vibe.  Well as positive as a futuristic society run by corrupt buisiness officials can be at least, but believe me this game aint afraid to get heavy.  Although it does get heavy the majoritiy of the game will be spent relaxing, listening to a kickass soundtrack, and laughing at how strange some of the conversations manage to become.  Seriously if you're looking for a relaxing game with some great jokes, and emotional moments.  Pick this one up. Oh and it also has NG+.

Here's a hidden gem that I just had to write a review for because it absolutely deserves more exposure.
This isn't something that I normally comment on, but one of the first things you will find striking about Gigantic is it's totally unique aesthetic, the art direction of this game is simply in a league of it's own, I have just never seen anything like it. There is this over-arching artistic cohesion to EVERYTHING, from the artwork, to the UI, to the environments, character models, animations, everything fits together just perfectly and the whole game just oozes quality, you can tell this was a real labor of love.
Gameplay is pretty tight. While it all looks very confusing and hectic at first (the game is pretty fast paced) it doesnt take long to make sense of what's going on. The game has it's own bold new game mode, it is quite original and fun. Props to the devs here for making something unique instead of just regurgitating tried and true game modes like domination and push the cart (*coughoverwatchcough*) The game runs great, good ol' UE3 engine, almost anyone can run it. Latency isn't an issue at all. Hero balance isn't perfect but it's close enough.
The main thing I would criticize is that the fps is capped at 60 (I think owing to the fact that this started out as an xbox exclusive or something). While the game DOES run beautifully at 60 fps and easy to adjust to (an untrained eye probably wont even notice) there are a lot of people that will probably be totally turned off by this. To me, it's annoying, and I hope for a future fix, but it's my only major gripe.
I'm totally in love with this game though and I hope it catches fire.

Lovecraft's books) and old hard as balls NES games. To quote a review of Dark Souls: "You will DIE. A LOT."
Story follows a young unnamed girl who I named Lily (why? I don't know honestly, it kind of fits to me), who's dropped at "Lafcadio Academy for Troubled Young Ladies" private school. One day Lily finds a weird book in the library, and begins to read it in the evening. In her following dreams she dreams of being a weird demon hybrid of herself disfiguring other monsters in worlds like out of the head of H.P. Lovecraft. However, in the morning she finds that her dreams are starting to affect her. I won't tell more about the story, but let me tell you, don't expect any MGS or Mass Effect depth of story.
Gameplay consists of the dreams Lily finds herself in. While her control scheme might seem really simple at the beginning, you'll find (either to your aproval or disaproval) that the difficulty of the game is not at all in the controls, but in player's SKILL of using them and the ENVIROMENT around you.
The levels will start out relatively easy, but will end up being hard as all hell unleashed (especially the last level. OH GOD THAT LAST LEVEL...).
The checkpoint mechanic in the game is really neat: your combos and points you gather throughout the levels fill up a special meter at your disposal. When full, you can make your OWN checkpoints anywhere... AS LONG as it is on solid ground, and in a certain distance from enemies or traps.
Other than that, this game does NOT hold your hand: traps differ from short spikes that take away one of three hit points you have per life, long INSTA-KILL spikes, to buzzsaws that are annoying when there's one but are complete and f.ucking AS.SHOLES in groups.
Enemies come in four/five types (the game does not give them names so I made up my own [EDIT: THE GAME DOES GIVE THEM NAMES IN THE ACHIEVEMNTS]):
Walkers: slow guys that attack you with extendable blades and block after you hit them a few times. Around 6-8 HP, not sure.
Squids: small flying squids that charge you like bullets. Annoying during hard platforming sections. 1 HP.
Gremlins: little guys armed with either swords or bombs. 1 HP
Bomb variant: Suicide bombers. They charge you and try to explode close to you so they can blow you up. Can be useful in fights to kill more enemies at once.
Sword variant: these guys are hard to kill, and are never a good sign, ESPECIALLY in small corridors where you can't jump. Best disposal method is to jump and use the downards attack while they are on the ground. The problem is that they know this attack as WELL, and love to use it. Only positive thing about them is their low HP.
Samara: oh god no. This ghost with long hair is here to do one thing, and one thing only: RUIN YOUR EFFIN' DAY. She is relentless, can fly through walls, has 7 HP, and teleports if you attack her with more than two times in a row. Method of survival: find a piece of ground without traps, and deal with her on ground. YOU CANNOT KILL HER IN AIR. I TRIED. AND THE DAMN LAST LEVEL OF THE GAME MAKES YOU FIGHT THREE OF THEM IN A ROW, WHILE CLINGING TO A WALL OVER A PIT OF F.UCKING BUZZSAWS AND SPIKES. WITHOUT A CHECKPOINT. GOOD LUCK AS.SHOLE.
A nice thing is that levels actually resemble their respective background- for example, one level looks like a giant grandfather clock from the inside- huge gears and such. The actual platforms you'll be jumping on will be gears as well. And this counts for all levels. Nice detail.
The game offers two difficulties- Novice, which is kind of the same as Normal, but with the exception that you can't access the last level of the game (AND FOR GOOD REASONS), and you only have to finish the level in order to move on.
Normal difficulty. That's where the shi.ts at. Only here will your progress be tracked, and only here can you get achievents for such things as combos, enemies killed with one attack, etc. Here you can access the last level (which I mentioned a few times already). Here you also get an optional objective: collect the secret Book of Blades pages scattered throughout the level (6/level). At the beggining, like with the levels themselves, they are... well not easy but let's say not as hard as it may seem. But later... The first problem is that sometimes you run through a level, realize you do not have 2-3 pages, and your initial reaction is "WHERE IN THE DAMN HELL COULD THEY BE!?!?". Yes, sometimes, even finding them can be hard. And in the later levels, getting them is not a challenge anymore- it's a damn suicide mission.
I have to mention the last level.
OH. MY. GOD. If you are not prepared, this level will F.UCKING DESTROY YOUR MIND. It will throw every obstacle you had to endure at you, with a god damn fighting marathon at the end. AND THAT'S NOT EVEN THE HARDEST PART. THE HARDEST PART IS THE ONE WITH THE ELEVATING PLATFORM SHORTLY BEFORE IT- IT MADE ME RAGE SO HARD, I LITTERALLY ALMOST RIPPED MY HAIR OUT IN FRUSTRATION.
BUT GOD DAMN IT IS IT A GREAT GAME.
This is one of the games that gives you the determination to go on, to try just one more time, and never give up. The kind of game that makes you celebrate just getting through a tough part. The kind of game that makes you sattisfied with your relentlessness at the end of the level. The moment I finished that god forsaken level was one of the best moments I ever experienced in a game.
The pixel art and graphics are really great and original, one of the best I've seen in a while.
The music is awesome and I'm considering buying the OST, although it's not my type of music.
...Sigh... But do I recommend this game?
I want to, I REALLY WANT TO... but this is a kind of game that only the hardcore fans of platforming will enjoy. Altough I fell in love with the game, I can't deny my rage that made me ragequit several times before finishing it.
... But I finished it. Two times in fact.(both difficulties) I can't say that about other games I like more and don't frustrate me as much.
...I RECOMMEND IT.
Understand that you are not going to play this game for a complex story. Or a great reward at the end. Or some epic boss fight at the end (No bosses in this game). YOU are going to play this game, so that when you are done, you can pat yourself on the back and say "I beat They Bleed Pixels.". No great celebration. No big reward. Only you. Your pc. and the glorious feeling of acomplishment after beating that god forsaken final level.
I realise that I haven't said everything about the game (Concept art unlocks, Bonus levels...), but It's currently 2:12 AM in my country, and I just finished the game, and felt the need to write this review.
Great job Spooky Squid Games. But seriously- F.UCK you for that last level

Given the simplicity of the basic mechanics (snake puzzles), and the obtuse solutions of many of the puzzles, it's not worth it's $40 price tag.
If you're a fan of pretentious philosophy and banging your head against a wall, it may be worth $20. For most others with a passing interest in puzzle games (such as myself), $5 or $10 would be a better price.

After about 4 hours and 180 puzzles I feel like I've barely scratched the surface.  This is a really incredible puzzle game.  You're constantly learning new rules and building on the skills that the game is teaching you.  It's like the Socratic Method of games.  There is no instruction just a progressive building and combining of elements.
This is not a game with action or violence.  The only obstacles are the various line puzzles, and your only tools are your senses and your wits.  You need to constantly be observing the scenery and listening to the ambient noises for subtle clues that might help you solve the next panel.
If you enjoy puzzle games and want a relaxing way to spend a few hours then this is the game for you.  You'll get your money's worth.

This game is a masterpiece.
I have no idea what's going on with the people in the ratings here who compare it to Snake or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ because this is not only the hardest puzzle game I've ever seen (and I've been around since Myst at least) but it's the most rewarding, and the deepest, and in small moments, piece by piece, it builds to incredible ideas. It's philosophically deep and extremely powerful in terms of emotion, but still totally accessible. It is the pinnacle of how complexity can be achieved through a simple set of mechanics.
The people rating this game poorly probably didn't like things like The Talos Principle or Portal either, let alone things like Myst or Riven. This game will challenge you at every step, and while it seems obtuse at first, it definitely has a thread and a message and something it wants to say.
If ever there was a game that is at once an amazing gaming experience *and* can be considered a monumental piece of art, it is this game. This was seven years work for the company/people that made it, and it shows. At no moment does it compromise, and it never, in any way, cheapens itself. This game is a love letter to science, and to religion, and to games and puzzles and space and Earth and if you let it, probably the inside of your own brain too.
10/10? ♥♥♥♥ that. It's unrateable. It defies categorization or ratings.

Luckily, I really like line-drawing puzzles.
6 hr update: I really, really like them.
40 hour update: this game isn't about line-drawing puzzles at all. Drawing lines is just the interface, the language, which the player uses to interact with the game. The puzzles themselves are vast and varied, it just so happens that you speak in Snake to answer them. Even at this point I am discovering new stuff and starting to appreciate the weightier themes of the game as I peel back the onion skin a layer further. I'm not even dismissing the audio logs as pretentious nonsense anymore. It really does all fit together. Just to give one little magic moment without spoiling anything too much. There is a statue you find of a man who is raising his hands to the sky and looks as though he is despairing. Viewed from a slightly different angle, however, his shadow aligns with stones on the ground and suddenly he looks like a guy juggling. And that's the game in a nutshell. It's a masterpiece, one of the very best if not THE best game I have ever played. Thank you Mr. Blow.

Undead Shadows is a wavebased zombie-and-other-monsters-from-minecraft-deflection simulator by Ignition Games.
The video review is here(warning! explicit langauge):
To make it short: I have found 18 reasons for you to not buy this game that are explained more elongated in the video. Here I will keep myself short and simply list those reasons:
1. The game has No Controllersupport even though it features partial controller support on the store page.
2. There are pretty much no steam features integrated into that game.
3. Because of reason number two, they have an own online service, that sends out no confirmation mail when registering... dogdy.
4. This game needs an internet connection for a singleplayer game with a multiplayer component. It's no always online system, but that doesn't make it any better.
5. The game has no FOV slider! Luckily for them the standard FOV is 90, so the problem is not that bad.

Got this one for $4 along with the three other Thief games during the 2017 winter sale... And at that price, it's definitely worth it! The game is a straightforward fantasy/steampunk first-person stealth game. The main story is a generic rollercoaster ride, 100% on the rails. To their credit, the devs threw in some optional side missions to spice things up. The production values are top notch, with beautiful graphics and art design.
As far as the story goes, Garrett is a fine protagonist, but the other characters and the plot are on the weaker side.
Unfortunately, the game fails where it matters - in its gameplay and its level design. If one sticks to the main story, there is little thieving to do, and little need to ever use Garrett's fancy kit. Due to the poor level design, consisting largely of narrow corridors, I think it's possible to complete the game - easily - without ever using anything beyond a few rope arrows.
Square Enix should learn from the success of the new Hitman and Dishonored games (and even Tomb Raider), and reinvent Thief in a proper way - with nice open-ended sandbox levels, rather than a banal fantasy rollercoaster ride.
The main story takes 7-8 hours to beat.
Rating 7/10 - worth at $4 with the other Thief games; but not otherwise.

One important thing first: You don't need to like trains to like Mini Metro, but if you enjoy, say, Transport Tycoon, that might be an indicator MM is a game for you. Nonetheless it is NOT a game seriously simulating the building of a transport network, there's just too many things random to consider it that. Money won't help you overcoming the challenges it presents you. In fact, there isn't even money. It's more like a subway-themed puzzle game. Solving problems with the resources you have and use them most efficiently, that's what Mini Metro is about. Not gaining as many as possible.
You pick your map from a slowly, but steadily growing list of cities around the world - literally around the world. From the US to Brazil to Germany to Egypt to India to Japan to Australia and many more. The most recent addition was Stockholm, Sweden. Your job then is to connect each stop to the subway system (or tram in some cases) of the city, wherever said stop decides to appear on the map. Sounds simple and it is, but that doesn't necessarily mean it is easy. You only have so many subway lines available, and only so many trains to run on them, and only so many tunnels or bridges, which you will need to cross bodies of water. The maps develop in a random way in each time you play, and so do the extensions you are presented to choose from each in-game week. The replayability of Mini Metro therefore is secured for a very long time.
Further, each of the cities comes with not only with its own map, but also, more subtily, with its own set of rules, which are slightly different in different places. One will bombard you with passengers once your network is past a certain size, some will allow you to run only so many lines at maximum, others will keep you critically short on tunnels or carriages or whatever it is you are in desperate need for all the time, on some the trains have less-than-standard capacity, in yet another, the stations do.
What I imagine is a big part to the success of Mini Metro, is that it is great for multi-hour play sessions - it's in fact heavily addictive at first. While that wore out after a while for me, the nature of its gameplay also makes it great to come back to if you have a few minutes you need to fill. Cooking and cleaning is done... "C'mon, let me draw some subway lines until the visitors arrive."
With gameplay being covered, let's move on to graphics. There's not much of graphics really, a whole lot of well done aesthetics nonetheless. The network you build as time goes by is displayed in the form of a map as they are commonly put up at real-world train stations. Some of these become really nice to watch, and the replay function after the game has ended (which it will, you can't beat Mini Metro) can be interesting as well.
So, you probably guessed already I'm very pleased by the game, but are there things that should be changed? Well, not many. Sometimes trains refuse to depart from a stop for some time for unknown reasons. There's two solutions to this coming to my mind: Either fix the bug or declare it a feature, call it a technical malfunction on the train.
The secon thing that can be annoying is if you want to draw a line from one stop to the next parallel to a river that makes a tiny little swerve toward the side there, so the direct way leads under a bit of water you could easily lay your tracks around in reality. A fix to this could be waypoints that the player could place on the map freely, where your lines will go by without stopping.
Those are really the only nitpicks coming to my mind, after way over 100 hours (PC and tablet combined).

First and foremost: I have had to base this review on a two hour play time. Reasoning: as of the date of this review: two hours is the maximum play time you can have a game for in order to request a refund if so desired. I desired that refund.
Moving on.
I found this game stressful, and at times frustrating. When I encountered the pathing puzzles: I quickly learned that navigating the maze was simply not enough. There was a particular method that was needed in order to solve all the puzzles in a given set. This makes sense to me. Find the overall method of solving a solution, and you can solve the rest of the puzzles with a little bit of elbow grease.
Kind of like a 'teach a man to fish' scenario.
But then the game decided that it no longer wanted me to do that. I attempted to solve a puzzle in the manner in which the game had taught me; only to find that it's rules had now arbitrarily changed.
Honestly with the time constraint that I had: I simply had to locate a guide online and use it's solution... And that's when I got frustrated. The solution in the guide was simply an alternate solution than the one I had attempted.
In my mind: the worse thing in a puzzle game is repeating the same puzzle over again. By their very nature: the vast majority of puzzle games suffer from a lack of replay value. I get that, and I accept it. We've all played the Portal series, and forced ourselves to forget it so we can enjoy playing it again in 6-8 months.
There was a part in my playthrough of this game where I failed to solve a pathfinding puzzle. Instead of letting me attempt again: the game reverted the
puzzle to a non solved state, and forced me to re-enter that one too. The worst part was that the puzzle was still
, and I jsut had to trace over what I had already done. Why?
There is no jumping or crouching. The game is not about physically demanding puzzles, and that's fine. However there are invisible walls
A minor ledge of say - half a metre - is an impass. It makes me have to walk back and forth between puzzles and areas the long way every time.

I really, really wanted to like this game. As a huge fan of the older Thief games (Deadly Shadows in particular, as blasphemous as it is to say that) and stealth games in general, I knew the latest iteration of the franchise wasn't going to be perfect. I knew it wasn't going to be a "true" Thief 4, building upon past gameplay mechanics.
In other words, I knew it was going to be "modernized" in an attempt to appeal to a wider audience.
And yet... I was still disappointed. 90 minutes in and I felt I'd seen everything the game had to offer. This game was so much of a disappointment that I refunded it before the timer ran out -
even though I only spent $5 on it during Steam's Winter sale.
There is no player freedom. Levels are incredibly linear, the story is unfocused and boring, the voice acting sucks and the characters are horrible.
The first character you meet - a fellow thief woman - is quite possibly one of the worst characters I've ever seen in any game - ever. She is so forgettable that I cannot remember her name for the life of me, and I looked it up prior to writing this review.
She's annoying, impulsive and hot-headed - and not in an endearing or even love-to-hate sort of way. She makes nonsensical, dumb decisions that are clearly a result of poor writing rather than poor character decisions (she kills a guard because it "had to be done" though there was both plenty of shadows and plenty of room to sneak by him and his companion without drawing attention - something literally ANY close-to-decent thief would have done, impulsive or not).
Did I mention the terrible voice acting? Because it's bad. REAL bad. Lines are delivered with all the charisma and feeling of a dog turd.
The developer's decision to move away from Stephen Russell as Garret's voice actor was an awful one, and the game suffers for it. Their reasoning for the decision was the same as it was for Ubisoft's decision to move away from Michael Ironside as the voice actor for Sam Fisher (another horrendous decision) - "full performance capture", I.E. making the voice actors do their own stunts. As voice actors like Michael and Stephen get on in the years, this sort of technology is no longer all that viable.
Stupid, stupid, stupid. And it didn't even pay off. The game's animations are unrealistic, exaggerated and downright bad in some areas. I do appreciate the developers' decision to go with the "full-body" first person view, as well as their decision to actually animate every single interaction Garret has with the game world (Picking up objects, picking pockets and locks, opening doors, peeking around corners, etc.), however. I wish more games did that sort of thing, it really does add to immersion.
Anyway, back to voices. Garret always had a gruff, manly voice, but it also had a musical charm - it's hard to pin down, but it just worked. The new voice actor sounds like he's trying way too hard to sound like every other badass action hero on the planet, and his emotions never fit the situation he finds himself in.
Sorry for the somewhat unfocused nature of this review, but I'm going to end it here. It's not a good game. Do not buy it - even if you aren't a classic Thief fan, you will be disappointed. There are far better modern stealth games out there than this one: Deus Ex: Mankind Divided & Human Revolution, Dishonored (and all of its DLC) & Dishonored 2 (and its DLC), Metal Gear Solid V, Hitman 2016 and even bloody Mark of the Ninja. Play those before you even think about playing Thief 2014.

Good concept; poor implementation. The game goes away from intuitive metro design that's organized and lifelike. Instead, the optimal solution for each level is often a tangled mess of paths that are very difficult to manage in a real-time game. I found myself pausing often to delete the entire track I had created (a daunting task - each node must be removed individually) and redesign my metro from the ground up because another shape had appeared.
The music, although soothing at first, quickly became a headache as the seemingly random dissonance roared in my ears.
The level-to-level experience felt very dry - little progression is made as you continue on throughout the game, and every new component can be unlocked in the first few levels. There is very little novelty from one level to the next, just a reorganization of nodes.
The first few moments of each level have a little charm as you watch what you've created, but the game quickly becomes a mess as you struggle to understand what you've developed. I felt little accomplishment from the beginning to the end of each level, because I had to completely destroy all my progress several times to even consider reaching a winning layout.
This game has potential, but dries up very quickly.

I don't want to just keep playing to see how high of a score I can get. I want to have at least some sort of clear milestones or objectives to help prevent me from feeling like I'm wasting my time. Even if I did want to try to challenge myself to get a high score, it would be needlessly tedious - every time I wanted to re-attempt, I still have to play through the slow-paced early and easy stages of a level until I reach the point where I left off last time.
Additionally, I found the core gameplay to get a little bit tedious after about 2 hours. The core gameplay loop in this game is one of fixing problems with something you already designed, and I find this to be grating after awhile. Once I finally have a design that works well for the nodes that I see right now, the game changes it up - adding more nodes, increasing the amount of people, etc...and now my current design needs to be modified / adapted. There's no sense of accomplishment - just an ongoing sense of failure.

In this game you are meant to move these things called crystals. You are meant to get get crystals of the same shape and colour in a row of 3 or more. Each addon to that 3 will be a new "ability" you can create. For example 4 of the same shape and colour will make one that when combined with 2 others of the same colour, or another "ability" of any colour will clear one column or row (depending on how you made it). This game brings in loveable characters from the hit disney movie "Frozen" Characters such as Olaf, Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff. With these loveable characters by your side it helps you imagine the world as the world in Frozen. This game has an addictive and enjoyable experience with over 300 levels to play!
This game allows you and your favourite characters from Disney's Frozen to tackle these challenging puzzles together using your head and sometimes the power ups of each individual character! There is also a mechanic known as "Power Ups" these include universal power ups and power ups that can only be activated if you are using a certain character such as Elsa who has a Snowflake Crystal. Using this you pick any one colour/shape and all others of the same colour/shape on the board go away. One of the universal power ups is "Snow Ball" this allows you to finish that pesky level when you need one more column or row to complete but you run out of turns. This Snow Ball gives you 5 more turns to finally get past that level and advance to the next one.
After time you will unlock more power ups and more of your favourite characters to use later on.
This is just the single player.
There's a fun and just as addictive multiplayer. You and your friend can get together in real life and play against eachother. Using the same mechanics as the singleplayer except after you make columns and rows of the same colour and shape the character you picked will throw a snow ball at the character your friend picked or vice versa. You can practice this game mode against yourself so when your friend comes over you have the upper hand.
All and all this game is garbage and it isn't worth the space on your computer or your time at all.

Beautiful game that exudes charm, character, and atmosphere. It's a real gem. I used to enjoy playing this game and eagerly bought an ultimate pack. When there were 5,000 concurrent players per day, this game was absolutely amazing! I easily had a dozen friends who also played Gigantic too. We'd team up and feel like we accomplished something together each time we won.
So why the negative review? Honestly, Gigantic is completely unplayable right now and you should avoid it until there's a big content update that brings back players. Matchmaking happily pairs newbies with veterans. It doesn't take long to get matched with some of the most toxic and stressful people in gaming. There's so few players for Gigantic that nearly every match has a bad mix of players. You won't find a helpful community of players working together -- you'll just find rage and stress. Gigantic is a gem ruined by its horrendous players and matchmaking. Worse, the developer thinks they can advertise their way out of a rapidly declining player base.

Super Meat Boy meets a solid combo-based combat system, based around getting the most possible punishment done on your opponents; wrapped in an intruiging amalgamation of lovecraftian and surreal themes. And amalgamation that is, because all the enemies are lovecraftian horrors from your worst nightmare.
But your real worst nightmare will be your own reaction times, and the potential lack of a controller.
This game is hard. Really hard. Like, solid rock hard. And that's not even beginning to see the meta that the game has practically built into itself. The super meat boy comparison is apt because the game likes to time and judge your performance, encouraging constant movement and concentration.
Also, it requests you use a controller. Unless you enjoy carpal tunnel, i suggest you follow it's advice; it can work on keyboard in the same way Meatboy can. Interpret that how you will.
All in all, it's fun if you've got the patience for failiure that you need for Super Meat Boy's latter levels.

They Bleed Pixels is a 2D Action/Platformer in where we take control of a young orphan girl that finds a mysterious book which slowly begins to transform her into a monster. She is then transported to a world within the book in where there are other monsters all wanting to kill you. Being a monster now, the girl is just as capable of brutally murdering them as they are at harming her. You have a basic attack, a dash attack and a kick that sends enemies flying through the air. You'll rarely just be button mashing as this game is more about using the hazards in the environment to your advantage rather than actual combat with your foes. Killing them in stylish ways will earn you more points which in turn will fill up your checkpoint meter that will allow you to place a checkpoint at a safe place of your choosing by simply standing still for a few seconds when the meter is full.
The real threat to you will be the environments as this nightmare world is filled to the brim with pointy objects like spike and floating saw blades. Usually you are able to take three hits before death from whatever harms you unless you fall on a spike and are impaled. Saw blades will be your worst foes as their hit-boxes are rather large and being scraped by one will send you bouncing all around the place like if you were a pinball, annoyingly enough. Starting up the game you have the options of picking either Normal or Novice difficulty. Novice difficulty makes the game far easier as well as removes the leader-boards, most of the games collectibles and the final mission of the game won't be accessible in this mode. Normal is far more difficult than it implies and I was happy just being able to get through a level, much less worry about collecting any of the secret pages or other collectibles set in hard to reach locations.
They Bleed Pixels is an extremely hard game and even if it only continues 11 missions in the story mode it will take you longer than you may expect as you cover the stage in your blood as you die repeatedly. There are no lives or anything of the sort so you are free to try as much as you like and with the addition of being able to set checkpoints wherever you please you'd think it would be a simple task but nothing can be further from the truth. Setting checkpoints requires quite a large area for it to be considered as a safe place to set it, though even immovable saw-blades can deem an area unsafe causing you to pinpoint just the right angle which seems a bit unnecessary. You can exit the game at any time and the next time you choose that level you can load up on the last checkpoint that you set meaning that you can rage quit a level without losing any progress but the leader-boards will be disabled now.
As you fight and maim your way across the level blood will be spraying everywhere from your defeated foes. The blood in this game is plentiful and will splatter across the environments in a satisfying fashion. Unfortunately the combat system itself is rather abysmal. All the attacks are tied to one button for some reason and accidentally triggering the dash attack was the lead cause of my death throughout. Even then it just doesn't feel right as it is difficult to connect your attacks and when you stay your ground it is impossible to harm them as you default to harmless kicks which can be problematic when there are no hazards to toss them to or when you are fighting a more powerful foe. Other than the basic enemies with stretchable limbs you will also be facing ghosts which can obviously phase through the environments, flying foes that will hurl themselves toward you and a short fella that jumps around with a giant blade. There is a lot of variety within the enemies which is no doubt a good thing but with the combat system in this game it is just a painfully awkward to face them.
In a game that requires pinpoint precision and has everything placed in a way to kill you stopping to fumble about with an enemy really breaks the flow. After finishing three levels you are rewarded with a cut-scene that reveals more of the story as well as gives you a key in which you can unlock some fan art in the extras menu. The story is there just for the sake of it and doesn't really add or detract from the game. In the extras menu you will find 150 badges that challenge you to do certain things and will take quite a while to complete if you are into that kind of thing, a decent amount of really nice fan art to unlock and five extra levels to play through. These levels are quite different visually from the normal campaign ones and are pretty well done.
Music is pretty solid across the board though I personally found none of it to be particularly memorable. Graphics are pretty simple with all the environments just being black blocks but having a different background each level so it doesn't get stale. The camera is just right and you never feel cheated due to something you didn't see coming. All in all it is a good game that is sure to challenge even the most hardened of gamers. It will constantly have you wanting to punch something but it is fair enough that it will keep you playing for “one more try”. While the combat part of They Bleed Pixels is sub-par, kicking an enemy into a saw-blade and watching the blood physics work their magic is impressive enough to make it less of a hassle. If you are looking to grow some gray hairs or brag about your gaming skills this would be an excellent title to do so.

Based on only an hour played, so take what I say with a grain of salt.
I was hoping this would grab me like Braid, or the Talos Principle. Solving puzzles in those games rewards you with insight into the world, the story, the themes. Along with being fun puzzles in and of themselves, there was a reason for solving them beyond 'because they're there."
I got no sense from the Witness that there was anything beyond the puzzlees. I never felt like solving a puzzle resulted in a tantalizing, fleeting glimpse into what lies beneath. It just felt like... puzzles. A bunch of puzzles.
If that's what you want, then this may be the game for you. But if you want puzzles in service of something else - ANYTHING else - then move along. There's nothing to see here.
(I'm sure someone (possibly many someones) will say I didn't give it enough time. To them I'd say that if Braid and the Talos Principle (and many others) managed to hook me in an hour, then the Witness should be able to do the same. From what I experienced, it seems utterly indifferent to my enjoyment. It offered no hooks. It simply exists, and much like the island on which it's set, it seems completely unconcerned with me or my actions. I'll give Blow credit for thematic consistency, but that doesn't change the fact that it was not enjoyable to actually experience.)
EDIT: Originally I refunded The Witness after the review above, but I bought the Humble Freedom Bundle that came with a copy, and I decided to give it another chance. I've gotten much farther in this time, but sadly it hasn't really done much more to win me over. On the second attempt I'm much more willing to meet it without my old expectations, but the end result is a sometimes clever, sometimes frustrating, but still ultimately un-engaging experience.
The Witness is basically like being stuck in a room with someone who doesn't speak your language, so you go through the painstaking process of total immersion learning. When you finally learn something, there's a great Eureka moment. When it feels like the game is doing nothing to teach what you need to learn, you want to bang your head into a wall. But there's also the added bonus of not knowing who you're locked in this room with, or what you hope to achieve by learning the language, as The Witness offers no context or reason to care about anything that you're doing. I'd be more eager to jump back in and try harder to solve these puzzles if I thought there was any sort of payoff at the end, or even if I thought there was value in the skills I was learning, but there's just not, so... why?

After putting 8+ hours (~215 puzzles) in, the game is a masterpiece in puzzle design. At about 2.5 hours in and a couple frustrating (in the best possible way) moments later I had to stop to write a review. Somehow this game is only "Mostly Positive" and it seems the people who are not pleased have some sort of surround sound bug (legitimate complaint) or simply played for an hour, maybe two and never reached a complex puzzle, never asked a single question, "What is that?" "Why am I here?" "How do I get there to do that?" There's no spoon feeding here. You must work your way through and you must want to do so.
The game is absolutely beautiful, and there are many subtle sounds and visual ques along the way which add to the whole vibe the game seems to be working toward. I have already taken several screen shots and I expect to take many many more by the end of the game. It's simply stunning.
So unless you're not a puzzle gamer, or you've got legit concerns about your surround sound headphones... this game is fully worth the full price.

First and foremost: I have had to base this review on a two hour play time. Reasoning: as of the date of this review: two hours is the maximum play time you can have a game for in order to request a refund if so desired. I desired that refund.
Moving on.
I found this game stressful, and at times frustrating. When I encountered the pathing puzzles: I quickly learned that navigating the maze was simply not enough. There was a particular method that was needed in order to solve all the puzzles in a given set. This makes sense to me. Find the overall method of solving a solution, and you can solve the rest of the puzzles with a little bit of elbow grease.
Kind of like a 'teach a man to fish' scenario.
But then the game decided that it no longer wanted me to do that. I attempted to solve a puzzle in the manner in which the game had taught me; only to find that it's rules had now arbitrarily changed.
Honestly with the time constraint that I had: I simply had to locate a guide online and use it's solution... And that's when I got frustrated. The solution in the guide was simply an alternate solution than the one I had attempted.
In my mind: the worse thing in a puzzle game is repeating the same puzzle over again. By their very nature: the vast majority of puzzle games suffer from a lack of replay value. I get that, and I accept it. We've all played the Portal series, and forced ourselves to forget it so we can enjoy playing it again in 6-8 months.
There was a part in my playthrough of this game where I failed to solve a pathfinding puzzle. Instead of letting me attempt again: the game reverted the
puzzle to a non solved state, and forced me to re-enter that one too. The worst part was that the puzzle was still
, and I jsut had to trace over what I had already done. Why?
There is no jumping or crouching. The game is not about physically demanding puzzles, and that's fine. However there are invisible walls
A minor ledge of say - half a metre - is an impass. It makes me have to walk back and forth between puzzles and areas the long way every time.
I get it; the game is gorgeous and you want people to experience the environment. But I couldn't help but feel like I was just a slave to the world's path, and not person taking a place within it.
On top of that, your character is slow to move. I found I was constantly holding the shift button to sprint, and my pinky got cramped. He also seems to have this strange acceleration when beginning to move in a direction. Starting off slow, and speeding up. While true to life: it feels out of place and indeed seems to serve no purpose in this particular game.
All in all: I do wish I had more time with it - (Thank steam). If these types of issues are not that important to you: then I can reccomend this game. For me: it was simply not what I expected.

I want to delve into this first to get it out of the way.  While this game does have MTs they are mostly non-invasive & involve buying skins/shaders or you can get them out of a lootbox & lootboxes have to be earned. Lootboxes have a very low chance of dropping shaders, especially the highest tier ones. The only other things you can buy are character level ups (after you get at least one to 20) & cosmetic changes to gear (which are both overpriced, imo).  Basically, they made a character customization system that revolves around real money & yea I hate it.  It still doesn't hurt the game itself, though, as it's just a ton of fun to play.  Everything is bought with Crystals & you can earn Crystals in game, up to a certain point but after that it takes forever to get anymore for free.
The tutorial in this game is great.  You know how most fighting games skip the whole "How to play" process entirely & basically throw you in like a newborn in the woods?  Well, this game not only shows you how to play, the basics & more advanced moves, it also has a seperate tutorial for every individual character!  It mainly shows the basics for each character, but it also rewards you with lootcrates for doing them.  I'm just glad there even is a tutorial. Also, it's all optional.  No forced tutor sessions here!
The gameplay is really fun & simple compared to other fighting games.  It still uses the light/medium/heavy style from MKX but adds a character power trait which adds a bit more strategy & helps make each character feel different.  One character might recieve a buff while another gets a projectile & each of which change up depending on the character used.  e.g. Batman gets robotic batarangs while Green Arrow gets arrows & more powerful arrows.
The game also gives a new ability gear slot that adds new or augments existing abilities which adds more depth to character builds & can make characters more powerful.  The same goes for gear sets, which can also add or augment existing abilities.  None of these can be used in competitive online modes, however, so if you're worried about balance in online matches no worries.  If you don't care about balance, there's a mode that lets you use all your abilities & gear as well.
The single Player content in this game is insane.  This game has more single player content than any other fighting game I've ever played.  The multiverse are like online events you can do to earn character specific gear & abilities or just earn credits & lootboxes.  You can tough them out all the way through or if your fingers are tired you can make AI builds to fight for you.  Having trouble with that level 20 boss?  Let the AI beat it for you!  Yes, it does seem rather cheap letting the game play itself but it helps players of varying skill level enjoy all the game has to offer & if you don't wanna you don't have to use it.
Then there's multiplayer AI battles which are fights where you make AI builds & fight other players AI builds.  This part feels sort of like a mobile game mode because the game plays itself, but it is still satisfying seeing your version of Flash or Batman or whoever kick another players' rear.
The real problem with the single player is how unfair the AI bosses get as you advance through the multiverse.  You could end up fighting all perfect matches, then suddenly the AI decides you don't deserve to win anymore & it will just win over & over again, forcing you to use the AI loadouts just to win.  It's incredibly frustraiting when this happens & there's nothing you can do about it.  The AI will always eventually decide to make you its plaything.
I don't know if it's the game, my controller, my fingers or what but after playing for a while the game will also decide to not register my inputs randomly.  I will be doing fine then suddenly nothing I press registers, then it works then it doesn't.  I don't know what exactly is causing this to happen.
The bread & butter of the single player mode is the games campaign, while it pains me to say that currently the PC version suffers from stuttering in cutscenes it's still one of the best stories in any fighting game.  Much better than MKX & slightly better than MK9's.  It's like watching an interactive DC movie, just be careful when playing it around the kids as there are some darker tones here.
I've only played a few matches but I haven't experience any significant issues with the online modes thus far.  Ping is responsive & stable with little input delay, if any at all.  Very good job done here.  I'll update if I encounter any issues at a later date.
The game also has guilds which you can make or join online & they work in similar style to MKX' faction system, though I think the faction system works better as it doesn't require long term commitment.  Guilds are basically groups of up to 50 people that team up in their own private multiverse events, earn buffs to help eachother or team up to tackle events together, up to 3 people at a time.
Personally, I dislike this system as I've played the game on consoles & a lot of guilds are just dead with high inactive player counts.  So, if a guild has say 30 people with all inactive, & 20 open slots you will see their guild activity mostly consisting of "Player Joined, Player left" & that's it.  This is where I wish they implimented a faction system instead.
On the plus side if you are in an active guild it's a lot better than the faction system, as you get the chance to interact with members of said guild & play together to earn more loot.  So, if you can, try to find a guild with an active player base.  Hopefully, it will last a long time.
This game is overall a fantastic fighter & much better than IJ1.  For me it's better than MKX, too.   If you like fighting games, DC or just a good time then get this game.  IMO, this game is worth the full price but it's completely up to you whether or not to get it now or wait for a patch or a good sale.

This game sucks and it doesnt deserve the positive ratings it has on steam as of the time of this review.
In rebooting the series they've stripped out some of the most interesting parts of the setting, and some of the mechanics the series was known for. "The City", which doesnt make sense anymore as a name as other cities are mentioned by name in the game, is a drab not-Victorian trash heap that is a boring chore to navigate through. The map doesnt help as it doesnt show closed gates or blocked roads, so you're supposed to discovered the right window to force your way through to get to the other half of a neighborhood. Speaking of the map, the drawn, possibly inaccurate maps that you had to buy or find and figure out where you were from landmarks from the previous games are gone, replaced by a regular minimap.
The game REALLY wants you to use a drug fueled cheato-mode detective vision that tells you where everything you can interact with in the environment is, trap disarming is pretty much built around it. You can only climb or use rope arrows are specific points, despite wooden beams and outcropping pipes being thrown around all over the place. You can wander around the city all you want, but unless you talk to a plot character about things to steal those things wont appear, to the point where you can wonder into the house its supposed to be in but it's just not there. The games platforming is automatic, you just go to the ledge and press space and the game does the rest, which leads to confusion where the game wont let you make a jump where you've SEEN Garret make harder ones just fine. There are three different groups of human enemies in this game and they all behave the same, they're all the same copy pasted "dude with sword" or "dude with crossbow" with no variation besides visuals and some voice lines.
The plot is a mess, it revolves around a character where Garret has a long history with them but the player doesnt know a thing about them, and all we see of them before they vanish for most of the game is them being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ so theres not much motivation to want to help them. Things are left unclear, character motivations dont make sense, the ending is confusing and supposedly leaves itself open for a sequel but I'm not interested in where it can go. The events that take place over the course of the game sound like and talk like they have wide ranging changes for the city, but things never change, the patrols you have to avoid never change routes or the number of guards. The loading screens imply theres crazy riots all over the place but the most you'll see is a group of five NPCs yelling at two guards.
Sound wise this game is a complete mess. The mixing is bad, things are loud and clear when they should be muffled, muffled when they should be clear, in cutscenes the volume levels of characters talking seems to fluctuate, where of two characters who are both yelling, only one is clear. Even for individual characters the who are the focus of a cutscene the volume of them speaking might suddenly drop for no reason. Some sound effects such as throwing a body might not work at all. The music for the game is pretty generic, especially when compared to the previous games in the series.
If you want a game about sneaking around and stealing♥♥♥♥♥♥ go play Thief 1, 2, and 3 with the fan patches, you'll have more fun than you did here, get more gameplay out of it, and probably save money.

Despite Spareware's lack of aesthetically interesting enemies or levels it serves
as a solid wave-shooter bringing rogue-like perma-death and tactical decision making to the mix.
Levels are selected from an overhead map traversing one hex to the next onwards towards its center where a main objective awaits. You usually have a choice of several hexs to tackle (unless occupied by enemy soldiers in which your only immediate mission is a survival bout; fending off the officers in a given time frame). Hex missions will vary between finding a new piece of equipment to add to your repretoire, objective hacking/destroying (to build up your collection of cells) or just simply trying to make way to the exit on the other end of the map.
Along the way, aside from equipment like torso, heads, legs and arms there are experience points to be earned to build up skills either serving as perks or gimmicks that can be assigned to three of your face buttons to use at certain times (ie; healing, speed boost,  shield, etc).
Missions cost cells so a major part of the game is not overspending and knowing where your next batch can be earned. Perma-death (death of the entire campaign! ) takes place when you fail a mission and no longer have the amount of cells needed to begin another.
Like A2 Protocol and Wasted, Spareware is another 'nobody' game very easy to overlook but does everything well enough
so as to addict the player and arrest their time away from bigger name companies and their bigger name titles.

Spareware is the debut Steam game by Rusto Games. Rusto Games are based out of Kajaani. Kajaani is a small city of just shy of 40,000 people and located in central Finland some 560km (348 miles) north of the capital, Helsinki. You can imagine just how small a populous the city has to lure game developers in so it's a mighty effort for a developer to get a game published on Steam.
Spareware is an arena twin-stick shooter that was released in a year where the market was flooded with them. For the game to have any chance, whatsoever, of breaking into the market and getting an audience it was going to have to be special. It would have to offer something unique. But most of all it was either going to have to be so good as to be unmissable or so bad that it lures a crowd like Sharknado did for the B-movie scene.
Unfortunately, for Spareware, it's neither bad enough nor good enough to capture a sizable audience. It's a slightly better than a mediocre game that will find some people becoming fans of it and much more turning away from it rather quickly. Therefore, it doesn't hit the sweet spot that small indie games need to to be successful.
It's a bit of a shame because it's clear that the developers are passionate about what they do. Perhaps that is the nicest thing that can be said about the developers at Rusto. It's a reasonable effort from what I am certain is a small studio. They can be proud of their achievement. And it is a solid title that I am certain they can use as a learning experience should they continue working on further titles which I encourage them to do.
The standout feature of Spareware is the destructible body parts system. Players have three layers of protection. These are your head and your arms. Enemies begin by attacking your head. If that layer of a shield is completely depleted your head explodes and you lose that body part. Being a mech you are able to continue and the enemies will target your arms. If this again is depleted you lose an arm and finally, if you lose your other arm you will die. However, you can shoot vehicles that are a part of the game's environment and replace your parts or pick up shields to regenerate health. It's a very easy system to learn.
Spareware is a much better title when playing with friends than playing solo. This is, I believe, the intention of the game. A number of the better skills in the game are balanced around team-based play. The game is so much more enjoyable when you have friends playing with where you take down enemies very quickly, power up together and destroy the unending supply of respawning enemies.
In the time that I played solo, I quickly found myself becoming bored. This is because the presentation of the game is relatively basic. The assets are relatively basic and the reskinning becomes obvious. Of course, I wouldn't have expected much more than what the game delivers given a clearly limited budget. This isn't a game from a major studio, after all. The other thing that becomes particularly noticeable when playing solo - more so than co-op - is that the level design doesn't differentiate itself nearly enough from level-to-level. It often feels like you are repeating levels. The aesthetics and environments are largely repeated even if the maps are marginally different.
The game started to shine a little when I put in a little time with friends. The game's deficiencies become less significant and I focused more on kicking♥♥♥♥♥with my friends by my side. This was the intention of the game and therefore I have to suggest that the devs did a good job in this regard. If you have friends and are bored of the more highly regarded games on Steam then I would recommend Spareware. It's an enjoyable co-op experience.
The game is not short on Steam features and kudos must be paid to the developers here. Clearly, they have considered the overall Steam audience for their game and have done a rock solid job in adding them to the game.
It's clear that the Rusto has put in a lot of effort in their debut title. However, that doesn't necessarily make the game very good. I've long held the opinion that the worst thing that you can be on Steam is mediocre especially if you're lacking product hype. Players are generally attracted to can't miss hit games, games that are full of hype (whether they deliver or not is almost irrelevant) or games that are so poor that they attract the attention of the more popular YouTubers, podcasters, etc. who are more than happy to create a video or spend time on their podcasts discussing how bad a game is and subsequently peddle the game to their audience.
Unfortunately, by being a marginally better than a mediocre title, the developers have missed the mark. There's a reason why, currently, there are only 6 reviews on Steam with mine becoming the seventh. There are better games on the market within the genre and there are significantly worse games.
I wouldn't personally recommend this title to soloists. There just isn't enough quality content to entertain you. You'll quickly become bored and move onto the next game in your library. If, however, you have a group of people to play with you - especially locally - and you've already played the well-known genre titles to death then give this game an opportunity.
Consequently, this is the type of game that I wish Steam would incorporate a middle option. I can't recommend the game to soloists but can do so to people seeking a multiplayer experience. Given that the intention of the developers was to create a multiplayer experience I will reluctantly give the game a thumbs up. Soloists beware.
