Sometimes you just might be in the mood for a game that will make you feel stupid. And sometimes those stupid people will stop playing less than 2 hours into the game and post a negative review complaining about how difficult the game is.
I had to take a picture of my screen with Snapchat and use the paint tool in the app to solve the last
100 puzzles I just did.
If you're stuck on a puzzle you don't understand the mechanic of, skip it, and come back later. There's no point in trying to brute force it, because there will just be more difficult versions of it beyond the door it unlocks. You will eventually learn how to complete it, at which point you can return and complete it with .
Also, if you reach a platform that moves you to a place it seems you can never leave, try to solve the puzzle on the platform in a different matter.
Really though, the bottom line here is that this is a massive puzzle-filled game which competes with the likes of the Portal franchise and The Talos Principle. If you're going to go ahead and sum up this game with, "so it's just mazes", then I'm going to go ahead and sum up Portal with, "so it's just portals". This is an atmospheric puzzle game through-and-through. The visuals are stunning, despite the complete lack of options related to them, which probably came about as a problem resulting from an indie developer trying their hand at creating a game engine from the ground up rather than using something already established like Unity, Unreal, Crytek, etc... If this game is "just mazes", I dare you to try and beat it without the assistance of somebody else. This game is hard. And while mazes are the core mechanic, just like portals are in the Portal games, there are plenty of twists on the mechanic that help change things up just enough, just like in every single other game with a core mechanic that is branched off of.
And after looking over a whole bunch of the other reviews, I'm really confused because this isn't a situation like Amazon's reviews where people can just willy nilly review products they didn't purchase. These are all people who legitimately purchased The Witness who are giving it negative reviews. Are these based off of reactions from watching trailers? Did people want another Braid? Where's the audience that gave The Talos Principle a 96% on Steam? This is The Talos Principle on steroids. This is The Talos Principle if the entirety of the game's content was open from the beginning, and you accidentally stumbled onto the last few puzzles of the game.
Don't chalk up the game's length to whatever amount of time it takes you to beat the game after having solved the first 5 puzzles on your own, and eventually breaking down and resorting to the use of a guide. These is Dark Souls-levels of difficulty and eventual satisfaction after having accomplished something you never thought you would. This is easily one of the biggest and most difficult puzzle games available on Steam at the moment, and don't let anybody convince you that it's nothing short of great.
This game is currently sitting at an 89% on Metacritic, and a 76% here on Steam, with various well-known critics like IGN, Destructoid, Telegraph, and Guardian giving the game perfect 10s. This game is a big deal, and hopefully the Steam userbase, being mostly populated by gamers playing a crate-opening simulator, recognizes that this is far more than just a bunch of mazes.
Once you've hit a certain point in the game, everything just starts to click. You begin to realize how crucial it really is to just straight up abandon a difficult puzzle and come back to it, especially if you feel like you're just brute forcing the thing at that point. This game turns into a unique kind of Metroidvania game right off the bat, in which every path is available for the player to explore, but the player soon finds out that some paths are more difficult or even impossible when compared to others. The game doesn't provide you with a unique ability that allows you to double jump up walls, or turn into a ball and roll through tight spaces. Instead, the game offers you the knowledge to go back to these difficult areas and know what you're doing through the use of little mini-tutorials that don't feel like they're holding your hand at all. They feel like they take the same approach that the start of the game does. They feel natural, which is once again why I must stress the importance of abandoning unfamiliar puzzles until you learn how to complete them later on.
This is as much a maze game as Dark Souls is a combat game. Sure, it's a pivotal gameplay mechanic, but it produces a much wider range of puzzles than I've ever seen before in a puzzle game, and you can't just take the word of someone who's put 1 hour into the game and called it quits.

Afghanistan '11 captures the spirit of the ongoing war in AFG and for that I commend it. The obvious comparison that must be made is to Vietnam '65, its predecessor. I was happy with the additional levels of complexity, units, and abilities introduced in AFG '11 but with that feature expansion also comes an increased time committment. A default 45 turn skirmish in vietnam would run about 1.5 hours, but in AFG '11 the campaign missions are 60 turns and each takes probably 2-3x longer to finish. I'm up to multiple hours on the 5th campaign mission alone, for example, and still have a third of the turns to go. The reason for this longer duration is the more complex gameplay over Vietnam, including the micro intensive supply system, multiple unit actions per turn, much higher unit cap, and more frequent combat over Vietnam 65. The end result is that the game has a lot of content, much more than Vietnam which was a simple randomly generated skirmish over and over, but it also risks dragging on. The campaign missions would probably be better served by a 45 turn duration.
The game currently does have some bugs in it, including crash to desktops, that presumably will be fixed eventually. The bugs havent been show stopping yet, but the CTDs force the odd turn to get replayed over which can take a while with the much higher unit count. There is no manual save option, but it autosaves at the start of each turn (instead of the end). There is also some wonky behavior like fuel trucks and the emergency fuel ability being able to resupply helicopters in flight. Little annoyances like being unable to use alternate abilities for an infantry squad when its in ambush stance without moving to a new tile could also use adjustment.
As an Afghan vet I can't help but notice the little idiosyncracies in the game where realism was sacrificed for gameplay. For example special forces cant collect intelligence from villages like infantry, and infantry cant train Afghan army units. The Afghan names generated for the political campaigns arent real afghan names, which is odd since a 5 minute search on google could probably turn up a number of real life names to randomly recombine. The pictures in the fake newspaper updates dont seem particularly relevant to Afghanistan. Opium fields are spawned in the random corners of the map, usually on steep mountain sides, instead of near the populated rural areas where farmers live in real life. The game spans a decade with its campaign but the technology is the same throughout, ex. MRAPS in 2001. Forgiveable because its a game but again, little things that jump out at me. The game captures the spirt of the Afghan war well but it is not a hardcore simulator.
All said I'm enjoying the game so far and I'm willing to overlook the odd crash and bug to recommend it to new players. Its playable now but if you arent in a huge rush waiting, for a patch or two couldnt hurt. I wouldn't be surprised if player feedback helps the team knock out some more of the wonky bugs and refine the gameplay a bit tighter.

This game is a gem. It's relatively simple in its layout, but extremely challenging. You're forced to wrestle with a lot of different factors: logistics, public opinion back home, trying to win over the locals, and finally deal with the insurgents.
To explain this balancing act, I'll relate something I faced in-game: My strategy was going to focus almost entirely on clearing out IEDs, and building relations with local villages. I didn't want to waste resources chasing Taliban through the mountains, as ultimately that's a futile endeavor, and I didn't see much point to it.
That was a mistake.
The third village I visited was on the far eastern side of the map, so I put together a convoy to just check things out (sweep for IEDs, talk to the villagers, make sure no Taliban were directly around the village). Well, about two thirds of the way to our destination, we run into two Taliban patrols inside a large valley. My two infantry squads dismount their MRAPs and engage, destroying the first patrol, but the second engagement sees the remaining Taliban flee and leaving  second squad with heavy casualties.
Damn.
I send a Chinook in to MEDEVAC the wounded squad and RTB, but they take fire crossing the mountain range. I re-route through the valley, pick up the wounded, and just as the Chinook is about to clear the valley... she takes fire once again, crashing into the mountain-side and killing all onboard.
I should have cleared that area. I should have had a FOB out there. I should never have sent that helicopter out un-escorted.
My reckless behavior has now given the Taliban a great victory, and destroyed all the confidence and goodwill I had started to develop with the Afghan people. This is an okay HOG, the graphics are pretty decent for the genre and this helps make the HOG scenes much more fun to play that some others, although there is a zoom function provided which probably gives the hint that some items are very small on the screen, although that isn't overused - and most items are hidden in reasonably logical positions, rather than scattered around randomly in impossible or unlikely spots.
The point and click segments and the puzzles are okay, so overall as a game it flows fairly well, and it is usually obvious what you are looking for and what you need to do to progress. One issue I did find was sometimes the hint system fails you and just has you shuffling from room to room without actually helping you work out the next step, but usually it does work correctly, but it did lead me to use a walkthrough in one section where I couldn't work out what to do and the hint system broke down in this way.
In terms of the story and characters, the story starts out okay but does get a bit silly - it seems very much aimed to be like a B-movie, but some of the developments at later stages get pretty weird and out of place compared to the tone for the first half of the game. While Sophia herself is actually a little interesting as a character, most of the rest of the game is populated by very one dimensional cliches - the businesslike police boss, the rich playboy, etc.
Overall then a decent HOG with a few flaws, but also a bit different from the standard for the genre, with a decent if somewhat strange storyline.

Also, the hint function is broken and tends to lead the player around in circles (it works in the HO scenes though).
Is the story good at least? No, it’s astonishingly bad, a mixture of low-budget spy movies and a female version of Danger: Diabolik. On the plus side, we have everything: a secret Egyptian sect plotting world domination, technical-looking gadgets everywhere (including
on the police station!), a predictable plot, clichéd characters, and even some horrible dialogues.
But it’s so incredibly terrible it’s hilarious; Black Viper is a prime example of the “so bad it is good” category. Thankfully the game is short, so if you ever need some cheesy spy story to laugh at, get it.

Written in the Sky is both free and extremely short, meaning that you should just go and read it yourself, because in the amount of time it takes to read a few reviews you'll probably already be done with the games. Now as for my take on it the game, it's not very good.
My biggest problem with the game, that preteen looking girl you see in all the screenshots? She's actually supposed to be a high school student. She both looks and acts like she's in elementary school, but for some reason we're supposed to just accept that she's not. It's almost as if they had the character drawn up from another game and just threw her into this one.
My second biggest problem with the game is the story. Azure, our selfish protagonist decides to tail someone suspicious after she sneaks out of the house due to getting grounded for skipping school. They end up at a warehouse and once the suspicious person leaves, Azure looks around the warehouse and finds a ring. Now despite the ring being too big for her she decides to play bride and try it on anyway only for the ring to change size and get stuck on her finger. She runs home after this and then goes to school like normal, but she ends being tailed by the suspicious person. After school this person confronts her and it turns out that she's actually cute alien princess named Sienna. During their conversation our dim-witted protagonist misunderstands what Sienna was saying and runs home. Once she gets home she finds Sienna has swapped her father's brain with a goldfish so that they can talk alone. Sienna explains that the ring Azure put on is a proposal to her and the key to saving the Martians from a civil war. Azure says she needs some time to think so she goes through a normal day of her life, but gets in trouble at school for not paying attention, since she's thinking about the space war Sienna just told her about, and when she returns home she asks Sienna to marry her since she wants to escape her life, there's then a sex scene if you have the 18+ version on. Azure and Sienna leave for Mars without telling anyone, which includes Azure's father who's brain was swapped back to his body as they were boarding Sienna's ship. There Azure who has shown zero redeeming qualities throughout the entire course of the game ends up becoming a good king for Mars.
Now while there's huge holes in the plot that I could criticize I think the easiest thing to attack here is just the general outcome. Azure decides to just leave home with a word to anyone, simply because she doesn't like the fact that she keeps getting in trouble. Since I feel like this is deserving of more detail I'll give it. Azure's mother was murdered by a criminal because her father is a detective. Ever since he has been very hard on Azure and, despite her protests, forced her to learn various detective skills. Azure then decides to just leave him without a word to go and live on another planet because she doesn't like that he was often angry with her and doesn't think he'll miss her. Not only did Sienna mindswap him with a goldfish for a full day, Azure leaves him without so much as a goodbye.
I'm sorry, but Azure's father was the only person in this game that seemed like a good person and Azure is a spoiled brat that just ran away from her problems.

They Bleed Pixels is a rhythm game pretending to be a platformer pretending to be a beat 'em up.
At first, it seems like a respectable beat 'em up. You're rewarded for killing enemies in creative ways, and there's a creative save point system that lets you place checkpoints whereever you want.
But slowly, like the game's protagonist, TBP starts to change, first into something strange, then something horrific. You realize, as the jumps become harder and the shallowness of the combat becomes clear, that no, this isn't a beat 'em up at all. This is a platformer, and a relatively tough one at that.
If it ended there, the game would be fine. Tough, but fair. But then, the transformation reaches its completion.
You start to realize that the game is intentionally limiting your checkpoints to pre-defined areas.
You start to realize that the game is limiting where you can wall-jump, where you can stand still.
You start to realize that placements of enemies block your jumps with dodgy collision detection.
You start to realize that your combat capabilities are gimped in the air.
You start to realize that some enemies don't follow the rules set by the game.
You start to realize that enemies that used to be fun to kill are now insurmountable obstacles, health-sponges that act as arbitrary walls.
You start repeating the same pixel perfect motion, over and over.
The game starts punishing you for not doing them fast enough.
You start to wish the game would kill you faster.
Why bother with a health bar when one misstep leads to your death anyway?
Why bother having spikes and saws that don't kill you in one hit when they send you careening fatally across the screen anway?
And then you realize that there's only one real path to everything.
You realize that you're playing a rhythm game where the steps are invisible and the music is bad.
You enter a cramped elevator shaft with enemies that never die and punch you to death in three frames.
And then you turn the game off, ship it off to the 'Beaten' section of your library, and watch the ending on youtube, if you even still care about its vague, cthulu-themed excuse plot by then.
In short, spend your money and your time elsewhere.

This game is a gem. It's relatively simple in its layout, but extremely challenging. You're forced to wrestle with a lot of different factors: logistics, public opinion back home, trying to win over the locals, and finally deal with the insurgents.
To explain this balancing act, I'll relate something I faced in-game: My strategy was going to focus almost entirely on clearing out IEDs, and building relations with local villages. I didn't want to waste resources chasing Taliban through the mountains, as ultimately that's a futile endeavor, and I didn't see much point to it.
That was a mistake.
The third village I visited was on the far eastern side of the map, so I put together a convoy to just check things out (sweep for IEDs, talk to the villagers, make sure no Taliban were directly around the village). Well, about two thirds of the way to our destination, we run into two Taliban patrols inside a large valley. My two infantry squads dismount their MRAPs and engage, destroying the first patrol, but the second engagement sees the remaining Taliban flee and leaving  second squad with heavy casualties.
Damn.
I send a Chinook in to MEDEVAC the wounded squad and RTB, but they take fire crossing the mountain range. I re-route through the valley, pick up the wounded, and just as the Chinook is about to clear the valley... she takes fire once again, crashing into the mountain-side and killing all onboard.
I should have cleared that area. I should have had a FOB out there. I should never have sent that helicopter out un-escorted.
My reckless behavior has now given the Taliban a great victory, and destroyed all the confidence and goodwill I had started to develop with the Afghan people. Another disaster like that and it's all over. We'll be packing up and going home. One thing is for sure though, we're not going to take this lying down.
Today, I'm going to exhaust as much political favor as I can, and we're going to go back into that valley with attack helos, special forces, and every other piece of hardware I can spare, and we're going to make them pay.

Original Review Jan 2015: If you like UT3, you will like this game. Literally the only difference between them is the weapons and the dodge jump. Toxikk is a repackage of the UT demo contained in UDK with only minor gameplay related changes and minor modifications to several models. There is nothing wrong with this, but if you think Toxikk is a polished game you should be impressed by what you can do with almost bone stock UDK content with a very small team.
If I had to guess, most of the time working on this game was spent on the menus and the leaderboard system. None of this means that the game is bad, but the only map available right now is very cramped, the weapons are not well balanced and the rocket launcher is overpowered to all heck. You can easily dominate a match by focusing on the rockets and timing the armor. But despite all that you can actually have fun with this game and if you want some of the feeling of UT3 mixed with a small amount of UT2004 you will probably enjoy what this game has to offer.
FYI, F is feign death and Q is turn invisible (yes everyone can turn invisible)
In the end I'm voting "No" on recommending this simply because the game is incomplete. The one map gets boring fast and if you aren't used to arena FPSes, you will die more than you will kill which is frustrating. Give this a bit more time in the fryer and it will be a decent game.

I will be honest I hesitated a lot at the idea of this game. My background with alcohol is one that can make me question it a lot and it took a fair bit of pushing from a friend to really sell me on the idea of this game. Honestly I am very glad for that since I really enjoyed it.
The basics, you are a bartender and you make drinks. However sometimes what they want isn't what they need and at other times the orders are cryptic at best. Consider this, you have a drink that someone wants with optional alcohol, do you add it? how much? why? what will happen if you do or don't?
Personally my stance on alcohol was unless asked for exclude it. However my next playthrough I am tempted to see just how differently things will go when I aim to add as much alcohol as possible. I already have been told there are differences from the friend I mentioned earlier trying it a bit. I also found a few spots I saved and kept a save to see other outcomes for instance when hanging out with others with multiple options. It can be really interesting how small choices make big differences. I played very careful (likely too carefully at some points) getting a bit more of a completitionist playthrough (but not completely perfect since some knowledge is hidden well). I had the message to my friend of " nooo don't end there, what about the promise of a ((removed for spoiler))? >.<", it really was good to see characters develop and I had the sad feeling of seeing it end since I was so engrossed in it.
Speaking of being engrossed this can actually be problematic, see I started it later into the day and was basically wanting to finish it in a single run till my brain was getting fried due to exhausion. It wasn't the game was overly hard work but I was just so focused on it, the characters and how they developed, making the drinks, picking up subtle hints and actually trying to avoid going too deep into spoiler areas to get things perfect (basically I was just checking with a friend on drinks I was questioning). I am actually a little sad to say I still can't remember how to make any of the drinks in the game by memory, but my memory was always bad so it isn't surprising. It kind of got me thinking about bartending like how it can require a lot of skill at making drinks but also how they deal with people (for better of for worse).
Overall I would highly recommend this game, the music and graphics I don't really think about since they fit well and are not at all bad. Visual novels go quite differently from over the top stupid and simplistic to an amazing piece of complex story telling. I wouldn't say this game is overly complex as in puzzling but it has a lot of though with the characters and how things go, those subtle hints to try and remember to get things going differently. I worried that if I put this game down for the night I would forget it loads and I partly did (against my bad memory more than anything) but I still remembered some of the drinks people enjoyed (still checked a little). If you are on the fence on if to buy this I would say go for it, I doubt you would be disappointed and this is from someone who has issues (likely just minor) to alcohol.

Edit: after someone in the comment brought up that in their opinion the game gets better later on, I decided to put some more playtime in Va-11 Hall-A. My overall rating for the game hasn't changed much, but I'll keep this edit on top, since it's rather short.
After the first day of chapter 2 (which is about 1/3 of the game, I think), I feel like there is nothing in this game for me. My previous advice is still valid, and watching a playthrough of the first 30-40 minutes should be enough for those interested to figure out if this is for them or not.
I keep having a hard time caring about the characters and the writing. I feel this is the narrative equivalent of humans finally encountering aliens, and then discussing the weather with them. You meet all sorts of people that look weird/interesting, and supposedly have weird/interesting jobs, but the game makes sure to instantly normalize every single one of them, and the dialogues end up being about the most mundane things you can think of (family, the monotonous parts of their jobs, etc). The setting is extraordinary, the characters should be extraordinary (except the protagonist), but so far, everything remains in the background (gunfights around the city? A sleepover and everything is over), and nothing of what would make such persons unique and worth listening to gets explored (cursory mentions, and then the mundane hammer falls down, reducing the interesting premises to everyday chit-chat). I can't force myself to play more than this, so even if it gets amazing from here, I'll never find out.
Previous review before the edit:
The protype for this game had me excited (and got a few laughs out of me), the demo later on had me worried (the writing was needlessly verbose, tedious and the philosophy on display was poorly argumented, as well as becoming a ghost story out of nowhere, and managing to have a crash to the desktop kind of bug if you went through a certain path). Now the game is out, and it confirmed the bad impressions left by the demo.
This is just a poor visual novel, in the first hour you are presented with info dumps disguised as dialogues, bland conversations that go on for way too long (they really need to work on being concise, the dialogues were often short monologues, opinion pieces about this universe you know nothing about), no plot whatsoever (just some random backstory for the first few customers you get to serve, and sparse details here and there about the city), moments that are supposed to be comedic in nature, but are hardly worth a chuckle: they follow some of the classic structure you see often in manga or anime, where you get someone saying/doing something silly, the protagonist going along with it for a while, before realizing how absurd it is and commenting on it, but the reactions are too subdued to sell the absurd comedy, and the writing for the absurd part doesn't ramp it up enough, some gags are also beaten to death by the end of day 1 already. You don't get to pick your answers, and you can only affect the situation by way of the drinks you serve, which ultimately hampers the gameplay, and it also serves to make the protagonist even more removed from the players (you really are just in for the ride in this game).
The best parts might just be when you are NOT talking to the customers, and these parts aren't all that great either. Be it the sadly uninspiring "buy stuff or your character is distracted at work" mechanic, the no challenge drink mixing (at least this is mildly satisfying, dragging and dropping ingredients while following the recipes works fine for what it is), or reading the newspaper/reddit before going to work (which is written a bit better than the dialogues provided by the clients), they don't have the pacing issues the dialogues suffer from, and seem to have more charm in them. Sadly, a visual novel lives and dies by the quality of its writing, so even if these parts were better than they actually are, they still wouldn't be able to salvage the game.

To be fully honest, I've never really played a F2P multiplayer game that I truly thought felt like a passion project through and through. Most of them feel like a bunch of high tier game developers had an idea for a game, asked the marketing team how it could make them money, and then go from there. This truly feels like all of the people involved had a fun time and were clearly inspired, and that speaks volumes for a game in a genre that is usually ridden with whaler paying schemes and uninspired designs. The fact that you can pay 30 dollars to get
hero in the game (forever! as long as they keep coming out!) without having to pay out your♥♥♥♥♥every time a new one is released blows me away in a sea of games that would rather you pay 10 dollars for each one.
Gigantic is a MOBA by name alone, it doesn't really share many similarities with games that you are currently thinking of as soon as you hear it. It's less "League of Legends/Smite crossed with Overwatch" like people have been advertising it to me and more like a wacky game mode in a largescale A-MMORPG. Rounds are less focused on player progression and base destruction since you level so fast and can repair part of your "base" in a few seconds, and more focused on pure skill and tactics with the 5 on 5 teamfights and solo duels. The gameplay feels extremely chunky, and other than the fact that I think melee heroes are a bit overpowered due to their excessive gap-closing and high damage I think is well balanced.
The graphics, sounds, voice acting... it's all there. I've heard some people criticize the VA for being lazy, but honestly in most cases I found it fitting. It all reminds me a lot of old disney cartoons I used to love watching. The menus are also well done too, and the daily "quest" system has a bunch of beautifully drawn cards for you to look at while you draw them from a deck. I have mild complaints about the in game graphics though- I have them set to max, yet it still feels like they are on the lowest setting. I know it's stylized, but the way that everything doesn't really have a texture and is just wearing straight color with blocky shadows makes it look cheap compared to the drawn 2D art. It's not a major issue though, and once you start playing the game it's hard to notice.
The only real massive complaint I have is accessibility. There are a lot of things that just aren't explained to you at all unless you go rooting around in a wiki or on the official site. How does crit chance work? How does armor piercing work? Do we all start with 100 armor? Is +20% armor piercing on your attacks just 20% bonus damage? Do the stat bars on the hero pages  reflect their starting stats, or just their skill layout? How do dash attacks work, do they deal more damage or are they just there for mobility? All of these things are questions you come up with in the game due to skills referencing these concepts. I know the answer to most of them now, but I wish they were more readily available to new players. Speaking of skills, I wish I could view them before I get in game. When the game starts there is a mad dash to quickly read every single one of my skills while I run towards the center of the map, just so I don't let my team down by standing around on the spawn platform looking at  lines of text.
But despite that taking up a whole paragraph, it's honestly not a huge detractor to the whole experience- just minor annoyances. It's kind of disheartening to see people rag on the game just for the lack of heroes or the fact that it's capped at 60 FPS... it almost feels like they didn't play the game for more than 5 minutes and want to find things to complain about regardless. Yes, there isn't many heroes out yet or many variations in maps, but I think in time this will blossom into a beautiful game due to the sheer amount of love and time that feels like was put in. It's a fun hero brawler, it's F2P, it's got a good paying scheme, and it feels passionate. I'm praying with all high hopes that this game doesn't die solely for the fact that I want more games like this to exist.

I'm going to say this flat out. I do not recommend this game. Game mechanics were a bit iffy - the puzzles and hidden object scenes works just fine, but progressing was slightly difficult as it was hard to know what to do or what you could pick up. And while nobody over the age of thirteen plays hidden object games for their story, it was a bit dumb.
The biggest problem I had was with text. Or with the way the text was written. Considering that hidden object games rely massively on text for their stories, they should be well written with decent grammar. You will not find that here. I feel that this is mainly because this game was made in another country in a different language, then was translated into English. But the person translating English does not know English well enough to translate correctly - so often there are words that don't make sense (too literal or a phrase translated literally). And because of this, there are a few items in the hidden object scenes that were difficult to find because you aren't exactly sure what you are looking for ('pocket' for example was a purse type object).
So in conclusion - this game was a bit of a bore and a bit frustrating. The badly translated text was too distracting to derive enjoyment from it - detracting from the story. If you must, buy this in a bundle or on sale.

Outstanding game.  They mangaged to keep all the positives of Vietnam 65 and build with a wide assortment of cool new features and combat choices.  If you want to make a sequel, A11 has shown the world the new blueprint on how to do it.  It manages to give you the feeling of actually being a part of the battle and where and what you do, directly affects if you win or lose.  On normal settings, this is a much more difficult game, but in a good way, as you find yourself trying to balance out choices like, "Should I send in the infantry first to clear out any dangers from partisans, or should i go right to the clearing of the IED's so they don't blow up when they take a step after they land"?  And the game actually forces you to put together convoys if you want to travel in any halfway safe situation.  Something I was personally impressed with.  Supply is much more forgiving then it's predessor, which is an improvenment.  If you run out of gas, you just have to send some, your equipment doesn't just blow up.  I'm still trying to figure out if the AI is decent.  But I can say it's doing a good job of frustrating my efforts to win the hearts and minds of the populations.  I can see that it will be necessary to use my special forces to train Afgan forces, but I haven't gotten that far.  So there is allot of pluses for this game, I'm going to rack up some hours on it for sure.  Great job developers!!

I have very mixed feelings about this game, and the only reason I'm giving it thumbs down is that it seriously lacks consistency.
It has a lot of potential and I hope they'll introduce some interesting goals and more variety to it, becayse in current state it's simply too grindy and outright boring.
After couple hours I feel burned out. All the ships seem like differently colored rehashes of same thing we flew before, just with boosted stats. At first, when you play tutorial and quite fun promissing PvE option, you get the general idea of how Star Conflict is supposed to look. Interceptors are fast and hard to hit, but fragile, gunships are your heavy punchers, and frigates are designed to bring some serious firepower to the frontline being able to withstand some punishment...
...but the moment we get into PvP this notion goes to absolute ruin. That is because higher ranked players overall have access to equipment with vastly superior stats, meaning you'll spend long minutes sitting on their tail scraping Hit Points with your puny gun, but it often takes three shots to turn your frigate into a flaming husk within a second or two.
Unlike with War Thunder, where vehicle and equipment stats are just an cherry on a cake (of your presonal skill) here it's complete oposite. It's all about upgrades, more dps, more energy, more stats, stats, stats and unfortunately it feels more like two metal boxes exchanging stats between eachother.
As I wrote there is plenty of ships, sadly most of them are slightly altered models (or not altered at all) of ships we've seen before already, thanks god they have different paintjobs! Upgrade costs are simply horrendous and tier progress it tiring, with a complete lack of interresting content. Game looks AMAZING, the graphic engine is top notch, ship design is perfect, they do look like warmachines and not flying dildoes, like in so many Space-Sims. I love the physics which deals with innertial and thus flight model doesnt feel like planes in Space, but actual spaceships.
If only INTERFACE was up to par. The main problem is that in game, where you get into the thick of battle, when all the flashes, explosions, muzzleblasts, thrusters, laser-beams and shiny pulse projectile go across your screen you have NO WAY of telling where the heck is your crossair! It's a tiny cross, two bars, each about half a milimiter thick just vanish in the chaos before your eyes. You can't tell what you're shooting at...
I love the immersion factor for what little we've seen so far. The factions are fun, ships have unique feel and style, spacestations are a neat idea, it's just... there's not enough 'fun' to keep me playing. PvE Co-Op was great Idea, doing missions with my friends, flying in organized wings and such, but the moment I went into PvP it sadly turned into a typical World of Stats(tanks)/(in SPACE), an extremely repetitive grindfest, where lower rank players are pretty much free frags, with little to do. And when you get to higher ranks you pretty much wipe everything on the map with little effort. What's then? Grind for a box with better stats? Till you can beat other boxes with higher stats? Grinding for sake of getting a better vehicle to do more grinding and yet better vehicle, and so on, and so on...
We are given three factions to choose from, but what's their purpose other than different starting ships? You can fly any faction ship you want anyway, there is no real conflict between them and for most those factions are used to paint the galaxy map somehow in clan-wars, because no other idea seemed valid, I guess. We don't get to explore the factions, they are just there, a symbol that literary means nothing. It is a false pretense we deal with fleshed out setting, in fact factions are nothing more then another grind table masked as a reputation system to unlock 'bigger' stats technology.... You know, so we can get exactly same gun we used to shoot for last week, just with little more damage per second. It feels like in current state, this game is just a load of mechanics that seem interesting at first, but boil down to even more grind, and more, and more, and more grind.
Don't get me wrong, this game has GREAT potential, it simply feels like it lacks direction and variety. At current shape and form it get's boring fast, extremely fast! It's hard find reason to support microtransaction system where there's little purpose to keep on playing.
Thus, for now, it's Thumbs Down, but I do hope devs (who proved that are capable) can one day introduce new ideas and make the gameplay more interesting.

A very qualified recommendation. By itself, the game is not great, it's also not terrible. Within the context of it's creation, it's kind of interesting.
By itself, the art style is enjoyable and the music and sound design works pretty well. The platforming is somewhat good and the combat sections are OK.
The negatives include a handful of crashes (Windows 10) and a frustrating restart system (~12 seconds on an SSD) where you hear the same handful of quips from the narrator over and over. The game feels like it had grand ambitions, yet delivered something much more modest.
The context for this:
The game appears to have initially been partially developed by an animation studio with lots of ambition before going to Kickstarter to complete the game. A non-linear metroidvania with skill trees, three very different stances / forms, lots of interesting narratives, releasing on several consoles and PC, etc. The game only made ~$40,000 USD on Kickstarter. I would imagine at that point the studio had to regroup and decide what was doable within the meager budget. Where they landed is kind of interesting: what is the core of each element they need to make the game?
- They reduced the scope of the three stances / forms. Originally, each would have a skill tree and different gameplay. In the shipped game, the main form is used for platforming and the fire and ice forms are used for combat. The fire and ice forms are identical apart from inflicting more damage on similarly colored enemies and blocks. In the Kickstarter pitch, one played out with stealth mechanics and the other with heavy combat. They were heavily involved in navigating the world. In the shipped game, these other forms are only used to break similarly colored blocks (gates) while outside combat.
- They probably reduced the structure from an interconnected level design to what ends up being essentially linear sections. You do cross over the paths a few times, but rarely go back to an area with new abilities that transform the way you see the space. Instead, "I couldn't reach that ledge and now I can".
- They reduced the narrative from "battling with your subconscious" to a "bad guy takes over the world, kill the monsters and you get the throne." There are hints of something more, but they never go anywhere. There is an unreliable narrator, whispers from unreliable ghosts, etc, but none of them really lead to surprises.
- They reduced the number of enemies to a handful. They don't show up often enough for this to be a negative, but they aren't interesting enough to be a positive.
- The bosses were reduced to two repeated mini bosses (golems) and one final boss with phases and attack patterns. The golems are not fun and they have difficult to read hit boxes. After many deaths, I learned to role back and forth and do upper cuts to chip away at them. It felt like I found a design flaw and exploited it rather than solved a combat puzzle. The final boss was OK, but a little finicky.
- They likely reduced the platforming elements. These are done OK. You get a typical double jump and wall jump, but the most interesting part is a hover ability and a dash ability. The dash can be used as up / down / left / right and the hover holds you in place or lets you slide left or right. Those get combined and are fairly interesting. However, the later part of the game places lots of fairly challenging sections that require more than the controls can handle. It's a lot of retries with ~12 seconds (SSD) to wait between goes. I read another review that said they waited ~40 seconds between goes and I would have stopped at that point.
In conclusion, there are a few clever moments and points that hint at something better than the game can achieve. It's impressive that the studio was able to take a small budget, distill game design elements into achievable cores and put something out the door. If you want something that plays great and does lots of new things successfully, this is not that game. If you enjoy metroidvania / platform games and like thinking about the game while you're playing it, give it a go.

The game is also somewhat heavy on surprise deaths. Many times beams trigger alaarm, then once it's actually 1hit kill spikes, and another it's literally lethal by itself. Or spikes suddenly popping through walls. Or laval at the bottom of a pit. Then it's loading... and try again. Not really fun at any point, just feels like the devs wanted to "outsmart" the players in a "Haha, got you didn't I?"  sort of way.
All in all I didn't enjoy most of the game simply because it was linear and boring, but at the same time it felt so close to being something actually good.
But because the gameplay itself is generally dull and boring, I can't recommend this title.

You wanted action? You got it, baby!
While it's true that this game delivers action and fun in spades it doesn't change the fact that it feels like Far Cry 3 Lite. It's got the same animations and many of the same icons on the map and HUD, even several of the weapons are the same. It's got the same type of setting, deceptively beautiful but filled with danger and violence and the villain is charismatic and insane. Which is great by itself but all of it feels like an offshoot of what made Far Cry 3 great.
Especially the characters. In Far Cry 3 most of the characters, especially the villains, were larger than life and just plain fun to interact with and while it shows they tried to do the same in this one it falls disappointingly short and feels like a cheap imitation. I was also able to identify a lot more with the main character in Far Cry 3, like his distaste for killing in the beginning and then gradually turning into a violent monster. In this one Ajay doesn't really react at all when people are killed right in front of him and he's given a submachine gun right away and just starts blowing people away like it's nothing. The lack of a proper character arc is heavily felt in this game.
The game also has that good old unpolished Ubisoft feel. Just to mention a couple of things, 2 of the discoverable locations on the map are almost impossible to "discover". One of them you have to use a buzzer to get because the spot to be in order to make it pop is several meters in the air and the other one is below ground so you actually have to glitch yourself under the map in order to get it. The game has been out for 2 years, I can't believe this hasn't been fixed yet.
Another one is that whenever you accomplish a mission with the Golden Path they shoot their guns in the air to celebrate and if you do the same they will get mad at you and ask what the hell you are doing. And finally, worst of all there was the when I finished the game and NPC's talked to me telling me I made a different choice in the end than the choice I actually made. I'm a lorerunner by heart so this one really ruined it for me. There are so many small things like this that just breaks my immersion completely and ruins the experience.
All in all I think it's a fun game but they will have to do something different next time in order to top Far Cry 3, instead of trying to replicate it.

VA-11 Hall-A (Valhalla) is a mix between a visual novel and an extremely simplified Papers, Please. You play as Jill, the bartender of the bar Valhalla, and your goal is to mix drinks and change lives.
The game tells its story through conversations with the clients you serve. Each character has their own interesting personalities, and equally interesting stories to tell. It doesn't provide any options for what you can say to your clients, but it does frequently allow you to choose a drink for them if they cannot decide on a specific drink. This allows you to get them drunk and - naturally, change the outcome of the conversation. If you so desire, you can even serve them the wrong drink, although this will affect you either sooner or later.
The drink mixing gameplay is fairly basic and can get rather repetetive, but that doesn't matter a huge amount if you're one who appreciates story over actual gameplay (although if you appreciate gameplay over story, why are you even looking at a visual novel?)
I wish not to spoil the story, but I will tell you that there are 6 endings you can get.
I can really recommend this game at full price (hell, the fact that I'm writing a review for it says something). I suggest you scroll up and buy it if visual novels and very enjoyable characters are your jam.

VA-11 Hall-A is one of the best games I have played this year, if not all time.

Sometimes a customer will make a vague order, so it's best to read up on the small description of the drink or figure out what they've ordered before and what they like drinking.
The best part of the game has to be the characters and atmosphere. I've beat the main game in less than two days, so it's quite short, but what really sells this is the diverse cast of characters and the fantastic stories behind each of them. Every character is three-dimensional and seem so life like, it's hard not to love them all, even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones.

Does the thought of helping a young goddess regain all her former power and wisdom appeal to you? Then this might just be the game for you.
Enter the mind of Devine, a troubled young goddess with a lot of burdens to bear. Starting off as weak and powerless she searches a forgotten realm for the memories of a life long lost and gradually gains the strength to take on her unknown enemy.
The characters in this game are great; I wanted to learn so much more about them and the world in which they inhabit. The story was very intriguing as well; although it is somewhat easy to figure out I was still very happy to see its conclusion. The game is not overly long but its long enough to get your money’s worth in my opinion, especially if you plan on collecting coins and character skins.
The art style was very pretty too, I loved the bright vivid colours and cartoonish design of everything. The exploding light effects when slaying an enemy are particularly impressive. The environments themselves are pretty and have diversity about them, from deepest caves to sweet happy little villages this game covers a lot in a short amount of time. The soundtrack is catchy too; I really liked it and found myself humming along to a couple of the songs a few times.
This game is a ton of fun, the powers and abilities we are given add a subtle depth to the combat and exploration that whilst having been done before is very well implemented in this title. The ability to switch the characters mask at will was a nice feature and stopped the combat from becoming stale. But fair warning the controls on the other hand were lacking and imprecise, in my opinion it added to the charm of the title I can see some becoming annoyed with them. Also towards the end there is a huge difficulty spike that drove me insane, but it felt so great when I finally overcame it.
At full price I would be really - hard pressed to recommend this due to its simplicity, a couple crashes and sometimes frustrating controls, but when on sale or if you are metroidvania fan then this is a buy, it’s still a nice adventure through a wonderful world and I am looking forward to any other titles in the series.

This'll be my first fully polished review, so this'll be quite long:
Wonderful to finally see this genre of arena shoters coming back ^^
As an Unreal veteran, I do tell you, I see very high potential with this game.
I'm pretty sure that until next UT will be released, this will be the one we'll be playing.
As this is still at beta or early access, I wish developers would see my points in negative aspects written down below.
So, I hope more maps ofcourse are coming out, graphically this game is very impresssive. You could add more variations to character looks, or classes whatever, but it's actually pretty ok. The only deathmatch map available, was pretty good map really, it was easy to learn the corridors and locations of pickups.
Controls, are very good, it's perfectly polished, and I wish them to stay like this.
Things that have improved since I first wrote this review, are things like, Options menu is now accessible in-game. Also option for weapon auto-switch.
And I don't know what they did with Raven, but it feels now far better balanced than it was at first. I still suggest as soon as you spawn, to search for other weapons immidiately, but now the first weapon you have is quite bearable. The weapon balancing is being done better by each patch and that is a sign of good developers, great job:)
So, there are plenty of things which would be wonderful if they are improved, so I'll talk about each small thing separately. You may call this nitpicking, but these are things that even classic arena shooters have, but not this, when it claims to be like that. But first of all, don't get me wrong, I'm very positive about this game, and it has much potential.
Menu music, is horrible, and very repetitive, would be nice for it to have some variation, maybe an ambient part in the music, but the style is good though. The music in-game is way better though but decent, I won't argue about that much.
As I mentioned before about character, yeah, it could use more variation than just the two models you can choose.
Oh yes, I might be in extreme minority here, but this is one of my major complains. I'm a left-handed shooter, and I would like to have the option to hold my weapon on the left hand. Though no modern games give you the choice, and not that I expected that from this game either, but it would have been nice. Though working on character models specifically for this reason is kinda stupid, I know, but UT didn't change character models for those though.
To change the difficulty of bots, or a map, you have to go all the way back to main menu... It's not too bad though but a quick menu could be implemented. Now that option is acceccible in-game, that is very good, but I wish there to be an "Exit to Desktop" button.
When you start a match, the first thing you have to do is to run to find any other weapon than your base weapon. Also the gameplay with these weapons, was a little bit boring, like there was no special things you could do with any weapon, not even load multiple rockets. Oh, I'm just being used to UT weapons, I was trying to sound silly.
One more thing.. how about a weapon bar? While playing I have close to no idea which weapons I'm having, and that's stupid.
Well, first of all, I rarely play online. I rather play with bots all the time. Would be nice to have few things, like to change the bot difficulty automatically according to player's skills just like in UT. Speaking of difficulties, why can't I see it on scoreboard, the difficulty I'm against with? Not that it matters, but it's a nice little detail for a screenshot.
Another thing.. double kills, multi kills.. that sound that it makes, is horrible, intrusive, and they all have the same sound. Wish they had at least a robotic voice to say out loud "Double kill" "Multi kill" etc.
And I guess that's it, if I find any more of small things that bothers me, I'll be adding them to this review then. And yeah I am seeing the good changes in this game, and has thus erased some details of this review.

If you liked Vietnam '65, you'll like Afghanistan '11 - A complete upgrade in almost every single way.
For me, definitely one of best strategy games released over the past year. I'm Looking foward to future developments on this game, as there's a lot of potential for expansions and DLC's.

Huge improvement over Vietnam 65 -- basically the same game mechanics, but MUCH more fleshed out.  (Ignore low number of hours, I've put more time into this offline.)
Just a few basic things that have been improved:  Forward operating bases are more detailed than the fairly basic system in V65 (you can build the basic FOB and then build additions like medical bay, artillery pit, etc).  Special Forces actually have multiple effective combat options in addition to recon (instead of being totally helpless in combat), and on top of that there are more recon options available.  Maybe most significantly, there's an objective-based campaign in addition to the randomly generated skirmish mode (which was the only game mode in V65).
This is only really scratching the surface of what's been changed and improved.  The big takeaway is that this game makes V65 look like a bare-bones prototype.
It's worth pointing out that there are some early launch issues like weird UI and control bugs, and some people are having problems with frequent CTDs.  I've only seen one CTD so far, so the game has been playable for me, but be warned that not everyone is having the same luck.  The game is brand new though, so I'm expecting that these will be fixed within the next couple weeks or so.

However, now that I'm in so deep and still liking it so much, I highly recommend buying it. The design captures tactical and political aspects of war that I've never seen modeled prior to Vietnam '65 (dev's previous game) and it is much more satisfying than the old tropes of force on force. I'm not sure why it works so well, but it has something to do with a combination of a 4x type goal constrained by logistics, asymmetries, and time limits that are grounded in the headlines we've all read for the past 15 years.

Afghanistan '11 (A11) improves no Vietnam '65 (V65) in everyway. That being said, those people who didn't enjoy V65 or never bought it because they thought it wasn't for them, probably won't enjoy this game. This review is kind of a comparison between V65 and A11.
TL:DR There are substantial changes to pace of the game, the PP system and support and many other smaller changes have a positive impact on gameplay compared to V65 ensuring that not only is this game not just a reskin of V65 but is a completely seperate game in its own right, and worth the price increase from V65.
The pace slows down quite a bit by introducing an expanded logistics and supply system. Forward Operating Bases (FOB's) Now need to be provided with supplies to repair units, refuel units to max Rations or Fuel instantly, and provide shells for Artillery, which is all provided from your main base. Helicopters were the mainstay of V65 but now they are expensive and easily destroyed because they travel over the areas that the enemy literally spawn from, so they take a lot of hits (The chances of the enemy hitting is reduced in my experience, with a chinook taking 5 shots in one turn and only getting damaged) Instead ground vehicles have come to the limelight, as a cheaper and less hazardous alternative. Mines, now IEDs are far more common, but the PP reduction from enemy base structures has been removed as far as i have seen, instead replacing them with Opium fields which provide funds to the enemy.
All round, the PP system has been improved. You have an income per turn which can be increased by building waterworks in villages, and this helps to balance out the game on lower difficulties (Haven't yet tried higher difficulties) There are turns when my PP is up in the 7000, then in two turns i take staggering casualties because a convoy hit IEDs and were ambushed which plunged it back down to 4-5000. It generally rises turn by turn unless i see a Taliban offensive (Marked by elections or sometimes just random) where i will lose a lot of PP ferrying troops to combat or rescuing damaged units with escorts.
The last big change is the support, in the form of drones, airstrikes and supply drops. The PP requirement to use these has been removed, and instead there is a cooldown the length of which depends on who is elected. This makes these life savers and far more worth using in ordinary situations. From scouting out mountains for Opium crops with drones to having an advanced scout position consistently being re-supplied by air, they take some of the weight off your poor grunts' shoulders.
There are many other smaller changes which make the game far more playable, for example the increased number of things to do mean longer games aren't such a slog, some units being either impervious or highly resistant to IEDs, adding extra health to Taliban units so there is the threat of them returning are but a few, and it has already led to some memorable scenarios in the short time i have been playing, and there are sure to be many more.
I'm not knocking the people who haven't enjoyed this game, but there are a few things that i want to point out to readers that have been mentioned in other reviews i have read. Firstly there is no bug in the fourth tutorial, you have to open the command eye to see the objective. Secondly, there are very few bugs that i have seen (the only one i remember being the radio on one model being skinned to the head not the body so the radio floats around with the head rotation) and no crashes to desktop. Lastly, people who are complaining this is impossible to win due to everything being killed are not playing it with enough careful planning. Rushing into anything usually results in casualties, but thorough planning combined with the support assets can limit even the most dangerous mission. This game really pushes you to think outside the realm of normal strategy games.

I am terrible at competitive shooters. I am worse at these hero based MOBA shooters. Gigantic is genuinely fun to play, even though I'm not very good at it, and that's an accomplishment. The graphics are charming, and even though I've barely begun playing and don't grasp most of the complexities of the game, I thoroughly enjoyed the matches I've played so far. I'm hoping a community forms around this game.

I'd like to preface this review by stating that I play Overwatch at a semi-serious competitive level with roughly 525 hours in the game, dislike pretty much every MOBA except HotS, and dislike Paladins because it has no character and is made by talentless hacks. So keep that in mind, I guess.
This game is an excellent mix between MOBA and shooter; something that I feel is oversaturated but not well explored in this current game industry. After the massive success of Overwatch, a shooter with VERY light MOBA elements, certain games seem to have sought after a similar mix of shooter and MOBA, adding and mixing the two genres in different capacities. The most outstanding example would be Paladins, which added more MOBA features while keeping the team  objective-based FPS gameplay of Overwatch intact.
The difference with Gigantic is that it is built not around the genres it encompasses, but around the game itself, and allows the mixed genres to be formed around each other, and doesn't try to build the two types of game separately and  forcibly mash the two into one abomination. The game feels fluid and comfortable, and is unique in its gameplay and concepts. The characters are well-designed, both in mechanics and visuals. Every single character in this game is interesting to interact with and shockingly balanced (except for one character that sucks, but no one likes her anyway). I, as someone who only enjoys only one of the two genres that this game presents, was captivated almost immediately. I'm suprised this game isn't absolutely exploding with popularity, to be honest.
To conclude, I would recommend this game to literally anyone that enjoys shooters or MOBAs in the slightest. It's free, what have you got to lose?
Also, I've had no technical problems with this game at all, not on my ~$400 budget desktop or $500 laptop. I'm suprised people are actually upset that they can't run this game; I don't know just how destitute they are, but PC gaming probably isn't for them. :/

It's not my fault that I had played Dishonored 1&2 long before I got this game. And I had also seen some of the earlier 'Thieves'. I was honestly going to give it a try and be as neutral as possible.
The good things first. It looks good. The visuals were impressive for its time, and they are still nice to look at. The setting certainly has its style and charm, with plenty of atmospheric views and places to see.
Now, to the flip-side. It's incredibly linear. The seemingly rich and interactive environment does not work as it should. Master Thief can only jump\climb over the 'special' objects, and a mere waist-high fence or a tiny gap can become an obstacle for him. Ropes can only be attached to the 'special spots' too, which kinda kills their purpose.  Such things are ok for a fighting\action game (e.g. 'Remember Me'), but we're talking about the 'stealthy thief sim', aren't we?
The story\writing could possibly save the day, but it's rather dull and lacklustre. Those omnipresent unskippable cut-scenes and forced scripted events do not make it any better. I'm fine with the idea of a 'flawed' PC, which can sometimes do stupid things and\or fail, but those moments reminded me of early  'Deus Ex: Human Revolution', with its gameplay-breaking bosses. Action or combat should only occur in a 'stealthy' game by the player's choice (or by the player's mistake), not because some level designer had told so.
TL;DR - If you're looking for the 'thief sim' gameplay - try older 'Thieves' instead. If you're into pretty graphics and the story- go for 'Dishonored' 1&2 (which are also filled with different paths, great gameplay and non-linear options).
I really wish that more games offered more custom difficulty options like this game.  "cough"Dishonored*cough*  It's just too bad that we'll probably never see another one of these.

Thief Deadly Shadows was one of the best games ever to be made, a masterpiece for the ages, so everybody had high expectations upon the fourth installment of the Thief series. To be truthfull, this game had bad reviews because it did not live to the expectations and the standards set by its predecessor. And the 10 year gap between both games, only provides more accumulation of expectations from the die-hard Garret fanbase.
But in all, as a stand-alone game it is fairly good. Nice graphics and physics. Very interesting missions, with well balanced foes, and a nice array of capabilities and gadgets given to the player.
The major let down was the map... A sh... Well, horrible for a game launched in 2014. Those rigid levels maps, with absolutelly no free-roaming, are suitable for a game of 2004 (like Thief III), but inadmissible for the modern gamer. Especially, since GTA and Skyrim and so forth, have settled the open-map sandbox as the pattern for and action/adventure/RPG game.
The story is also a let down. They decided to reboot the series, but there are vague and incoherent references to the early time-line. So..... may centuries have passed, but the thief world is still Medievalish?? I mean, either you tottaly reboot the game, or you continue the story. That "not-meat-nor-fish" (a Portugues expression, y'all can use now) thing is the worst of both options.
3/5
2/5 (if you are a die-hard Thief franchise fan, and expect a sucessor to Deadly Shadows)

VA-11 Hall-A (Valhalla) is a mix between a visual novel and an extremely simplified Papers, Please. You play as Jill, the bartender of the bar Valhalla, and your goal is to mix drinks and change lives.
The game tells its story through conversations with the clients you serve. Each character has their own interesting personalities, and equally interesting stories to tell. It doesn't provide any options for what you can say to your clients, but it does frequently allow you to choose a drink for them if they cannot decide on a specific drink. This allows you to get them drunk and - naturally, change the outcome of the conversation. If you so desire, you can even serve them the wrong drink, although this will affect you either sooner or later.
The drink mixing gameplay is fairly basic and can get rather repetetive, but that doesn't matter a huge amount if you're one who appreciates story over actual gameplay (although if you appreciate gameplay over story, why are you even looking at a visual novel?)
I wish not to spoil the story, but I will tell you that there are 6 endings you can get.
I can really recommend this game at full price (hell, the fact that I'm writing a review for it says something). I suggest you scroll up and buy it if visual novels and very enjoyable characters are your jam.
It's time to mix drinks and change lives.
I really, really wish the game had trading cards, though. I'd totally buy my way up to a level 5 badge.

Born in the most obscure and deepest parts of the country known as ''Venezuela''. Developer Group ''Sukeban games'' bring forth VA-​11​ Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action or ''Valhalla Bartending Action'' for short.
I have no particular ''match up'' for this game likely to be due to my lack of experience in the field, but let me tell you there's a ride to be had if you can engage in several layers of fiction. humor and parody
VA-11 Hall-A - Cyberpunk Bartender Action introduces you to a post-dystopian environment in the year 2069. A world in which nanomachines are a running disease or the very opposite as they can be taken for a ''enhanced'' Life. Corporations reign to alter and experiment with the social balance of the world and White Knights for law enforcement.
Despite the world's problems. You are a mere bartender named ''Jill'' who lives in Glitch City with her cat ''Fore''  and she has the strong motto of ''Time to mix drinks and change lives'' that being said. Brace yourself for the concept of Bartending in a small bar downtown essentially codenamed ''VA-11 HALL-A'' or Valhalla for simplicity. as the most ridiculous clients come to grace you with Social Interaction brimming to the top with satire-like humor parody and bartending experience.
Let's avoid dwelling into more paragraph territory and go to Pros & Cons:
+ Post-Dystopian Future World setting in the Year 2069 with a decent level of depth/detail involving the concept of Bartending after all it is described as a ''booze em' up about waifus, technology, and post-dystopia life.''
+ Well-designed and Interesting set of characters with all kinds of personalities - traits and ''humor'' to be found in each one packed with social interaction obviously. You'll find a waifu in there.
+ Contains all kinds of humor and references that perhaps is what I could consider to be ''Parody-like Satiric and black humor'' all within the range of remaining blunt and harmless and simultaneously funny.
+ It is a visual novel and targets story/exposition lovers the most. and while you may actually spend 100% of your time clicking to scroll through text. The concept and game-like/aspect mechanic of Bartending is more than a simple mechanic and plays an important role in most of your social interactions while remaining fun and important specially to keep getting more of that satiric humor and references. (It can decisively get you a different ending if you serve the ''right'' drinks) Presentation and style are fairly well done to fit this ''Cyberpunk Bartending'' style.
+ This game has an amazing OST. I won't even bother describing it. It's a shame theres no OST DLC to purchase -YET- but untill then feast your ears on it with the Bandicamp Link

Overview:
Poi seems like a cute little adventure game where you are tasked through levels to find these adventure medalians. The game starts off talking about how you and your twin love to adventure, but it never really expands on that, it seems like your twin is the there so you have the option to play as a girl/boy. The game starts in this valley where you meet this old man who tasks you with finding these adventure medalians, and once you get it you return it to his ship where he tells you his story about how he was an adventurer etc. That is really all your given, not really a purpose other than to explore, which is fine, but it is a little barebones. My main issue with the story is how unexplained it is, it gave me very little reason to want to explore to find the medalians.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is pretty basic, and reminds me of some 3D mario games, such as mario 64. However the controls are really clunky and frusterating to use. You need to stomp on enemies in the levels, but I find that it is inpercise and you are constantly landing right next to them, only to take damage. However the climbing and movement otherwise is very nice and clean. This game in general is kind of a call back to 90's platforming, however with a little twist on it.
Final thoughts:
For $15 I would not suggest buying this game for the full price, unless you really know that you like this game. I would recommend this game to anyone who loves 90's 3d playforming games, in a cute atmosphere where the only thing you need to do is explore and collect medalians.

The art direction may be a bit generic, and there are only four full-sized levels before the final obstacle course, but this game is full of heart, and the devs did a good job giving you plenty of stuff to do. I especially like the little fossil exhibits, which make collecting fossils feel more rewarding than just filling out a checklist.  The levels themselves are dense playgrounds with plenty to explore without being pointlessly oversized and tedious to navigate.
My only real issue with the game is that the enemy hit detection can feel pretty wonky and inconsistent.  The game's difficulty is fairly relaxed, though, so it wasn't a huge problem.

is a masochistic technical platformer, in the same overall genre as Super Meat Boy and Dustforce. It's got a heftier feel to it than SMB, though: your character has a bigger hitbox, you don't always die instantly on taking damage, and levels are much, much longer. Plus there's a light but engaging combat system, where you earn greater rewards by defeating enemies with speed and style instead of simply button-mashing them to death. One of those rewards is the game's clever make-your-own-checkpoint means of saving your midlevel progress. Charge up your combo points enough over time and you can conjure a save point, replenishing your health and taking a bit of the edge off the levels' grueling length. The whole package fits together brilliantly, making it worth pushing on even in the face of a few rough edges in level design.
I also give
props for its protagonist, who gets to be badass, feminine,
non-sexualized, a rare combination even among the female main characters (still a minority) out there. There's not much in the way of plot, but the game's cutscenes basically tell a delightful "self-rescuing princess" story. That gives some extra shine to the thumbs-up the game already deserves for its gameplay, making this an all-around winner!

In Death Road to Canada, you are a survivor making their way from Florida to Canada in a brutal zombie-infested roadtrip. Along the way you'll meet friends, enemies, and frenemies with their own randomized skills and characteristics. You can also create your own survivors and set their appearence and traits. The undead, bandits, and your own ineptitude will put your survival skills to the test as you collect food, fuel, medicine, and bullets. All of which are important on the Death Road.
The highlight of Death Road to Canada is the absurdity of it. Mexican wrestlers, giant bug-eyed anime girls, or a Monday-hating orange cat can be meet on the road as
characters. Reading SWOLE magazine increasing your strength or transforming your dog into a Dogman, the randomized events on the Death Road make each attempt more interesting than the last. All while making you laugh, this game will punch you in the gut with its difficulty and other game modes to mix things up.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game for its replayability, awesome soundtrack, and the comedic tone that makes it a memorable roadtrip simulator.

I can't recommend this to anyone unfortunately, i was excited about it, but it just feels a bit too bland. It doesn't do anything terribly wrong, but there's not enough that it does to make itself worthy of a recommendation.
The story: Its a bit convoluted as its all apparently taking place inside of your soul or your inner being, the world is actually you? Something metaphysical and quite honestly maybe some people will appreciate the uniqueness of it, it comes across to me as bland and uninteresting. I don't usually mind stories that are a bit out there, I loved transistor, but that story worked well because of all the great personalities within it, this game doesnt have that. Its a lot of restore your memories and remember the past events, and the enemies are manifestations of your anger and fear but they're also golems which are being sent by the king to kill you so... which is it game? I always thought trying to be a bit out there doesn't work for this style of mainly combat and platformer focused gameplay. But again, this is more personal, some people may enjoy where i just kinda feel eh about it.
Visuals: The background art is pretty good, but the actual character models, enemies, and townfolk are all pretty bland or lifeless as far as animation ect is concerned. It looks pretty good in screen shots, but as for certain story sequences, the lack of appealing visually interesting story characters makes it seem very generic. Although this is party due to the  writing helping it feel so very cliche, villagers say "i am very busy i don't have time to talk to you" but literally stand there lifeless without any animation at all. I have to give them credit though, for a team of 6 people that made this, it is an amazing amount of work, but its just such a shame that it feels incomplete, like they just didn't have the time to finish giving the game that final polish it needs to come to life.
Music and sound: Music is decent, nothing amazing so far but not terrible, suits the backgrounds pretty well but nothing memorable so far. Unfortunately, the narrator doesn't exactly make the story interesting. The narrator is ok, a bit monotone mostly, and everyonce in a while seems to be evil and against you, its very odd. But since its basically the only voice in the game there's not much too it, I suppose I'm not overly enthused about him tho partly due to my disinterest in the storyline.
Gameplay: While it does have the metroidvania's nonlinear worlds, everything is very linear as far as exploration. Area's are locked off until you collect x amount of crystals, they're not hard to find, and really doesn't leave any optional exploration beyond this. There hasn't been any side power ups to find on the side (minus skins which are hidden), no destructible walls, and while there are upgrades, so far they are mostly unlocking basic mechanics for the game. There are a few interesting movement mechanics like levitation that come in much later, but a case of too little too late. The game moves smoothly and controls are responsive and feel good for platforming. However the action is very basic. There are red and blue enemies, so once you have the red and blue forms unlocked, you simply turn the color of the enemy and punch them to kill. You have a regular punch, an uppercut, and a special punch which uses mana. There is a roll to dodge while in your rage or fear forms, and in your regular form you get a few extra platforming abilities. Again, its not bad and it works at a basic level, but it fails to be interesting enough to really get excited over. In your regular form you get a special to posess enemies, but it doesn't really amount to anything interesting since the only thing you can make them do is self destruct. I thought the concept would have been cool to possess enemies and use specific mobs to solve puzzles but it never gets that complex
Final thoughts: For a game made by an small indie studio I can recognize the huge amount of work that went into this, but I think a stronger focus on unique interesting mechanics would have made the game better overall. If you're really urging for a metroidvania this one might rub the itch, but definately will leave you wanting something with a bit more to it.
