You and I both visited this page for one or maybe even two of the same reasons:
* you enjoyed playing Candy Crush, and you were looking for a similar Steam game
* you loved the movie Frozen ,so you figured you would give this game a go
Before you install this game, I suggest you read a few of the reviews that actually give you some of the pros and cons of the gameplay of Frozen Freefall. I probably started off like you, reading some of the 5 to 6 word reviews and thought to myself, ehh I will just give it a try and see for myself. Here are my thoughts on this game.
When you start up the game, you will quickly realize that you do not have mouse support while using this game. You are to solely rely on the keyboard to navigate throughout the game. For me, this was already an annoyance, but I still wanted to give the game a fair shot. Once you continue through the story portion, you can then begin the actual game play. Like you can gather by screenshots and other reviews, it is a simple “match three items” kind of game. Once you match certain items on the board, you can either cancel out the items and make room for new items to drop, or you can create a special item that has special powers that may in a later turn cancel out multiple items on the board. (Very much like Candy Crush) However, what you may not have thought of is that you can only use the keyboard, so what used to be a simple task with the mouse, turned into a confusing mess.
Since this is a free-to-play game, I opted to give it a fair shot. I do think it is a cute game for young gamers, but it can be frustrating and even confusing at times. One other quick thing to keep in mind prior to installing this game is although it is free-to-play, once you run out of lives, you will have to purchase more lives to continue.
The pricing is as follows:
5 lives for 99 cents, 32 lives for $4.99, and 70 lives for $9.99
If you like having to answer a Yes/No question after every menu decision you make then this is the game for you!

I guess it's a game about American refugees fleeing to Canada after a major disaster.

Didn't like the results of the American presidental election? Tired of paying out the♥♥♥♥♥in medical bills? Or do you just want a convenient excuse to shoot things without getting in trouble? Why not take the Death Road to Canada?
Drive across the country from state to state, collecting supplies, fighting off bandits, and slaying zombies along the way. There's a bit of an Oregon Trail vibe as you have to keep your party healthy, and make decisions as to where to go to collect supplies. There's also roguelike elements as you can increase the stats of your characters, every run will be different, and death is permanent. You can however make custom characters that you can start the game off as, or perhaps even run into them in future runs.
The game is both addictive and challenging, and I highly recommend it. If anything, it'll be good practice if the worst happens should our next presidnet screw everything up!

My experience with death road to Canada:
-Created custom characters: Stronk, and myself.
-Run started great, found shotgun, ammo, fuel and a hockey stick for stronk.
-Find a magic gnome riding a rat.
-Gave the gnome a pistol.
-Run turns even better, food, fuel and ammo are abundandt!
-Find a man covered in boxes by the roadside. My character steals his shotgun.
-In the middle of a siege, my character's rusty machete breaks. Not good!
-Half mauled, we manage to escape.
-On the way to Canada, we run into Joel, one of my other characters.
-I immediatly take Joel's hatchet for my self.
-We are caught in another seige in a Y'all mart. Stronk dies!
-We manage to barely escape, and mourn the loss of Stronk.
-Running low on food, I plan to have Joel mauled so me and the gnome don't starve.
-My plan horribly backfires. My character is caught in an alley and brutally mauled. My last words were "This is all YOUR fault!". My character is selfish.
-Jeol grabs my loot and kicks♥♥♥♥♥ with the gnome not far behind. They manage to escape.
-The car runs out of gas, Joel and the gnome hunt for a car in town. Gnome is beat up badly.
-Caught in a siege, it's either Joel or the gnome. The gnome seems to willingly sacrafices himself for Joel.
-After the brutal mauling of Gnome, Joel drives off.
-Joel seems to nearly break the fourth wall and asks himself why the zombies aren't running.
-On the road, Joel runs into a clown who he eagerly accepts into his car. Maybe the clown could help scavenge for food.
-Joel and the clown head from town to town, narrowly escaping death each time, each car not seeming to last even a day.
-They have just about had it. With a few shells in his shotgun, Joel heads into a tunnel with clown, the highway packed to the gills with zombies.
-Together, Joel and the clown sprint down the infested road, being grabbed as they go by. The clown is too slow. Giving a small nod to Joel, the clown gives off a final honk, which echoes against the cement ceiling.
-Clown is gone.
-Joel uses every shell, mowing down the horde until he reaches a car. Joel gets in and locks the door.
-He knows what he must do. The infected moan and scrape at the car, throwing themselves against the glass.
-Joel takes a final breath and closes his eyes as the hood of the car is torn off, the unknowing zombies scraping at the delicate machinery within.
-The car explodes, and infected fly in every direction. Burning or shredded by the debris, every one of the zombies in the tunnel falls to the ground. Their spirits at rest.
-The tunnel is deathly quiet. Ashes coat the cement and Joel is nothing.
-The game-over screen pops into existence.
-Exit to the main menu.
-Wash...
-Rinse...
-Repeat...
10/10
RIP Stronk

This game is a perfect example of "less is more".  The mechanics are straight-forward, and anyone could replicate these graphics.  The gameplay however, is open-ended to the point where perfect play is impossible; this is a good thing.  Stations pop up, and your duty is to move shapes from one type of station to another.  This is achieved by creating transit routes so that they can get there efficiently and quickly.  The stations and passengers are (mostly) random, so replayability isn't a fear.  This game falls under "easy to play, hard to master".  This game skates the line between leisure and intense strategy, and it satisfies either angle, no matter what you are looking for.  If efficiency and replayability is your thing, this is a must play.

I have a lot of things to say about Thief (2014) and a lot of them are not very good. I would never play this game for the story as it is quite terrible, in part because of the absolutely awful deuteragonist/damsel-in-distress/antagonist, who is precisely what I'll be starting this review with...
Right off the bat, you meet Erin - neo-Garrett’s former apprentice he had taken under his wing when she was young. They had split because of their differences (see: because she murders people).
After making the same mistakes as before (see: murdering an innocent - specifically, a young guard) and neo-Garrett calls her out on it, Erin gets pouty and accuses Garrett of being jealous of her and
. I found her to be a very poorly written, one-dimensional character all throughout the game and quite detestable as a result. I had a hard time
to feel bad for her because the game constantly begged me to do so.
Going further into my opinions on Erin here, but I’ll admit it’s ¾ b*tching about her and ¼ critiquing how they could have made her more meaningful to the player:
You aren't going to find people who LOVE Erin. There are people who like her or don't mind her and people, like me, who absolutely despised her character and found she brought no value (
) to the story whatsoever.
Gameplay? Well, it’s fun, I suppose. Very streamlined and railroaded, like most games these days. This was the case because the devs supposedly wanted to focus on the story. Whoops - the ball was dropped on that one! Anywho, as I mentioned before, it’s good mindless fun. Even on the highest difficulty, I didn’t find it difficult and never used the Focus ability. You’ll find most of your time spent stealing tea cups, cutlery, and plates and it’s kinda soothing. I must admit that over the course of the 40 hours I played, I DID find it very amusing that someone who is a master thief is pocketing ink bottles and letter openers and other knick knacks worth between 6g to 20g for profit… but when he comes into possession of items of high value (paintings, bangles and bracelets, and brooches), he just collects them in his clock tower home. The only explanation that would make sense to me would be that the items (like family heirlooms) are too hot for a fence to sell within The City, but that reasoning doesn’t really explain everything away.
Sound definitely could have used work. “Are those footsteps right next to me or are they coming from upstairs?” is a question you’ll often ask yourself. Also, hearing conversations/guards whistling without any sort of dampening effect through massive stone walls is a thing. Basically, it was very unreliable to focus on sound to get a clue on the positioning of NPCs. Sometimes, it was accurate enough to get the job done. Other times, I wondered why I even bothered sitting in a dark corner waiting for a guard to pass by when he was actually pacing inside a locked room down the hallway. It’s disappointing that a AAA game couldn’t get this right, but a dying game company consisting of 20 people absolutely nailed it…. In 1999. C’mon, Eidos Montreal.
I’m not even gonna bother breaking down the story. I’ve already ragged on Erin for being a poorly written piece of sh*t and she is the center of the damn story! The plot is the obvious product of the revolving door of lead devs on the Eidos Montreal team. It shows and not in a good way. It doesn’t help that the game’s ending basically leaves it open for a continuation
. If this is truly the case, I hope it is a far more solid game to bite into.
Overall, I’d rate this game a 5/10. A solid “meh”, but easy and fun to dive into as long as you ignore the glaring flaws like I mostly did (Erin just really agitates me). Basically, just focus on collecting loot (my favorite part!) and the little “challenges” on each level and put your blinders up to everything else in the game and it’s entertaining!

I won't say that this game has no redeeming qualities, but it's still a thumbs down for me.  The main reason is that, no matter how hard I tried, I could not get invested in either the story or the two main characters.  And the reason for that failure is that I found both of these characters to be utterly preposterous.
The girl, Nina, is a pretty young lady who (the game goes out of its way to point out and show you in half of its pictures) has a lovely rack.  Yet she constantly talks about how no guys have ever told her that she is hot.  This is a girl who has posted a picture of herself in her game's forums and who attends nerdy conventions.  Women like this don't get ignored.  They get absolutely showered with attention -- so much that they usually complain about it.  Girls like this typically have nerds swarming around them like a cloud of nanobots.  If this game were realistic, then the primary game mechanic would consist of deleting messages from her inbox asking to see pictures of her bare boobs.  We male gamers have probably all, at one time or another, entertained fantasies about unearthing that hot nerdy girl who doesn't know that she is hot.  But it's a unicorn, and seeing this fantasy portrayed as a "realistic" character in this story is downright insulting.
Equally insulting is the game's attempt to convince me that this girl would fall for the antisocial♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that is her love interest.  He is decent looking but he isn't funny.  He isn't charming.  He is a misanthropic dork with no self esteem who doesn't even strike me as being intelligent.  And Nina falls for him so hard that she takes half naked selfies for him and then practically begs him to fly across the continent to have sex with her.  She even has a shopping list on her desktop of all of the sexy underwear she is going to buy to impress this guy.  You can only stretch a romance so far before you break my sense of disbelief, and with Cibele, that happened before I was halfway done with the game.  It is a cruelly dishonest portrayal of young adult romance.
I'm not madly in love with the concept of "games" that aren't actually games, but I do think that this is one that could have worked.  However, it would have needed a better developed, more believable romance for me to have swallowed it.

Cibele is a narrative-driven game which stands out for its story and presentation. It's a hard decision whether to choose to recommend this "game" or not.
Firstly, no, it's not a game; it's an interactive multimedia story. And that's its strength. I was really enjoying the means of the narrative, the way you explore Nina's files and overhear her chats in real time. (And, on a personal note, this means of delivery and the theme of the plot really hit close to home, paralleling many of my own experiences.) So, for all these reasons, I would say, yes, worth playing.
However, after the hour or two of its duration, it had one of the stupidest, laziest, disappointing, uninspired endings I've ever seen. What seemed like the typical "end of the second act" - wherein crucial plot points are unresolved and you are anticipating resolution in the following final chapters - the end credits roll. If this were a Hideo Kojima game, I'd expect a fake-out ending and some major plot twists afterwards, but, no, that's all she wrote, literally.
Because this game is not a game but rather a narrative, and that narrative was so poorly structured, this is the primary reason I say that I cannot recommend it. I do hope other developers will use a similar medium to convey their stories, but with a better sense of pacing and, most importantly, conclusion.

This is a pretty damn fun game. The gameplay is an interesting mix between that of Overwatch and MOBAs, with some extraordinary agility added into the mix, resulting in a very fast-paced game that feels engaging. One could possibly even describe it as having platformer elements. The time-to-kill is surprisingly high, although I consider this a bonus as it means one can actually counter an engaging foe. Another bonus in my eyes is the fact that this game actively rewards teamwork and strategy; a team that knows when to play it safe and when to steal enemy power is almost guaranteed a win.
The levelling system allows for a degree of variety in character playstyle which I find very welcome; take the Margrave for example. One can either build him to deal out tonnes of damage, at the cost of survivability, or build him to tank incoming blows and interrupt enemies, which can be really helpful in securing rampages.
That brings me onto the guardians; the entire point of the game is to secure power so that your eponymously gigantic guardian can pin down the enemy guardian, allowing your team to deal damage to said guardian. Power is be gained by defeating enemy players or by harvesting it at nodes scattered around the map which one can summon creatures ontop of to automatically collect power. This concept allowing for a surprising variety of gameplay; storming the enemy's side of the map is just as likely to let you win as playing completely defensively. However, there are unfortunately only three maps available in the game right now. Hopefully there are more to come.
The cast is a diverse mix of characters with clearly expressed personalities in the quality voice acting this game has. Each character also has little snippets of lore spread about the game, which I found to make for some rather intriguing reads. Characters range from the endearing (Mozu, Pakko) to the suave (Charnok) to the zany (Uncle Sven) and to the edgelords (Margrave, Tripp). I've had a fun time simply listening to character lines on Soundcloud.
All in all, this is an incredibly enjoyable game which is in dire need of more players.

Gigantic is really quite something that caught me by surprise. I've really tried to like MOBAs and have never been able to be invested. I enjoy watching them, but they've never been my forte. Gigantic is a MOBA, in a sense, but it's really not in the context that most think of MOBAs (common correlation is to DotA, LoL). Gigantic is really it's own breed, and you could spend hours drawing comparisons to games like Overwatch (another I never really got into, despite my FPS-centered background), but you'd never actually hit the nail on the head.
The combat and movement is amongst the smoothest I've experienced. The game just flows exceptionally. The heroes, while currently at a count of 23 with more to be added perpetually, are immensely diverse and while they have stark similarities to those in other games, still differentiate in unique ways that evoke the "ohh that's cool" response.
The game is free, but you can buy an Ultimate Pack for $30 that has some unique skins, currency, fortune cards (awards things for various in-game goals on completion) and all heroes now and ever (Smite does this, it's a cool idea). There is no P2W at all, purchases are purely cosmetic or for heroes, which require personal skill to succeed with. Heroes can also be earned via soft "crown" currency over time for free (fortune cards help this), but it takes time.
The Art style is really unique and for a game that's flew under the radar it's really a must play. Once you get a couple games in it becomes familiar and deceptively addicting.

I want to recommend this game but I also have quite a lot of gripes. I just recently beat it, and want to write down my thoughts on it. That said, if you're into cyberpunk themes, visual novels, anime, cute girls or 4chinz, this is probably worth your money. The basic premise of this game is that you serve people drinks and talk to them, though you never actually make the dialogue choices yourself, only advance it like you would in a visual novel. From a gameplay perspective you mix drinks using a recipe book and do some other things along the way. This review will contain spoilers.
I started the game and was quickly sucked into the world and the laid back feel of the game. The game is set in Glitch City, a neo-tokyo esque city based in the USA, controlled by a mega corporation called Zaibatsu corp, the city is home to new experimental AIs called Lilim that function just about as well as humans do, as well as other oddities like talking dogs and brains in jars.  Everything is dark and dingy and the music is pretty great, a lot of "neo 80s" synth is used which really fits the game. The soundtrack has a good range of ambient, dark and upbeat songs, but none of the tracks have vocals. The game actually lets you choose up to 12 songs for each shift you take when bartending, which is a nice touch. I felt the ambient music complemented the conversations nicely, with "Everything Will Be Okay" being my favourite track in the game.
The gameplay is shallow at best, you are given a recipe book with all the drinks you can create, each with their own set amounts of ingredients that you have to follow to serve the drink. It was a fun gimmick at first but it never got much deeper throughout the entire game. The difficulty comes in clients ordering things using cryptic codes, and these were fun and rewarding parts of the game, but they only showed up 4  times in the game, specifically being with Stella and Virgilio (probably didn't get his name right) At other times you are supposed to remember a client's favoured drink which was also rewarding. But these moments are rather sparse in the entire game, and I found late game that clients would just ask for whatever drink they wanted by name. No puzzles, no thinking required, just bartending. I feel like this game could have doubled down on the gameplay if they wanted to, and made it the "cyberpunk bartending action" it's advertised as, emphasis on "action". I suppose they didn't want to upset the chillout mood to the game with puzzles. I like puzzle games, by the way.
The story itself is also pretty shallow, but fun nonetheless. The writing isn't going to impress a literature enthusiast but it's enough the average joe. Where do I start? Jill is a bartender stressed out about having to pay for bills and the occasional shoulder massager for times when she is super stressed. There are happenings in Glitch City that clients (who are often involved in said happenings) discuss with Jill, with large scale events  like terrorist attacks and superstar concerts. This leads to a varied cast of characters which I can honestly say is one the best parts about the game. Donovan is a man's man, Dorothy has the best jokes and Virgilio is an eccentric fedora tipper who I'm pretty sure is a homage to the Phoenix Wright games, but maybe only in appearance.
There is an air of mystery placed on characters like JIll, Gillian, Boss, Jamie and Art. Only one of these mysteries  gets cleared up, and that is the one concerning Jill and becomes a central part of the game from midway all the way until the end of the game. The breakup between Lenore and Jill and Lenore's untimely death is introduced quite suddenly, and the player is expected to feel bad for Lenore's death when we only have Jill's stories and an old photograph shown offhandedly as information of what she was like. I really didn't feel invested in this at all, other than how Jill's mood goes rock bottom but gradually improves. I feel like it would have been better if it was introduced from the first day.
Finally the story doesn't go anywhere in regards to the bar's closure. The player is told that Vallhalla, the bar, is scheduled to close in a few months, but that doesn't really go anywhere, even at the end of the game. No breakup of the three people staffing the bar, only for Jill to open her own bar in the future with white hair and a mechanical arm and a cyborg eye (what?). I'm just saying that there was a lot of wasted potential on the story in regards to the the ending and the mystery behind some of the characters.
Double finally this game has no romance options. Why? WHY?! Sukeban games, you made Jill a lesbian, added potential romance options like Alma, Dorothy, Betty and Boss but you didn't actually make it a part of the game?! Goddammit guys, I wanted to like this game and I did for the most part, but I can't let these gripes past. I just wanted to romance Boss. ;_;
EDIT: Oh yeah, the ending, can we talk about how untimely that was? You don't even get to do anything in the new year's party, which would have had new interactions with Gaby, Sei, Stella, Betty, Deal, etc.
EDIT 2: Re-reading this I feel like I focused quite a lot on the negatives. I will say I enjoyed the game as a whole, but had some issues on untapped potential in the gameplay and story. I didn't touch on drinking with Boss or the truth or dare sections which were fun, as well as the phone article/blog posts which added a bit of depth to the story.

You know that one game where you run around various worlds jumping on bad guys and collecting coins? You know the one! Where the character can triple jump, wall jump, ECT. It's Poi of course! Wait, what game were you thinking of?

I'm not entirely sure how to talk about Poi. I don't think most, myself included, expected this to be the next "Super Mario 64." Its important to look at Poi for what it accomplishes in its own right, even if it can't match the greats that clearly inspired it. But since Poi doesn't really have any contemporaries (yet,) this kind of comparison is almost bound to happen. Trying to give level-headed praise or criticism is almost like trying to walk a tightrope.
At the end of the day, we should try to like Poi for what makes it unique. A game may not have the same level of quality as its predecessors, but a unique twist or hook that at the very least makes it distinct and enjoyable in its own right. For me, that's what ultimately tilts this towards a non-recommendation. Poi gets the basics down pretty well but by and large struggles to move beyond a gameplay skeleton we've seen several times before.
So yes, Poi is undoubtedly a 3D platformer collectathon. Believe me when I say the "collectathon" is strong with this one and the game plays off the explorer motif rather well. You need to find gears, keys, fossils... all sorts of stuff. At your disposal are several explorer tools like a shovel and compass that you can purchase and a bevy of movement options that will be familiar to fans of the genre. If anything Poi is straightforward and to the point, and if you want a game to just auto-pilot on for awhile Poi can definitely fill that role.
In general, Poi is pretty laid-back. The simplistic graphics and music are charming and the gameplay pretty chill. Even in death, there's not much to lose since most areas are filled with checkpoints. The game also tries to inject its own personality through the explorer spin, having you scope out landmarks and photograph wildlife to fill out a journal. There's almost always something to do or find and you can explore it at your own leisure.
But despite the depth of content, there are parts where the execution just feels dreadfully lazy. This goes beyond simply having a lot of the same collectables, which arguably would be expected. Its the fact that the game settles on mundane, cut-out tasks again and again as a means to dispense rewards. Need to wash off the bell? Move this object. Fix the tower? Move this object. Power up the windmill? Again, these fetch-questing and button-pressing escapades are nothing new to the genre, but there is only a thin creative layer over top of it. The collection aspect isn't necessarily the problem here; its the means of collection that can quickly become tedious.
Do the environments themselves help make up for this? Unfortunately, we're definitely in well-trodden territory here as well. Canyons, volcanoes, snowy fields... been there, done that. Its here that the simplistic graphics sort of work against the locales, as they struggle to infuse much-needed personality into the different worlds. I don't recall many times when I looked off in the distance, eager to explore. Particularly in the first half of the game (and there's only about a half-dozen core worlds,) the locales aren't very large or interesting.
However, I will give credit where credit is due and say the latter half of the game does step things up a little. The worlds get a bit bigger, and the end-level in particular I found to be a satisfactory challenge (at least compared to the rest of the game.) Again, Poi has the foundation in place... I just feel like it drags its feet a little too much, then ends right when it starts to finally click the pieces into place.
No doubt Poi is going to find its audience if it hasn't already. In particular, I feel like it would be great for a beginner who is less familiar with the 3D platformer niche. All that being said, I still personally give this a reserved non-recommendation. There was some fun to be had in my playthrough, but the extremely "paint-by-numbers" nature of this game is something I'm not giving a pass on.

TL:DR - Far Cry3++, still amazing though, recommended.
Far Cry 4 is an improvement over the third game in every respect, here are some things that caught my attention:
First off, performance. I have an old setup, however the game ran on low settings at 45-60 fps, so I'm definately not complaining about that. I can't really say anything about the graphics for the above reason, however visuals for me aren't the most important thing in a game.
The storyline is more flexible that ever, your choices influence how the playthrough turns out more than just who you kill at the end. If you choose one side or the other, missions change accordingly.
There are even more weapons, and something that I can't thank the devs enough for is the return of some guns from Far Cry 2, specifically the mortar (although stationary), and the flare pistol. A personal favorite would be the throwing knives - makes you feel like J. Statham :P
Overall combat feeling is about the same as Far Cry 3, however there are some things that were added to keep you under pressure, best example would be mortars - enemies can and will use them, and ignoring them is not an option as they kill you pretty fast.
Collectibles and side quests? More than ever. Propaganda posters, hunting missions, courier takedowns, armed convoys and much more. Certainly enough to keep you busy for a while after completing the story.
Crafting is largely the same as in Far Cry 3 as is the inventory system, however items that you collect from around the world are now more valuable.
There were some things that I didn't like, for example when you are given a choice to shoot or leave a character alive, there's no time to think about it, there's no "press this for that" on the screen. That caught me once and while it isn't a massive problem, it definately is annoying.
And so, overall Far Cry 4 in an improvement over 3, however the core mechanics are almost the same. Those seeking a completely new experience will be slightly disappointed. If you loved FC3 and want more of it then you should love this aswell.
Judging by the content of the game, I'd give it an 8/10. While at it's core it's very Far Cry 3'ish, it certainly doesn't lack in things to do.
And yes, there are missions that involve being drugged. Quite a few actually.

~~~~~ A THIEFY REVIEW ~~~~~
Yes, I played them. All of them. They were literally the first PC games that captured my imagination. The story. The environments. The quirky attention to detail that was Thief The Dark Project, The Metal Age, and Deadly Shadows. Hands down one of my Top 5 Favorite PC Games Of All Time. (Grouped together, of course)
This Thief is still Thief. It's not that dissimilar. The obligatory horror mission. The ever-changing City. The fantastic stealth gameplay, which is quite honestly very good. Guards that occasionally change their rotation, while still predictible, does happen. Bumping into the map environment and giving away your position. Those long-range spots where you swear nobody was nearby.
The AIs audio perception isn't quite as hard core as The Metal Age was, it's more refined and predictible. Slow sneak over glass. Don't bump into the detritus laying on the floor. It's good if a bit more railed, but kinda beats the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that would happen in The Metal Age, where one wrong step would give away your position sending you on a spiral of quick saves and quick loads.
Okay I get it. People don't like that it's more story/action oriented. Well truth be told, the previous Thief titles were also quite story and objective oriented as well. Every map had one singular objective, in fact. They also had their fare share of cutscenes. The problem I think is people don't like that there's a mini-map and waypoints. I don't either. Know what's fantastic? They let you toggle it on or off, so you can play how you like. #StopWhining
[What Thief Does Well]
+ Mature stealth gameplay. I loved every moment of sneaking around. That's the core of the game: It's a stealth title and it does it VERY well.
+ ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic map design. Very dynamic environments and not always intuitive. Exactly like the previous games, only better. From bounding up a sheer wall and creepin' in the rafters, to opening hidden passages and discovering secrets where none appeared. A lot of areas have that diaorama feel to it in the look of the map, like they were designed by Disney Imagineers. I'm not sure how else to explain that, but I like it. Whoever designed the maps, I tip my hat to you sir. Job well done.
+THE CONTROLS! The precision of your first person control over Garrett is amazing. I remember Deadly Shadows had some "mech rotation" control. Seems they took a page out of the book and improved on it. From your legs moving on their own when you are simply rotating your FOV, to the slight lean when you are sprinting, to the perfectly accurate and comfortable feeling of just looking around. It's good. Great. It puts many FPS titles to shame with just how damn polished and precise it feels.
+ Graphics. They're good. I feel like for a 3+ year old title this was probably ahead of its time in certain areas, and to me is a game that does shadows VERY WELL. Not over the top, but selective, and high quality. The skin texture on NPCs is pretty good. There's quite a few low quality meshes if you bother to look around, but that doesn't bother me. Most people would never notice that some random potato in the corner has polygon edges on it from the right angle. It does look quite nice all in all, and most importantly, was optimized with a passion. Solid FPS with zero dips ever. Okay I'm on a Ryzen build maybe that's overkill for a 2014 title @ 1080p, but my graphics card is the same age and that has to count for something.
+ Sound quality. It's impressive but not ground breaking. Good dynamic shift in audio based on things such as obstacles between the source and Garrett's ears. Good moody ambiance that will keep you on your toes, and tell tale clues that blend into your stealth gameplay for a seemless experience. Solid A+.
+ Tons of loot to steal. I liked the quantity of collectibles in this one. Don't know what getting a full set does for you really, besides the satisfaction of knowing you found them. Which is fine by me. Some people hate the animations of actually stealing stuff, and it does get a little repetitive after a while, but it also forces you into an uncancellable animation which means you need to be extra perceptive and choose your timing carefully. It's also cool to see Garrett acting everything out I think, adds some immersion that I wouldn't mind seeing in the next Thief title, if that ever happens.
+ Story seems decent. I haven't quite finished it but I'm not complaining. If you've ever played a really badly translated Asian MMO and feel totally lost about the random and crappy nature of the storytelling and dialogue, you should know that this is nothing like what the story in Thief is like. It's fairly interesting, character driven, and does keep you wondering what the next Chapter has in store. 3 out of 5 stars.
[What Thief Does Badly]
- Where's the factions? Where's the Keepers? The Pagans? The Thief universe feel is not really here, in this title. In a very disgusting sort of way, it reminded me a lot of Dishonored. Save the girl. Some nameless plague is killing people. All the NPCs have the same ♥♥♥♥ing dialogue. It's almost like the two games were written by the same person at the same time. Not cool. Not good. What made the previous Thief games so damn captivating was the character! The mood! The quirky and mysterious nature of the various NPCs and protagonists.
I'll never forget exploring the Pagan realm in Deadly Shadows, white-knuckling my way through the Mechanist stronghold dodging cameras and traps, or laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off at Benny and random NPC hilarity. All of the Thief games were memorable asf, and there's a reason for that. Whatever essential spark those games had, this one does not.
~~~~~CONCLUSION~~~~~
Is it worth $30? I think so, yes. I'll be replaying some missions I can tell you that for sure. Is it a good stealth title? Definitely. Just keep in mind that if you are purchasing this title with rose-tinted glasses coloring your eye holes, thinking on the nostalgic experience of the days of yonder yore.... you will be disappointed. I said it's not that dissimilar and I'm not lying. But that doesn't mean that is exactly similar, either. It's it's own thing. It's own story. It's own world.
So if you can be objective about that fact and enjoy Thief for what it is, you will find that its a pleasurable stealth title and totally worth your time. There are honestly so few GOOD stealth titles out there that should mean quite a bit if you are a fan of the genre. It might not be the same captivating quirky and mysterious world of the previous titles, but it's still a damn good stealth experience. IMHO. I would recommend to play it hardcore. Turn the difficulty on max and turn the mini-map off and go for the 100% silent playthroughs. It will give you the most similar experience to the other games that you can get.
Hope that helps you decide.

Under any other title, I might have called Thief 2014 a decent stealth game. Alas, since it happens to ostensibly be a reboot of one of my favourite game series, I’ll definitely be biased going into this one.
The story places you once again in the shoes of Garrett, who may or may not be the same Garrett as you saw in the original (it’s complicated, though I’ve forgotten most of what the game told me). I suspect the answer is ‘may not’, because instead of a cynical down-to-earth master thief who’s just trying to make ends meet, we’re instead given a glum gloomy kleptomaniac who “survives to steal” (actual quote).
You are placed into The City, a nameless medieval-steampunk metropolis stretching into the murky horizon. I have my doubts as to whether this is the same city as the original, since it seems to have become strangely desaturated over the years. Either depressing colours are suddenly in vogue here, or this is yet another example of a game developer mistaking misery for gritty realism. Strange to think that the original city managed to feel more believable despite its quirky characters and saturated colours, or more likely because of them. The originals were also dark in tone, but more so in a low-fantasy sense, where the Monty Python-esque humour of the dialogue didn’t feel as jarring as one would expect. The rebooted city has plenty of detail weaved into its decrepit streets and written notes scattered about inside buildings - but the place is so dull and depressing that it’s hard to work up any enthusiasm to delve further into it beyond the surface level.
The writing was of course a strong point in the original - with its strange mixture of low fantasy and subtle magic that made the world unpredictable and dangerous. The reboot seems to imply at the start that you’ll be playing some kind of father-daughter style bonding story as Garrett has taken on a new prodigy, a young woman named Erin, and begun training her in the art of stealing. After she predictably becomes
Unfortunately, this assumes that you’ve become invested in the character, and everything about Erin’s character is, to be perfectly blunt, repulsive. Throughout the prologue, she’s surly, petulant, shows nothing but contempt for Garrett, and even murders an innocent guard at one point - bearing in mind that in the Thief universe killing is considered sloppy and unprofessional, so not only is she a terrible person, she’s also a terrible thief.
All of that might be fine if she was the antagonist, but Thief strangely expects us to like this character. They may have tried to subvert this later on, but the story becomes such an incomprehensible and badly-structured mess that I gave up trying to understand it by the halfway point. Considering how much this game throws behind its cutting edge mo-cap cutscenes, the story has very little to show for it, and the less said about the dialogue the better...
The gameplay of the original was an effective fusion of sprawling labyrinthian levels and slow-paced stealth gameplay with a focus on evasion over killing (killing was even forbidden on the highest difficulty). New Thief gets only the first half wrong - the levels are all ugly messes of constricted corridors which have to be segmented by loading level airlocks every twenty paces - this is made even more obvious because the game forces you through a quicktime event to jimmy open windows which gets tedious
quickly.
In truth though, the stealth gameplay is actually quite well executed. It doesn’t have the same depth as the original, but it’s still more elaborate than its more action-focused contemporaries like Dishonored. I could gripe about the sticky cover system or lack of a jump button, but the fundamental appeal of moving quietly from room-to-room is still intact in Thief. The AI itself seems more proactive than the relatively basic system in the originals (it was 1998 after all), becoming suspicious if you open doors or operate light switches. It made me more cautious about moving into the next room than I ever had been in the original games. Suddenly I was once again thinking carefully ahead, planning my next move and being meticulous in making sure I left everything as I found it - a guard might get suspicious of an open drawer.
That’s ultimately what leaves me deflated about Thief - it has a handful of potentially really good ideas buried under an insipid mess of bland storytelling, poor level design and a fundamental misunderstanding of what made the original games tick. It feels like Eidos Montreal have extracted all of the quirkiness that gave the original its charm and replaced it with a dull-as-dishwater aesthetic populated by stock characters and utterly generic warring factions.
If you’re a stealth gaming fan who isn’t familiar with the franchise, then Thief isn’t a half-bad experience once you get past the weak story and into the core gameplay, and is still worth the price in a Steam sale. But if you’re a fellow Thief fan like me, then you may seriously struggle to forgive this reboot’s casual disregard for everything that made the originals special to begin with.
A good stealth game with an even better story.

It's a fun enough game. I mean, sure it's got its problems, but I can look past them and just in say that in the context of a subjective, pointless review that I've found this game enjoyable, to a point (he says, in a foreboding tone).
I guess if I were being honest, and I most certainly only ostensibly defend them with this point, the majority of the issues you could list with this game would be thematically similar to those you would raise with most reboots, invariably related to the game being at points - and quite often, important ones - inexplicably tone-deaf with respect to what made the original great.
I don't think we're ever going to establish exactly why we end up with so many instances of a re-imagining of a beloved game IP where the developers or publishers will insist that it's most certainly a continuation or at least definitely connected with the original games, yet simultaneously go about introducing so many elements which are either ill-fitting or downright counter intuitive to what you would expect from another iteration of the original games.
While Thief is most certainly yet another solid example of that situation occurring, much like all the others, it will inevitably come down to personal taste for the changes and each individual's ability to accept them for what they are, and with the game now three and a half years old at the time of writing this review, I imagine those elements are familiar to the majority of readers, and if not they are easily discovered elsewhere.
Were I choosing to be needlessly dramatic I might describe this as requiring a sort of gaming cognitive dissonance ("this is a Thief game but also I can't jump, over trap pads or at all, except for pre-defined locations, but this is definitely a Thief game") but using a more reasonable tone I'll merely insist that it comes down to accepting those changes despite their disparity with the game it is claimed to be continuing the legacy of.
Were this a normal review, following normal review protocols, I might point out that for me the most frustrating departure from the originals is the inability to be allowed to knock out civilians on the Master difficulty. In both my opinion and with respect to the original games this firstly makes no sense, subsequently makes the game pointlessly frustrating, and finally seems little more than a prime example of the contemporary design mechanism of making a game or elements of it illogically difficult but then terming it as "hardcore", which seems to be either fast becoming or simply already a synonym for "masochistic"; but this, much like the mystery behind remake design decisions, is a discussion for another forum.
I will, however, allow myself a further brief but admittedly self-indulgent sidetrack into that specifically raised issue, as it is my primary bugbear: on normal difficulty the guards are most accurately described as deaf and blind, but set to Master, where they finally have an appropriate level of ocular and auditory faculties, you now can't knock out civilians without instantly failing. Additionally and inexplicably, the game still presents you with the contextual option to perform this action; your blackjack when swung does not knock people out, you need to press a defined key to perform a 'takedown' to render someone unconscious. Some people complained about Thief 3. I thought it was pretty decent. This new game, essentially Thief 4, or a reboot, kind-of, is the biggest downward spiral the Thief franchise has experienced, in my opinion. Although I could talk about not liking the way the game tracks specific pieces of loot and nags at my OCD tendencies, making me feel like I missed something important that probably wasn't, I would rather discuss the loss of good lore in Thief.
In the older games, you had factions and things of interest, such as  the Hammers, who were the city's religious order of builders with their own holy texts, and the Pagans, who revere nature and also worship things. You also encounter undead and other things while exploring, and the lore was pretty cool, even though I wasn't really into the first game (though I did get quite far into it). The second game added in the mechanists, which were a group of steampunk-robot-building people. Cool stuff! I completed the third Thief game but don't remember much about it. Whatever factions were in it were pretty decent, as I recall.
With this new Thief, however, it appears that these factions do not exist in any capacity, and during my time with the new game, no other interesting factions were discussed. If they were mentioned, the game didn't bother making them of interest to me before I quit playing. The city was just fairly grim-dark with various places to burglarize, and some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ guards wandering about. The setting didn't have the same "personality" of an older Thief game, or even one that could compete.
I'm no victim of nostalgia and will gladly sell out a game that I feel another game has outdone, but in my opinion, this new Thief game has not outdone its predecessors in anything but graphics, and even then, the art style of the older games is superior to me. I love stealth games, so when this Thief game left me bored and never wanting to play it again, I found myself not interested in recommending it to others.

As a long time Thief player, and fan of the series, since initial release of The Dark Project back in '98... Thfourf is, kinda, somewhat, partially what Deadly Shadows should have been (IMHO). Though Deadly Shadows was *good*, a major highlight was Stephen Russel still voicing Garett, and his ability to deliver the non-chalant, devil-may-care attitude to our beloved thief, while still conveying the "what the hell did I get myself into" take on things... which isn't delivered nor fully fulfilled in Thfourf.
That being said, Thfourf does do a major attempt to convey much larger game world "maps" than Deadly Shadows was capable of, and even with revisiting the City hubs, it still feels more expansive... though after a while a little cumbersome. The actual mission maps are more expansive than those of Deadly Shadows, yet no where near the scope of any mission in The Metal Age. Stealth dynamics are still the front of the series, and continue to oust any competitor - from Styx, to Splinter Cell, to Dishonored and the "questionable" Metal Gear series. Though, I fell the 'Focus' ability was aimed more at new-comers to the Thief world, at the least, for us long term taffers, it can be disabled and ignored. One does not need the 'focus' ability to enjoy the game, quite the contrary, abstaining from it's use is far more challenging... far more vanilla Thief.If you want a struggling RPG experience, better look towards Dishonored, Metal Gear of Styx. The 'focus' ability isn't only really partially fledged out, and felt more like a catering fan service to new players of the genre to strengthen their experience short-comings.
The missions can be expansive at times and require the patient approach to figure out strategy for each small area you come across; though one specific mission felt like a straight call out to the epic "Shalebridge Cradle" of Deadly Shadows, with a very similar approach and engagement to the mission getting into full swing. I felt it was a very good effort, was very enjoyable to run through, but lacked the impression Shalebridge did first time running through Deadly Shadows (i.e. was a good mission, but didn't stand up to Shalebridge's earing a 10-page layout in PC Gamer).
All in all, I would say Thfourf is a solid installment to the original series, if one can set is aside from being a direct followup. As much as we fans were loathe of Deadly Shadows at time of release, we learned to appreciate it, and Thfourf is in that category. It's good, is "Thief," it has it's faults, but is still enjoyable to stealth.

We all have those days. You feel tired for one reason or another. A long day at work or maybe you’re feeling a little under the weather. You want to wind down and play a game, but nothing overly complicated or taxing. Fortunately, Mini Metro exists and is possibly the most relaxing game ever.
For everyone who has played Mini Metro before I’m talking about Endless mode here. This mode unlike any of the other equally brilliant parts of the game has no fail state. You can just continue to expand, refine and enjoy the little subway you’ve created. Usually, you have to deal with congestion. This means that slowly people will get grumpy because their train is taking too long to arrive. When they become mega-grumpy and file a complaint with the transport commission it’s game over. This is fine and it starts off nice and relaxed. Everything is all lovely jubbly, in say Osaka, but inevitably somewhere isn’t quite as efficient as it should be and people start to complain. And then, Mini Metro flips from relaxing to stressful, and some days that is just too much stress to handle.
So stay with me here, I promise Endless mode is different. Pick a city that takes your fancy. Maybe today you want to play with bridges instead of tunnels as you create wonderful tram lines instead. Mini Metro has you dragging various coloured lines for your engines to run on and each one depicts a shape. These can be anything from a circle and square to a star and diamond. Each shaped station is going to have shaped passengers who want to go to their corresponding location. Triangles to triangles and so on. Each time you reach a new milestone of passengers taken to their stations you get some new toys to play with. This could be more carriages, new tracks and trains or even something special like an interchange station that makes it easier for large numbers of passengers to pass through a specific place. In Endless mode, you are left to tinker with this lovely visual puzzle entirely stress-free.

In many other reviews I like to give a thumbs up and explain what flaws these games still have.
Here it is the other way around: This "free" game sucks even though it provides you with SOME entertainment.
What is this game?
Well, it doesn't seem to be THE official PC game about the Disney movie "Frozen" (also it doesn't look like it, just look at the menues).
It's a clone of "Bejeweled", the addictive, colourful casual game where you put at least three gems of the same kind together to make them disappear and win points.
In "Frozen Free Fall: Snowball Fight" you're suppoused to achieve different goals in each level: In one level you need to achieve a minimum of points, in another you have to beat the clock and so on.
It has very little to do with the movie outside of the Frozen-themed menues and the animated characters standing next to the game board as decoration.
But what makes the game bad is the "Pay to win" principle.
Sure, in a lot of levels you do fine without paying crap but in others you feel like they were created intentionally hard or you have far too little tries and time. So you buy stuff. And if you don't pay attention, soon you'll be paying way more than this game is worth.
Personally I've tried to get as far as I could, buying as few objects as possible (for about 5 € in total and yes, I am ashamed) and now I'm stuck in Level 32 which always has the same order of gems.
Everytime I lose a level or just discontinue I get told that I lose a life. And somehow I always have 5 lives, they won't get fewer. Is it a bug? Well anyway, at least the pressure about buying lives (yes, you also buy lives) is not there.
So this is what pretty much ruins the fun.
Why couldn't the developers say "You know what: Pay us a few bucks and you get a fun game which does not suck more money out of you"?
Oh yeah, THEN they would not get a piece themselves of the cash cow that is "Frozen".
I love playing games like "Bejeweled" but this one I cannot recommend or play much more of it. Screw "free" pay to win games.

Great writing and realisation does not save what is ultimately a strange and somewhat chore to sit through. I love games
that are narrative-driven and experiment with interactive storytelling, and have a huge amount of patience for "walking sim"-style games. All that said, Cibele was a weirdly frustrating and unintentionally alienating experience. The "gameplay" segments, wherein you essentially play as Nina playing an MMO, are mind-bogglingly boring to the extent where I would have honestly preferred they be left out the game and Cibele solely be a desktop-exploration style experience.
The drive of this game is its story and the relationship between the two characters - why, then, does the narrative completely stop and force its characters into silence until I click enough enemies for the next beat to occur? The story is constantly interrupted and halted because the player has not killed enough enemies or opened the right documents. It made me feel as if I was stripped of any agency, and made the narrative feel as if it were moving at a completely unnatural pace. It's strange for a game that goes to such extreme lengths to make the dialogue and actions of the characters believable to suddenly have them both awkwardly go silent for an indefinite period of time. Not to mention, there is a certain amount of creepiness in forcing the player to read a teenage girls emails - maybe everyone didn't get that feeling, but once I knew I HAD to for the story to progress, I suddenly felt quite gross.
I don't mind an open-ended narrative, but Cibele merely stops. The game ends the moment it introduces any actual narrative drama, and though I am hesitant to slander a game for not sticking to the tired three-act structure, Cibele would have really benefitted from another chapter. As is, we don't learn how the characters dedal with the situation they're put in, we don't know how it effects them emotionally and we don't get to see them change or grow. A story doesn't need catharsis to work, but it does need to have a point. As-is, Cibele feels like it never really knows what it's trying to say beyond the vague "exploration of falling in love" tagline.
There are things I like about Cibele. I love the core conceit, I love the sections of the game where it lets me discover things at my own pace, and I think both the actors do a fine job of delivering fairly believable dialogue (even if it is quite hard to like the male character). However, by the end of the game, I found myself in the weird middle ground of being frustrated the story was over, and relieved the gameplay was over.

One of the worst games I've ever played. Would be a cute student project or honestly I'd be proud of a personal friend if they made something of similar quality. But as a consumer product, I urge you, save your money and your time.
Allow me to clarify a bit. Some people say this game is cool thanks to ... "the narrative," and how personal the story is. Sure. But it's not a good narrative for entertainment. It'll do fine as 'art' for personal expression. But unless you buy family photos from your local retired school art teacher, I can guess that you probably don't really care about art for personal expression.
The main characters are unlikeable. The acting and dialogue is forced and weird. It has some discoverable tidbits, sorta like a walking simulator might, but since the game doesn't give you any reason to care about these people, it's a waste of time.
There is 'gameplay' but I can honestly say any free mobile title would be better than what's here for the gameplay. I really can't overstate how boring, tedious and un-fun it is.
I'm gonna monologue for a sec here:
The medium of games is unique because it lets the player be part of the story. Through gameplay, game devs can communicate emotions and pressures that stick better than what you might enjoy through passive entertainment. As a result, players can get deeply attached to characters and plots, and so powerful narratives do very well in gaming. But you can't just marry a horribly bland story, and horribly bland gameplay, and expect that to fly. It needs to be the best of both worlds. Calling this game a narrative achievement would be a disaster for all the real narrative achievements in gaming, both in indie and AAA. Anybody who has given this game awards or attention should be ashamed.

It's hard to recommend Cibele as it is a pretty boring game, and its story isn't making up for it at all. But the game itself is original enough to keep me interested to the end.

I was not intending to write a review of this one but after seeing the horror that is the review section for this game I find that I have to weith in and give an actual review rather than the complaints of jaded perverts that populate the section.
For the sake of providing consumer advice I have to stress that this title is both unsuitable for a yonger audience and does not provide any form of engaging "Gameplay" instead this Cibele seeks to tell a story in a way that immerses the viewer in the life of the subject and provokes empathy for her. in fact a major complaint being made in most revies is that the combat in the mmo-esque segment is dull, reppetitive and largely pointless. The point that they are missing however is the fact that us purposely ment to be this way. Nina in the first chapter forgoes moving on to a new game with likely better gameplay to instead stick with a more boring experience that happened to also be where the guy she likes hangs out. She can see that the game is boring but sticks around for him. if you engage with the narrative and allow yourself to feel for Nina then this truth becomes obvious. that is the mentality however that is needed to enjoy Cibele. If you cannot step into another person's shoes then this game simply is not for you.
Furthermore a point needs to be made and respect must be given where due. This project was a personal one for the creator and she assumes the role of herself in it. That includes all the more risque actions taken in the narrative. This took courage that most game developers are never even asked to exhibit. The waves of vitriol that spew from the review section demanding she provide them hardcore poornography of herself if she wants a good rating for her project are frankly disgusting and are undewserved by this sincere piece of interactive narrative.

There is no 'game' as such. Pretty much whatever you do, everything plays out linearly. So all the posts that mock the game for having a 'boring' or 'non-existent' gameplay are missing the main point - the game is about the character Cibele, her life and what she goes through. You're just a tourist on a tour. Your main point is to try and understand her. And this is by reading her blog posts, seeing her journal entries, her pics, what she says and communicates. The game is about internet love, and all the dark horrors that lurk just behind the shadows. It is about vulnerability, about fearing the worse. To be perfectly honest, towards the end I was in my mind conjuring up the worst things that could happen, I knew they wouldn't actually take place, but it still made me think, and wonder why this cliche story evoked those emotions. The game's purpose, it's 'art', is to make you think of that. It's just another medium that hides a short film underneath.

For some reason i thought it would be fun to read a bad story, didn't realize "bad" in this case just meant "badly written."
The story started out building something interesting, but it took way too many words to say not much at all. The devs shoved in a ton of what i would call "sci-fi nonsense," filling the story with all this weird fantasy stuff about Mars and not doing anything with it. There were even some really nice space pictures, but nothing actually happens in space and nothing meaningful develops between the main characters. Eventually i was just mashing space, reading every fifth section to get a general point of the plot. I can't really complain because it's free, but I wish the devs knew what they wanted out of the story. Near the end there is a Lesbian scene (which I didn't know about until after i started playing), and i can't see a reason for it storywise other than the devs wanted to have some lesbian art.
TLDR: Use less words, and cut out the unimportant sci-fi bits you don't build on.

I want to recommend this game but I also have quite a lot of gripes. I just recently beat it, and want to write down my thoughts on it. That said, if you're into cyberpunk themes, visual novels, anime, cute girls or 4chinz, this is probably worth your money. The basic premise of this game is that you serve people drinks and talk to them, though you never actually make the dialogue choices yourself, only advance it like you would in a visual novel. From a gameplay perspective you mix drinks using a recipe book and do some other things along the way. This review will contain spoilers.
I started the game and was quickly sucked into the world and the laid back feel of the game. The game is set in Glitch City, a neo-tokyo esque city based in the USA, controlled by a mega corporation called Zaibatsu corp, the city is home to new experimental AIs called Lilim that function just about as well as humans do, as well as other oddities like talking dogs and brains in jars.  Everything is dark and dingy and the music is pretty great, a lot of "neo 80s" synth is used which really fits the game. The soundtrack has a good range of ambient, dark and upbeat songs, but none of the tracks have vocals. The game actually lets you choose up to 12 songs for each shift you take when bartending, which is a nice touch. I felt the ambient music complemented the conversations nicely, with "Everything Will Be Okay" being my favourite track in the game.
The gameplay is shallow at best, you are given a recipe book with all the drinks you can create, each with their own set amounts of ingredients that you have to follow to serve the drink. It was a fun gimmick at first but it never got much deeper throughout the entire game. The difficulty comes in clients ordering things using cryptic codes, and these were fun and rewarding parts of the game, but they only showed up 4  times in the game, specifically being with Stella and Virgilio (probably didn't get his name right) At other times you are supposed to remember a client's favoured drink which was also rewarding. But these moments are rather sparse in the entire game, and I found late game that clients would just ask for whatever drink they wanted by name. No puzzles, no thinking required, just bartending. I feel like this game could have doubled down on the gameplay if they wanted to, and made it the "cyberpunk bartending action" it's advertised as, emphasis on "action". I suppose they didn't want to upset the chillout mood to the game with puzzles. I like puzzle games, by the way.
The story itself is also pretty shallow, but fun nonetheless. The writing isn't going to impress a literature enthusiast but it's enough the average joe. Where do I start? Jill is a bartender stressed out about having to pay for bills and the occasional shoulder massager for times when she is super stressed. There are happenings in Glitch City that clients (who are often involved in said happenings) discuss with Jill, with large scale events  like terrorist attacks and superstar concerts. This leads to a varied cast of characters which I can honestly say is one the best parts about the game. Donovan is a man's man, Dorothy has the best jokes and Virgilio is an eccentric fedora tipper who I'm pretty sure is a homage to the Phoenix Wright games, but maybe only in appearance.
There is an air of mystery placed on characters like JIll, Gillian, Boss, Jamie and Art. Only one of these mysteries  gets cleared up, and that is the one concerning Jill and becomes a central part of the game from midway all the way until the end of the game. The breakup between Lenore and Jill and Lenore's untimely death is introduced quite suddenly, and the player is expected to feel bad for Lenore's death when we only have Jill's stories and an old photograph shown offhandedly as information of what she was like. I really didn't feel invested in this at all, other than how Jill's mood goes rock bottom but gradually improves. I feel like it would have been better if it was introduced from the first day.
Finally the story doesn't go anywhere in regards to the bar's closure. The player is told that Vallhalla, the bar, is scheduled to close in a few months, but that doesn't really go anywhere, even at the end of the game. No breakup of the three people staffing the bar, only for Jill to open her own bar in the future with white hair and a mechanical arm and a cyborg eye (what?). I'm just saying that there was a lot of wasted potential on the story in regards to the the ending and the mystery behind some of the characters.
Double finally this game has no romance options. Why? WHY?! Sukeban games, you made Jill a lesbian, added potential romance options like Alma, Dorothy, Betty and Boss but you didn't actually make it a part of the game?! Goddammit guys, I wanted to like this game and I did for the most part, but I can't let these gripes past. I just wanted to romance Boss. ;_;
EDIT: Oh yeah, the ending, can we talk about how untimely that was? You don't even get to do anything in the new year's party, which would have had new interactions with Gaby, Sei, Stella, Betty, Deal, etc.
EDIT 2: Re-reading this I feel like I focused quite a lot on the negatives. I will say I enjoyed the game as a whole, but had some issues on untapped potential in the gameplay and story. I didn't touch on drinking with Boss or the truth or dare sections which were fun, as well as the phone article/blog posts which added a bit of depth to the story.

I had played a demo for it at E3 and I loved what I played there but this was not the same experience. I was drawn to this game by its comedy factor and how you have to craft drinks to meet client needs but those moments are seperated by long boring dialogue.
The dialogue is just there to tell you about the characters and the world so if you don't care about those then there isn't much to really gain from reading it. The humor was not that good and rarely made me smile. At this point you are probably saying "Well then you are just not easily impressed" or "well then this is the wrong game for you" or "well maybe it gets better" but really I find it hard to call this a game when there is so little game play besides the ocasional part where you have to make a drink for the client which is not very challenging since you have the recipes and the client tells you if they want you to make any changes to the original drink.
The main character was a hard one to resonate with and was kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥ at times.
I will give the game another try some time. As I said this was just my first impression so my views mght change later on but as things are currently going I doubt they will. I would reccomend this game to more casual people who prefer story over gameplay.

游戏总体很不错，让玩家们体验到了在战争中生存的不易。
游戏中你需要收集材料，做家具来满足一些生活需求。比如床，如果没有就只能睡地板了，第二天角色就会出现睡眠不佳状态。以及录音机和炉灶做饭之类。细节方面挺到位的
如果要说游戏的缺点，我列举几个。
第一个，就是感觉心情系统有待完善，有些举动会影响角色心情，即使你觉得没什么。比如我操作角色去别的难民家偷东西，或者杀了人，都会影响全部角色的心情。按实际来说的话，你既然都干出这种行为了，有什么要后悔或者悲伤的？而且你不告诉同伴谁知道你干了这种事？
第二个就是有些难民见人就开枪，都是同胞好不好？至于见人就打吗？
第三个就是游戏存档功能很操蛋，只能保存你当天晚上回来的时候。有时候白天辛苦忙活了半天，出现什么问题关游戏了，那就都白费了。
还有就是游戏后期比较无聊，设施齐全后基本不愁吃穿，天天吃喝睡就到了战争结束。
我个人比较喜欢里边罗曼这个角色，战斗力很高，不仅适合守家，也适合去坏人家替天行道，而且即使杀了人，心情也不会有影响。
总之游戏值得一试。

Gameplay wise, it's a 2D crafting/survival game, but can be very punishing if you miss something or make a mistake. Pretty much anything an kill you, from the cold, to lack of food, being attacked by a normal civilian, lack of base defence, or lack of medicine. I also found that each campaign added a lot of replay value, for me, and have played this through a number of times now. Your morality and the decisions you make during the campaign also influence the ending, and your survivors can emotionally suffer, based on what's happened in-game.

Yes, it can get bland at moments, but for those going into a space combat sort of game, that is kind of expected. Many games in this genre are very boring and dull, but this has the graphics to make it that more exciting.

My first in the Far Cry series being Far Cry 2, I came to this game with some negative thoughts.
First of all, the stealth gameplay is very rewarding.(In fact, most of the time it's the recommended path to take.)
Being able to mark your targets feels a bit cheap, and I'd like for it to be more temporary.(Similar to the Hunters.)
The visibility marker is very well balanced, not too fast, but not at all too slow. If you're being detected, you can easily run to cover, but you can't just charge into view from a distance.
Enemy FOV seems a bit lacking, they can't see anything past 50 feet, so apparently Kyrat has very poor ophtalmology.
(Side note, the heck is with calling them Rupees? An omage to Zelda? But I digress.)
A few of the side missions feel a bit broken. For my first Armed Escort, I destroyed one of the enemy cars, but the truck refused to move past it. And then the driver died, dispite taking no damage. Probably a failsafe for the game, but it was very irritating.
Combat is very unique to the Far Cry series, very... Soft, is how I would describe it. You don't feel involved at all, recoil is non-existant, also damage is very strange.. Some weapons deal a huge amount of damage, while other weapons are almost laughably under-powered. How is a pistol less powerful than a bow and arrow? Accuracy is also an issue, you can shoot something in the middle of the Dot, but you'll miss? Enemy AI accuracy is stupidly good. These are apparently footsoldiers, almost untrained, but they can accurately hit a flying, moving target with every other shot.
These are very small issues, in my eyes. The game isn't as unplayable as FC2 with the stupid Malaria mechanic.
The skills are very interesting, and very well done. You can play the game without them and be fine(albeit it would be more difficult), or you can use them for a bit of an easier time.
The story isn't very gripping. Who's Pagan Min? Why should I care? I'm only here to kill people and climb towers.
The charactors are also pretty shallow, I don't feel a lot of connection to any of them, they're just shoved into your face in a slideshow.
Overall, the gameplay is very rewarding, all the issues I've noted feel minor compared to how fun it is to play the game
The weapons choices are limited, but unique. The crafting system is simple but elegant(Being able to see the general location of animals is also very handy.) The side missions are a bit grating, but quite rewarding, with the new weapons, money, replaced ammo...
It also rewards exploration, without making it a necessity.
Overall, I'd give it a 7/10. (Or maybe a 5/7, best game ever.. Kudos if you get the reference.)

*Review contains spoilers*
Overall I liked this game
It has a nice art style, good backing soundtrack with some good dialogue from a nice cast of characters
But I do have some criticisms of the game
One minor one is that in the english translation there are multiple misspelt words and some grammatical errors.
But my major gripe are the leopard cat endings (I may just be salty that he ran me over with a car)
The specific ending I am referring to is the 2nd leopard cat bad end: Loving gaze (I think that's what it's called)
Having gone through the true leopard cat ending I feel as though Leopard cat would have ended up developing feelings for the protaganist which would make him question the whole consuming his soul thing (if you go pure senpai affection)
I think a neat, alternate bad end would be he takes you to his house but instead of killing you tells you about what he was planning and about Senpai being dead, that he had planned to kill you and eat your soul but refrained due to developing affection for you, then he decides to leave for real, maybe because he feels bad for misleading you or something. I think this ending would impact the player just as much as the other 2 bad ends, if it's their first run and they trust leopard cat (like I did) it still comes as a big shock to the player.
Overall I feel like Leopard Cat as a character has potential but could've been written better, with more hints at what he wants and maybe more thoroughly (in the scenes where it comes up) display his internal conflict because it seems somewhere deep down he doesn't want to eat souls for a living, saying that he would rather have been born human or as another kind of spirit and seeming genuinely sad about it.
I know my review probably won't change anything in the game, but I'm just putting my views out there.
The game is still very good and worth playing, just don't get run over by soul-eating trickster cats.

Poi is very barebones, it's pure 3D platforming, levels are thrown on our faces with not that much cohesion, there's a lot of teleportation from one area to the other, lots of hidden useless collectibles, our abilities are straight off stolen from Super Mario 64 and that's it.
There are lots of filler missions and excuses to hold a Medal (the game's "Stars") behind some grinding. The worst offenders I can remember is this one mission I simply had to rotate 4 levers and this one character that gives you a Medal once you've "Jumped 500 times, Rolled 250 times".
All boss battles sucked and were there just to mark the checklist.
Although sometimes too easy, there are some quality platforming to be done and the collectibles can be really fun to hunt if you're into this sort of stuff.
Overall Poi really did scratch that unstoppable itch I've had ever since finishing Banjo-Tooie and was a great surprise to start the hopeful "Comeback of 3D Platformers" we're about to have!

It has the abstract environments of mario64 with the production value and level size of mario sunshine with a musical style and flair of mario galaxy so in a sense POI celebrates all 3 current types of 3D mario games.
More than merely a tribute, the game is fun.  Fun to play and fun to find the last few items to complete the game. This is one of those games where I wish there was a "Maybe" button, because the game itself isn't bad, but it isn't good either. Yes I'm judging this game with minimal time invested in it, but that should be more a red flag against the game, rather than in its defense.
I do like that this game is a call back to the era of 90s platformers, which still holds a dear place in my heart and several places on my top 10 favorite games of all time.
However
This game does nothing to improve upon those old school games. The story is bland, with the entire premise being that you need to collect medals from different worlds to become a better explorer, or something. There really isn't any driving force behind the plot; and if there was one, it clearly wasn't memorable enough.
It has some interesting mechanics, so I'll give it that; for example, rather than an overworld, you help pilot a small airship to different worlds, and at times other airships will appear in the hub world that you can glide to with your parachute thingy. Other than that though, the mechanics are basically Super Mario Sunshine, minus the FLUDD capabilities.
The soundtrack is pleasant, but again with limited playtime, I haven't heard all of the tracks, or at least I hope I haven't. The sound effects are on par.
When it comes to level design and challenge, this is where I feel there is a HUGE disconnect. From what I have played so far, this game is not challenging at all. Not even in the slightest. And the worlds are not very interesting. They all feel like a mishmash of objects rather than a carefully designed world. One of the biggest things that 90s platformers like Super Mario 64 or Banjo Kazooie had going for them was that they were designed for all ages.
Let me explain: Take SM64 for example. To get to the Bowser fights (which weren't hard), you needed 8, 30, and 70 stars, respectively. Before going to any of those fights, you have a ton of options for which stars to go for. Before the first fight, you can get around 40 stars; the second, around 65, and the third, 119. You didn't need to get everything, so there were stars that were really easy to get (get to the top of the tower, for example), and then stars that were much more difficult to get (get 100 coins in each level, for example), which made the game winnable for kids, but provided enough challenge for adults to stay interested.
And that's my main problem with this game. It feels like it caters far too much to children. There is not enough challenge to keep my interest.
The game is not memorable. It has good core concepts, but fails in execution. It feels far more like a clone of old school platformers than a new idea, and has absolutely no degree of difficulty. What it lacks in story and plot development it does not make up for in gameplay and level design.
I'd give it a solid 6/10, so again a maybe.

The levels are surprisingly varied, some featuring unique architectural puzzels, one has a really good horror vibe. There are almost always a bunch of different ways to get from A to B and there's a good deal of verticality in most areas. There are some steampunk and magical elements to the world as well.
There are a lot of gadgets and mechanics to allow for a variety of stealthy play-styles.
I also switched off most of the UI which made the game even more immersive than it already is.
The story is good and did interest me throughout - it's easy to follow.
Running around on the city's rooftops at night, looting gold from a big mansion, breaking into a prison or sneaking past a sleeping guard - everything feels great.
On the technical side, the game ran fine for me.
