Poi is a great return to 3D platformering collectathons.
I was incredibly curious going into this game; hoping that it really would allow me to return to the enjoyment I got out of game like Banjo-Kazooie, DK64, and Ty the Tasmanian Tiger. So far, it's delivered fully in that aspect.
The gameplay is incredibly solid, with relatively tight controls. There are some minor quirks, like the roll jump having relatively precise timing to pull off, and enemies sometimes being a little annoying to jump on; but overall the controls are solid and you won't find yourself fighting to keep a handle on your character. The movement of your character is incredibly similar to the Super Mario games, with the ability to Triple Jump from a continous set of jumps, do sideflips, walljumping, and a dive jump that allows you to slide.The game also includes movement familiar to other games, like having a double jump in the air, and a jump that you can execute out of a roll for extra momentum. Chaining the roll jump into a dive jump can create some incredible speed if you like moving fast. The game also takes further inspiration from Mario by having you jump on enemies to kill them; you can also kick stunned enemies/items by walking into them.
Like collectathons before it, this game has several forms of ways to collect items, all with the ultimate goal of collecting the explorer medals. These include but are not limited to: The Explorer Medals themselves, Golden Cogs, and a Picture Book. As you progress, new types of collections appear, and new things to explore and discover are revealed. This game doesn't appear to have a lack of things to collect and in turn feels like you'll have plenty to do besides just beating the game.
The music in this game exceeds my expectations. They suit the levels and the environments, and they're incredibly pleasant to listen to. They're pretty whimiscal. I would heavily suggest in buying the soundtrack if you're into that.
This will mostly fit the rest of the stuff, like Graphics and Story. As far as the graphics are concerned, they're pretty good. The 3D graphics look a little more out of the PS2/GameCube era of gaming, but a bit more polished. However, I don't see that as something that detracts from the experience. Instead, it brings a level of charm that really hearkens back to an era of gaming now long lost. The only downside is that the environments feel a little... empty. Maybe a bit more on the basic side.
The Story is pretty basic, you're asked to go out and collect some Explorer Medals from an old adventurer so he can vicariously live one more adventure out through you. I haven't seen a hint of an ulterior story boss or anything. The story might be a bit on the lackluster side, but seeing as how this game is far more colorful and lighthearted, and likely built to help revive a genre slowly coming back; a deeper story really doesn't feel needed.
The game does have a few extra things, such as hidden hats to collect and a new game+ mode for you to play through after you've completed the game. These help establish replayability along with the collectathon aspects of the game.
I feel I should at least point out a few things that might detract from the experience for some.
-Environments feel a bit bare. Thematic in nature, but they feel a little empty towards that theme for me in some way that I just can't explain.
-Level Design is average. It's not incredibly good, but it's nowhere near bad. Nothing stands out as silly with placement, and nothing seems terribly pointless. The flow of the levels just feel a bit off to me; it might go hand in hand with the previous point of the environment feeling a tad bare for me.
-Story is fairly simplistic. This isn't really a con for me considering the colorful, lighthearted nature of the game, it doesn't feel like it needs to go all out with a story. So far, I haven't yet had an inkling of a deeper story. This might detract from your experience a bit depending on how much you care.
-Barely any invincibilty frames. The first time I got knocked by an enemy, it proceeded to ram me twice more before I could get a proper jump on it since I was a little stunned that it was hitting me so quickly.
Overall, this is an incredibly solid 3D platformer, and perfectly fits in with the collectathon genre. There's plenty to do and plenty of time to be spent in this game. It does have a few flaws, but none of them are glaring, and you likely won't notice or care about most of them while you're enjoying your time playing. I would heavily suggest buying the game and it's soundtrack.

I've owned since very early access and it's probably the best early access game I've purchased. There were constant updates, each update improving on the last and adding features, but the release is just fantastic. I love the new location, the new art, the costumes are a nice touch. The worlds might seem small at first, but there are a lot of hidden objects.
If you rush the game, you can finish it in about 2-3 hours, although this was pretty standard for most platform games in the 90's. However, you won't want to rush this. You'll want to revisit each location to get all the explorer medallions, you'll want to do the challenges (I think I'm still top of leaderboard for a few of them).
The controls are very smooth and responsive. The only issue is the camera in some areas. There are some areas where the camera locks and I'd really like to be able to rotate it around. Other than that, the camera is pretty good.
You can also choose to be one of two characters, covering both genders (boy/girl), so it's pretty biologically accurate.
Lastly, this is great for kids. My daughter calls this the "game with the whale boat" and she loves to watch it played. Older kids (6-12) will really enjoy this one, although some of the challenges and a few bosses might be tricky.

-feels and plays like an old-school choose-your-own-adventure book
-interesting story - you are a Craft-wielding (magic) law student working to make partner at your law firm
-diverse persona creation - can decide name, gender, goals, sex orientation

-handy stats menu that records your current standing with each main character, as well as abilities and characteristics (ex: whether you are more of a socialite or ambitious individual)
-fair requirements for achievement hunters
-costs about the same (if not cheaper) as a choose-your-own-adventure book
-definitely not for everyone, this is strictly a digital choose-your-own-adventure book; if you do not enjoy reading, you will probably not like this
-no visuals (besides the stats bars), no music or sound - everything relies on your imagination
-no extra save slots, so you will have to do multiple playthroughs to explore the different story paths
Choice of Games consistently releases high-quality choose-your-own-adventure games, and I have thoroughly enjoyed many of their products. Very good if you like this genre and enjoy reading.
Recommend!

First of all I have to say that I don't need the fanciest graphics but I'm used to 120 fps and my eyes hurt when I have to play a game on 60fps. When you're fine with playing on 60FPS or have a NVIDIA Graphics Card then this review probably won't be very helpful to you since I can't tell you anything about gameplay. I started the game with the graphics settings on high
I recently got Farcry 3 and I had a lot of fun with it so I figured why not buy Farcry 4 during the Summer Sale. Huge mistake.
It started off great, the Cutscene in the beginning ran smoothly on 250+ fps. Once the cutscene ends a scripted scene inside a house starts where you just sit there and can't move for about two minutes. The highest I got on the lowest settings was around 75.
I tried out some fixes for fps drops I found on the internet but none helped me.
I'm very disappointed, was really looking forward to playing this game. Maybe I'll pick it up again If I were to buy a NVIDIA Graphics card in the future.

A small, but great game about surviving in a town plagued by a war. In This War Of Mine, you play as a group of people (or just one guy, your choice) to survive in the fictional town of Pogoren during a conflict between some rebels and the army. Each character has his/her own story. It's best to find out the game's mechanics first, then restart your story and play through it again. You'll search for food, bandages, weapons and medicine to battle sickness, wounds and hunger. People will die, but if you help others they will help you. You can steal or barter, kill or get killed. Each action has consequences, some small, some gigantic. You need to battle winter, outbreaks of crime and the army storming the town. You can betray your friends for rewards and guilt, or keep them safe and suffer.
In the end, it is your choice, and the ending will be based around the choices you make.
A con would be that the game isn't too full of content, but in my opinion it doesn't need that. This game is great with the ammount of resources to play with it gives you, you make your own content.
By buying this game, a small percentage will go to charity, which I find great.
Anyways, buy the game!
EDIT: The soundtrack and style of the game is also pretty nice, and even a very basic PC can run it well (those Intel graphics ones, ♥♥♥♥ those)

Death Road to Canada
Game is fun, funny and technically endless as you and your team trek from the wastes of Florida to bristling perfection that is Canada in the zambi alpacalyspe.
Throughout your journey you must maintain proper fuel levels, car damage, food, and the health of your survivors by exploring randomly genereated towns full of the undead and rest stops that allow you to buy and loot supplies and weapons to use or trade. There are random events with skill checks and also little hidden events in towns to help boost ratings for your travelers. Combat is simple and addicting, however knowing when to run is often a critical choice. Side note: kiting skills are a plus.
You can also create your own team of survivors, equip them with certain professions and skill sets like Pistoleer- Good with pistols, or Car nut - Bonus mechanic stats. You can take up to 2 of them to start the game and hope to run into the other on your journey to Can-a-dia. Your teammates can leave you depending on their stats so be careful of who you choose, or they can bring your morale down if they are annoying or a whiner.
The games old 16bit feel is welcoming and is good for a quick periods of gaming. My only gripe is that the events arent as vaired as I'd like but that is very fixable with patches and more writing from the dev team. All in all good game to play in both long plays and short bursts

All right, let's start off with talking about what this game is not. This is not the origional "Thief". The origional Thief series where very open world, giving you up to fifteen paths to take to accomplish a level. This game gives you at most three, in a chapter. I loved the origional Thief, and Thief II. I played them when they first came out, and if you have not played them, I would suggest you go and give them a try as well (Thief: Gold Edition is highly reccomended as it streamlines the origional game). I even played Thief III on Xbox, and while it was not the same as the origional two, it had a few interesting mechanics, and some of the oddest glitches out there (I had my game lock all enemies into only using horizantal attacks once, so I could stay crouched and never get hit for almost an hour and a half of gameplay, with saving and loading, no idea how it happened)!
This Thief, while more linear in it's approach, is still a great game! I have looked through all the negative reviews, and it is usually, "This game is not as good as Dishonored." Here is the thing, they are two very different games! Is Dishonored great? Yes, it is. However, it plays completely differently. Don't judge a game for not being something completely different than what it is meant to be. I had a great time playing through the game. I personally wish there had been more puzzles to advance, because I felt the puzzles available where a little too simplistic. But I have not only played through it once, I am now playing through it for a second time.
This version of Thief reintroduces us to "The City", a setting I have seen through three previous iterations. Now I am seeing the City as it decays from the inside, dying from its own corruption. I am getting to see Garret, the main character, deal with the world he has known and saved many times, crumbling around him. We are shown how humanity will turn on itself, when some disease runs rampant through the populace. The game deals with having a mass of dead bodies, and what needs to be done to clear them from the domain of those still living to protect them from the horrors of the more filth and diseases caused by it. We are introduced Garret's rival, trainee, and love interest.
So, yes, I would reccomend getting this game. Especially if you can grab it during a sale event!

Star conflict is my go to game when I just want to blow things up for a little bit.  The game is more popular in Russia than in the US which means that if I'm up late at night there's plenty of people to shoot at!
There's a ton of different ship types and content to play, especially for a free to play shooter.  There are three factions, each with its own preffered mix of shield, armor and speed and it's own preferred weapon type (EM, thermal, or kinetic).  There are three sizes of ships and each size has three possible roles for a total of 9 distinct ship types.  Plus, each ship can be fit with custom modules to fit your play style and tweak your ship's manueverability, weapon strength, tankiness or repair abilities.  As you progress up in tiers, you find about a dozen different distinct weapon types as well.
There are several pvp combat styles which will be recognizable to veterens of shooters including capture the flag, king of the hill and protect the leader style modes.  There are also pve missions where you and 3 squad mates team up to accomplish a specific strategic goal like sabotaging the construction of a dreadnaught, ambushing a supply convoy or protecting your own shipyard from attack.
Progression tends to be fairly slow.  This means there are more people playing the early-mid game than the (more complex) late game.  There are 5 tiers of ships in the game, and the first two tiers come pretty quickly, but in the third, progression in terms of synergy (xp) and equipment comes markedly slower.  Since your reward after a battle is weighted heavily by how well you did in that battle and ships that get blown up need to be repaired, it's entirely possible to *lose* money on tier 3 pvp and higher.  I don't view this as a negative.  Lower tier pvp is practically consequence free pew pew where one skilled pilot can turn the course of a battle.  Higher tier pvp with high tier ships requires you to think through your ship set up and work with your team mates -- solo wolves die fast.  In tier 3 and up, I rarely see the one stupid team mate ruin the game for everyone -- those sorts tend not to progress that far.
The cash shop for this game is a bit baffling.  There are premium ships you can buy that have significant perks.  These aren't in battle perks, but things like gets more loot, xp and money perks.  However, they are wildly expensive -- $30-50 US -- and so they aren't seen very often.  Small microtransactions are more common, so that you can put custom stickers on your favorite ship, buy a day of double xp or transfer xp from a maxed out ship to some other ship.
All in all, highly recommended!

Since Poi is one of the only real 3D Platformers on Steam i want to give my opinion about it.
First off im glad that theres people trying to create 3D platformers again (and on PC aswell) i really appreciate it!
But to the point how good is Poi actually well here is a list about things  i liked and disliked about the game :)
Pros:
+ Great controls (the way how the character moves and everything else feels great which is a very important point since there are a lot of games i just couldnt play because of boring or bad controls)
+ Big amount of playtime (i completed this game to a 100% and it took me a total of 10 hours which is a lot considering that i mostly play platformers and am a completionist)
+ A variety of minigames and certain tasks in the game
+ Progression feels rewarding
+Creative use of the hubworld
+Some missions had cool ideas ive rarely seen before
+Online leaderboards for all challenges
+ Good price
Cons:
- Bosses felt kinda boring: (with the expection of the final boss being OK) my reasoning for this is because almost all of the bosses only had 3 hitpoints and their patterns get repetitive fast and are rather easy in fact i beated the second boss in 12 seconds.
- Only jumping as an attack: This one really kind of annoyed me over the long run to be honest, theres no kind of punch move or something similar its always jumping, not that big of a deal since platforming is more important but id still like that to be improved.
- It tries way too much to be Super mario 64 instead of making its own thing: Ok this opinion is probably a thing which lots of people agree and disagree but the game really tried too much of the same (basically the Explorers Badges are the same as Stars in mario theres even the 100 coin challenge in each level) a great example which is inspired by other games but still mostly does its own thing would be a Hat in Time.
- Once completed theres not much reason to come back: This is probably my biggest problem with the game, theres just a really small replayability factor the reason for this is probably because the levels themselves are not worth playing without getting the badges/stars since they have not too much to offer themselves.
- Both playable characters feel the same: I kind of hoped they would make more out of it instead of just (wanna play a boy or girl ?)
- Completing some tasks completely, feels unrewarding: For example getting 50/50 golden gear parts you expect something special happens but instead you just get your last explorers badge :/
- Costumes/Skins: Those were a great idea but are sadly just recolours
- Soundtrack gets kind of repetitive fast: (either its used in too many levels or loops to quickly)
- Too easy for my taste
- Story was really boring sadly
Final words:
Despite some of the negative points ive mentioned for this price the game is absolutely fantastic and a step in the right direction for 3D platformers to be relevant again.
I can recommend you buying this game and trying it out yourself.
A worthy contender to the recent revival of the 3D collect-a-thon genre. Polished with a great level of care and packed with content, check it out.

It's a pvp third person hero shooter, like Team Fortress 2, Paladins and Overwatch; with more in common with the last two. The main mode of the game consists of nothing more than facing the oponent in the map trying to gather energy for your deity to attack the other. You gather energy by killing the enemy heroes or killing the monster they can summon to protect the spawn points of energy. After you gather 100 points of said energy, the enemy deity or "base", is open for attack and to receive damage.
Do that over and over until you get bored of it.
Because the game is so offensive focus, there's no place for support characters, because if you aren't killing the enemy, you aren't winning and since both teams receive spawns of energy at the same time, the opening for attacking the enemy base goes to the team that has the best offensive. Playing deffensively is not an option.
It's a game that only rewards one type of gameplay.
Add to the mix a bunch of visual effects covering your screen on team fights and the difference of angle from your camera's aim reticle and the actual angle from which the attacks are sent out from your character, and you have a gigantic mess that in most cases is won by the team with most AoE attacks.
Also because this game was made as a windowns 10 exclusive first, you don't have fullscreen mode, only borderless window AND you need to use a second launcher to even play the game, just like Ubisoft's UPlay. If you have your own launcher, why your game is on steam?
The only unique aspect of this game is its art style, which is nice, but the art of the game will only make it better if the mechanics are already good.

Okay, so having played through the first world of the game and a few of the optional side levels, I think this may be a good time to write my first ever review! I will be brief, this game is very fun. If you enjoy Super Mario Sunshine, or even 3D platformers in general, you will feel right at home in this game. The controls are great, and the flow of movement in the game is even better. Back to my reference of Sunshine, I can see a lot of inspirations from SMS in this game. The movement is very similar to SMS, which is great because it was pretty good. Excellent game
It reminds me of Dysfunctional Systems by succeeding in a big way where that game failed.  In Dysfunctional Systems, we were deluged with information which was ultimately worthless, and learning that information in no way paid off.   The character knew everything she needed to know whether we read logs or not, and it left me feeling cheated.  This game, on the other hand, uses the bartending game to get you to engage with its characters and remember the little things about them, and it rewards you for it.  This turns what would otherwise be another boring kinetic novel into a very engaging experience.  It really shows just how much you can do with even a little gameplay.
Music and art are excellent.  The aesthetic vision is very nicely realised in character designs and backgrounds, and it's all wonderfully complemented by the soundtrack.  I'd like to applaud the artists for their efforts.
Continuing a bit about the writing; the setting opens up in a very gradual sort of way that's really nice to see, and consistently leaves me wanting to see what will come next.  Lots of mysterious details keep me interested in seeing how it unfolds.  The same goes for the characters themselves.  It's a level of world-building that I haven't seen in awhile, and it's nice.  My one complaint is that more should have been done with Anna.
Anyway, great game.  In some ways, it reminds me of Papers Please, largely on the play side.  Highly recommended.

I've been waiting to play the full version of this for quite some time now, ever since the very early demo enraptured me with its snappy writing, strong characterisation and wonderfully distinctive take on the dystopian future setting. And I'm delighted that the full version has, so far, surpassed all my expectations and hopes.
VA-11 Hall-A is kind of hard to pin down. At heart, it's basically a visual novel, but rather than making binary choices that filter you off down one of several discrete routes, the choices you make as protagonist Jill when going about her daily life at home and at work affect what happens next in the story, including the characters you encounter, how Jill gets along with her clients and co-workers and how everyone reacts to the events unfolding in the backdrop.
Interestingly, VA-11 Hall-A presents its overarching narrative almost entirely from the perspective of Jill behind the bar and in her apartment. Significant things happen in the world, but you don't see them directly; instead, you tend to see the people involved immediately before and/or after the events, or read about them on the news web pages and forums the morning after. Sometimes whether or not you dosed them up with alcohol before the event in which they were involved has an effect, too; prepare to feel guilty if that happens!
To give too many examples would be to spoil the experience, so I'll leave it at this: VA-11 Hall-A does a much better job of almost any visual novel I can name at making its world feel "alive" and like the actions you take actually matter, rather than simply picking a route through the story. There's nothing wrong with the latter approach, of course, but this way of doing things helps keep the people who expect a bit more in the way of traditional "gameplay" happy as well as those of us who are along for the ride primarily from a narrative perspective.
To sum up: great writing, wonderful characterisation, superb music and a glorious, beautiful PC-88 style aesthetic (with perfect pixel aspect ratio even scaled up to 1920x1080) makes for an absolutely lovely, unconventional and entirely memorable game.
I adore VA-11 Hall-A and pray with all my heart that it sees the success it deserves, both here on Steam and elsewhere on the Internet.

There's something quite to be said about a game which takes itself so simply. Rather than be wrapped up in pointless mini-games or timesinks, VA-11 Hall-A has opted instead to deliver the core experience of what it is without the need for too much bells and whistles, and in this case, it works in its favour.
VA-11 Hall-A is less a game per se, and more of a story. It's more of an experience, something completely wrapped up in strong characters and woven threads. Everything that makes the game is given to you straight, and because of that, there's nothing that distracts you from the core experience.
But what IS this game? Some have compared it to a visual novel, and some have compared it to a simulation. The truth is, it lies somewhere uniquely between the two. There is the lightest of puzzle-solving elements that require you to make drinks for the trickle of customers that visit the bar, and that is done by leafing through an in-game book and creating very simple concoctions.
However, it's not really a time-management game, it's more like a game of understanding, a game which asks you to be invested in the story to be able to cater to your client's needs. The game challenges you to think laterally, encouraging you to do your job -- in essence, the game-play of figuring out and mixing drinks feels very organic and does not distract from the main purpose of the game, which is to deliver stories to you.
Ah! The stories. The stories are what makes the experience real, and what makes the game fantastic. The game takes place in a dystopian future where you have to find out more about the world through a shared experience of a day in the life of the main character. The whole game is about you learning and reading a story, much like how a visual novel would pan out, minus more dire choices. However, the game doesn't presume to hold your hand nor withhold things entirely due to its format. Although the game thrusts you into the head of the protagonist, you still get to more than adequately learn about the world through interaction with the characters and by reading articles on your mobile device.
And it is ultimately very rewarding due to the game's intensely dedicated world-building, both in world and in cast, and through the unique way the story is presented.
While there are the odd typos here and there, there's nothing that can be addressed as signs of incompetence (just getting straight, for the grammar nazis, this means that they DO know their 'its' from their 'it's'). And while the game has a large focus and takes inspiration from Japanese media, the problems of the world are weighty and the reality of the characters make us able to absorb the absurdity of it all and enjoy it as both social commentary on the human condition and also a fun character-sim based on a very colourful cast.
The soundtrack is between good and great. Certain songs popped out at me enough that I stopped reading to hit that 'jukebox' button in order to find out the name of the track that I was listening to so that I could find it a permanent slot on the edit-able BGM list.
The money that you earn from the bartending sequences allow you to 'help' your character in a variety of ways, and in fact, there is a replayability - although very slight - in purposely doing things wrong and disregarding your character's needs. The other elements of replayability come from the multiple endings that result from how well you cater to your clientele.
In essence, much like the drinks that you serve in the game, VA-11 Hall-A is a whole bunch of different elements and flavours given to you in the perfect amounts to create something rather delicious indeed.
And believe me, I'll be coming back to this bar for more if the tender mixes up new drinks.

At first, I didn't want to recommend this game. And then I did. And then I didn't. So on and so forth, until today, when you can see my final verdict.
Cibele is not a good game. I mean it in the most traditional sense: it is not "fun". It even has many flaws, which could be easily avoided without interfering with the author's apparent artistic intention. You will have to play to some fake MMO RPG. All you will do is some grinding, and of top of that, you only have one attack. If the game designer just added some spells, I'm sure the game, without being fantastic, would have been a lot less repetitive. On top of that, the game has a gigantic bug. Bosses appear and go into some zones that you can't reach. For some reason, your online friend has no problem following them and keeping fighting them. Either the bosses shouldn't go into those unreachable zones, or your character should be able to. The game may be intended to offer something different than the others, it should however not be a pain to play it (except maybe if there were a discourse along with it; for example, a game about suffering may make the player suffer in some way).
A good thing about Cibele is that it dared to explore some themes that are rarely tackled in video games. It could have use its medium better instead of alternating between live-action cutscenes and a tedious RPG, but I'm happy that it tried to.
I know it's a bit bad to recommend a game because of what it could have done instead of what it actually does, and I have to admit that I wouldn't recommend it to a real-life friend, but this is a path I want the video games industry to explore further, without of course letting aside the kind of games we're used to.
So yeah, this is all a very confusing review but in summary, I recommend more this game as a case study and as an example to developers of what I want to see in more (but not most) games than I recommend it as a product that will be appealing to gamers. So play it if you're involved in the game industry or if you're someone very curious who's not affraid of experimental games.

The facade of an MMORPG that most of it takes place in isn't really a "game" but it adds to the immersion - it makes you feel like yeah, I'm actually there, this is happening to me. I see a review calling it the equivalent of "embarrassing teen poetry" as a negative, but that's almost the point - it's about a particular teen experience. The game may not be as compelling if you didn't have those experiences, but I think it's really wonderful, perfectly written story. Ideally you'll admittedly want to get it in a sale but it's very emotional and made me cry.
Before starting the MMORPG sections, make sure you click through everything on the desktop, there's lots of stuff there. You can also reply to the ingame chats (the mailbox at the top) which gives some more writing/story.

Full review:
Tribloos 2 is one of those games that are just a pleasure to play. It’s really peaceful and provides quite the laid-back experience amidst all of today’s more violent games.
This is a time management game. You’re tasked with getting stuff done in a certain amount of time using the provided Tribloos. This usually entails building a certain amount of buildings or collecting a certain amount of items. For example, I may be tasked to build three homes, each of which adds five Tribloos to my workforce, or I could be tasked with making bread, which is a multi-step process for the Tribloos.
The game does have a story to it, although negligible. Trey’s village is in danger due to storms. Yes, rainstorms and such. Matilda the dragon, who usually blows the storms away, is too tired to blow away these new storms and the Tribloos are now tasked with protecting themselves from the dangers ahead. I don’t see how this story actually plays into what I do in the game, however. Does making bread help protect the village? Now that I think about it, this may be because they’re stockpiling food, although I’m unsure.
The game’s graphics are all hand-drawn and look fantastic. The Tribloos themselves look great, as do the game’s various buildings. Oh, might as well throw the backdrops in there as well, which are all very well done. The game also has its own original soundtrack, which was excellent. I wonder if the soundtrack is available for download separately?
The game has plenty of content to go around, for a game of this scale at least. There are 90 levels. Each takes a couple of minutes to beat on average. This is, however, if you just play through the game without the goal of getting all perfect scores, which I had difficulty with. A lot of times I would simply run the clock until I got a bronze rating, not on purpose though. I’m obviously doing something wrong with my time-management here, not that I have any in reality (okay, maybe I do).
Overall, this game is quite a treat. It may be lost in the flood of indie games coming out these days, but I can give this game my recommendation. It may not be for the more hardcore gamers, but I certainly enjoyed it, and I consider myself one.

TL;DR If you liked Morenatsu you will absolutely like this as well.
Nekojishi is an absolutely wonderfully crafted visual novel featuring same-sex male relationships between a man and beast-mean (better known as furry) characters. Each choice contains weight to it and watching the reactions to the other characters based on each choice makes you want to replay the scenario later to see what happens when you choose differently. Not to mention the endings are emotional roller coasters that really play with your emotions, especially if you get one of the bad endings and makes you want to try for a better ending. The characters are memorable and enjoyable, leaving you with a sense of guilt anytime you disappoint one of them. The music is very well done and heavy amplifies the feeling in major scenes. Despite having heavy moods sometimes, it still manages to find appropriate times for moments meant to give you a chuckle and doesn't lose sight of the spirit aspect to the beast-men. The only minor complaint I can think of is the translation errors, but after having done about half of the endings, I only had 1 time where I was unsure of what they meant to say. All in all, if you want a gay furry VN, Nekojishi will do more than satisfy you

The gameplay is horrible: most of the time you "play" a fictional MMOG Valtameri by running around a small 2D map and clicking on monsters. Yes, we already know that online games eat up our time and offer nothing in return,
However, this is just a background for the story, which is about a relationship that forms between a teenager girl and a teenager boy. I believe every adult already has an idea how that ends. And not to spoil anything, but yes, that's not worth suffering through the terrible gameplay for an hour - this is what it takes to finish the game.

First things first, this is definitely more an experience than a game. It follows Nina and her experience with user Ichi on an MMO-RPG type game. The experience is replicated extremely well. As someone who has had deep intimate connections with people over similar games, I can appreciate the level of realism put into this. The narrative unravels as you explore into Nina's computer, her images, her blog posts and messages etc. I didn't feel creepy doing this, however I could see why people would. If you've ever had an experience with somebody online, even just a long distance relationship I'd highly recommend this game. It sparked an immensely deep level of introspection in myself.
I would say as a girl you're more likely to get something out of this game. Nina is relatable, with her interests in anime, alternative fashion and poetry. Her character ( or herself, as the game is autobiographical) is deeply charismatic and compromising. You feel a connection with her and share her sensitivities.
As much as I personally drew out of this game, I would have to say I had some issues with poor frame rate. However it didn't bother me awfully. What did was the short length. Perhaps it went fast as I'm a fast reader but I found the three arcs of the game far too short, and I find myself searching for more.
Overall I'd say as an experience I don't regret it, but I would say a length increase would be nice. Buy on sale if you can.
Really beautiful realistic relatable story otherwise, and I'm glad I played it.

A very short and intimate take on MMO culture, specifically two socially awkward young people who start to fall in love without any idea of how love actually works. You "play" by going through Nina's desktop, her recent chat logs and photos, before logging into the MMO to co-op with the guy she's increasingly attached to. Its strengths all lie in showing how awkward yet interested people can get with each other over the barrier of the internet, both helping and hindering understanding. For that, Cibele's worth taking a look at, but it doesn't go nearly far enough - it ends abruptly, just when the characters most need to unpack why they're doing what they're doing. It feels like half of a story arc.

This War of Mine is a really well done gem of a game. There aren't any keboard controls, it's all mouse. You're stuck in a war torn city, trying to survive by gathering supplies and improving your base. There are many locations to visit on the map. During the day you will be upgrading your base, cooking, purifying water, distilling alcohol, crafting bullets, and things like that. During the evenings you will be scavenging the city while the rest of your part defends the base from looters. In the city there are many different groups and locations that you can trade with, sneak in and rob, or try to kill.
It's a short game. In its current state you must survive around 40 - 50 days in game. That's not a very long time as each day may take 'guestimation' 10 minutes? But there is a fairly high level of replayability as there are many unique characters to use with their own traits as well as many locations that were not in your game.
The animations are simply beautiful. I don't know what you call this style of graphics but it is 3D without being 3D. It's like many layers of 2D that sum to 3D. It's very pretty and immersive. I think that's the biggest takeaway from this title is that it is immersive. Choices matter. You grow attached to your friends. You don't want them to die, but sometimes they do.
It's a very good game. I purchased it very cheap on summer sale and for that price I feel like I got an incredible bargain. If I had paid full price for it then I would say it was a fair price. Still a great game and I hope the devs made enough money to do something like this on an even grander scale. I definitely recommend this game.

I haven't played much of this game, so take my review with a grain of salt. They Bleed Pixels is a 2D platformer/beat-em-up game. I haven't gone too far into the game, but feel I have played enough to give an opinion.
Story-8/10
I haven't really grasped the story in its entirety at this point but i'll try explaining it. The story is you are a girl going to a girl school. One day you are at the library and see a book bleeding. Curious, you grab the book and realize it's evil or something, so you bury it. The book wasn't happy about that, so in your dreams it turns you into a monster trying to escape other monsters that want you dead. You die in your dream, you die for real or something.
Gameplay-9/10
The gameplay is outstanding for me (although a bit repetitive). This game is very fast paced and is relatively difficult. Not only do you platform across stages, but you fight enemies along the way (I'll talk more about enemies later). The combat isn't limited to punches and kicks, however. The monster you become has claws and stuff that can stab enemies and perform several different moves. As well as your own weapons, the environment is a weapon as well! There are spikes and saw blades you can throw and kick enemies into (among other things), allowing for a wide range of ways to kill your enemies. The most unique part of this game to me is the Checkpoint system. In this game, you don't get a checkpoint halfway through the level. In this game, killing enemies and collecting certain objects in levels will allow you to CREATE the checkpoint (so long as there are no enemies or hazards nearby). There is a bar that, once filled, will allow you to create a checkpoint if you stand still and are not near anything hazardous to your health (a circle will grow and shrink around you to show the 'safe zone'). I feel this self checkpoint system is very unique and makes your deaths feel more like your fault rather than the games. This game also uses a 'heart' system for your health, allowing a few hits before death.
Enemies-9/10
The enemies are varied throughout the game. I'm only a couple levels in and I have seen many different enemies. You've got the generic enemies, you've got bomb enemies (that can blow up other enemies), you've got flying enemies and so on. As well as the enemies you have saw blades that hurt and spikes that can insta-kill should you miss a jump. Both saws and spikes are abundant, but they are placed in ways you can't really fault. The saws are placed in places where you should think before acting, while spikes are basically a replacement for the 'bottomless pit' insta-kill from other platformers. The enemies all have a certain amount of hits and repeating attacks can not only make killing an enemy difficult, but may also give you less Checkpoint progress.
Sense of Progression-7/10
Maybe I didn't play for long enough, but I had no real feeling of progression besides going to the next level. Cutscenes between levels were the same and I never really felt like I was going anywhere besides a new level.
Graphics-8/10
The name may have tipped you off, but this game is in pixels, although that's not a bad thing. Colors are abundant and animations are smooth, making this game a treat to look at compared to other pixel games. However, textures are repeated time and time again to the point that seeing that enemy get impaled on a spike for the 7th time loses its charm. I won't fault the game for having simple graphics, just for not changing the formula often enough to make them seem like they actually attempted to make a pixel game look gory.
Overall-8/10
Is it perfect? No. Amazing? Less no, but still no. Worth playing? Definitely. If you're a fan of 2D platformers but are tired of games like Mario where jumping on the enemy is enough, this game would be a good choice. Don't go spending $30 on it, but if you can get it for $10 or less, I would recommend getting this game. It's difficult and it quickly loses its "Wow!" after a few levels, but if you can enjoy the gameplay and not the graphics or story, this game will give you a good time.

I find most MOBAS too hard to play, due to their controls. Gigantic however, takes my one complaint with the gameplay of games like DOTA, or LoL, and fixes it. Rather than clicking your character into the right direction from a birds eye view, you control your character with the WSAD and space bar keys from a third person view. This comes with the ability, upgrading system, and strategic teamwork that make a MOBA, A MOBA. The objective is that the enemy team has a certain entity or object that you need to get to and destroy, which is a reoccurring theme in this genre. However, Gigantic twists it up a little. Either team works along side a giant guardian. When you collect enough energy (By killing enemies and their summonables, or harvesting it) Your guardian makes its way to pin the other guardian down. This is when you attack. The concept encourages regrouping to strike as one, and you really won't win without doing so. I haven't played enough MOBA's to know if Gigantic encourages teamwork more that others, but it certainly does a good job of it. I'd also like to state that there's a character for everyone (And that's not something you hear out of me very often. Or ever, really.) There are hard hitting tanks, fast slashing assassins and fighters, tactical shooters, healers with plenty of utilities under their belt, and much more. I ended up finding my favored characters much faster compared to other games.
Now of course, I'm still gonna have problems with a game. That's just how it is, the devs are only human beings. I only have two cons to talk about. One of them is even the dev's fault. Its how some teams are just not willing to use teamwork, and you can get several teams like this in a row, making it hard to claim a victory. My other problem (and the bigger one) is the match making system. While players can't leave the team for whatever reason after the match starts, they can still do so all the way up to the character selection. If this happens the other players on both teams have to find another match. This wouldn't be such a big problem if it didn't take so long to find a match. It takes 30 seconds to 3 or so minutes, depending on your connection and luck.
Anyways, that's my review for Gigantic. Sure, it has poor matchmaking, but the wait is worth it. Even if you lose, the match is always a fun one. And the game is free, so there's no reason to not give it a shot!

Frozen Free Fall: Snowball Fight is a military shooter in the same vein as the Battlefield or Medal of Honor franchises. The majority of the game takes place in war-stricken Afghanistan, a desolate and barren wasteland torn between military mercenaries and armed insurgents. You play as Captain Elsa McTavish, an American Forces Captain turned renegade after the loss of your dog 'Boner' in a midnight raid gone wrong.
The game claims to be open world but really this is a facade, in fact you spend all of your time in closed mission areas or a main base from which you can move out. The missions themselves usually consist of taking out military targets by force or by capture, and a few have driving sections at the beginning or end which can provide a frantic and thrilling chase. The vehicle mechanics are good but unfortunately the thing that lets this game down is the FPS element itself.
I have to say in my experience that combat just did not feel satisfying. There is a gratuitous amount of gore in this game which although realistic could be a bit over the top. The 18 rating is justified as often things come down to hand-to-hand combat, with Elsa using knives, hammers or even mislaid pens as deadly weapons.
Another important part of the game is the 'interrogation' mechanic. Sometimes to progress in a mission Elsa will take a hostage and question them for information, letting you use the environment as a weapon with which to torture your captive. The way the dialogue unwinds here is quite subtle and believable, the intense story being very well written, and smashing out somebody's teeth on a urinal to find out what they know somehow manages to retain the atmosphere of drama without seeming too funny or out of place.
Overall the game is a massive improvement on Frozen : Reckoning, but in the end it can never bring the series back to the glory of Frozen II. I'd recommend this if you want a game that's casual in terms of difficulty but still carries a heavy plot. Otherwise you'd be better sticking with the previous iterations.

Good things:
- The 3 main characters were all very well-developed. They grew on me gradually., and also develop relationships with each other. The contrasts between their characters were more complicated than the too-common manga "the crazy one, the smart one, the tomboy" etc. choice. Each of these charcters is both appealing and annoying, in different ways.
- The fast-forward (hit CTRL) is VERY useful!  Wish I'd noticed it earlier.
Bad things:
- The opening feels like a typical manga "loser guy suddenly has a harem of hot babes competing over him" scenario.  It gets better quickly, but it's bad to have the opening feel so generic.
- Characters never ask two crucial questions: why
.  Liao is trying to make his big decision without getting the information he needs to make it.
- There was no 'G|PG|R|X' rating anywhere--no way of knowing whether I was going to see pictures I didn't really want to see. It turns out there's a paid version that has such images, so you're safe if you don't pay. But nothing on the Steam store webpage or in the game said anything about it.
- The English translation had extremely bland, just-the-facts writing. The writer or translator needs a can of "Show, don't tell."
- The plot points, where you get to make a decision, were chosen for game mechanics reasons--as places to adjust the emotion scores for each cat--rather than for story reasons!  So you get to decide whether to go on a date with a cat or not, but get no say in some of the most-important decisions your character makes, like
.  The entire story is framed as you deciding between the 3 cats,
It's very weird that you have to figure out the game mechanics and beat them over weeks of story time just to accomplish something that your character could do with a few words.
- This is made worse by your narrator-character being a total wuss, so he sits back and watches things unfold a lot of the time.  Seriously, Liao is annoying.
- The plot points are VERY far apart. We're talking hitting the space bar over a thousand times between decision points sometimes.  Spend less time painting backgrounds and more time writing dialogue, guys.  Personally, I think this game would have benefitted if each separate location were an adventure-style world, so you could type commands like "TALK TO LEOPARD" or "DANCE", and feel like you had some control.
- I wish that the controls let you set the printing to be instantaneous.  Even the fastest speed is quite slow.

So Steam won't let me post this review without giving it a "Recommend" or "Do not Recommend". Since it's well made, and with love, I'm giving it a thumbs up. But don't let that override my original "review":
So... this game is... fine. Just fine. Let me explain:
It's in early access. When I got it, I wondered why; it seemed pretty damn near complete. It was a great "zen game", to just space out with, enjoying the instantly gratifying physics and mechanics of this Mario64-esque platformer. Some content was clearly missing, but it was obviously "complete" enough for the devs to be fine with selling, none too cheap. The platforming was just challenging enough to not be boring, while it was an overall carefree and stress-free easygoing gameplay experience, with a matching artistic aesthetic. Very kid-friendly.
Then I took a break from it for a few months. Updates were made.
When I came back to the game, it was changed. Not unrecognizably, but in the essence of what it was. I don't know if it was always the devs' plan (which is likely), or if it was in response to/anticipation of mainstream criticism, but they had added enemies.
This changed everything. At the point I was then playing it at, the mechanics had not changed, so there was no new attack function, save jumping on the enemies' heads, which it seems the game was not built for. There is a reason Mario64 added a "punch".
Moreover, the addition of enemies and timed challenges stripped this game of its originality and unique appeal. The 3D Mario games already exist, and if I wanted to play them, I would already do that. It has lost its "zen game" feel, and some of its accessibility to small children (which it clearly had prior to the new additions).
Which is not to say that these new additions ruin the game, or make it "bad". It's just sad that when I thought I had found something truly unique, original, and fun - a new itiration of an old formula -, it turns out this was considered "incomplete", and was changed to match consumer expectations of a 3D platformer, following a 20-year-old formula to a T.
If you like the 3D Marios, and want more of the same, the current game is great, and I recommend it. And I hope they can salvage some originality here, going forward. If it's innovation you're looking for though, the current iteration of this game is not the place to find it.

TL;DR at the end.
Okay, first things first. I started playing Thief games when Thief 4 (what became simply "Thief") was announced. Played all 3 of the previous games, and became a fan instantly. Stealth is just so well done in this games. I'm not sure if I've played such great games in this genre ever since. The story, the characters, the atmosphere.... Garrett is simply the best main character in video games' history with his "antihero" role. (for gamers who played the first title: "Could you possibly be any more helpful?" - it was just a sentence that made like Garrett instantly. He said it to a drunk guard. :D) But now I should start talking about this specific game.
Okay, so I hadn't bought the game on release nor did I preordered it (wish I had tho...), I started playing this relatively late. I hadn't watched any gameplays or walktroughs, so when I finally started playing it, it was still fresh and new for me.
And here comes the review:
The game is different from the ones from before. You no longer have the mechanical eye, you no longer have a dagger or a sword. Your only weapon is the Blackjack (which became cooler) and the bow with different types of arrows (blunt, rope, water...) Personally, I think it's an improvement. In Thief 1, I've died many times, because I wasn't used to stealth games, and the sword seemed to be much more security, then what it actually was. The atmosphere haven't changed a single bit. even if the city became more "modern". The game is pretty dark. And I don't mean only the story, but there is not a single place where it is sunny, and colorful, and bright (okay, there is a bright place in the game at some point, but it's not the kind of bright that brings happiness and joy). If I would have to use colors to typify the game, I would say dark-blue and gray. These colors are the most dominant (with some greenish, and dirty-white at some playces). Garrett hasn't changed a bit (even if it's not the original Garrett....), and his VA made a damn good job as well. The cinematics are  beautiful (if I can use this word to describe something that dark and (at some places) depressing.
Now about the gameplay:
Graphics: I was never the kind of person who would play a game for the graphics (my favourites are Thief, Legacy of Kain, Rayman.... they are all old games, with not super-ultra-lifelike graphics, and I still prefer them over titles which comes out these days). That said, I think the graphics are great for a 2014 game. The environment is well built, the characters are differrent from one-another (okay, there are guards who looks like twins, but I don't really care about that, playing at ultra stealth is not the mode where I can stare at guards' faces....). I think that's enough about graphics.
Story: Actually, I liked the story pretty much, even if it made the game a bit linear. I don't want to spoiler it for anyone, so I'll just going to say that, the ending was something unexpected. First I felt a bit betrayed by that. Playing such a cool game for an ending like that. But then I realised what a great ending it was actually. I couldn't forget it, so it done it's job very well. Even now, months after I finished the game, I still remember the whole ending scene. There can be (and I think there are) mixed reviews about this game because of the end, but if you ask me, I would say it's a masterpiece, that not too many games can have. It doesn't just not answer all of the questions. It actually doesn't answer any open questions. It just leaves everything as it was (with some exceptions), and I'm the type of guy who really appreciate it. So the story is one of the best parts of the game imo.
Gameplay: So, I think I'm not the only one, who hates when the character is invisible in first person (like in almost every FPS games for example: CS, overwatch, bioshock (still a masterpiece tho)...). Well, I have good news: not just Garrett's hands are on the screen the whole time (even if they are empty) but if you look down, you can see his legs as well. You might say, that's really unnecessary, but think about crawling on a narrow board. Now you can imagine how big of a help it is. There are idle animations for his hands as well. The "parkour" system is something I like as well. Don't expect something like in Assassin's Creed (however there are parts like that, and even the camera goest to a third person view at these parts), but the movement is just simply fluid. Something like in Mirror's Edge (another of my favourites). The rope-arrow is still badass (however you can't shoot them anywhere unlike in the old games). Combat is another strong thing in the game. You can't combat face-to-face. I mean, you can, but like in the old games, it's not supposed to happen. 1 on 1 is hard, but not impossible, however going against more than 1 opponent at the same time is kinda unwinnable (is this word exist at all?). However, since you are a thief, you should never kill, except if there is no other option. Well, at hard difficulty, it's kinda impossible to win a face-to-face combat, so you better prepare for that, if you want to do a predator playtrough. Well, that's for the gameplay I guess.
Soundtrack: I think it's the almost the last part of the review. You should know that, if I like a soundtrack, I will listen the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it (like with Final Fantasy XIII, Total War, Rayman: Revenge of the Dark...). Well, I think I've listened more than just the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game's OST. It's fantastic, how well it goes with the game, and how great it is even without the game at the same time. I really must congratulate to the ones, responsible for the music.
And now the so called cons, which made some players giving a negative review, or just simply made them to not like the game. As I told earlier, you can't shoot the rope-arrow anywhere, only to given spots. Well, this seems like a minor con, but actually, playing this after playing the previous games, it feels like, (I think I read it somewhere, and I think it's really well said, so I will write it here) it's not your playtrough when you play the game, but someone else's, who prepared everything for you, by marking the only places, you can attach ropes to. So the game is a bit linear in that aspect. Another con is the Bank Heist DLC, which feels like a level, that was just ripped from the game,  and sold separately. Well, I enjoyed it and all, but it definitely doesn't worth full price, unlike the game. Well, and last, the game felt a bit short, (20 hour for the main story, I'm kinda used to Final Fantasys, so it's actually decent length, but still...)
TL;DR and suggestions: Played it after the old games, still LOVED it. I don't know what others talk about, this being the worst of all Thiefs.... Graphics, Story, Gameplay and music are absolutely perfect (at worst they are still better then many games coming out nowadays). The game might be a bit linear at parts, but there are plenty of sidequests to do, and the game is  hardly repetitive. Buy the Bank Hesit DLC only, and at discount. The game worth full-price, but it's summer sale right now, so even the Master Thief edition is so cheap, that you really should buy it (and the old ones as well!).
My 20 hours is because I only played the main story, and none of the side-quest. As soon as I'll have more time, I guess this number will go up to a much bigger value. If you have any questions, or if you are not sure about buying it, just send a message to me with your questions, and I will answer them. Best whishes, and don't get caught!

Is it a reskinned Far Cry 3? Sort of. Is it repetitve? Certianly. All the Far Cry games contain the same basic principles, capture bases, kill bad guys, topple dictatorships, craft items, spend skill points, buy weapons. Any quad-core and a GTX 750 should be fine.
My only gripe I have is that the animals drive me crazy.  Seriously, It's even worse than FC3.  Eagles come out of knowhere and attack you from the sky... CONSTANTLY. Iv'e experienced a few minor glitches here and there, but overall it's a very well polished, good looking, good running game. I suppose it is basically more of the same, but I would still  highly recommend if you are a fan of FC2 and FC3.

it plays like a moba. except, instead of the isometric bird eye view camera, you play in 3rd person. So good aim is a requirement. If you try soloing everything, you're likely to die. Theres no farming of little lower enemies to level up. You upgrade your character as you gain points, or EXP. Theres different builds you can do.  Each character has a main attack, then 3 other abilities and an ultimate attack unlocked by gaining focus.
While the game is fun, I have 1 big problem with the game. You'll wait a minute or so for a game, then one person wont load in time, or just deny the match queue. So instead of just removing that person from the queue and filling it with someone else..it just removes you from the queue and you have to do it all over again. This happened to me three times in a row before I found a game. After the 7-10 minute match, I went to look for another game. 2 queues failed because ONE person denied or couldnt load in time. Then I found a match. After that match, 3 more failed queues because of people denying/not loading. This is a really bad system. Any other game would just replace that slot with someone else and startup.
Now, the next problem I have isnt really a major gripe I have. Because this IS a F2P game and the devs need to make money somehow. Its more of a warning, to people who dont really like grinding and grinding. Ive introduced some friends to some pretty great games before that used this sort of paywall/unlock system before, and they got pretty turned off. The unlock system gives you a set of free characters, that get rotated throughout the roster every few weeks. From what it looks like, they give you 5. To unlock characters, its about 10,000 ingame credits. After each match, you'll get about 70-100 coins. Although, maybe its based on how you perform. And I'll admit, Im not the best player there is.  You can of course buy the characters out. For about $5 each, or just buy the bundle for $30. And whats really annoying, is when you spend all that time to unlock a character you've been wanting..but people pick them. So you cant pick them.
-AGAIN, not a complaint, just a warning-

On the positive side, Cibile explores how the game medium can creatively be used for story telling purpose. I like it when someone attempts something new, and Cibile definitely falls into this category.
However it falls flat on the face concerning actually delivering something enjoyable.
The story is a probably realistic depiction of teenage first love from a pink haired girl's point of view. It's told by means of selfies, chatlogs, emails, high school poetry and online conversations during playing a mock MMORPG. But even the creative use of these artefacts can not overcome the fact that the whole thing is just boring.
Apart from the lackluster story it's a technical disaster. There's a desktop simulator where you can't move windows or click them in the back- or foreground. There's a MMORPG simulator with history's worst pathfinding algorithm.
If you're a fan of Gone Home or Firewatch you might still like this. For everyone else I recommend to watch a playthrough on Youtube in fast forward.
Prayed this had a happy ending from the very beginning scene. Agree it's not much of a game, but it's a worthy loveletter to MMORPG relationships and first loves.

(Don't mind my play time -- I was offline for the most part. I played this game for about an hour, which is the entire length of the game).

This should've been a documentary/movie. It's kind of sad to say (especially since this is based on a true story), but what looks like an interesting idea on paper (a game based on a romance in a game) just doesn't work. There are things to be said about the...less-than-average quality of the video's or the game-within-the-game, but I probably wouldn't recommend this game if those were great either.
The first impression you get from Cibele is from within a 10-second clip and her desktop. It's meant to get to know her, but because of the way it's presented I felt more like a creep invading her privacy than someone wanting to know more of Cibele.
I'm sure I know plenty of women to whom the sort of flirtation in the virtual gameworld feels familiar, but as a guy I knew where this was heading from the start. Perhaps if the gameplay was better than just a barebones "click at the thing" I would've followed through, but I got bored and did a quick google to find out if I was right (unfortunately, I was).
Are there good things to be said? Absolutely. The story is absolutely believable and is most likely still happening right now. So it has a better message than easily 95% of the games out there. So when I said this should've been a documentary, it wasn't out of a "boooh! don't pollute my games with your emotional message"-kind of way but because the medium games require more interaction and choices to both identify with the protagonist as well as tell the story in a more straightforward line. Telling this story in the best medium possible would IMHO serve much better to convey the message to the intended audience (see also: the documentary 'catfish')

Both this game and Dishonored are "Thief, but new". Both suffer from bad modern design trends, but Dishonored manages to pull it off without ruining the core game even if the sense of vulnerability is missing. Thief fails to an extent where it pollutes its own name.
The whole game feels like a quick time event, every action is contextual. You cannot jump at will, you hit q to knock people out, picking up anything triggers a lengthy animation. "Tap E to hide a loading screen". At its best it feels like a more restrictive FarCry 3.
Once you get past most of the mechanics being poorly thought out, the rest of the game is better, but still problematic. Most of the stealth feels like those tight sections between the larger areas in a Splinter Cell game. All levels are very small and the sneaking is almost always absurdly close quarters. There's a lot of this in the older Thief games, but it feels like that's the only part that the devs really grasped at all.
It has an upside, though. The game is pretty as hell and the world is cool. If you're someone that enjoys linear story based games like Metro or something, then you'll probably enjoy this.
If it wasn't called Thief, I'd recommend it.

They Bleed Pixels. Right off, I reccommend this game; however, that being said, I have some major issues with the game. The game is an excellent, 8-bit style, hack and slash--which incourages stringed combos--somehow, reminicient of arcade platformers like Tekken and Streetfighter. The game insinuates a story, that really had potential, but like all too many platformers, completely fails at delivering. Performance is patchy; some surfaces and enemies cause near unplayable lag (drops as low as 3-8 fps), but as soon as they de-render, the game returns to the regular 50~fps. The game's controls are completely rebindable, which is great, as the defaults aren't optimum. I really wish there were some resolution options as well (locked at 720p, I think?). I read some reviews when the game came out, outlining these same issues--and purchased only recently, hoping that developers would make an effort to fix some pretty basic issues. My last, and biggest, issue with the game, is that hitboxes are terrible. I love platormers of this style, for quick-paced, careful gameplay. When hitboxes are larger or smaller than the displayed npc/surface, it's crap.
Summarized::
Pros:
-Cheap
-Fun to pick up and play whenever
-Interesting, dark style, that's actually well done
-Actual fighting combos
-Replayability
-Rebindable controls
Cons:
-Garbage hitboxes
-Lack of npc variety
-Basically half a story?
-Graphics issues
Buy it on sale, worth a few bucks, and a few more if things were fixed. The more you pay for this, the less enjoyable it is.

Pros: clever level design, fancy fight moves, helpful checkpoint system, beautiful pixel art/animation, John-Carpenterish synthy disco music.
Cons: Finicky fight control and jump mechanic take some time getting used to; expect lots of misfired moves and missed double jumps until you nail it.  Levels get tough real fast (this has been rectified by a rewrite; see below.)
Update (2015/06/03): TBP has gone through a
over to a new engine.  It's now cross-platform, lighter on the system resource, and runs at 60fps (was 30.)  It also features brand-new leaderboards with playback ability, and two additional bonus levels.  Special novice difficulty levels, which are a subset of re-balanced earlier "full" levels, are also introduced to ease the player into the game mechanics.
I usually don't care much for precision platformers, but TBP was a welcome exception.  The main reason was, cruel as the game may be, it plays remarkably fair.  The enemies and deadly traps communicate clearly to you with visual and aural cues, with anticipation time long enough for you to react.  So when I died, I knew it was due to my poor judgement or execution, that I could do better next time.  It reminded me of the first 2D Prince of Persia, in a good way.
Also, the dynamic checkpoint system comes in real handy - you can set one down anywhere (with reasonable limitation and cost,) which effectively split a level into shorter, manageable chunks that you can practice on.  It's kept between game sessions as well, so you can always pick up just where you left off anytime.  I certainly wouldn't have lasted without it.
And when all else fails, you can always unleash your trusty claws and vent your frustration on the nameless things that wander about in your way.  Which also grants you more checkpoints then health refills, so it all adds up to a surprisingly encouraging play experience, despite all the bloodbath and body counts.  Make no mistake; you *will* die often - and so will the enemies.  It's all fair and square, and there's certain grim beauty to it.
I heartily recommend TBP to anyone with an intrepid mind who takes pleasure in the mesmerising recursion of experimentation, realization, and execution.  Practice does make perfect!

Haven't played the game for very long, and historically have not been terribly fond of MOBA or MOBA-esque games, but I find this one to be a blast. The perspective and immediacy of action end up making the game feel much more like a brawler than how stuff like DOTA felt to me, and the speed at which combat happens is engaging and frenetic without feeling rushed.
Although that said, I guess it's not precisely like a MOBA. There's critters to kill, but you don't push them towards an objective. Rather you summon creatures who give you benefits and gain energy. After a certain amount of energy gained either by them or your team killing enemy creatures and players, your team has a chance to score a point. It's a good, quick cycle of gameplay.
The art style is really interesting, and I have yet to get tired of seeing any of the environments or characters. The music is also pretty wonderful.
I see a lot of complaining about the launcher but it's not really a big deal. A minor annoyance once, but with your login info saved, it's just an extra click on the mouse. If it bothers you here, you can also get the game directly through Arc Games (which will have cross-play with Steam) or the Windows 10 store (which will have cross-play with Xbox One).
If there's anything I dislike, I don't care for the rate of currency earned, but this might be common to MOBAs and games similar to them. It does have about six or so heroes for free that cycle each week, so you're not forced to spend real money on anything. I'm also not crazy about how every game with a new player has to take place in a specific arena, because I feel like it ends up over-representing that arena. I also don't like that you can use in-game currency to buy slightly better creatures to summon, but again, since I can earn the currency in-game, I'm not as bothered by it.
Those are relatively small annoyances, though. It's a great game, and worth a shot if only because it's free to play with no pay-to-win aspects that I've seen.

This game is pretty good for the reasons I will list now. Lets kick off my review.
====Gameplay====
The gameplay is quite awesome, teeming amounts of frigates, fighters, and interceptors, all desperately trying to complete their objective. While you are either hanging back and providing firepower in your frigate, or hunting down every last enemy with an interceptor under your command.
====Community====
The community is nice, but it is impossible to coordinate attacks. They all have their own motives and completely ignore anything told to them, this makes strategy not an option. The only way to actually be coordinated is if you are calling someone on steam or skype, some kind of internet voice chatting program. But thats it.
====Mechanics====
There are a few main mechanics you need to get a handle for until you can get good at this. I will list them now.
---Controls---
The controls are pretty simple, easy to get a handle on, but not so easy you can fly blindfolded with one arm tied behind your back. It is a perfect balance between mouse controls and keyboarding.
---Ships---
This is a pretty big part of the game, there are three main types of ships and a bunch of minor types for those. I will only go into the main ones. Frigates, fighters, and interceptors. Frigates pack big firepower but are slow with heavy armor and shielding. Fighters are a balance between speed and firepower, able to go toe-to-toe with a lot of things, even frigates if played correctly. Interceptors are very fast, and good for taking out fast moving things to keep them from getting in the zone where frigates cant shoot and tearing them up.
---Hull and Shielding---
These are two simillar things so I will knock them both out at once. Your shields protect your hull and they recharge. When your hull hits zero you are as dead as a can of Spam, and hull wont recharge.
---Items and Abilities---
Two more simillar things, yay! Items are disposable things that can only be used a few times per life. Then you die and get 'em back, simple as that. Abilities can be used as many times as you want but usually have a cooldown.
====Overview====
So all in all, this is a pretty awesome game. But fix that whole coordination thing by adding voice chat or making designated squads at the beginning of a fight. And also, I would love to see a dreadnought as a playable ship in the game. They would have so much potential as heavy hitters or being able to dock fighters for repairs.

A short, poignant story about the romantic misadventures of a 19 year old woman. It might make you want to yell at your screen at points, but it's worth playing as an example of compelling quick storytelling in games.
I met a dude on the internet. We did some kinky stuff and then he never called me back. Game Over.

This is a modern day love tale. A neo-Romeo and Juliet. The story of a romantic fling of the 21st century. And it's a true story.
The main premise is that you are a 19 year old girl, named Nina, living in the golden age of the internet. There is no direct control of your character; rather, you are controlling how she navigates her computer desktop. Exploring her file directory, subtle details including photos, blog posts, and instant messaging sequences reveal glimpses of her outside life. You can even read (presumably real) archived blog posts from a 12 year old Nina, ranting about important topics such as popular fandoms, and how proper spelling and grammar is for nerds (I may be projecting a little here).
The plot device is a game within the game, called Valtameri, a superior version of World of Warcraft. In order to defeat enemies, you just click them over and over, filling a meter until it's full. When that happens, a boss appears, and you have to slowly grind down its health. There are no quests, no additional areas, and you are the only player besides this other dude who...who is he? I think he might have a crush on you or something? Whatever.
Anyway, back to the main game at hand. Valtameri is an example of what MMORPGs should really be like. When I log into WoW, my computer can't handle the influx of players appearing on my screen. I've had 5 CPUs burn out because of that game! MMORPGs were meant to be played singleplayer, not this multiplayer garbage! Valtameri is honestly the most innovative MMO I've ever played, not only because of the small fanbase, but the endless content. In WoW, you get kicked for inactivity if you stand in one place for more than 15 minutes. In Valtameri, I could stand in one place for 25 hours! (I timed it!) Upgrade your servers, BLIZZARD! I hope they see their place once this masterpiece of gaming gets revitalized in sales!
Oh yeah, this guy talks to Nina through the aforementioned superior MMO, they flirt, they meet, they meat, and break up. Some message there...maybe don't online date? I wasn't really focused on that sappy nonsense. It didn't help that the live action cutscenes juxtaposed the other, better part of the game. Where can a guy play a singleplayer MMO in peace without some hippie message getting embedded in the works?
In conclusion, I nominate Cibele, containing Valtameri, for Game of the Year 2016. We found the WoW-killer.
