I am currently a little in love with this game. If you're looking for something that has the feel of Oregon Trail, but you get to slice up some hecking zombies. Then I'd definitely recommend this game. It's got some great dialogue too.

There are certainly ups and downs to the game, like having the procedural map generation bone you at times or your team mates not pulling their own weight during a fight despite you telling them what you want them to do. These few grievances never seem to affect my gameplay however, as I usually find myself rising to the added challenge this presents for good or bad.
My first play-through I didn't know what to expect, most of it is hard to differentiate between my many play-throughs since but I will never forget a particular moment where my group happened across a strange old woman running a bed & breakfast; there were a few choices I could choose from but none of them really beneficial so I decided to throw the dice and selected "Say it don't spray it!" expecting the absolute worse to follow. To my surprise the old woman not only gave us a place to stay for the night but fed us the next morning, after recovering from the initial shock I laughed out loud for a good minute before trailing off into sporadic chuckles while I continued my journey to Canada. I couldn't recommend this game enough to anyone who has a fondness for rogue-likes with a sense of humor and a nostalgic love for Oregon Trail.
Extra Tip: If your vehicle is destroyed or runs out of gas and you don't want to lose your ammo (which might or might not happen until you find another vehicle) try loading up your character's inventory with as many guns of each ammo type as possible. I've found that you won't lose ammo if it's loaded into a gun and carried on your person, just be sure you put it back into your storage when you do get a vehicle or don't if you like to live dangerously.

Poi, to put it bluntly is a love letter to platformers that have been extinct since the 90’s, where Mario 64 changed the game as we know it. We’ve had Banjo Kazooipoipove, Donkey Kong 64 and others of the same type, Poi can stand right along beside them. There are two characters to choose from, a boy and a girl. They don’t really stand out and to be honest they are kind of generic and lack the personality of Mario but they do the job. Maybe it’s the nostalgia talking, or the great art style, but it nails the feel. You have your triple jump, your wall jump, the run and the quickly juke back into a somersault move maneuver. All is missing is the slide into a jump move.
The first world that I played inpoimedallion was colorful, with enemies abound, and you can guess how to kill them. Platforms were floating, wires acting as bridges to the next mountain, were set. Everything is as what you would expect of the genre.
I haven’t played much, and I played very little in fact, but I was so excited I just had to write something down.
There are items to collect, aka red coins, medals aka stars, and regular coins. You access the different worlds via a helm of an airship acting as the hub. I look forward to playing more, in fact I’m off to play right after this post. I enjoyed it quite a bit, and I give this first impression a silver trophy.

I was very excited to play Poi last time, and now I’ve put almost 3 hours into it and have a clearer view on it. Yes, I said it’s a Mario 64 clone, and that hasn’t changed. There are different worlds that have their own unique theme. For example, Cozy Canyon was all about greenery and water, it was a relaxing, fun, place to play in. Then there’s Magma Canyon that has a desert tone to it, with reds, and grey towers.
You start off with access to only one world, Cozy Canyon. Then you have to earn enough Medallions to enter the next area, in my case 10 to enter Magma Canyon. Each area has multiple Medallions, for example, CC has one for collecting 7 Coins, another has you simply climbing a windmill. They get more creative with one having you play hide and seek or collecting seeds. Your airship aka the world hub, introduces new characters that have their own ships. To reach them you simply jump off your boat and
Along the way you collect coins that go into your stash. These coins can then be used to purchase items that help you. You can buy the very useful compass, that points you in the direction of the objective. A telescope that allows you to see far, or a shovel to dig fossils.
I haven't even made it pass the first level.

Having already played numerous "Choice of " games I believe it is safe to say that I’ve seen the different styles of writing within each adventure. The writing for, “choice of robots” was philosophical and aided by generic technological terminology, and “heroes rise” was filled with comic book ability terminology interlaced with futuristic technology reasoning.
With this game, “choice of the deathless” you can tell that this writer has done not only his supernatural and spiritual research, but he is also well versed in the poetic styling of demonic fiction. Honestly, I went into this adventure expecting something a little more heaven vs hell, or even dealings with the devil type story. Surprisingly, the story was closer to demonic bureaucracy and internal politics.
Personally, I ‘m rather fond of finding love in the “choose your own adventure” style settings, and I can honestly say my choices gave me a rather enjoyable end to that journey. Although, love aside, I feel the pace of the story was rather rushed in the beginning which kept me from really grasping the world I was entering. I’m sure the effect that I felt starting the adventure was intentional after seeing just where the journey took me, but I think it also had a side effect by not allowing me to fully connect to the characters in a meaningful, remember able way. I would play this “Choice of” game again, only to give myself a better grasp of the world within.

Choice of the Deathless is one of the better games released under the developer's official "Choice of" titles. This game is not the best one that Choice of Games has to offer, but it is great and certainly worth the time and money. The story is very well-written, the humour used is witty, and the world is original and intriguing. The gameplay is not too linear, and the choices you make do matter. The characters are interesting and they have a certain level of depth to them.
The opening scene isn't great and some people could even find it dislikable enough to lose interest in continuing the game. The opening scene may be boring and fail to grab your attention, but that is not indicative of the quality of the rest of the game.
Some scenes could be difficult to picture because the story takes place in an entirely original fantasy world where you have no basis from real-world examples and would need to rely heavily upon your imagination. The replay value is low and the story is also very short. Nevertheless, fans of interactive fiction and beginners will enjoy playing Choice of the Deathless.

I loved farcry 3 but found this one a bit dull and repetitive once I'd got past how amazing the graphics are.  Essentially the game boils down to;
1. Clear radio tower
2. Capture bases
3. Kill animals
4. Repeat
A lot of effort has been made with the storyline, but I didnt really care about the characterors and found it a bit boring. I also really don't like the stealth system / missions as the enemies can find you too easily, even when you are well hidden.
I have completed about 40% of the game but have become frustrated and bored by some of the mission, so I won't likely complete it.

Cons: Unfortunately it just wasn't that great. It took a lot of stuff from Far Cry 3 (which is okay) but failed to add almost anything. The features added are more comparable to a mod or a dlc than a new game. The story is really saddening when compared to the quality of Far Cry 3; the characters in Far Cry 3 are so well done (for the most part), but in FC4 the character development is so much below the standard set in the last game: throughout the entire game I just don’t get the players motives; he far too silent (it worked in Half-Life because the story was explained by the environment and the motive was mostly just survive or told to you by a character), I get no sense of likes, dislikes, or any actual emotions. This guy is risking his life to put his mothers ashes in the place where she wanted them, but he never even shows any emotions about his mother; surely if is risking his life for her burial he must have some pretty strong emotions toward her but they never show up. Pagan Min is just not as good of an antagonist as Vass was, no comparison can even be made. It is hard to imagine that these two stories were made by the group.
Pros: The world feels like it is actually inhabited by other people, you see people working in the fields and relaxing against walls, this was really missing in FC3, very few people were anywhere other than the villages. The game does add some new features that are quite nice (although not nearly enough). The graphics are wonderful, significantly improved over FC3. The animal life (except eagles) was vastly improved, while I think they were a bit too aggressive *cough cough eagles* there is a lot more variety and importance with the animals in this game, riding elephants into battle is a unique experience that is new to the game. There does seem to be a lot more side quests in FC4 than there were in FC3.
Verdict: It is a fun game but it lacks what made FC3 great: indepth story and new features. If it is on sale and you enjoyed FC3 it may be worth it, but otherwise you might as well pass.

They Bleed Pixels is a fun but very unforgiving platformer. The difficulty curve goes up rapidly, so don't expect to finish this in one sitting. As of writing this, I have not completed all of the levels.
The main thing you want in a precision platformer is good controls. They Bleed Pixels succeeds quite well in this regard, since you essentially have one button for attack and one button for jump. You can double jump and you grab walls just by falling into them. The jump physics provide very good precision. Various attacks can be performed by pressing or holding the attack button in combination with other buttons. This all becomes fairly intuitive, and doesn't require you to learn countless moves each requiring different buttons to execute.
As was mentioned before, They Bleed Pixels is a precision platformer. It requires precision, timing, and trial and error. It also requires patience, because you will fail over and over. There are a decent variety of enemies with interesting and challenging behaviors. The game is well-designed, such that even the most basic enemy can prove to be a legitimate obstacle in the right circumstance. You can't just button mash your way to victory. You have to approach enemies intelligently and exploit their weaknesses.
Needs more work, but its fun as hell! Very fast

NOTE: I have played Dota 2, SMITE, Paladins, some Battlerite and Heroes of the Storm.
Gigantic is a mix between the current FPS MOBA type of games like Paladins and Overwatch with the view and some gameplay of SMITE and it feels to have been done well.
I would say there are 2 types of ways you can play this.
1. The shooter type which basically lets you play as a 3rd person shooter
2. Brawler Melee type which makes you play like SMITE but has the capability to use abilities at different angles and not just in a flat plane.
The game mixed both quite well. Gameplay is like ARTS or ASS♥♥♥♥♥♥S (Dota 2\LOL\HON etc)  where you defend your "Guardian"and defeat the opposing side. To do these you summon and protect creatures that collect Power orbs OR defeat\Kill he opposing forces players and creatures. Each time you get up to the threshold,Your Guardian attacks and immobolizes the other one where your team must know deal sufficeint damage 3 times for you to win the game
Pros
1. As stated above the mix between the most popular Genres of MOBA\FPS\ARTS was done well. It isnt as space constrained as some Arena Shooters  and wasn't designed to be since you need to rely on team composition as well to have the Melee heroes to Tank\Frontline or initiate most of the fights.
2. Gameplay gets you to move around the map A LOT. either to catch points or trying to escape death. The skill and moveset you are given varies but the impact on the game makes it very hectic. CLashes are all about movement and aim.
3. Controllers are supported (but as what i stated above regarding aim and movement this becomes a liability)
NOTE: I will detail my experiences between using a Controller and Mice and Keyboard in the next section
4. Everything can be bought by ingame currency
Needs Improvement
1. Controller support is nice, I use my PC as a console as well. But as with how awesome the game is with movement, controller LACKs the preciseness needed to be as competitive as K\M. A=Aim assist seems to work only for SHooter heroes. Melee type seems to be not working as well and I would assume they should have higher aim assist for those.
Movement and AIming wins you games. The skill and mvoeset of some heroes makes it niegh impossible to keep up using one.
2. As a F2P I am comparing it as how much P2W is the game. They decided to use the LOL\SMTE\Paladins route in having timed hero rotation. Right now i do not see any balance issues or hard counters between heroes.
What I do see is the "possibly" P2W of the creatures you summon. I played the game without buying or upgrading them but will do so soon. From what we can see you are the ones that "buy" the creatures. The only information shown is that they seem to be slightly more powerful in terms of health. I will be checking if other info as attack speed or defense balaces them.
3. Fortune cards are the "Quests" you take to get "crowns" or in game currency  I would like the Devs to "FORCE" players to set it up first before playing a game once you have Free draws. Some of the quests are Hero specific which leads to
4. The game needs to have the heroes to all be available to play at least in bots. WIth Quests being hero specific and you clicked on the wrong card, you just wasted 1 quest until you are able to use that hero.
The benefit of also being available in Bots fixes the major flaw i have for these games is that
"Why should I buy these hero when i havent even played him\her\it"? (Basically saying we want your money first and if you dont like it sucks to be you)

I recommend this game, first and foremost, to people who want an unfair platforming challenge. You will die. A Lot. I'm not JUST saying that because I died a lot, but because the games platforming and level design is such that you won't always know what lies ahead. Some quick reflexes may save you in most situations, but it's likely that the game's architecture changes at that one critical moment to make you slide instead of stop, or have floating enemies chase after you through intense buzz saw blade platforming elements.
I had fun though. I tried to get all the pages, but around chapter 3 they start placing them in unkown sectors of the level and you'll have to send your little girl flying out into a bed of spikes to try and find where they placed it. Still, if you like that kind of platforming challenge, the control and execution in this game is really technical and can satisfy that urge to "get it perfect" and a lot of the levels, though they took me a half hour to get through, can be beaten in under 5 minutes.
So yes, I recommend this game, It's fun, well built, has that unfair platforming design, but some people like that. I did, until I just couldn't take it anymore.

Stupid design decisions (ridiculously short phase timer), constant crashes, and limited card pool are just a few of the things that detract from what could actually be a good digital magic experience. Unfortunately, as with previous entries this game is only really good for a new player looking to learn the mechanics of Magic and not much else. Even that is undercut by the awful phase timer, I could see a new player not even grasping that you can respond to triggered ablilities in this game. There are dozens and dozens of flaws I could point out with this game, but I want to uninstall and forget about it at this point.
TLDR: Avoid unless you are looking for an easy and free way to learn/get into Magic, and be prepared to move on to paper or hopefully MTG Arena if that turns out ok.

The claw in this game is an awesome addition that makes using the environment to your advantage a lot easier and more versatile than previous Thief games and successfully ghosting past enemies is pretty damn hard (even on normal difficulty).
Unlike Dishonored and previous Thief titles, though, you don't have a blade, so if you do go in for a confrontational play style you'll want to rely on your bow and the different arrow types. It's beautiful. All the other weapons handle perfectly, it's like someone walked back to the late 1990's, found Unreal Tournament, blew the dust off, cradled it lovingly in their embrace, and went "It's okay, you're safe now, modern game developers might have forgotten the concept of the pure deathmatch shooter, but we won't forget. We will make you shine, we will make you stand tall once more."
And they did.
Oh god, they did. Toxikk is effectively what happens when you pull Unreal Tournament out of the 1990's, put it in the hands of developers who loved, absolutely loved Unreal Tournament, and then decided to take all that was good about the game, and make it -better-. The graphics, beautiful. The sound, meaty. The gameplay, tight. The effects, lush. The core levelling concept - pitch perfect. Everything about this game save the one thing I mentioned right at the outset is wonderful, wonderful, wonderful.
What we've got here, is a beginning, and if the devs keep up the good work from this point on, we're going to see an explosion, a return of the FPS arena shooter on the PC in a big way. This is worthy of your time, and your money, and even with the one map it runs right now, it's glorious. Get it. Love it.

This is based off of a true story.
Everything was fine. Kiara, Rosaline, and their dog, Billy, were cruising down the Death Road to Canada. They had over 200 gas, over 30 food, 20 medical kits, and more ammo and weapons than they know what to do with. They were a happy family, eating marshmallows and telling scary stories around the fire.
Then... everything changed when the group of bandits attacked.
Kiara was killed. But that wasn't the worst part. The dog was killed. Sweet little Billy. Struck down in his prime. Rosaline was all alone.
So she traveled on. The car broke down. She walked alone, through the rain. She didn't have time to mourn the lost of her dearest friends... her only friends. Then, when all hope was gone, while looting an apartment, Rosaline found a dog, Jeanette. She adopted Jeanette and they traveled onwards.
The two comrades happened upon a junkyard that had a decent car. At the junkyard was another dog that joined them in their new car. Jeanin was one of them now. Their family was growing. They were all smiles and laughs. Jeanette loved to stick her fluffy doggy head out the window.
And another dog, Virginia, found them on the road and joined them! Rosalin was surrounded by sweet, loving, zombie-killing dogs. What more could she ask for?
But one apartment... there were too many zombies. Rosalin was seperated from her beloved dog. She slashed at the rotting zombies with her rusty machete but she was too tired. Her arms went limp at her side as she felt teeth rip into her flesh. She looked at Jeanette one last time... her last breath was a single, whispering word:
"Canada."
The fluffy little dog gathered up her friends, her comrades, her family, and fled the apartment, leaving behind the skeleton of her beloved master. With that one word echoing in her mind, Jeanette jumped in the front seat of the car and taught herself to drive. They were going to get to Canada.
The three dogs fought and fought for over a week. They battled their ways through sieges, through swarms, through factories, through grocery stores, through the skeletons of the hundreds of humans who had died in their journey to Canada. So many had died. But these little dogs were making it.
They were less than two days away. They stopped at a trading camp one last time. The traders took pity on the three dogs and gave them some free ammo. The dogs were eterneally grateful.
But Rosalin had had all the guns.
The dogs didn't have any guns.
One last stop before reaching Canada.
They were trapped in a house.
It was a siege. They just had to survive long enough and then escape.
Zomies were raining from the ceilings, flooding through the door as a flood of death and gore. No other human had ever gotten this far before. Not even close. But these dogs. These brave dogs, Jeanette, Jeanin, Virginia... they had done what no other human had done. They had gotten to Canada.
Almost.
Jeanette was the first to die as she desperately tried to lead the pack of zombies away from her comrades and from the door which would soon be open. But the house was too small. She was overwhelmed.
Jeanin took over. Sweet little Virginia was being overwhelmed. Jeanin ran in, batting the zombie away, scratching and biting them to protect Virginia, who was quickly becoming tired. Jeanin succeeded in her goal, but only after she died.
Virginia. She was all alone. The zombies were busy feasting upon the carcasses of Jeanette and Jeanin. Virginia ran towards the door. The siege wasn't over but it was almost time for that blessed door to be free. She would be ready.
But the zombies were far more ready than she was.
They were waiting right outside the door and came rushing in to greet her. Virginia fought her way to the door and tried to leave.
"It is unsafe to go outside right now."
She couldn't leave. Not yet. She tried to run away. She fought and fought and fought... but it was all for naught. She was less than a foot away from the exit.
The zombies circled her and Virginia's body fell to the floor as they bit and scratched her. Her blood was ripped out from her veins and her limbs were devoured by the growling mass of zombies. As her soul slowly left her eyes, she could see one last sign...
"The siege is over. It's safe to go outside."
One day away.
One driving day away from Canada.
Almost.
10/10 would get a pack of dogs to drive a car to Canada again.

This game has become a real personal favourite. I've looked for a fun 3D platformer reminiscent of those I enjoyed on the Nintendo 64 back in the days, but was constantly disappointed with games that didn't feel right, some with really odd control schemes and other things that marred the experience, but then I found this game. Playing with a gamepad, the game captures that classic feel while incorporating all the modern elements I've come to enjoy like beautiful graphics (a cel-shaded style in this case). It has a well thought out gradual difficulty curve, features a variety of tasks (reaching and beating a boss, coin or item collection, finding a hiding NPC and such) over multiple vibrant worlds each with it's own atmosphere, enemies and friendly NPCs and interesting nooks and crannies to explore. I could not recommend this game any more to those searching for a great 3D platformer.

The Nintendo platforming vibe is all over this.  And that's a good thing in every way.
Everything from the jaunty opening music to the clever cartoon style to the endless array of secrets to find to the perfect mix of casual-friendly game design crossed with fiendish speedrunning pitfalls is pretty much perfect.
Sure a lot of people are going to dismiss it as "childish" or "too easy" - their loss.  (Personally, there were more than a few sections that were not nearly as easy as they initially looked.  Or maybe it's just my rubbish gaming skillz... :))
No, it won't take a determined player long to get to the "end" (and, at present, it's not clear what that "end" might actually entail!) That's not really the point.  It's the journey this time, not merely the destination.  And what a ride.
edit: now that the "final" game is out, I still stand by everything here.  The final boss is the only thing that really lets the game down, failing on all the things that made the rest of the game so much fun.  It's not a deal-breaker in any way though; just a disappointment, that's all.

The game is set in a world where lawyers are demon-binding blood mages, deities are bound by contracts and corporate profit rules above all, yet somehow feels exotic and strange. The imaginative and borderline satirical setting coupled with evocative prose give this title a very special flavour. Struggling with student debt while considering the pros and cons of becoming a fleshless immortal is rarely encountered in any medium, interactive or otherwise.
However, the consequences your choices have on the story are not on par with most other games from Choice of Games. While the writing shines, multiple replays reveal very shallow reactivity. Different outcomes lead to superficially different conclusions without significant branching, and often the whole choice thing seems tacked onto a very rigidly fixed structure.
I recommend playing this on the strength and intelligence of its narrative. Just don't expect the illusion of influencing the story to hold after the first playthrough.

I bought this game from Humble Bundle along with a couple of other FMV games. While this game was more of a bonus as I wouldn't have bought it otherwise, the story behind activating it and actually finishing it is rather simple and amusing.
I was rather appalled by Nina's appearance with her pink hair and whatnot and this fascinated me. I wanted to know why does my stomach churn at her mere image and if I was going to throw up during gameplay or if I am able to pass over this gut reaction. Truth be told, I had to close the game halfway because my feeling of sickness got worse, but in the second half of the game, this reaction subsided.
As far as gameplay is concerned, Cibele is far off from being a full fledged game and should be considered a kind of experiment. There's a game within the game, but that thing is so overly simplified and useless that the whole game could have been a form of kinetic visual novel.
There's basically nothing to do in the game. You have a form of emulated desktop, with private pictures, conversation and miscellaneous articles that you can peruse, a emulated mail and chat client and the actual game : Valtameri. That's basically it. You click stuff, read someone else's conversations and see some FMV's every now and then. Valtameri itself is very dumbed down form of clicker type game without any redeeming qualities.
This is absolutely mundane and it doesn't offer any kind of excitement. If you've ever needed to fix someone's computer then this is the exact same experience sans pink background, poems and maybe with more articulated text messages.
This piece of software is more of an social experiment. It's all about the feeling and for the most part, it represents a forced tentative of identifying with the main protagonist and (re-)living some sort of nostalgic experience based on a real-life experience. Well I call it more of a miss, but honestly, i liked the ending. My respects to Ichi.
As my personality is completely opposite of the heroine, Cibele manages to gather all the things I hate about the current state of gaming, MMO players, people and society as a whole. Here are a couple of examples this game manages to perfectly recreate:
Don't get me wrong, I'm not accusing anyone, it's just my one personal view on things.
As far as pricing is concerned, the game feels overpriced for so little content and next to no replay value. 9 euros is quite a lot to ask for this piece of software and even if the game was around 2 bucks or something, it would be worthwhile to just skip this game altogether and buy something else.
Personally I don't recommend buying this game, but in the end, everyone is free to do as they please.

This is as if someone who kinda knew how to make a game and someone who kinda knew how to shoot a short film got together to produce something less then the sum of their parts.
The 'gameplay' is clicking on a monster and either watching your character twirl around for a minute or two until the monster dies or watching your character run into a wall as the pathfinding fails and wait until Ichi kills the monster for you (he apparently got the 'walk through walls/over gaps' upgrade that Nina ignored).
Looking at the Feature list:
The '3 full acts' equate to three conversations between Nina and 'Ichi' where they flirt together and they occasionally say 'nice hit' or something similar; during which you'll be clicking on monsters, waiting for a bar to fill up and wishing for death to relieve you from the utter boredom.
The story is probably true, which is a point in the game's favour. However, it's a predictable story which is a point against it. On top of that, the story lacks gravity as it doesn't show any fall-out from the *twist* at the end.
The 'mutiple short films' last less than 5 mins all together and still feel dragged out; there's a scene where two characters slowly walk down a corridor and then slowly walk up some stairs.
The game world is comprised of four maps, one of which is a straight corridor. The other three I can't remember at all as they're all just flat and dull, each with areas you can walk and can't walk (which the 'boss' and Ichi ignore). There was nothing memorable or 'richly illustrated' in any of them. As for the musical score, I honestly believed that all the maps had the same music as the damn repetitive sound that your attack makes drowns anything else out.
The desktop is not fully interactive; you can't move anything around, unlike 'Her Story'. That might seem like a small and petty point, but it adds to the pile.
Also, as you'll see if you scroll through the play times for this game, it doesn't last much longer than an hour and certainly not two. Even reading all the chat logs and viewing all the pictures I barely logged more than an hour; though it certainly felt longer.
While writing all of the above, I tried to think of positives and came up kinda short. The stuff on the desktop was kind of interesting, if lacking. It was sort of nice that the messenger continuously, yet not instantly, updated when you replied (though that sort of made the lack of replies on the emails really apparent).
All in all, I didn't enjoy this game at all. It was a chore to play and I didn't have any sort of positive experience playing it. If I hadn't gotten it from a HumbleBundle I would have gotten a refund.

Nina Freeman is a force to be reckoned with.  She manages to tell a touching tale of first love through the ever changing desktop of a young woman as she meets and falls for a young man she met through an online game.  The hidden treasures of Nina's thoughts and dreams are voyeristically on display for the perusal of the player and as I sifted through her folders, photos and messages and listened in on her conversations I learnt more about Nina and found myself smiling and cringing as her relationship evolved.
Although the game is quite short, the numerous story telling elements give the story more depth and flesh out Nina's background through blog entries, mail, photos, messages, voiceovers and video sequences.  It is a well planned and excuted piece of story telling and I look forward to Nina's next release into to the gaming world.

They Bleed Pixels is one of the coolest 2D action\platformers I've seen in the last few years. It's a bit short, yet it compensates with a high replayability of the levels, which are meant to be beaten over and over in order to get the highest rank and unlock all the secrets. The combo system is simple yet functional, and the jumps require extreme precision and timing. Level design in this sense is excellent, presenting hard but calculated sections, with no impassable or glitched spots - read: if you fail it's YOUR fault.
If you're into Lovecraft-inspired themes and pixel art you'll love this title, but beware: you're going to yell out all of your curses while playing it.

First of all, thanks to my friend Albion who gave me FC4 as a birthday present – that was in April and now, in June, I’m still playing it, which speaks volumes about the game.
To the game itself. This is a superb open-world shooter with a well thought out and cohesive story-line that is as thought-provoking as its predecessors and explores further a lot of the philosophical issues brought out in the brilliant FC2, where we are made to think about the consequences of our actions in the theatre of war. Here the good guys and bad guys are, to a large part, interchangeable and we are made to think about what exactly “doing the right thing” really is. As such, this sort of game is the point at which gaming and literature meet and this is a welcome coming of age for gaming, in my opinion. I’m glad that we’ve left behind the mindless shoot-‘em-ups for to a more considered approach to what we are doing within a gaming context.
I’m surprised that there are those detractors in the Steam community that are less than pleased with the story telling in FC4, which is surprising because the story and characterisation here is as good as it gets, in my opinion. I have two degrees in English Literature and am working on a third and I found the game wholly satisfying from a story point of view as well as from the less cerebral aspect of shooting ‘em up. NPC’s are three-dimensional and believable, from the hilarious offbeat Yogi and Reggie to the intensity and motivated passion of Amita and Sabal. I sense that Ubisoft have taken a leaf out of the Borderlands book in that this iteration of FC takes itself a bit less seriously than its predecessors. I was particularly amused at the DJ Rabi Ray Rana’s comments about using a bidet. This notwithstanding, the humour is there just as a mild seasoning rather than a main ingredient and the occasional light relief is just that.
The game graphics are excellent. No other way to put it. I was stunned by the vistas of the Himalayas along with the diverse wildlife (which is often more dangerous than the bad guys). I thought FC1, 2 and 3 were good, but this takes it to the next level. The availability of gyrocopters to get around provides many opportunities to ogle the scenery from great heights while going about your business.
There are always niggles though and I’m pleased to say that these are mainly of a technical nature. First, many Steamers have commented that the game features jerky gameplay where the screen can freeze for a long as six seconds. I’ve found out that this is nothing to do with your hardware, so don’t go running out to spend cash on an upgrade; simply Google  “Far Cry 4 jerky gameplay” and you’ll find a simple hack that sorts the problem out. Why this couldn’t have been done at “factory” level, I don’t know. Second is a minor annoyance and it concerns choice of video format. For some reason Ubisoft seem to think that PC gamers like to play with the game windowed, as opposed to full screen. Maybe many do, but I prefer for the game to remain in full screen for maximum immersion. Why then, does the game frequently want to switch back to windowed mode when your left pinkie accidently hits the [Caps Lock] key? Why can’t we just pick a locked mode and stick with it?
Niggles aside, this is a highly addictive game that can stand many playthroughs without becoming tedious or predictable. You get many hours of gameplay for your buck, pound, rupee, whatever, and if you can get this on sale, then do so.

Nekojishi is good not because of giant cat husbandos and stunning visuals(Though it certainly helps), but because it develops its characters and makes you attached to them. I initially downloaded Nekojishi with the expectations of a cheesly written romance novel with no real direction, but I was pleasantly taken aback as to how fleshed out and well
it truly was.
The gist of the story is that we follow Liao, a college student living a hum-drum life who is granted the power to see cat spirits who all happen to need his help in one way or another. It's here where the player must guide Liao down a path with one of these spirits and make choices that are difficult, funny, saddening, and the rest of the whole nine yards. It's these choices that make the game particularly awesome only because the writing is so good and it makes you consider the shades of grey within' each scenario, sort of like Night In the Woods.
As for the visuals? There's very little to be said beyond stunning, one can tell that heart and soul went into the making of this novel. All in all, I would highly recommend this to anyone as an endearing story worth remembering and playing many times over for all the different paths and endings.

While its 7 expansions in the Campaign are meaty enough to keep you occupied, Wizard has announced that they will no longer support future Magic expansion packs in Duels any longer, starting with Hour of Devastation. Of course, this is different from what was initially promised, that Magic Duels would be the platform where all future expansions would exist. Such contradictions in their promise is ludicrous, considering how lesser card games like Pokemon achieved Wizard's MTG promise on their online Pokemon trading card game. Most of Pokemon's expansion (save a few) packs are available in the game platform. I don't see why Wizards couldn't do this, but I would guess that it has to do with money money money - meaning the next platform would either by even more P2W than Duels, or not available for F2P at all. Such greed in abandoning platforms would merely result in consumers like myself turning to other card games that don't try to short-change those of us who paid money for the in-game gold, for those of us who have always been loyal to the company. It's unethical and leaves a bad taste in our mouth. This is practically like Sony abandoning PS Vita. "Have fun with your limited amount of content from now on. We're jumping ship for a bigger catch."
And it's a shame, for the game is a quality replication of the actual card game. Yes, it's grindy, yes, the gold cap is annoying, but the story is well-written enough to keep things interesting, and the different mechanics of the various expansions (the introduction of Vehicle, Crew, Revolt, etc.) promise diverse strategies. Unfortunately, all of that fresh content have now come to an end. Talk about killing a golden goose. Had there been infinite expansions, the "bonus" stuff like the card sleeves would actually have been worth buying.
For those newcomers who want to have a try at what MTG is like, go ahead and play this. But for those interested in a more lengthy relationship with an online game, I suggest looking somewhere else, for there lies a dead-end on this path.

Only recently have I gotten into MTG; this game helped me learn the more complex details of what I've come to believe is an amazing game.
That being said... There are a few issues I have with this game.
The story mode I believe is where it shines. Your are given a deck for each oppenent and It's undeniable that the deck has the cards you need to win. You just have to play the cards right or... sometimes you have to hope for the right cards... but thats the name of the game. Overall it's a great way to understand how the cards in each set work with eachother and how to use them most effectively.
The deck builder is semi-easy to navigate but once the cards are in your deck, its a little harder to sort.
The versus mode however is lacking. The gameplay works well enough however there is a distancing between opponents in a game that seems to be very personal in real life. Theres no way to talk or rematch through the game, though this may sound trivial to some, i think its an important part of the game.
There is also a pay to win aspect of it which exists in the real card game as well. It is possible to buy the best cards and create the decks you find on youtube channels and such and have a very good chance of winning every versus battle. I feel a digital version of this game could benefit from leveling the playing field and only allowing coin income via batteling. Only the most skilled should have the rarest cards. Too many times I've played people with 3 planeswalkers in one deck and no idea how to play them.
Overall I recommend the game, but thats more so because I recommend MTG. It's great for learning and improving and is an easy way for people to get immersed without buying a few hundred cards.

Thief is a new spin on the old classic games with the same title.  It is fundamentally a sneak game with heavy emphasis on staying undetected.  You play as Garrett who wants nothing more than to steal mountains of gold and stay out of jail, but Garrett get cought in a grand plan to solve all the world's ills gone wrong.
The good:
1. Good sneak actions.  The guards are moderately intelligent.  Gone are the days when you could stand right in front of them in a shadow without then notising.
2. Great loot collections.  And it is not easy to get all the loot.
3. In my view the original Thief games are legendary because of their amazing level design - the best I have ever experienced.  This Thief does not quite match them, but it is still great.
4. Some great scenery. All areas are highly detailed and look like real cities.  Sadly you can interact with very little of it.
The bad:
5. The characters are as interesting and loveable as stale bread.
6. The game creators have killed off some of may favourite game charactersof all times from the original Thief games.  No more Hammers, Pagans or Mechanists.  That is all I will say about the death of the Thief franchise.
7. This game has a combat system.  What for I don't know.  This is Thief, not a first person arcade game.  I never bothered learning the controls and never needed to.
8. Those ♥♥♥♥ing birds.  Someone should be shot for the birds.  And how come in a city full of mass starvation no-one has eaten them?
9. The games quite a bit of adult content and dialogue which totaly turned me off.  The creators tried way too hard to be edgy.
The ugly:
10. The missions are great, but the city is repetitive and soul numbingly boring.  The same gaurds, guard the same spot all the time.  Knock them out, move to another map, move back and woilla the have spontaneously rematerialised with total amnesia of what you did to them last time.  This you experience hundereds of times throughout the game.
11. The game is drawn out way too long.  I was really happy to end this torment.  This game would have scored much higher if you could play the missions only and not the rest.
More of a chore than an enjoyable experience.  Get Dishonered, not thief.

What happened?  Really, what happened.  The game is like a person being touched by Midas, and turning to gold.  Before, he was turned into gold, the person functioned in society, showing plenty of potential, and accomplishing things the person could've never imagined.  But once turned into gold, the only good things are that the person looks pretty, and it'll sell for alot.  This is exactly what the game did to the franchise before.  For those of you not seeing the analogy, the older thief games were old but gold.  One of the best stealth franchises of all time in fact.  It forced players to use the environment, to use the gadgets at your disposal.  You can also spend money aquired in the previous mission to purchase additional gadgets if you think you'll need more.  Every mission in the old thief games would give the player a major disadvantage; sometimes, players won't even realize it until later on the mission.  Whether if it is having an unclear view of the map, or simply the surface you would walk on.  Yes!  The surface mattered in the old thief games too!  They put that much detail into this game.  In the old thief games, exploration was vital to gathering extra supplies, and getting rewarded.  In thief metal age they even added secrets!  The story was extremely intrigueing, going as far as giving details on how Garret (the main character) even got the map!  On top of that, the maps were amazing, a huge city?  Sure, more than one anyways.  A luxury mansion?  Not a problem!  A religious temple?  Not a problem.  A secret society of a group of cultists?  Sure!  A FREKING VAULT?  who do think I am.  The new thief game threw literally every.....single.... one of them, not to mention every mission would have the same exact theme!  How boring and obnoxius can the devs get.  I mean really.  In the old thief games, you could also peak whenever you wanted,  in this game you have to be up against a corner, which makes zero sense.  It's not realistic, and you might be saying, "why the thief game's weren't realistic in the first place."  you're not wrong, but this isn't even realisim, it's common sense.  The devs seem to be a council of autistic people!  Despite the map handicap, in the older thief games, the map was still maueverable!  In this game, oh my god.  You all wonder why I have 11 hours on this crap game, and giving it a crap review.  Becaue at least half the time, it was me either scavenging for the same piece of loot, that respawns mesteriously (this didn't even happen in the previous thief games either! And this is supposed to be a more advanced, "realistic" engine!)  or I'M TRYING TO MANUEVER THE MAP FOR 4 HOURS.  The map is so confusing, just period, you spend have the time grinding for a trinket that ends up most of the times not even worth it, sometimes not even knowing how you get past a stupid window that you can't open.  Also in the thief games before this one, you get a special item always with you, except in thief the dark project, alows for you to zoom in, whether to identify the identity of an ememy, eavsedrop on a conversation, or checking if what you're staring at is loot.  And just like every other aspect of the original thief games, there's a story to the mechanical eye too!  I'm not going to explain it here, but make sure you check it out, but DON'T DO IT UNLESS YOU WANT SPOILERS!  There's also the obvious lockpicking, but it comes with a slight twist, in the first two games, you need to switch between two types of lock picks, not your normal lock picking mechanic now is it?  In this game, you spin your mouse, and press e, a blind person, could do that.  The final thing I would like to say before moving on to negative aspects of this game, is the story.  Oh boy, I might end up spending ALOT of time talking about this.  In the original games, the story was fantastic, a masterpiece, still one of my favorite plot lines in gaming history.  All those religious temples and cultist hideouts I mentioned are all a part of the story.  In thief the dark project, you're a thief......well self explanatory.  You find places to burglarize, knocking out or killing people with your vast arisnal, and unlike every other game, you're not overpowered for once.  You face SEVERAL challenges, even thinking you're good to go.  With this enters a new character or two, who hire you to steal an object, and this can go SO MANY ways.  I mean really, alot of ways. For me, the thing that really makes this game fun is putting friends and family into the game and watching the chaos that ensues.  The game plays a bit like Oregon Trail in terms of managing resources like food and bullets while traveling across the country.  You also have to make decisions about how to handle various situations that come up, like running into a massive group of zombies and having to decide whether to take a detour or try to plow through them.  Depending on the traits of your characters, you may have additional options in these instances.
The other half of the game is running around city streets and various buildings searching for supplies while avoiding getting killed by zombies.  The combat can feel a little clunky, particularly when dealing with doors and corners, but doesn't detract from the game too much.  Character movement also feels a little flawed.  Navigating corners and narrow spaces can get a bit frustrating when your character seemingly gets stuck on nothing.  I also found the companion AI to be a bit annoying at times.  Their path-finding can be frustrating, they will often continue to walk into objects instead of just walking around them.
This game really shines in it's character design, decision making, and quirky humor.  You're able to give your characters a perk, like mechanical or medical skills, and personality trait, like being calm under fire or paranoid.  It creates humorous situations like when your co-worker complains about Mondays the whole trip, or when your fitness obsessed friend challenges bandits to a body builder pose-off.
Overall I found this game to be a very enjoyable experience.  I would recommend this game to people who enjoy replaying games to see all the different outcomes to different decisions you make.  If your goal is to just get through the game to see the end, there may not be enough value here for you.  Otherwise, there's enough content to warrent playing the game multiple times, even after finshing it.

I'm a proponent for changing what "playing a game" means, but experimentation can't come at so great an expense.  "Cibele" as a vehicle for a story, isn't a strong one and the story itself felt like one I didn't need to be witness to and eventually, simply forced me to turn it off.

It's a very short game that tells a pretty personal story. I enjoyed it, but it's definitely not for everyone. Probably something good to pick up on sale and burn through in an hour. If you're looking for a brief experience in the life of a teenage girl, this is as good a place as any on Steam to find that.

Cibele is a short game for sure, and very light on play elements; the game-within-a-game MMORPG exists merely as a point-and-click excuse for the MC's online voice conversations with a distant love interest. The rest of the game is more like a cross between "Gone Home" and "Emily is Away" - it's all about exploring bits and pieces of digital ephemera to get a sense of who the main character is (chat logs, pictures, emails, scanned pencil drawings) and what her relationships are like with those around her. As a person who grew up in the late 90's/the 00's watching anime, playing an MMORPG, making blog and
profiles, drawing bad fanart, and talking to friends online at least as much as I did in person, this game had quite a few relatable elements. It was a little shorter and more content lite than I would have liked, but I found the story compelling and refreshingly realistic. And though the MMORPG in the game doesn't offer much from a play standpoint, its visual design and art style was charming and engaging. Get this game on sale and wile away an hour on a nostalgic, bittersweet love story!

If you love narrative games, Cibele is a must-play.
If you are offended by games that can be beaten in an hour, or don't have a ton of action, this is not for you.
I went into this game completely blind (did not even know who Nina Freeman was), and I'd recommend doing that. Nina definitely poured her soul into this game. All of the blog posts, messages, and online conversations felt real.

The game itself has a good lore and story, which can actually pull you into the game very easily. The choices, like the other games from them, have real choices which affect large parts of the story. They aren't what I would call 'fake choices' as some, and even most, can lead to big consequences. My biggest issue with this game is probably just within the biggest cliche that the developers use. I do recommend this game, along with the others. I can't wait to see what's in the remaining games they have to offer and whatever games might come in the future from them.

If you haven't played Far Cry 3, this is a sandbox game where you murder animals craft sexy new wallets and ammo pouches from the animal skins you tore from the murdered animal carcasses. Oh, and there are bad people who shoot at you or something, and some kind of plot. Oh, and skill upgrades for an RPG aspect. Yeah, so the animal-murdering and wallet-crafting is quite literally the most fun thing about the game, and that's not a dig on the game. You might think "Wow, you're a terrible person!" That just means you haven't played these games yet, because if you had, you'd know that crafting animal skins into wallets and ammo pouches is amazing. The Far Cry games don't have an overarching plot or main protagonist, so you may as well start with this game unless you are just super bored, in which case you could play Far Cry 3 first.
If you -have- played Far Cry 3, this is basically the same game in a new setting, with improved user interface and graphics. There are a couple of new features such as swinging and climbing from climbing gear ropes, and riding on elephants. Vaas was a great Joker-style villain in Far Cry 3, though he wasn't used long enough and the last time you see him, it's really confusing, anyway. In Far Cry 4, Pagan Min is your baddie, and he's a classy, smug, eccentric fellow. You can choose to join one of two sides of a faction opposing him, though I was a bit disappointed that I couldn't actually just join his side and crush the rebel scum. I really, really liked the cut of his jib!
There's not much else to say. If you like character upgrades, stealth kills, driving in vehicles, exotic locations, collectibles that give you experience points and are marked on the maps you can buy with the money you earn in game, then you'll probably enjoy this game. Huh, I kinda just described an Arkham game, to an extent. Anyway, good stuff! The actual story is just okay. The gameplay is where it's at. Seriously, though, if you haven't played FC3 or 4, you don't realize the excellence of killing the wild animals and making them into wallets. You have to try it.

Are you prepared for some old-school, Nintendo-hard platformer with a pixelated Lovecraftian aesthetic? Just making it through the levels is pretty challenging, but if you're going for completion, get ready to start tearing your hair out. The platforming on its own is fun, and you start off with double jump and wall climbing abilities (the latter being an obvious application of having claws for hands), and the enemies that aren't shamblers require some deftness and skill to dispatch safely, but combine them and things can quickly get hellish.
Fortunately, you get three hitpoints to work with, and when you activate a save sigil (read: checkpoint) you get them all back. Save sigils aren't located at designated points, but are earned through collecting blood drops and killing enemies (higher combos earn sigils faster), and can then be created on (non-icy) flat ground a safe distance from death traps (stationary floor spikes don't block sigils, fortunately).
Unfortunately, some of the difficulty comes from controls or mechanics that could use minor tweaks. Movement (especially while jumping) could be a little tighter, and this is particularly noticeable on sections full of icy platforms, when landing with even no horizontal momentum still causes the player to slip forward at surprising speed, often towards spikes or buzzsaws. The two button controls can be unecessarily restrictive. Stab and kick are assigned to the same button, depending on whether you press just attack or also hold left/right. The problem occurs when you want to dash, which uses the exact same key combination as stab, but when you're already moving. This is an issue that could have easily been avoided by making kick and stab two different buttons. Additionally, the rebound from hits is pretty severe, which can be incredibly frustrating on small platforms, and while recovery is fairly quick, there is no temporary invulnerability following a hit, which combined with the knockback can turn a minor misstep into instant death.

The game is not a hack and slash platformer as one might assume by the theming and combat tutorial placed at the beginning of the game, which is a shame because combat is fun and well-designed. It's actually about 90% monotonously difficult precision platforming. Reviews claim that it is "easy to learn, hard to master," but this is not the case. There is no difficulty curve whatsoever- after the third stage the game rapidly increases challenge to rediculous levels, and requires far more patience and effort than can be balanced by the meagre early game exposition in the way of motivation.
Or, to put it simply, it offers too little and demands too much.

Oh, this war of mine. What can I say?
For all of the touching moments I've had in gameplay, the one where Zlata, the musician in our group, slit her wirsts and died was one of the realest for me.
For all the terror I've felt in gameplay, the moment I saw "SNIPER" scrawled on a wall just as I heard the gunshot, gripped me the most.
and for all the potential I've seen in a game, this one keeps it all hidden away.
This game will reach out to you in a way nothing I've ever experienced could come close to, but there are plenty of other reviews for you read from if you want that. On a base level? Buy this game. Right now. It will change you, and your life.
But what about those of you who want something more. Something... realer than the short paragraphs we are given or the mechanical way characters interact.
The saddest thing about this war of mine, is that it does it's job so well, it highlights ways it could be so much better. The basic needs; Food, warmth, shelter, cease to become important by the 30th day, as the dreary mechanical rinse and repeat cycle ruins everything that made the game special. The characters which at first seem so full of life, quickly become puppety playthings, devoid of any real meaning or character.
What I mean is, this game is excellent at a base level. Replayability-wise? You'll lose interest after your second run. Relationships between characters, love interests, feelings, hope. People really just SITTING DOWN and TALKING about LIFE and LOVE and really, truly caring for each other, attempting to pull through the nightmare, the terror that has torn them from their homes and turned them against their neighbours, the loss, the sorrow they feel when a father loses a child or a bright spark takes their own life. These are the things this game stresses the most, and yet it is what it lacks. A daughterless father can drink alcohol and be totally cool with his daughter's death two days later. Two people who have been surviving together for months can be totally indifferent if their conterpart is killed in cold blood. You assign people to chat with a child not because they want to... but because the child gets a mood penalty if they don't.
So I go back to ticking boxes. Going to location X, to collect Y for the survivors to Z. Min/maxing, learning exploits until each game is just far too easy, and I watch as the same endings for each character happen over and over again, until I just can't bear to play such a well-crafted husk anymore.
Buy this game, and like everybody else, play it for maybe twenty hours, and let it's brilliance touch you.
But know that it could be so, SO much more.

I used to really, really love this game. It was practically the definition of a good space-dogfighting game, blending the simple fun of an arcade title with the variety of a futuristic space-combat "simulator" in a way that captured the best elements of both. Unfortunately, development has taken a turn for the worse and I've recently joined the roughly 40% of the registered playerbase that's quit within the past year.
This game has become a classic example of a great idea with a poor execution. Players new to this title can expect some fun gameplay at first, marred by some big problems. More time is spent queueing for matches than actually in them. It takes forever to unlock new levels and upgrades. The game is almost entirely server-side and Russian-based, so EU and US players can expect input lag. The monetization scheme is overpriced and somewhat pay-to-win. The developers will try to deny or cover up the existence of bugs rather than fix them. There is no actual anti-cheat software of any sort (although admittedly the game's server-side nature somewhat limits cheating). The developers have a very limited and somewhat antagonistic relationship with the community. The game's glaring problems are common, known to the playerbase, and rarely fixed.
A year ago I still recommended this game, but now this free title isn't even worth the download time. Check out the variety of other space-combat games Steam has to offer; give this one a pass.

This game is pretty shiny! Being a lover of shiny things and arenas of death, this game was pretty magnetic to my eyes when it was shown to me. so now a early on review that WILL change at a later date. Oh and heres a summary of everything im about to say. This game is fabulous. It has really good core gameplay. It has what id expect from an arena shooter and adds more sugar to the amazing cup of tea that it is. There are some weapon balancing things I would do such as buffing the spawn pistol and reducing the default ammo count on the rocket launcher. The visuals need to be a bit less blurry for a pc game. Id recommend this game simply because it plays very well and it doesnt require a top of the line pc to play it.
And now on to what I love about this game in detail.
*The weapons! They look amazing and feel right when its in the hands of my character who really looks like a spartan from halo 4/5. Being a long term halo fan, I actually really like this. Anywho, the weapons are nice! The rocket launcher is a strong power weapon as it should be buut compaired with the other weapons, I feel it needs less rockets upon pick up. Maybe a longer respawn time too because out of the matches I have played thus far, it basically will give you victory if used right. You will never run out of rockets if you and run the map just right. Maybe the rocket launcher simply doesnt belong on the one map we have right now. I also feel the pistol can use a slight buff. Its the only weapon that seems to struggle to hold its own among all the other weapons from my experiance. I dont have much of an issue with the other weapons cause they seem perfect. They arent op and they all hold their own against eachother pretty nicely.
*The map! The layout of it is nice. Pretty generic and what id expect from an arena shooter. It runs smoothly and theres combat basically everywhere. I cant wait to see more. The one map we have right now consists of 3 or 4 floors which dont really have a direct line of sight on eachother. Around the center, theres a lift and a jump pad so you can go from basement to roof really fast. Mobility is no issue on this map to say the very least.
*Player movement. Its really really smooth. Its way beyond my expectations. I don't actually have much to say about it other than its gonna take me some time to get use to the dodging mechanics.
*The audio. 90% of the time, I mute my games audio cause I hate the way things sound in most games. A lot of times, its just the bgm cause I hate the bgm games use. The sfx I turn down but not off most of the time simply cause I like hearing my guns shoot or my swords swing. This game is one of the few that I play that has audio that i actually like to listen to!
*The bullet holes! Yes really, this minor detail! SOOO many games dont even bother with this detail. While they arent perfect or even the best looking ones, they are there so I know my gun is actually shooting and missing vs me thinking I am shooting and not knowing that I am missing then assuming my game lagged or glitched causing me to rage quit then never playing the game again. Bullet holes and scorch marks are highly important for any shooter game. I only wish they stuck around a while longer for simple asthetics added over time sense there's nothing destructable.
More will be added im sure as more is put into the game.
Now for the things that bug me or what id consider to be bad.
*The textures. You have this glowy tv screen sign thingy that looks absolutly amazing on a wall that is so blurry, it would probably look like a solid color from 50m away. The floors are okay but still pretty blurry.
*Gibs arent juicy enough. They look like rocks too.
yep. those are my only two dislikes about this game. Two minor details. The gameplay is solid.

Choice of the Deathless has one of the most interesting names for a game I have seen on Steam. Admittedly, that was what first drew me to the game (as well as a recommendation from a Steam friend), as well as another friend taking note of the title. There's not much to say for the game visually; you are presented with words and the occaisional pop up saying you've completed an achievement. What it lacks visually it makes up for with writing because this is some of the wittiest writing I've seen on Steam, and its title seems fitting of its content.
Given that this is a straight Choose Your Own Adventure game, the choices you choose will matter a lot in determining what happens down the line. The writing itself is very good at giving you a taste of the world, and yet not holding your hand through ever single aspect of it. This can be a little daunting to new readers, because you can quickly become lost with all the facets of this universe. Luckily, this story is set in the same universe as the author's published "Craft Sequence" series, which may be of interest to anybody who thoroughly enjoyed this game.
The characters you encounter (as well as the dialogue options for yourself) feel fresh and amusing, and the choices allow for a broad range of answers. As I mentioned earlier, it's incredibly witty and so if you love writing like that this will be perfect for you. The kinds of scenarios written also feel very interesting, though the one thing that may be a downside to some readers is how some of the events/scenarios don't seem to connect to each other much, aside from a brief mention by a character or so (this is, however, wholly dependent on the choices you make I believe - I am currently going through each possible route). Overall, however, there is a story that does weave its way through your adventure, and while the ending itself may feel like a cliffhanger, it was still an enjoyable read. If you're unfazed by the text only visuals, then I highly recommend giving this a go. And when it's on sale for a cheap, cheap price, why not?

The two words that come to mind when I think about Cibele are "genuine" and "personal". This is an honest representation of a series of events that happened to the creator in real life. It does not romanticize or exaggerate, but instead shows things as they really are - intriguing at first, then confusing, and finally somewhat anti-climactic - just like life could be.
This is a purely narrative piece about the author's experiance of falling in love with a stranger in an online game. The minimalist interractivity and gameplay serves as a vessel for the player to get inside the skin of the main character and follow her conversations and mail with her friends and her online boyfriend. A lot of reviews point out that there is no actual game in here and that they wasted an hour of their life. While I see waht they mean, I disagree completely. Yes, you don't kill enemies and don't level up, but you experiance a story. I grew up playing RPGs, but this is the first game ever that genuinely made me insert myself in somebody else's life. The cheesy desktop with girly wallpaper and the folders filled with poetry and selfies surprised me and even made me somewhat uncomfortable at first, but they served as a window to Nina's life. For the first time ever I saw first-hand what is like to be somebody else - a girl in the internet, with her own interests, friends and life, that are different from my own. Another tool that helped me immerse were the short movies that show the main character alone in her room. They just feel real and personal. This is also reinforced by the fact that the actress in these videos is the creator of the game herself.
Cibele is a brilliant little experiance and an excellent proof of concept. It shows what a true roleplaying game could bring to a player to make them feel like somebody else for an hour. That being said, it has plenty of flaws. The UI is clumsy and just bad, lacking simple features like the ability to scroll through photos without having to open them one by one. The "game" that Nina plays is not really a game - you just click on enemies while you listen to her conversations with Ichi and there is no failure state or progression of any kind. But there doesn't need to be. If anything, the fact that the in-game MMO is boring helps you focus on the important bits - her chat box, e-mail and voice chat, which is convinsing and voice-acted extremly well (plenty of cringe included, we've all been there).
I think the main flaw of the game is the somewhat misleading marketing - on the page it promises a story about sex that is 1.5-2h long. It is not these things. It's exactly 1-hour long roleplaying experiance about what it is to be a college freshman girl who falls in love with a person she knows nothing about, and the consequences of that. I see a lot of complains about the price, too. While these things are subjective, I agree that the game should cost less for what it is.
I would highly recommend this little game to anybody. Just make sure you know what you're getting into - a short snippet of somebody's life, without any real choices or gameplay to speak of. How much you'll enjoy it will depend on your mood and your expectations (or lack of such). Maybe this title will make you look at some aspects of gaming and real life with a new perspective. At least that's what happened to me.

This game does not work at all. When it runs normally on ultra settings at 1440p, I get 100fps with 2 oced 970s, an i5 469k oced, 32gb of 1866mhz ram, and whatever storage device I put it on. It's alright I guess. The overall story seems genuine and relatable, even if it's kind of obvious where everything is going, but no individual piece of it really stood out. Being able to poke around in someone's computer to discover bits of their life is probably the most interesting thing that was done with it, while the pseudo-MMO gameplay is pretty janky. The dialogue and acting was mostly passable, and some of the awkwardness actually felt appropriate.

A very personal window into the relationships that can form online, Cibele certainly has a draw in its voyeurism. The protagonist feels very real, and left me feeling almost like an intruder to the intimate conversations, private messages and spaces that are open to explore. The FMV could be a little more polished and does suffer from being a little too cardboard at times, but not so much that it detracts from the overall plot and can easily be forgiven from a small developer.
Perhaps not worth the regular pricing -- I finished the game in around an hour or so -- but does make for an interesting and fairly emotional experience.

Death Road to Canada is an overwhelmingly fun homage to the Oregon Trail (or more accurately the Organ Trail). I bought it on a whim due to the art style and zombies, as I have a soft spot for these types of games, and I honestly couldn't be more in love with it. The game is funny, original, creative, interesting, and above all else it's hard as hell. You face some serious challenges on the death road, and it takes a really long time before you're even competent enough to reach the final days leading up to Canada. On top of that, the sound track is absurdly catchy, to the point where I find myself going around my daily life whistling or humming to the music that's in this game.
This is all without even mentioning the fun I've had playing this couch coop. I only picked up the game two weeks ago shortly after its release on steam, but my friends and I have taken every opportunity possible to meet up at my place and get as far as we can. We still haven't even beaten the game once, possibly because we're terrible, but more likely because the game is just that challenging, and that's something I simply love.
If you are the kind of person who enjoys rogue-like games with difficult but rewarding gameplay, or if you're just looking for a good game to hang out with some friends and play, then this is a great choice for you.
I give Death Road to Canada a 9/10.

I hate going against the popular vote, especially when a game has 90% positive reviews out over over 1,000 reviews like this one does, but I am staying with my initial, unflinching diagnosis of this game. It is unfortunate and I feel stupid going against so many positive reviews, but user reviews on Steam do not always signify a good game. See: DayZ. If not for the two problems that cripple this game, it would otherwise be a masterpiece. I recently reviewed Teleglitch and said it was by far one of the hardest games ever made. It is infinitely easier than this game. This game is the hardest game in the history of gaming, in my opinion, and for all of the wrong reasons. I have played some legendarily hard games and beaten them, some with not as much effort as most people say they needed to beat them, but this game I just couldn't do anything because the controls are in my opinion so poorly done. Of course 90% of other reviews here disagree with me, so catch this game on sale and decide for yourself.
The first are the horribly over-responsive and loose controls. You fly around like a pinball in a pinball machine in levels designed with every pitfall and hazard imaginable covering about 99% of each level. Over responsive in that in air after a jump is way too responsive. If I press right or left, I go way too far in that direction. Loose in that when you stop running, your character does not stop or even slow down quickly, she keeps sliding a bit. These things are the very single reason I ever died in the game. I never, not even for a second, felt challenged as a gamer because i just could not do anything with the horribly loose controls. The other issue with the game are the fighting controls. I struggled to remember exactly what to do on each zombie fight even though it is so simple. Simple yet so unnecessarily contrived. Even on the third level when I was getting it down, it still felt incredibly awkward. And that is where I gave up in utter disgust at the controls, level 3. Level 1 told me on the end screen I had died 30+ times. Level 2 I died 40+ times. Level 3 it was endless deaths and that was because, in addition to the hyper/loose controls, they put ice on every floor and platform in the level. I tried dozens and dozens of times from each checkpoint, slipping, sliding, bouncing, and being knocked into spikes, more spikes, buzz saws, and more spikes. And that leads me to the second game killer.
The second thing in the game I could not do anything to guard against or improve: knock back. When you get hit, you bounce way away from your point of contact. You very, very seldom get lucky and get bounced to safely land. Nearly every single time you ever get hit, you are bounced right into another hit or into death. Enemies knock you into other enemies and death pits. Non-lethal spikes knock you into other enemies and death pits. And one of the worst enemies I have ever seen in a game, the flying creatures in this game are unbearable.
So to cut it short, I can say that since you are a pinball in this game, this should have just been a table add-on for Pinball FX.

Let's clear the air: There's some obvious comparisons that can be made between this and other popular games of the now. There's heroes with various powers, there's "towers" of sorts as well...but any amount of time actually *playing*
will reveal a delightful truth: it may be similar but it is differnet in all the right ways that make it unique and worth your time.
The quick and dirty: Two teams of 5 summon and protect creatures that generate power orbs, so they can send their Guardian to attack and exploit the enemy Guardian. Matches proceed in phases of attack and defense determined by kills and power colleciton, capped off with a final "clash" stage where the map adjusts to a smaller area and the two guardians fight more regularly. Frist team to Wound the enemy Guardian 3 times during the Attack phases, wins.
Now some thoughts.
1) It's free. Or 30 bucks gets you all hereos now and forever. I'm a sucker for those deals and I find them very fair when you're a "play all the heroes" kind of guy at first and don't want to be shackled to a progression system. Everything in game can be earned by playing.
2)
The animations are fluid and interesting, the guardians are exciting to watch and engaging. Character abilities are clear, as are hit markers. The minimap is intelligent and the UI, while minimal in some ways, is clean and effective.
3) Great heroes. The set they have so far all have various strengths, and some are in need of nerfing/adjusting, but they are a fun bunch to play and to look at with a fair amount of skins already in game for earning.
4) New player friendly. The game's community is pretty solid, the game has a good tutorial stage and the "Vs AI" difficulty is a medium at it's meanest, so it's easy to learn the game. Everyone's got a sprint, Hold "1" to auto-upgrade your skills, and poof...all players can easily access the game's systems without hassle, and become pros at it as they progress.
Gigantic is great, really it is. Will it totally replace your competitive gaming schedule? No, but it should have a place, it really has earned one on mine. Not just becuase the current product is so good (hint: it is), but because the future of the product could be quite interesting as well (more maps, more heroes, more guardians, more creatures, etc). Give it a shot, I am sure you'll enjoy it!
