This game is among some of the best games I have ever played. It is so dark, so depressing, makes you feel so terrible, but it reveals so much about humanity... For instance: One of the guys, who was scavenging, had to kill 2 people in self defense. After that, he kept getting more and more depressed, and everyone else barely managed to keep him sane. He was drowning in guilt, and I can't even put it in words how much you connect with these characters. It is creepy, they honestly seem like real people, you can feel their emotions, grieve with them when something happens. One of the characters was wounded by bandits, and needed medical equipment. I sent someone to go raid a house nearby, the house had an elderly couple with lots of medicine. The husband begged me not to take the medical supplies, because his wife needed them, I took them anyways. His wife died, and when I came back, I had to kill him, he tried to kill me. After that, my character just got back to the house, curled up on the floor, and sobbed. He didn't eat or anything. The next day he committed suicide. I was near tears, I can't even describe how much this game messes with your emotions. You start out thinking "its just a game, I can't be bothered by it" but you will end up either sitting there, feeling horrible as you watch your group slowly die one by one, until the last one left just kills himself, or you will "beat" the game, surviving to the end, after which it runs through a timeline of every morale dillemma you had, and your choice for it, so that you get stuck having to stare at how selfish and cruel you were, whether that was denying medical supplies to children who were running through a warzone just so they can heal their mother, or denying orphans food after their mother died because of lack of medical supplies(probable connection), or maybe it was having a guy hammer on your door going PLEASE HELP MY NEIGHBORS GOT HIT BY A SHELL and you do nothing. In this game, there is no win-win situation. There is no way you come out the "good guy". You just either survive, or you die.
This game is not a game. It is art.

1. This game is good times, simple as that. My biggest complaint is it's not yet finished and I want to play more.
2. As of the middle of September 2016, gameplay feels really solid. There are some glitchy bits here and there but overall the mechanics feel pretty complete. It controls basically in the manner of more or less every 3D platformer ever and that is just fine.
3. The story elements are not nearly so close to being finished. You play as a boy or a girl who has to go places and do things for some reason.
4. The thing that continually impressed me was how you could miss a jump or fall off a ledge you were following and somehow wind up in a new area w/ new things to explore. I would routinely get sidetracked on the little missions you are given and would often find myself doing something completely different than what I sent out to do.
5. I really enjoyed the music but could not shake the feeling it was bit generic.
6. My least favorite part of
was the enemy design. I can't quite put my finger about what bugs me about them but they mostly struck me as a bit cheap.
7. There is only one boss battle in this so far and it is honestly not great.
8. All of the various worlds both looked different and had different elements that made them play different. I think this could be pushed farther but it's a good start.
9. I am not sure if it's in the plans but the characters are all minimally voiced. They just make a grunt or say hi or something when you talk to them and then you have to read the text on a screen.
10. Number 9 is actually a good thing in my point. Having everything voice acted is overrated.
11. The one thing that is a bit wonky about gameplay is sometimes when you manually adjust the camera, the game will re-take control over it too quickly, which is annoying as all get-out but not game-breaking or anything.
12. This has a solid amount of content already for early access. I imagine if you are one of those 100%-ing goofballs, it could take over ten hours to do everything. I played about six and am waiting for new content before diving back in.
13. It bears repeating that I will dive back in and play this once there is more to play. It's relaxing, it's cute, it's fun. It's worth playing.

First, the problems, and there are quite a few, so bear with me: there is not much connection between this game and the previous Thief games in terms of story or lore - no Hammerites, Pagans, or Keepers except for the odd logo or sculpture that references them. The lean feature is less useful and more cumbersome than before. For some reason the game prevents you from saving in certain circumstances (why? It should be up to the player to make that decision). Sometimes the sound design shows some flaws - guards regularly repeat conversations and the propagation doesn't feel as seamless as before. There is a bug that sometimes causes initial suspicions to be recorded as detections (this mostly happened when sneaking over broken glass - as soon as a guard heard the slightest sound the game recorded my cover as blown despite the fact that no-one had seen me). Also, in every single small gap to slide through between crates, there's a bloody post in the way, and to move it requires an annoying quick time event. Why couldn't it just be a few of them? There is also an awful section in which you have to negotiate a fire, which turns into effectively one long quick time event/platforming hybrid. Whoever thought that was a good idea needs a stern talking-to. Freedom is slightly curtailed by the fact that rope arrows can only be used at certain points, rather than any wooden surfaces. Oh, and the map. For whatever reason the developers have made the use of mission markers necessary as the map is next-to-useless - it is unlabelled and doesn't tell you where you've been a la Thief II. And finally the main problem. I don't know about everybody else, but I definitely had some performance issues with this game. After a certain amount of playing time there was lag, especially in cutscenes where characters' speech was slow and didn't match the lip-syncing. To be fair it wasn't so noticeable in the gameplay itself.
And yet, despite all this, and I surprise myself in saying this as I'm as big a fan of the Thief series as anyone and therefore have very high standards for it, but I still really enjoyed this game. This game still succeeds in making you feel like a thief. The atmosphere is outstanding - the graphics and weather effects are top-notch, and in the main city level especially the developers have really captured a feeling of squalor, poverty, and repression in the game world. It feels like a really run-down and oppressive place whose few riches Garrett is trying to take all for himself. Sure, the levels themselves are a bit smaller than in Thief II, but they are packed with detail. It really encourages you to search everything you can, and searching you will be doing a lot of, as you now have the ability to do things like snuffing out candles to create more shadows, and also stuff like rifling through cupboards and drawers, which is a very nice thief-y feature.
And back to the city again. One really good thing about the game is that there are a lot of opportunities to travel via rooftops and makeshift wooden bridges, just like in Life of the Party (Thief II). Yes, the Thieves' Highway is back! This allows you to explore lots of areas and buildings that would be inaccessible from ground level, and also creates the feeling of ground level being inherently more dangerous, as there are more enemies here. Not to mention it also allows you to find hidden loot in unexpected places - again making you feel like a really skilful thief. And in general throughout the game: secret areas also make a comeback! The city hub and the individual missions all have them, some easy to find, some challenging. These may be hidden panels in brick walls, secret tunnels behind a vent, or places really high up that are difficult to access by conventional means. You will also be pleased to know that the city and the missions all have multiple paths to take to fulfil your objectives - sometimes these are difficult to spot. It takes thorough exploration to get the most out of a level: in a later one I incapacitated some guards to reach a door, and when I opened it and got to the other side I suddenly realized I could have gone a better way!
The basic act of sneaking is still very satisfying. Skulking around and between shadows feels tense, and the AI of the guards and other NPCs is good enough to know where potential hiding spots are, react to doors opening, and noticing when the players put out fires close by and lighting them again. There is an especially spooky level halfway through the game which takes place in an asylum (yes, an asylum - think Shalebridge Cradle), which works so well due to the fact that it leaves your imagination to create the threats. There are also side missions you can complete, and I'm happy to report that the ones I did play were fun and worth spending time on - more opportunities to sneak around and steal stuff is good. The final sequence was also surprisingly good - at first I thought it would be a rubbish boss battle, but it turned out that stealth and timing were once again the key.
Overall, this was a challenging game, at least on the difficulty setting I played on. The Bank Heist was especially tough and required a real sense of timing, and the later missions were also satisfyingly tough. I can't tell you whether they can be truly ghosted or not, but you will definitely need to make use of the tools you have in hand. Luckily, you can buy them in between missions and sometimes there is even a merchant hiding away in some secret area of a mission who can sell you stuff! I would definitely recommend this game to all who simply want a game that holds its own as a stealth title that rewards real skill. Approach it with an open mind and you'll probably enjoy it. Just a shame about the rope arrows and the limited jumping.

7/10/2016 – This is a review of Far Cry 4.  I’ll solidly recommend this game in spite of a few problems that most shooter games have these days.  I like the (somewhat crowed) map and the ability to move quickly between safe houses.   There’s plenty of opportunities to make money by searching bodies, stashes, and skinning animals.  This is in addition to having plenty of missions and conquering strongholds and towers.  Capturing a tower removes the fog of war for that particular area.  The game has a grappling hook for use when crossing cliffs and hard to reach locations.  The grappling hook isn’t anywhere near as useful as that used in Just Cause and Dying Light.  There are plenty of weapons ranging from a bow and flame thrower to a suppressed semi-auto .50 caliber sniper rifle.
For game play, the player will want to arm with a suppressed sniper rife and something like the heavy PKM.  For side-arm I always carried the grenade launcher that seemed to work well from vehicles and the truck protection side missions.  The game plays in part from a dope and drug filled psychedelic perspective.  This isn’t my cup of tea by far but perhaps some will like it.  I didn’t care for the racing side-quests but again, that’s me.  The gyro-copter was fun and contributed significantly to the game play.
The most addictive and fault laden aspect of the game is the Arena, an enclosed area where your character is subject to various battles using a variety of weapons. This is where the player is really exposed to the “nerfed” weaponry and the lack of situational awareness. With most of the weapons, nothing less than a headshot or multiple body shots will bring down the opponents. The most difficult part of the Arena are the large black wolves that come out of nowhere to disable the player. During the pooch attack, the game controls appear to lock momentarily.  This is a tactic straight out of the L4D playbook if you know what I mean; a lame attempt by developers to simulate speed.  The animals and especially the badgers will take multiple hits from explosions, flame throwers, grenades, and continue to attack. Sometimes when a badger or bear are in hot pursuit but you turn your head since you think you have enough of a lead, nope, they suddenly make up that distance in a millisecond and attack removing most of your heath.  The most frustrating part of the arena play occurs during those levels of “Endless” past 40 or so when the health kits stop coming.  Opponents and animals will come out of their (adjacent!) door immediately knowing where you’re at and begin attacking.  It seems the game could be made challenging without resorting to these kinds of adolescent nonsense.
During the campaigns, I didn’t care for the wild predators constantly attacking.  Everything from badgers, wolves, tigers, bears, indigenous wild dogs, guard dogs, and even eagles.  Sometimes, I’d be attacked simultaneously by both the bad guys and one of the predators.  The yaks and rhinos were especially bad tempered.  One thing that drove me crazy is that you can't cancel out of the healing process and has cost me game time.  Once started, you're committed; very uncool!  The AI at times went crazy; I’d stop to help a civilian for some extra karma and money but the civilian sometimes would run away screaming.  After I’d start leaving, then the saved civilian would say “come here” in order to offer me my reward.  Too much drawn out dialogue was present in the game but perhaps I’m just impatient.  Once one of these long-winded speeches started, the player is unable to escape past.  The developers must be really proud of this game and don’t want us skipping anything.  Another gripe is the large number of “turd” hunts.  These hunts also include searching for anchor points for the grappling hook.  Often the player is forced to take the long-way around a mountain in order to reach a designated point on the map.  Again, developer’s pride I guess.

Gigantic Review - Huge Potential
TL;DR - In spite of the crowded MOBA marketplace, Gigantic manages to elbow its way into the big-leagues with an intelligently tweaked combat system, excellent character design, and a slick art style. I’ve enjoyed my 14+ hours in the game, but like the other mainstream MOBAS, there’s a lack of content that keeps me from falling head over heels. Keep your eye on this one - I have a feeling Motiga will continue to innovate and expand on the solid foundation they’ve built.
The question is this: does the world really need a new competitive MOBA/FPS hybrid with the likes of Smite, Paladins, Heroes of the Storm, League of Legends, and DOTA 2 already commanding huge audiences? The clear answer is no, nope, nope-aroos - but boy-howdy, I’m sure glad Gigantic is here in spite of the oversaturated market. It’s got stylish art, deep gameplay, a (mostly) cool roster, and a well-balanced free to play model. It’s not the game we needed, but it’s a damn good game nonetheless.
If you imagine a sliding scale of MOBA-ness with DOTA 2 (very MOBA) on one end and Overwatch (just a wee bit MOBA) on the other, Gigantic exists somewhere in-between, integrating an in-match leveling system and unique abilities with a Smite-esque combat system that includes both melee and ranged characters. Motiga has wisely mixed up the formula by eliminating creeps, replacing turrets with living point-control creatures, and replacing the nexus with the titular big ol’ monsters you’re tasked with bringing down.
Being that they’re competing in a pretty saturated market, I worried that developer Motiga felt the need to innovate just to differentiate Gigantic from its competitors, but I’m happy to report that they generally hit the mark. It feels very satisfying to bring down the other team’s giant, and each hero has a smartly designed kit. Tanks tank, flankers flank, and the “Utility” characters have a nice mix of buffs, debuffs and crowd control abilities. Heck, for a recently released MOBA-like, it’s also pretty damn well balanced (with a few exceptions).
Melee characters land blows with a combination of heft and dexterity, while spell-casters dish out damage from a safe distance. The “shooter” characters stand out as some of the most fun to play. They’re nimble enough to get out of harm’s way quickly, but still pack a punch when it comes to dishing out damage.
All that hard work on character design and innovation would go right down the toilet if the gameplay was no good - so Praise Yeven that Motiga nailed it. Gameplay is a slightly different take on the standard MOBA fare: each team competes to gather power faster than the other by slaying enemies, taking down the other team’s stationary monsters, and collecting power orbs from contested nodes. When a team fills their power meter, their Guardian rushes across the map and slams the opposing Guardian to the ground, allowing the attacking team a few moments to “wound” the enemy Guardian. The first team to land three wounds wins.
Sounds familiar, right? It should, as most MOBAs and MOBA-alikes share a similar set up. It’s important to note, however, that there’s a steep learning curve when dropping into the game for the first time. The tutorial is longer than I’d like, and in spite of its length it felt like Motiga stuck a Flaming Fire Hose of Information (+5 against Noobs) in my mouth and rolled a crit. In fact, I feel like I explained how the game works in the previous paragraph better than it was explained in the aforementioned tutorial… but then again I might be a bit biased.
Even with a cursory knowledge of League and HotS, there were concepts unique to Gigantic that I didn’t fully grasp until my second or third hour of online gameplay (which only unlocks after the tutorial and a bot-match). Maybe I’m just slow, but I wouldn’t suggest this booting up this game unless you’ve got experience in the genre or a friend to explain what the hell is going on.
Arguably, MOBA-alikes aren’t generally known for their art styles, with Heroes of the Storm and Smite coming off as quite bland, while LoL and DOTA 2 end up looking  confused due to their ahem...gigantic rosters. Motiga clearly (and intelligently) invested in art and design, as their characters, world, and menus share a nifty pastel-cartoon style that facilitates a clean look without sacrificing important detail.
It’s not entirely good news in the art-department though, as a few of the characters (Imani, Vadasi, and Tripp in particular) come off as lumpy and uninspired. I imagine this will bother me less as alternate skins become more common, but considering how good the rest of the game looks, it’s a bummer that a few of the characters fell out of the ugly tree.
Speaking of skins, this is a free-to-play title, which means that there are plenty of things to purchase from the in-game store, including heroes, creatures, fortune cards (equivalent to Hearthstone’s “quests”), boosters and skins. I ended up spending $15.00 on a bit of premium currency and a starter pack, mostly to permanently unlock a few heroes. Happily, none of the available purchases provide any unfair advantages, and as long as you’ve got a few fortune cards going in-game currency isn’t too hard to come by.
Performance wise, Gigantic runs well at mid-to-high settings on my decidedly ho-hum PC, and I imagine you could get it to work pretty well on your average toaster-oven should the need arise. Occasionally I’d run into a bit of stutter or frame-drop during team fights and respawns, but that could just as well be my rig as the game.
Currently, matches are easy to find (with the exception of one evening early on when I was dropped from a few pre-game lobbies without explanation, which I’ll chalk up to server issues close to the release date) and none of the toxicity that’s found elsewhere in the genre is present in Gigantic - perhaps because there aren’t that many people using mics at the moment, and there’s no in game text-chat.
That said, my biggest gripe with this game is the same complaint I have about every other MOBA - namely there’s only one game mode to be played on a limited number of maps. For those of you who don’t mind digging deep and really getting to know the roster this likely isn’t an issue, but I did find myself signing off just to go play something different for a while. Certainly, I wouldn’t expect this title to be all things to all people, but it would be nice to see Motiga introduce a horde defence or 3v3 mode just to let easily bored types like myself mix things up a bit.
So - would I recommend you spend some time in Gigantic’s battle arena? If you’ve got some experience in the MOBA genre, or a friend to help get you situated -  absolutely. Especially considering the price of admission (free!) there’s a lot to like, and hours of battling to enjoy. That being said, the lack of additional game modes and unfriendly new player experience might deter the very audience that Gigantic is hoping to capture.
The best news is that free-to-play titles like Gigantic tend to have very long life cycles, which means that Motiga will likely have ample opportunity to continue their innovation streak and push out new and better content. Gigantic’s launch is a strong start, and I’m looking forward to watching Motiga make it even better in the months and years to come.

This game is among some of the best games I have ever played. It is so dark, so depressing, makes you feel so terrible, but it reveals so much about humanity... For instance: One of the guys, who was scavenging, had to kill 2 people in self defense. After that, he kept getting more and more depressed, and everyone else barely managed to keep him sane. He was drowning in guilt, and I can't even put it in words how much you connect with these characters. It is creepy, they honestly seem like real people, you can feel their emotions, grieve with them when something happens. One of the characters was wounded by bandits, and needed medical equipment. I sent someone to go raid a house nearby, the house had an elderly couple with lots of medicine. The husband begged me not to take the medical supplies, because his wife needed them, I took them anyways. His wife died, and when I came back, I had to kill him, he tried to kill me. After that, my character just got back to the house, curled up on the floor, and sobbed. He didn't eat or anything. The next day he committed suicide. I was near tears, I can't even describe how much this game messes with your emotions. You start out thinking "its just a game, I can't be bothered by it" but you will end up either sitting there, feeling horrible as you watch your group slowly die one by one, until the last one left just kills himself, or you will "beat" the game, surviving to the end, after which it runs through a timeline of every morale dillemma you had, and your choice for it, so that you get stuck having to stare at how selfish and cruel you were, whether that was denying medical supplies to children who were running through a warzone just so they can heal their mother, or denying orphans food after their mother died because of lack of medical supplies(probable connection), or maybe it was having a guy hammer on your door going PLEASE HELP MY NEIGHBORS GOT HIT BY A SHELL and you do nothing. In this game, there is no win-win situation. There is no way you come out the "good guy". You just either survive, or you die.
This game is not a game. It is art.

After completing all levels in the game. I can finally write a review.
Frozen Free Fall is a matching game at its core and can be compared to games like: Candy Crush, Soda Saga, and Bejeweled. The only main difference is that it's based on the world of Frozen.
First things first, if you don't like Frozen, you will NOT enjoy this game.
A few quick things before I list the Pros and cons:
1) You don't have to pay anything to complete all levels, I didn't so you shouldn't have to either.
2) This game will make you want to buy stuff, trust me.
3) All characters can be unlocked for free.
4) There is now partial mouse support.
Pros:
+Lots of Levels
+Based in the world of Frozen
+Free to play
+Beautiful Unity based game (I was actually suprised at the character design looking so good)
+More content in the future (Hopefully Free)
+A well made port from the web based version
+Devs listen to the community for the most part
+Lots of variety in the levels
Cons:
-3 songs in the game. 1 song you hear so much that you will want to rip your hair out.
-An Obvious cash grab. I don't blame the devs for this though. Blame Disney.
-Some levels are so stupid hard that you are ALMOST forced to buy items without playing the levels over and over.
-Sound glitches when getting too big of a combo, its actually very funny XD

In conclusion, the game itself isnt all that bad. Yes it is a cash Grab for people that don't want to try hard. I give props the the Developers for making the game look so good on the unity engine! There are definitly better matching games out there though and I recommend you play them. Unless you really like Frozen. I will Recommend this game solely on the fact that its free and you dont have to pay anything other then your time.

Everyone wants to live 10 years in the past. I wouldn't mind it, life wasn't that bad then, my dad wasn't really depressed and my mom wasn’t a scary religious zealot. Smart phones weren’t released, so people had to have real books, and real friends. Life didn’t feel like a meaningless nightmare of suffering quite yet. Ahhh, nostalgia. That’s exactly how Poi wants to make you feel.
“Remember those games you liked that were released in the 90s, with the platforming and fun?” It seems to say.
I do remember those games quite well, actually. I never played Banjo and Kazooie, but I did play Super Mario 64, a lot. As a kid I beat the game at least over 10 times, and screwed around in it a lot more. I probably played the game over 200 hours. Of course, I was a kid, about anything is fun to a kid. I bet Poi would even be fun to a kid, but it certainly was rather mediocre to me.
Poi is a platforming game that, as I said before, tries to net the nostalgia of 90s platformers. In gameplay, it does it fine, though the controls are exactly the same as Super Mario 64, the jumping, the literal everything. Could that be a gripe? Maybe, but there certainly is a market for games that are “Super Mario 64, but better.” There is, however, not much of a market for games that are “Super Mario 64 with absolutely no personality.” That’s the biggest problem with Poi, it’s really generic. The levels are really quite boring, and while they are very different from each other, they have the same feel of being completely nonexclusive. Mario 64, however, had distinct music that gave every level a different mood, with way more different aesthetics and themes. Poi misses the mark there, big time. Also, Poi (at this point) doesn’t have very many levels at all, 5 big levels and a collection of challenges. Super Mario 64 had 15 big levels, and another 15 unique challenges with unique themes as well.
Okay, so the world is lacking in Poi, but what about the character themselves? “The Explorer” (who apparently isn’t named Poi) is really generic as well. Sure, they make noises when they get hurt, but they don’t really say anything about who they are, and they aren’t funny. Super Mario 64 was a funny game. Mario made funny noises and had little reactions to things, like when he would throw Bowser, he would say “goodbye me Bowsy” in a really funny Italian accent. The character in Poi is rather annoying.
Another issue I have with Poi, is that the collectables are chore to get. Super Mario 64 had red coins and regular coins, that were easy to see and somewhat fun to collect because you got to see the interesting levels. Poi not only has silver keys and coins, but locations and artifacts as well. I completed all of them in one of the stages, and I wanted to rip my eyeballs out with a spoon. Even then, the compass in the game really ruins a good part of it, because most of the time it feels like you’re just walking in a certain direction trying find a patch of dirt to dig up a dead thing.
The plot in Poi is also lacking, mainly because it's not a very good Plot. There is no antagonist, really. I suppose you could say the environment is an antagonist, but it's not a very good one. In Super Mario 64 though, Bowser brought all of the villans in all of the levels to screw things over, who also kidnaps the princess, giving Mario a reason to do anything. There is no call to action in Poi, you're just helping out an old man, and he doesn't really seem very appreciative.
The game also has bugs, one of them making it so a boss can't be killed. I didn't finish the game, because I couldn't. Also, the camera likes to go through the ground a lot, which is really annoying. By the time you buy it, it may have less bugs, but as of now it's a bit of a mess.
In conclusion, the game has alright enough gameplay, but has no personality, annoying characters, bugs, and too many ♥♥♥♥ing collectables. It’s definitely not worth 15 bucks, but 5 bucks seems okay, if you’re into that sort of thing. Emulators, however, are free, and then you can just play the 90s platformers that you remember.

It is a sore disappointment to know what could've been done with this progenitor of stealth games and then be served a lackluster and claustrophobic fetch quests with a tacked-on story. Thief's first three games were remarkable in their stories, voice acting, mechanics and they led to various off-shoots, most famous of which is obviously Dishonored, which puts shame on Thief 4 by doing what Thief could/should have done by an epic margin - two full years earlier.
Thief is a bit of a reboot. The protagonist and his character is the same: Garrett the Master Thief, sour, sarcastic and materialistic. Even his comic relief / foil Basso the Boxman is still there. However, the setting is a bit different now. Back in the older installments, there was a huge city, where opposing factions of technocratic Hammerites battled naturalist Pagans, overseen by the enigmatic Keepers, of which Garrett was a former member.
That's all gone now. The city is there, as the City. Garrett does his thieving jobs, assisted and obstructed by his rash partner/protégé Erin. The short relationship between the two is clunky, cliché and out of place (considering she's sort of probably the continuation of the young girl at the end of Thief III).
In comparison to Dishonored (not an unreasonable thing), Thief is so cramped. Despite the fact we are in this huge, sprawling city, we're almost always confined to narrow alleys, dank corridors and courtyards. Dishonored was hardly an "open world" game but at least there was the illusion of a wide expanse, for instance, when you'd climb to the top of Kaldwin's Bridge halfway through the game. Adding to this limited aspect of the game, the navigation mechanics are sparse at best. There is probably one or two viable routes in-and-out of a given location and possibilities of using Rope Arrows or such devices are confined to maybe a single occasion per mission.
There is also the issue of loading screens. While they can be fine while transitioning between vast zones, it's so irritating to go through these almost forced elements every time you visit your home, try to break into a house et cetera. Coupled with the frankly lacking world design, these stops are very disruptive to the overall immersion.
There are some good stuff, obviously. the Swoop mechanic -although not a huge factor- gives the sense of mastery while shuffling about amongst guards and such. There was also a glimmer of a parkour experience first at the opening sequences with Erin, then around Chapter Four, where the game really gave a sense of rush and excitement like Mirror's Edge or indeed the Dishonored's Challenge Modes against that train.
It's unfortunately not worth the full price, which may be why the Steam price of this game has been discounted progressively lower price. It's worth a shot if it's on sale and if you're a oldtime fan. Otherwise, Dishonored is cheaper, looks and plays better and its replayability offers different stories, rather than just different mechanics.

I was a fan of Thief series for almost 15 years, played the original series and fan missions for the most of my life. I always liked the atmosphere of those games, story, Mechanists and Hammerites and of course the main character - Garrett. The missions and the locations were always top-notch.
When I heard about the new game I was more than happy. Ok, there were many doubts like not involving Stephen Russell, but after playing the game...
I can say that it is still really interesting game. It has its moments and tries to catch your interest with good graphics and new refreshed story and also "powers" that Garrett can wield - I believe that it is mostly aimed for new players not knowing much about older Thieves and just looking for nice stealth game in semi-medival-steampunkish style. And that is good at some point, they are trying to show Garrett to new players (because not everyone likes the pixels in "vanilla" Thief and that's ok, we have our tastes).
For me (somehow older Taffer) it was nice game, spent some time in it and I think I will return to it one day, but... It wasn't THIS Thief. It lacks the magic and the atmosphere of older series, it was just... Too medival and raw? Where are the Hammerites, Keepers and Pagans who mostly builds the story? Why the powers when you can mostly count on your skills? Why the controls are so sluggish and for the most of time you are slower because you are trying to jump in the right direction? Why you can't shoot rope arrow anywhere you want?
And for the most - WHY SO MANY LOADING SCREENS IN LOCATIONS!?
After all I can recommend this game as a separate stealth game, not Thief series. It's still entertaining, I love some locations, story plots and old Garrett's cynical humor. But it lacks many wonderful Thief's elements that build this series for many years and also have some strange mechanical silliness.
As I said it is a good game for "new players", that want to spend some time in stealth style, not knowing many details about older parts, and not to worry so much about being *that* stealthy (because I think in this game Garrett can be pretty powerful with his skills).
For the end... I do not why this game tries to be a little bit "Dishonored" with more agressive paths of ending some missions. Garrett was and always will be a sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ - he doesn't have Corvo skills or character and you can see it in older games.  So why not leaving it as it was with really amazing, classical character and lore?

Hopefully everyone remembers the choose-your-ending books from when they were younger; you flip through the book reading and then come to a point where you have multiple options, and the option you pick determines the outcome of the story for you. This game is one of those, and although there are no real mechanics or graphics to speak of, it's an enetertaining experience, just the same. The detail in how the story is told (as well as how it all unravels ultimately) are interesting, and although I wish there were a few more options or alternate events than there are, it still makes you want to continue through to the end.  It's entertaining, and it doesn't discriminate based on gender - you're free to call yourself man or woman and still have the same romantic options available to you, both men and women. I've put four hours into this thing already and finished the story several times, and I'm still not bored with it; there are more outcomes I haven't found even at this point and achievements still to be unlocked. I'm praying for a follow up to this particular storyline or at least something else in the same world as this was set; it's easy to get addicted to this, but if you're not a big fan of reading, you'll want to look for something else to occupy your time.

Choice of the Deathless is a text-only interactive fiction game that takes place in a post-cataclysmic world that is a mix between high fantasy and modern day Manhattan. The Gods have been slain, and demons are bound by magic to serve mortals, but they are always looking for ways to threaten the physical realm. There is a lot of awesome bits of lore like these that hint at a greater world. Your character is a member of a law firm that deals with demon contracts, so you are an interesting mix between lawyer and wizard.
You start off by just getting out of school and getting a junior position in the firm, shackled by crippling debt. Your goal is to earn money and power, while also dealing with interpersonal dilemmas. Each chapter ends in a personal conflict related to your case, which can be resolved in multiple ways. I chose to employ powerful magic and political backstabbing, but there are also options to deal with these by means of charm and friendship, sheer force of will, or trickery. The game keeps track of your stats depending on how you handle a situation, and you also develop reputation with certain characters.
There is a lot of great descriptions of the other lawyers, especially the more powerful ones, and ideas about magic that can only be expressed in text. I don't know how well the game will hold up on a second playthrough, but I suspect the scenarios will be the same, but with different side stories and reactions. I think there is more in depth characterization, even romances, if you specialize in charm, but I was a pretty ruthless guy who only had time for work. The ending was a satisfying conclusion. My bosses loved me.
It's cool to see Steam branch out into interactive fiction. It's a pretty underrated genre of video games. At the end, it's a well told story with a unique setting and an interesting take on demons, so I'd give this a full recommendation!

Death Road To Canada follows two survivors of a zombie apocalypse as they try to make their way to the safe confines of the beautiful country of Canada. There is no specific story since the vibe of the game is almost a make-your-own adventure type and RNG does play a high role in the gameplay. Although there is no story as such, along the way you’ll meet new survivors and NPCs (if you stay alive long enough) and there is plenty of dialogue and little random events.
When you start the game you’ll begin with a few supplies like food and medicine and your car (which is where a good chunk of your gameplay will be spent). You’ll travel in your car (or on foot if you happen to run out of gas or break your vehicle) and it’ll be from there you’ll encounter random events, traders, new locations, bandits and even sometimes new survivors to join your group. Travelling in your car will consume gas and travelling no matter how you do it will also consume food which is one of the most important resources. Without food your group will starve, the more they starve the lower their ‘morale’ drops and once a person's morale is completely gone it is highly likely they will abandon the group. The more group members you have the more manpower you wield but also you’ll consume more food so remember that when picking up new survivors.
Along your journey you’ll find various location that you’ll have the choice to loot if you wish too but you can also choose to pass them by. Sometimes you’ll find a solitary location and others you’ll find two to pick from and each location's name will be kinda relative to what you find at that location e.g supermarket = food, hardware store = melee weapons. Displayed alongside the location name will also be details of the location you’re about to enter such as the size of the zombie swarm, how aggressive they are and the time of day. These three things massively affect whether you’re successful at that location or not so you do have to take them into consideration when playing or you’ll quickly end up as zombie chow. Once you’ve assigned any weapons you may have to your survivors you can enter your location where you’ll be able to loot and kill at will. You’ll usually find a bit of loot and maybe an NPC, sometimes you’ll find something a little more rare.
Each survivor has hidden stats which you won’t be able to see until they need to be used or you level them up for example you won't know if John is a good Mechanic until he tries to fix a car or increases that specific skill. Most survivors start pretty weak but the progression system in the game increases each trait that survivors randomly have as you complete specific things throughout your runs.
My favourite part of Death Road To Canada is the ability to add all your friends/family/enemies/acquaintances to the game as survivors you’ll have a chance to meet along the way. You’re able to name them, choose what they look like and wear and their traits and then either load them into your game from the start as your starting survivors or hope to come across them randomly in normal gameplay. There is a mode that increases your chances of coming across custom survivors so if you want to play a game where you’re likely to find all your friends then you can. The Custom Game Mode isn’t the only game mode you’ll find though, there are several ranging from change in difficulty to change in your trip length so there are lots of options for replayability if you manage to beat the normal main campaign (good luck).
The graphics are pixel graphics and though I do enjoy the ‘old-school’ feel to them sometimes I have trouble seeing some things clearly, especially the larger the screen I play it on.
The soundtrack is truly fantastic though! Instead of what you’d expect of a normal zombie survival game it takes an upbeat approach instead and the juxtaposition is fantastic. The whole package has a very nice retro feel to it and brings back some nostalgic feelings of the games on older consoles.
--- Randomized events, survivors and locations for replayability.
--- Local Co-Op so your friends can help you smash some zombies.
--- Fantastic soundtrack.
--- Difficult yet rewarding gameplay.
--- Customizability with survivors you can create yourself to encounter when you play.
--- Various game modes
--- Awesome soundtrack (yet not available for purchase )-: )
---
--- Full controller support yet instructions are keyboard keys only.
--- No achievements?!?!?!?!
--- Sieges can be a real pain in the...foot. Some are just a little too difficult.
Death Road To Canada to put it plainly is a great game with a hell of a lot of fun to be had. The randomization and various game-modes adds a great deal of replayability and the fact you can customize the game and add your own characters gives it a great feel. There's plenty of content included and for the hours of gameplay you’ll get out of it the price is more than fair. If you’re not willing to part with the cash right now it’s still a must buy during one of the Steam sales.

It's hard in a way that becomes incredably satisfying to win without being all the time controller snapping frustrating. It's as they say fiendishly difficult, but you can see where you messed up as opposed to there being no clear path or idea of what you should do. Even dieing as much as I did the game never felt unfair in how it did things. Every death was pretty obviously my mistiming something or making a bad jump, there was never the feeling that the game pulled some trick or some other new thing out to spite me and make it overtly hard.
It's a challenge that is fun and satisfying to beat if you can without feeling like the game is cheating against you.

Straightforward controls, straightforward physics, straightforward enemies.
The complexity of the game comes from the level design, and it's brilliant. Instead of making any one mechanic too complicated, they string together a series of simple and intuitive mechanics together to make something complex.
The difficulty on the first run is pretty stanard in the precision platformer genre. You die a lot as you get aquainted with the game, and the parts that seem hard are all because you're generally still improving. After you've done a section it gets significantly easier less because you've memorized the level and more because you've just gotten better at the game, although knowing a level layout doesn't hurt.
The game also handles replayability extremely well. You have two ways to play the game "better". Speed running and score running. Both require you to essentially give up on placing checkpoints, which help you survive in your initial runs. But how you approach a level in is vastly different depending on what you're going for.
Speed and score runs require memorization, but that's because figuring out what to do is half of it.
Speed runs are all about avoiding combat and getting through the levels quickly. Occasionally that means taking damage to rocket yourself across the screen, and actively avoiding the free point orbs.
Score runs, on the other hand, are all about forcing the AI to do what you want, then using the map to perform the most point intensive combos. The combos aren't obscure either, which is refreshing. Each attack has a clear job and is easy to perform, and the map is what decides the best combo.
My only gripe is that there's no map editor.

Poi is a very charming game. A very Solid throw-back to 90's platformers and collect-o-thons (hell the gameplay is almost identical to Mario 64).
The art-style/character design is quite childish in my opinion but again, thats more than likely to fit in with the type of game its going for so it doesn't really bother me, however I can see it turning a lot of people off if they haven't played it yet.
The music is actually very good, not something I was expecting for a game looking like this, with each world having its own theme and giving the correct ambiance.
Controls are solid and gameplay is very smooth, making play this game for extended periods at once, which is something I don't get from most current games anymore.
I only really have 2 major gripes with this game though. First being that its incredibly short. I get its still in early access but I almost feel a game like this can't really get away with it, Its fun, charming and engaging but because of that it ends far too soon. More worlds and such are going to be added but for now, lets just say I'm glad I got this through the humble monthly and not paid outright for it.
The second thing being they just added in a new collectable (50 Golden Gears), which is lovely, it adds more time to the game however is now the only collectable without any tacking of how many are left in a world.
So for right now, its a fun time killer however be cautious paying full price for now as the content isn't exactly plentiful.

To quicky describe this game, I use, "It's like World of Tanks, but with starfighters instead of tanks." Now, for a longer description, this game is actually pretty damn good. It's got solid gameplay, nice visuals, and I really like it. There are three classes of ships, and three sub classes for each. The three classes are 1: interceptors, which are fast moving lightly armored ships, 2: fighters, which are medium armed and armored and overall versatile ships, and 3: frigates, which are big, heavy, and slow moving ships. I won't go in depth with the sub classes, but for interceptor they are recon, covert ops, and ECM; fighters get gunship, command, and tackler; and frigates get long range, engineering, and guard. Each sub class has there own special main ability, or 'module' and a selection of other modules which are unique to that sub class, and there is also a selection of other multi-purpose modules that are avialible to all ships, no matter the class or sub class. Now, I think I've gone on ranting enough for this game, and if you've read this far, you've probably got the general idea of the game. I hope to see you up in the battle feild!

The gameplay setup is identical to its predecessor with minor changes that improves the overall experience. Several new vehicles and a slightly tweaked combat system allow for a better playing experience. While this may feel like a drawback, in all fairness Ubisoft games are more memorable for their story than the gameplay.
It’s important to note that the story is not just an improvement over its predecessor but a moral journey in the backdrops of a civil war. The story will explore themes of redemption, the emotional consequences of a broken heart along with the internal conflicts of traditional values vs. modern values. The biggest driving force in the story are the two characters who are in conflict with each other but bound by a sense of duty to an adopted country.
Unlike Jason Brody from the last game, Ajay Ghale is not some annoying brat who acquires combat skills after taking some hallucinogens. Instead he is a man with a troubled past that wants to put his mother to rest while exploring his families heritage.
On the other side of the spectrum is Pagan Min, who seeks to keep control of Kyrat by what ever means necessary. This is a villain that could easily be described as a J-Pop star with the personality and style of the Joker. While he lacks the junkie-style savageness of Vaas Montenegro, he makes up for it with his charismatic charm.
Despite being total opposites, they have this twisted relationship that is very similar to what is shared between Batman and the Joker. A relationship that is best demonstrated in how Min doesn’t taunt or provoke Ghale but instead converses as if they are friends.The common theme that bounds these characters is they have a Western upbringing but have have come to Kyrat for a purpose that evolved into an odyssey to better themselves.
Far Cry 4 preserves everything gamers liked about its predecessor while introducing a more memorable story that is rich in context. While it will feel like a familiar game, the journey will make players explore a new world with many wonders.

For starters:
A good game that takes the gameplay of the original games and makes it a little more fluent (and lineant) for modern games. While you can try and knock out every guard, you can also lift their pocketbooks, or just evade them. Choice is yours. There are side missions you can do for extra gold, which can go toworads upgrades for equipment, or trinkets to offer other bonuses. If you screw up in one of the chapter missions or client missions you can replay them at most any point in the game, which allows you to experiment with different approaches. There are a number of paths to take, so explore the environment.
Technical:
I need to stress that the only reason you need an AMD R9 or nVidia GTX 660 is if you desperately need the tesselation enabled or want to try and force this game into resolutions above 1080p, aside from that my laptop's ATI chip handles this game pretty well at 720p, high res textures, normal res contact hardening shadows, parallax occlusion mapping, no Anti-aliasing. (FPS: 20~34 Avg \ Peak: 49)
This game does utilize multi-core, so your multi-core CPU helps.
As I said above, most complaints for compatibility stem from people who are using Windows 8 and above, Windows 7 has yet to cause problems for me.
Some anti-virals may hinder the dynamic loading of areas. Excluding this game from being scanned may help load times and reduce in-game pauses, since there's normally a large and constant flow of data being read for this game.
Automatic Texture Quality Limiting is a good idea, but will constantly limit your texture quality to Very Low if your video driver can't report the right amount of VRAM. You can disable it in the launcher's options.
Gameplay:
You aren't a member of MSF or Diamond Dogs. You buy or find your own arrows and gear.
Your most supernatural power is a form of focus.
Moving through the city does feel "On-rails" at times, but keep in mind you don't have a grapnel gun.
You are a thief, the last thing you want is a brawl, or to be seen. The shadows are (mostly) your best friend.
Documents and the environment may hold safe codes and puzzle solutions, try listening to some pipe knocking in Chapter 5.
Complete Immersion is possible, HUD can be disabled and you don't -need- the lockpicking guide, just watch your arms.

In an industry where you see heartless sequels and cash grab titles, it is a breathe of fresh air to see a title such as VA-11 Hall-A not only succeed at being a fun and interesting experience, but be a dark horse candidate for video game writing of the year. A seamstress would be jealous at the way that VA-11 Hall-A is able to weave a story that connects from the start to its finish, while still hooking the player into wanting more. This is going to sound like high praise (and it is), but this is an Edgar Wright movie if it was in a video game form. Everything feels well thought out in terms of its implementation, as even the small side elements of the story and presentation help to complement the overall product. It's gameplay mechanics, while minimal, do help in create a branching plot, and making you feel like you're affecting the story. Patrons will get mad at you for getting them drunk the night before against their supposed wishes, or will love you for helping to cheer them up, because you gave them a drink they didn't ask for, but truly wanted. Look, it's not going to blow you away with gameplay: it's there to complement the story, but it's done with reason: to make the overall experience better. And of the games that I played this year, there's only one or two that I will probably remember 10-20 years down the road: And VA-11 Hall-A is most definitely one of them (along with Danganronpa 2). It's a game that shows the best of what games as a storytelling medium have to offer: and for the 15 dollar price tag, you can't ask for more bang for buck. It's a must buy if you like ANYTHING to do with storytelling.

UPDATE: I have completed at least one of the routes in the game, so now I can say with certainty that everything I originally wrote in this review is valid. This game was super wonderful and I'm definitely gonna be playing more of it!
VA-11 HALL-A, or Valhalla, is a cyberpunk, PC-98 inspired game set in a crapsack dystopia, where there is constant political strife, riots, and crime. A Big Brother-Esque association known as the White Knights watches over everything, a hacker group is constantly trying to disrupt the status quo, and a group is trying to overthrow the white knights and secure freedom. However, unlike most games with this kind of setting, you are not one of those big players. You are, simply, a bartender named Jill, and you serve the people of this world, both important and not, who are looking for the comforts of the bottom of a glass.
Hearing such a premise, there's a concern that it might end up being boring, but it really isn't at all. The minute I started playing, I was hooked in for several hours, and I'm certain I'm gonna be hooked for even longer. The world feels so engaging, and it rewards you for paying attention to the dialogue. Not every game could get away with telling rather than showing, but the writing style in Valhalla makes it work beautifully. It's got some great humor, lots of memorable characters, kickass music, and a gorgeous artstyle that enforces the tone of the game perfectly. All the parts of it seem to work together cohesively, and I love it!
Gameplay wise, you are, well, a bartender. So you mix drinks for your patrons based on their requests. You do this by mixing various substances together, mixing them, aging them, and so on. The system for it is very intuitive, and the way you are given orders is great since you never really grow too comfortable. Some people know exactly what they want, others have very vague ideas. Some will want a drink based on some obscure information you'll pick up while playing, some want gimmick drinks. What's wonderful too is that this actually is how you make decisions in the story. The game has different branches and can unfold differently based on the drinks you make, whether it be you ♥♥♥♥ing the order up, giving certain drinks without alcohol, doubling up the contents to make the drink huge, or picking one drink out of a list of possible drinks that fit the request. It's simple in concept, but it's executed very well and I think will inspire several playthroughs for people like me who will want to see all the details of this game.
I'd been eyeing up this game for years since it was first made for a Game Jam, but I was eagerly waiting to try it when it finally was finished and released, and I am happy to say it has met my expectations! I really recommend this game for anyone that likes unique games like Papers Please, enjoys anime, enjoys sci-fi games, or just enjoys a compelling world in general. Definitely check it out if you can!

I love this. Maybe it's the ambient music that follows your every move, or the predictable back-and-forth of the trains, or simply that there's something inherently and mysteriously satisfying about the design of the London Underground map.
Whatever the case, this game about moving blobs between blobs is an entertaining jaunt through logistics and logic. Connect lines between an increasing number of randomly-appearing nodes so that the blobs can get between them through a 24-hour period. It starts easy. You even get a prize for completing a whole week!
And then it's not so easy. And then it's a nightmare. And then you die.
Maybe not that last bit. But that's what it feels like, as you watch your hard work rapidly unravel and the first overloaded station explodes like the big blob it has become.
It manages to be incredibly relaxing and supremely frustrating at the same time, You'll get mad, walk off, and then come back for another try. In fact, if you were Minister for Transport, the blobs would rally their local MP to have you replaced because they were delayed getting to the star when you were distracted by building more lines to the pentagon. But it's fine. They'll forgive you. However, when square then explodes because you got up to get some tea, you may not forgive yourself.

Let's be honest here.
This game is the next generation of PC gaming. Vibrant graphics, amazing UI controls, stunning mechanics, this game is the whole package. This game provides the practice of self control by showing you the characters you COULD buy, but would rather not to. Children these days need to practice self discipline to increase independence, responsibility, and self worth. Not only are these characters unlocked through microtransactions, but they are shown with vibrant colors and interesting gestures making the player feel absorbed into the world of Frozen. These amazing visual effects are the tiny things modern games need, as they provide an overall thrilling experience to the player, resulting in some delicious eye candy. But it doesn't stop there. The amazing orchestral soundtrack is another plus to this already truly beautiful game, as the melody provides a melifluous, enthralling sound to help the player feel as if he/she are playing in the soft powdery snow. The stunning soundtrack includes about 3 different songs, looping about every ten seconds to clearly portray the mesmerizing experience of winter. The game made me feel like I was a child in the winter again, hot chocolate with Jumbo Marshmallows, fireplace roaring, smell of delicious sweets being baked, and seeing the smiling snowmen outside my bedroom window. If I were to describe the atmosphere of the game in one word, I'd choose, "Captivating."
Now, the game holds many different hypnotic (In a good way) features that engross the player into living the "Winter Wonderland." The mechanics aren't complex, and very easy to learn: Using the arrow keys, match 3 or more of the same color/type to clear it off the board. The basic instructions make it easy for a player to jump into the game, and almost instantly begin improving player skill. The elementary mechanics allows the player to waste very little time learning how to play, and spend more acutally PLAYING the game. After that, the player is free to learn/play whatever they want, and set goals for themselves. For example, once you learn how to play, the game quickly transitions you into gradually progressingly difficult stages. These stages allow quick thinking and cognitive excercises to help train that funny thing inside your head. Now here's the best part. Ever find yourself really tense, agitated, and anxious? Well, once you go through your MANY attempts (Or "Hearts" in this case), they provide a 30 minute life regen time. Now what does this do, you ask, well patience of course! The simplicity of this game along with it's relaxing atmosphere and gameplay makes it a wonderful stress reliever after work, school, and stressful moments. This is why I love this game.

Frozen Free Fall is getting a lot of flack that I don't think it deserves. I actually find the game enjoyable, but was taken aback by a difficulty spike that came out of nowhere. Let me explain - The game currently has no mouse control. That isnt a problem at all until you reach level 16, which is where the developers introduce the time mechanic. They give the player 90 seconds to score a certain amount of points.
This would not be difficult in the least if the game had mouse control. Instead I'm left rushing around the board one gem at a time trying to line up swaps before the timer runs out.
The game also has a decent amount of microtransactions, but in this single player game they are more or less useless. (Took me 3 hours to beat the game in its current state, except for the bugged boss. That includes doing all the challenge levels and spending some time just digging up fossils.)
Poi is Super Mario 64 stripped down to its skin and bones right now. It's got tight controls that gives a good platforming experience, but one of the bossess is bugged so it can't be beaten and the world is lackluster both in level design and overall world design, which doesn't work too well together with a limited and basic set of mechanics.
Mechanically you have the basics, you can jump and double jump, far jump (roll + jump), sprint, pushing objects and wall jump. This makes for a very familiar but lacking platformer experience, as no attack moves, stomps or anything of the sort limits your interaction with the world, its currently limited to buttons you jump on and that one incident where you have to push an object onto a square (the push is otherwise only used to turn things).
They've added a shovel to the game to dig up artifacts which is just random fossils plopped down on the map which you gather to gain a medallion when you've found all of them in a level, wholly pointless and just more stuff for the sake of it. Same with the "locations" feature where there are set places in the world which triggers a location reveal, which if you find all of them in a level you get a medallion for. This is further pointless because you can buy a compass that shows you the location of both the fossils and locations when you're nearby them.
The world design is a nonexistent sloppy mess of random things put together to become platforms and a level. There is no coherency to the obstacles, the world or the enemy designs, its just random stuff cobbled together.
The level design is as basic as it gets and works more as a proof of concept than finished levels, it has all the elements of a platformer, moving platforms, ropes, thin walkways, ice, slide ramps danger zones, basic clearly-based-on-S64 enemies and all that, but its put together like a playtest. There is no consideration for why the things are there in the world, it doesn't show off an identity to the world, it just is there, because it's a game and platformer.
The art is relatively good, but also, pretty generic, the game in its current state is mostly carried by texture alone, lightning in the game seems almost nonexistent, with it just seemingly being fullbright lightning, no fancy shaders going on here, except for metal objects and water. Which is a shame since they are very much going for the "Nintendo look", it just lacks the fancy lights for it. Though that shouldn't be a priority at this stage of development either way, I'm just hoping its not looking like intended.
I'm really looking forward to seeing this game in its finished state, it shows a lot of promise and I had fun playing it for sure, despite all of its downsides, I just hope they can pull it through, the long time between updates is not reassuring, especially not when there is a critical bug with a final boss that's been in there for months.
I wouldn't really recommend buying it in its current state unless you're really desperate for a classic platformer in your library, and you can't wait for Yooka-Laylee. On the other hand, the price isn't terrible for what you get, and it was fun to play.

Poi is a charming 3D platformer that follows in the tradition set by classics such as Super Mario 64. You play as a young adventurer aspiring to become a great Explorer by collecting 100 Explorer Medallions scattered across 4 major "worlds" as well as several smaller side areas. The game offers both a male and female protagonist, and allows the player to freely switch between the two of them between levels.
Despite being in Early Access, the game is exceedingly well-polished with beautiful visuals and an endearing soundtrack. The controls are spot-on, the levels are enjoyable to explore, and the difficulty is set just right so as to remain approachable by children while still offering an entertaining experience for adults.
It is worth pointing out that in its current state the game is still unfinished and lacks a proper ending, but you do get a good feel for where the development team plans on taking things. Despite this, Poi offers one of the best platforming experiences that I've seen in years, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the genre,

I thoroughly enjoyed the game when I had it. I got bored of it fast though, but decided to pick it up again.
It's a fun game, but a little imbalanced when it comes to what ship you're flying and what ship is shooting at you. It makes sense though, because an tackler should be able to take down a gunship easily, and a gunship should be able to destroy an interceptor pretty quickly.
I'm a little upset on how the frigates work though. It takes a good amount of time before you get your first damaging frigate, and even then it's expensive to arm it with the weapons you wish to take into battle.
If anyone is familiar with the World of Tanks series, then you know how most of the game works.
Two teams composed of pilots flying different ships playing in one of the gamemode types. You choose what ships you want to take into battle, three at the most. If you leave the battle, then those three ships become locked until the end of the battle. There is a respawn in the control beacon game mode, but there is no respawn in search and destroy or any of the other arena style gamemodes.
After all of this though, I still enjoy flying a frigate into a swarm of fighters and winning against all the odds. If that's not you then you'd probably be interested in flying an interceptor capable of in-battle warp jumps, or a tackler that uses a beam to slow ships and paint them for extra damage. All in all it's a really fun game when you know what you're doing.

The main story of Cibele is a "first love" story between Nina and Blake, which in summary is painfully cliche - Nina essentially falls head over heels for some guy online who calls her hot (like, a lot. The two of them calling each other hot and not-so-humbly saying "no" is about 80% of the dialogue), and starts sending him sexy pics. Over the course of a few months this tenuous relationship falls apart (crazy, I know).
On top of that, you get to explore Nina's computer, which is just a bunch of photos, bad fan art, very teenage blog posts, and very college freshman chat logs. Once you're done with that, though, most of the story takes place on a little MMO inside the game, and it is tedious as f*ck - it's the exact same mouse-mashing for all three little fights, with the world's dumbest AI partner and an avatar that spends more time getting stuck on landscape borders than fighting. But, you have to fight in order to progress the story - there's no way around this monotonus little minigame.
TL;DR: the focus of the game is supposed to be this painfully awful love story, but you'll spend more time button-mashing a jillion little octopi to death. It's tedious, boring, and altogether a major "pass."

To call this a choose-your-own-adventure story would be doing it an injustice. This is far more sophisticated. This is a beautifully constructed game that takes a fun format and brings it to the next level. The story is completely engrossing, I couldn't turn the game off, it was that engaging. The writting is immersive and a pleasure to read, the choices are well constructed and satisfying (with just the right amount of humor thrown in), and the world is unique and intriguing. I was sad when the game was over, I wanted to explore the world more.
I'd also like to note that I found no offensive content in this game during my play-through: nothing sexist, racist, homophobic--in fact it is very easy and satisfying to play as male or female, gay, straight or bi, and the race of your character is never mentioned or assumed. Initially I really enjoyed this game. The aesthetic and the promise of a slower paced Super Meat Boy platformer with some combat mixed in was the main pull for me.
When I started playing the game I had some trouble with the controls, it felt very fumbly and the amount of actions expected out of a single button seemed a bit much. I figured, hey I'm bad at platformers generally speaking so I'll just have to take some time to improve. While I did improve, the problems with the controls did not.
As the difficulty of the levels increased I discovered that my initial concerns may not have just been my own incompetence. The controls are too sensitive in some places, not sensitive enough in others. The attack animations are very awkwardly timed (the overhead slash, in particular), and too much is expected out of the "attack" button. To lay out what all the buttons are in this game (using an X360 pad), it's Left Stick to move, A to jump, and B to attack. But What attack you do depends on context or how the button is pressed. Left Stick + B = standard stabbing attack, Left Stick + B = dashing attack as well, if there is nothing immediately close to you. Just tapping B makes you kick, holding B makes you kick straight up. Left Stick (up) + B = overhead slash, while in the air B = ground slash, unless you're next to an enemy, then B = attack enemy.
Too much expected of too little, and combined with the less-than-impressive responsiveness of the controls this creates more frustration than is bearable. There were times during wall-jumping sections that require a double jump, but falling from the wall is considered a jump, and even thinking about moving the Left Stick away from the wall causes you to fall. This created no end of terrible moments of being unable to control the character well enough to accuratly move around the obstacles.
Some might say I am bad at platformers, but I have played more difficult levels than what They Bleed Pixels has to offer in games like Super Meat Boy and 1001 Spikes, and succeeded without much, or any, frustration. I could not finish They Bleed Pixels because of the control issues, but combined with the lack of resolution options or really any basic graphics settings, I would not recommend anyone play this game.
Jokes aside this game is amaizing.
For masochists only.

They Bleed Pixels is a 2-D sprite based platformer combat hybrid, it offers a variety of well designed levels and indie style music from DJ Finish Him. While this game is well made, a good port on PC, and has controller support, I will say its definitely not for everyone, because of one factor.
The Difficulty
This is one of the most difficult platformers I've ever played, and it isn't for reasons you'd expect. For one unlike other notoriously hard platformers, you are given a wide variety of abilities, such as a dash, double jump, wall jump, and a plenty of combat moves to work with against enemies. You also get a system that replaces lives and continues with your own checkpoint at any point of the level when a certain score is reached by defeating enemies and collecting items. However, the levels don't get truly challenging until you hit the 3rd world, which is referred to as dreams in this game.
"THEN HOW COULD THIS GAME POSSIBLY BE HARD!?" You scream at me
Well the enemies are designed to be aggressive, all of them, even tiny squids are your worst enemy as the level design shows you more saws in one area then at your local hardware store. Because there is a heavy hitting knock-back similar to that of the Castlevania games on NES, you'll more likely die from hitting one cleverly placed saw or enemy, because there is no recovery time in the game you could lose all 3 of your hearts in less than a second.
All in all, this was a great game to play, and an amazingly designed one at that with a cool style and music, I'd recommend it, but to actually finish it is a question you can only answer by your skill level.
Also you play as a little girl, so that's cool.

A rouge with survival elements with a splash of internet humor. The game presents itself in two different play-styles: an Oregan Trail like decision making rpg overworld, and a Nuclear Throne like top down fighter where you scavenge for supplies and weapons. There is also a character customisation where you can design your own characters and give them particular traits to spice up the character, or you can find randomly generated characters to adenture with, topped with some preset special characters that have unique dialog, abilities and weapons. All of this is presented in beautiful and detailed pixel art.
I only have two gripes with DR2C,
-Its difficulty if the first. While I understand that it is a rougelike and your chances of winning consistantly without a high level of practice are very low. This game also heavily relies on good RNG on your characters stats and the events they are put in; which may turn people off. Generally I find there are two ways you can play DR2C, you either play silly in order to have fun, often resulting in bad things happening due to you telling everyone to "COOL IT", or you can play super optimally and boring, usually resulting in higher chances of victory but takes away some charm the game has.
-The second is the small amount of bugs the game has. So far my game is unable to enter fullscreen and just makes the screen black, which I assume is a resolution issue. The other problem that has only happened once is the game randomly crashing presenting you with an error code. However, being a newly released game with updates coming out every day, these problems are sure to be fixed if not shortly, in the future.
Overall DR2C is a great pick up game with runs lasting around 30-60 minutes, packed full with hilarious dialog and a vast array of characters. Good times will be had with this game, but if RNG reliant games bug you, you might want to wait till this title is on sale. If not, I highly recommend it!
