A fun little 3D platformer game that reminds me of games from my childhood on Nintendo 64, like Super Mario 64, Banjo & Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64. It's rather short at the moment, I finished the current content in around 4 hours, but it's clear there will be more to come. I've noticed a few bugs, but nothing too major.
Pros:
* Basic 3D platforming mechanics are solid. Jumps, double jumps, triple jumps, long jumps, wall jumps and wall sliding are all present and used extensively. Probably the most important point.
* Levels are varied and fun to explore.
* OST is simple, but relaxing.
* Character designs and the overall visual design is cute and cosy.
* Two characters, though they are essentially identical other than gender.
* Full controller support.
Cons:
* Camera clearly needs work. In some segments it spins automatically, due to climbing towers or doing puzzles, but it's hard to keep it from doing so when not needed.
* Some mechanics are present but are not really fleshed out or used to its potential. I trust this will be expanded upon.
* One level could not be completed due to a bug, I trust this will be fixed.
* A few level designs feel as if they borrowed too much from platformer classics, especially SM64.
* The challenge runs are often either too messy or too uninteresting. Also, see above point.
* Enemies are more of a nuisance than a threat, in addition to not being particularly varied.
All in all I recommend this game if you played the old 3D platformer games, and want what's essentially a modern old school platformer. I will return and update this review at a later time, to see which ones have changed.

Bright
Colorful
Simple
Such is the world of Poi.
You can Jump, Double Jump, Wall Jump, Triple Jump, Long Jump, Reverse Jump, Combo Jump, Deep Fried Jump, Stir, Fried Jump, Gumbo Jump, Pineapple Jump, Lemon Jump, Coconut Jump, Pepper Jump, Jump Soup, Jump Stew, Jump Salad, Jump and Potatoes, Jump Burger, and dig. That about wraps up your list of available moves.  Now throw in compact stages with a central world hub and call it a video game.  It seems like four developers from Mario 64 were kidnapped, frozen for 20 years or so (wow, has it been that long already?), recently thawed out and forced to invent a new IP.  And then some composer was hired off the street or something.
As stated before (like at the very beginning so you probably don't remember), Poi is a really simple game.  All of the objectives are very clear and close in proximity.  To make up for this lack of scale the creators saw fit to add stop watches per objective.  Nothing like getting a gold medal on a challenge stage, then realizing that you are, in fact, little♥♥♥♥♥♥number 497.  Congratulations.
In Poi, you are... Poi.  A boy (or girl, depending on your gender identity of the minute) who has been tasked with retrieving an old man's lost explorer medals.  And Poi, in ze's (or... zer's?) ADD-ridden state who can't sit still in a classroom to save zis life, kindly obliges.
The graphics in Poi are bright.  Lots of color everywhere and appropriately placed sections of minimal pallette variety.  What's missing here is detail and more polygons, not to mention that the textures are rather underwhelming.  I'd also hate to appear nitpicky, but the API doesn't like to stay at 144 frames per second on my GTX 1070.  At least there are some modern lighting effects in use.  Yay.
The gameplay itself is mixed.  It is seamless and smooth for the most part.  The level design allows the player to speedily bounce from platform to platform and the double jump and edge grabbing mechanics are very forgiving in most cases.  That being said, Poi is slow in opening up new areas.  It's a common symptom of games with little content to keep the player repeating the same stages over and again in order to advance.  Small challenge stages fill the gaps between the levels, but their variety and simplicity makes it quite transparent that these are meer time killers.  Some refinement is in order at this point as well, like the hitboxes for enemies.  Even the simplest little buggers can be very annoying and will kill you all the way dead unless you're extra careful.
For the bottom line, Poi is a nice early access game to keep your kids occupied for a time.  The pace is faster than Mario 64 and the game itself is a lot more pretty, but there are still some glitches that need to be worked out.  For now, where Poi sits fills a giant gap in the PC gaming segment, but it only leaves me desperate for something better.

I love this. Maybe it's the ambient music that follows your every move, or the predictable back-and-forth of the trains, or simply that there's something inherently and mysteriously satisfying about the design of the London Underground map.
Whatever the case, this game about moving blobs between blobs is an entertaining jaunt through logistics and logic. Connect lines between an increasing number of randomly-appearing nodes so that the blobs can get between them through a 24-hour period. It starts easy. You even get a prize for completing a whole week!
And then it's not so easy. And then it's a nightmare. And then you die.
Maybe not that last bit. But that's what it feels like, as you watch your hard work rapidly unravel and the first overloaded station explodes like the big blob it has become.
It manages to be incredibly relaxing and supremely frustrating at the same time, You'll get mad, walk off, and then come back for another try. In fact, if you were Minister for Transport, the blobs would rally their local MP to have you replaced because they were delayed getting to the star when you were distracted by building more lines to the pentagon. But it's fine. They'll forgive you. However, when square then explodes because you got up to get some tea, you may not forgive yourself.

Magic Duels: As of October 2017, I wouldn't recommend this game to new players without considering the release of Magic Arena.
Magic Duels is a  great way to play Magic The Gathering, especially for beginners. It allows one to earn the in game currency through the story line quests which give a back story to all of the Planeswalkers, wizards who can travel the multiverse. Each of these introductory battles are themed and utilize various strategies, mana colors, creature cards within your own deck and the opponent's deck. They offer a coin reward which can be used to buy booster packs to create and improve your own decks. There are also online battles with real opponents utilizing these self made decks or simply battling an AI.
The interface of the game is simple and easy to use, although sometimes the user can experience minor glitches such as skipping parts of the turn or getting stuck on zoom in for the cards. In contrast to that, the card artwork is absolutely stunning and creatively themed in the realms of fantasy, adventure and even horror genres. The strategies that these cards offer range from simplistic to mind boggling and each user is the creator of their own game in this regard. Within some game rules, a user has almost endless possibilities in regards to their own personal strategy and theme.
The best part for me is that the game is utilizing the current card sets that one can use in real life so I feel I am learning a game that not only can be enjoyed on PC, but my knowledge gained there can be taken into my real life and utilized between my friends or at my local game shop that offers MTG events.
As of Fall 2017 I can say that there is plenty to dislike and it is enough to discourage me from putting much effort into this game again with the release of Magic Arena on the horizon. This game is pretty much abandoned by Wizards. Spending money at the cash shop does not seem worth it to me and I notice that many players use selfish tactics to boost their scores without having to actually play against you, after disconnecting their internet. All in all, I'd only suggest getting into Magic Duels this late in the game if you want to give it one last hurrah or you are already an MTG player just looking for some quick matches to get into.

If you've played Far Cry 3, you know what you are getting in Far Cry 4.  Take all of the same mechanics, the stealth gameplay, the animal hunting the item crafting, add a few extra mission types, vehicles and gimmicks and you basically have this game.  There has been some polishing done.  It fully supports co-op play and includes the ability to summon AI companions if you don't have a friend handy to play with but still want an extra gun.  Still, Far Cry 4 feels oddly hollow to me.  Though the plot of Far Cry 3 wasn't entirely believable, it nonetheless had a compelling theme.  The game was centered around your main character's descent into barbarism.  Thus, each perk that made him better at combat or strengthened his inventory was tied to him losing a piece of his former self, becomming that much more infected with the savage morality of the island he was on.  Far Cry 4 doesn't have the same plot development, and while the main villain is amusing, he doesn't have the same kind of power and presence that Vaas did.  Far Cry 4 simply jumps into the action with you apparently already comfortable with the terrible things you have to do.  While your protagonist does grunt in disgust at the task of skinning and butchering animals, he kills people with an absolute gusto.  Far Cry 4 does try to play around with moral ambiguity in that you have to choose between two conflicting leaders in your mission selection, one appearing to be a moral idealist and the other a pragmatist, but that doesn't really match the depth of the previous game, even as those characters develop.  Nonetheless if you really enjoy chaining knife kills, doing ridiculous trick shots from the back of an elephant and sandbox gameplay, then this is definitely the game for you.

At first some people may pass this off as a basic interactive story about dating furries, but as you get deeper into the game the plot can take many twists and turns, it becomes far more deep and will have you thinking of the characters in a variety of different ways depending on your choices. You may come to care for each of the characters, you'll feel sorry for them, feel happy for them, feel disappointed, hopeful, and more. The writer does a fantastic job fleshing out the characters in ways which makes you like them without giving away the whole truth behind them.
There are many endings in this game, some good, some bad. One of the things which made me play through he game multiple times is that I wanted things to be better, to make the right choices so everyone could be happy, and each ending made me see the characters in a completely different light.
The art in this game is quite good, though except for changes in facial expressions you'll only ever see the characters in the same few poses through the whole game and it will leave you wishing for something different after a while.
The beautiful music helps to enhance parts of the story really well, the soundtrack is one of the main things which will play with your emotions, the happy bouncy tune when characters are being silly makes you feel good. The slow soft tunes in some of the more sad and serious moments make you feel sorry or sad for the characters, and it will tug at your heart strings more as you get deeper into the story.
I understand that this type of game may not be everyone's cup of tea, especially if you're not into the whole furry scene, but I would highly recommend it to people who do find these kinds of games fun. You'll have a good time reading a well written story and will enjoy seeing where your decisions take you.

This game is a good example of why difficulty for it's own sake is not a positive. This game is made difficult by...
A.) A character with little weight and poor traction
B.) Checkpoint starvation disguised with a place-your-own-checkpoint system. The game allows you to place your own checkpoints, but only in places with non-icy, non-buzzsaw-infested ground. Instead of directly starving you for checkpoints, the game instead starves you for clear ground upon which to place said checkpoints.
C.) A difficult obstacle, which is then duplicated five times before you reach a place where you can set a checkpoint. Doing the difficult obstacle once is clearly not difficult enough, so you must do it five times in a row instead, with very little variation besides adding more buzzsaws.
D.) Oversaturation of spikes, buzzsaws, and icy ground. Even in the inferno level there is ice to prevent you from walljumping or having any fun. Difficulty that relies on depriving the player of options and control over the character is not enjoyable.
6 out of 10

In Cibele, you play as Nina Freeman (a.k.a. the director of this) and it follows the story of how she meets this dude online in a video game and how they "fall in love." I really hope this isn't the word-for-word conversations they had back then; and if it is, I really hope both parties stepped their social game up since then.
The gameplay involves playing another game inside Cibele, which just so happens to be the most lackluster game ever created. You click on enemies and... that's about it. Just keep doing that while the convos play out in the background and wait until the boss decides to show up. Other than that, you read blog posts and look at pictures of Nina and her friends.
I got this in a humble bundle and still feel ripped, let alone the people who paid $8.99 for it. This is what "Life is Strange" would have been if it didn't have excellent writing and a good sense of direction.
A Facebook "game" would provide a deeper gameplay and story ...

Cibele is a 1-hour mildly interactive narrative experience about the type of remote love MMO and chatroom users have with people they've never met. Don't expect game mechanics or variable story; this is an interactive movie.

For me, having played an MMORPG intensively in a raiding guild for almost 4 years, this story line is plausible. I think that fact made it even more uncomfortable for me to play this game. Why I clicked through the first wave of grinding to get to  a boss mob that dropped no loot was beyond me. Then to see your character making these decisions that I personally thought were, at best, flighty. Its a shame the character didn't ruminate over her situation until the end. In the end, it just brought back memories of online friends that had been through a similar situation, and all the time lost raiding some damn buncha pixels in a game for 4 years.
However, for someone who has never been addicted to Evercrack, or WoW, this might be a way to see inside that world (from a young naive female gamers perspective).
For the time I spent I think it was worth it.  Interesting look at an online relationship between college students.  Again short but pretty sweet.

I feel like this game could have had real potential, if only it was a little more, well, gamey. From a visual standpoint, it's pretty nice (others may disagree), and I enjoyed going through the chatlogs and understanding the relationships of Nina through them. The way each episode was set up was also a good idea. However, there are no real gameplay elements. Even if it is an artsy, autobiographical interactive story, it lacks the interactive part. Just a few thoughts: Why not give options for replies to messages? maybe different endings depending on what you do? What happens if you ignore all messages and dont reply to any of them? what if there was a "Shut down" option on the desktop? Missed opportunities.
The Story itself was really short and kind of foreseeable. Which is precisely why I would have liked the option to save Nina from that obvious fate. I imagine giving people options to avoid this kind of scenario might have been a better way for the author to "get over" the experience, and would have had a much stronger impact, instead of just replaying/recording what happened.
It wasn't badly made. It's just kind of boring and uneventful.

I have always been fascinated with simulations of real life things. As a kid, I dug SimTower trying to build the greatest skyscraper everrrrr (unfortunately, it took a lot of micromanaging so I got bored after I hit 4 stars).
With Mini Metro, I lay my hands on a very simplistic type of simulation: You have to connect different spots on the map (which is based on real life cities) in order to build a functioning public transportation system. Starting out slowly, you soon hit the point where your passengers get annoyed and complain because they have to wait too long (it's not like nobody has ever been in that state of mind). It takes careful planning and managing your lines to be successful until the inevitable overcrowded station. Different cities also have different assets to their system such as high-speed trains or interchanges that don't overcrowd as fast.
It is a lot of fun on the way there and adds some variation by the Daily Challenge as well as a sandbox-like endless mode. I enjoy playing it whenever I am sick of the fast-paced multiplayer games I usually play.

I'm impressed. This is probably the most polished Early Access game I've ever played, and also one of the best-looking ones as well. Especially for an indie developer. The game is perfectly stable, crash-free, and runs smooth as silk on my PC. Was able to set my options and join an online match within seconds, no problems whatsoever. The game runs on Unreal Engine 4.
It has all of the settings you would expect from a proper PC game. World detail, shadow detail, light shafts, AF level, multiple forms of anti-aliasing, different framerate caps, V-sync, and FOV slider that can go well over 100. I'm playing it on the "Very High" preset with a few extra tweaks. I'm sure I can run it on "Ultra" just fine, but I haven't bothered trying yet. It's such a fast-moving game that there isn't much point in stopping to admire the pretty graphics (but it's a very pretty game anyway).
The menus are laid out well, the server browser is slick and functional, and - as I said - the whole game feels extremely polished.
Fans of Quake and Unreal Tournament will feel right at home here. The devs have been pretty straightforward about their resentment toward F2P games and microtransactions. There's no leveling, loadouts, XP, or any other "modern" FPS features. No sprinting, no ADS. Bunnyhopping is alive and well. The rocket launcher is the most devastating weapon in the game (as it should be), but it's not fast enough or explosive enough that it doesn't require skill.
The weapon spawn points actually have a timer floating above them to show when they will respawn. A clever feature that I have never seen in an arena shooter before.
The one little gripe I had is that I couldn't modify my settings during a match. Had to back out to the main menu to change my mouse sensitivity. A bit frustrating but something you'll only have to deal with once.
The other thing I should point out, is that there is, literally, only one map right now. But it's a very fun, polished, and well-designed map. Lots of branching paths without feeling too cramped. My understanding is that the developers are working on balance right now, and will release maps over time; the next map probably being sometime in early February.
Really glad I took the risk on this game. The people making it are obviously pretty passionate. If you're looking for classic deathmatch-style gameplay with a modern coat of paint, it's a must-have.

I enjoyed this game. I knew about most of it's faults beforehand, so I think that actually helped me to look past them and enjoy the rest of the game.
There some annoying problems with this game. I will lay the ones I found most notable out here before I get to the good stuff.
1. There are annoyingly long scripted animations for doing very common things: opening windows, knocking out guards, stealing loot, opening doors/wardrobes/cabinets, opening grates. This is the biggest problem of them all, in my opinion. It kind of disrupts the flow of the game, breaks the immersion. You get used to it after a while, and then it's ok.
2. The city map is split up by multiple loading screens (this is a joke, they should have been able to fit it all on one map without any load times, it's not that big).
3. It could be pretty difficult to get to certain areas of the map at times, but you get there after some snooping around and observations. Many people point out the lack of a fast-travel system. This should have been included, but you can get by fine without one once you get used to the layout of different areas.
4. (Only important to fans of the Thief Franchise) There are loads of differences to the previous Thief games. In essence, this should be called something else as the gameplay mechanics are seriously lacking compared to the previous games.
I enjoyed this game for multiple reasons:
1. The side-quests were varied and helped scratch the completionist itch I have.
2. The environments are very atmospheric (there is however a very small colour palette and it's really depressing/dreary. Many people will not like this, but I thought it was fine)
3. There is a variety of ways to complete each mission and travel through the map.
4. It was an excellent immersive experience at times.
5. Many different tools and arrow types making the gameplay more diverse (again, not as good as the previous Thief games, but for a newbie it would be fine)
6. Good pacing. The game progressed along nicely.
Look, I'll be honest, I could list many more smaller faults. It's a shame it was so different from the previous games which had excellent lore, better characters, interesting factions, more dynamic game mechanics. If you are new to the franchise, then these things don't matter, and you can enjoy the game more. However, if you are a fan of the series, then you'll have to accept all these caveats and treat the game differently. It's so different to the previous titles that you should probably treat it as a completely unrelated game. You'll have a chance of enjoying it then.

Mostly for people who like hardcore gaming experience.
This game is not only retro for its graphics and style, but also for the mechanics. Expect a whole lot of spikes, deathtraps, difficult jumps and enemies set in weird places. Many times this game will force you to rush, perform some sick combo, but without telling you directly - it's not exactly your "press JUMP to jump" game. It's kinda frustrating at times, but it's equally exciting and satisfying.
The gameplay is pretty simple - go on, defeat enemies (or don't), reach the objective. It's got a checkpoint system (no quick save/load), but it's kinda different compared to other arcade/platformer games - you get points by collecting them or by killing enemies (bigger combo - more points), it fills up your meter and when it's full you can set a checkpoint. The environment is pretty hazardous, not only for you, but also for the enemies, as you can kick people sending them into the air.
The soundtrack is pretty goddamn amazing as well and for a chiptune (it's pretty close to that) fan it's a feast, also giving the game a lot of momentum.
Fantastic game, beautiful art style, fun and challenging gameplay. Highly recommended for people who like Super Meat Boy.  It's a challenging game but it is really fun.

Each chapter in Cibele plays in two parts: a desktop interface, and a simulated MMORPG portion where you'll log in and talk to Nina's contacts. There are three chapters, so three desktop and MMO experiences. I wanted, initially, to support the game and give it a recommendation because I think games like this are important, but Cibele would only be important if it was fun. Playtime clocks in at 90-120 minutes for the egregious price of $9.
There are plenty of great stories in our world, and plenty of great games. Cibele is a good story and a bad game: you'd be better off just watching a Let's Play on YouTube. The MMO is a top-down 2D experience with fairly nice art, but with only one mechanic: click to attack. You'll quickly understand the goal is to click a few mobs and check your notifications across your various software, such as 'whispers' and what appears to be an Instagram simulacrum. As you do so, you'll trigger listening to Nina talk to her womanizing schmuck love interest; an organic and painfully probably-accurate depiction of how these relationships usually go down. She turns down every compliment he gives her, seeming surprised she might be attractive, meanwhile taking selfies displaying her large chest. I suspect such pictures are the main driver for the game's price and its success.
I want to find some good points, some reason you may want to play rather than watch YouTube, but there's just nothing. You make no choices. It has no replayability. The desktop interface is a chore to use, and the MMO portion couldn't even get pathing done properly. Often, you'll click on a mob to kill in order to progress the narrative, and get stuck on what hardly passes for a corner. Given these issues, Cibele should just float around as her partner's avatar does. Play for the voyeurism, I suppose?
It's just not fun. You will likely not enjoy your experience; it didn't need to be a game, so don't play it. If a developer wants to make waves in gaming while providing meaningful story and narrative, the end product -- the vehicle for that story -- must be fun.

I usually like story driven games without much interaction, although the style that Cibele does it in is tedious and vexing. The desktop interface where you can see Nina's personality is good at first, but having to open and close them to read all the documents especially when they pop up later on every so often can slow everything down. Having the player be able to "play" while listening to the two character's dialogue is great in concept, but just boils down to randomly clicking just to get the story to move forward with grinding, getting repetitive and annoying each time you have to do it.
The story itself is okay, but nothing special. Just a typical story of two people who met while online gaming with things being not as good as it seems overtime.
This really isn't that worth it to playthrough.

I don't generally write negative reviews for the simple reason that enjoyment of a game is subjective, and I prefer to talk about things I like than things I did not, but there is a lot of good press out there about Cibele, and after playing through I cannot understand why.
I am assuming that this is recounted from or based on a real event or series of events from the life of the creator, and that they are therefore very close to the subject matter. Unfortunately the interactions between characters do little to bring this out to the point where it can be engaged with on a meaningful level. Sure, it's a simple enough story, but the problem doesn't lie so much with the barebones plot, but the lack of character development. This, I believe, is probably related to the story being so personal - just a few lines can conjure up a lot of memories and depth for someone who lived the events depicted, or who experienced something similar, but for anyone else, there's not much here.
Compounding this is the irritation of having to play that accursed MMO/ARPG. The game-within-a-game is there purely because that is where some of the major interactions take place, and unfortunately the fact that the gameplay itself is secondary is painfully evident. I would rather have had the onscreen character on autopilot and focus more on the chat elements than be forced to click on things until I have clicked on enough things for the next dialogue line to trigger. This negatively impacts your experience particularly as it leaves the already poorly written and acted dialogue even more broken up and stilted feeling.
The game itself suggests that first love is a complex thing, and indeed it is. Unfortunately Cibele does not allow itslef the room to explore the theme, and this isn't helped by a clunky interface and a truly awful representation of MMO/ARPG gameplay interrupting the flow. After having this compared to Her Story in some reviews I can't help but be hugely disappointed, and could not recommend this to anyone.

VERY short story (My game time is a single play through and I thoroughly inspected every environment), that is intriguing but falls short due to the nature of the "online game" Cibele shares with her new internet friend. If you think about the story without the terrible online game game play, it is actually a very interesting concept and ends with a good message. I definitely would not have purchased this game, but if you are like me and received it from a humble bundle deal then it might be worth your time to check it out. My negative rating is merely to show people, that for what this game has to offer it is not nearly worth the price of $9 The music was pretty good at least.

Poi is like a spiritual successor to Super Mario 64 on the PC.
Unfortunately it falls short in that regards. While its a fun game, it does not hold a candle to the Mario game. The levels here while are clearly inspired by Super Mario 64, are nowhere near complex enough to be challenging. The monsters also are more of an annoyance than presenting an actual challenge.
Like Super Mario 64, each map has 7 medals (stars) to get. While, Mario had a large number of big maps, Poi only has 5 maps which are very basic along with some challenge maps which are even smaller and usually give you less than a couple of minutes of playtime unless you wish to beat the top guys on the leaderboard.
I bought the game for $2.50 from someone who bought the Humble Monthly Bundle, and for that price, I am going to say that I am satisfied. While it was very easy and basic, it certainly did satisfy the Super Mario 64 itch I had, so it succeeded in that regards. The controls and camera are much better than Super Mario 64, and I have no complaints on that front. On the whole, I would hesitatingly recommend this game if you can find it on a sale or a cheaper price like I did. It has its fair share of bugs, due to which I am unable to complete the game, but considering its an early release, that is to be expected.
Basically if you really liked Super Mario 64 or other 3d platforming games, its worth a shot, but if you are not a fan of the genre, this game will not make you change your mind.

Everyone who loved classic 3D platformers like Super Mario 64 will feel at home here. Even though the game is in Early Access, there is a lot of content and a lot to come, too.
The visuals are not the most detailed, but in my opinion that fits the game very well. The aesthetics and theme of the game are really cute and there's not a lot of violence – if you jump on enemies, they vanish in smoke –, so in my opinion you can very well let children play it.
There's a progressing story and the levels ("worlds") of Poi introduce the core mechanics one by one with cute little text boxes. There's a lot to explore and you can collect various artifacts and medaillons. I found some mystery island and I wonder what happens there later in the game!
Poi is developed on top of the Unity3D engine, so if you can run other Unity3D games well, this will be no exception. I only had one crash in a few hours of gameplay on 64 bit Arch Linux which I'll attribute to my system and not the programming of Poi.

Mini Metro
First of all I have to admit that I think this game is presented in a very appealing style. As an architect it is my day to day job to think about graphical appearances of drawings and diagrams so I see myself capable to state that the art and graphic style of the game is phenomenal. The greatness of the presenation starts with the use of pictogram's and symbols, includes great color management and concludes in a nearly flawless minimal design game.
The game is a great "time killer" for optimizing fanatics because fully understanding the game takes quiet a while in my opinion as it is not a as straight forward game as it looks like in the beginning. Its not mastered by thinking "I am going to connect these stations and lets see what happens!". A situation which shows that there is more effort put into the design of the game than in a strait forward browser games. The game also has great balancing as each factor is important but no game factor has a ridiculous overwhelmingly impact. For example the drawing style of each player is different and the game sometimes draws the metro lines so that he trains actually lose some time on each station. If the player redraws and tries to put the lines in the right angel he achieves a optimization of some milli second. A factor that helps the player to make a better score but it is also possible to make good scores by concentrating on other "small factors" like the one just explained.
Finally I have to also state that the game has an factor of addiction as the player always things "one more time, this time I'm going to make a score over 2.000". A situation (which again) shows very good inventing, designing and balancing potential by the developers of the game. So putting all together this game is totally worth its money as the player will play for a throughout great design and thought through little puzzle game.

This is a great game to play to relax to. The music is atmospheric and soothing. The gameplay mostly lets you watch your creation at work. The graphics are simple yet easy on the eyes.
If I were to have a problem with it, it would be the fact that new stations and problem stations aren't easier to notice. The gong of a new station appearing is often lost in the hustle and bustle, and the chirp of a station being overcrowded doesn't exactly tell you where, if there are several one might get lost in the shuffle.
I don't normally strive for achievements, but the ones in this game are worthy challenges if you are up to it. Many people complain about the spawns, but unless you play with the permanent tunnels option, there's nothing stopping you from redesigning and moving your trains around whenever you feel a redesign is in order. I often have several trains crisscrossing between stations to keep the variety of stations favorable.
Islands though can be a pain. Tunnels and bridges are given sparingly, and often at a cost of a new line, or train car which would increase your capacity. I often find it better to have longer cars move people around on an island of just circles, with a short rail with two long cars taking all the squares and triangles to the nearest one on the other shore. Islands with multiple rare symbols are often best split up if you can manage it as well.
In short, it's a game that can keep your mind active while you wind down for the evening. The graphics and music are minimal, but entrancing, and the challenges are well chosen. I hope they add more content at some point.
I also bought this for my Android for $4.99 I liked it so much so I can play it on the go. Touch controls are a bit touchy, but that's for another review.

Star Conflict is one of my favorite games! For a brief period about a year ago, I was reading tons of science fiction, and I wanted to get in on some space battles.  This game is PERFECT!  It's like a 3rd Person Shooter, except you're a space ship.  Run through on like 10v10+ TDM's or Capture the Beacon (like domination).  The best part about this game is that it's FREE!  Similar to league, you CAN buy stuff on there, but you can save up in-game credits and buy all the same stuff. Some of the ships are premium ships, like you have to use the actually paid for credits to purchase them, but they don't provide any advantage.  I beat kids in premie ships all day.
The ships are very customizeable, offering a nice range of weapons to choose from.  You get one main weapon (obv) and then you can load your missile bays with all kinds of different missiles, from homing missiles to armor piercing and everything in between.  You also get active modules that you can equip your ship with.  You can equip shield boosters, or like tractor-beams, you can put IR Flares into one module, and whenever someone sends a missle at you, just pop them bad boys and you're able to get away.
There are fighting/command ships, Dagger/assassin-style ships, and there are huge slow moving tank/frigates to choose from. You end up gaining enough experience and move through the different tiers of ships.  So you fully upgrade and customize your ship, then get enough experience with it, and buy the next one higher (always better and worth it).
There's also 3 different factions in the game.  There's Federation, Empire, and Jericho, and they all compete for sectors of space near where the FIRST alien artifact was found.  There's a bunch of different PVP game modes, and there's also some PVE missions that are very dope and fun as well. This is a very awesome game and I just can't say enough good things about it.  Oh yeah, did I mention that it's FREE! lol.

I picked up Far Cry 4 during the steam summer sale, and waited almost a year before playing it. I've been wanting to play it since I got it, but I just didn't get into it. Far Cry 3 was good, but I was not that impressed actually. I played through the story pretty quick and I didn't do any sidequest. I just didn't like it that much, beside the main story.
Far Cry 4 has really changed my mind about far cry though. Sure, it somewhat repetitive and similar to far cry 3. But I think that Ubisoft really improved upon the concept and made something even better. Kyrat is a beautiful place and such a nice combination between sunny paradise and snowy mountains. When I powered up my computer with 980 SLI and 1440p monitor recently my jaw just dropped when playing this game. It's so cool to sit in that mini-helicopter and just fly over the map.
The story is interesting and you actually make some choices. Side with the guy that wants Kyrat to be like old times, or with the girl that want to change Kyrat into something better. On top of that you have the new villain, Pagan Min, which is crazy and funny guy, just like Vaas from previous game. The story is filled with crazy missions that are fun for the most part. Sidequests in far cry 4 is really good! I ended up completing almost every single one of them. I think that assasination missions, kyrat fassion week and the quest where you blew up propaganda was the most fun ones. I don't really like racing, so I skipped some of them. Not that they were bad either, I just hate race games with timers and missions with fail-state. This game has almost no timer on missions, which is something I usually have a problem with in Ubsoft games (looking at you assasins creed..)
Thought I was just going to play this game really fast, just like far cry 3, but ended up spending huge amounts of time in Kyrat. All in all im very happy that I've played this game. The story was good, graphics is outstanding, upgrades/skills are really useful and for every mission it actually feels rewarding. The powerful weapons you get later on, with upgrade possibility and paint, you can really create a nice loadout. I spent time to hunt so I could carry more ammo and many weapons at the same time. I really liked the feel or getting better and better gear, without feeling like it was to difficult to achieve.
In the beginning outpost was hard, even on medium difficulty, but with all skills and all weapons at my disposal I just ran through the fortress in the end. It was just a blast and I had many fun moments. I found very few bugs, I guess it pays to wait a bit before playing a AAA-title, cause I heard that far cry had issues at launch. Not anymore anyway, running at 100+ fps on 1440p with settings around high. Game goes way higher though, up to very high and ultra, and game supports SLI.
To wrap this up, far cry 4 is a great experience and a massive improvement over far cry 3 in my opinion, with new weapons, animals and interesting quests. It will take you 50+ hours to do most things, but if you really want everything you can spend even more time. In my opinion this game is worth full price, but if you get it even cheaper then it's a steal! Recommended for players that want a story-driven FPS with open world questing and a big map to explore.

As much as I am not a fan of visual novels, Nekojishi convinced me that this genre have some hidden gems.
Actually, the only one thing that make me played this novel were characters, cat characters more precisely. They are very nicely drawn and look truly friendly from the very beginning.
Technically, this game does not have tons of graphic content. There are few characters that doesn't change much during gameplay and several backgrounds that might not be the most beautiful pictures I have ever seen. Even though it is visible that devs tried their best to make it attractive - characters slides (which imitates their movement) and, in some points, lightning changes giving backgrounds and characters different hue.
The most important part of visual novel is a story, and the story of Nekojishi is truly solid. There is lot of fun, but also sadness and uncertainty in this game. Choices truly matter and they are not always easy. If you play visual novels for sexual content, you will be surprised how little amount of it Nekojishi includes. Especially that the game is about big furry cats. It rather focuses on feelings of the characters and their relations between each other.
As much as long texts of visual novels make me usually bored, it was absolutely different in case of Nekojishi. It took me long hours to get to the first ending and I was surprised how easy it was to read. I will definitely try to reach rest of endings in the future.
So far... I can recommend this game, even for those, who are not into visual novels.
And one of the reasons why they should try Nekojishi is because it is for... free. Actually this is the biggest surprise since it is the best visual novel I have played so far.

Although Magic Duels had good anime effects, the game entirely break the charming part of Magic the Gathering.

Third, the game has just killed itself. It stopped updating. Forget about it, take your MTG cards and go to your local card store to play with your friends or local players, never waste your time on Magic Duels.

This is a free to play online Magic: The Gathering game that seems like it is in early beta, but in fact is no longer under development.  When you first start playing, there are single player campaigns you can do, following the stories of different planeswalkers.  In these campaigns, you get predefined decks and gain incrememntally more coins for each mission.  Finishing any campaign unlocks the starter deck for that expansion.  When you have finished all the campaigns, you'll have a lot of free starter deck cards and a considerable amount of money to buy booster packs.
Then you move on to building your own decks and playing against other human players to gain coins, either through victories or completion of daily quests.  A victory grants you 30 coins +20 for the first victory of the day. Daily quests grant 80-120 coins, depending on what they are.  Booster packs cost 150 and give you 6 cards.
The game is entertaining for a while and nostalgic if you used to play Magic: The Gathering, but there are two main reasons why I give it a negative review:
1. It is a very long and frustrating grind. It takes 100 booster packs to get all the cards in any set, and there are 8 sets, so at 150 coins per booster, that means 120,000 coins.  You get 30 per victory and 0 per defeat. Due to the way matches are ranked, you're likely to win about half of your matches, so that means 8000 games to get every card.  At 15 minutes per game, that'd be 2000 hours.  It will take about 100 hours before you even start to feel that your cards work well enough together to be able to build a good deck.  During that time, you'll be constantly playing against decks that make you think, "Yeah, sure I could win easily if I had those cards."  Of course, you can also pay real money for boosters, if that's something you do.
2. The game is incomplete.  There are some basic features that were simply never implemented. For example, when you create a new deck, you can either use the deck wizard and choose between a set of deck themes, or you can build your own custom deck from scratch.  If you choose the deck wizard, at the end you will be able to choose a background and portrait for that deck.  If you make a custom deck, you can't.  All custom decks will have the same portrait and background.  You can also duplicate decks to make changes to one but keep the other as it is, but when you do, you don't get to change the name, so if your original deck was called "Firestorm", the second one will be called "Firestorm [2]" or maybe something like "Firesto[2]".  There's no way to change names, portraits or backgrounds of existing decks.  This is not gamebreaking by any means, but it is certainly sloppy and clearly reflects on how little the developers care about the game.  There's also no option to chat in multiplayer, or communicate with your opponent in any way, and there are ocassional bugs where you have a limited time to do something, but the buttons don't respond, so you either do nothing, or the game just gets stuck there until you quit.  And, upon the release of the last expansion, it was announced that it was the LAST expansion, so they're not even developing it any more.  The developers seem to be much more interested in releasing new MTG games as often as possible where you can spend time and money to build up your deck before they move on to the next one, than in creating one game that is complete, good, and long-lived.
In summary, the game is somewhat fun, but it's more frustrating and disappointing.
This game is good for learning how to play magic, but experencied players will be disapointed as they may be expecting something closer to Magic Online.

Choice of the Deathless is a choose your own adventure type text-based adventure. As the store page mentions, you can choose your gender and sexuality without this affecting anything in the storyline, and thus you start your journey working at a “law firm” dealing with demons and other beings that exist in this world.
Quickly you have to get used to your new work environment, and choose how you budget your expenses (Live downtown but pay high rent? Give yourself less pocket money?) These choices don’t affect the story at all as far as I can tell, maybe unless you either go broke or completely pay off your student loans, none of which I’ve done yet (I went for a neutral path moneywise).
You get to meet a variety of characters, some colleagues, some superiors, some clients, human, demon, and others. What you choose to say and how much time you choose to hang out with them affects your friendships and possible romance with them, which is pretty interesting - socializing matters! And if you’re an♥♥♥♥♥people remember… So I’d say this aspect is pretty interesting and where the game actually branches.
Scenario wise, I think you usually get the same most major scenarios to progress the story, and the choices you make in between aren’t able to cancel a future major event happening. It will just affect what options you can choose to do in the scenarios. For example if the major scenario in year 3 is happening and you have some allies by spending time/ helping them in the first few years they may help you out. Or if you became enemies they might mess you up.
Storywise I found it quite entertaining, the writing style is alright, I’d say 7/10 in terms of smoothness and clearness. Would have liked some more details in how their world with humans and demons and other forms of life work, but how the author paints is it interesting and vivid enough on a small scale.
Overall I really enjoyed the 1.5 hours it took to finish this story, and there are way more paths I could choose. As mentioned though major scenarios are mostly the same, what makes variety is your relationships with other characters. Just like a real life workplace! (Minus the necromancy of course) :p

Most of the difficulty from this game comes from the fact that the controls simply do not work well.  Movement feels sloppy, for lack of a better term.  On "stable" surfaces, you slide small amounts, but just enough to screw you up.  On deliberately slippery surfaces, (of which there is no shortage) you accelerate extremely rapidly, but slowing down or changing direction is disproportionatly difficult.  Jump controls are adequate.  What really ruins the game, though, is the combat.  The combat controls are unintuitive, and all attacks are needlessly condensed into one button.  You'll find yourself performing dash attacks into spikes when you meant to simply perform a melee attack, because the input for a melee attack is to hold a directional button and tap the attack button, whereas the input for a dash attack is to tap a direction and attack at the same time.  In a game that requires delicate platformining in conjunction with delicate combat, this kind of assignment is just frustrating in a "♥♥♥♥ this, I have better platformers to play" way.  And it's not like there is some kind of technical constraint requiring this; pretty much every PC controller made in the last 10 years has at least 4 face buttons.
If the game was purely a platformer, it would have been great.  If they had split up the combat controls, the game could have been great.  If they had just split the levels into clearly defined platforming and combat sections, the game could have been amazing.  Instead, it's disappointingly frustrating because the challenge is in overcoming the horrible way input is handled, rather than challenges presented by the environment.
The game is very nice aesthetically.  The music and environments are both very enjoyable.

(tl;dr: I got this game in a bundle for very cheap, played on a whim and thought it was interesting for the time spent.) This game is about being a hormonal teenage nerd girl, the ups and the downs. It's so well-written (although the voice acting is either a little self-consciously wooden or brilliantly intentionally awkward?) that I was having flashbacks to my own complicated and awkward social experiences from being 18-19 years old. Made me want to hug the protagonist and punch the love interest! So as a story, if you can relate to the subject matter at all it's going to make you feel things.
The gameplay is visual novel-style, but not the choose-your-own-adventure type with multiple endings that's popular; this game is linear. I enjoyed how, aside from the cutscenes with "IRL" video, the interaction with the game is through using Nina's computer. Looking through her horrifyingly organized folder tree (she names photos 'blah' sometimes) at the new pictures and poems and chatlogs between sessions in her MMO adds atmosphere and a sense of advancing time to the story. I got a good sense of her personality. The MMO game-in-a-game is 'played' by clicking on monsters to auto-fight while Nina and her gentleman caller voice chat and she simultaneously checks her email, insta and in-game inbox. There's a certain humour in her doing 17 other things while also talking to the guy character in a manner that would suggest all her attention is on him... and then he's also putting photos online so he's doing the same thing on his end. I don't know, it's a super interesting immersive experience, and worth checking out for cheap. No replay value unless you want to relive the saga again, though, and the game only lasts for an hour and change.

+ Absolutely full of charm! If you enjoyed 3D platformers from the N64/Playstation->Gamecube/PS2 era you will feel like a kid again when you play Poi. ♥
+ Heavily influenced by Mario 64 / Sunshine. To some, this may sound like a bad thing, but everything just feels so right almost like you are playing a new Mario game. There are tons of references I could list, but triple jumping, and jumping on enemy heads to defeat them are things you will notice right away.
+ Visually the game is just full of appeal. Somewhat "polygonal" in nature, but I feel like this was to mimic games of old, and personally I just think the game looks fantastic.
+ The gameplay or I suppose I should say "the controls" feel almost perfect! Plenty of ways to jump, hop, climb, run, roll, and lunge around. Really shows off the right way to make a 3D platformer, and is a ton of fun to play.
+ The level design is spot on. You really couldn't ask for better obstacle courses, and areas to jump, flip, and collect all sorts of things. Also, very similar to Mario, you can replay areas with new objectives to get additional medallions (stars). Along with this, each time you play a level the weather / day / night cycle changes so you get a new perspective of the stage each time.
+ The soundtrack.... feels so nostalgic... it is sooooooo goood! Good enough to be background music in movies! The composer Lyndon Holland deserves a reward! The music fits the game so well, I loved every moment!
+ The game is a bit casual, but I honestly thought this was a good thing. You rarely every have to replay stages or reset your progress. There's plenty of checkpoints, and enemies are not very hard to avoid or defeat. (This is also a great game for kids!)
+ Lots of side-levels or challenge stages that are short and sweet that help keep the game feeling fresh. (I especially liked the slide level)
- The one thing that is sort of missing from Poi is that there doesn't seem to be any challenging enemies or bosses to defeat. Most of the enemies are just distrations that you try to avoid, or you jump on them to kill them easily.
- I was frustrated a bit with the hitbox when jumping on enemies. Sometimes you will go to jump on something only to get damaged when you land. This happened a lot with the mole creature.
[Side Note: This review may be a little biased as I have not played a good 3D platformer in a long while]

I was looking forward to this game when it came out, I wanted to be optimistic about a continuation of the Thief series. The setting, the characters, the story - it was a really fun little universe and I missed having a pure stealth game to play with the kind of open, sprawling levels and dark corners you could hide in while you listened to guards and NPCs gossip and♥♥♥♥♥♥ There really wasn't any of that in this game?
There are *improvements* to the detection system and some neat little gimmicks like swooping (moving quickly from one corner to the next to try and avoid being seen), but movement in general is limited and clunky. It's hard to distinguish what you can and cannot climb on initially, and once you realize what you're able to mantle up on ... it's a bit disheartening, to say the least. You cannot jump (a LOT of puzzles and simple obstacles could easily be avoided if the player could jump over them), you cannot place rope arrows in areas that would be practical, etc. Not all doors, windows, etc are accessible when you're in the City.
It's a minor nitpick but I also cannot stand how clunky combat is should you actually end up in a situation where you are detected. I realize the justification behind it is ~Garrett doesn't fight / kill~ and ~you should try to ghost this game~ but ffs, you really do need to smooth out combat just a little so you can properly defend yourself enough to back out of a fight if you want to encourage your players to be nonlethal. There are other ways to motivate a player to try a ghosting / nonlethal route, annnd this is not really the way to go about it tbh.
The City and levels are pretty much barren via a plague plot device and it's depressing - and not in a good way. NPC types are severely limited, lowering any challenge you could have in planning your approach to each level and client job. The story itself is incredibly short, disjointed, and reaches an unsatisfying conclusion. Levels feel repetitive and dull. I *did* enjoy the shorter client job missions you could pick up optionally from various NPCs throughout the CIty, but even then it didn't feel worthwhile.
Framerate issues abound, no matter what your settings are. Cutscenes love to crash and load oddly - animation is awkward despite the use of mocap to try and (I guess?) inject realism into the characters' facial expressions and body movement. Dialogue is unnatural and - again - severely disjointed.
From what I understand of the history behind this game, it's no wonder it turned out to be a mess. It's just a shame - really disappointing. It can be fun at times, and I see the potential behind it, but as it stands it's just ... Yeah.

Star Conflict is by far at the top of any free-to-play games I've ever tried. It's fast-paced, quick-to-learn but hard to master game with great emphasis on skill. As all free-to-play games, the game has a lot of premium content, including unique maxed-out premium ships, but everything else is available to all players, including vast choice of weapons and active/passive modules for each ship. Most of the premium features affect how quickly you can level up the ships (gain synergy), which also happens to be the threshold for gaining access to new ships.
The Ships and Factions are well thought-out and balanced, and although you choose a faction in the start, you're not limited in anyway to that, but can instead switch factions on the fly. What matters is the ships you choose. Factions have different ships, which all follow the basic classification system between Interceptor, Fighter and Frigate, but each faction has its own core variant with unique special abilities and stat variation, with some occasional cross-over. The balance is overall very good, and with vast selection of weapons and active/passive modules, you have a very good and considerably meaningful customization options throughout the game.
I thoroughly recommend Star Conflict to space sim fans. For guilds, there's also corporate-only sector warfare, which is Star Conflict's endgame. You can also play PvE in co-op, though the missions currently lack variation and are good only for better cash. Other than that, I'd hoped the game would have a proper newtonian flight model, but even as it is, the experience is very enjoyable, with lot of room for tactcs and skill.

If you read my review, read carefully and READ IT ALL:
This game is not fun.
Because its not meant to be fun; at least not in the normal sense of the word.
This War of Mine sets you in a war-torn city, already some time into its siege. You either choose from severel pre-set scenarios or you create your own story. Once you start one of these, anything can happen.
You control a few civilians, trying to make it through the worst.... trying to stay alive until the war ends... or, if you own the "The Little Ones" DLC, until you manage to escape.
You have to protect them, feed them, improve their shelter and guide them through several challenges, both on-screen and off-screen. Each of your survivors has certain talents, each of them reacts a bit different to what's happening and each has his or her own story.... and depending on how good or bad you do, his or her own ending.
This War of Mine has rather simple controls, but it doesn't teach them to you; it's up to you to figure them out, discovering what you can do while you play. There is a Wiki that explains a lot about this game, but if you really want to immerse yourself in this I recommend you only visit the Wiki when you're really at your wits end.
As I said at the beginning, this game is NOT fun.
But in its own way it drags you in, giving you a special experience few games manage to deliver like this. And in this regard, This War of Mine is quite.... entertaining? No, immersive, thats it. And in an odd way I find it to be relaxing. Don't ask me how or why.....
Highly recommended.

I wanted this game for a long time because I liked its style and presentation. When it went on sale I eargly grabbed it and...was just so disappointed. I was looking forward to a challenging plat-former with an interesting visual style. Well I certainly got something "Challenging" but for all the wrong reasons. The game is artificialy difficult. The whole thing is basically like those Super Mario hacks where the game is almost impossibly hard because the person put a lot of effort into making sure you get screwed over at every turn. I couldn't tell you how many times I died because something popped out at the last second from hiding, and would demand the reflexes of a coked up 8 year old to dodge on the first try. Which bassicaly turns large portions of the game into less of a plat-former and more of a memorization puzzle with the added difficulty of having to jump around.
The game employs a unique check point system, when you have absorbed enough blood you are allowed to drop down a check point which heals you and allows you to continue from that sport if you die. The only limiting factors are that you can't be moving, and can't be near a saw blade or an enemy. And because of those two factors a good portion of the time these check points were useless because the developers would place a random saw blade, or cover EVERYTHING in slippery goo to make sure you can't actually stop moving and drop a check point. Forcing you to do large portions of a level without being able to employ a system the developers put in. In some cases I wondered why the check point system existed because 80% of the level was created so I couldn't drop a check point at all. It's pretty frustrating to have that purple glow around you indicating you could place down a check point and take a breather, only to notice that there is NO where to drop it down.
Jumping is a big problem. Under normal circumstance the jump and double jump work fine but when you attempt to double jump off a wall, if you do it wrong, the double jump fails. As far as I can tell its a timing issue, you need to cling to the wall for the right period of time to be able to jump off it an then perform a second jump. It's only a fraction of a second difference between getting your double jump and not. Normally this isn’t a big deal but it you're getting into a groove, or you NEED to be fast to get past a part this becomes a huge problem. It turns some parts of the game into an annoying game of timing the wall jumps juuuuuuuust right so you're still moving quickly, but cling to the wall long enough to perform the second jump you need.
Combat can be fun at times; kicking an enemy into a saw blade is immensely satisfying. However this part of the game also is greatly flawed. the developers like to throw lots of flying enemies at you while you're performing difficult jumps. Which make sense in a game with combat, only they don’t give you any way to dispatch these enemies, forcing you to try and complete already difficult platforming while also dodign enemy attacks. Usually I had to get part way through a tricky jump situation, then double back so I could dispatch the flying enemy who followed me. It made difficult jumps tedious and frustrating. As for normal combat, everything gets the kick. Really, there isn't much more complexity to the game than that. Kick an enemy into a trap or kick them into the air and air juggle them. That's as complex as the game gets. Even when fighting multiple enemies just kick them all into a corner, kick them all into the air, and air juggle them all. At first combat was fun but after a while the lack of variety became really boring. Most of the time if I didn’t need a check point I avoided combat because despite how easy it can be sometimes to dispatch enemies, other times its really hard because of the broken controls.
The game has no invisibility frames so its not only possible you can get killed in a few seconds by one enemy who got in a bunch of hits or a trap you bumped into, its a guarantee its going to happen. And the knock back from taking damage is ridiculous. Its not so bad for enemies, but for traps it makes no sense and is extremely frustrating. If you land on spikes you jump up and way from them by about 3 pixels, meaning you will die on those spikes because the odds of being able to jump away are slim. Its pretty pathetic dying on a single set of spikes because being damaged by them doesn throw you far enough away from them to actually do anything about it. Saw blades are the total opposite, one of those babies touches you you go FLYING! and its pretty much a guarantee that if the blade doesn’t kill you, where ever it sends you will.
The game is challenging, yes, but because of bad design. The entire game is just a test of how perfect you are able to play the game, because yes, you HAVE to be perfect in what you do for many parts of the game. No room for error, or creativity. You have to do it exactly as the developer intended. It makes for a frustrating and boring experience. I’m glad I got it on sale and didn't waste more money on it.

I love this game. But, there are some heavy critic points.
First, this game is completely soundless and pictureless. That there are no pictures is actually a good point since the picture in your head is mostlikely way better, but I still would have wished for music. But I can understnad that it's pretty hard to put music in this kind of game. How do you put music in, when you don't want to influence the players view on the happenings in the text?
Second, the game is short. In about two hours you can play it though, if you don't skip the textes. This is way too short. Even the point that there is no calm moment is not improving it, maybe even working against it. When I play a game in which I have so much controll over a actuall storyline, I want to experience the consequences more and heavely, not so subtly. For example: You begin an afair with a workmate and now you have a drama at your workplace. Maybe even a forced payless vacation, because this had influence on boths productivity. Or if you find a partner, why can't you two just enjoy your time with idle talk? That would be an additional chance to see a character in a new light and you could like them more.
Everything else is just small stuff, like the game never told you it would save itself. I myself felt at first forced to play it though in one go.
But, if you want to read, no, to play a fantastic story, then this game is still perfect for you. The game is in a wonderful world, with easy and yet complex rules. Depending on your choices, you can do about just anything. Cause the death of a god, make a god your ally, become a skeleton, become a partner in your company etc.

I just hated waiting for the dialog to be over and then the boss would come.  I think they might be an easier way to do the grinding but it really broke it down to the basics of what a game is. Click and something happens. I do think Ichi is a hacker, how did he go through walls like that?
Characters:
I am surpised by the fact I actually did care about them. Nina and myself had a lot same interest in manga and anime which will be a little bias on that fact. I just wished the best for her in the story, but things don't always work out like we hope for in real life.

I would recommend this game because it affected me.
At its heart, Cibele is a game about a typical first love. I found myself relating to a lot of the events unfolding onscreen.  It's painful to read through, but it's a good kind of pain. It's authentic.
It's a really honest depiction of the uncertainties of love, sex, and identity.
As most people would agree, it's more of an interactive movie than a game, and having the gameplay elements (pointing and clicking on monsters) does not positively add to the experience as a whole. I can guess what they were going for -- getting to know this online character by playing together and sharing experiences with him-- but the effect is missed because it's tedious and not dynamic in the slightest. I feel that the experience would have been stronger if either we were able to build meaningful memories with the character, or if we were just able to watch the characters bond without interacting with them. In this regard, the shortness of the game is a high point.
The other nitpick I have with this game is that I wish Ichi (the male character) wasn't so... upfront about his feelings at the end. Him introspecting feels like we're being lectured at --- by this point, we have already spent 60 minutes hearing this character talk and those who have been through relationships can pick up on a lot of things through his dialogue and inflection. This is a problem with a lot of narrative games, though --- when it comes time to present "the answer" of a character, the character will often go an on introspective spiel just to make sure we got it (The Beginner's Guide is really guilty of this). There is both showing and telling in Cibele, and I think it would be better if there was less telling. After all, the entire journey of Cibele is learning about Ichi. It dampens the experience if we are told about his emotional conditions by Ichi himself.
Anyway, I would recommend this if you can get it for cheap. It's nice to see a game that focuses on online relationships like this.

When Thief4 was first released I asked a friend if the game was any good. "It's a great game, but Thief it is not." was his answer. Honestly I agree with the former, yet disagree with the latter. :) Let's say it out loud: Thief4 is a great game! :) I hope nobody disagrees with that. :)
Thief4 (just called 'Thief' or 'Thi4f') was long awaited and the devs of Eidos Montreal had a difficult job of meeting the players expectations. Thief1 and Thief2 were magnificent and they are legends of the 90s! Thief3 was kinda flat, nothing of a life changing experience, yet it was a nice addition to the Thief series.
I believe that Thief4 fullfills the expectations of both being a modern game (at the time when it was released back in 2014 - well it's a bit outdated by now) and living up to its predecessors reputations. OK, fans do complain that there are differences, which they hate. For example, rope arrows are limited to specific spots only. In Thief2 you shoot a rope arrow into any wooden surface, so you would try to make your way into a building. Another example is climbing, which is -again- limited to certain spots. In the old games a blackjack was yuor best friend. Some of the fans even played only to meet a 'perfect thief' principle. In Thief4 you take down the guards by punching them. Different. Lockpicks work in a different way as well. The surfaces are all the same in Thief4. In the old games there were some surfaces, like tiles, that when you walked on them, the guards could hear you. These are not minor tweaks, these significantly change the gameplay.
Some fans go extreme and call Thief4 a Thief-parody game. I strongly disagree. Thief4 is indeed simlified as far as the mechanics go, so you're sort of limited in what you do out there, in the shadows. However it still an enjoyable Thief experience and you still need to figure out the best way to solve the problems and to advance further in the game. And after all you have everything the old Thief games had in a modern game: looting, blackjacking (sort of), picking pockets, picking locks, dirty secrets, dark alleys.
Oh, and you don't have Hammers. And Keepers. If that matters to anyone.
I've also heard the complaints that the DLCs are too short and too expensive. I don't know... All I can say is that I fully enjoyed Bank Heist DLC. I suppose if you're a fan you will enjoy the DLCs. Although don't expect anything new. Well... if you like a rollercoaster ride, it ends, you immediately get back in line to register for the next ride. :)
After listing the drawback, let's now praise Thief4. :) The visuals are stunning. The atmosphere created is amazing. Thief1 and 2 were all about a rotten environment and so is Thief4. Dirty parts of town... Sewers. Rats. Spiders. Thief's solitude. The sound of the guards' footsteps and the constant worry never to be seen. Always stick to the shadow. Avoid the light. The clinking sound of looting treasure, so sweet for the ears. You could simply stand still and analyze the guards patrol patterns, spend long minutes before making your move.
The storyline is a good one, the cutscenes are flashy. The story is a little dark, but it's the nature of the series. If that is your cup of tea. Some of the fans complain that the story has little to do with the former games (isn't it that the events of Thief4 take place before Thief1 and 2?). To be honest, I agree. Constantine and Victoria in Thief1 and 2 were so exceptional... yet in the new game we were presented with old friends like Basso. And last but not least we have Garrett, the main protagonist. The same Garrett. The voice of the master thief was excellent in Thief1 and 2 and so is in Thief4.
To sum it up, Thief4 is a must play, especially for Thief-series fans. If you've never played Thief before, you should still play Thief4. You can't go wrong here.

I would definitely pass on this unless you are a hardcore puzzle player, huge Frozen fan, or don't mind spending money on free-to-play games.

Ah, the joys of Far Cry 4.
Being my first game in the Far Cry series, and one of the first real open world shooters I've played, Far Cry 4 really was a new experience for me, and a good one at that, still sitting near the top of my 'favorite games' list. First off, the visuals are truly beautiful. As much as it murders my framerate to do so, I can't help but get to a high point, turn the settings up to Ultra, and just look down at the landscape. But as many of us know, graphics don't make a game good. Luckily, FC4 doesn't disappoint when it comes to gameplay.
I do have some pet peeves with this game, like the reused animations from FC3, but overall it takes everything from its predecessors and polishes it to a shine. The guns are responsive and each feels very unique, surprising with such a wide variety to choose from. There's also the satisfying feeling of exploding an enemy vehicle with some well-placed mines or C4. Wingsuiting is probably the most fun way to get around in any video game to date. Not only that, there's also co-op! While it's not perfect, I'd be lying if I said I hadn't had fun messing around with a friend in tuk-tuks, or shooting rockets out of the back of a truck.
The story is good, although there are definitely better ones out there. You're a man named Ajay looking to spread his mother's ashes in her home country, Kyrat. When you enter, you realize quickly that the country is run by a flamboyant dictator named Pagan Min. In true Far Cry fashion, you decide that the best way to improve this country is to grab some guns and ravage the countryside, blowing up everything in sight. Jokes aside, there are some interesting characters and entertaining moments throughout the story mode that I'll leave you to discover for yourself.
9/10, definitely worth $60.

I just feel that the game was won in the south and only continued in the North to complete.

The basic setup of Cibele is quite similar to the .hack games for Playstation2. You start out on a fictional computer desktop on which you can read some mails and watch some images, then you enter and play a fictional MMORPG. The story is told mostly through audio chat that happens while you play the game, while mails and images providing some context. Between chapters the game features FMV sequences that detail what is going on in the real world. The navigation on the desktop is a little annoying as you can't raise or move windows, only close.
The fictional MMORPG itself isn't much of a game, as all you do is click on enemies to attack them. Once you have attacked enough there comes a boss that you also attack, which then ends the chapter. There isn't a healthbar or different attacks or spells, a single click is all you have and need. You can however read some chat and email messages while in the game and you have all the audio chat to listen to, so it doesn't get boring.
Overall this is an ok game/interactive-movie-thing. The basic setup is interesting, but it doesn't go very deep and the game is over in less than an hour. There are also only two characters in audio-form, everybody else just enters the story as text messages or email. For the current price it's a little to expensive, but if you can find it in a bundle it's an interesting game to play, as it has a more intimate and personal feel to it than your average game.
I don't normally like text-only games, but the system was interesting and well-polished, the writing was amazing and the world is just so inventive I'm utterly hooked.
